Set tools.lockPlatforms to list the exact platforms instead (the current machine is always kept), for example to prepare for another build environment. See tool lock coverage.

Command Effect on the lock First oyzu build with no lock Resolves what the builders need and writes the lock, without editing your TOML oyzu pin Locks requirements and installs nothing. --dry-run previews oyzu install <tool>@<version> Declares the tool in oyzu.toml and locks it, together oyzu update [tool] Moves to the newest version within each existing request; never edits configuration oyzu uninstall <tool> Removes the declaration and its lock entries oyzu pin --refresh Refreshes install recipes, keeping the selected versions Configuration and lock change together: a failure leaves both files as they were, a simultaneous edit fails with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT, and an interrupted write is recovered the next time you run install, update, uninstall or pin.

Once a lock exists, builds and installs use it as written and never quietly re-resolve. If you change a request so the lock no longer covers it, Oyzu stops and tells you what to run. For example, after changing go = "1.24" to "1.23": $ oyzu install --frozenCopy ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: configured tool request is not pinned; run oyzu pin, then oyzu install Next: Run oyzu pin --refresh to refresh the lock, then oyzu install. Two flags make this explicit: oyzu install --frozen needs an existing matching lock and never resolves a new version. Use it in CI. oyzu install --offline uses no network. It needs the lock plus either an installed copy or a cached archive, which it checks against the locked digest before using. A cached archive that doesn't match its locked digest fails instead of being replaced by a fresh download.
documents.s: The lock stays as written until you change it

documents.t: Organization policy can allow or lock tool versions. The lock is checked against those rules before anything is installed or used, so a hand-edited lock that maps an allowed 22 to 26.1.0 is refused, naming the rule and the lock file. When a policy applies only in some contexts (say, an exact Rust version for release), the lock keeps one entry per request, so local and release entries sit side by side. See policy constraints.

On your machine, the action cache identifies tools by the digest of oyzu.lock. Changing a locked version re-runs the affected work, and changing it back can reuse earlier results. A tool that isn't in the lock, such as a system C compiler, isn't part of the cache key, so use oyzu build --no-cache after changing one. See The action cache.

Commit oyzu.lock. It's what makes other machines match yours. Don't edit it by hand. Change requests in oyzu.toml or with oyzu install, and let Oyzu rewrite the lock. One lock per project root. A nested project with its own build.yaml has its own lock. Your user-level defaults (oyzu install -g) use the lock beside your user configuration file. Review lock changes like dependency updates. A changed version or digest is a changed toolchain.
Lock inspection Pin declarations without installing Requirement discovery and pinning

"Build it for Linux and macOS" and "test it on Node 22 and Node 24" sound alike, but they're different requests. The first changes what ships: there are two artifacts. The second changes only how the build is checked: there's still one artifact, tested twice. Oyzu keeps them apart. Platforms are declared in build.yaml; extra runtime versions to test against are toolsets in oyzu.toml.

Every platform is written os/arch[/abi]: Platform Meaning linux/x86_64, linux/arm64 Linux on Intel/AMD or ARM 64-bit darwin/arm64 macOS on Apple silicon windows/x86_64 64-bit Windows linux/arm64/musl, windows/x86_64/msvc With an explicit ABI You can also type amd64 and aarch64; output, records and dist/ folders always use the names above. The ABI is optional and only matters where an OS has several (gnu or musl on Linux; msvc, gnu or gnullvm on Windows). Without one, the builder picks its default. Rust cross builds for Linux default to musl, which can break code that relies on glibc features such as dlopen or NSS name lookup; declare linux/<arch>/gnu where that matters.

Two terms stay separate: The target platform is what an artifact is built for. The executor is where its build actions run: your machine, a cross toolchain on your machine, the container executor, or a remote pool. A Linux arm64 binary might be built natively on an arm64 machine, cross-compiled on an x86_64 laptop, or built in a container. The executor is recorded on every target and is part of its cache key, so these three results never stand in for each other. See Execution modes.

A build lists the platforms it ships for in build.yaml: builds: cli: uses: rust/app platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64, darwin/arm64, windows/x86_64] A build with one platform keeps its name. With several, each instance gets a platform-qualified ID, and each platform's output goes in its own folder, dist/<target>/<platform>/, so bundles from different machines merge without collisions. A build that declares nothing builds for your machine.

Command Builds oyzu build Your machine's platform. If a target declares platforms but not yours, it builds the one declared platform your machine can build, asks for --platform if there are several, or is skipped with the reason if there are none oyzu build --platform

(repeatable) Exactly those. A declared platform that can't be built here fails before anything runs, with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE oyzu build --all-platforms Every declared platform, through the container executor; fails if any can't be built The plan says how each platform would be built. Platforms your machine could build are listed with the flag to use, and the rest are listed with the reason, such as "needs a macOS runner (Apple SDK and linker)". Today only Rust has a native cross toolchain. Go, Node, Python, Java, .NET and Helm build only for your own platform natively.

By default, a platform is built on your machine if it matches, otherwise with a cross toolchain when the builder has one. You can instead set the executor per platform in oyzu.toml, per folder and per context: [build.executors] "linux/arm64" = "cross-toolchain" # always cross-compiled "darwin/arm64" = "host" # only on a macOS arm64 runner [context.release.build.executors] "linux/x86_64" = "container" # release builds use the container executor A declared executor is the only one used for that platform. When it's unavailable, the platform isn't built here and the plan says why; asking for it explicitly fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. Nothing falls back to another executor, so a release builds each platform exactly as its plan says. See declaring a platform's executor.

You don't have to hand-write your CI matrix. oyzu build --plan --json includes a matrix with one entry per declared platform of every selected target: the runner that can build it natively (os as CI providers name it, and arch), the declared executor, and the targets that declare it. The matrix doesn't depend on what the planning machine can build, and with --affected <ref> it holds only the affected targets. Feed it to your workflow's matrix and run, in each job: oyzu build <targets> --platform <platform> Mapping each runner to your provider's runner labels is up to your workflow. When the artifacts are published, Oyzu checks that every declared platform is present. See a CI matrix from the plan for a complete GitHub Actions example.
documents.s: A CI matrix from the plan

documents.t: To check that an application also works on another runtime version, define a toolset in oyzu.toml. The shipped build is built and tested once, with the [tools] versions. Each toolset adds a verification run that repeats the build and test stages with its tools and records the result. A verification run never produces an artifact, so publishing still sees one artifact. # build.yaml: nothing about runtime versions builds: app: uses: node/app # oyzu.toml [tools] node = "22.14.0" # builds, tests and ships the app [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" # also tested on Node 24 Command Runs oyzu pin Locks Node 22.14.0 and the node24 toolset's 24.14.1 oyzu build Locally: the app alone oyzu build --verify-with node24 Locally: the app and its Node 24 run oyzu build --context ci In CI: the app and its Node 24 run A toolset runs in every context except local, unless it lists contexts = [...]. Each run is its own target in the plan (app-verify-node24). It skips lint and format checks, which don't depend on the runtime, and never packages or publishes. A failing test in a run fails the build. Runs are listed under .verify in the plan JSON, so CI can give each its own job. The global --toolset <name> option uses a toolset's tools for exec, run, env, activate, which and install, so you can reproduce a run's environment by hand. A build can require passing verification on certain tool versions before publishing with verification.<tool> (for example verification.node = ["22", "24"]), and policy or [constraints] can make versions required. A version no toolset covers adds a run, and oyzu publish refuses a release without a passing result for each. A version outside the project's own range, such as below the go line in go.mod, is recorded as not applicable instead of failing the build. See verification toolsets. Runtime versions never go in build.yaml: the old matrix.<runtime> field is refused with a message showing the toolset form. Profiles can't hold tools either. A toolset is the one place to define an alternative set of tools.
Native cross toolchains exist only for Rust so far. The container executor needs Docker. See platform requirements and platforms and executors.
Platforms and executors Verification toolsets and platform matrices Build bundle layout CI guide

Oyzu starts from the files your ecosystem already has. A go.mod is a Go module, a Cargo.toml is a Rust package, a package.json with a lockfile is a Node project. You don't have to describe your repository before Oyzu can build it. When you want the list of builds to be explicit and reviewed, add a small build.yaml; from then on that file decides.

Term Meaning Example Project root The folder Oyzu treats as the top of your project The Git worktree root Target (also called a build) One buildable unit with a name api, a Go module in api/ Builder The ecosystem support that finds, plans and builds one kind of target go/app, rust/app, node/app, python/app Discovery Reading native files to find targets and pick their builders, without running project code oyzu discover Inventory The list of builds in build.yaml builds: {api: {uses: go/app, path: api}}

Inside a Git repository, configuration is inherited from the worktree root, and the nearest build.yaml above you decides the builds. Outside Git, the outermost folder with Oyzu configuration or a build.yaml is the project; failing that, the folder you ran the command in. --root <dir> sets the root explicitly, and -C <dir> runs from another folder as if you'd changed into it. A nested project with its own build.yaml is independent: running Oyzu inside it uses that project, with its own oyzu.lock and dist/. Parent inventories aren't merged. See inspection and selection for the exact rules.

Without a build.yaml, Oyzu walks the tree from the root. When a builder recognizes a folder, that folder becomes a target and the walk doesn't go deeper there, because the builder owns everything below it. Dependency and output folders, nested Git repositories and folders with their own build.yaml are skipped. A small repository with two Go modules and no Oyzu files: shop/ api/ go.mod main.go main_test.go worker/ go.mod main.go main_test.go $ oyzu discoverCopy 2 targets · 12 tasks discovered without running project code Project root: …\shop ​ project-api · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location api … ​ project-worker · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location worker … Without configuration, names follow the folder: a target at the root is project, and one below it is project-<path>, here project-api and project-worker.

Inside a target, a builder still has choices to make: which package manager, test runner or formatter. Each option comes with evidence, and the strongest evidence wins: Strength Examples declared a test script that runs exactly one recognized test runner native a lockfile, packageManager in package.json, a [tool.*] table in pyproject.toml conventional a declared dependency, a uv.lock that locks no packages default the documented default when nothing else applies, such as npm or Ruff If two options have equally strong evidence, Oyzu doesn't guess. Discovery fails, names both, and prints the build.yaml line that settles it: $ oyzu discoverCopy ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: conflicting Python formatter candidates black, ruff: black via pyproject.toml tool.black; ruff via pyproject.toml tool.ruff; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {formatter: black}` or `with: {formatter: ruff}` oyzu build --plan shows every choice and its reason in a Discovered table. Each builder's options are listed in discovery decisions and build.yaml selectors.
documents.s: How a builder makes its choices

documents.t: A build.yaml at the root turns discovery into an explicit list you can review. With one present, only its builds exist. Discovery never adds a build on its own. builds: api: uses: go/app path: api worker: uses: go/app path: worker depends_on: [api] Field Purpose uses The builder. Optional when exactly one builder recognizes the folder path The folder, relative to the root depends_on Builds that must finish first (ordering only) materialize Artifacts from another build to place in this build's inputs platforms The platforms this build ships for, such as [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64] inputs Extra source paths the build reads with Options for the selected builder, such as formatter: ruff With that file, oyzu discover reports the names you chose (api, worker), shows Chosen by build.yaml, and confirms that build.yaml declares every folder where a build was discovered. build.yaml holds only what changes what ships. Tool versions, check levels, tasks and environment variables go in oyzu.toml; see Configuration layers. A build.yaml that belongs to another tool (Dart's build_runner uses the same name) is recognized by its keys and skipped.

Once you have a build.yaml, a folder someone adds later won't build unless it's listed. Oyzu helps you notice: oyzu discover lists folders a builder recognizes that no entry covers, with the line to add for each. oyzu build --plan names up to five of them under Not in build.yaml. A real build never builds them. oyzu discover --check exits 1 with INVENTORY_UNDECLARED while such a folder exists. Add it to CI. oyzu discover --write adds an entry, with uses written out, for every folder exactly one builder recognizes. It keeps your comments and order and adds an editor-schema comment. exclude: lists folders that are deliberately not builds, for example exclude: [tools/scratch, tooling/**]. Folders that a declared build's native workspace already includes (Cargo members, go.work use, npm, Yarn or pnpm workspaces) are covered by that build. Inside Git, only folders with tracked files count, so files a CI job creates can't fail the check. See builds build.yaml leaves out.

If a native file already says something, Oyzu reads it there: The go and toolchain lines in go.mod set the minimum Go version. rust-toolchain.toml selects the Rust channel and components. Lockfiles decide the Node package manager. Native workspace manifests decide which folders belong to one build. Oyzu configuration only adds what native files can't say, and when both mention the same thing they must agree. See Tools and toolchains.

Command Use it to oyzu discover See targets, builders and how each was chosen oyzu discover --json Get the full discovery record, including each task's environment oyzu discover --check Fail CI when a recognized folder is missing from build.yaml oyzu discover --write Add every undeclared folder to build.yaml oyzu config schema build.yaml Print the JSON Schema for build.yaml oyzu run list See the tasks each target offers
Discovery decisions and build.yaml selectors Build inventory fields and errors Set up projects guide The build graph: what happens once targets are known

Oyzu has two ways to do work: oyzu run <task> runs one named task now, with live output, the way you'd run go test or npm run lint yourself, but with the project's pinned tools. oyzu build produces the project's outputs. It runs stages across every selected target in dependency order, reuses unchanged results, and leaves a bundle in dist/. Both use the same tasks. The difference is what happens around them.

A task is a named operation on a target, written target:task, such as api:test. Builders infer the common ones from your native files, so most projects need no task configuration: Task Purpose Part of builds build Compile or package the target yes test Run the tests and collect JUnit and coverage where supported yes lint Run the ecosystem's linter yes format-check Check formatting without changing files yes format Rewrite files to the formatter's style no, development only install Fetch dependencies no, development only $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 13 across 2 targets ​ Task Source Command api · go/app (7) api:build Inferred · go go build ./... api:smoke oyzu.toml go run . api:test Inferred · go go test ./... … The Source column shows where each task came from: inferred by a builder, or written in oyzu.toml.

$ oyzu run api:smokeCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks › api:smoke Running · native tool output follows Hello, Oyzu! ✓ api:smoke Succeeded (exit 0 after 1.16s) oyzu run runs in the target's folder with the project's tools on PATH, streams native output as it happens, and uses your terminal's input. A bare task name works when only one target has it; otherwise write api:test. Arguments after -- are passed on: oyzu run api:test -- -run TestPrice. Task runs are never cached. They're for the edit-run loop.

oyzu build runs the same tasks as stages, with more around them: oyzu run <task> oyzu build Scope One task (plus its prerequisites and hooks) Every stage of every selected target Ordering That task's prerequisites The whole build graph Reuse Never cached Unchanged actions are reused Output Live native output Live progress, then a summary of outputs, tests and coverage Record Test runs can write a test bundle Always a bundle in dist/ Checks You choose the task Chosen by check levels and context

A plain local oyzu build is a fast build: it runs the build and package stages and only the checks set to required, and shows the rest as skip · fast local build. A full build runs every check that isn't off. You get one: with oyzu build --full on any machine; automatically in the pr, ci and release contexts, which Oyzu detects from CI variables, so CI needs no extra flags; with oyzu --profile ci build. Each check (tests, coverage, lint, format) has a level in oyzu.toml: off, advisory (a failure is a warning), enforce (the default; fails full builds) or required (runs in every build and fails it). No flag skips a check the project chose; turning one off is a committed change. See check levels.

Tasks go in oyzu.toml under [tasks]. Each one is either argv (an argument list, recommended) or run (a shell command): [tasks."api:smoke"] argv = ["go", "run", "."] A task with the same name as a builder stage replaces that stage's command. The stage's requirements still apply: a replacement test stage must still produce the reports its builder needs. Which builds a task applies to depends on its name: Key Applies to [tasks."api:smoke"] Build api only [tasks.post_build] (a hook) Every build below that file's folder that has a build stage [tasks.test] (a stage name) Replaces test in every build the file reaches; refused if those builds use different builders [tasks.lint-docs] (any other name) At the root, a workspace task: oyzu run lint-docs Names are checked before anything runs. A misspelled build or hook target is an error naming the file and line and suggesting the nearest name. See which build a task belongs to.

A hook is a task named pre_<task> or post_<task>. It runs with that task, both in task runs and in builds. Prerequisites use depends_on: [tasks."api:pre_test"] argv = ["node", "scripts/check-api-inputs.mjs"] depends_on = ["schema:verify"] [tasks."schema:verify"] argv = ["node", "scripts/verify-schema.mjs"] schema:verify runs once per command even if several tasks need it, in the schema target's folder with that target's tools. A custom command never installs a new tool by itself: the tools it calls must be ones the project already uses.

A hook can say when it applies with when and unless, using facts such as the build context, platform, whether the build is optimized, and for post_build hooks the artifact. It can receive values through placeholders like {artifact.path}: [tasks."cli:post_build"] argv = ["{artifact.path}", "--version"] when = { optimized = true, platform = ["linux/x86_64"] } Conditions choose behavior; they aren't a security control. Use check levels and constraints for checks that must run. See task and hook conditions.

Builder stages are cached without any setup. Oyzu can't see inside a task you wrote, so a target containing one runs every time, unless the task sets cache = true with outputs, or the hook declares outputs. See authored tasks cached on request.
Build tasks Task settings Run native tasks guide

A build is only as reproducible as the compiler that ran it. Oyzu manages toolchains itself, so your laptop, a teammate's machine and CI use the same Go, Node or Rust without anyone installing it by hand. You say what you need, Oyzu picks an exact version, verifies the download once, records it in oyzu.lock, and puts it on PATH for builds, tasks and your shell.

Oyzu collects tool requirements from three places and combines them, keeping track of each source: Source Example What it adds Native files go 1.22 in go.mod; rust-toolchain.toml Minimums, channels and components the project already declares The builder Go's builder needs a Go compiler; Rust's test stage needs nextest and cargo-llvm-cov Tools for the stages that will run [tools] in oyzu.toml go = "1.24" Explicit requests, for tools with no native pin or to pick within a range Tools follow checks: when a check is off, its tools aren't installed. With [checks] format = "off", the Rust builder no longer adds rustfmt. oyzu build --plan shows the combined list without checking or installing anything: $ oyzu build --planCopy … Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:go minimum-version >=1.22 all 2 targets go.mod go oyzu:go request 1.22 all 2 targets api/go.mod (native pin); worker/go.mod (native pin) …

If a native file already pins a tool, that file is the request, and Oyzu configuration either adds nothing or must agree: a [tools] value in the pin's folder, or nearer the build, must name the same version line, or preparation fails naming both files; a [tools] value farther away loses to the pin and is shown as overridden; native ranges, such as npm devEngines, stay constraints. Today Oyzu reads the Rust toolchain files and the go and toolchain lines in Go's go.mod and go.work. Go's lines count as a minimum, not an exact pin, because Go treats the toolchain line as a suggestion. Oyzu requests that minimum when no [tools] go is set, and a configured version below it fails with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT. Support for other native pin files, such as global.json, Gradle and Maven wrapper properties and packageManager, varies by ecosystem; the build guide for your ecosystem says which it reads. See Go version selection and Rust toolchain files.

Installing a tool takes the same steps whichever command starts it: Resolve the request ("1.24") to an exact version (1.24.13) for every platform in the lock, from the publisher's catalog or Oyzu's signed public tool index. Download the archive for this machine. Verify it: the archive digest against the publisher's checksum, the publisher's signature where available, and the unpacked layout. Store it in the shared tool store with an install record, and write oyzu.lock. After that, the tool is trusted. Running a command doesn't re-hash the installed files, and a damaged installation may simply fail when run. Checking happens once, at install, which keeps every command fast. $ oyzu install go@1.24Copy Installing requested tools Resolving every platform, then installing this one ✓ Installed (reused existing installation) go 1.24.13 Declared "1.24" in …\shop\oyzu.toml (project) Locked in …\shop\oyzu.lock for 4 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc) ​ Store: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Oyzu\tools Configuration keeps what you typed ("1.24"). The lock records the exact version and an archive for each platform. Only this machine's archive is installed; here Go 1.24.13 was already in the store, so nothing was downloaded. go@1.26 is a prefix, go@1.26.8 is exact, go@latest is the newest eligible version, and plain go keeps an existing declaration. Several tools in one command are applied together or not at all.

Installed tools live in one store per user, shared by every project: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\tools on Windows and ${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/oyzu/tools on Linux. Two projects that lock the same Go version share one installation. oyzu uninstall never deletes shared files; oyzu tools list shows what uses each installation.

The selected tools reach every place you run commands: Where How Builds The build installs any missing pinned tool and uses the exact selection for each action Tasks oyzu run <task> puts the selected tools on PATH One command oyzu exec -- go version Your shell oyzu activate adds the selection to PATH as you change directories Lookup oyzu which go prints the selected executable $ oyzu exec -- go versionCopy go version go1.24.13 windows/amd64 oyzu which and oyzu exec never fall back to a program elsewhere on your PATH when the selected tool is missing; they fail and tell you to install it. Shell activation applies a project's environment variables only after you trust the folder, because environment variables can run code in shells and interpreters.

Command Declares in Locks in oyzu install go@1.24 project oyzu.toml project oyzu.lock oyzu install -g node@22 your user configuration the oyzu.lock beside it oyzu install --local go@1.24 oyzu.local.toml project oyzu.lock Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT instead of guessing.

Oyzu installs supported tools from their publishers: Node, Go, Python, Java, Maven, Gradle, Helm, kubectl, k3d, npm, pnpm, Rust and the Cargo helpers it needs, among others, plus experimental registry packages (aqua: and github:). It doesn't install operating-system components. A Windows Rust build that needs the MSVC build tools and SDK, or a system linker, reports it as an executor prerequisite with setup instructions; oyzu pin --dry-run lists these separately from managed tools. Tool commands are supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64); support for individual tools varies. See tool commands.

Command Use it to oyzu install <tool>@<version> Declare, lock and install a tool oyzu install Install everything declared; --frozen never changes the lock, --offline never uses the network oyzu update [tool] Move to the newest version within each requirement; never edits configuration oyzu uninstall <tool> Remove a declaration and its lock entries oyzu pin Lock requirements without installing oyzu tools current / list / versions / info See what is selected, stored, available and why oyzu which <command>, oyzu exec -- <command> Find or run a command with the selected tools
Tool commands The lock file Manage your first tool guide Shell activation

Oyzu builds container images from ordinary Dockerfiles and packages Helm charts from ordinary chart folders. Neither needs configuration. With a little build.yaml, the pieces connect: a binary built by one target is copied into an image, and the image's exact digest is written into the chart that deploys it. Image builds produce an OCI archive in dist/ and never push. Chart builds produce a packaged .tgz and a rendered manifest, and never contact a cluster. Publishing is a separate, explicit step (publishing). Note: The Docker and Helm builders are experimental. They run as the oyzu/docker and oyzu/helm plugins. Images are Linux images only (linux/x86_64, linux/arm64). Builds that need an engine use Docker with a Linux engine, on Linux or Windows. macOS is not supported yet.

Files Builder Tasks Dockerfile docker/image build, lint (Hadolint), format-check and format (dockerfmt) Chart.yaml or chart/Chart.yaml helm/chart build (helm package), test, lint (helm lint), format-check and format (yamlfmt), install (helm dependency build) If both chart locations exist, discovery fails as ambiguous, so declare the path in build.yaml. If a folder with a Dockerfile also looks like an application (a package.json or pyproject.toml), select the Docker builder with uses: docker/image.

Oyzu looks at the Dockerfile and picks the cheapest safe path for each target. You don't set anything. Daemonless assembly. If the final stage only copies files onto one base and edits image settings (COPY, WORKDIR, USER, ENV, LABEL, EXPOSE, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, STOPSIGNAL), and the base is scratch or pinned by @sha256: digest, Oyzu writes the image itself, like ko or Jib. This build needs no Docker engine. Base images are fetched anonymously by digest and cached. BuildKit in an isolated worker. Anything else (a RUN in the final stage, ARG, ADD, a tag-only base, .dockerignore) runs in Oyzu's rootless BuildKit worker with no network. Base images must already be in your local Docker image store. On this path Oyzu doesn't pull them or read registry credentials. # Daemonless: a digest-pinned base and only COPY and settings FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12:nonroot@sha256:7f0c72cd138b442ae0deeb69c08b1acf5525439ba251a49ad93c320a061567e5 COPY bin/server /server USER 65532:65532 ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] The full list of instructions daemonless assembly accepts is in daemonless assembly.
documents.s: Two ways an image is built

documents.t: A Linux Docker engine for BuildKit builds and for the quality checks. You also need the base execution image and, for RUN steps, the pinned rootless BuildKit worker (published execution images). Oyzu pulls both by pinned digest the first time it needs them. Set OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL=1 to forbid pulls on an offline host. Hadolint and dockerfmt ship in the Docker plugin package for builds. To run oyzu run lint and oyzu run format on your machine, they must be on PATH. oyzu build --no-docker builds a daemonless target without contacting Docker. A target that needs the engine stops with exit status 3 before anything runs.

lint runs hadolint --no-color Dockerfile and honors a .hadolint.yaml next to the Dockerfile. format-check runs dockerfmt with --check and honors a nearby .editorconfig. Both are build gates with --full and in CI. See Dockerfile linting and formatting. A successful image build records: Output Contents <target>-<version>.oci.tar The image as an OCI layout archive, with its digest in manifest.json JUnit report Integrity and platform checks on the archive Dependency record Each base image's requested reference and verified digests, the Dockerfile digest and the build path used Every image is checked against its target platform, and an image for the wrong architecture fails. To build for both supported platforms, list linux/x86_64 and linux/arm64 in platforms. (linux/amd64 and linux/aarch64 are accepted spellings.) Oyzu builds one image per platform plus an OCI index over them. A Dockerfile with RUN in a target-platform stage needs the worker and target platforms to match.

with.repository names the image's eventual registry repository, such as registry.example.com/team/app. Building never contacts it. A chart binding reads it (below). To load a built image into Docker or a k3d cluster without a registry, set docker.load and run oyzu run load. See loading the image locally.

oyzu build packages the chart and renders it with helm template --dry-run=client and an empty kubeconfig, so you get both a .tgz and a rendered.yaml. With --full or in CI it also runs: Validation. Rendering plus values.schema.json checks for an application chart, or strict lint for a library chart. Reported as junit.xml. helm-unittest, when a chart or subchart has flat tests/*_test.yaml suites or recursive unittests/**/*.yaml suites. Reported separately as unittest.xml. Rendering alone doesn't count as a passing unit test. Snapshot baselines are inputs, so creating or changing one during a build fails it. helm lint and a read-only yamlfmt check of the chart's YAML. Templates aren't formatted. Coverage is recorded as not applicable instead of as an invented percentage.

Charts build in the isolated worker with the Helm in your lock; the base image has none. Declare the version and install it, which records the exact archive in oyzu.lock: # oyzu.toml [tools] helm = "4.3.0" oyzu install helm@4.3.0 Helm takes an exact version only. yamlfmt comes from the lock too. When a chart has unit test suites, Oyzu fetches its pinned helm-unittest release and restores it for the test stage, so a pinned Helm must be able to run that plugin. Isolated chart builds are supported on Linux amd64. See pinned Helm.

A chart can use the identity of an image built in the same oyzu build, so nobody passes --set image.digest=… at deploy time: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/greeting chart: uses: helm/chart path: chart bindings: - from: image artifact: image type: image-reference repository: /image/repository digest: /image/digest The destinations are JSON Pointers into the chart's values.yaml, and each must already be a string there (an empty digest: "" is the usual shape). Oyzu writes the repository and the image's real manifest digest into a private copy of the chart before packaging. The packaged defaults and rendered.yaml carry the produced reference, and your checked-in chart is never edited. A changed image rebuilds the chart, and a failed image blocks it. See image bindings for the reference form and the limits.
documents.s: Bind an image into a chart

documents.t: This example is examples/builds/image-and-chart/project in the Oyzu repository. Copy it to a new folder and run git init. It has a Go command in app/, a Dockerfile at the root and a chart in chart/: FROM scratch COPY bin/server /server ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] build.yaml connects them. materialize copies the Go target's binary to bin/server in the image's build context, and the chart binds the image: builds: app: uses: go/app path: app image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.invalid/team/greeting materialize: - from: app to: bin/server platforms: - linux/amd64 chart: uses: helm/chart path: chart bindings: - from: image artifact: image type: image-reference repository: /image/repository digest: /image/digest The chart's values.yaml holds the placeholders the binding fills: replicaCount: 1 image: repository: registry.example.invalid/team/greeting tag: development digest: "" oyzu build --plan shows how the three targets depend on each other: $ oyzu build --planCopy Declared task ordering Task After app-platform-linux_x86_64-a7b09986ced7:build image:build app-platform-linux_x86_64-a7b09986ced7:build chart:build image:build Output shortened. Read the plan this way: The image's platforms: [linux/amd64] makes the Go binary a linux/amd64 build too, so the copied file matches the image. Oyzu names those variants app-platform-linux_x86_64-…. The image needs no Docker engine: FROM scratch plus COPY is assembled in process. The chart waits for the image and receives its OCI archive as .oyzu-bindings/0.oci.tar, the data its binding reads. The Go binary and the chart still run in the isolated worker, which needs Docker. With --full, the image also runs lint and format-check, and its placement changes to Docker engine required, because Hadolint and dockerfmt run in a container from the Docker plugin package. oyzu build then produces the Linux binary, a versioned .oci.tar image archive with its JUnit report, and the chart .tgz plus a rendered.yaml whose image.digest is the image's real manifest digest.
documents.s: Worked example: binary, image and chart

documents.t: You see Cause Fix Preparation names a missing base image (BuildKit path) The base isn't in your local Docker image store Pull or provision it your usual way. Or pin it by digest and keep the final stage free of RUN, so the daemonless path fetches it A private base fails on the daemonless path Only anonymous registry pulls are supported Use a public base, or provision it locally and use the BuildKit path A foreign-platform RUN fails before any action RUN in a target-platform stage that differs from the worker Build on a matching worker. Or compile in a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM stage and only COPY into the target stage Hadolint or dockerfmt fails A lint or format finding Fix it, or run oyzu run format and review the change helm lint reports missing dependencies A vendored subchart under charts/ isn't declared in the parent Chart.yaml Declare it (name and version, no repository URL) A unittest snapshot fails the build A baseline under __snapshot__ would be created or changed Update baselines deliberately with helm-unittest, review and commit them A binding fails during configuration The destination is missing from values.yaml, the image has no with.repository, or both binding forms are set Add the string field, set with.repository, or use one form NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON with --no-docker (exit 3) A selected target needs Docker, such as lint or format checks under --full Run with Docker, or select only daemonless work

Images are Linux only (linux/x86_64, linux/arm64). Native Windows images and emulated RUN aren't supported. Registry credentials, private bases on the daemonless path, remote ADD, and secret and SSH mounts aren't supported. Binding a multi-platform image (an OCI index) into a chart is refused. Chart dependencies from remote or OCI repositories, Go-template formatting, and chart publishing or signing aren't supported. See capabilities and known limitations for the whole product.

Docker image inputs and offline builds, including offline dependency contexts for pip, npm, Yarn, pnpm, Go modules and Cargo Oyzu's BuildKit frontend and declared fetches Helm charts and chart tests Publishing finalized artifacts, including OCI destinations

Oyzu builds an SDK-style .NET solution or project with no configuration. It honors global.json for SDK selection, restores NuGet packages through a controlled mirror, then builds, tests and packs offline in an isolated Linux container. Test results become JUnit, and every packable project becomes a NuGet package in the dist/ bundle. Note: The .NET builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/dotnet plugin and builds only in the isolated Linux executor, so you need Docker. Supported on Linux (x86-64) containers, with SDK 10.0.401 by default. There are no Windows or macOS builds yet. You can start the build from Windows, but it still runs in the Linux container. The .NET reference has the full details.

.NET builds always run in the isolated executor, with no host build path. You need: Docker with a Linux engine. The plan says Docker engine required. The base execution image. Oyzu pulls it on first use. The SDK in oyzu.lock. Run oyzu pin. Without a [tools] dotnet setting it locks the default SDK, 10.0.401, and restores it into every action. See provisioning. To run on an image of your own, pass --image dotnet=<image>. The locked SDK is still used. You don't need the .NET SDK on your machine.

A folder is a .NET target when it directly contains a solution (.sln, .slnx) or an SDK-style project (.csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj whose root names an MSBuild SDK). Legacy non-SDK projects aren't claimed. The version comes from a literal <Version> in the root Directory.Build.props. A literal Version or VersionPrefix in the entry project works too. The tasks are native dotnet commands: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 5 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · dotnet/sdk (5) project:build Inferred · dotnet dotnet build project:format Inferred · dotnet — Unavailable: No native configuration or registered integration was discovered project:install Inferred · dotnet dotnet restore project:lint Inferred · dotnet — Unavailable: No native configuration or registered integration was discovered project:test Inferred · dotnet dotnet test There are no format or lint integrations for .NET yet, and the list says so.

Every native command gets one entry: the single solution, otherwise the single SDK-style project. If a folder has more than one candidate, the build fails and names them. Pick one in build.yaml: builds: app: uses: dotnet/sdk with: project: Greeting.slnx with.project is the only option. Any other key is refused (invalid .NET with options: unknown field …, expected project).

global.json in the target folder selects the SDK the way the dotnet host does: sdk.version, sdk.rollForward (default patch with a version, latestMajor without one) and sdk.allowPrerelease. Without global.json, the locked SDK is used. global.json must be strict JSON, so comments are refused. Oyzu doesn't predict the result. During preparation it lists the SDKs in the container and asks dotnet --version which one your folder selects. If nothing installed satisfies the request, preparation fails before restore. The message names the request, the available SDKs and oyzu pin as the remedy. --plan shows the request. Current versions list the SDK requirement as oyzu:dotnet; the output below may show an older image default. $ oyzu build --planCopy Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source dotnet-sdk tool 10.0.400 rollForward latestFeature; default image SDK project global.json /sdk 10.0.401

Command What runs oyzu build --plan Nothing. Shows the SDK request and the stages oyzu build Restore, dotnet build (Debug by default, Release with --optimized), then dotnet pack oyzu build --full Also dotnet test, with results converted to JUnit In CI the test stage runs without --full. Inside the container: Restore runs once during preparation with no network, through a loopback mirror. The mirror reaches only the public https://api.nuget.org/ flat container (and its vulnerability data) through Oyzu's scoped broker. Feeds and credentials from NuGet.Config, user settings or RestoreSources aren't used. If any packages.lock.json exists, restore uses --locked-mode. Build runs dotnet build <entry> --configuration Debug --no-restore (Release for an optimized build) with -p:Version=<snapshot version>. Test, when selected, runs dotnet test --no-build --no-restore with TRX output (VSTest, or Microsoft.Testing.Platform when global.json selects it). All TRX files become one JUnit report. A test run that produces no TRX fails instead of reporting an empty suite. Pack runs dotnet pack --no-build into one directory artifact, nuget-packages-<version>. It fails when no project is packable.

Preparation restores with NuGet audit on and reports what it finds as a NuGet audit step (for example known vulnerabilities: 1 high), as NUGET_AUDIT warnings and in the dependency record. Findings never fail the build, and they can't turn into compile errors under TreatWarningsAsErrors.

This is the .NET fixture from the Oyzu source tree (tooling/fixtures/dotnet-app): a solution with a packable Greeting library and an xUnit test project. global.json: { "sdk": { "version": "10.0.400", "rollForward": "latestFeature" } } Directory.Build.props: <Project> <PropertyGroup> <Version>1.2.0</Version> <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework> <Nullable>enable</Nullable> <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors> </PropertyGroup> </Project> Greeting.slnx lists src/Greeting/Greeting.csproj (with RestorePackagesWithLockFile and a checked-in packages.lock.json) and test/Greeting.Tests/Greeting.Tests.csproj (IsPackable false, referencing Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk, xunit and xunit.runner.visualstudio). oyzu build --plan --full shows the target running in the Linux container, whatever your host is: $ oyzu build --plan --fullCopy project · dotnet/sdk · unresolved until executor selection Executor: captured-worker Profile: development · local dist only (--configuration Debug) Placement: runs on any platform · Docker engine required · Isolated steps run in the captured worker on a Docker engine Discovered Selection Reason sdk 10.0.400 rollForward latestFeature native global.json /sdk Output shortened. The request 10.0.400 with latestFeature admits 10.0.401. Now build: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building dotnet-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ NuGet audit no known vulnerabilities 22.5s ✓ Version 1.2.0-dev.gb0a8e2fc937d · 1 package 0.4s … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project prepare dotnet/sdk restore executed 14.7s ✓ project build dotnet build Greeting.slnx --configura… executed 9.7s ✓ project test dotnet/sdk test executed 3.6s ✓ project package dotnet/sdk pack executed 6.3s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/linux/x86_64/nuget-packages-1.2.0-dev.gb0a8e2fc937d 3.4 KB development ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 1 skipped (1 collected reports) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 61.9s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 46700-1792554997213667400-1 Output shortened. The artifact is under linux/x86_64 because the build ran in the Linux container.
documents.s: Worked example: a library with tests

documents.t: Output Contents nuget-packages-<version>/ One directory artifact with every packable project's .nupkg reports/junit.xml All TRX results converted to JUnit, keeping class names, failures and skips Dependency record SDK version used, lock digests, each restored package's digest and audit findings The version is a snapshot from your declared version and Git history, passed to restore, build and pack as -p:Version. See version inference.

You see Cause Fix Several entry candidates named More than one solution or project in the folder Set with.project in build.yaml No installed SDK satisfies the request global.json asks for an SDK the locked one doesn't satisfy Change global.json, or set a matching [tools] dotnet and run oyzu pin Restore fails under --locked-mode packages.lock.json no longer matches the project's dependencies Update the lock with dotnet restore and commit it NU1503 or an MSBuild SDK not found A NuGet-supplied MSBuild SDK whose version is a property, range or wildcard Write a literal version (Sdk="Name/1.2.3" or msbuild-sdks in global.json) so Oyzu can restore it in preparation Pack fails: no packable project Every project sets IsPackable to false Make the library packable, or build a different target A test fails The test run failed JUnit is kept and the package isn't exported

Linux (x86-64) containers only. There are no Windows or macOS builds. Private feeds, credentials, package source mapping and workloads aren't supported. global.json and Directory.Build.* files above the target folder aren't copied into the build. No coverage, lint or format integrations. No per-package artifacts, dotnet publish outputs or NativeAOT publishing stage. A repository without a root solution needs with.project. The default SDK, memory and timeout limits and the builder name may still change. See the reference.
.NET reference NuGet sessions: managed NuGet for oyzu exec, separate from builds Build bundles

Oyzu builds Go modules and workspaces from go.mod and go.work alone. It picks the Go version your module asks for, installs it, and runs the native go build, go test, go vet and gofmt commands. It collects the binary, JUnit results and statement coverage into a verified dist/ bundle. Note: The Go builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/go plugin, whose releases are previews: opt in once with oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true. Applications build on your machine. Libraries and workspaces build in the isolated executor and need Docker. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet. The Go reference has the full details. The tutorial walks through a Go project step by step, including a failing test and reuse.

Project Builder Where it builds A module with a main package (go.mod) go/app On your machine A module with no main package go/app, packaged as a module In the isolated executor (Docker) A workspace (go.work) One target for the workspace In the isolated executor (Docker) Discovery reads files and runs nothing. Go itself decides workspace members, which packages are main, dependencies and cgo during preparation. To package a module as a library even when it also has commands, set uses: go/library in build.yaml. The inferred tasks are plain Go commands: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · go/app (6) project:build Inferred · go go build ./... project:format Inferred · go gofmt -w . project:format-check Inferred · go gofmt -l . project:install Inferred · go go mod download project:lint Inferred · go go vet ./... project:test Inferred · go go test ./... format rewrites your files and never runs inside a build. The build uses format-check, which fails when gofmt -l lists anything.

Command What runs oyzu build --plan Nothing. Shows the stages and the Go minimum read from go.mod oyzu build go build with -trimpath and VCS stamping off, then collects the binary oyzu build --full Also go test -json with a coverage profile, go vet and gofmt -l oyzu run test Only the tests, on your machine, writing a test-only dist/ bundle In CI the checks run without --full. Arguments after -- go to the task's command, so you can select tests the Go way: $ oyzu run test -- -run TestGreetingCopy · project · Testing TEST_EVIDENCE: Test evidence project:test Command passed Results 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped Coverage 50.0% of statements (1/2) Acceptance accepted ✓ project · Testing Succeeded (exit 0 after 2.30s) Output shortened. Oyzu adds -json, a fresh -coverprofile and -count=1 to the implicit go test ./..., converts the events to JUnit and keeps Go's coverage profile. Coverage is statement coverage, as Go measures it. If checks.coverageMinimum is above zero, the test action supplies the target's coverage report, and the build fails if that report is missing or below the minimum. See build check requirements.

Go's own files decide. Oyzu runs Go with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so Go never downloads a toolchain behind your back. Oyzu selects and installs it instead. The go line in go.mod (or go.work in a workspace) is a minimum. With go 1.22 and nothing else, Oyzu locks the newest stable release of that line. A toolchain line is honored too. The newer of the two lines is the minimum. [tools] go = "1.24" in oyzu.toml picks a release at or above that minimum. The exact choice goes in oyzu.lock with the minimum recorded beside it (for example go-minimum:>=1.22). Commit the lock. The Tools row of each build says what ran: go 1.22.12 already installed detected from go.mod. If you change [tools] go (say to 1.23), the next build refuses to guess and tells you to update the lock: $ oyzu buildCopy ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✗ Tools failed: preparation did not complete <0.1s ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:go 1.23; run oyzu pin Next: Run oyzu pin --refresh to refresh the lock, then oyzu install. A request below the module's minimum (here [tools] go = "1.21" with go 1.22) is refused before any work, naming both files: $ oyzu pinCopy ✗ TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT: project: [tools] go = "1.21" in oyzu.toml is below the go minimum 1.22 that go.mod declares (go line); set [tools] go to 1.22 or later in oyzu.toml, or remove it so the native file decides The Go reference has the complete rule, including toolchain lines, workspace files and oyzu.toml values in different folders.

Everything lands in the dist/ bundle. The Outputs section prints each artifact's path, and manifest.json records it with its digest. The bundle layout describes the directories. Output Contents <target>-<version>[.exe] The application binary, or one per named command module-<n>-<version>.zip, .mod, .info For a library: the module archive, its go.mod and proxy metadata reports/junit.xml Test results converted from go test -json reports/coverage.out Go's coverage profile manifest.json Every file with its digest, plus the plan and build evidence Versions are snapshots: 0.0.0-dev.g<source> without a tag, or a tag-derived base with the same suffix. For a /v2 module the snapshot is v2.0.0-dev.g…, so it satisfies Go's module path rules. A snapshot isn't a release; see version inference.

This is the same program as the tutorial: a go.mod with go 1.22, a main.go that prints a greeting, and one test. It lives in examples/builds/go-app/project in the Oyzu repository. Copy it to a new folder outside any other repository and run git init. Preview the build: $ oyzu build --planCopy project · go/app · windows/x86_64 Executor: host Profile: development · local dist only (no difference: the Go compiler always optimizes) Placement: runs on windows/x86_64 · no Docker engine needed · Runs as host processes without a container engine Stage Selection Details build selected Native commands and report bindings resolve during preparation format-check skipped fast local build lint skipped fast local build test skipped fast local build ​ Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:go minimum-version >=1.22 project go.mod go oyzu:go request 1.22 project go.mod (native pin) Output shortened. The application runs as host processes, so no Docker engine is involved. Now build with every check: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building go-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tool versions Resolved and locked 3.5s ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 0 installed now 0.2s go 1.22.12 already installed detected from go.mod … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=fals… executed 1.2s ✓ project test go test -json -coverprofile=C:\Us… executed 1.8s ✓ project lint go vet ./... executed 1.1s ✓ project format-check gofmt -l . executed <0.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/project-0.0.0-dev.g933478b85fef.exe 2.0 MB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 9.0s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 60212-1792553348765929400-1 Output shortened. Go 1.22.12 was already in the shared tool store. On a fresh machine the Tools row says it was installed now. Check the result with oyzu inspect dist, as in the tutorial.

A module with no main package, or a go.work workspace, builds in the isolated executor. The plan says so before anything runs: $ oyzu build --planCopy project · go/app · unresolved until executor selection Executor: captured-worker Placement: runs on any platform · Docker engine required · Isolated steps run in the captured worker on a Docker engine Output shortened. Isolated builds download public modules through Oyzu's scoped Go proxy, verify them against go.sum, then build, test, vet and package with no network. They run on the base execution image, which Oyzu pulls on first use. The image has no Go: the Go in oyzu.lock is restored into each action. See the Go reference.

You see Cause Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:go …; run oyzu pin (exit 4) [tools] go or the module's go or toolchain line changed since oyzu.lock was written. go get and go mod tidy can rewrite them Run oyzu pin and commit oyzu.lock cannot select oyzu:go for request "…"; declared requirements: >=… from go.mod go The configured Go is below the module's minimum Raise [tools] go, or remove it so go.mod decides format-check fails gofmt -l listed files Run oyzu run format, review the changes, rebuild A test or go vet fails The Go command failed The failure section names the log under dist/logs/ and the command to rerun one target. The previous good binary is kept A library or workspace build can't start its worker The isolated executor needs a running Docker engine, the execution image and Go in oyzu.lock Start Docker, make sure the execution image is available, and run oyzu pin

Private module sources, direct VCS fetches and module publication aren't supported. Cross-compiling with GOOS and GOARCH as a build option isn't supported. Platform matrices select matching provisioned toolchains (toolchain platforms). cgo builds work only through the coarse isolated plan. Full cgo portability isn't supported. Libraries and workspaces need Docker. See capabilities and known limitations for the whole product.
Go reference and Go installation Direct tests: what oyzu run test records Build bundles

Oyzu builds Maven reactors and Gradle builds from pom.xml and build.gradle alone. It provisions the JDK and Maven or Gradle itself, runs your normal lifecycle, collects JUnit and JaCoCo reports and records the jars it produced. You don't need Java installed, and you don't write an Oyzu build file. Note: The Java builders are experimental. They run as the oyzu/maven, oyzu/gradle and oyzu/ant plugins. Maven and Gradle build on your machine. Ant needs the isolated executor. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet.

Signal in your project What it decides pom.xml A java/maven target. A reactor (parent POM with <modules>) is one target, and Maven owns module order, inheritance and profiles build.gradle or build.gradle.kts A java/gradle target. A multi-project build, including includeBuild composites, is one target, and Gradle owns membership and task dependencies build.xml An Ant target, built only in the isolated executor mvnw or gradlew committed Oyzu runs the wrapper instead of mvn or gradle and provisions only the JDK maven.compiler.release, maven.compiler.target, maven.compiler.source or java.version in the root POM The minimum JDK JavaLanguageVersion.of(…) or sourceCompatibility in Gradle build scripts The minimum JDK Discovery reads files only. It doesn't start Maven or Gradle.

The example is examples/builds/java-maven-reactor from the Oyzu repository. Copy it to an empty folder and run git init. It's a reactor with two modules, library and app, each with a JUnit 5 test. The root POM declares <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>. $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · java/maven (6) project:build Inferred · maven mvn -B verify project:format Inferred · maven java OyzuJavaQuality.java format project:format-check Inferred · maven java OyzuJavaQuality.java format-check project:install Inferred · maven mvn -B dependency:go-offline project:lint Inferred · maven java OyzuJavaQuality.java lint project:test Inferred · maven mvn -B test test is a development task, not a build stage, because mvn verify already runs your tests. oyzu build --plan shows Executor: host, so Maven runs directly on your machine with no Docker, and names where the JDK floor came from: $ oyzu build --planCopy Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:java minimum-version >=17.0.0 project pom.xml properties.maven.compiler.release oyzu:java tool from configuration / native project JDK for the selected Maven build stages oyzu:maven tool from configuration / native project Apache Maven for the selected build stages Output shortened. Now build: $ oyzu buildCopy Building java-maven-reactor windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · fast ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tools 2 tools pinned · 0 installed now 0.2s java 17.0.20 already installed detected from pom.xml maven 3.9.16 already installed detected from pom.xml … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build mvn -B -ntp org.jacoco:jacoco-maven-plug… executed 19.0s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/library-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar 1.8 KB development project dist/project/windows/x86_64/app-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar 1.9 KB development ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (2 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 lines) Coverage project: 66.7% (2/3 lines) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 1 executed · 22.0s Output shortened. Oyzu selected JDK 17 from the POM and Maven 3.9, locked them in oyzu.lock, and ran one Maven verify with JaCoCo around it. Each module's Surefire XML and JaCoCo report were collected (one coverage line per module), and both jars were published to dist/ because every test passed. Your checkout isn't modified, because the build runs in a private workspace. On a fresh machine, the first build downloads the JDK and Maven first.

The example is examples/builds/java-gradle-multi-project: an app and a library subproject plus an included support build. rootProject.name = "oyzu-gradle-example" include("app", "library") includeBuild("support") $ oyzu buildCopy ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Tools 2 tools pinned · 0 installed now 0.4s gradle 8.14.6 already installed detected from build.gradle java 17.0.20 already installed detected from build.gradle … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build gradle -I C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\T… executed 16.4s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/app.jar 820 B development project dist/project/windows/x86_64/library.jar 729 B development project dist/project/windows/x86_64/support-0.1.0.jar 717 B development ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 lines) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 1 executed · 55.9s Output shortened. Oyzu reads Gradle's own model through an Oyzu-supplied init script, which reports each project's archive and test tasks. It then runs gradle --no-daemon build with an init script (-I) that applies JaCoCo, and publishes the jars the model reported, including the included build's support-0.1.0.jar. Only library has tests, so there's one report.

You don't configure tests or reports. Maven. verify runs Surefire and, where a module declares maven-failsafe-plugin and has IT*, *IT or *ITCase classes, Failsafe. Each module with test sources must produce JUnit XML in target/surefire-reports (and target/failsafe-reports). JaCoCo 0.8.13 runs around verify, and each module's target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml is collected. Gradle. build runs your Test tasks. Oyzu collects each tested project's JUnit results and the JaCoCo report its init script writes under build/reports/oyzu/<test task>/jacoco.xml. A failing test fails the build with the native output and publishes no jars. A module with test sources but no XML (for example because tests were skipped) fails its report requirement. Oyzu never invents a passing report. To run only the tests on your machine and collect the same reports into a test-only bundle, use oyzu run test and then oyzu inspect dist. That path needs Maven or Gradle and the JDK already provisioned, and it runs them offline. See Maven and Gradle.

lint and format-check are build stages, selected by --full or a CI context. The defaults are Checkstyle 10.21.4 (unused and redundant imports, empty statements, equals and hashCode consistency) and google-java-format 1.28.0. They check .java files under the target and skip target, build, .gradle, out, dist and similar directories. format rewrites files and runs only when you ask: oyzu run format. Oyzu doesn't download these two tools yet. On a fresh machine, --full stops before building: $ oyzu build --fullCopy ✗ Report preparation failed: preparation did not complete <0.1s ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: Java lint and format-check need Checkstyle and google-java-format, which Oyzu does not provision automatically yet: run `python tooling/provision-java-quality.py --destination <absolute directory>` from the Oyzu repository and set OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME to that directory, replace the task in oyzu.toml (for example [tasks.lint]), or build without --full (see docs/reference/java-quality.md) You have three ways forward: Provision the defaults. From a checkout of the Oyzu repository, run python tooling/provision-java-quality.py --destination <absolute directory>. It downloads checksum-pinned upstream JARs. Then set OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME to that directory (export OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME=/opt/java-quality, or $env:OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME = 'E:\tools\java-quality' in PowerShell). Use your own quality tasks. If the project already uses Checkstyle or Spotless, replace the defaults in oyzu.toml. The tasks must exist in your build: [tasks.lint] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "checkstyleMain", "checkstyleTest"] [tasks.format-check] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessCheck"] Build without --full until one of those is in place. Oyzu doesn't infer Maven quality-plugin bindings or Gradle quality tasks, read your own Checkstyle XML, or run Kotlin or Groovy linters. See Java quality.

Native files come first, then oyzu.toml. The result is always recorded in oyzu.lock. Tool Default request Override JDK The declared Java level (maven.compiler.release and friends, or the Gradle sourceCompatibility or toolchain level), raised to 17 if lower. lts when nothing is declared [tools] java Maven 3.9 [tools] maven Gradle Gradle 8, or 9 when the project declares a Java level above 24 [tools] gradle The declared level is a floor. A project declaring release 21 gets JDK 21, not the newest JDK. A project declaring 8 or 11 gets JDK 17, the oldest JDK that Maven, Gradle and Oyzu's Java support run on. JDK 17 compiles the older level correctly with --release. To choose explicitly: [tools] java = "21" # latest 21.x, "lts", or an exact "21.0.8" maven = "3.9" # or gradle = "8" oyzu pin --dry-run previews what would be locked, and oyzu exec -- mvn -version runs a command with the locked tools. JDKs are Eclipse Temurin, checked against the SHA-256 the Adoptium API declares. Maven comes from the Apache distribution server and Gradle from services.gradle.org, each checked against its published digest. A build sees JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_HOME and GRADLE_HOME from these tools only. It never inherits a machine-wide JDK. See Java, Maven and Gradle installation. Wrappers. With a committed mvnw or gradlew, Oyzu runs the wrapper and provisions only the JDK. The wrapper downloads its own Maven or Gradle outside Oyzu's checks, so pin distributionSha256Sum in maven-wrapper.properties or gradle-wrapper.properties. The Maven wrapper's only-script form also needs curl or wget on PATH.
documents.s: Choose the JDK, Maven and Gradle

documents.t: Project What lands in dist/ Maven reactor (native build) Each module's jar under its own name, such as library-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar Gradle build (native build) Each archive Gradle's model reports, such as app.jar and support-0.1.0.jar. Same-named archives are prefixed with the project path Isolated Maven or Gradle build pom, jar and war (Maven) or JAR, WAR, EAR, ZIP and TAR archives (Gradle), with snapshot versions from version inference written into private copies of your build files dist/manifest.json records every artifact with its digest, the tests and coverage, and the logs. oyzu inspect dist verifies them. A build artifact isn't a publication or release approval.

oyzu build runs Maven and Gradle on your machine when the project fits: Maven. A reactor whose jar names can be read from the POMs (literal or inherited versions, jar packaging, no finalName or classifier). Gradle. Any build whose archives Gradle's model reports. Everything else, and every Ant project, uses the isolated executor: a Linux container with captured dependencies and no network during the build. It needs Docker. Oyzu pulls the base execution image on first use. The JDK and Maven or Gradle come from oyzu.lock, and Ant and its pinned integration files are fetched and restored for you (see the Maven, Gradle and Ant references). Isolated Maven and Gradle builds on the base image are not supported yet. Request the isolated path explicitly with oyzu build --isolated, for example oyzu build --isolated --full for Gradle. The isolated worker restores the JDK locked in oyzu.lock since the image has none, and refuses a selected JDK older than 17 with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION.

Symptom Cause Fix Java lint and format-check need Checkstyle and google-java-format… --full without provisioned quality tools Provision them and set OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME, replace the tasks, or build without --full (above) Build fails with a JUnit failure and no jars in Outputs A test failed, and jars are never published from a failing build Fix the test. The Surefire output and log path are in the failure section A module fails its report requirement Test sources exist but no JUnit XML was produced (skipped tests, disabled reporting, or a custom report directory) Let the tests run, or move reports to the default directory. Custom report directories aren't collected on the native path Dependency or JaCoCo download fails Maven Central was throttled or unreachable. Coverage tooling is fetched by Maven or Gradle Retry. --offline builds need those artifacts already in the local repository TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION An isolated build selected a JDK below 17 Remove the low [tools] java pin. JDK 17 compiles older --release levels Ant build refused before any work No Docker, and Ant has no host build Start Docker (Oyzu pulls the execution image itself) Gradle refuses the daemon JDK vendor gradle-daemon-jvm.properties names a vendor other than Adoptium (isolated builds) Use Temurin, or provision a matching runtime yourself For anything else, start with the Log path in the failure section and Troubleshooting.

Outside isolated builds, Java quality tools aren't provisioned automatically. Private or custom Maven repositories and corporate credentials aren't supported. Dependencies come from Maven Central (and, for Gradle plugins, the Gradle plugin portal). Custom JaCoCo destinations, aggregate reactor coverage and custom test report directories aren't collected. Isolated Maven and Gradle builds on the base execution image are not supported yet. A green build shows that the stages passed on this source. It isn't a release approval.
Maven · Gradle · Ant · Java quality Java, Maven and Gradle installation · Native host builds · Version inference Recipes: Maven application · Maven reactor · Gradle application · Ant application

Oyzu finds Node packages and workspaces from package.json, the lockfile and your native configuration, so you don't need an Oyzu build file. It installs the Node version your project asks for, runs your build, tests, lint and format checks, and collects JUnit and LCOV reports and the packed or built output in a verified dist/ bundle. Note: The Node builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/node plugin. It supports npm, pnpm and Yarn (Classic 1.22.22 and Berry 4.17.1 with nodeLinker: node-modules), with different limits for each (see Limits). Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet.

Discovery reads files only. It never runs npm, project scripts or configuration code. Signal in your project What it decides package.json A Node target. Packages are discovered as node/app. Set uses: node/package in build.yaml to force package behavior package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock The package manager: npm, pnpm or Yarn packageManager in package.json The manager and, for an exact npm or pnpm release, the version to pin workspaces in package.json, or pnpm-workspace.yaml A workspace, built as one target scripts.build, scripts.test, scripts.lint, format-check or format:check The commands for those stages. Root scripts always win over Oyzu's defaults A node --test, Jest, Vitest or Mocha script, configuration or dependency The test framework, which decides how JUnit and coverage are collected eslint.config.*, .prettierrc*, biome.json The linter and formatter. ESLint and Prettier are the defaults, and biome.json selects Biome for both A vite build script A Vite application, whose dist/ output becomes a directory artifact engines.node A constraint every Node version Oyzu selects must satisfy When two equally strong signals disagree (for example two test frameworks), discovery fails and the error names the with: setting to add in build.yaml, such as with: {test-framework: mocha}. See discovery and selection.

The example is examples/builds/node-package from the Oyzu repository. Copy it to an empty folder and run git init. It's a package with a build script and node:test tests: { "name": "oyzu-example-package", "version": "0.1.0", "private": false, "type": "module", "scripts": { "build": "node build.mjs", "test": "node --test" }, "engines": { "node": ">=22" }, "files": ["dist"], "exports": "./dist/greeting.mjs" } oyzu run list shows what Oyzu will run: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · node/app (6) project:build Inferred · npm npm run build project:format Inferred · npm prettier --write . project:format-check Inferred · npm prettier --check . project:install Inferred · npm npm ci project:lint Inferred · npm eslint . project:test Inferred · npm npm run test oyzu run <task> runs one of these on your machine with your installed dependencies. oyzu build is different: it runs the same stages in an isolated, offline worker and records the results. oyzu build --plan lists every decision Oyzu made and why: $ oyzu build --planCopy Discovered Selection Reason formatter prettier default, no stronger evidence linter eslint default, no stronger evidence output-profile native-package default, no stronger evidence package-manager npm native package-lock.json lockfile test-framework node-test declared package.json /scripts/test Output shortened. A plain oyzu build runs only build. --full adds the checks: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building node-package windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Source captured 9 files · sha256:85ba8a7663bd <0.1s ✓ node toolchain 24.22.0 · verified against the lock 0.1s ✓ Version 0.1.0-dev.g2274557f5896 · 1 package 0.3s … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project version node -e // Writes the planned OYZ… executed 0.8s ✓ project prepare node /oyzu/npm.mjs install /depen… executed 1.5s ✓ project build npm run build executed 0.9s ! project test npm run test -- --experi… executed 1.1s · 1 warning ✓ project lint node /oyzu/node-quality.mjs lint executed 2.5s ✓ project format-check node /oyzu/node-quality.mjs forma… executed 1.0s ✓ project package npm pack --ignore-scripts --pack-… executed 1.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project 351 B development dist/project/linux/x86_64/oyzu-example-package-0.1.0-dev.g2274557f5896.tgz ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 100.0% (3/3 lines) ​ ✓ Build succeeded with warnings 1 target · 7 executed · 24.4s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 53932-1792554128072680700-1 Output shortened. In order: Prepare copied the 9 source files, selected Node 24.22.0 (the newest LTS release satisfying >=22), wrote it to oyzu.lock and computed the snapshot version. version wrote that version into a private copy of package.json. Your checkout is never edited. prepare installed the locked dependencies. Every later action runs offline from that install. build, test, lint and format-check ran the commands. Lint and format-check are read-only. package ran npm pack and put the archive in dist/, only because every gate passed. The warning came from the test run. Warnings never fail a build. Check the result with oyzu inspect dist: $ oyzu inspect distCopy ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded ​ Artifacts Path (under dist/) Kind Size Platform Digest project/linux/x86_64/ file 351 B linux/x86_64 sha256:1bad82c807ef oyzu-example-package-0.1.0-dev.g2274557f5896.tgz ​ Reports Report Path Status project:test project/linux/x86_64/reports/junit.xml collected project:coverage project/linux/x86_64/reports/coverage.lcov collected ​ Verified: every recorded file matches its digest. This does not show who produced the build or that it may be released. Output shortened. The platform is linux/x86_64: the build ran in a Linux worker even though the host is Windows. Commit oyzu.lock and keep dist/ out of version control.

The plan's Executor: line tells you. For most Node builds it's captured-worker: Oyzu copies your source, downloads the locked dependencies through its broker, then runs every action in a sandbox with no network. Windows and macOS need a running Docker engine for this. Linux uses Docker when an engine answers. Otherwise it uses the daemonless crun sandbox, which needs unprivileged user namespaces. --no-docker (or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1) forces crun. The build.isolation setting in oyzu.toml chooses between them; see configuration. Image. Every manager runs on the base execution image, which Oyzu pulls on first use. Node and npm, pnpm or Yarn come from oyzu.lock, and the pnpm and Yarn lockfile parsers ship in the Node plugin. To run on your own image instead, pass --image npm=<image> (or pnpm=, yarn=). Some applications build directly on your machine and need no Docker: npm and pnpm applications whose build writes the conventional dist/ directory (for example a Vite app), single-root Yarn applications, and explicitly declared single-root npm packages. Oyzu installs Node itself for these. See native host builds and Node applications.
