An npm workspace root is one target, and each member becomes its own versioned package. examples/builds/node-workspace has a private root and two members, @oyzu-example/shared and @oyzu-example/app, where app depends on shared: { "name": "oyzu-workspace", "version": "0.1.0", "private": true, "workspaces": ["packages/*"] } $ oyzu build --fullCopy ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project 367 B development dist/project/linux/x86_64/oyzu-example-shared-0.1.0-dev.gfe03e51cecc5.tgz project 346 B development dist/project/linux/x86_64/oyzu-example-app-0.1.0-dev.gfe03e51cecc5.tgz ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (2 collected reports) Coverage project: 100.0% (1/1 lines) Coverage project: 100.0% (1/1 lines) Output shortened. Each member got its own archive and its own JUnit and LCOV pair. Inside the archives, app's dependency on shared points at shared's snapshot version. The private root produced no package. How the work is divided: Stage Root script present No root script build Runs once with npm's lifecycle hooks Each member's build script, in dependency order test Runs once and owns one report pair Each member's script or detected test framework, with its own reports lint, format-check Runs once Root-owned files are checked by default. Each member uses its script or the default tool A failed member build stops its dependents. Test and quality failures continue through the other members so you see every problem, then fail the build. Every member needs a distinct package name and a real version (see member names). pnpm workspaces (pnpm-workspace.yaml with packages) and Yarn workspaces use the same planner with their own installation and packing. Their isolated builds use the same execution image. See npm workspaces, pnpm and Yarn.

You don't configure reporting. Oyzu instruments the detected framework and collects JUnit and LCOV for every package: Framework Detected from Notes Node's test runner A node --test script, or the default Oyzu passes Node 22 flags, so pin Node 22 or later when tests run Jest Script, configuration or dependency Jest 29 is supported Vitest Script, configuration or dependency Needs its matching coverage provider installed. Runs with one worker Mocha mocha script, .mocharc*, package.json section or dependency Mocha with c8 for coverage. See Mocha Reports land under dist/<target>/reports/, with digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. A failed test blocks packaging but keeps its reports. To get the same reports without a full build, run the tests directly on your machine: oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist This writes a test-only dist/ bundle from your installed dependencies. It packages nothing and doesn't isolate the run. See direct tests and workspace test bundles.

lint and format-check are build stages, selected by --full or a CI context. format writes files, so it's never part of a build. Run it yourself with oyzu run format. Tool Default version Behavior ESLint 10.11.0 Uses your configuration when present, recommended JS/TS rules otherwise. Never fixes Prettier 3.9.9 Uses your configuration, .editorconfig and ignore files Biome 2.5.15 Selected by biome.json or biome.jsonc for both roles A tool your project installs wins over the default. A tool you declare but haven't installed fails instead of silently using another version. The defaults check JavaScript and TypeScript sources only and skip node_modules, dist, build and coverage output. To pass your own flags, write a script ("lint": "eslint . --max-warnings 0"), because the defaults reject extra arguments. See Node quality.

oyzu build --plan ends each Node target with a Static analysis section. For each stage it lists the files the stage is predicted to read and write, the tools it needs and anything it couldn't bound, each with a confidence level and a file:line source. It parses files and runs no project code. An excerpt: $ oyzu build --planCopy project:build · confidence: over-approximate · scope: predicted 9 exact, 1 over-approximate, 0 unknown Reads Path or name Confidence Source Why package-lock.json exact package-lock.json lockfile package.json exact package.json manifest src/greeting.mjs exact build.mjs:3 file-read · copyFileSync Writes Path or name Confidence Source Why dist/greeting.mjs exact build.mjs:3 file-write · copyFileSync Narrow the view with --stage <name>, ask about one file with --why <path>, list only the uncertain facts with --unknown, or skip the analysis with --no-analysis. All of these need --plan. The analysis also runs rules that catch problems visible only across files: phantom-dependency, escaping-reference, undeclared-env, public-env-secret-name, exports-target-missing, lockfile-manifest-drift and others. They're advisory by default. oyzu build --check applies them without preparing or running anything: $ oyzu build --checkCopy ✓ Check passed: no blocking findings Static analysis only: nothing was installed, downloaded or executed. To make a rule fail builds, set its level in oyzu.toml: [analysis.rules] phantom-dependency = "enforce" # off | advisory (default) | enforce [[analysis.suppress]] rule = "escaping-reference" path = "legacy/**" reason = "vendored fork, tracked in the migration plan" Only a warning backed entirely by exact facts can block. See Node static analysis for every rule and its limits.

Native files come first. Oyzu reads them in this order: packageManager in package.json. An exact stable npm or pnpm release ("packageManager": "pnpm@10.20.0") becomes a tool requirement and is locked beside Node. A Corepack +sha512.… suffix is accepted and ignored. Ranges and tags select nothing. Yarn is pinned the same way with an exact yarn@1.22.22 or yarn@4.17.1; see managed Yarn. engines.node limits every Node selection. It doesn't pick one. No pin. The default is lts: the newest LTS release that satisfies every engine constraint, or the newest stable release if no LTS release does. In the run above, >=22 selected 24.22.0. oyzu.toml, to choose explicitly. It must agree with packageManager and satisfy engines.node: [tools] node = "22.12" npm = "11.6.2" # or pnpm = "10.20.0" .nvmrc and .node-version aren't read yet. Set [tools] node instead. The first build writes the exact choices to oyzu.lock, and later builds reuse them, including offline. oyzu pin --dry-run previews what would be locked, and oyzu install node@22.12 declares, locks and installs in one step. The isolated worker restores the locked Node and npm, pnpm or Yarn. The execution image has no copies of its own. See Manage your first tool, Node selection and npm and pnpm installation.
documents.s: Pin Node and the package manager

documents.t: Project Artifact Package (npm, pnpm, Yarn) An npm pack-style .tgz named <name>-<version>-dev.g<source>.tgz. The embedded package.json carries the same version Workspace One .tgz per member, plus one for a publishable (non-private) root node/app with Vite or a dist/ build script A directory artifact application-<version> holding the built output. A configured Vite build also records the resolved output metadata Versions come from your version field, Git tags and commits; see version inference. Artifacts appear only when every required stage passed. Creating an artifact never publishes it.

A test fails. If you change the greeting in the example and rebuild, the other checks still run so you see every problem, but package is blocked because no artifact comes from a failing build: $ oyzu build --fullCopy ✗ project test npm run test -- --experi… failed 1.5s · 1 warning ✓ project lint node /oyzu/node-quality.mjs lint executed 4.3s ✓ project format-check node /oyzu/node-quality.mjs forma… executed 1.1s ⊘ project package needs project · test ​ ── Failure: project · test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── actual: 'Hi, world!', expected: 'Hello, world!', Exit 1 Log dist/logs/0003.stderr Next oyzu build project re-run only this target ​ ✗ Build failed 1 failed · 1 blocked · 5 succeeded · 17.8s Output shortened. The exit status is 1, and the full log is at the path shown. Symptom Cause Fix NPM_WORKSPACE_MEMBER_NAMES Two members (or a publishable root and a member) share a package name, or a member's version is latest Rename them so each name is used once, or mark the root "private": true. Give each member a real semver version. "private": true on a member doesn't exclude it. See member names npm, pnpm or Yarn rejects the lock during preparation The lockfile no longer matches package.json Regenerate the lock with your package manager, commit it and rebuild. The lockfile-manifest-drift rule in --plan often shows the exact entry pnpm capture does not yet support configuration <key> in <file> A pnpm setting outside the supported list, such as hoistPattern or nodeLinker. .npmrc and .pnpmfile.cjs aren't supported either Remove the setting. catalog, catalogs, overrides, patchedDependencies, minimumReleaseAge, allowBuilds and trustPolicy are supported. See pnpm workspace settings Yarn capture does not yet support <file> setting <key> A setting outside the supported subset. .yarnrc.yml is Yarn Berry configuration Use a supported Yarn Classic setting, or use a Berry project that meets the Berry limits. There is no automatic PnP conversion Lint fails with a missing tool Your package.json declares ESLint, Prettier or Biome but it isn't installed Install the project's dependencies with its package manager and retry Discovery fails on conflicting evidence Two linters, formatters or test frameworks claim the same role Remove one configuration, or select one in build.yaml with with: {linter: <name>}, with: {formatter: <name>} or with: {test-framework: <name>} Test stage fails with bad option Node is pinned below 22, and Oyzu's reporting passes Node 22 flags Pin Node 22 or later NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON (exit 3) No Docker engine for the isolated worker Start Docker. On Linux, use the crun sandbox NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES (exit 3) crun can't create user namespaces on this Linux host Allow unprivileged user namespaces, or use a host with Docker TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE An organization catalog has no LTS markers for the lts default Pin an approved exact version or a named line such as lts/krypton For anything else, start with the Log path in the failure section and Troubleshooting.

Yarn Berry support is for exact 4.17.1 with a literal nodeLinker: node-modules. Single-root applications work natively and in the isolated executor. Workspace packages work natively only (publishable root, app and shared members, or a named private root). Pack hooks are limited to analyzed local copy and helper scripts. PnP, aggregates, project plugins, yarnPath and custom or non-registry sources aren't supported. Yarn Classic 1.22.22 supports single-root applications natively and in the isolated executor. Classic workspace packages work natively only, with a private root and members. Project plugins, custom registries and extra rc settings aren't supported. pnpm isolated builds support pnpm 10.11.0. Vite builds need one written Vite 8 client environment. SSR, library, watch, multiple-environment and no-write modes fail with an explicit message. npm TypeScript workspaces work natively on Linux (x86-64) with a literal tsc -p tsconfig.json and noEmitOnError. .nvmrc and .node-version aren't read. Cyclic workspace graphs, affected selection inside a workspace and member task groups aren't supported. Default lint and formatting cover JavaScript and TypeScript only, not JSON, CSS or other files. A green build shows that the stages passed on this source. It isn't a release approval.

Oyzu builds Python distributions from pyproject.toml, uv.lock, poetry.lock or requirements.txt. It selects and installs CPython for you, builds wheels with your own backend, runs pytest with JUnit and Cobertura coverage, and checks your code with Ruff. You don't write an Oyzu build file for a package. Note: The Python builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/python plugin. If no release of it is available to your installation, the build stops with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet. Which of two paths your project takes matters: Native (on your machine): pip projects with a pyproject.toml. Oyzu installs CPython and builds a wheel. No Docker. Isolated (in a Linux container): uv, Poetry, requirements-only and legacy projects, and anything you request with --isolated. Dependencies are downloaded first, and every action runs offline. This needs Docker and the base execution image, with CPython in oyzu.lock. uv and Poetry builds also need an image of your own with that manager installed, passed with --image uv=<ref> or --image poetry=<ref>.

Signal in your project What it decides pyproject.toml with [build-system] A python/package target built with pip through your declared PEP 517 backend uv.lock uv manages the project, and the lock's hashed export owns the dependency set poetry.lock Poetry manages the project requirements.txt only A requirements-only application, with no invented distribution metadata uses: python/app in build.yaml with one [project.scripts] entry An application. The isolated path also produces a runnable .pyz requires-python A constraint every selected CPython must satisfy .python-version The default CPython request pytest.ini, [tool.pytest.ini_options], [pytest] in tox.ini, [tool:pytest] in setup.cfg pytest configuration (pytest is the default either way) Discovery reads files only. It never imports conftest.py, runs Python or collects tests.

The example is examples/builds/python-api from the Oyzu repository. Copy it to an empty folder and run git init. It's a small setuptools project with one console script and two unittest tests that pytest runs: [project] name = "oyzu-api-example" version = "0.1.0" requires-python = ">=3.10" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] oyzu-example-api = "api:main" [build-system] requires = ["setuptools==80.9.0"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" Its build.yaml contains only uses: python/app for the api target. $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 5 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command api · python/app (5) api:build Inferred · pip python -m build api:format Inferred · pip ruff format . api:format-check Inferred · pip ruff format --check . api:lint Inferred · pip ruff check . --no-fix api:test Inferred · pip python -m pytest oyzu build --plan shows Executor: host, which means the native pip path. The only tool requirement is CPython, constrained by requires-python: $ oyzu build --planCopy Discovered Selection Reason formatter ruff default, no stronger evidence linter ruff default, no stronger evidence package-manager pip default, no stronger evidence test-framework pytest default, no stronger evidence ​ Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:python minimum-version >=3.10.0 api pyproject.toml project.requires-python Output shortened. Now build: $ oyzu buildCopy Building python-api windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · fast ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 0 installed now 0.2s python 3.15.0 already installed detected from pyproject.toml … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ api build python -m pip wheel --no-deps --wheel-dir \\… executed 16.7s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── api dist/api/windows/x86_64/wheels-0.1.0 1.8 KB development Checks not requested api: format-check, lint, test ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 1 executed · 19.5s Output shortened. Look at the selected interpreter: CPython 3.15.0. With only requires-python = ">=3.10" and no pin, Oyzu picks the newest stable CPython, which can be a very recent release. Pin a version for predictable builds (below). pip then ran its PEP 517 wheel build, downloading the setuptools backend from the package index, and the wheel was published as the directory artifact wheels-0.1.0. The native path produces a wheel only. It doesn't assemble the runnable .pyz application. That's part of the isolated path.
documents.s: Your first build: a pip project

documents.t: oyzu build --full adds test (pytest) and lint and format-check (Ruff). On the native path, Oyzu doesn't install pytest, pytest-cov or Ruff for you, so on a fresh machine the checks fail: $ oyzu build --fullCopy ── Failure: api · test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytest' Exit 1 Log dist/logs/0001.stderr Next oyzu build api re-run only this target ​ ── Failure: api · lint ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── cannot execute ruff: program not found ​ ✗ Build failed 3 failed · 1 succeeded · 13.2s Note Local binaries were not updated; existing binaries are from the previous successful build. Output shortened. The wheel built, but required test evidence is missing, so the build fails and Oyzu keeps the previous good outputs. To fix this, create a .venv in the target folder from the Python Oyzu selected, install your dependencies, pytest, pytest-cov, coverage and your quality tools into it, and build again: oyzu exec -- python -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install pytest pytest-cov coverage ruff # .venv\Scripts\python on Windows # also install your project's own dependencies the usual way oyzu build --full Oyzu checks that the .venv was made from exactly the Python it selected. A .venv made from another Python, or with system site packages, is refused: recreate it from the selected base. Activation, VIRTUAL_ENV and PYTHONPATH don't select the environment. You can also replace a stage's command in oyzu.toml with [tasks.lint] and similar. A replacement test task must still produce the JUnit and coverage reports. See native preparation.
documents.s: Tests and checks on the native path

documents.t: uv, Poetry and requirements-only projects use the isolated executor. The example is examples/builds/python-uv-library: a setuptools package with a committed uv.lock and a dev dependency group that holds pytest and pytest-cov. $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · python/package (6) project:build Inferred · uv uv build project:format Inferred · uv ruff format . project:format-check Inferred · uv ruff format --check . project:install Inferred · uv uv sync --locked project:lint Inferred · uv ruff check . --no-fix project:test Inferred · uv uv run --locked pytest oyzu build --plan shows Docker engine required. The isolated Python path runs on the base execution image with the locked CPython 3.12. uv and Poetry aren't restored from the lock yet, so those projects need --image uv=<ref> or --image poetry=<ref> (Python applications). Image names in the output below may differ from what your version prints. $ oyzu build --planCopy project · python/package · unresolved until executor selection Executor: captured-worker Placement: runs on any platform · Docker engine required · Isolated steps run in the captured worker on a Docker engine Discovered Selection Reason package-manager uv native uv.lock lockfile test-framework pytest default, no stronger evidence Output shortened. A full build goes through these stages: prepare downloads binary wheels for the uv export --locked closure, the build backend and the test and quality tools, through Oyzu's broker to public PyPI. Each wheel's digest is recorded. build runs the backend once in a private workspace, with a PEP 440 snapshot version of the form 0.1.0.dev0+g<source>. Your pyproject.toml isn't edited. test installs the built wheel offline and runs pytest against it, so coverage measures the installed package, not your checkout. lint and format-check run Ruff read-only. package publishes the wheel and source distribution once every gate has passed. The example folder contains a .python-version file with 3.12. Without it, requires-python = ">=3.10" selects the newest CPython, and prepare fails with coverage-… is not a supported wheel on this platform, because the lock holds wheels built for Python 3.12. See Choose the Python version.
documents.s: Your first build: a uv project (isolated)

documents.t: pytest is the supported runner, and it also runs unittest.TestCase suites, as in the pip example. Oyzu records JUnit and Cobertura for every build and stores them under dist/, with digests in dist/manifest.json. You don't configure reporting. Manager Development command (oyzu run test) pip python -m pytest uv uv run --locked pytest Poetry poetry run pytest oyzu run test runs on your machine with your installed environment and writes a test-only dist/ bundle. Pass pytest arguments after --, as in oyzu run test -- -k health. pytest, pytest-cov and coverage must already be installed there, because Oyzu doesn't install them for development tasks. pytest owns test collection: testpaths, file patterns, markers and conftest behavior. Your coverage settings, including fail_under, are kept. Expect this behavior: An empty suite keeps pytest's exit code 5 and fails the build. Add tests or fix collection, because an empty directory isn't a passing result. A failed coverage threshold fails the build even when every test passed. Assertion failures keep their reports and block packaging. See Python testing.

Ruff runs ruff check . --no-fix for lint and ruff format --check . for format-check, reading its own configuration as usual. Both are selected by --full or a CI context and never modify files during a build. oyzu run format runs ruff format . and does write files. In the isolated path Ruff is downloaded during preparation. On the native path it must already be installed, as shown above.

Oyzu picks the version in this order: an explicit oyzu.toml request, then .python-version, always constrained by requires-python, and finally the newest stable CPython. Source Role [tools] python in oyzu.toml The request, when present .python-version (one release such as 3.12 or 3.12.4) The default request requires-python in pyproject.toml A constraint every selection must satisfy None of these The greatest stable release available Set it in oyzu.toml: [tools] python = "3.12" # latest 3.12.x; ranges such as ">=3.11 <3.14" also work Run oyzu pin --dry-run to preview the choice, or oyzu pin to write oyzu.lock (the next oyzu build also does it). Commit the lock. Pre-releases, free-threaded and debug builds are never selected. A requires-python specifier that uses !=, === or pre-release versions can't be turned into a tool range and fails with the specifier named. Set [tools] python instead. Interpreters come from Python Build Standalone for Linux (amd64, arm64), macOS (arm64, amd64) and Windows (amd64), checked against the publisher's checksum manifest. oyzu exec -- python --version runs the locked interpreter, and pip runs it with -m pip. Oyzu doesn't provision uv or Poetry; the isolated images bring their own. Isolated builds use Python 3.12 regardless of this selection. On Intel macOS you can install Python 3.11 and run pip with it, but wheel builds there aren't supported yet. See Python installation.

Project Artifacts pip with pyproject.toml (native) A wheels-<version> directory holding the built wheel Package (isolated) Wheel and source distribution, named with the PEP 440 snapshot version such as 0.1.0.dev0+g<source> python/app (isolated) Wheel, source distribution and a runnable <target>-<version>.pyz containing the wheel's files and runtime dependencies Requirements-only application (isolated) A .pyz built from app.py or __main__.py, versioned 0.0.0-dev.g<source> Versions come from your static version, Git tags and Conventional Commits; see version inference. A .pyz needs a compatible Python to run, requires pure-Python wheels, and isn't a release approval.

Symptom Cause Fix No module named 'pytest' or cannot execute ruff: program not found in a native --full build The native path doesn't install test or quality tools Create the .venv described above Wheel build fails on Windows with [WinError 3] The system cannot find the path specified under build\bdist.win-amd64 The project is in a very deeply nested folder Move the checkout to a shorter path The build picked a brand-new CPython Nothing pins Python, so the newest stable release wins Add .python-version or [tools] python Poetry lock is missing or stale; update it with poetry lock poetry.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml Run poetry lock and commit the result Direct URL requirements need an approved source adapter A dependency points at a URL or Git source outside uv.lock Use a registry release, or a public GitHub Git source locked by full commit in uv.lock Source package NAME needs build requirement maturin... A dependency must be built from Rust source Not supported. Use a project or version that publishes wheels Dependency group NAME is not defined A [dependency-groups] include names a group that doesn't exist Fix the include. Only the dev group is selected The build fails with no tests run pytest collected nothing (exit 5) Check testpaths and file patterns. Run the manager's test command to see collection --offline build fails fetching the build backend pip downloads the backend during the wheel build Build once online so pip has the backend cached NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON or a missing image The isolated path needs Docker, the execution image and, for uv or Poetry, an image of your own Start Docker, make sure the execution image is available, and pass --image uv=<ref> or --image poetry=<ref> The full list of preparation errors is in Python preparation. For anything else, start with the Log path in the failure section and Troubleshooting.

The native path covers pip projects with pyproject.toml and produces wheels only. The isolated path needs Docker and the base execution image (plus your own image for uv and Poetry) and runs Python 3.12 only. Private package indexes aren't supported. Dependencies come from public PyPI. On a Windows host, the package stage of isolated builds failed in earlier testing (No such file or directory or environment variable not found), so the wheel and source distribution weren't exported there. The checks before it ran normally. Source builds of Git, sdist-only and local dependencies work only for uv projects. Poetry and pip Git or path sources are refused. Only the dev dependency group is selected. A green build shows that the stages passed on this source. It isn't a release approval.

Point oyzu build at a folder with a Cargo.toml and it compiles with Cargo, runs your tests with coverage, checks Clippy and rustfmt, and writes a verified dist/ bundle. You don't write any Oyzu configuration for a normal Cargo project. Note: The Rust builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/rust plugin, which Oyzu selects and records in oyzu.lock. If no release of it is available to your installation, the build stops with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet. The Rust reference has the full details.

Oyzu treats any folder with a Cargo.toml as a Rust target. It reads manifests without running Cargo or any of your code. Project Target A single package, binary or library One rust/app target A Cargo workspace ([workspace] in the root manifest) One rust/app target for the whole workspace. Cargo decides the members The target delivers every enabled binary. A package that is publishable also gets a .crate archive when you build in the isolated executor. A library-only package gets its .crate and no executable. You need a checked-in Cargo.lock, because Oyzu runs Cargo with --locked and a stale lock fails instead of being rewritten. oyzu run list shows the tasks Oyzu infers. They are plain Cargo commands: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 8 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · rust/app (8) project:archive Inferred · cargo cargo package --workspace --locked --offline project:build Inferred · cargo cargo build --locked --workspace project:fetch Inferred · cargo cargo fetch --locked project:format Inferred · cargo cargo fmt --all project:format-check Inferred · cargo cargo fmt --all --check project:install Inferred · cargo cargo install --path . --locked project:lint Inferred · cargo cargo clippy --locked --workspace -- -D warnings project:test Inferred · cargo cargo test --locked --workspace oyzu run <task> runs one on your machine. build, test, lint and format-check are also the stages of oyzu build. format edits your source and is never part of a build. fetch and install are development tasks only, and oyzu run install -- --root <dir> passes its arguments to cargo install.

Command What runs oyzu build --plan Nothing. Shows the stages and the tools Oyzu read from your files oyzu build Compiles the workspace and collects the binaries. Checks are skipped locally oyzu build --full Also runs tests with coverage, doctests, Clippy and cargo fmt --check oyzu build --isolated The same build in a Linux container (needs Docker; see Isolated builds) In CI the checks run without --full. See build selection and checks. Tests run through cargo llvm-cov nextest, so the test stage needs cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov and the llvm-tools-preview Rust component. Oyzu pins and installs the first two for you. Doctests run in the same stage, because nextest doesn't run them.

Oyzu reads the files Rust developers already use, in this order: rust-toolchain.toml (or the older rust-toolchain file). Everything rustup accepts is read, including components. A channel such as 1.99.1 is an exact pin. package.rust-version in Cargo.toml is a minimum. [tools] rust = "…" in oyzu.toml, only when you have no native file or want a different value in one folder. A native pin file wins over a farther oyzu.toml. With none of these, Oyzu locks the newest stable Rust on the first build. Either way the exact choice goes in oyzu.lock, so commit it. After you change a pin, run oyzu pin to update the lock and oyzu install to download what it names. oyzu pin --dry-run previews the change. The Tools row of every build says which compiler ran and why, for example rust 1.99.1 already installed compilation (detected from rust-toolchain.toml). You never install Rust yourself. You do need the platform's linker: on Windows, Microsoft Build Tools with the Windows SDK (MSVC) or LLVM-MinGW; on Linux, the system C toolchain. Oyzu checks the linker with a tiny test build before compiling.

A successful build writes one dist/ bundle. The Outputs section prints each artifact's path, and manifest.json records it with its digest. The bundle layout describes the directories. Output Contents <binary>[.exe] Each enabled Cargo binary <package>-<version>.crate Crate archive for each publishable package (isolated builds) reports/junit.xml Test results from nextest (with --full or in CI) reports/coverage.xml Line coverage in Cobertura format reports/doctest.xml One case per package that has doctests manifest.json Every file with its digest, plus the plan and build evidence Packages with publish = false get no .crate, but their binaries are still delivered. A binary that needs required-features is delivered only when that feature is enabled. Versions are snapshots from your declared version and Git, such as 1.2.3-dev.g<source>. A snapshot isn't a release; see version inference.

You need a build.yaml only to change something Cargo can't express. The Rust builder accepts two options under with: Option Values Default Meaning features List of Cargo feature names none (default features stay on) Applied to build, test, lint, doctests and packaging artifacts all, binaries all binaries delivers only enabled binaries and skips crate packaging builds: greeting: uses: rust/app with: features: [loud] Unknown with keys are refused. To build for other platforms, declare platforms on the build; see cross-compiling.

In a workspace you can make chosen packages share one version number, using the same release metadata cargo-release reads. Oyzu only reads it and never runs cargo-release. shared-version = true joins the workspace's shared group. A string such as "suite" joins that named group. false leaves a group. Matching version strings, or version.workspace = true alone, don't group packages. tag-prefix sets the Git tag namespace used to find each group's last release, for example suite/. # Workspace root Cargo.toml [workspace.metadata.release] shared-version = "suite" tag-prefix = "suite/" # A package that versions on its own [package.metadata.release] shared-version = false tag-prefix = "helper/" Every member of a group must have the same native version and tag mapping. Private or unselected members count too. Conflicting versions or overlapping tag namespaces make the build fail. This applies to Cargo workspaces only. The Rust reference lists every inheritance rule and refusal.
documents.s: Keep selected packages on one version

documents.t: This is a tiny binary crate with one unit test, from examples/builds/rust-app/project in the Oyzu repository. Create these files in a new folder and run git init there. Cargo.toml: [package] name = "oyzu-greeting-example" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2021" Cargo.lock: version = 3 [[package]] name = "oyzu-greeting-example" version = "0.1.0" src/main.rs: fn greeting(name: &str) -> String { format!("Hello, {name}!") } fn main() { println!("{}", greeting("Oyzu")); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn greets() { assert_eq!(greeting("Oyzu"), "Hello, Oyzu!"); } } rust-toolchain.toml: [toolchain] channel = "1.99.1" components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"] Run oyzu build for a fast build. The first build also writes oyzu.lock, which you should commit. The binary is under dist/: $ dist/project/windows/x86_64/oyzu-greeting-example.exeCopy Hello, Oyzu!

The first build locks only what a fast build needs. If you then ask for --full, Oyzu names the missing lock entry instead of guessing: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building rust-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✗ Tools failed: preparation did not complete <0.1s ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: cargo:cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1; run oyzu pin Next: Run oyzu pin --refresh to refresh the lock, then oyzu install. Run oyzu pin to lock every tool the project's builds can need, including the test-stage tools, then build again: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building rust-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tools 3 tools pinned · 0 installed now 1.7s cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 already installed coverage, if enabled cargo-nextest 0.9.146 already installed testing, if enabled rust 1.99.1 already installed compilation (detected from rust-toolchain.toml) … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build rust/app build-host executed 0.6s ✓ project test rust/app test executed 2.1s ✓ project lint cargo clippy --locked --workspace… executed 0.4s ✓ project format-check cargo fmt --all --check executed 0.2s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/oyzu-greeting-example.exe 143.9 KB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 66.7% (6/9 lines) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 7.1s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 53896-1792554065729458000-1 Output shortened. Running the same command again without changes reuses every stage and labels it reused from an earlier run, not run now.

$ oyzu inspect distCopy ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded ​ Actions Action Status Exit Gate project:build succeeded 0 required project:test succeeded 0 required project:lint succeeded 0 required project:format-check succeeded 0 required ​ Reports Report Path Status project:test project/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml collected project:coverage project/windows/x86_64/reports/coverage.xml collected ​ Verified: every recorded file matches its digest. This does not show who produced the build or that it may be released. Output shortened.

oyzu build --isolated runs the same stages in a Linux container with no network. Oyzu first downloads every locked crates.io dependency and checks each archive against the SHA-256 in Cargo.lock, then builds offline. Isolated builds also package publishable crates with cargo package and verify them. You need Docker and the base execution image, which Oyzu pulls on first use. Rust and its test tools come from oyzu.lock, and cross builds fetch pinned linkers. See the isolated-build image.

You see Cause Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE: cargo:cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1; run oyzu pin (exit 4) oyzu.lock came from a fast build and lacks the test-stage tools, or a pin changed Run oyzu pin, commit oyzu.lock, build again COMMAND_FAILED: provision llvm-tools-preview before Rust tests: missing llvm-cov The Rust installation used for tests has no llvm-cov Set LLVM_COV and LLVM_PROFDATA to the tools from a toolchain with the llvm-tools-preview component (under lib/rustlib/<host>/bin), or delete oyzu.lock, run oyzu pin and rebuild LINK : fatal error LNK1104: cannot open file '…\linker-arguments' (Windows) The project path is too long for the MSVC linker. Compiler state lives under .oyzu/native/rust/ in the project Move the project to a shorter path invalid Rust with options: unknown field … A with key the Rust builder doesn't accept Use features or artifacts, or remove the key A test fails The Cargo test failed The failure section names the test, the log under dist/logs/ and the command to rerun one target. The previous good binaries are kept Formatting and Clippy findings are build gates too. Fix them with oyzu run format and oyzu run lint, then rebuild.

Private or alternate registries, private Git dependencies and credentials aren't supported. Locked crates.io dependencies and public GitHub sources pinned to a full commit are. Coverage is line coverage from nextest. Doctests aren't measured, and the doctest report counts packages, not individual examples. Isolated builds need Docker and the base execution image.
Rust reference Native local builds Tool commands: pin, install and tools Build bundles Capabilities and known limitations

Use the zig/project plugin to build a Zig project with its own build.zig and collect what the build installs: programs, libraries and resources. Zig keeps full control of the build graph. Oyzu selects the compiler, runs zig build with a private install prefix and caches, and records the installed files in a verified dist/ bundle. Note: The Zig builder is experimental. The plugin isn't in a released CLI or plugin catalog yet, so you build it from the Oyzu source and bind it in your user configuration (see Set it up). It works with Zig 0.15.2. Native builds work on Intel macOS (x86-64). Isolated builds work on Linux (x86-64, GNU). Windows and macOS on Apple silicon aren't supported yet. The Zig reference has the full details.

Oyzu doesn't detect Zig projects automatically. Declare the build in build.yaml beside your build.zig: builds: hello: uses: zig/project Choose the compiler in oyzu.toml: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" Build the plugin from the Oyzu source and bind its absolute path in a user configuration file: oyzu exec -- cargo build --locked -p oyzu-plugin-zig --features plugin # User configuration, not the project [plugins.development] "zig/project" = "/absolute/oyzu/target/debug/oyzu-plugin-zig" Set OYZU_USER_CONFIG to that file's absolute path, then run oyzu build in your project. See local plugin bindings.

oyzu build runs: zig build --prefix <output>/install --cache-dir <output>/cache --global-cache-dir <output>/global-cache Oyzu collects the install directory as the build's artifact and keeps both Zig caches out of it. The path of the collected files is in dist/manifest.json (for example hello/darwin/x86_64/install), so run your program from there: install/bin/hello. Discovery never evaluates build.zig or downloads anything. Oyzu reads build.zig.zon for the package identity, the compiler minimum and the declared dependencies. .minimum_zig_version limits which compiler Oyzu selects. It doesn't pin one. Task Command Notes build zig build Installs into the private prefix test zig build test Runs the native step, but Oyzu collects no test report from it format zig fmt . Rewrites files. Never part of a build format-check zig fmt --check . Native format check If you replace the build task in oyzu.toml, your command runs exactly as written. It must produce the install directory itself and doesn't get the options below.

Put these under with in the build: Option Values Default Meaning steps 1 to 16 step names (letters, digits, _, -; start with a letter; up to 64 characters) the native default install Run these build.zig steps. Flags, paths and shell text are refused definitions Map of up to 16 option names to strings, booleans or integers none Each entry becomes one -Dname=value argument. Compiler, target, cache and fetch options are reserved and refused install-format directory, tar.gz directory tar.gz packs the install tree into one install.tar.gz, keeping relative links and executable bits String values can be up to 1,024 bytes with no control characters. All arguments together are limited to 4,096 bytes. Values are never evaluated by a shell. Other option names are passed to your build.zig, and its failures show up normally. You can keep build.zig and a tracked dist/ folder in place and send Oyzu's own bundle elsewhere: # oyzu.toml [tools] zig = "0.15.2" [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" # build.yaml builds: ghostty: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: steps: [lib-vt] install-format: tar.gz inputs: [dist] adds your tracked dist folder as a source input. oyzu inspect then reads .oyzu/bundle by default. See bundle placement. definitions selects project options the same way, for example definitions: {xcframework-target: native}.

Declared packages in build.zig.zon (URL, transitive, path and lazy dependencies) are prepared before build.zig runs. Oyzu downloads each archive through its scoped broker, checks it against the native package hash, and gives Zig only local files through --system. Native macOS (Intel). Preparation needs network access on every invocation. It supports archives and GitHub repositories pinned to a full 40-character commit, within size and metadata limits. Nested Xcode projects are limited to the exact Xcode and Swift versions in the reference. Isolated Linux (x86-64, GNU). The build runs with no network, -j1 and the install prefix described above. After one online build, the prepared packages let an offline build reuse them. This path needs a plugin package that includes the Linux build, so a single local binding isn't enough. See the reference. Native host builds that declare dependencies are refused unless they take one of these paths.

If your build.zig runs other tools, such as Pandoc for documentation, pin them in oyzu.toml next to the compiler. Pins apply to every build in that folder. The compiler stays first on PATH, and the other tools follow. [tools] zig = "0.15.2" "github:jgm/pandoc" = "3.12.1" oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 oyzu pin 'github:jgm/pandoc@3.12.1' oyzu install --frozen oyzu build --isolated Pandoc 3.12.1 works on Linux (x86-64, GNU). Oyzu accepts complete publisher tar.gz and tar.xz packages whose commands match their file names. Archives that need an interpreter, command aliases or missing executables are refused. Offline builds need the publisher archives cached by an earlier online build. The tools run during the build and aren't part of the collected install tree. See native documentation installation tree.

The isolated build reserves 4,096 MiB of memory plus virtual machine overhead. The default Docker Desktop memory limit is too small, so raise it (6 GiB worked on an 8 GiB Mac) and keep at least 2 GiB of free disk.

You see Cause Fix Metadata error with a file, line and column Invalid build.zig.zon (duplicate field, expression or unsupported escape) Fix it at the reported location A build that installs nothing fails artifact collection build.zig installs nothing Add an install step, or select the right steps Refusal about a required test report A selected check needs a native test report, which Zig builds don't produce Build without the check Dependency or hash refusal An archive doesn't match its package hash, or the source form isn't supported Correct the hash, or use a supported source Options refused next to a build task replacement with options need the standard build command Remove the replacement or the options Native failures from build.zig are passed through as they are. A failed build never produces a successful artifact.

Zig test reports and coverage aren't collected. A required test check is refused with an explanation. Only Zig 0.15.2 is supported. Other compiler versions and other platforms are not supported yet. Isolated builds need Docker, a plugin package that includes the Linux build and the memory above. Native macOS dependency preparation needs the network each time. There is no offline reuse. Git dependencies other than a full-commit GitHub repository are refused. Native dependency packages can't contain links other than a direct link to a sibling regular file. An install tree with links fails the directory format. Use install-format: tar.gz, which keeps links that stay inside the tree.

use std::{env,fs,path::PathBuf}; fn main() { println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=../channel.txt"); let channel=fs::read_to_string("../channel.txt").unwrap(); let generated=format!("pub const CHANNEL: &str = {:?};",channel.trim()); fs::write(PathBuf::from(env::var_os("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("channel.rs"),generated).unwrap(); }

Change channel.txt to preview, rebuild, inspect the new bundle, and run its delivered executable: expect Release channel: preview. oyzu install --frozen oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Read each exact regular-file artifact path, digest and output ID from the manifest. The selectors below illustrate the reactor's named outputs; use the exact IDs in your inspected bundle. <project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"><modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion><groupId>example</groupId><artifactId>reactor</artifactId><version>0.1.0</version><packaging>pom</packaging><modules><module>shared</module><module>app</module></modules><properties><maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release><project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding></properties></project>

Use independently accepted provenance and signing roots. The local verification harness is an explicit test builder: it observes a real build, signs those observations before publishing, and clearly makes no protected-origin, keyless, transparency or SLSA-level claim. It cannot attest an earlier unobserved build. Production acceptance and managed controls remain separate. [publish.destinations.local] kind = "oci" registry = "http://127.0.0.1:26111" repository = "examples/files" artifacts = ["APPLICATION_OUTPUT_ID", "LIBRARY_OUTPUT_ID"] [publish.destinations.github] kind = "github-release" apiUrl = "https://api.github.com" repository = "your-owner/your-disposable-repository" tag = "your-preexisting-test-tag" tokenEnv = "EXAMPLES_GITHUB_TOKEN" artifacts = ["APPLICATION_OUTPUT_ID"] [publish.destinations.github.evidence] mode = "destination" [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."APPLICATION_OUTPUT_ID"] bundlePath = "application.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted builder public key>" builderId = "<accepted exact builder identity>" [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."LIBRARY_OUTPUT_ID"] bundlePath = "library.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted builder public key>" builderId = "<accepted exact builder identity>" [publish.requirements.signing] keyEnv = "PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED" publicKey = "<matching publication public key>" Replace APPLICATION_OUTPUT_ID and LIBRARY_OUTPUT_ID with the exact target/name selectors from the inspected manifest. This is illustrative configuration requiring real evidence and roots. Keep it in the normal configuration owner; destination maps replace atomically across the cascade. Secret settings are environment references. Required managed controls still apply. The Rust build guide walks through a Cargo application with real output: discovery, toolchain pinning, oyzu build --full, the output bundle and common failures. For more projects, use the first build recipe and the catalog for workspaces, features and generated sources. The Rust reference covers every Rust builder setting.

Oyzu builds, tests and runs tasks for your existing projects using the conventions they already follow. It installs the exact compilers and runtimes each project needs, so the same project builds the same way on every machine. You need no account and no configuration file to start. Early release Oyzu is in early development. Support varies by ecosystem and platform; check what works today before you rely on a particular combination.

Install Oyzu. It is one executable. Follow the tutorial to build, test, inspect, rebuild and debug a small Go program, or use the four-command version on your own project. Manage your tools: lock exact versions for your whole team. Read your build results: what ran, what was reused and what was recorded.

Run these from your project root: oyzu discover # what Oyzu found: targets, builders and tasks oyzu run list # the tasks it found and the native command each runs oyzu build --plan # preview the build; runs and downloads nothing oyzu build # fast local build oyzu build --full # build plus tests, lint and format checks oyzu history # past builds

No configuration to start. Oyzu reads Cargo.toml, go.mod, package.json, pom.xml, pyproject.toml and other native files. You add a small build.yaml only for the exceptions. The same tools everywhere. Exact tool versions are recorded in oyzu.lock, checked against their published digests when installed, and used the same way on every machine and in CI. Clear results. Output says what ran now and what was reused from an earlier build. Reused test results are never shown as a fresh run. One interface for every ecosystem. Rust, Go, Node, Java, Python, .NET, Docker and Helm builds use the same commands and produce the same kind of output bundle.

Guides for everyday workflows: adopting Oyzu in a repository, CI, monorepos, caching. CLI reference for every command and flag. Concepts to understand how a build is planned and run. Known limitations before you commit to Oyzu for a project.

Run these four commands from the root of an existing Rust, Go, Node, Java, Python, .NET, Docker or Helm project. You don't need a configuration file. For a step-by-step walkthrough with full output, see the tutorial. oyzu discover # 1. what Oyzu found oyzu build --plan # 2. what a build would do oyzu build --full # 3. build, test, lint and format-check oyzu inspect dist # 4. check the output

$ oyzu discoverCopy 1 target · 6 tasks discovered without running project code Project root: ~/hello ​ project · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location . Manager go Version 0.0.0 Part of builds build, format-check, lint, test Development tasks format, install ​ Target names are what `oyzu build <target>` accepts. Next steps: oyzu run list every task and the command it runs oyzu build --plan preview the build stages without running them Use --json for the complete discovery record, including each task's environment and dependencies. Oyzu reads your native files (Cargo.toml, go.mod, package.json, pom.xml, pyproject.toml and so on) and lists each target (a buildable unit, here project), the builder that handles it and its tasks. It runs none of your code to do this. oyzu run list shows the exact command behind each task.
oyzu build --plan shows which stages run for each target (build, test, lint, format check) and which tool versions they need. It installs, downloads and runs nothing.

oyzu build # fast local build: build stages only oyzu build --full # also run tests, lint and format checks The first build picks tool versions, writes them to oyzu.lock and downloads any tools that are missing. The output has the same sections every time: Prepare, Plan, Build (one row per action) and Outputs, then a result line. A failed action gets its own section with the error, the exit code, the log file and a command to re-run just that target. oyzu build exits with 0 on success and non-zero on failure, so it works in scripts and CI. Add --json for machine-readable output. Commit oyzu.lock and add dist/ and .oyzu/ to .gitignore.

oyzu history # past builds oyzu inspect dist # check the output bundle against its recorded digests Build again without changes and Oyzu reuses the earlier results, and labels them as reused. See Read your build results.

Problem Where to look A tool is missing or can't be installed Manage your tools The build fails The failure section and the log it names, then Troubleshooting A target is missing or uses the wrong builder Add a small build.yaml: Adopt Oyzu in an existing repository
Run your project's tasks. Adopt Oyzu in a larger repository. Command details: CLI reference, local builds, build tasks.
Oyzu is a single executable, oyzu. It needs no account, agent, daemon or desktop app, and no administrator rights to install.

On Linux or macOS: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | sh On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex The script: Picks the newest release (previews included) that has an executable for your platform. Downloads it and refuses it unless its SHA-256 digest matches the one GitHub reports. Installs oyzu into ~/.oyzu/bin (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\bin on Windows) and runs oyzu --version. Runs oyzu shell install to set up your shells and PATH (see What it sets up). It prints the release it chose, one line with the tag, asset, digest and install location, and the installed version. Preview releases Every release is a preview. Releases are binaries and notices published on the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository, so you need no account or token. No release has been published there yet. Until one is, the script stops with no published release of oyzuai/oyzu-releases has .... The scripts don't check release provenance yet. To use Preview plugins, run oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true once. It applies to all your projects and leaves the Stable defaults unchanged. A GitHub token is optional. It lifts the anonymous API limit of 60 requests an hour: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) sh $env:GH_TOKEN = (gh auth token); irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex

Each script is under 250 lines. To read it before you run it, download it first: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh -o install.sh less install.sh sh install.sh --version v0.0.4 --version (or OYZU_VERSION) installs one release tag instead of the newest. In PowerShell, pass parameters like this: & ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1))) -Version v0.0.4 The install script reference lists every option, the exit codes and the errors.
documents.s: Read it first, or pin a version

documents.t: Your shells need to activate oyzu, and programs that never start a shell (IDEs, GUI apps, scheduled jobs) need to find oyzu and your tools. oyzu shell install handles both: Shell activation goes into ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc and the PowerShell 7 profile, for each of those shells you use. oyzu and the shims folder go on your PATH, so node, go or cargo run at the project's locked version everywhere, without oyzu exec --. On Windows this is your user Path in the registry. On Linux and macOS it is your login profile. Open a new terminal, and restart any IDE, afterwards. You can run oyzu shell install again at any time. To install the file only, pass --no-modify-path (-NoModifyPath in PowerShell). With fish or Windows PowerShell 5.1, the installer prints what to run or which folders to add yourself.

Run the same command again to upgrade. It replaces oyzu and oyzu-shim in place. To uninstall, run oyzu shell remove to undo the shell and PATH setup, then delete those two files from the install folder.

oyzu --version oyzu --help The version shows the release (or source revision) and platform of your build. A source build says local. oyzu --help groups commands by job: develop and build, project tools, environment and configuration, platform, and diagnostics. The platform group (auth, release, secrets) needs an Oyzu platform account. Everything else works without one. oyzu <command> --help works offline with no project open. Then run it on a project. The tutorial builds a real program step by step, and Your first build is the short version. Something wrong? See troubleshooting. You don't need to install Go, Node, Java or any other ecosystem toolchain first. Oyzu acquires the tools a project asks for. See Manage your first tool.

The install scripts are tested on Linux and Windows (x86-64). They also have asset names for macOS, ARM64 and musl Linux, but those aren't tested yet. Support for builds differs by ecosystem and tool provider. See what works today and known limits.

This is for contributors, or when you need an unreleased change or a platform with no release executable. You need a checkout of the Oyzu repository and either an existing Oyzu, which provides the repository's managed Rust, or the Rust toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml. The first run needs network access unless the managed Rust and the locked Cargo dependencies are already cached; the build uses --locked. On macOS, native builds also need Apple's Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install). tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh export PATH="$PWD/.oyzu/bin:$PATH" oyzu build cli The script builds the CLI, the native shim and the Rust and Node plugins, copies them to .oyzu/bin and restores the repository's own locked tools. The source bootstrap section covers the user configuration it writes, when it refuses to run, and CARGO_TARGET_DIR. Later, to bring the oyzu on your PATH up to date with the checkout, run oyzu run bootstrap from the checkout. It rebuilds the CLI and installs it in place, on Windows or Linux. See Refreshing the oyzu on your PATH.

Isolated builds (oyzu build --isolated) run a Linux oyzu inside the container. On Windows and macOS the install scripts set this up from the release. For an oyzu you built yourself, pass the Linux oyzu built from the same source: oyzu engine install --linux ./oyzu-linux-x86_64 If you have a compatible development engine archive with its identity and digest, you can install it for your user: oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> This doesn't change your PATH or pin a project. The installed executable, and any byte-identical copy of it such as the oyzu on your PATH, supplies its own isolated-build workers without an engines.packages entry. Explicit project pins and administrator pin requirements still take precedence. Add --json for a machine-readable record. The engine staging reference covers package requirements, offline use and recovery.
Every build ends by telling you what ran now, what was reused from an earlier build, what the tests reported and where the full record is.

$ oyzu build --fullCopy Building hello linux/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tool versions Resolved and locked 5.2s ✓ Source workspaces 1 private target workspaces ready <0.1s ✓ project dependencies Ready <0.1s ✓ Output bundle Ready <0.1s ✓ Compiler cache 0.0 MiB / 8192 MiB retained budget <0.1s ✓ Source evidence 4 captured/observed entries recorded in 0.00s <0.1s ✓ CLI identity Verified in 2.17s 2.2s ✓ Report preparation Contracts and bindings ready <0.1s ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 1 installed now 22.8s go 1.22.12 installed now detected from go.mod ​ … ​ ── Plan ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── format lint test build project run run run run ​ profile project · development · local dist only ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 00:30 .. project build started 00:34 ✓ project build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=fals… executed 4.4s 00:34 .. project test started 00:40 still running: project test 5s · 2 waiting 00:41 ✓ project test go test -json -coverprofile=/tmp/… executed 6.3s 00:41 .. project lint started 00:42 ✓ project lint go vet ./... executed 1.0s 00:42 .. project format-check started 00:42 ✓ project format-check gofmt -l . executed <0.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/linux/x86_64/project-0.0.0-dev.ga0bde8664a74 1.9 MB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 42.2s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 1410-1792893472911570613-1 Output shortened. Prepare sets up configuration, tools and workspaces. Plan shows which stages run for each target. Build has one row per action with its native command, executed or reused, and the time. Outputs lists the artifacts. The summary gives tests, coverage, the result and where the details are. A failed action gets its own section with the cause, exit code, log file and a command to re-run just that target. CI logs show the same sections without live progress. Add -q for less output or -v for more. Every section is explained in Read output, receipts and history.
documents.s: Read the output top to bottom

documents.t: Wording Meaning executed The command ran in this build reused Inputs are unchanged, so Oyzu restored an earlier result. The row shows how long the original run took blocked Not run, because something it depends on failed unknown Oyzu couldn't confirm a final result for the action Tests run now Tests that ran in this build Reused test evidence Test results from an earlier run with the same inputs. The tests did not run now Oyzu never presents reused tests as a fresh run, and it never shows a coverage percentage it didn't measure. Here is the same build repeated with nothing changed: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building hello linux/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full … ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── · project · linux/x86_64 Reused from an earlier run · not executed now · originally ran 2026-10-25T01:58:35Z (key e2c2f69bdfe3) 00:01 ↺ project build reused was 4.4s 00:01 ↺ project test reused was 6.3s 00:01 ↺ project lint reused was 1.0s 00:01 ↺ project format-check reused was <0.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/linux/x86_64/project-0.0.0-dev.ga0bde8664a74 1.9 MB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Reused test evidence 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports; not run now) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 statements) · reused from an earlier run, not run now Evidence origin local · producer 1410-1792893503389005878 · completed 2026-10-25T01:58:35Z ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 reused · 1.5s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 4502-1792893522584342917-1 Output shortened. Change a source file and only the affected actions run again. See Cache build results.

Each build writes an output bundle to dist/: the artifacts, test and coverage reports, logs, and manifest.json, which lists everything that was built with its digest. The previous bundle moves to .oyzu/history/. oyzu history # past builds, newest first oyzu history <id> # one build: outcome, why each stage ran, file paths oyzu history <id> --json # the same, as JSON oyzu inspect dist # check every recorded file against its digest oyzu inspect tells you the bundle is intact. It doesn't tell you who produced it or whether it may be released, and its output says so.
Every command accepts --json. Standard output then holds only the JSON result. The exit code is 0 on success and non-zero on failure either way.
Read output, receipts and history CLI output, build bundles, action cache, affected builds Build evidence

Oyzu treats the tools a project needs (compilers, runtimes, package managers) as part of the project. It records exact versions in oyzu.lock, installs them and runs your commands with them, so your team and CI get the same versions without installing anything by hand.

Native files your ecosystem already has: rust-toolchain.toml, the go and toolchain lines in go.mod, global.json, the packageManager field in package.json, Gradle and Maven wrapper properties. oyzu.toml, under [tools], for anything a native file can't say. oyzu.lock, which records the exact version and download digest Oyzu picked. Write each version in one place only. If a native file already says it, leave it out of oyzu.toml.

$ oyzu pin --dry-runCopy Build requirements · preview ​ Consolidated across 1 build target(s). ​ Tool requirements Requirement Requested version Needed for Installation support Applies to oyzu:go 1.22 Declared requirement Oyzu All targets ​ Executor prerequisites Requirement Needed for Availability Applies to ​ Check tools are required when their checks are enabled by the build or policy. ​ Tool execution platform coverage OS Architecture ABI linux amd64 gnu Metadata coverage only; native installation support varies. ​ No files changed. Tool resolution complete. Installed availability was not checked. Nothing was installed. Use --json for sources, constraints and discovery limitations. --dry-run writes and installs nothing. Add --json to see where each requirement came from.

oyzu pin # pick exact versions and write oyzu.lock oyzu install # install the tools declared in oyzu.toml $ oyzu installCopy Installing tools Checking pinned tools and verifying reusable installations Tool installation ​ Tool Version Result go 1.22.12 reused ​ Selected installations verified. Use oyzu tools current to inspect availability. Oyzu checks each download against its recorded digest and publisher information before using it, and trusts the installed tool after that. You often don't need either command: oyzu build locks and installs what it needs. Commit oyzu.lock. Command What it does oyzu install go@1.26 Adds Go 1.26 to oyzu.toml, locks it and installs it oyzu update Moves locked versions forward within what oyzu.toml allows; never edits oyzu.toml oyzu uninstall go Removes the declaration and its lock entries; the installed copy stays in the shared store

$ oyzu which go && oyzu exec -- go version /home/you/.local/share/oyzu/tools/installs/d966a600…/payload/bin/go go version go1.22.12 linux/amd64 oyzu which shows the exact executable a command would run. oyzu exec -- <command> runs any command with the project's tools on PATH. To have your shells and IDEs pick up the tools (the install script already ran this unless you passed --no-modify-path): oyzu shell install # every shell found, plus oyzu and the shims on your PATH oyzu shell install bash # or only one shell Open a new terminal afterwards. With the shims on PATH, plain go or node use the project's locked version and you do not need oyzu exec --.

oyzu tools current shows the versions in effect here and where each came from. oyzu tools list, oyzu tools versions <tool> and oyzu tools info <tool> show the shared store, the available versions and where a tool comes from. Not every tool installs automatically on every platform; when one can't, the command says what is missing.
Pin tools for your team: exact versions, updates and scopes. Tool commands, shell activation, configuration.

In about ten minutes you build a tiny Go program with Oyzu: you see what Oyzu detects, preview the build, build and test it, check the result, rebuild it from cache and read a failure. The output on this page comes from a real run on Linux; your times, hashes and paths will differ. You need the oyzu executable (Install Oyzu) and network access for the first build, so Oyzu can download Go. You don't need to install Go yourself.

mkdir hello && cd hello git init Create go.mod: module example.com/oyzu/hello go 1.22 Create main.go: package main import "fmt" func greeting(name string) string { return "Hello, " + name + "!" } func main() { fmt.Println(greeting("Oyzu")) } Create main_test.go: package main import "testing" func TestGreeting(t *testing.T) { if got := greeting("Oyzu"); got != "Hello, Oyzu!" { t.Fatalf("unexpected greeting: %q", got) } } That's the whole project. There is no Oyzu configuration file: Oyzu works from the files Go already uses.

$ oyzu discoverCopy 1 target · 6 tasks discovered without running project code Project root: ~/hello ​ project · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location . Manager go Version 0.0.0 Part of builds build, format-check, lint, test Development tasks format, install ​ Target names are what `oyzu build <target>` accepts. Next steps: oyzu run list every task and the command it runs oyzu build --plan preview the build stages without running them Use --json for the complete discovery record, including each task's environment and dependencies. Oyzu found one Go application, which it calls project. It only read files; it ran nothing. To see the commands behind each task: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · go/app (6) project:build Inferred · go go build ./... project:format Inferred · go gofmt -w . project:format-check Inferred · go gofmt -l . project:install Inferred · go go mod download project:lint Inferred · go go vet ./... project:test Inferred · go go test ./... ​ Run one with: oyzu run <task> (extra arguments go after --) Commands show argv; task dependencies and hooks may also run. Use --json for full task records. These are ordinary Go commands. You can run any of them with oyzu run, for example oyzu run test.

$ oyzu build --planCopy Planning hello Linux x86_64 (host) · Local · context local · Fast build requested ​ Build preview Execution: host · No tools installed, dependencies downloaded or build actions run. ​ project · go/app · linux/x86_64 Executor: host Profile: development · local dist only (no difference: the Go compiler always optimizes) Placement: runs on linux/x86_64 · no Docker engine needed · Runs as host processes without a container engine Stage Selection Details build selected Native commands and report bindings resolve during preparation format-check skipped fast local build lint skipped fast local build test skipped fast local build ​ Platforms · how each is built here Target Platform Here CI runner Note project linux/x86_64 builds · host linux x86_64 ​ Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:go minimum-version >=1.22 project go.mod go oyzu:go request 1.22 project go.mod (native pin) oyzu:go tool from configuration / native project Go compiler for selected manifest build stages ​ Declared task ordering Task After project:build ​ Static analysis analyzed from the working tree · read-only, no project code executed ​ Unresolved until preparation • Tool installations and executor prerequisites have not been checked. • Application dependency availability and native metadata require preparation. • Exact commands, additional native stages, artifacts and report bindings require preparation. ​ Run oyzu build with the same selection flags to prepare and execute. This preview is not build evidence. The plan shows what a build would do without doing it. Two things to notice: Oyzu needs Go 1.22 or newer, and it read that from the go 1.22 line in go.mod. A plain oyzu build runs only the build stage. Tests, lint and format checks are skipped to keep local builds fast. --full turns them on.

$ oyzu build --fullCopy Building hello linux/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tool versions Resolved and locked 5.2s ✓ Source workspaces 1 private target workspaces ready <0.1s ✓ project dependencies Ready <0.1s ✓ Output bundle Ready <0.1s ✓ Compiler cache 0.0 MiB / 8192 MiB retained budget <0.1s ✓ Source evidence 4 captured/observed entries recorded in 0.00s <0.1s ✓ CLI identity Verified in 2.17s 2.2s ✓ Report preparation Contracts and bindings ready <0.1s ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 1 installed now 22.8s go 1.22.12 installed now detected from go.mod ​ … ​ ── Plan ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── format lint test build project run run run run ​ profile project · development · local dist only ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 00:30 .. project build started 00:34 ✓ project build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=fals… executed 4.4s 00:34 .. project test started 00:40 still running: project test 5s · 2 waiting 00:41 ✓ project test go test -json -coverprofile=/tmp/… executed 6.3s 00:41 .. project lint started 00:42 ✓ project lint go vet ./... executed 1.0s 00:42 .. project format-check started 00:42 ✓ project format-check gofmt -l . executed <0.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/linux/x86_64/project-0.0.0-dev.ga0bde8664a74 1.9 MB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 42.2s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 1410-1792893472911570613-1 Output shortened. Read it from the top: Prepare loads configuration, picks the Go version and installs it. Here Oyzu downloaded Go 1.22.12, the newest 1.22 release, and checked it against its published digest. Plan shows which stages run for each target. Build has one row per action, with the real command (go build, go test, go vet, gofmt -l), the result and the time. Outputs lists the program Oyzu built. The last lines summarize the tests that ran, coverage and the overall result. The build added two things to your project: Path What it is Commit it? oyzu.lock The exact Go version and download digest Oyzu used Yes, so everyone gets the same Go dist/ The output bundle: the program, test reports, logs and a manifest No, add it to .gitignore

Every build keeps a record. oyzu history lists them: $ oyzu historyCopy Invocation evidence Invocation / run Outcome Scope Started 1410-1792893472911570613-1 succeeded 1 targets · 4 actions 2026-10-25T01:58:23.389005878+00:00 0 older entries omitted · 0 incomplete bundles Next: oyzu history <ID> for a bounded summary and evidence paths Recorded observations; this summary does not verify artifact contents. oyzu inspect checks the bundle in dist/: $ oyzu inspect distCopy ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded Run 1410-1792893503389005878 · source sha256:50d4437e1473 · uncommitted changes ​ Targets Target Builder Platform Path project go/app linux/x86_64 . ​ Actions Action Status Exit Gate project:build succeeded 0 required project:test succeeded 0 required project:lint succeeded 0 required project:format-check succeeded 0 required ​ Artifacts Path (under dist/) Kind Size Platform Digest project/linux/x86_64/ file 1.9 MB linux/x86_64 sha256:bc329b1b6748 project-0.0.0-dev.ga0bde8664a74 ​ Reports Report Path Status project:test project/linux/x86_64/reports/junit.xml collected project:coverage project/linux/x86_64/reports/coverage.out collected ​ Verified: every recorded file matches its digest. Content integrity alone does not identify a producer or grant release authority. Use --json for the full inspection result, including the plan and execution envelope. inspect confirms that every file in dist/ is exactly the file the build recorded, by comparing digests. It tells you the bundle is intact. It doesn't tell you who built it, and the last line says so.

Run the same command again without changing anything: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building hello linux/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full … ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── · project · linux/x86_64 Reused from an earlier run · not executed now · originally ran 2026-10-25T01:58:35Z (key e2c2f69bdfe3) 00:01 ↺ project build reused was 4.4s 00:01 ↺ project test reused was 6.3s 00:01 ↺ project lint reused was 1.0s 00:01 ↺ project format-check reused was <0.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/linux/x86_64/project-0.0.0-dev.ga0bde8664a74 1.9 MB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Reused test evidence 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports; not run now) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 statements) · reused from an earlier run, not run now Evidence origin local · producer 1410-1792893503389005878 · completed 2026-10-25T01:58:35Z ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 reused · 1.5s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 4502-1792893522584342917-1 Output shortened. Nothing changed, so Oyzu reused the earlier results instead of running the commands again: 1.5 seconds instead of 42. Each reused row shows how long the original run took, and the test summary says not run now, so you always know whether tests actually ran. See Read your build results.

In main.go, change "Hello, " to "Hi, " and build again: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building hello linux/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full … ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 00:01 .. project build started 00:01 ✓ project build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=fals… executed 0.1s 00:01 .. project test started 00:01 ✗ project test go test -json -coverprofile=/tmp/… failed 0.2s 00:01 .. project lint started 00:01 ✓ project lint go vet ./... executed <0.1s 00:01 .. project format-check started 00:01 ✓ project format-check gofmt -l . executed <0.1s ​ ── Failure: project · test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── --- FAIL: TestGreeting (0.00s) FAIL example.com/oyzu/hello · TestGreeting FAIL coverage: 50.0% of statements FAIL\texample.com/oyzu/hello\t0.003s FAIL example.com/oyzu/hello Exit 1 Log dist/logs/native-2e05b5df14bb75bffc73cd4b76b6b9f01ba018113cbfb2f6ec747663d1de7a60.stderr Next oyzu build project --full re-run only this target ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 2 succeeded · 1 failed ​ Tests run now 0 passed · 1 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ Test evidence project:test Command failed (exit 1) Results 0 passed · 1 failed · 0 skipped Coverage 50.0% of statements (1/2) Acceptance rejected · required evidence is absent, invalid or failing ​ ✗ Build failed 1 failed · 3 succeeded · 1.8s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 4551-1792893524068393468-1 Note Local binaries were not updated; existing binaries are from the previous successful build. Output shortened. The command exits with status 1. The failing test gets its own section with the test output, the exit code, the full log file and a command that re-runs only this target.
