After that, builds never pick new versions on their own. If a native minimum moves past the lock (for example go get raised go.mod), the build fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE; run oyzu pin again.
documents.s: 2. Lock what the native files ask for

documents.t: Native files often give only a minimum or a release line. For Go, a toolchain go1.24.5 line selects exactly 1.24.5, while go 1.22 with no patch number selects the newest stable 1.22.x (Go version selection). To move the team to a newer version, declare it: oyzu install --dry-run go@1.24 # show what would be declared, locked and installed oyzu install go@1.24 # declare, lock for every platform, install for this one $ oyzu install go@1.24Copy Installing requested tools Resolving every platform, then installing this one ✓ Installed (reused existing installation) go 1.24.13 Declared "1.24" in …\shop\oyzu.toml (project) Locked in …\shop\oyzu.lock for 4 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc) ​ Store: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Oyzu\tools oyzu.toml now holds what you typed, and oyzu.lock holds the exact version: [tools] go = "1.24" Spec Meaning go@1.24 Newest 1.24.x go@1.24.13 Exactly 1.24.13 go@latest Newest available version go Keep the existing declaration Several specs in one command are applied together or not at all. Tools Oyzu can install: node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm, rust, cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov, plus aqua:<owner>/<repo> and github:<owner>/<repo> packages (experimental). Zig 0.15.2 can be installed on Intel Macs (experimental); see Zig installation. The full list is in tool commands. The lock covers other platforms too, so teammates and CI runners get a matching download. Platforms the publisher doesn't build for are left out and reported.

Commit oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock. Teammates and CI then run: $ oyzu install --frozenCopy Installing tools Checking pinned tools and verifying reusable installations Tool installation ​ Tool Version Result go 1.24.13 reused ​ Selected installations verified. Use oyzu tools current to inspect availability. --frozen fails instead of changing the lock when it doesn't match the configuration. Each download is checked against its locked digest; installed tools are trusted after that. oyzu install installs tools declared in oyzu.toml. When every requirement comes from native files, it says so: $ oyzu installCopy Installing tools Checking pinned tools and verifying reusable installations ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: configure a tool before running oyzu install Next: Correct the reported cause and retry the command. That's fine: oyzu build installs every pinned tool it needs on its own.
documents.s: 4. Commit, and let everyone else install

documents.t: $ oyzu tools currentCopy 1 tool ready ​ Tool Requested Selected Source Status go 1.24 1.24.13 project ok ​ Use --details for paths and identities, --all for overridden declarations. ​ Store: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Oyzu\tools Installed state comes from stored receipts; payloads are not re-hashed. Command Shows oyzu tools list Installations in the shared store, their size, and whether this project or your global configuration uses them oyzu tools versions go Versions you could install, newest first oyzu tools info go Where the tool comes from, accepted names, platforms and how it is verified oyzu which go The exact executable a command would run oyzu tools current statuses: Status Meaning Fix ok Ready not installed Locked but not in the store oyzu install stale lock No matching lock entry oyzu pin blocked Not allowed by tools.allowed Ask the policy owner ambiguous Conflicting lock entries or tool names Use the exact tool name the message lists

oyzu exec -- go version # anything after -- runs with the locked tools on PATH oyzu run test # tasks always use the locked tools To have your normal terminal pick up the tools inside the project, set up shell integration once with oyzu shell install bash (or zsh or pwsh). See shell activation.
documents.s: 6. Run commands with the pinned tools

documents.t: oyzu update go # newest version within the declared request ("1.24" -> latest 1.24.x) oyzu update # every declared tool oyzu install go@1.25 # change the request itself oyzu pin --refresh # refresh download details, keep the selected versions oyzu uninstall go # remove the declaration and its lock entries update never edits oyzu.toml. Commit the lock change like any dependency update.

Flag Writes to Use for (none) Project oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock The team's tools --local oyzu.local.toml (the project lock is still used) A personal override you don't commit -g, --global Your user configuration and the lock next to it Tools you want in every project Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT instead of guessing.
An administrator can limit which tools are allowed with tools.allowed. Other requests fail with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED, naming the rule. See configuration.

Code Meaning Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE The lock has no entry for a request, or a native minimum changed oyzu pin, then commit the lock TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT (exit 3) A configured version is below what a native file requires Raise the request, or lower the native minimum TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT Specs combined with --frozen, --offline or --update Run two separate commands TOOL_NOT_DECLARED uninstall or update of a tool this scope doesn't declare The message names the scope that does PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT / PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED Another or an interrupted lock edit Run oyzu install, update, uninstall or pin again; they recover first TOOL_LOCK_MISSING install --frozen with no lock Run oyzu pin or oyzu install online once Reference: tool commands, configuration. Offline and proxy setups: Work offline or behind a proxy.
Find your symptom below. Every Oyzu failure starts with a code (such as TOOL_LOCK_STALE) or a plain cause, then a Next: line with the fix. Read those two lines first.

oyzu --version # the exact Oyzu you are running oyzu build --plan # what Oyzu will do; runs nothing oyzu -v build # debug detail; -vv for trace oyzu history # past builds, with invocation IDs oyzu history <invocation-id> # result, why each stage ran, file paths Every failure also prints the invocation ID, the Oyzu version, the executable and the directory: $ oyzu build nopeCopy … ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: unknown build target nope; available targets: api, worker Next: Correct the reported cause and retry the command. Invocation: 36620-1792552675147666000-1 oyzu … · windows/x86_64 Executable: …\oyzu.exe Directory: . With --json, the failure is an object with code, error, exitCode and nextStep. For detail from one area, set for example OYZU_LOG=warn,oyzu::tools=debug. Areas: commands, config, discovery, tools, acquisition, executor, builders, reports.

A project folder is missing from oyzu discover. Discovery stops at the first folder a builder recognizes and skips nested Git repositories, folders with their own build.yaml, and dependency and output folders. With a root build.yaml, only listed builds exist. Add the folder: builds: web: uses: node/app path: web oyzu discover --write adds such folders for you (builds build.yaml leaves out). Oyzu picked the wrong package manager, test runner, linter or formatter. oyzu build --plan shows each choice and why. Override it in build.yaml with the with key the plan names, such as with: {package-manager: pnpm} (selecting a role). conflicting … candidates …; declare the intended one … with: {…} Two native files disagree equally. Add the suggested with: setting to that build, or remove the stale file (for example an old lockfile from another package manager). … is recognized by docker/image and node/app, so discovery cannot choose Name the builder: both: {uses: docker/image, path: both}. Another tool's build.yaml (for example Dart's) is in the way. Oyzu only treats a build.yaml with a builds, members or exclude root key as its own. Others are listed as skipped.
documents.s: Discovery: Oyzu doesn't see my project as expected

documents.t: Message Cause Fix CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming a build.yaml field Unknown field or root key, or builds not under builds: Put builds under builds:. Each build accepts only uses, path, platforms, depends_on, inputs, materialize, bindings, fetches, with CONFIG_SCOPE A setting in a file that can't hold it: cache.remote, cache.ciRemote, cache.dir, platform.url or platform.account in a project file, or [publish] outside the root oyzu.toml Move it to user configuration (oyzu config set --global …), the environment, or the root file CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN A task key, depends_on or publish setting names a build, task or output that doesn't exist (the message suggests the nearest name) Fix the name CONFIG_REFERENCE_MISPLACED A task key for a build sits in an oyzu.toml outside that build's folder Move it to the root or the build's folder CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS An unqualified stage replacement such as [tasks.test] reaches builds with different builders Qualify it per build: [tasks."cli:test"] build.yaml changed between discovery and source capture The file was edited during a build Finish the edit and run again Run oyzu config validate after every edit, and oyzu config explain <key> to see where a value comes from. CONTEXT_INVALID: an unknown --context or OYZU_CONTEXT value. It fails every command that reads configuration, including install and exec: $ oyzu build --context nightlyCopy ✗ CONTEXT_INVALID: --context has unknown context "nightly"; use one of local, pr, ci, release Next: Correct the reported cause and retry the command.

unknown build target nope; available targets: api, worker: build arguments are exact target names from oyzu discover, not task names, paths or patterns. ambiguous task test; choose api:test, worker:test: several targets define the task. Add the target name: oyzu run api:test. TASK_NOT_FOUND (exit 5): the task doesn't exist in this folder. The message lists the tasks it found; pick another project with oyzu -C <dir> run <task>: $ oyzu run nopeCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks ✗ TASK_NOT_FOUND: no task "nope" in …\shop. Available tasks: build, format, format-check, install, lint, pre_build, smoke, test. Run oyzu run to list tasks, or oyzu -C <project> run nope Next: Check the selected directory and name; use oyzu -C <project> to select a project. --affected builds everything. The JSON plan says why: oyzu build --affected origin/main --plan --json selection.affected.fallback Fix baseline-unavailable The ref isn't in the local clone. Run git fetch origin main, or use fetch-depth: 0 in CI. configuration-or-lock-change build.yaml, oyzu.toml, oyzu.lock or a native manifest changed. Commit it and later builds narrow again. If changedPaths lists files you didn't edit, line endings differ between your files and Git; fix them with .gitattributes. SOURCE_TRACKED_IGNORED: tracked source .oyzu-tool-lock-edit.lock is excluded …: an ignored file was committed. For Oyzu's coordination file, untrack it with git rm --cached .oyzu-tool-lock-edit.lock and keep it in .gitignore. If the build really needs the file, list it in the build's inputs.
documents.s: Selection: the wrong things are built

documents.t: Message Cause Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE The lock has no entry for a request, or a native minimum moved (for example go get changed go.mod) oyzu pin, then commit oyzu.lock TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT (exit 3) A configured version is below the minimum a native file sets Raise [tools], or remove it so the native file decides configure a tool before running oyzu install Nothing is declared in [tools]; all requirements come from native files Nothing to fix: oyzu build installs those itself. Use oyzu install <tool>@<version> to declare one TOOL_LOCK_MISSING install --frozen or --offline with no lock Run oyzu pin or oyzu install online once TOOL_NO_PROJECT A tool command outside a project without -g Run it inside the project, or add --global PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED / PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT An interrupted or simultaneous lock edit Run oyzu install, update, uninstall or pin again; they recover first CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED The tools.allowed policy excludes the tool Ask the policy owner, or choose an allowed tool tools current shows not installed Locked but not in the store oyzu install --frozen tools current shows stale lock No lock entry for this platform or tool oyzu pin The tool store is shared per user: Platform Location Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\tools macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/tools Linux ~/.local/share/oyzu/tools Tools are checked when installed and trusted after that, so a damaged tool simply fails when it runs. Reinstall it.

Read the Failure section, not just the last line. It names the failing action, the native error, the exit code, the full log and the narrowest re-run command. Here a failing test in api blocked worker, which depends on it (the tutorial shows a single-target failure): $ oyzu build --fullCopy … ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 00:03 .. api build started 00:10 still running: api build 6s · 8 waiting 00:11 ✓ api build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false… executed 8.6s 00:11 .. api test started 00:20 still running: api test 8s · 7 waiting 00:21 ✗ api test go test -json -coverprofile=C:\Use… failed 9.3s 00:21 .. api lint started 00:22 ✓ api lint go vet ./... executed 1.1s 00:22 .. api format-check started 00:22 ✓ api format-check gofmt -l . executed 0.2s 00:22 ⊘ worker pre_build needs api · test 00:22 ⊘ worker build needs api · test, worker · pre_build 00:22 ⊘ worker test needs api · test, worker · build ⊘ + 2 more blocked · -v lists them ​ ── Failure: api · test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── --- FAIL: TestGreeting (0.00s) FAIL example.com/shop/api · TestGreeting FAIL coverage: 50.0% of statements FAIL\texample.com/shop/api\t0.613s FAIL example.com/shop/api Exit 1 Log dist/logs/0001.stderr Next oyzu build api re-run only this target ​ Checks selected 6 actions · 2 succeeded · 1 failed · 3 blocked ​ Tests run now 0 passed · 1 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage api: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ Test evidence api:test Command failed (exit 1) Results 0 passed · 1 failed · 0 skipped Coverage 50.0% of statements (1/2) Acceptance rejected · required evidence is absent, invalid or failing ​ Test evidence worker:test Command blocked (exit 1) Results missing · required Coverage missing · required Acceptance rejected · required evidence is absent, invalid or failing ​ ✗ Build failed 1 failed · 5 blocked · 3 succeeded · 22.7s api/ ✗ 1 target 19.2s worker/ ✗ 1 target Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 40716-1792553002522238800-1 Note Local binaries were not updated; existing binaries are from the previous successful build. Output shortened. blocked actions didn't run because something they depend on failed. Fix the first failure. After a failure, .oyzu/bin still holds the programs from the last successful build. Passes locally, fails in CI: CI runs every check. Reproduce with oyzu build --full. CHECK_ADVISORY warning: an advisory check failed, but the project set it to warn only, so the build succeeded. Another build is running in this folder. A second build in the same folder fails before running anything. Wait for the first one. Don't delete .oyzu/build.lock; the lock is released when the build exits. An existing dist/ blocks the build. Oyzu only replaces a dist/ that contains an Oyzu manifest. If your project writes its own dist/, move that output, or set [build] bundleDirectory (bundle destination). Oyzu never deletes it. An error names a .oyzu/bundle-… folder. dist/ couldn't be written, so the results were kept there. Inspect that path with oyzu inspect, fix the disk space or permission problem, and rebuild.

Symptom Check Fix A result was reused that you didn't expect oyzu build --explain, oyzu cache explain <target> Oyzu doesn't see changes outside the key, such as an environment variable a tool reads. Run once with oyzu build --no-cache Nothing is ever reused oyzu history <id> lists the reason per stage Hooks without outputs, secret environment values, or a changed oyzu.toml oyzu cache clear says the cache is busy A build is using it Retry when it finishes A test row says reused The result is from an earlier run, labelled as such Use --no-cache to run the tests now Details: Cache build results.

Code Meaning PROXY_INVALID A proxy variable is set but isn't a valid URL. Oyzu never falls back to a direct connection TRUST_BUNDLE_UNREADABLE / TRUST_BUNDLE_INVALID SSL_CERT_FILE is missing, unreadable, empty or not PEM SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE The download failed after two retries. Check your connection and the proxy SOURCE_TIMEOUT The 45-second download deadline passed SOURCE_DENIED No approved source allows the request or redirect BYTE_LIMIT / REQUEST_LIMIT A download or session went over its size or request limit TOOL_OFFLINE The command needs the network and --offline forbids it With --offline, a missing tool or dependency stops the build instead of being downloaded. Go online once and run the same build. See Work offline or behind a proxy.

Code (exit 3) Fix NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON Use a runner with Docker, or the host path for builders that support it NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES The Linux crun sandbox can't run here. Allow unprivileged user namespaces, or use Docker PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE This platform's executor isn't available on this machine. The plan names the runner it needs See Isolated builds.
See the failure tables in Remote builds and Publish artifacts.

A new PATH entry isn't picked up. An open terminal keeps the PATH it started with. Update the session ($env:Path = "C:\path\to\bin;$env:Path") or open a new terminal. Line endings. With core.autocrlf, files on disk can differ from what Git stored, and --affected counts that as a change. Set explicit eol rules in .gitattributes. Paths in messages may start with \\?\. It's the same path.

Collect oyzu --version, your platform, the full failing command, its output with -v, and oyzu history <invocation-id> --json. Oyzu hides credentials in URLs, headers and key=value text, but native tool output is passed through unchanged, so check it for secrets before you share it. Reference: CLI output, build logging, build bundles, tool commands, acquisition transport.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/acquisition-transport.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. When Oyzu downloads tools, helper archives and container-build dependencies, the requests go through one HTTP client with fixed rules: which sources may be contacted, how credentials are used, how retries work and how large downloads may be. This page explains those rules, how to use a corporate proxy, and what the download errors mean. Native package managers still read their own lockfiles, resolve dependencies and check package integrity. Oyzu only fetches bytes from allowed sources; it doesn't resolve dependencies. Note: The download client is experimental.

Each builder supplies the sources it may use. A source is an HTTPS origin and path prefix, with an optional authorization header held on your machine. Every request and every redirect must match an allowed source, or it fails with SOURCE_DENIED. A redirect uses the destination source's credentials. A token is never forwarded to another source. Some sources only accept redirects. For example, Go's proxy.golang.org sends large module zips to https://storage.googleapis.com/proxy-golang-org-prod/; a request that starts there is refused. go.sum still pins every zip. Plain HTTP is only allowed for local loopback endpoints. Base URLs with credentials, a query or a fragment, and encoded path escapes, are refused. Downloads happen while the build prepares, before the plan is frozen. Build actions then run with networking off. A missing input or integrity failure during an offline build never falls back to downloading. oyzu run tasks such as oyzu run install run on your host with normal network access.

The download client reads the standard environment variables of the process that runs oyzu. They apply to tool metadata and archives, helper archives and container-build dependency downloads. Variable Effect HTTPS_PROXY / https_proxy Proxy for HTTPS sources (CONNECT tunnel). HTTP_PROXY / http_proxy Proxy for HTTP sources. ALL_PROXY / all_proxy Used when the scheme-specific variable isn't set. NO_PROXY / no_proxy Hosts, domains and CIDR ranges that skip the proxy. SSL_CERT_FILE A PEM bundle of extra trusted certificates, for corporate TLS inspection. The built-in public roots stay trusted. Loopback addresses (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) always skip the proxy, so local endpoints and their credentials never go through it. Proxy URLs may include credentials. They are never printed. An invalid proxy URL fails with PROXY_INVALID. An unreadable or empty SSL_CERT_FILE fails with TRUST_BUNDLE_UNREADABLE or TRUST_BUNDLE_INVALID. Oyzu never silently connects directly instead. A proxy doesn't widen the allowed sources; it's only a route. A TLS-inspecting proxy can see request headers, including source credentials. Only use a proxy you trust with them. Extra trusted certificates don't replace signature checks: a tool's publisher signature is still verified against its own trust root. Not supported: proxy authentication other than credentials in the URL, PAC files, system proxy settings and per-source proxies. Proxy support is tested on Linux and Windows. macOS isn't supported yet.

Rule Value Retries per download 2, after the first attempt Network deadline per download 45 seconds, shared across redirects and retries Redirects per download 5 Requests per session 4096, counting retries and redirects Backoff 200 ms, then 400 ms, or longer if the server sends Retry-After Statuses 408, 429, 502, 503 and 504, and connection or transfer failures, are retried. A partial download is discarded before retrying. Statuses such as 401, 403, 404 and 500 fail at once. So do denied sources, invalid redirects and size limits. If Retry-After asks for a wait longer than the remaining deadline, Oyzu returns the failure instead of retrying early. These limits can't be configured. A package manager may make its own further requests; its own retry behavior applies to those. Delivery edges still filling. An organization's delivery edge that is still fetching an artifact from its publisher answers 503 with Oyzu-Fill: pending and Retry-After. Oyzu waits the Retry-After seconds (1 to 30, default 5) and asks again with a fresh deadline, for up to 15 minutes, without counting it as a retry. Without that header, a 503 is an ordinary retryable status.

Each successful response may be up to 256 MiB, and one session may read up to 1 GiB in total, including failed attempts. Pinned tool archives (Rust, Node, Go, Python, JDK and Maven) download in sequential 8 MiB ranges, up to 512 MiB in total. Each range has its own 45-second deadline, so a large archive can take longer overall while a stalled request still times out. Ranges must line up exactly; an inconsistent server response fails with SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, and a total over the cap with BYTE_LIMIT. The archive's SHA-256 is checked before use. Up to eight downloads run at once, sharing the session limits. Error response bodies from servers are discarded. You get a fixed message with the HTTP status.

Errors Oyzu generates include a code and a fixed message, without the URL, query, token or server error text: Status Code Meaning and next step 400 REQUEST_INVALID A malformed request from a builder. Report it as a bug. 403 SOURCE_DENIED No allowed source matches the request or redirect. Check the source configuration. 413 BYTE_LIMIT A size limit was exceeded. Check the dependency's size. 429 REQUEST_LIMIT The session ran out of requests. Check how many dependencies are being resolved. 502 SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE The download failed after retries. Check the source and your connection, then rerun. 502 REDIRECT_INVALID, REDIRECT_LIMIT An invalid or too long redirect chain. Fix the source endpoint. 504 SOURCE_TIMEOUT The network deadline expired. Check the source and your connection, then rerun. For BYTE_LIMIT, the error also reports which limit was hit (response, session or artifact), the bytes observed and the limit. The pnpm adapter includes these in its failure message. When a server itself returns an error, its real status is kept with a redacted body, and the package manager shows it its own way. Maven runs with -e so nested resolution causes appear in failed builds. A failed preparation produces no dependency snapshot or build plan. The next build prepares fresh inputs.

Container npm builds fill npm's cache with npm cache add, 16 archives or 16 MiB at a time. When that fails, the message names the batch, archive count and size, the exit status and signal, and any recognized OS error code, errno and system call, for example: npm cache seed batch 1 (16 archives; 4066624 bytes): npm cache add failed (244): status=244; signal=none Oyzu may read the end of npm's debug log for these codes. Raw log text, arguments, configuration and URLs aren't included, and the log isn't kept in the bundle. An exit status like 244 alone doesn't mean the worker ran out of memory; use the reported cause to decide.

Artifact set installs use the same client, with one source per host route, and two differences: A source with redirects = "server" treats any 3xx response as ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNEXPECTED and doesn't follow it. A redirect to a host that no route allows fails with ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNROUTABLE. A redirect to a host with its own rule is fetched from that rule's destination. With no tools route configured, redirects may reach any HTTPS host. Redirect targets and their query strings are never stored or reported.

Rust helper archives (nextest and cargo-llvm-cov) download through this client. Public downloads use GitHub and its release-asset redirect host. A configured tool connector replaces that public source, with no fallback to the public one. The recipe is checked against its metadata before download, and the archive digest before extraction. See helper installation.

Downloads in progress can't be interrupted immediately when a session ends. Private registries other than those builders support, and automatic credential refresh, aren't supported. A successful retry doesn't authenticate a dependency or make it eligible for release.
Declared fetches for pinned downloads in build.yaml. Artifact sets for routed tool installs.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/action-cache.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A repeat oyzu build skips targets whose inputs haven't changed and restores their earlier results. You configure nothing: you never write cache keys or per-language cache paths. This page covers what is reused, what invalidates it, how to see why a stage ran, and how to share results through a registry. Note: The action cache is experimental. The remote cache is unsigned, so a remote hit tells you which run produced a result, not that the result was verified.

oyzu build # first build runs and stores; repeats reuse oyzu build --affected HEAD # Git-selected targets also reuse unchanged results oyzu build --full # quality stages and their reports are reused too oyzu build --no-cache # run every action; read and write nothing oyzu cache status # where the store is, how large, how many entries oyzu cache clear # remove every cached result (bundles are untouched) oyzu build --explain # after the build, why each stage was reused or ran oyzu cache explain api # why target api's key (and its stages' keys) last changed Every oyzu cache command supports the global --json flag before or after the subcommand. They read no project beyond configuration. Output shortened. A project with four targets, one run each: $ oyzu build # cold ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 4 executed · 9.4s $ oyzu build # unchanged repeat ↺ api build reused was 1.2s ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 4 reused · 1.8s $ echo "// edit" >> api/src/greeting.mjs && oyzu build ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 3 reused · 1 executed · 3.1s Reuse is local to one user on one machine unless you configure a remote cache. Every output says plainly that a restored result was not executed now: Receipts keep reused test evidence apart from fresh tests. When known, reuse.source records whether the local or remote store served the result. An unavailable cache is different from --no-cache. If the store can't be used, permitted native builds continue with a warning and run everything.

Control Effect oyzu build --no-cache No lookup and no storage for this build. The summary shows disabled (--no-cache). cache.local = false Same, from configuration (default true). cache.dir Absolute directory that replaces the default store location. User or system scope only. A project oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml that sets it is rejected with CONFIG_SCOPE. User-scope configuration is ignored in CI. oyzu cache status / clear Show or empty the store. status also reports the Docker image budget. oyzu build --explain, oyzu cache explain <target> Explain why stages were reused or ran. Read-only. cache.remote, cache.read, cache.write The remote OCI cache: destination, lookup (default on) and publishing (default off). cache.ciRemote, cache.immutableTags The CI repository, and whether the registry refuses to replace tags (default off). build.host-workspaces-dir Absolute directory where native builds park private copies of your source. User or machine configuration only. Doesn't affect cache keys. See configuration. Keys and cache paths are never user-authored. Native builds work from a private copy of each target's source, kept in a host-workspaces folder next to the action store. It follows the platform cache location, not cache.dir. Use build.host-workspaces-dir to put it on another drive. It must be outside the source tree. Oyzu renames the copy into place when it can, and otherwise copies only the pruned source, keeping file times and permissions so native tools such as Cargo still see unchanged files as fresh. A real source edit still invalidates native compilation. Oyzu never copies compiler, dependency or tool caches. Changing the setting doesn't move existing parked workspaces.

Host Default store Linux $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/actions (fallback ~/.cache/oyzu/actions) macOS ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/actions Windows %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\actions The store is per user and shared across projects. It holds blobs/sha256/ (file bytes), results/<key>.json (result descriptors), quarantine/ (rejected data) and tmp/. Output trees are stored as a manifest plus one file per blob, not as a compressed archive.

At the end of a build, if the store is over 10 GiB, Oyzu removes the least recently used results until it fits, then removes blobs no result references. A hit refreshes an entry. Eviction touches only the cache. Bundles in dist hold their own copies. The budget is fixed. Builds hold a shared lock on store.lock while they read or write the cache. An unused store isn't created. Runs with the cache disabled, or with nothing cacheable, leave it alone. oyzu cache clear needs exclusive access. While a build uses the cache it fails with a retry message and leaves active staging alone. Retry when the build finishes. If end-of-build eviction hits contention it warns, and the store may briefly exceed its budget. A later build retries. If a store is busy with maintenance, builds proceed without it and cache commands return an error. Don't delete store.lock to clear contention. The lock protects cooperating Oyzu processes, not external deletion or filesystems without working locks.

Oyzu hashes file bytes while copying them into the cache and again when restoring them. It checks every file of a restored action before accepting the hit, and it replaces each destination file only after its copy succeeded, so a missing or corrupt blob leaves the previous file in place. Corrupt cache data is rejected, quarantined and recomputed (see Failures and recovery). A restore that touches several files isn't rolled back if a later file operation fails. Artifact and report gates still run after a restore.

The unit of reuse depends on what Oyzu knows about the target: Per action for targets whose actions carry a stage contract (today node/package on the captured path). Each action (for example api:version, api:build, api:package) has its own key and result. See Per-action reuse. The target's group record lists its action results, so an unchanged repeat restores the whole target in one step. Per target for every other builder: one key per target, restoring all its actions together or none. A reused target or action keeps: its artifacts, byte for byte (each is checked against its recorded digest); its original JUnit, coverage and other reports and their producer evidence; the original run ID, key and completion time, in a reuse record. Oyzu stores a target only after all its actions succeeded and its reports were collected. Failed, blocked and cancelled targets aren't stored. Built-in builders declare their own actions, so their stages are cacheable with no configuration. Declared source inputs are included in the target's key on both native and captured paths.

These targets simply run, and the output says why: Targets with authored tasks or task overrides that don't ask to be cached, and targets whose hooks ([tasks."api:pre_build"]) declare no outputs. An authored task with cache = true and outputs is cached (see Authored tasks). A hook that declares outputs is followed on targets reused action by action (see Hooks). Targets with hooks on a path that reuses a target only whole (native host targets with hooks, and captured targets without stage contracts). Restoring them would skip hooks that must run on every build. Targets that use secret environment values ({ secret = "…" }).

For native npm applications with dependencies, the target includes the prepare action (npm ci). A hit restores the successful result without reinstalling. A miss installs into the private target workspace before pre-build hooks. Results stored by an older Oyzu simply miss. Nothing needs clearing.

Before looking up actions, the captured npm path validates native metadata and downloads locked dependency bytes with lifecycle scripts turned off. That script-free step can be reused from the local store. The key covers the full source and target tree, the worker image and platform, the admitted tools, the command and environment, configuration and the download routes. Any change to the source, lock, tools, routes or configuration needs a new download. Tools are checked before lookup, and restored files are verified before use. The later offline install and lifecycle scripts aren't cached. The journal records a reused step as not executed now, with its original time and key. These entries share the local store, lock and 10 GiB budget. They are never uploaded to a remote cache. A missing or damaged entry falls back to a fresh download. Partly restored trees are discarded. --no-cache, cache.local = false and --verify-contract turn this reuse off. Builds with managed configuration, secret environment values or authenticated routes don't use it. Offline builds can reuse earlier captures.

Native builder actions can bind exact prepared-resource files. The plan records those files and their content digest, and execution mounts the same selection even with --no-cache. Native Go tests run in fresh copies of the captured workspace with empty report folders. Their writes are discarded, and validated reports are captured into the build bundle. Reused reports keep their original producer evidence. Workspace consumers of generated files, and --verify-contract, aren't supported on this path. See Go.

Captured path: oyzu build and oyzu build --affected on targets that use the Docker executor and its toolchain images (for example node/package). Native host path: builds that run on the host with Oyzu-provisioned tools (node/app dist applications, Go, Rust, Python wheels) reuse unchanged targets the same way. See Native host builds. Targets built by a host-coordinated image worker aren't cached yet and say so. oyzu run executions are never cached. No account is needed. Ephemeral CI runners start with an empty local store. With a remote cache they reuse results other checkouts pushed. Tested mainly on Linux. On a Windows host, shared edits conservatively re-run unrelated work. macOS isn't supported yet. On Windows, action tracking records native symbolic links and the Linux links Docker creates in a captured workspace without following them, so pnpm links stay usable by later native actions. A change that contains links can't be restored from the cache. Other Windows reparse formats fail with an error.

In the live Build section, restored actions show ↺ (the word reused without color) in place of executed. The summary counts them apart from executed work (2 targets · 3 reused · 1 executed). With -v and in JSON you also get each target's reuse origin and the Cache line. The final receipt marks test and coverage lines from restored reports as reused from an earlier run, not run now. In the build bundle a reused action keeps status: "succeeded", so every gate applies unchanged, and gains: "actionKey": "sha256:…", "reuse": { "actionKey": "sha256:…", "originalRunId": "…", "originalCompletedAt": "2026-10-07T08:43:02Z", "originalDurationMs": 812 } manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"] records the mode, whether the cache was active or disabled (and why) and each target's outcome: reused, executed (with stored, and rejected if a damaged entry was replaced) or not-cached with the reason. Journal events in logs/events.jsonl use the finish status reused. Logs for reused actions aren't recreated. A hit never skips a gate. On restore, every report is parsed again from its stored bytes and judged by the current contract (for example the coverage minimum). A report that fails there rejects the entry, and the target runs normally. Preflight, policy and required-check enforcement are unchanged.

Two read-only views answer "why did this stage run or get reused?". Both name the first key component that differs from the last build of the same target or stage, so a miss points at what changed. Each key is made of named components, compared in this order: Component What it covers Parts named on a change builder The builder ID and digest (an Oyzu upgrade changes it) platform, variant The target platform and variant toolchain The toolchain: image content digest or resolved tool lock, host platform dependencies The prepared dependencies (for Node, node_modules) source The source digest in scope: the whole target scope, or a confined action's predicted reads definition The frozen action definitions, field by field and environment variable by variable: argv, env.<NAME>, cwd, limits, report contracts, configuration digest, input mounts api:build env.MODE (group key) or env.MODE (action key) materialized Digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets The artifact ID upstream Output digests of the earlier actions an action follows The action ID When several components differ, the first is the reason and the rest are listed after it. The key alone decides reuse. Components only explain it. source comes before definition because an action's environment can carry values derived from source, such as the development version. Every lookup also records the subject's latest key in history/ under the store: the run that first and last used it, and the distinct key before it. A subject is a target or, for targets reused action by action, each action. History is written even when nothing is stored (a failed build, an always-run target), is a few kilobytes per subject and is removed by oyzu cache clear.

After the receipt, it shows at most eight action decisions, with a count of the rest. The manifest has complete detail. A blocked or failed action keeps its failure cause. An expanded entry looks like this: Why each stage ran or was reused api:build — Executed Recorded selection: api (requested) Reuse: source files in scope changed Source comparison: run previous-observation changed: shared/greeting.mjs (reads-source) Native provenance: applications/api/build.mjs:2 (path, exact) Other reasons you may see: no earlier build of it is recorded in this cache (first build, or after cache clear) inputs unchanged since run …, but no result is stored (not stored, evicted or cleared) the stored result was rejected: … (damaged entry) a hook runs on every build… a note that the result came from a remote A stage of a target that is reused or run whole shares the target's reason. A target that isn't cacheable shows its not-cached reason. --explain conflicts with --plan and --remote. It changes only the human output. The reasons are always in the manifest, under manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target> as explain ({reason, changed?, previousRunId?, sourceChanges?}) and, per action, actionExplain.<action>, so --json carries them without the flag. A failed local lookup is recorded as lookup: unavailable with the cause, which is different from a stored result that failed validation.

Oyzu keeps a source inventory per captured context in the cache history. sourceChanges compares the previous build's file identities with the current ones under the action's read scope (or the whole target scope), including added and removed files. Exact reads are labeled reads-source, approximate bounds bounded-read, and unmodeled relationships scope-input. sourceChanges.status is available, unavailable or scope-changed. Oyzu never guesses file names when the inventory is missing or the boundary changed. These inventories follow the history rules: --no-cache writes none, and cache clear removes them. Windows has no confined actions, but captured whole-scope comparison works. Native builds without captured context explain at target level only.

Reads the key history for a target ID (its group key and every recorded action) or one action ID such as api:build. For each it shows the latest key, the runs that first and last used it, whether a result is stored and the first component that differs from the previous key. It reads no project and runs nothing, so it works between builds and on another checkout that shares the store. An unknown name exits non-zero with no key history for <name> in this cache. $ oyzu cache explain api Cache key explanation api api (whole target) Key 3608cd663130 · since run 26520-… · last seen run 26520-… (2026-10-10T10:04:22Z) Result stored · the next build with these inputs reuses it Changed since run 25996-…: source files in scope changed (also: action definition: api:build env.OYZU_VERSION, api:build env.PROOF_VALUE added and 7 more) api:build (stage) Key f700515a6d9c · since run 26520-… · last seen run 26520-… (2026-10-10T10:04:23Z) Result stored · the next build with these inputs reuses it Changed since run 23970-…: source files in scope changed (also: action definition: env.OYZU_VERSION, env.PROOF_VALUE added and 1 more; output of an earlier action: api:version) --json returns kind: "action-cache-explain" with subjects[] (id, kind, target, actionKey, firstRunId, lastRunId, lastSeenAt, stored, previous, reason, changed). Limits: History keeps two distinct keys per subject, so cache explain compares the latest keys, not an arbitrary older build. To look at a finished build, use history. A stage's previous run can be older than its target's, because a build that restores a target whole doesn't look up its actions. Builds that share one store at the same time can interleave history writes. Each write is atomic and the later one wins.

A target's key is a SHA-256 over these inputs and nothing else: Input Notes The target's actions Command, environment, working directory, platforms, limits, report contracts and configuration digest. Scheduling settings such as build.jobs aren't part of it. Source in scope The target's own directory, the directories of every target it declares as a prerequisite (depends_on, materialize, task dependencies, the same edges --affected uses) and every file no target owns (root build.yaml, oyzu.toml, locks) Toolchain The resolved image's content digest, not its tag Prepared dependencies The dependency snapshot's content (lock digests, prepared tree, manager identity), not where or when it was prepared Builder The builder's digest Materialized inputs Digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets, known once producers finish Host paths, run IDs, timestamps, credentials and the number of parallel jobs never enter a key. A serial build, a --jobs N build and a host with a different core count share hits, and so do different checkouts, worktrees and branches. Changing one target's inputs re-runs exactly that target. One thing to know: execution-only settings such as --full are part of the configuration digest, so changing them re-keys every action.
documents.s: Inputs and what invalidates a target

documents.t: The native path has no plan of captured inputs, so its key is built from what the host build actually saw: Input Notes The target's actions Each eligible Rust action, otherwise the whole group: command line (per-invocation locations such as temporary output folders become fixed tokens), environment variable names, working directory, report contracts and configuration identity Source The digest of the target's private source copy: its own directory plus declared inputs. Native tools are host processes, so ambient reads outside this are not in the key. Tools The digest of oyzu.lock and the host platform Builder The Oyzu executable's digest. For a target built by an external builder plugin, also that plugin's identity. Materialized inputs Digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets A tool that isn't in the lock (a system C compiler used by cgo, or sh) isn't part of the key. Use --no-cache after changing such a tool. A restored native target keeps its materialization receipts, and promoted local binaries (.oyzu/bin) are refreshed from the restored artifact as after a run. Conventional native Rust stages have independent results. Adding --full to an unchanged build reuses the existing executable and runs only the new checks, and a repeat full build restores the checks with their original reports and compiler warnings (labeled as reused). A compile that succeeded stays reusable if a later check fails. Stdout and stderr logs stay available after reuse. Independent Rust stages get separate private source copies and Cargo target folders and can overlap within --jobs. Coverage has its own instrumented compile. Hooks, task replacements and materialized inputs stay serial and whole-target. This is host execution, not a sandbox. The pinned tools must include the selected check helpers. An incomplete lock reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE; run oyzu pin and retry.

The cache trusts the declared target graph, like --affected. An action that reads another target's directory without a declared edge is invisible to the key. For example, if api and web copy ../shared but declare no relationship to it, editing shared/ reuses their old results, while oyzu build --no-cache rebuilds them. Native cross-root dependency discovery isn't implemented. Declare relationships in build.yaml (depends_on: [shared]), or use --no-cache, for builds that read across target directories.

A target built by an external builder plugin (a plugins.development or plugins.packages binding) is reused like a built-in target. Oyzu writes the plugin's verified identity on the target record as extensions["oyzu.dev/builder-plugin"] and includes it in the target and action keys next to the Oyzu executable digest: {"reference":"go/app","source":"package","package":"oyzu/go","version":"0.1.0", "release":"sha256:…","executableDigest":"sha256:…","runtime":{"os":"linux","arch":"amd64","abi":null}} {"reference":"go/app","source":"local-development","executableDigest":"sha256:…", "runtime":{"os":"linux","arch":"amd64","abi":null}} runtime uses the plugin package names (linux/darwin/windows, amd64/arm64, gnu/musl/msvc). A development executable's ABI is unknown and recorded as null. A changed plugin executable, package release or version, runtime or reference re-runs the target, and explain reports builder identity changed. Reverting reuses the earlier result. How the plugin was selected (resolved now or locked) doesn't change a key. A plugin-built target never shares a key with the built-in builder it replaces. For a development binding, the digest covers only the bound file. If that file isn't a native executable (a wrapper script or .cmd file, for example), what it runs is outside the key, so its targets are not-cached with the reason "is built by a development plugin binding that is not a native executable". Bind the plugin executable itself to get reuse. A native wrapper executable is keyed on its own digest alone, so rebuild or rebind it after changing what it starts. Plugin-built results stay in the local store. They are never sent to cache.remote or cache.ciRemote, and --slice refuses the target with EXTERNAL_BUILDER. The usual exclusions still apply: --no-cache, cache.local = false, --verify-contract, secret environment values and hooks without declared outputs keep a target out of the cache.

Planning attaches a stage contract to each action of an analyzed target: the reads, writes, environment names and tools the static analysis found for the stage, the actions it follows, and whether its outputs are bounded. A target whose actions all have a contract is reused action by action. Today that is node/package on the captured path. Step Behavior Lookup The target's group record is tried first (unchanged target: one step). On a miss, each action is looked up when it becomes ready. Action key The action's frozen definition, the target scope, toolchain, builder, variant, platform, prepared dependencies (only if the action reads them), materialized artifacts and the output digests of the earlier actions it follows Action result The files the action published to the bundle (artifacts, reports), their records and the workspace changes it made (files created, modified and deleted, new folders) Reuse Records enter the manifest as succeeded with a reuse record. Reports are parsed again and gated by the current contract. Workspace changes are restored before the next action that has to run, so later actions see what running it would have left. A fully reused target never touches its workspace. Early cutoff A re-run action that produces the same workspace changes leaves its dependents' keys unchanged, so they are still reused. Always runs An action without bounded outputs never gets reused on its own. It runs every time, and what it produces still feeds what follows. A target holding such an action isn't restored whole. Storing Results are saved only after the whole target succeeded and its reports were collected. Without a confining contract (see below), an action's key uses the whole target scope. Targets with an authored task or override that doesn't set cache = true with outputs, or a hook without declared outputs, are not cached. An action that creates a symbolic link or special file can't be restored, so it still runs and feeds its dependents but isn't stored. The manifest records each action's outcome (reused, executed, always-run) under manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target>.actions.

A hook ([tasks."api:pre_build"], post_<stage>) that declares outputs doesn't make a per-action target uncacheable: [tasks."api:pre_build"] argv = ["node", "hook.mjs"] outputs = ["generated"] # workspace paths, folders or globs the hook writes Aspect Behavior The hook Runs on every build. It is never restored and its record never has reuse. The action record shows always-run. Its output The files it changed are recorded, and their digest enters the key of every later action of the target. A hook that writes something else re-runs what follows. A hook that writes the same bytes leaves it reused. Target outcome reused when every other action was reused. Otherwise executed. The target's group record isn't stored. Undeclared effects A hook that changes a file outside its declared outputs isn't followed. Nothing of the target is stored, and the outcome carries a rejected note naming the files, so the next build runs it again. No outputs The target is not-cached ("hooks without declared outputs"). Whole-target path On the native host path and on captured targets without stage contracts, a target is only restored whole, which would skip its hooks. It is not-cached and its hooks run every build. outputs paths are relative to the hook's working directory (the target, unless cwd says otherwise). Use / or \. Editing a hook script counts as a source edit, so it re-runs actions keyed on the target scope and any confined action that reads the script. On Windows no action is confined, so any source edit re-runs the whole target, though an unchanged repeat is still reused. Whether a script edit also changes the development version, which is in every action's environment, depends on the hook: Hook Development version Comment-only edit of its script pre_build with outputs, on a builder that finalizes versions (Node) Finalized after the hook (below) Keeps the version. A confined api:build is reused. Any other hook (pre_test, post_build, …) or another builder The script stays in the version scope Changes the version, which re-keys every action of the target

On captured Node targets, Oyzu moves the version action after the followed pre_build hooks, so nothing that writes the version runs before them: Planning records every action in plan.json with the pre-hook source version (the version scope without the hook's script). The target record carries extensions["oyzu.dev/version-finalization"]. The actions before the hook run with the pre-hook version. When the hooks succeed, the files under their declared outputs are digested from the workspace (so --no-cache gives the same result) and folded into the version. The target is planned again, and the remaining actions run from that post-hook plan, written to plans/<target>.post-hooks.json. plan.json itself isn't changed. The manifest's target record is the post-hook one. manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/version-finalization"].<target> gives preHookVersion, version, hookOutputs, planPath and planDigest. A hook edit that changes what it writes changes the version and the package. A script stays in the version scope if it isn't named as an argument of the hook's command (for example run = "node hook.mjs" through a shell) or if a builder stage reads or writes it. Other builders, other hook phases and the native host path aren't finalized. Effects outside the workspace (network, global state) are invisible to Oyzu, so declare them away yourself.

An authored task or task override isn't cached by default, because Oyzu can't see its effects. Opt in with the cache and outputs task fields: [tasks."api:test"] run = "node --test" cache = true inputs = ["src/**", "test/**"] # optional; may only add to the target scope outputs = [".events"] # workspace paths, folders or globs the task writes Aspect Behavior Opt-in cache = true and at least one outputs entry. The plan marks the action cacheable: true and records the declaration in extensions["oyzu.dev/authored-cache"]. cache on a hook is ignored: hooks always run. Key The task's frozen definition (command, environment names, working directory, report contracts, configuration digest) and the target scope, as for a builder stage. Editing a file in the target, or the task, re-runs it. inputs Relative to the task's directory. Entries inside the target are already covered. An entry outside the target isn't supported yet: the target is not-cached ("declares inputs outside its target …"). Per-action targets (captured node/package) The task is a reusable action. Its workspace changes must lie inside its declared outputs, otherwise nothing is stored and the outcome carries a rejected note. Around a hook it is reused while the hook's output is unchanged. Whole-target path (native host, other builders) The target is reused whole when every action is a builder stage or a cached authored task. Reports are restored and gated again. Declared outputs aren't checked here. A target with hooks isn't cached on this path. cache = true without outputs not-cached: "<task> sets cache = true but declares no outputs, so it is not cached" --no-cache, cache.local = false Nothing is reused or stored. A task that leaves nothing in the workspace must still name an output (for example the folder its tool writes logs to). Reusing a task around hooks needs per-action reuse, which only captured node/package targets have. A command the builder doesn't recognize for report instrumentation keeps today's reporting behavior.

A narrow key is only sound if the action can't see anything the key left out. So Oyzu keys an action on the files its contract reads only when the action also runs confined to them. This needs the captured path and a Unix host. Linux is tested. macOS isn't supported yet. Windows doesn't support confinement, so every action there keeps the whole-target key. Step Behavior Eligible The stage's own command was modeled by the analysis, none of its facts is an unbounded unknown (a bounded one adds its bound to the reads, see bounded unknowns), and its outputs are bounded. For an analyzed Node package that covers build and test from its scripts, plus the builder's own commands: version, the npm install (prepare), npm pack (package) and the default ESLint and Prettier checks (lint, format-check) of a package without such scripts. pnpm and Yarn installs and packs, workspace plans, application packages, Biome and authored replacements keep the whole-target key. See builder-owned stages. Key The digest of the source files the contract reads, the output digests of every earlier action of the target (except a check ordered before it only to share the workspace, see checks that run at once), the frozen action, toolchain, prepared dependencies and materialized artifacts. Editing a file the stage doesn't read leaves its key alone only if the edit also leaves the development version unchanged. Any other edit changes the version, which is in every action's environment, and re-keys every action. View Before the action runs, the executor builds a private view of the workspace with only the declared reads, what the earlier actions created, and the artifacts materialized for it, and mounts it as /workspace. Other files don't exist for the action. Merge When the action ends, what it created, changed or deleted in the view is merged back into the workspace. Not confined Any action without a contract, with an unbounded unknown fact or write, on a builder without analysis, on the native host path and on hosts without view support. These keep the whole-target key. Example: oyzu build --full on a Node api target after appending a comment to api/test/greeting.test.mjs: · api:build Reused from an earlier run · not executed now · originally ran … (key 0452eeca9fb2) › api:test Running Cache active · 3 targets reused The same edit also reuses api:version, api:prepare and api:package (it packs only files: ["dist"]) and re-runs api:lint and api:format-check, which read every JavaScript file of the target. manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target>.confined lists the confined actions. --no-cache and cache.local = false turn off lookup and storage, but eligible actions keep the same private views, so a fresh run sees exactly the files a reusable run would.

Static analysis sometimes meets a construct it can't resolve, an unknown fact. An unknown can carry a bound: the files, globs, task environment or installed packages the construct can't read outside of. A stage whose unknowns are all bounded has scope widened. Its reads gain each bound, and it still runs confined with a narrow key. One unbounded unknown keeps the whole stage on the whole-target key, unconfined. Bound Covers Example Hard What the tool's own rules allow npm pack files entries (the package folder), an unexpanded test pattern (the runner's root), a computed environment mode (<envDir>/.env*), a missing relative import (the files resolution probes), a tsconfig extending a package (installed packages and the config's folder), computed process.env access (the task's environment) Heuristic Where a tool usually stays A command with no tool profile (prettier, biome, oxlint, tsup) or an unmodeled subcommand or flag (next lint, ng test, vitest --coverage): its folder, the files directly in each folder above it, and installed packages. Task runners (turbo, nx, lerna, ultra, wireit) are never bounded. A bound that relies on installed packages counts only for an action that reads the prepared dependencies. If a confined widened action reads outside its bound, it fails with the path and the inputs fix (see below). Declared inputs add to a bound but never bound an unbounded unknown. oyzu build --plan shows scope: widened and each bound in the Why column. --why <path> answers covered-by-bound for a path only a bound covers.

The check stages of one target (test, lint, format-check, scheduled by --full or CI) don't produce anything another check consumes, so the plan marks the edge between two consecutive checks as order-only. A hook between them, or a declared depends_on, keeps the edge a real dependency. When build.jobs is above 1, a check starts as soon as what it really needs (for example build) has finished, beside the checks ordered before it, if all of these hold: the check runs confined (and --verify-contract isn't set); every action of its target already running is a confined check; no two of them declare writes that could meet (a glob counts as its literal folder). Otherwise it waits its turn. Serial and parallel runs give the same keys and outputs: Behavior View A check's view leaves out what the checks ordered before it left, and checks that may overlap get copied files instead of hard links, so one check's in-place write can't reach another. Key A check's key follows the actions its view shows, not the checks ordered before it. package still follows every check. Failure A failed check doesn't block the next check. It still blocks package and everything after it. A check that finishes early is recorded after the checks ordered ahead of it. Different targets still run one action at a time per branch. The native host path and Windows have no views, and oyzu run stays serial.

A development snapshot version (1.2.3-dev.g<digest>) is written into package.json by the version action, so it feeds every later action. Oyzu derives it from the target's source scope, minus files that only a quality stage (test, lint, format-check) is known to read exactly. A test-only edit changes neither the version nor the artifact names. A new test file, which only a glob finds, does. An unknown fact of a shipping stage (build, package) counts as reading its bound, or every file if it has none, so a test-only file that a computed import of build may reach stays in the version. If several targets share the folder holding a file, the file is left out only if every one of them reads it only from a quality stage. The script of a followed pre_build hook leaves its own target's scope, and what the hook wrote is folded in after it runs (version finalization). For a captured target whose final commands are all bounded, cacheable and confinable, the suffix uses the files its shipping commands read, plus configuration, lock files and declared inputs. This needs Unix view support. Targets with hooks, authored replacements, source projections, materialized inputs or cross-target prerequisites keep the wider scope. See version inference. Tagged and history-derived versions don't change. The version reaches every action as OYZU_VERSION.

If a confined action fails and its output names a file that exists in the target but not in the view, the build reports the stage, the path, the missing fact and the smallest fix, in human, NO_COLOR and --json output (diagnostic confined-read-outside-contract, with details in manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-violations"]): ERROR api:build read extra.txt, which its stage contract does not declare, so the confined view hid it. Missing fact: reads-path extra.txt Fix: declare it as an input of api in build.yaml: inputs: ["api/extra.txt"] (Or make the reference static so the analysis sees it.) Declare the path as an input. The declaration is relative to build.yaml, while the read path is shown as the target's own files write it. --json carries the same declaration as fix.declare.inputs. Oyzu finds the file by scanning the action's output for paths, so a tool that fails without printing the path is reported only as a failed action. The builder's node --test stage also runs the spec reporter on stderr, so a test file that reads an undeclared file is explained like any other stage. The behavior is the same when targets run in parallel.
documents.s: When a confined action reads something undeclared

documents.t: A target's inputs in build.yaml name extra source paths it reads (files or folders, relative to build.yaml; see target workspaces). On the captured path each one: joins the target's source scope, so the whole-target key and the development version cover it; joins the reads of every stage contract of the target, so a confined action sees it and its narrow key covers it. A target-level input re-keys test too when the file changes, even if only build reads it; only adds. It never removes an inferred read, and it never makes an action confinable. An input that leaves the workspace (the folder holding build.yaml) or names no captured file is a CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE error before anything runs, so a typo can't silently declare nothing. Globs aren't accepted. A folder covers everything beneath it. --affected doesn't yet treat a change under another target's declared input as affecting the declaring target.

oyzu build --verify-contract # also: --json, --full This can't be combined with --no-cache or --plan. A normal build runs. In addition, for every confined action: The action starts from a copy of its target workspace and runs confined, as usual. The same action runs again from an identical copy with the whole target visible. Oyzu compares the results: exit code, every workspace file created, changed or deleted, and the artifacts collected. Test and coverage report files aren't compared, because they carry timing. Equal results pass. If they differ, Oyzu re-runs the action with subsets of the hidden files (at most twelve extra runs) to find a minimal set that explains the difference, and names those files and the declaration that fixes them: Contract check failed · 8 confined actions run again with their whole target visible · 7 equal · 1 diverged · 20 not confined (not checked) api:build Diverged · also reads optional.json · declare inputs: ["api/optional.json"] A divergence fails the build, including when independent targets run in parallel (diagnostic contract-diverged; manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-verification"] has status, counts and one record per action). The check uses a throwaway store, so it reuses and stores nothing. It doesn't run on the native path. Each confined action runs at least twice with copies of the workspace, so it is slow on large installed trees. Actions that aren't confined are counted, not checked. If the search stops at its budget, the record says minimal: false.

You can share action results through any OCI registry. Share them from CI to developers, or between a team's machines. # oyzu.toml (project): where results are shared [cache] remote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache" # user configuration: this machine also publishes what it builds [cache] write = true Supported registries: zot, CNCF Distribution behind a token service, and a Harbor proxy-cache project, on Linux. Other registries (Artifactory, Nexus, Docker Hub, GHCR) aren't supported yet, and neither are Windows and macOS clients.

Setting Default Meaning cache.remote unset The OCI repository to share results. Accepted only in user/global, machine or administrative scope. cache.read true once cache.remote is set Look results up. cache.write false Publish results. cache.ciRemote unset The CI repository, see CI and development repositories. Same scope rule as cache.remote. cache.immutableTags false The registry never replaces a tag. See CI and development repositories. A project or local file that sets cache.remote or cache.ciRemote fails with a scope error, even in trusted project folders. Use the environment variables OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE and OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE for one invocation or CI. They override ordinary files and stay subject to administrative constraints. cache.read and cache.write are per-machine preferences and don't change action keys, so readers and writers share entries. A loopback host (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) is reached over plain HTTP. Every other host uses HTTPS with the shared proxy and trust settings. The remote is used only while the local cache is active. --no-cache, cache.local = false and --verify-contract use no remote.

Per-action results, for targets reused action by action (captured node/package and node/app targets with stage contracts). Whole-target results, for targets reused only whole (the native host path, other builders). These appear under the target's ID in the build record where an action ID would be. A per-action target's group record is never pushed. A client rebuilds it from the action results, so an unchanged repeat after a remote hit makes no registry request.

Step Behavior Lookup After a local miss, one GET of the manifest under the action's tag. On a hit, two blob GETs (config and layer). No HEAD requests, no tag listing. Verify Manifest shape, media types, key annotation, config and layer size and SHA-256, the uncompressed archive's SHA-256, every archive entry against its name, and the entries against the blobs the config references. Only then is the result committed to the local store. Push After an action's result is committed locally and cache.write is true: one GET of the tag (to check for a racing writer), config and layer uploads, then the manifest PUT, which is the only write that makes the entry visible. Offering a reused result If a build reuses a result this machine produced but never sent to this remote (stored before the remote was configured, or while it was down), it is pushed the same way. The store then marks it sent, so later reuses ask nothing. Results that came from a remote aren't offered. Racing writers Equal output identity (artifact digests and workspace changes; reports are excluded because they carry timing) converges and writes nothing. A different one is a conflict: recorded, never replaced.

A registry that requires sign-in is supported through the registry token flow. The credential is an environment variable, never a setting: export OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN=… # the token your registry's token endpoint accepts In a CI job that offers OIDC ID tokens the way GitHub Actions does (OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL and OYZU_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, which the Oyzu runner sets), leave OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN unset. The client signs in with the job's ID tokens and asks for a new one when needed. The credential is first sent as a bearer token. A 401 with a Bearer challenge names the registry's token endpoint. Oyzu uses it only if it is on the registry's own origin (scheme, host and port). Otherwise the request is denied and the credential is never sent elsewhere. The client then asks that endpoint for one token per repository, with OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN as the Basic password (user name oyzu), or with no credential if the variable is unset or empty. Tokens ask for pull, plus push when cache.write is true. A rejected or expired token is fetched again once. A second refusal is a denial. With ID tokens, the Basic password is the job's ID token: GET $OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL with ?audience=<registry origin> and the request token as a bearer, answered with {"value": "<jwt>"}. It is reused until 30 seconds before it expires. The request token goes only to that URL, and neither token is recorded. A blob response can redirect to another host (for example a separate blobs host with short-lived signed links). Redirects are followed without the Authorization header when they change origin, at most 5 times, and never from HTTPS to HTTP.

Repository <prefix>/v1alpha1/<first two key hex>, tag lookup-<64-hex key>. An OCI image manifest with artifactType application/vnd.oyzu.action-result.v1alpha1. The action-result descriptor as config (application/vnd.oyzu.action-result.config.v1alpha1+json) and one layer (application/vnd.oyzu.tree.v1alpha1.tar+zstd) holding every blob the descriptor references, named sha256/<hex>. Annotations: dev.oyzu.action.key, dev.oyzu.action.output and, on the layer, dev.oyzu.tree.uncompressed-digest.

The build record gains manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].remote: location, read, write, status (active, unavailable with reason, or unusable for a cache.remote the client can't use), counts of hits, pushed, converged, conflicts and rejected, the requests sent by kind, and per target the actions in each list. A result materialized from the remote carries extensions["oyzu.dev/remote-origin"] in the local store. The summary line adds the remote part, for example remote 7 reused · 0 pushed.

A project can name a second repository that only CI writes: # oyzu.toml (project) [cache] ciRemote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache/ci" # CI writes, everyone reads remote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache/dev" # optional: developers share here immutableTags = true # the registry never replaces a tag write = true # CI ignores user configuration Build Reads (after a local miss) Writes (with cache.write) CI (the execution context detects a CI provider or CI) cache.ciRemote only. cache.remote is recorded as skipped. cache.ciRemote Anywhere else cache.ciRemote, then cache.remote cache.remote only, never cache.ciRemote No cache.ciRemote cache.remote cache.remote The registry, not Oyzu, makes the CI repository trusted. It must refuse writes to that repository without the CI credential. Detecting CI only narrows what a build accepts. A build that sets CI without the credential is refused (403), keeps building and writes nothing. A CI build never reuses a developer's upload. It doesn't read cache.remote, and a result in its local store that came from a development remote is looked up again in the CI repository. A remote hit is recorded with its scope (ci or development). Nothing is signed, so a hit from the CI repository says where it was read, not who produced it. The registry credential is OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or, without it, the CI job's ID tokens. It is never a setting, and it is never written to a record or log. OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN is sent as a bearer token on every request to the configured registry host (over HTTPS or to a loopback host), and dropped when a redirect leads elsewhere. Immutable tags. cache.immutableTags = true says every configured cache repository refuses to replace a tag. A push then skips the racing-writer read, so a pushed action costs 6 requests instead of 7, and a refused manifest PUT (409 or 412) counts as the conflict. Don't set it for a registry that replaces tags, or the last writer silently wins. Either way, a hit is used only after the digests its manifest names verify.

Counted from the registry's own log for a project with one node/app target and seven cacheable actions (oyzu build --full): Build Manifest GET Blob GET Upload POST Blob PUT Manifest PUT Total Cold push (7 executed, 7 pushed) 14 0 14 14 7 49 Warm hit, second checkout, empty store (7 reused) 7 14 0 0 0 21 Partial hit, test-only edit (1 reused, 6 executed and pushed) 13 2 12 12 6 45 Unchanged repeat after a warm hit 0 0 0 0 0 0 A hit costs 3 requests per action. A miss that pushes costs 7. Signing in adds one token request per repository the build touches. With a storage-backed registry, a push can cost many more storage operations than the 3 objects an entry consists of (about 25 write-class operations per entry on CNCF Distribution's S3 driver), which matters if your object store bills per operation. Harbor's proxy cache revalidates every manifest with the upstream registry, so it saves blob traffic, not manifest requests.

Remote failures never fail a build: Situation Behavior 404 under the tag A miss. The action runs (and is pushed when writing). 5xx, 408, 429, timeout, connection failure Retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff and jitter. Then the remote is off for the rest of the build and everything is computed. 401 / 403 After sign-in (one token renewal), not retried. The remote is off for the build and no other route is tried. A wrong OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, no credential where one is required, and a read-only credential with cache.write = true all end here. The build computes and succeeds. 409 / 412 on the manifest PUT The registry refused to replace the tag: a conflict. Not retried. The entry there is kept and not read back. The remote stays on. Digest, size or shape mismatch, missing blob, conflicting config The entry is rejected and its bytes are quarantined in the local store (quarantine/remote-<key>-<part>). The action runs. The remote entry isn't repaired. Push failure The build succeeds. The record says why the entry wasn't pushed. Push interrupted before the manifest PUT Uploaded blobs stay unreferenced. Nothing is visible under the tag.

Sign-in uses only OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN (as a bearer token or through the registry token flow) or a CI job's ID tokens. There is no Basic auth to the registry itself, credential helpers, Docker configuration, login command or OAuth2 POST token form. Immutable tags are declared, not detected. Results aren't signed and producers aren't verified. Lookups aren't batched. Transfers are sequential. Entries above 256 MiB aren't pushed. There is no remote retention or pruning. A damaged remote entry is rejected by every reader but never repaired or replaced. An entry pushed by an older Oyzu without keyComponents in its config is rejected like a damaged one.

Situation Behavior No entry The target runs and is stored. Damaged blob or descriptor, mismatched key, unreadable entry Rejected and quarantined. The target runs and replaces it. The summary notes the rejection. Report gate fails on restore The entry is rejected and the target runs normally. Cache location missing, unwritable or unusable The build runs normally and stores nothing. cache.local = false / --no-cache Everything runs. Cancelled or failed build Completed actions that are valid on their own can still be reused. Failed or interrupted actions and failed targets have no stored result. Writes are atomic (stage, then rename), and a descriptor is published only after every blob it references. After a failed build, an eligible action's outputs, workspace changes and reports are sealed when it completes, so a later writer or target failure can't change them. An action whose required reports are missing or malformed isn't stored. Upgrading Oyzu invalidates entries, because the builder digest is part of the key.
