Nothing is migrated, and old entries age out through retention. Python application targets pass the whole-tree digest to the build (OYZU_SOURCE_DIGEST), so they miss on any edit.

The cache trusts the declared target graph (see Trust model). Targets built by a host-coordinated image worker, and authored tasks around hooks on the native host path, aren't cached. Version finalization after hooks covers only pre_build hooks on captured Node targets. Narrow keys are limited to the stages listed under Confined actions. Everything else keys on the whole target. Python targets miss on any edit until their source digest is scoped. Execution-only settings such as cache.local and cache.nativeMaxMiB currently change keys. Windows has no confined actions. macOS isn't supported yet.

Build bundles for what reuse records in the manifest, and build logging for the live view. Affected builds for Git-based selection, and native Node static analysis for stage contracts. Configuration for the cache.* settings.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/affected-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build --affected <git-ref> builds only the targets that changed since a Git commit, plus the targets that consume them and whatever those need to build. Use it in pull requests and CI to skip unchanged parts of a monorepo. Note: Affected builds are experimental. oyzu build --affected HEAD --plan oyzu build --affected origin/main oyzu inspect dist The ref must already exist locally; Oyzu doesn't fetch it. Git must be on PATH. --affected can't be combined with target names. No project configuration is needed. Without --affected, every target builds as usual.

Oyzu compares your current source with the committed files at the ref, including deleted files and executable-bit changes. A project nested inside a repository is compared with its own subtree. The usual source exclusions apply to both sides, so changes in dist, .oyzu, dependency folders and other excluded folders don't trigger builds. Checkout filters and line-ending conversion can make working files differ from committed ones; such differences count as changes. A changed file selects every target that contains it. Selection then follows consumers through depends_on, materialize.from and cross-target task prerequisites, transitively. The producers and task dependencies those targets need are added. Each selected target runs its normal checks and packaging. A native workspace (for example a Cargo workspace) is one target; individual members aren't selected separately. Oyzu doesn't detect one project reading another's files, so declare those dependencies. Execution follows the plain-build rules: native when every selected target supports it, otherwise the container executor.

--plan returns an empty preview and leaves dist alone. A build writes an empty, inspectable bundle with no tools, actions or artifacts. Old artifacts aren't copied into it, and unselected targets aren't reported as successful.

The plan and manifest record oyzu.dev/selection with mode: "affected", the impacted targets, the final selection and the excluded targets. Its affected object records the ref, the resolved commit, the source digest, changed paths, the reason each target was selected, and any fallback to a full build. The human output shows a Selection section: counts of changed, dependent and unaffected targets, the base and its short commit, or a Not narrowed notice with the fallback reason. See result output. These records describe the selection. They aren't release or CI evidence.

Oyzu builds everything when it can't safely narrow the selection: the ref can't be read locally; a file is new compared with the ref; a changed file belongs to no target; build, configuration or lock files changed; inputs of a root task with cross-target prerequisites changed; the configuration is managed by policy; Git object limits or unsupported entries prevent comparison. The recorded fallback says which. If the ref was missing, fetch it and run again. A fallback may need tools that a no-change build wouldn't.
documents.s: Falling back to a full build

documents.t: --affected works in a clone made with git clone --filter=blob:none, which has full history but only the file contents a checkout needs. Git fetches the contents of changed files from the remote on demand, so the clone needs read access to the repository. If that fetch fails, Oyzu falls back to a full build. Git fetches these one file at a time, so a very large change takes longer to plan. This is how a platform pool plans a remote run.

Changes to external configuration, tools or environment aren't seen by Git. Run a full build when those change. Reuse of cached actions isn't part of --affected itself; see the action cache. Discovery and validation still cover the whole workspace. Reading the baseline needs no network, but preparing selected targets may download dependencies. Git metadata never grants signing or publication rights.
Build tasks for target selection. Native local builds for the CI matrix from --plan --json --affected. Action cache for reusing unchanged results.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/ant.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The java/ant builder builds conventional and custom Ant projects in a container and exports versioned JARs. oyzu run test is a separate workflow on your machine that produces test and coverage reports without packaging a JAR. Both use the same Ant reporting integration. Note: The Ant builder is experimental. Captured builds run on Linux (Docker required). The builder is supplied by the oyzu-plugin-ant plugin (profile java/ant); see plugin catalog.

oyzu build --isolated --full oyzu inspect dist You need Docker and the base execution image. Oyzu pulls the image when it's missing. Ant 1.10.18, JUnit 4.13.2, Hamcrest 1.3, JaCoCo 0.8.13 and the Java quality tools are pinned upstream files. Preparation fetches them, checks them and restores them read-only at /scratch/java-integration, so there is nothing to build or install yourself. There is no host build path for Ant: captured builds always need the container. --isolated selects the container. --full adds the test and quality checks to build, archive and package. Isolation alone doesn't run all checks, and plain oyzu build keeps the fast defaults. Checks you marked required still run. Oyzu chooses the archive targets and JAR paths from what Ant reports for your project. It doesn't assume a layout. Ant projects with ivy.xml are refused, and arbitrary downloads from Ant aren't supported. The bundle contains the versioned JARs and the reports from the checks that ran. A failed check or a missing required report blocks the JARs and keeps the available reports in the failed bundle. A custom task that exits zero without writing its reports counts as incomplete reporting. To make the reports mandatory, add a [checks] section with tests = "required" and coverage = "required" (check levels). See direct reporting for how command success differs from verified results.

The JDK comes from oyzu.lock; the base image has none. It is used to evaluate the project and for every build action. For example: [tools] java = "21" Run oyzu pin, then oyzu build --isolated --full --frozen. The locked archive is restored read-only, and JAVA_HOME and PATH are fixed in the plan. Oyzu's Java integration needs JDK 17 or newer. Offline runs need the archives already captured. A missing or incompatible pin is refused before any action runs.

Captured builds use version inference over the native version property and your Git history. Oyzu asks Ant again with the chosen version and oyzu.version user properties before planning. The artifact name, the bundle version and the JAR's Implementation-Version agree. Qualifiers that can't take part in SemVer inference are kept. An exact tag produces a snapshot, not a release.

An Ant project with a conventional test target can run oyzu run test to write native test and coverage reports to a test-only dist/ bundle. It needs no Oyzu configuration. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist To use a different Ant target, replace the task: [tasks.test] argv = ["ant", "verify-contract"] One literal ant <target> command is instrumented, including the equivalent literal shell form. Compound shell commands and other replacements run unchanged and must write the required JUnit and JaCoCo reports themselves, at the paths in OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT. Extra arguments forwarded to the automatic reporting aren't supported and fail with an error. Target-qualified names and pre and post hooks work as in the common task engine. A failed test skips its success-only post hook. Discovery always provides an implicit test task. Without a test target in build.xml or a replacement, running it fails with Ant's missing-target error. Oyzu doesn't invent a test suite.

Install these before running: a JDK with java and javac, with JAVA_HOME set (or both on PATH); Ant, with ANT_HOME set to its folder; JaCoCo, with JACOCO_HOME set to a folder containing jacocoant.jar and jacocoagent.jar; your test libraries. JUnit projects need JUnit and Hamcrest in Ant's lib folder. Oyzu compiles its own Java integration into a temporary folder and starts Ant with your platform's classpath separator. It doesn't install tools or download dependencies.

The manifest links JUnit results and JaCoCo coverage for your application. JUnit suites keep individual tests and skipped cases. Forked Java assertion programs produce one case per run. They need fork="true" and failonerror="true". Coverage follows the src folder convention and the javac output that Oyzu observes. Test classes are excluded. Builds without line debug data keep the instruction counters they have instead of inventing line coverage. Other source layouts, alternate task implementations and the JUnit Platform need explicit reports. Direct tests keep your project's version properties, run the target's compile prerequisites, and can update your build output. They don't package snapshots or run lint and format checks. oyzu build --isolated --full applies versions, runs the quality checks and collects JARs. A missing tool, a compile error, a failed test, a missing or invalid report, or an unmet coverage constraint fails the command. The reports available at that point stay in the failed bundle. Fix the cause and rerun. See direct tests for output handling and provenance. Direct tests run on your machine with your network and environment, so they aren't isolated.

Run oyzu inspect dist after a build or a direct test run to check the bundle. A failed check, or a required report that is missing or invalid, fails the command, and the bundle keeps the reports that exist so you can see what happened.
Captured builds run on Linux only. Other source layouts and test frameworks need explicit reports.
Java quality tasks, direct tests, version inference.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/artifact-sets.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A resolved artifact set is a JSON file that lists, for each tool, version and platform, the download URLs, archive facts and verification evidence for a community-recipe tool. oyzu install --artifact-set reads such a file, decides which platforms are usable, writes their entries to oyzu.lock, and downloads and verifies the host artifact. Later installs replay the lock without the set file. Note: Experimental. Flags and error codes may change. Installing from the signed tool index is the normal path; use artifact sets only when you have a set file to install from directly. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. Installed recipe tools are not runnable yet (see Limitations). You can produce a set with oyzu tools resolve followed by oyzu tools evidence. No account is needed, and install and tools info never evaluate recipes themselves. # Check eligibility only: nothing is written or downloaded oyzu install --dry-run --artifact-set terraform.verified.json oyzu:terraform@1.16.5 oyzu --json tools info --artifact-set gh.verified.json aqua:cli/cli@2.102.0 --details # Pin a record by its digests.full, lock its platforms, download and verify the host artifact oyzu install --artifact-set go-task.verified.json --artifact-set-digest sha256:<digests.full> \ oyzu:go-task/task@3.54.0 # Replay from the lock alone (the set file can be gone); --offline reuses the verified cache oyzu install --frozen

Flag Meaning --artifact-set FILE A set file (JSON, format: 1, kind: "artifact-sets"). Repeatable. Accepted by install SPEC and tools info. With --frozen it is checked against the lock. --artifact-set-digest sha256:D Trusts one record by its digests.full. Repeatable. Without it, each file is a local set that you vouch for. --connector-bindings FILE Connector endpoints for routes. --details (tools info) Show every check and route. The spec can be oyzu:<name>@version, oyzu:owner/name@version, aqua:owner/name@version or recipe:owner/name@version. It matches records whose tool.id is aqua:owner/name or recipe:owner/name. The version matches either the upstream form (v1.16.5) or the normalized form (1.16.5). core: records (Oyzu's own providers) can't be installed from a set (LOCK_ID_UNREPRESENTABLE). Sets work in the project scope only; -g and --local aren't supported.

The whole file is rejected, and nothing is written, if: it is over 16 MiB, is malformed JSON or has a duplicate key; format isn't the integer 1 or kind is wrong (SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED); it has unknown top-level fields, more than 4096 records, a duplicate record, or records not sorted by tool ID, version and platform (SET_SCHEMA_INVALID). A single record is unusable (other records still count) if it has unknown fields or values, a URL that isn't plain https (no user info, fragment, backslash or dot segments), evidence that doesn't match its URLs, is over 1 MiB, or its recorded digests don't match its content (SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH). A set doesn't vouch for itself. Each record needs an anchor: a --artifact-set-digest pin, or your choice to use a local set.
documents.s: What a set file must look like

documents.t: You get one result per platform. Checks run in this order: Check What it checks Codes tool-admitted tools.allowed CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED set-integrity record is valid, anchored and not expired SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, SET_SCHEMA_INVALID, SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH, SET_UNANCHORED, SET_ANCHOR_EXPIRED, SET_DISAGREEMENT record-status resolved passes; unsupported means unavailable; error means invalid the record's own reason code evidence-floor verification tier and evidence TIER_BELOW_FLOOR, EVIDENCE_BELOW_FLOOR, EVIDENCE_VERIFIER_UNAVAILABLE, EVIDENCE_ORIGIN_NOT_ACCEPTED routes every download and evidence host can be reached through your routes ROUTE_UNROUTABLE, ROUTE_EGRESS_UNROUTABLE lock-representable (install only) the record fits in oyzu.lock LOCK_ID_UNREPRESENTABLE, DIGEST_NOT_SHA256, ARCHIVE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED Outcomes: Outcome Meaning eligible Usable. denied A rule blocks it; someone can change the rule. unavailable The set says there is no asset for this platform. It is left out of the lock and listed in unavailablePlatforms. Selecting that platform later fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. invalid The record can't be used. If set-integrity or record-status fails, later checks show skipped. The exit status is 1 for denied, invalid or an unavailable host platform, and 2 for argument errors. Human output starts with the outcome, then platforms, reasons and a "Denied by" table (rule, scope, reason, fix). --json prints the same result (outcome, results[].checks, denials, routes, code, written). Secrets, query strings and redirect targets are never shown. The minimum tier is verified and there is no evidence minimum. You can't change these yet.

Oyzu uses the lock first, then an anchored set, then a local set. It never falls back to evaluating a recipe. A record that matches a --artifact-set-digest is anchored. Without any digest, every record is local. When you pass digests, only matching records are used. The host platform must match; other unmatched platforms are left out of the lock. Two anchored records for the same registry snapshot with different content fail with SET_DISAGREEMENT, and neither is used. In managed mode, local sets are refused (SET_UNANCHORED; use the catalog instead), and installs from sets are rejected.

To send downloads through a mirror, add a tools route in registries.routes whose scope is a host (for example github.com). Its connectorId selects a connector from the --connector-bindings file: format = 1 [connectors.corp-github] base_url = "https://mirror.example.com/gh/" redirects = "server" # or "client" (default) authorization_env = "CORP_AUTH" # optional; never printed The request goes to base_url plus the original URL's path and query, unchanged. With no tools route, Oyzu downloads directly and follows redirects to any https host. Once any tools route exists, only listed hosts are reachable. Two rules for one host fail with ROUTE_RULE_CONFLICT. redirects = "server": the mirror follows redirects; a 3xx reply fails with ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNEXPECTED. redirects = "client": each redirect host needs its own route (ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNROUTABLE otherwise). Redirect targets are never stored, logged or printed. registries.routes is administrative configuration.

Each accepted record becomes a normal oyzu.lock entry: id is recipe:<owner>/<name>, whether the record said aqua: or recipe:. version is the normalized version; digest and size come from the verified artifact. The entry records the download URL and digest. Direct and mirrored installs produce identical lock entries. Digests must be lowercase sha256:<64 hex>. oyzu install --frozen downloads (or reuses the cached copy of) each locked recipe: tool and checks its size and digest. With --artifact-set, it fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE if an anchored record disagrees with the lock.

Installing downloads and verifies the artifact into the tool store cache, but doesn't extract it, create shims or write [tools]. A recipe tool isn't runnable yet. Signatures and attestations aren't re-checked at install; only the digest is compared. oyzu tools evidence verifies GitHub attestations when the set is produced. No organization catalog source, no update for sets, and no settings for the minimum tier or evidence. Supported on Linux x86-64 only.
Resolving recipes into artifact sets Tool commands Tool index and tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/auth.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu auth signs you in to an Oyzu platform account and keeps the session in your operating system's credential store. Remote builds and runs (--remote), oyzu secrets and oyzu release check then use it. Everything else Oyzu does is local and needs no account. Note: Platform sign-in is experimental. It needs a platform that publishes the sign-in endpoints described below; until it does, login reports discovery as unsupported. It hasn't been tested yet against a real identity provider or each operating system's credential store. oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments oyzu auth login oyzu auth status

Command What it does oyzu auth login Shows a web address and a short code. Approve the code in any browser, on any device. Oyzu then checks that you're an active member of platform.account and stores the session. oyzu auth status Shows the platform, account and local session state: absent, active, refreshing, reauthentication-required or logged-out. Reads local state only; contacts no server. oyzu auth logout Deletes this account's local session, then asks the issuer to revoke it and reports that result separately. oyzu auth conformance Checks the client against a built-in fake issuer on your machine. Needs no account. Exits 1 if any scenario fails.

platform.url and platform.account set in user, machine or administrator configuration. Project and local files can't set them, so a checkout can't choose where your credentials go. For login, a terminal where you can read the code. A credential store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or a running Linux Secret Service provider (GNOME Keyring, KWallet). There is no plaintext fallback. Without a store, login stops before asking you to approve anything. A platform that publishes OAuth protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728) naming one issuer that supports the device authorization grant (RFC 8628) for the public client oyzu-cli.

Oyzu reads /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource from platform.url (with the URL's path appended, if it has one). Its resource must equal platform.url, and it must list exactly one authorization server. Oyzu reads the issuer's metadata. The issuer must match, and its device and token endpoints (and revocation endpoint, if any) must use HTTPS on the issuer's own origin, with no credentials, query or fragment. Plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host. Redirects aren't followed and no token is sent. Oyzu starts the device grant for oyzu-cli, with no client secret and no scope (it never asks for offline_access). A verification address on a different origin isn't shown. Oyzu polls at the issuer's interval for up to 15 minutes. Oyzu calls GET /api/v1/access-context?account=<platform.account>. The answer must show an active membership of exactly that account; another membership is never used instead. If the account requires stronger sign-in, you get AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED; without a membership, AUTH_NOT_A_MEMBER. In both cases the new sign-in is revoked and nothing is stored. The session is stored only after every step succeeds, so a cancelled, denied, expired or failed login leaves nothing behind. The device code is never shown or logged.

Every command that talks to the platform gets its credential the same way. The rule is fixed, and a failure never falls back to a different identity. Situation Credential platform.authentication.provider is environment OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Without it: AUTH_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE. platform.authentication.provider is session The stored session. If OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN is also set: AUTH_PROVIDER_CONFLICT. platform.authentication.provider is workload, private-key or execution AUTH_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED (not available). No provider set, OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN set That token, as given. It's never stored, refreshed or replaced. No provider set, at a terminal (stdin and stderr) The stored session. No provider set, unattended (CI, scripts, agents) AUTH_PROVIDER_REQUIRED. A stored session is never used implicitly. If the platform rejects a token, the command reports *_UNAUTHENTICATED; it doesn't try your stored session instead. The credential is sent only to the origin of platform.url, never to a redirect or any other address.

Setting Values Default Meaning platform.authentication.provider session, environment (workload, private-key, execution are reserved) unset Chooses the credential source, as above. Environment variable OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER. User, machine or administrator configuration only. OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN holds a credential. It isn't a setting and doesn't belong in a configuration file.

The refresh credential and the cached access token are stored as separate entries in the credential store. A small non-secret file under the user data directory (auth/) records the issuer, subject, state and expiry. When several commands need to renew at once, only one renews; the others wait and reuse the result. If a renewal answer is lost (timeout, crash, failed store write), the session ends with AUTH_REFRESH_AMBIGUOUS or AUTH_STORE_FAILED and you sign in again. A rejected renewal ends it with AUTH_REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED. An issuer outage or lost network leaves the session as it is. logout wins over a renewal already in progress, which can't bring the session back. Local logout can succeed while remote revocation can't. The result says so with remote: refused, unreachable or not-advertised. Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire. A separately supplied OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN isn't affected.

Human output leads with the outcome. With --json, each command prints one record (auth-login, auth-status, auth-logout or auth-conformance) with session facts only. The login address and code go to standard error, and only when it's a terminal, so JSON on standard output stays clean. Without a terminal, login fails with AUTH_INTERACTION_REQUIRED before contacting anything.

Failures exit 1. If a session can't be renewed, run oyzu auth login again. Code Cause Fix AUTH_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account is missing. Set them with oyzu config set --global. AUTH_INTERACTION_REQUIRED login isn't running at a terminal. Run it in a terminal. AUTH_STORE_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_STORE_FAILED The credential store is missing, locked or failed. Start or unlock the store. AUTH_DISCOVERY_UNSUPPORTED, AUTH_DISCOVERY_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_DISCOVERY_INVALID, AUTH_DISCOVERY_AMBIGUOUS The platform's sign-in metadata is missing, unreachable, invalid or lists more than one issuer. Check platform.url; ask your platform administrator. AUTH_ISSUER_MISMATCH, AUTH_ISSUER_UNTRUSTED, AUTH_ISSUER_CHANGED, AUTH_REDIRECT_REFUSED, AUTH_GRANT_UNSUPPORTED, AUTH_DEVICE_UNTRUSTED The issuer's metadata or endpoints failed a safety check. Ask your platform administrator. AUTH_DEVICE_EXPIRED, AUTH_LOGIN_DENIED, AUTH_LOGIN_CANCELLED The code expired, was denied or you cancelled. Run oyzu auth login again. AUTH_NOT_A_MEMBER, AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED You aren't an active member of the account, or it needs stronger sign-in. Check the account, or complete the stronger sign-in. AUTH_CONTEXT_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_ISSUER_UNREACHABLE The platform or issuer couldn't be reached. Retry later. AUTH_LOGIN_REQUIRED, AUTH_REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED, AUTH_REFRESH_AMBIGUOUS No usable session. Run oyzu auth login. AUTH_DESTINATION_MISMATCH, AUTH_AUDIENCE_UNSUPPORTED A credential would have gone to the wrong place. Check platform.url. AUTH_PROVIDER_* See which credential a command uses. Set the provider or token.

Tokens, device codes and refresh credentials never appear in output, logs, configuration, command arguments, error text or the metadata file. There is no plaintext credential file. Coding agents and unattended jobs don't inherit your session. Don't give an agent your OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN: a copied token still identifies you.

Supported credential stores are macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager and the Linux Secret Service, but none has been tested with real sign-ins yet. The workload, private-key and execution providers, browser-redirect (PKCE) login and a background agent aren't available. To switch accounts, change platform.account and run login again.
Remote runs Secrets Checking whether a build would ship

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-bundles.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every oyzu build writes its results to a bundle, in dist/ by default. The bundle holds the manifest, the plan, the execution record, logs, reports and the artifacts themselves. Use oyzu inspect to check a bundle and oyzu history to look up earlier builds. oyzu build oyzu inspect # check this project's bundle oyzu history # recent builds A failed build still writes a bundle. Read manifest.json for what actually happened.

If your project already uses dist/ for its own files, put the Oyzu bundle somewhere else in the root oyzu.toml: [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" Setting Values Default Where build.bundleDirectory dist, .oyzu/bundle dist Root oyzu.toml only (including root context and profile sections, and policy). Component, local and per-folder values are refused. Other paths aren't supported, and Oyzu doesn't pick a destination for you. The destination doesn't change artifact names or identities. Artifact paths in the manifest are relative to the bundle. .oyzu/bundle is never treated as source. If a build reads your own dist/, declare it with inputs: [dist] in that build's build.yaml entry. Being tracked in Git isn't enough. oyzu inspect (with no argument), history, scan, publish and local image loading all use the chosen destination. They never fall back to an old dist/. oyzu inspect <path> with an explicit path reads that bundle directly, without opening project configuration. Connected publishing (oyzu publish --server ...) and oyzu release check read dist/manifest.json by default. Pass --manifest .oyzu/bundle/manifest.json if you moved the bundle. The manifest records the destination in extensions["oyzu.dev/bundle-directory"]. To inspect a bundle you moved by hand, pass its path.

Each target's artifacts and reports go under <bundle>/<target>/<platform>/: dist/ manifest.json plan.json envelope.json logs/ cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu-shim.exe cli/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml docs/windows/x86_64/application-0.1.0/ The layout is the same for local, multi-platform and CI builds, so bundles from different platforms merge without collisions.

The platform folder is os/arch, such as linux/x86_64, windows/arm64 or darwin/arm64. An ABI is added to the architecture only when you declared or requested one that isn't the OS default: --platform linux/arm64/musl writes linux/arm64-musl/, while linux/arm64/gnu writes linux/arm64/. Output that is platform-independent uses any. Build Platform folder Native host build The host, such as windows/x86_64. Isolated build The platform of the execution image the action runs on (such as linux/x86_64), or the target's single declared platform. Docker image target under a native build The worker's platform. Output a builder declares platform-independent any. No built-in builder does this for a whole target yet. OCI image index any, since it covers several platforms. Node applications, including static dist/ and Vite sites, are kept per platform. The folder follows the platform you declared or requested, not the ABI the toolchain picked. If a target declares linux/arm64 and is cross-built to musl, it lands in linux/arm64/ even though the asset is -musl. Declare the ABI (linux/arm64/musl) to keep GNU and musl builds apart.

The manifest and plan record each artifact's path relative to the bundle (for example cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe). oyzu inspect, oyzu publish and the action cache read that path; they never assume a layout. reports is reserved for a target's reports. No artifact can be named reports. Builder-internal files, such as Docker's container/image.tar, also live in the platform folder. Vite's vite-state.json stays in dist/<target>/.
documents.s: Paths in the manifest and plan

documents.t: Each artifact records profile: development or optimized, the profile its build actually used. It's shown on its Outputs row. Which profile a target uses depends on where its output goes, build.optimized and --optimized / --no-optimized; see optimized builds. optimized is recorded only where the profile changes the output: Rust binaries (cargo build --release) and .NET packages (--configuration Release). Rust .crate archives and other builders' output stay development. Output from a custom task that replaces the builder's command is development.

Each target records the platform it was built for (os/arch[/abi]), including the ABI when the OS has several, for example {"os":"linux","arch":"arm64","abi":"musl"} (recorded for Rust today). extensions["oyzu.dev/platforms"] records how the target was built: Field Meaning target The logical target all platform variants share. declared The platforms the target declares. declaredExecutors The executors declared. platform, executor What this record was built for and with: {"kind":"host"}, {"kind":"cross-toolchain","toolchain":"rust-lld","target":"aarch64-unknown-linux-musl"} or {"kind":"container"}. rows One entry per declared or requested platform with selected, executor or reason, and the runner that builds it. oyzu publish uses declared to refuse an incomplete platform set. See platforms and executors.

When Oyzu collects a native executable (Rust and Go binaries), it checks the file without running it, so cross-built binaries are checked too. It must be a valid ELF, Mach-O (including the matching slice of a universal binary) or PE file for the target platform and architecture, and must not be empty or truncated. The record gets extensions["oyzu.dev/executable"] with platform and, once checked, verified.format (elf, mach-o, pe) and verified.architecture. A failure stops the build with EXECUTABLE_INVALID: artifact <id> is not a valid <platform> executable: <cause>. Known architectures: x86_64, arm64, 386, arm, riscv64, ppc64le, s390x. A plugin's executable flag only places a file in .oyzu/bin; it isn't checked.
A Python wheel that turns out to be py3-none-any still stays in the platform folder. oyzu run <target>:test puts reports under the host platform.

oyzu history oyzu history <invocation-id> oyzu history <run-id> --json oyzu inspect <bundle-directory> --json oyzu history reads the current bundle and earlier ones kept under .oyzu/history/. It doesn't load project configuration, so old builds stay readable even if your configuration is broken or the bundle moved. It doesn't install, use the network, run anything or hash artifacts. Look up a build by the invocation ID or run ID from its summary. Old bundles without an invocation ID can be found by run ID. An invalid ID fails with INVOCATION_ID_INVALID; an unknown one with INVOCATION_NOT_FOUND.

A listing shows up to 20 builds, newest first, with counts of what was left out and up to 8 notices about incomplete bundles. A summary of one build shows: action counts, test totals (fresh, reused, unknown origin), warnings, and up to 8 failed or unusual actions and 8 diagnostics, with short excerpts; up to 8 recorded action decisions (why each ran or was reused), the selection, and cache status; unavailable cache tiers (cacheLimitations) and selection fallbacks (selectionFallback); paths to the full records. Lists are capped at 8 entries, with a *Omitted count beside each. The full manifest has everything. oyzu build --explain shows the same summary.
documents.s: What a listing and a summary contain

documents.t: Native log bodies and environments aren't included. Open the returned paths for the full records. A summary isn't artifact verification. Use oyzu inspect for that. Later source or configuration changes, or oyzu cache clear, don't rewrite a past build's recorded decisions. Older records without file-comparison detail say it's unavailable.

checks shows which checks each target ran, from the build's recorded oyzu.dev/build-checks facts. Up to 8 targets are listed; totals count all of them. Each target's tests is selected, not-requested or unknown. Missing or malformed records stay unknown; current configuration never fills the gap. checks.status is recorded when every target has a record, partial for a mix, and unknown when none do. unknownTargets gives the count.

Totals are split into fresh, reused and unknown origin. Each also counts zeroTestReports: reports that say they ran 0 tests. If passed, failed or skipped is missing, that total is null (shown as unavailable). Zero tests, skipped tests, missing required reports and missing records are always reported separately.

When a policy constraint changed a target's setting, the plan and manifest record extensions["oyzu.dev/policy-overrides"], one entry per override: setting and the effective value; constraint: source, kind (lock, minimum, maximum or required), bound, selector, and label (org policy, admin policy or project constraint); replaced: the value, source and scope it replaced; a human note. See policy constraints and selectors and project constraints. In a release build, when a nearer folder lowered a check below a farther [context.release] value, the target records extensions["oyzu.dev/release-lowerings"]: the setting, the value used and its source (such as app/oyzu.toml:2), and the releaseValue and its releaseSource (such as oyzu.toml:5). See per-context values.

History is local. Nothing is uploaded or shared. Nothing expires automatically and there's no delete command. Remove old bundles yourself when you no longer need them. A command that stops before the bundle is created leaves no history entry. Crashes, write failures and full disks can leave partial or missing records. Remote runs don't appear in history. Use the platform's run link.

oyzu inspect checks a bundle against its own records. It confirms the files match what was recorded; it doesn't prove who produced them. To check a downloaded artifact against signed GitHub provenance, see release provenance verification. Plan and manifest agree. Target records and artifact identities must match the plan. Relabeling a variant in the manifest alone fails. Generated versions. A target whose version was set by declared hooks must match its recorded post-hook plan; only the declared version fields may differ. Successful bundles are complete. Every planned artifact, required action and required report must be there. Reports are re-parsed and checked against the plan's rules (including coverage), rather than trusting stored summaries. OCI images. The image's OS and architecture must match the target. See Docker target selection. Plugins. See plugin provenance. Reports for runtime variants are tied to their own target records; see runtime matrices.

A build holds an OS file lock on .oyzu/build.lock until it finishes. A second build in the same workspace fails before running anything. The lock file existing on disk doesn't mean a build is running; the lock is released when the process exits. Staging happens in .oyzu/bundle-* on the same filesystem as the destination. An isolated build only replaces an existing destination that contains an Oyzu manifest. Any other existing folder, even an empty one, is refused. Oyzu never deletes files it doesn't own. Use .oyzu/bundle if your project writes its own dist/. With .oyzu/bundle, native builds and direct tests also require Oyzu ownership. Your native dist/ stays where it is and isn't copied into the bundle. Symlinks (including broken ones) and Windows reparse points are refused for the lock, state, bundle and history paths. Just before replacing the bundle, Oyzu checks that the destination hasn't changed since the build started. A new destination, changed manifest or existing history slot stops it rather than overwrite anything.

When a build finishes, the previous bundle moves to .oyzu/history/<new-run-id> and the staged one becomes current. Nothing is appended to the old manifest. This step is local and never uses the network. If the second step fails, Oyzu tries to put the previous bundle back. If that fails too, the error names the history folder holding it. oyzu build --plan is a read-only preview and never replaces the bundle.

The previous bundle's artifacts move to history even when the new build fails. They aren't copied back into dist/, which would block a later retry. Unrelated native files are kept. .oyzu/bin stays at the last successful build. If an older bundle recorded old binaries as unclaimed output, move that bundle aside before rebuilding. A matching file name alone doesn't allow replacing them.

The new staging folder is kept and its path is in the error. If its records are complete, inspect it directly: oyzu inspect .oyzu/bundle-EXAMPLE Use the path from the error message. Keep the conflicting destination and fix the filesystem problem before rebuilding. A kept staging folder is never treated as a successful build or reused. Abandoned staging folders are cleaned up normally.

When a build uses an external builder (see plugin packages), the plan, execution record and manifest each carry extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"]: one entry per plugin with its source (package or local-development), identity and executableDigest. oyzu inspect fails with plugin records differ from plan or ... from envelope if the manifest's or execution record's copy is missing or edited.

Note: Slice handoff is experimental and is mainly used by platform pools. oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://host/path builds only the named targets and, on success, uploads the complete bundle (plan, execution record, logs, artifacts and reports) to the OCI repository before writing it locally. Ordinary builds never need a registry. Part Value Repository and tag <handoff>/v1alpha1/<first two manifest-digest hex>:bundle-<64 hex> Artifact type application/vnd.oyzu.build-bundle.v1alpha1 Config The manifest.json bytes, application/vnd.oyzu.build-manifest.v1alpha1+json. Its SHA-256 is the tag. Layer One application/vnd.oyzu.build-bundle.v1alpha1.tar+zstd archive with the other bundle files Annotations dev.oyzu.build.manifest (config digest), dev.oyzu.bundle.uncompressed-digest (raw tar digest) The archive is reproducible: sorted paths, zero owner and timestamps, files 0644 or 0755, folders 0755. Links are refused. The config plus layer, and the unpacked tar, are each limited to 256 MiB. Your normal registry credentials and proxy settings are used. Uploading the same bundle again is harmless; a different bundle at the same tag fails. The plan records each target's oyzu.dev/execution (needsDaemon, executionPlatform) and oyzu.dev/slice (transferable, repeatable, reason, detail) facts. transferable doesn't mean a cache hit. If the upload still fails after retries, the build ends with HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED and exit status 5. The actions' real outcomes are kept, along with the exact upload bytes, so the upload can be retried without rebuilding.

Replacing the bundle is two renames, not a crash-safe transaction. If the process or machine stops in between, there's no automatic recovery; the error or history folder tells you where the previous bundle is. The path checks and lock protect against other Oyzu commands, not against a hostile process that can replace folders. Bundles aren't stored remotely, and there are no automatic retention limits.

Direct Node, Python and Go tests use the same process. With the default dist destination, a test run can copy your existing native dist/ output into the new test bundle and keep the original in history. Those copies are listed separately and aren't build artifacts. With .oyzu/bundle, your native dist/ is left alone. Earlier reports in the current bundle move to history.
Local builds and build tasks for what fills the bundle. Action cache for reuse recorded in the manifest. Publishing for what uses a finished bundle.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-logging.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build shows its work as it happens: preparation steps, parallel targets, commands, live output and a final receipt. It also saves complete logs and an event journal in the bundle. How output is shown never changes what is built or which checks run. oyzu build oyzu build api web worker oyzu build --output plain oyzu build --output interactive oyzu build --plan oyzu build --json > result.json 2> events.jsonl For the section-by-section layout of the default view (Prepare, Selection, Plan, Build, Failure, Outputs, Warnings, summary), see build transcript. This page covers the output modes, the interactive dashboard, CI output, saved logs and interruption.

Option Behavior --output auto (default) Compact linear view: named preparation steps, one row per action and one final receipt. --output plain The same linear view. Never uses an alternate screen, fixed panes, key input or full-screen redraws. --output interactive The full-screen dashboard. Needs a terminal on stdin and stderr. Works in CI too. --json Stdout holds the final manifest or plan JSON; stderr holds JSON-line events only. Takes precedence over --output. -q Quiet output. Takes precedence over --output. On a capable terminal, each active step shows a header and its last eight output lines. Routine successes collapse; slow steps and problems stay in scrollback. Redirected output is append-only, never redrawn. Color is separate from interactivity: ui.color = auto | always | never. A nonempty NO_COLOR wins, and CLICOLOR_FORCE can color a pipe without turning on redraws. GitHub Actions gets the same linear view, wrapped in collapsible groups.

--output interactive opens a dashboard that stays in place while the build runs. The header shows the project, elapsed time, phases (Prepare, Build, Collect) and the selected platforms with readable OS and architecture names. During preparation it shows how many tools are verified or pending, and up to two pending tools. Finished setup collapses when the build starts. Each row shows its current operation, elapsed time and, for active rows, how long the output has been quiet. One live pane shows the selected step's last seven output lines. New parallel work doesn't steal focus from the step you're watching. Warnings and failures stay pinned above the pane. Reused actions show Reused · not executed now. After a process exits, a step may show Checking outputs until its reports and artifacts pass validation; a clean exit alone isn't success. Blocked tasks show which prerequisite they're waiting for. Resizing recalculates the layout; very small terminals show a resize hint. Long lines are clipped, and you can pan to see them. Scrollback is kept in a temporary file on disk, deleted when the view closes. The saved build logs are the permanent record. When the build ends (or fails), your previous screen is restored and the permanent receipt is printed. Key Action Up / Down Select the previous or next step. Enter Expand or collapse the live output pane. a Follow active work automatically. p Show or hide preparation details, requested versions and the selected work's stages and outputs (up to eight setup rows; see oyzu build --plan --json for the rest). d / l Show or hide the full combined log. Escape Return to the compact live pane. Page Up / Page Down Scroll the log. Left / Right Pan long lines. f / End Follow new output again. n Select the next failed task. Failures only raise a notice; they never move your selection. q Close the dashboard and continue the build with plain output. Doesn't cancel anything. Ctrl+C Restore the terminal and interrupt the build. The dashboard never needs input to finish.

When output is redirected, or the build runs in a detected CI system, the view is append-only: Each action prints a start line (00:12 .. api build started) and an end line with its outcome and duration, both led by the elapsed time since the build began. In builds with more than twelve actions, only end lines and the final tally are printed. Every ten seconds a heartbeat line names what's still running: 00:31 still running: api build 10s · auth-lib test 12s · 6 waiting (up to three actions, then + N more). A heartbeat shows the build is alive, not that a tool is making progress. Output is laid out at 100 columns on every host. Terminal width comes from the console, so COLUMNS doesn't change it. Without color, marks are padded words (ok, reused, warn, FAIL) and rules use dashes. Terminal controls in every value are escaped. Redirected files never contain cursor movement. Recognized CI systems: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Buildkite, Jenkins and TeamCity, with a generic CI fallback. Detection only affects presentation (and the build context); it never grants any permission. GitHub Actions. Preparation, dependency and planning phases are wrapped in collapsible groups, closed before actions run. When GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY is set, Oyzu appends an HTML-escaped receipt to it; if that write fails you get a warning and the build result doesn't change. In JSON mode, no group commands are printed. Oyzu doesn't upload artifacts or add source annotations. The sectioned view described in build transcript applies to local oyzu build runs. --plan, --check, remote runs, oyzu run, oyzu scan and the dashboard use their own layouts.

The heading names the project, the host or platform selection, the execution mode and the requested checks. Which targets were selected, and why, is in the Selection section; stage status is in the plan table. Preparation runs as named steps: configuration, tools, dependencies, output bundle, compiler cache, source snapshot, CLI identity and report setup. › running, ✓ done, ✗ stopped by an error. A step that's still running when an error stops the build is shown as stopped, not done. Fast successful steps collapse. Steps that take ten seconds or more, and failures, stay visible. A slow step that succeeds is still a success. Tool installation shows the requested version. A reused tool collapses to one Ready line; a real download stays visible. Host prerequisites say they're checked during compilation. Optional tools that aren't used aren't listed. Each running subprocess (formatting, linting, tests, compilation, hooks, tool installation) gets a short preview under its row, showing its latest eight lines in dim text. Each parallel task has its own preview. The preview area is limited by the terminal height and says when activity is hidden. On success, the preview collapses into the totals. On failure, the first useful eight lines of error context are kept (or the last eight lines if no error marker is found), with the exit code. The receipt names the saved log. -v shows the full captured output, including successful preparation.

A finished step shows a mark, a name, a short result and its duration. Durations read <0.1s, 5.9s, 149s and 10m 06s. ✓ Source captured 2781 files · sha256:668b3844b9d7 13.0s ✓ Rust compiler 1.95.0 · reused the packaged copy from an earlier build 0.8s ✓ Compiler in container restored into a read-only volume 19.5s ✓ Cargo crates 371 locked · all from the cache 5.6s ✓ Project metadata 8 container runs · slowest `cargo metadata` 9.0s 25.0s ✓ Build inputs ready compiler, crates and project metadata 60.8s On a terminal, a running step shows in the live pane (› name detail). Redirected output prints a step when it finishes, with heartbeats while it's slow. With several targets, each step names its target (Cargo crates · cli · linux/x86_64). While Cargo compiles, individual Compiling lines aren't printed. The running status shows the count and latest crate (Running · 60s elapsed · 271 crates compiled · latest oxc_ast_visit), and the finished line shows the total (Succeeded · 276 crates compiled). Warnings and errors still print in full. -v prints every crate. With -v, a finished build also shows where the time went (Preflight 71s · Build 174s · Collect 4s). After the last action finishes, Collect does its own work: it saves the private source copies for the next build (Source workspaces), records results and verification evidence (Build records), and writes the local bundle (Output bundle). Each is a step like the ones above. It shows in the live pane while it runs, a redirected run prints › Source workspaces saving private copies for the next build · 10s every ten seconds while it is slow, and a finished step appears only if it took ten seconds or more, failed or warned. Generated platform IDs such as cli-platform-windows_x86_64-157f0d1f6adb are shown as cli · windows/x86_64. The event journal has the same steps and durations (Step events with duration_ms).

An isolated (container) build prepares these steps for each target: Step What it does Rust compiler Unpacks the locked Rust installation once per build and packages it for the container. The package is cached under cache/rust-packaged in the Oyzu user data directory. Compiler in container Restores the package into a read-only Docker volume named oyzu-tools-<hash> (the hash covers the worker image, compiler archive and format). The volume is kept between builds, so a repeat build reuses it in under a second instead of about 20 seconds. Cargo crates Captures every crate in Cargo.lock into an offline registry for the container, which has no network. Archives are checked against the lock's checksums and cached under cache/cargo-crates; registry index entries are cached for seven days. Project metadata A few short container runs (cargo metadata, rustc -vV, lock file generation). Shown as one step naming the slowest run; -v lists them all. Source snapshot, Dependency snapshot Private, hashed copies the offline build uses. Version The version stamped into the artifacts. About the compiler volumes: A companion volume, oyzu-tools-<hash>-ok, marks a finished restore. A volume without it is rebuilt. A lock file under cache/ in the user data directory stops concurrent builds from restoring the same volume twice. Each new compiler or worker image adds a volume of about a gigabyte. After each build, Oyzu removes older oyzu-tools-* pairs, keeping the current one and the three most recent others. Volumes in use by a running container are skipped and retried next time. Other Docker storage is limited by the Docker storage budget. A native (non-isolated) build shows Source workspaces (a private copy of the sources) and one step per executor prerequisite (a small compile-and-link check of the linker). The › Tools determining… line is a placeholder while this runs.

Native output is shown as it arrives. Oyzu can't show output a tool hasn't written yet, and Cargo can be quiet for a long time while compiling or linking. Silent tasks show elapsed time every ten seconds. Each excerpt names its task once and keeps the tool's own indentation and carets. Color codes from tools are removed in the human view; other terminal controls are escaped. The saved logs keep the original output. Parallel tasks never interleave within a line. Lines from one stream stay in order; the order between different tasks or between stdout and stderr isn't a strict cause-and-effect order. Cargo JSON is shown as short compiled-target and status lines. go test -json shows native output and failed test names instead of JSON. A single record over 1 MiB isn't shown; read the saved log instead. Native warnings appear once, in the receipt's Warnings section, and as NATIVE_WARNING diagnostics in JSON. Cargo warnings keep their source location, and Cargo's repeated summary line doesn't add another warning. npm and Node warnings are recognized too. Oyzu never decides an action's result from warning or error text. Warning and error excerpts have separate budgets, so warnings can't hide a later failure. Installer messages from rustup go through the same view. Its advice to add a temporary folder to PATH is hidden, because Oyzu activates the installed tools itself; JSON and saved events keep it. Rust doctests stream live; see Rust direct test evidence. The command shown for an action is redacted for display. It isn't a portable shell script.

The receipt is the summary at the end of a build. See receipts and history for what it counts. A build that fails during preparation says Build failed during preparation and No build actions started, and keeps the count of selected targets. Fresh tests and reused test results are counted separately. Reused results name where they came from and never count as tests run now. Missing reports never mean zero failures or 100% coverage. Coverage isn't averaged across unrelated measures. Receipt sections show up to eight entries and say how many were left out. -v adds the manifest and report paths. An empty result says No artifacts produced. Error and recovery paragraphs wrap at word boundaries (100 columns if the terminal width is unknown).

Every build saves these files in its bundle (dist/ by default): Path Contents logs/events.jsonl The event journal, including preparation output. logs/<target>/… Numbered stdout and stderr files for each action. manifest.json, plan.json The build's result and plan. plans/ Sealed plans for independent branches. If setup fails before the bundle exists, no journal is saved. The terminal, JSON and redirected output still have the error. oyzu run test and other bundled tasks also save their full stdout and stderr, in text and JSON modes. A task marked interactive = true uses your terminal directly, so its log files are empty. See task output. oyzu build --plan creates no bundle; see read-only build preview. See build bundles for how bundles are kept.

Each line of events.jsonl (and each JSON event on stderr) has schemaVersion, sequence, elapsedMs, scope, severity, target, invocationId, operationId, parentOperationId and an event: event Contents diagnostic A warning, error or other message, with code. heading, fact, inventory The build heading, context facts, and the selected targets, platforms, check mode and color preference. preparation, phase, task, progress Lifecycle changes. plan Target IDs and builders, action IDs, dependencies and artifact versions. Never action environments. command The redacted command. output stream, text and continued. finished status, and optional exit_code and duration_ms. Every warning and error is saved, whatever the console showed. Debug and trace messages are saved only when enabled. Environment maps are never included. New event types may be added; ignore ones you don't recognize. The format is experimental and separate from the plan's identity and from release records.

Logging uses no network. Your project's commands can print sensitive values, and Oyzu doesn't try to detect secrets in arbitrary output. Credentials Oyzu uses for downloads are never passed in a command's arguments or environment. A failure to write a log never changes a tool's result.

Builds use the global diagnostic controls. Event Level Routine lifecycle info Command details debug Failed step error Blocked task warn Native stdout and stderr are always saved, whatever the threshold. A line on a tool's stderr isn't an Oyzu error.

The first Ctrl+C (or SIGTERM, or SIGHUP when the terminal closes) asks the build to stop. No new work starts and running container steps are removed. A signal that was already ignored when the build started (such as SIGHUP under nohup) stays ignored. Steps blocked inside a native tool or Docker call can't respond right away, so Oyzu prints a notice ending waiting up to 10s for running steps. Press Ctrl-C again to force exit. The notice goes through the normal log, so it's a JSON line with --json. After an interrupt: Actions that never started are not-started, and the build is interrupted. On Unix, native tasks that were stopped report cancelled. On other platforms the tool's own exit is reported. In the dashboard, Ctrl+C restores your terminal first.

A second Ctrl+C, or the end of the 10-second grace period, forces exit: Oyzu removes the containers this build started (named oyzu-* or the build worker names). On Windows it also ends tracked child process trees. All of this shares one five-second deadline; cleanup that doesn't finish in time is abandoned. It names any container or process tree it couldn't remove, then exits with status 130, even if Docker isn't responding. These time limits are fixed. Forced exit is best effort. It can leave containers, processes and partial staging behind, and there may be no failure bundle. Once Docker is responsive again, remove the named leftovers before retrying, and see bundle recovery. Cleanup messages go to stderr even with --json and aren't a JSON result. Limits: On Unix, forced exit doesn't kill native child processes in other process groups. Containers left by an earlier hard kill (for example kill -9) aren't cleaned up.
CLI output for the section layout, JSON and diagnostic controls. Build bundles for inspect and history. Local builds

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-tasks.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build runs each selected builder's stages (format, lint, test, build, package), together with your own tasks, prerequisites and hooks, and collects the results into a bundle. Use this page to choose which targets and checks run, to add or replace tasks in oyzu.toml, and to understand how oyzu run tasks behave. Builds show live progress and command output. Add --json to get the final manifest and plan as JSON.

oyzu build # fast local build oyzu build --full # run every check that isn't off oyzu build api web --plan # preview two targets oyzu build --jobs 4 # limit concurrency for this run oyzu run list # list discovered tasks oyzu run test # run a development task Choose which checks run, per context, in oyzu.toml: [checks] format = "off" # never run; rustfmt isn't prepared for it lint = "advisory" # failures are warnings; the build still succeeds [context.release.checks] tests = "required"

A plain local oyzu build is a fast build. It runs the build and package stages and only the checks set to required. Other test, lint and format-check stages are skipped (skip · fast local build in Plan). Every check that isn't off runs in the pr, ci and release build contexts, and with --full, the ci profile or --remote. You change these defaults per context with checks.run, and set each check's level in oyzu.toml (check levels): Level Behavior off Never runs. Plan shows off and where it was turned off. The builder doesn't prepare the check's tools. advisory Runs where checks run. A failure is a CHECK_ADVISORY warning. enforce, required See check levels. Required checks and report validation always apply to stages that run. Test and coverage requirements apply to each target as a whole. The compile step doesn't need to produce coverage when the test step does. A positive checks.coverageMinimum needs a selected step that produces coverage and a valid report that meets the minimum. Missing coverage, a disabled test with no other coverage source, or a replacement task that omits required reports fails the build. oyzu run tasks have their own report rules; see direct test reports. On the native Rust path, --full can reuse an unchanged build while format, lint and test run at the same time, within --jobs. A failed required check still fails the build. See native cache behavior. A native build command may run tests itself. For example, Maven runs tests in verify. Skipping the separate test stage doesn't turn those off.
documents.s: Local fast builds and CI checks

documents.t: A local build that only writes its own dist/ uses each builder's development profile. A build is optimized when its artifacts leave the machine: handed off (--slice), written to a shared remote cache, packaged by another selected target, or published (the release context). Plugin-built results are handed off but never written to a remote cache (action cache), so a remote cache alone does not optimize them. --optimized and --no-optimized choose for one run. build.optimized in a folder's oyzu.toml (optionally per context) chooses for the targets under it. Policy wins over both. Optimized Rust runs cargo build --release; optimized .NET uses --configuration Release. Builders where it makes no difference stay development. Plan shows each target's profile and why (profile cli · optimized · --optimized), and Outputs labels each artifact. Optimized and development results never reuse each other from the action cache. For Rust and .NET, a CI build that writes the remote cache (optimized) doesn't serve a local development build; build with --optimized to reuse it. See optimized builds. Platform selection is covered in platforms and executors.

oyzu build oyzu build api oyzu build api web --plan With no arguments, every discovered target builds. Arguments are exact target IDs, not task names, globs or paths. Duplicates are ignored. An unknown ID fails before anything is prepared. Use oyzu discover to see target IDs and oyzu run list to see task names.

The targets you name, plus their depends_on and materialize.from producers, transitively. The owners of prerequisites and hooks reached from those targets' stages. Each added target runs its full set of build, check and package stages, not just the task that was needed. A custom task that no build stage reaches doesn't select its dependencies. Unselected targets get no tools, downloads, actions or artifacts. Concurrency uses the smallest build.jobs among the root configuration and the selected targets. Selection doesn't change which build a task belongs to: an unqualified root hook belongs to every build it reaches, selected or not. Discovery, configuration checks and source capture still cover the whole workspace. Broken metadata in an unrelated project can stop a build of another target.

The plan and manifest record oyzu.dev/selection: requested and selected IDs, the mode (all, explicit or affected), and excluded targets with reason outside-selection. Excluded targets aren't reported as successful. oyzu inspect dist fails if the manifest's selection doesn't match its plan. Runtime toolsets and affected builds also change the selection.

Oyzu reads build.yaml once per run and uses that copy for selection, ordering, platforms and artifact passing. If the file changes between discovery and source capture, the build fails with build.yaml changed between discovery and source capture. Finish the edit and run again. Changes after capture don't affect the running build.

Most projects need no task configuration. Builders supply build, test, lint and read-only format-check tasks. oyzu run list shows them. A format task that rewrites files is for running by hand. It is refused inside a container build. You can replace a builder stage with your own command. The replacement runs instead of the original. It keeps the stage's hooks, required reports and policy, so it must write the required reports to their assigned paths. Oyzu adds native reporting only to commands it recognizes.

A prerequisite uses the normal TOML task syntax: [tasks."api:pre_test"] argv = ["node", "scripts/check-api-inputs.mjs"] depends_on = ["schema:verify"] [tasks."schema:verify"] argv = ["node", "scripts/verify-schema.mjs"] Here api and schema are targets. Each script path is relative to its target's folder. Both tasks need Node available; a custom command doesn't install new tools. schema:verify runs once per build, even if several tasks need it. It runs with schema's folder, tools, configuration, environment and report paths. Its own dependencies and schema:pre_verify / schema:post_verify hooks follow the same rules. api:pre_test waits for the prerequisite and its post-hook before api:test starts. Hooks don't get hooks of their own.

Builder stage order always applies. A stage that already ran as an earlier prerequisite doesn't run again. A target's own prerequisites run in the order listed, after the previous stage. Another target's prerequisites follow that target's order. A cycle between prerequisites, hooks, stages, target dependencies or artifact passing fails before anything runs. Fix the relationship; reordering YAML entries doesn't help. A root workspace task (neither a hook nor a stage) reached through a prerequisite uses that prerequisite's target and tools, but keeps its own working folder. In a build with several targets, a root workspace task needed by more than one target is refused as ambiguous. Qualify it with the target that should run it.

A task key in any oyzu.toml belongs to builds by these rules. They are checked when configuration is read, before anything runs. Key Belongs to Errors [tasks."api:pre_test"] (qualified) Build api only. Wins over an unqualified definition of the same name for api. Unknown build (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN); file outside api's folder chain (CONFIG_REFERENCE_MISPLACED); a hook of a task api doesn't have (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN, with the nearest name). [tasks.post_build] (unqualified hook, pre_* or post_*) Every build whose folder chain reads the file and that has the hooked task (package always counts). A root hook reaches every build, including the root's own. At the root it is also the hook of a workspace task with that name. A hook of a task none of those builds has (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN). [tasks.test] (unqualified builder stage) Replaces that stage in every build the file reaches that runs it. Reaching builds with different builders: CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS. Qualify it per build. [tasks.lint-docs] (any other name) At the root, a workspace task (oyzu run lint-docs). In a subfolder, a task of every build below it. — A nearer folder's definition, or a qualified key, replaces a farther one for that build. Hooks can be narrowed further with when/unless. Stage replacements take no conditions. A task runs in its build's folder unless cwd says otherwise, relative to the file that declares it. Every depends_on entry must name an existing task, by id (schema:verify) or name (verify). # root oyzu.toml, with builds cli (rust/app), docs (node/app) and the root's own [tasks.post_build] # every build, the root's included argv = ["scripts/attest.sh", "{artifact.path}"] [tasks."docs:test"] # one build's stage: docs only argv = ["npm", "run", "test:ci"] [tasks.lint-docs] # a workspace task: oyzu run lint-docs argv = ["node", "tooling/check-docs.mjs"] Writing that docs:test replacement as [tasks.test] would also reach cli, a Rust build, and is refused: CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS: oyzu.toml:5:1: [tasks.test] replaces the test stage of builds with different builders: cli (rust/app), docs (node/app); one command cannot replace stages of different builders. Qualify it for each build instead, such as [tasks."cli:test"] In a single-build project, [tasks.test] works as before. Its task id is the build's own (project:test), and oyzu run test still finds it. oyzu config validate checks task keys' build names and placement. Hook targets and depends_on need the discovered tasks, so oyzu build (including --plan), oyzu run and other commands that discover the project check them. See names that cross files.
documents.s: Which build a task belongs to

documents.t: A task or hook in oyzu.toml can say when it applies (when, unless) and receive build values through {namespace.name} placeholders. Both are plain data from a fixed vocabulary. Anything that needs logic belongs in the program argv runs. For example, a post_build hook that runs the built binary: [tasks."cli:post_build"] argv = ["{artifact.path}", "--version"] when = { optimized = true, platform = ["linux/x86_64"] } unless = { artifact = ["bin-oyzu-shim"] }

when and unless are tables over these facts. They use the same form as policy constraint selectors. Fact Values Notes context local, pr, ci, release The context the build runs as (--context, OYZU_CONTEXT or detection). provider CI provider names (github-actions, gitlab, …) fork true, false false outside a pull request. Read from GitHub Actions and GitLab; using fork where the provider doesn't report it is an error. target Target names Matches the target's id and, for a platform variant (cli-platform-linux-x86_64), its declared target (cli). An unknown name is an error that lists valid names. platform os/arch[/abi], with the usual aliases A value without an ABI matches every ABI. optimized true, false The target's build profile. artifact Logical artifact names (bin-oyzu, as Outputs and the manifest show them, not file names) Only on post_build and post_package hooks. An unknown name is an error, except for a target with several platforms, where it may be built elsewhere. Every when key must match; a list matches when any value does. One matching unless key excludes the task. A task with neither always applies. Unknown keys, wrong value types, artifact on other tasks, and conditions on a stage replacement fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE when configuration is read. Put conditions on the stage's pre_ or post_ hook instead. A task under [context.release.tasks."cli:post_build"] already applies only in release; it needs no condition. Note: Conditions aren't a security control. A job with only the generic CI variable can lower its context with --context local. Use check levels and policy for checks that must run. Conditions are decided when the build is planned. A task that doesn't apply isn't scheduled, and anything that waited on it keeps its order. Plan shows one task note per conditional task: task pre_build · skip · unless context = local post_build · run for bin-oyzu · unless artifact = bin-oyzu-shim The plan and manifest record each conditional task under oyzu.dev/task-conditions: the conditions as written, run or skip and why, and for each run its action id, artifact and resolved argv. oyzu build --plan shows the same notes and taskConditions records; a per-artifact hook shows once per matching artifact there.

A placeholder is {namespace.name}. It is replaced with plain text inside one argv element at a time, and in the task's own env values. Nothing goes through a shell. Placeholder Value {build.context}, {build.provider}, {build.optimized}, {build.version} The context, comma-separated providers, true/false, and the version this build gives the target. In oyzu run, the version the project declares. Not available in container builds for builders that set versions after hooks, such as Node. {build.root} The build root, relative to the task's working folder. {target.name}, {target.dir}, {target.builder} The task's target. dir is relative to the working folder. {platform.platform}, {platform.os}, {platform.arch}, {platform.abi} The target's platform (abi only when it has one). {artifact.path}, {artifact.name}, {artifact.kind}, {artifact.platform}, {artifact.os}, {artifact.arch} In a post_build/post_package hook, the artifact it runs for. path is the packaged file, relative to the working folder. {env.NAME} A literal value from [env] in oyzu.toml. In argv, only when it doesn't look sensitive. {build.<target>.artifact.<field>} Another target's artifact, only along a declared depends_on or materialize edge. A producer with several artifacts needs materialize.artifact. What counts as a placeholder: Only {word.word…}. Everything else is left as written: {.Dir}, {a,b}, a lone brace. Go and Docker templates such as {{.Id}} or {{json .}} pass through unchanged. To write a literal placeholder, double the braces: {{env.HOME}} gives {env.HOME}. This applies only to the namespaces build, target, platform, artifact, env and tool. Doubled braces in other namespaces are ordinary text, so Jinja, Ansible and GitHub expressions ({{item.name}}, ${{github.sha}}) pass through. A single-brace {item.name} is still PLACEHOLDER_UNKNOWN. There are no functions, defaults or filters, and a substituted value is never expanded again. A run script can't use placeholders, because it goes through a shell. Use argv. Per-artifact hooks. A hook that uses the artifact fact or an {artifact.*} placeholder runs once per matching artifact, as actions such as cli:post_build[bin-oyzu], one after another. post_build runs for the artifacts the build produced; post_package for every artifact packaged into dist/. A target with no package stage (such as a native Rust build) still runs a declared post_package hook, after all its other actions. Before each run, the artifact is copied to .oyzu/artifacts/<target>/<platform>/<file> in the target's private workspace; {artifact.path} points there. A hook with no matching artifact is skipped, with the reason. Every run executes even if an earlier one failed; then any failure fails the build. Oyzu never runs an artifact unless you declare a hook that does. A per-artifact hook can't declare outputs (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE). Sensitive values. argv is recorded as written in the plan, manifest and command log, while task env values are recorded as [REDACTED]. So an {env.NAME} whose name or value looks sensitive (names containing TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, API_KEY, CREDENTIAL, AUTH and similar, or a value that looks like a credential) is refused in argv with PLACEHOLDER_SENSITIVE. Pass it through the task's env instead (TOKEN = "{env.API_TOKEN}"), or use the tool's own credential mechanism. Path values are relative to the task's working folder, in the platform's path form, and never expose your checkout path. That way the same build resolves the same argv on every machine, and cache keys match. Placeholder errors. Placeholders are resolved when the build is planned. Errors name the task and argv element: Code Cause PLACEHOLDER_UNKNOWN Unknown name. Lists valid names and the nearest one. PLACEHOLDER_UNDECLARED An {env.NAME} not declared in [env] or the environment. PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE An [env] entry that is a secret reference, path list or table; or a value that doesn't exist where it's used, such as {artifact.path} outside a post_build/post_package hook. PLACEHOLDER_UNREACHABLE Another target's artifact without a declared edge. PLACEHOLDER_SENSITIVE A sensitive-looking {env.NAME} in argv.

Command Conditions Placeholders oyzu build (native) Evaluated per target All, including per-artifact hooks oyzu build --isolated Evaluated per target All but artifacts: a hook that reads artifacts fails with PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE oyzu build --plan Evaluated; per-artifact hooks pending Rendered for decided tasks. {build.version} shows (resolved during the build) oyzu run Evaluated with the host platform and development profile A hook that reads artifacts is skipped (TASK_SKIPPED). A requested task that doesn't apply fails with TASK_NOT_APPLICABLE Limits: {build.dist}, {artifact.digest} and {tool.NAME.*} aren't available (PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE). Placeholders in cwd are refused. Artifacts built by an image worker aren't staged for hooks. Per-artifact runs of one hook run one after another. when/unless on [context.*] setting tables isn't supported.

Limit how many workers run at once for one build, without editing configuration. Remote and CI runners use this to fit a build into a fixed amount of memory: oyzu build --jobs 4 # or -j 4 OYZU_BUILD_JOBS=4 oyzu build Source (highest first) Notes --jobs / -j Accepts 1–65535. OYZU_BUILD_JOBS A value outside 1–65535, or not an integer, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. An empty value is ignored. build.jobs From configuration files and profiles. CPU count The default. --jobs and OYZU_BUILD_JOBS replace every build.jobs value, so the whole build shares one limit. Policy constraints on build.jobs still apply, and available memory can lower it further. The build prints the worker count, the plan records it in oyzu.dev/execution.jobs, and oyzu config explain build.jobs shows where it came from. oyzu run has no --jobs, because tasks run one at a time. The limit doesn't affect threads a compiler starts inside one action.

build.jobs limits both dependency preparation and build actions. In container builds, each worker reserves memory, and Oyzu runs only as many as fit in three quarters of the container engine's memory (docker info MemTotal). With default 2 GiB workers, a 16 GiB engine runs at most six at once. Dependency download workers reserve 4 GiB each and may run for up to 30 minutes. Native host builds have no engine to ask, so build.jobs alone applies. Each long-running container action gets an even share of the engine's CPUs, at most one CPU per 512 MiB of its memory reservation and never fewer than two. The chosen share is printed. Cargo sizes itself from it.

Free slots are refilled as soon as an action finishes and its reports and artifacts check out. Two actions never write to the same target's workspace at once.
