A target's check stages (test, lint, format-check) can overlap only when each runs in its own private view (see checks that run at once). A failed check doesn't block the next check, but it blocks packaging. A failed prerequisite blocks the actions that depend on it. Independent targets can prepare, run and package while others are still preparing. Each target's plan is saved in plans/ in the bundle, and oyzu inspect checks it against the final plan. Container execution uses the inputs captured during preparation. Task dependencies don't grant network, credential or host access. oyzu run uses your host environment.

Diagnostic When What it tells you worker-out-of-memory An action or preparation worker exits with 137, or its output ends with ENOMEM, cannot allocate memory or a heap-limit message. The action, its memory reservation (memoryMiB) and how many ran at once (jobs). Lower build.jobs or give the engine more memory. worker-file-sharing-error Windows only: an action's output ends with an I/O error. Docker Desktop file sharing failed a read. Build from a checkout inside WSL. On Windows, the out-of-memory message also notes that Docker Desktop file sharing can fail large writes with the same error, and that building inside WSL avoids it. Oyzu doesn't retry these.

oyzu run tasks get the project's pinned tool folders on PATH, plus tool variables such as GOROOT and JAVA_HOME. For example, argv = ["bash", "scripts/test-database.sh"] can call the pinned go by name. The tools must already be installed. oyzu run doesn't install them; run oyzu install first (or install --frozen --offline when cached). On Windows, a bare bash or sh skips the WSL launchers in System32 and WindowsApps. Oyzu looks for a native shell on PATH, then Git for Windows' shell next to git.exe, then standard Git install folders. If none is found, the task fails with the places searched; it never silently enters WSL. Git Bash converts the Windows PATH itself, so pinned tools work in scripts. shell = "bash" or shell = "sh" tasks use the same lookup. The default shell is PowerShell on Windows and sh elsewhere.

oyzu run <task> reports configuration, the selected task, tool verification and execution as they happen. Silent preparation shows an activity update every ten seconds, and a running task shows a heartbeat. Task kind Output Text mode, no bundle Uses your terminal's stdout and stderr directly. Records a bundle (oyzu run test, with its prerequisites and hooks) Shows output live and also saves it in the bundle's numbered dist/logs/*.stdout and *.stderr files. Bundled task with interactive = true Uses your terminal directly. Its output can't also be saved, so its bundle logs are empty. --json Stdout is one final result including captured output. Diagnostics stream on stderr. The task's streams aren't terminals, so prompts appear only at the end; use text mode for interactive prompts. Tasks receive your stdin, including piped input, in text and JSON mode. Container builds get no stdin. -q hides Oyzu's progress and keeps the task's output and logs. When output is saved, the task's stdout and stderr are pipes, which can change its buffering, color and terminal detection. PowerShell shell tasks need interactive = true to drop -NonInteractive. The task's own color handling, including NO_COLOR, is unchanged. For example, a task with argv = ["sh", "-c", "read x; printf 'got:%s\\n' \"$x\""] prints got:hello for printf 'hello\n' | oyzu run ask -q.

On Windows, each oyzu run command, prerequisite and hook runs in its own job object that is killed when closed. Child processes stay in the job. If Oyzu is killed, the whole task tree stops and releases the ports it held. When a task finishes, any processes it left behind are stopped. Don't leave background services running after a task returns; run a service in the foreground instead. stdin, arguments, exit codes and Ctrl-C behave as usual. This is process cleanup, not file or network isolation. If the job can't be created or the task's main thread can't be found or resumed, the task doesn't start and you get a TASK_JOB_* or TASK_PRIMARY_THREAD_* error. An enclosing job that doesn't allow nesting, or denied OS access, must be fixed first. If leftover processes don't exit within ten seconds, the task fails with TASK_JOB_CLEANUP_FAILED.

Native builds use the same task planner as container builds. Independent targets run in parallel up to build.jobs. depends_on: [api] under builds.web makes web wait for api's stages to succeed. A failed dependency blocks its consumers, not unrelated targets. Use materialize to pass files between targets; see target workspaces.
Container builds run each target in its own private workspace.

Prerequisites order tasks; they don't pass files between targets. When a consumer needs a producer's files, declare artifacts and use materialize (see directory artifacts). dist/plan.json records each action's owner, tools, dependencies, environment and required reports. The manifest records results, reports and artifacts. See build bundles. Packaging waits for every selected task of that target. A failed prerequisite, post-hook or required report blocks dependent actions and packaging. Whatever evidence exists stays in the failure bundle, and independent targets can still succeed. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's integrity, not whether it may be released.

Container builds capture your source once and give each target its own copy from that capture. Capture follows in-tree .gitignore rules (case-sensitive), including rules above a nested build root. Untracked files that aren't ignored are included. Tracked files that are ignored are left out with a SOURCE_TRACKED_IGNORED warning. To include an ignored file, list it in the target's inputs. This never includes Oyzu state, Git metadata or a nested repository. Listing a file includes its ignored parent folders but not their other contents; listing a folder includes everything ordinary inside it. Global Git excludes and tool-specific ignore files don't affect capture. Each copy is checked against the capture (size, digest, executable bit). A changed or missing file, a symlink or reparse point, or a copy failure stops the build; fix the problem and rerun. The plan and manifest record the selection in source.selection (container builds) or source.projections (native builds), so it can be replayed later. Compare the result with source.treeDigest to confirm the bytes are the same. When oyzu.lock is part of a container build's source, it is recorded with the source and tool evidence but hidden from the builder's view of the project, so license scanners don't treat it as project source. Listing it in a target's inputs keeps it visible.

Docker preparation commands have fixed time limits, separate from action timeouts: Operation Limit per command Image and platform inspection, daemon checks, tagging, worker control and volume operations 30 seconds Image pulls and exports, worker file copies and tool restoration 30 minutes Removing a failed restoration or a running worker 5 seconds They can't be configured. When one expires, the command fails with a deadline error and the Docker client is killed. Failed pulls keep Docker's error message. Before retrying, check the daemon, registry access and free disk space. Killing the client doesn't stop work inside the daemon. After the daemon recovers, look for and remove leftover Oyzu containers. Cancelling a build has its own cleanup budget; see forced cancellation.

oyzu build --frozen uses the plugin selections pinned in oyzu.lock and fails with PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING instead of resolving or rewriting the lock. --store picks the store that holds installed plugins. See plugin packages.
Error messages for cycles don't yet show the shortest cycle path. Oyzu doesn't infer a task's generated outputs; declare them. Long-running interactive services aren't supported as tasks.

Native local builds for the host path, platforms and slices. Action cache for reuse, affected builds for selection by Git history, and build logging for live output. Configuration for check levels, contexts and names that cross files.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cargo-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this when your crates come from a private sparse Cargo registry and you want Cargo to get its token without cargo login or a credentials file. Each time you run Cargo through oyzu, oyzu asks a local credential agent for a session and hands Cargo the token in memory through Cargo's own credential-provider protocol. Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Bash (Cargo 1.95). Isolated oyzu build runs don't use this yet.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [cargo] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning cargo.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain Cargo Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there. In your project, depend on the registry by name as usual: [dependencies] example = { version = "=0.1.0", registry = "internal" }

Run Cargo through oyzu exec, or in an activated shell: oyzu exec -- /absolute/path/to/cargo build --locked eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" cargo fetch --locked Supported commands are build, check, test, fetch and generate-lockfile. --help and --version run without asking the agent.

Sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "cargo", "arguments": [...]}. Reads the agent's answer: { "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential", "name": "internal", "index": "sparse+https://packages.example.com/index/" } name uses lowercase letters, digits, _ or - and can't be crates-io. index is sparse+ followed by an HTTP(S) URL ending in /, with no credentials, query or fragment. credentialEndpoint must also be on 127.0.0.1. Starts Cargo with CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_INDEX and CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER set for that registry, and CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_TOKEN removed. The provider is oyzu itself, run as cargo-credential-oyzu. When Cargo asks for a token, oyzu accepts only a read request for that exact index. It POSTs {"ecosystem": "cargo", "request": <Cargo's request>} to credentialEndpoint, which must answer {"token": "..."}. Cargo may reuse the token for the rest of that one Cargo run, but not for other operations. Your CARGO_HOME, caches, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and other Cargo configuration are left alone. Any provider you've configured for the same registry is overridden for that run only. The agent is asked every time, even for a warm offline build. Requests to the agent time out after 10 seconds and don't go through a proxy.

The token never goes into a file, a command argument or an environment variable. It's in Cargo's memory, so anything with access to that process (for example an administrator) can read it. Read-only access has to be enforced by the registry account the agent uses. If the agent fails, Cargo gets a generic error; the agent's response isn't shown. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command. oyzu never falls back to running Cargo without a session.
Cargo's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID The endpoint isn't 127.0.0.1 HTTP, or the agent's response is too large or malformed Fix the endpoint or the agent CARGO_SESSION_INVALID The registry name or index in the response isn't valid Fix the agent's response CARGO_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED The Cargo command isn't one of the supported ones. cargo publish isn't supported Use a supported command. Publish with oyzu publish CARGO_ROUTING_CONFLICT You passed --config, --token, --registry, --manifest-path, -C or -- Remove the override

One named registry per run. Other registries, Git and path dependencies, crates.io replacement, source replacement and Cargo aliases aren't covered. Arguments after -- aren't supported. Linux and Bash only. Windows, macOS and other shells aren't supported yet.
Cargo credential-provider protocol Cargo registry configuration Rust installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-help.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu --help lists every public command, grouped by workflow: Develop & build, Project tools, Environment & configuration, Platform and Diagnostics. Common examples follow the options. For one command's arguments and options, run oyzu <command> --help or oyzu help <command>. This works for nested commands too. oyzu --help oyzu build --help oyzu help config oyzu config set --help oyzu --json --help Help works offline, outside a project and without a platform account. It never runs the examples, installs tools or changes files.

On a color-capable terminal, help shows cyan headings, green command and option names and yellow placeholders. Redirected help is plain text. Variable Effect NO_COLOR=1 Turn help color off. CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 Turn help color on, even when redirected. Don't set both. The project ui.color setting doesn't apply to help, because help prints before any project configuration is read.

With --json, help and version requests return the unstyled text in output with exitCode: 0. Put --json before the command or after the command's --help. For oyzu help <command>, put --json before help. The human help layout can change between releases. Don't parse it; use --json.
CLI output for result and error formats.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-output.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every public command prints readable text for people by default and accepts the global --json flag for machine-readable output. This page shows what each kind of output looks like, which flags and environment variables control it, and what scripts can rely on. Choosing an output mode never changes policy, configuration, lock contents or exit codes.

Control Effect --json (before or after the subcommand) One machine-readable result on stdout; diagnostics on stderr as JSON Lines. See JSON results and errors. -v, -vv Debug and trace diagnostics; more detail in build output. -q, --quiet Hide routine progress. Results, warnings and errors stay. --log-level error|warn|info|debug|trace Set the threshold explicitly. See Diagnostic controls. OYZU_LOG Per-area log levels. NO_COLOR Turn color off. CLICOLOR_FORCE Force color (any nonzero value). NO_COLOR wins over it. ui.color Project or user setting: always, never or auto. Doesn't apply to help.
Run oyzu or oyzu --help for an overview of every command. Bare oyzu prints the same help and exits 0. See CLI help for nested help, help color and JSON help.

oyzu reshim (under Project tools) refreshes the shims folder and existing activation launchers. Human output shows the shims folder and the commands it holds; --json returns directory and commands. See the shims folder. oyzu shell install and oyzu shell remove manage shell startup profiles.

oyzu --version identifies the executable you're running: oyzu 0.1.0-local.8aee8560a0ca.dirty (debug; x86_64-pc-windows-gnu; build 1791211857) Part Meaning 8aee8560a0ca Short source commit (unknown.source-unknown without Git metadata). .dirty The worktree had uncommitted changes when it was compiled. debug Cargo profile. x86_64-pc-windows-gnu Target triple. build 1791211857 Build time in Unix seconds. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH sets it at compile time. Locally compiled builds are labelled local, including optimized ones. This is diagnostic identity, not a release version or a signed statement. --version never opens project configuration, runs Git or contacts a service. --version --json returns the text in the usual JSON envelope.

Pulling new source doesn't replace an installed oyzu. To see which one your shell runs, use command -v oyzu (POSIX shells) or Get-Command oyzu -All (PowerShell), then compare versions: oyzu --version ./.oyzu/bin/oyzu --version On Windows, use .\.oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe. oyzu build copies executable artifacts into the project's .oyzu/bin only after a successful native build. A failed build keeps the previous binaries. Compiling with Cargo through oyzu exec writes Cargo's own target/ output and doesn't update .oyzu/bin. Don't assume target/debug/oyzu is the one your shell runs. In an activated shell, ordinary commands run the first oyzu on PATH, so a project-local .oyzu/bin on PATH takes over. See shell activation.

Ordinary builds show a Facts section after preparation and before Selection, Plan and the actions. It needs no flag, login or network. Fact Meaning Branch / Commit The local branch and the commits recorded for versioning. Different targets keep their own commit. This doesn't prove that Git HEAD matches the files that were built. Git state Always shown as not verified. Source digest Content identity of the build inputs. Shortened by default; -v and JSON show it in full. Version / Basis Each target's or package's planned version and why. Packages in a target that share a version and basis are grouped: by count, or by name with -v. When some differ, each differing package gets its own row, the rest are grouped as others, and a basis they all share is shown once; -v lists every package with its own Version and Basis rows. Distinct native artifact versions get their own Artifact row. Kind The version kind; currently snapshots. A release context alone doesn't make a release. Context The build context (local, pr, ci, release) and where it came from. Protection unknown · not queried. Oyzu doesn't ask your Git host. Release Whether the build is eligible for release, or unknown. Version facts never allow publishing on their own. When independent targets prepare at different times, each new plan shows only new or changed facts before its actions. A version set by a hook shows pending post-hook finalization; the final version appears under Build. --quiet hides this section. In JSON, each plan event carries the facts in buildFacts. Environments, credentials and arbitrary extensions are never included. Uncertain Git or protection facts don't change the exit status, cache identity or release rules.

A default build shows compact linear progress, with one plan table before work starts. Sections always appear in the same order, and any section with nothing to say is left out. Every row, the title and the section rules share one width (80 columns, or less on a narrower terminal). Routine successes are collapsed; -v, --plan, oyzu inspect, oyzu history and --json keep the detail. Section What it shows Title line Project name and, right-aligned, the facts under Title line. ── Prepare ── One row per preparation step, then the pinned tools. ── Selection ── Plugin builder selection, and why the build isn't every declared target. ── Plan ── A table of targets by stages, with reason lines. ── Build ── One row per finished action. ── Failure: <target> · <stage> ── The native cause of a failed action. ── Outputs ── Artifacts with sizes and build profile. ── Warnings (N) ── Each distinct warning once, with its owner. Summary The outcome and counts, then a dim Details line. Title line​ The title line names the project and, right-aligned, shows: the host platform; local or the CI provider; the build context (context pr, context local). Where it came from is shown in Facts and by oyzu config explain context; see build context; fast or full, then optimized or development when you passed --optimized or --no-optimized. Under a CI provider the right-hand side may wrap onto the next line. If you pin a lower context while a CI provider marker is present, you get a CONTEXT_OVERRIDE_IGNORED warning. Prepare​ ── Prepare ── shows each preparation step as a row: mark, name, detail, duration and warning count. The Tools row summarizes the tools (2 tools pinned · 0 installed now) and lists each one with its version, already installed or installed now, and why it's needed (the detected requirement, or pinned in oyzu.toml). Toolchain components and host prerequisites follow. With several targets, the tool list prints once and each tool appears once. If the reason differs by target, each reason is shown (detected from …; pinned in … · not detected for <target>). The Plugins row follows the tools on every build that uses a builder plugin (2 plugins · 1 installed now). Each plugin release gets one line with its version, where it came from this time and the targets it builds: plugin store, installed now from <registry> (with its size when known), local package binding, or local development executable · not locked. A newly locked plugin adds recorded in oyzu.lock now. A plugin missing from the store, or not yet adopted, gets a warn mark and says what the next build does. Why each plugin was chosen stays in Selection. -v adds the release digest and the full route. The Images row follows on every build that runs in an execution image, such as --isolated (1 image · 1 pulled now). Each image gets one line with its digest, where it came from and the targets it runs: local Docker engine, pulled now from <registry>, unpacked now from … or unpacked root reused (from …) for the daemonless sandbox, or no image; built in process. -v shows full digests and sources. Plugin and image lines wrap rather than being cut, so no target or source is lost. In --json runs, the event stream carries the same facts as an executionImages inventory event (target, reference, digest, and origin with its kind). If another build holds the workspace, a Build lock row waits for it (waiting for pid N, started Ns ago) instead of failing. Ctrl-C stops waiting. Housekeeping after Prepare (such as cache cleanup at the end) is shown only when it's slow, fails or warns, or with -v. Attention rows. Tool detection is best-effort. Problems show as yellow ! rows under the tools. They warn and never fail the build (only an explicit pin can). tools.ignore silences a detection; ignored detections show with -v. Row Meaning ! protoc needed by prost-build · no catalog entry; pin or provide it Oyzu doesn't know this tool. A tool Oyzu can manage shows as an ordinary detected from Cargo.lock row and is locked and installed. ! protoc needed by prost-build in Cargo.lock · no usable checksum; pin it in oyzu.toml or silence it with tools.ignore A detected tool couldn't be resolved or installed. The build continues. host prerequisite … · not found on PATH A host prerequisite is missing. fetches <what> outside the lock (<file>) The build downloads something the lock doesn't cover. detection failed: <reason> · nothing extra detected Detection couldn't run. Live and redirected progress​ Interactive terminal. Work in progress shows under its section as one line per step or action with a spinner. Long status is shortened with …, never wrapped. Queued actions waiting on others show as ○ <target> · <stage> waits for <target> · <stage> (at most three, then + N more waiting), with an N of M finished line. Redirected and CI output never redraws. Each action prints a start line (.. target stage started) and an end line with outcome and duration, both led by the elapsed mm:ss. Every ten seconds a heartbeat names what's still running, for example still running: api build 10s · auth-lib test 12s · 6 waiting. Redirected output uses 100 columns on every host. Failure text wraps, Windows \\?\ prefixes are hidden, and long log paths keep their tail. On a narrow terminal or without color, every table turns into records. Nothing is dropped. Interrupted, --plan and --check builds have their own summaries. Selection​ ── Selection ── appears when a target is built by a plugin or when the build isn't every declared target. Plugin-built target: the builder selection. The full record with fixes appears when the build adopted or installed a plugin; otherwise one line per target. See plugin catalog. --affected: what it compared with (compared with origin/main at 0123456), the changed targets and paths, their dependents and the unaffected count. Fallback: ! Not narrowed with the reason, the code, and a fix when one is known. Explicit request: requested and required (prerequisites pulled in). Plan​ ── Plan ── prints once. Rows are targets; columns are the stages the builders declare, in the order format, lint, test, build, package, then any others. Cell Meaning run Runs in this build. skip The builder has the stage but this build doesn't run it (for example a fast local build), or it isn't available. off The check level is off: never run, and its tools aren't prepared. - The builder has no such stage. Under the table, one dim line per distinct reason names the stages it covers: Label What the line says off Where the check was turned off (format · disabled in oyzu.toml, test · disabled in oyzu.toml [context.pr]). skipped Why stages were skipped (lint and test · fast local build). advisory Stages whose failure is only a warning (lint · failures are warnings; the build still succeeds). profile Each build profile in use, its targets and why (cli · optimized · --optimized, cli and docs · development · local dist only, cli · optimized · release builds are published). policy Each policy override: the setting, the value policy enforced and why (format enforce · admin policy minimum in pr, release (project oyzu.toml sets off)), prefixed with its targets when not all targets share it. project Overrides from the root oyzu.toml's project constraints, in the same form (tests required · project constraint minimum in release (project app/oyzu.toml sets advisory)). lowered In a release build, each check a nearer folder lowered below a farther [context.release] value (tests advisory · app/oyzu.toml:2 lowers required from oyzu.toml:5 [context.release]). task Each conditional task or hook: whether it runs (and for which artifacts) or why it's skipped (pre_build · skip · unless context = local, post_build · run for bin-oyzu · unless artifact = bin-oyzu-shim). A per-artifact run's Build row names its artifact (post_build[bin-oyzu]). note Notes about the table. oyzu build --plan prints the same task lines as Task: lines under each target. Large and multi-platform plans One target built for several platforms (--all-platforms) shows one row per platform and says 1 target · N platforms. Above twelve rows, targets with identical stages share a counted row (29 targets) with a note. A narrowed build says N of M targets, and an affected build adds a why column (changed, uses <target>). -v lists every target. If the table doesn't fit, each row becomes a record (cli build run · package -, then its skipped stages on the next line). When a platform is built off the host, or a target declares platforms this run doesn't build, each row names its platform (hello · linux/arm64) and a built by column names the executor (host, cross toolchain (rust-lld)), or a footnote if it doesn't fit. An other footnote lists declared platforms you could build here with --platform; a not here footnote lists the rest with the reason (darwin/arm64 · needs a macOS runner (Apple SDK and linker)). See platforms and executors. --plan adds a Platforms · how each is built here table: target, platform, what builds it here, the CI runner it needs, and why. Grouping by directory. When targets live in more than one top-level folder (./ for targets at the root): plan rows are grouped under a dim folder heading such as services/; a prerequisite in another folder shows in a final needs column when it fits; Outputs are listed by folder; the summary adds one line per folder (services/ ✓ 2 targets 58.1s, the sum of that folder's action times); the twelve-row grouping applies within each folder. Build​ ── Build ── has one row per finished action: mark, target, stage, the command (shortened with …), executed or reused, and the duration. With more than twelve actions, clean successes fold into one tally such as ✓ 91 finished · 78 reused · 13 executed (-v lists them all). Running, warned, waiting, blocked and failed actions keep their rows, and the heading says 143 actions. A failed advisory check is shown once, as a warning: its row reads warn … failed · advisory, it gets no Failure section, Warnings has one CHECK_ADVISORY entry with the exit code and cause, and the summary counts it separately (1 advisory failed). The build still succeeds. Failure​ A failed action's row reads ✗ … failed <duration> (FAIL without color). After Build, a ── Failure: <target> · <stage> ── section shows the native cause (line breaks kept, terminal controls escaped), the exit code, Log with the log path, and Next oyzu build <target> re-run only this target. Actions that didn't run because a prerequisite failed are blocked (⊘) and counted separately. A blocked row says needs <target> · <stage>. Only the first three get a row; the rest become + N more blocked · -v lists them. The summary counts only outcomes that happened (✗ Build failed 1 failed · 12 blocked · 130 succeeded · 4m 02s), then Details and, for a host build, a note that local binaries weren't updated. A preparation failure ends after Prepare with a ── Failure: preparation ── section and no Build section. -q prints only Failure, Warnings and the summary line. Outputs, warnings and summary​ Outputs. ── Outputs ── lists artifacts as project-relative paths under dist/<target>/<platform>/ (any for platform-independent output; see the bundle layout), with size and build profile (cli dist/cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe 64.1 MB development). -v and --json show absolute paths; the JSON artifact record has the profile as profile. Warnings. ── Warnings (N) ── lists each distinct warning once, with its owner (for example docs · npm). Warnings aren't repeated inline during the run. The generic NATIVE_WARNING code is hidden by default and shown with -v and in JSON; Oyzu's own codes are always shown. Summary. The summary counts only outcomes that happened (2 targets · 1 executed · 1 reused · 235.3s), followed by a dim Details line with the manifest and event paths and the invocation ID. -v adds reuse and cache details. Marks and colors​ With color, state is a symbol: ✓ ok, ↺ reused, ! warning, ✗ failed. Without color (NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, redirected output), marks become padded words (ok, reused, warn, FAIL) and headings become -- Name ---. No state depends on color. -q prints only warnings and the summary line (failures keep their full report). Receipts and history​ The final summary of a build is its receipt. It counts targets and actions separately, and shows fresh tests, reused test results, warnings and where the records are. It separates checks that were selected (with their outcomes) from checks that weren't requested. That comes from the recorded build, not from a fast/full label or a missing report. Reports that recorded zero tests are labelled Native zero-test reports. Skipped tests keep their own count. Missing numbers show as unavailable, not zero. Old records without check selection say Check selection unavailable. A missing required report still fails the build. A successful build doesn't by itself make it eligible for release. A successful build says Build succeeded, or Build succeeded with warnings. invocationId ties a build result to its live and saved events; runId identifies the build that produced the bundle. oyzu build --explain and oyzu history <id> show recorded selection and reuse decisions; they never recompute causes from your current checkout. oyzu history lists up to twenty builds, and oyzu history <invocation-or-run-id> --json gives a compact summary with causes. See retained invocation lookup. Contract check​ oyzu build --verify-contract adds a Contract check block after Outputs. It shows the outcome (passed, failed, nothing to verify), how many confined actions ran again with the whole target visible, how many matched, diverged or weren't confined, and one Diverged row per mismatch naming the extra files and the declaration that fixes them. --json has the same data in manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-verification"]. A divergence is also an error diagnostic and a nonzero exit. An undeclared read by a confined action is the diagnostic confined-read-outside-contract, with the stage, path, missing fact and fix on indented lines. See verifying a contract.

Inspection, configuration and discovery commands use titled, indented views. pin shows a compact requirements table, task lists show readable labels, and which prints the selected path. Diagnostics from every command use the same status / subject / message layout, including env -v, which -v and shell payload commands. -v adds detail within the same layout. Multiline causes keep their line breaks. Lookup and payload commands print diagnostics append-only, with no redraws or cursor movement. Their stdout (paths, environment data, shell code) is unchanged.

--json works before or after the subcommand. Arguments after -- belong to the task or program, so its own --json doesn't affect Oyzu. oyzu pin --dry-run oyzu pin --dry-run --json oyzu --json config show oyzu tools inspect-lock --json oyzu --json tools resolve --registry registry.yaml --tool hashicorp/terraform --version v1.16.5 oyzu exec --json -- ./my-program argument Stdout holds one result, with no headings, color or progress. Oyzu's diagnostics go to stderr as JSON Lines, including warnings. Read stdout for the result. Native pass-through streams keep their own behavior. Errors (setup, operation or argument parsing) contain error and exitCode, and the process exits nonzero. JSON help and version return their text in output with exitCode: 0.

exec --json captures the child's output in stdout and stderr strings and returns its exitCode, which Oyzu also exits with. Input is still inherited. Output appears when the child exits, not live. The capture object says how streams were handled: inherited stdin, piped stdout and stderr, no terminal, not streamed, and UTF-8 decoding with replacement characters for invalid bytes. invocationId ties it to diagnostics. run --json outcome records describe capture the same way. Without --json, task output passes straight through.

activate, deactivate, environment hooks and env --shell SHELL print shell code by default, because headings would break evaluation. With --json they return { "shell": "…", "script": "…" }. Evaluate the raw code, never the JSON envelope. oyzu env inspection redacts credential-like values; shell payloads you ask for contain the real assignments in both modes. oyzu config schema build.yaml and oyzu config schema oyzu.toml print a JSON Schema document even in human mode, so you can redirect it to a file. With --json they return a config-schema record with it under schema. See editor schemas.

install SPEC, update and uninstall lead with the outcome (✓ Installed go 1.26.8), then what was declared and where, the lock and its platforms, replaced requirements and notes about other scopes. --dry-run starts with Dry run · no files were changed. Inspection commands show an outcome line, a table and an Attention section for unresolved rows. Statuses are words (ok, not installed, blocked, deprecated, stale lock, ambiguous), never color alone. All support --json. See tool commands.

oyzu tools list groups installations by tool (rust (core) · 12 installations · 17.0 GB), each with a Version / Platform / Size / Used by / ID table. ID is the start of the installation digest. It tells apart installs of one version that differ by recipe or platform ABI. --details adds location, tool identity and the full digest. The first line totals installations, tools, unreferenced installs and disk use.

tools resolve and tools evidence (see tool resolve) show a title, an outcome line (✓ complete, ! attention), the snapshot, a table of records, then Unsupported platforms, Errors, Needs attention and Next steps. --json prints exactly one document on stdout. Diagnostics such as EVIDENCE_FETCH go to stderr. Exit 3 means the document is complete but some items are undecided or unverified. Text from recipes has control characters escaped.

oyzu discover answers "what does Oyzu see here?". It prints one block per target (the name oyzu build <target> accepts): builder, whether build.yaml or native files chose it, package manager, version, location, which tasks are part of builds and which are for development only. It reads configuration and native files without running project code. oyzu run list shows tasks and their commands. --json returns the full discovery record. With no targets, it explains what to add or where to run. See build tasks.

A Not in build.yaml section lists each folder where discovery recognizes a build the file leaves out, as a Folder / Recognized by / Line to add table. --json adds an inventory object. Command Human output oyzu discover --check Build inventory is current (exit 0), or error[INVENTORY_UNDECLARED] with the table and a fix: line (exit 1). oyzu discover --write What it declared (Declared 1 build in …, Created build.yaml with 2 builds, Nothing to write, or, in yellow, A choice is needed: …; nothing was written), a Build / Uses / Folder table, and a Needs a choice table (exit 1) for folders several builders recognize, with an example: row and a <…> placeholder for uses. Folders listed as workspace members of a declared build are counted, not tabled: Build inventory is current · 2 builds declared, 10 workspace members, or Covered as workspace members: cli 10 folders. below a table. An unreadable workspace manifest adds a yellow warning: build web: cannot read the workspace manifest package.json: … line, and its members stay in the table. Both print a build-inventory record with --json (workspaceMembers, warnings). See builds build.yaml leaves out.

A bundle is the folder oyzu build writes (dist/ by default) or an exported OCI archive. oyzu inspect with no argument checks the current project's bundle; a project root also works. A missing bundle says where Oyzu looked and suggests oyzu build. On success the view starts with ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded|failed, then the run and source identity and tables of targets, actions, artifacts (path, size, platform, short digest), reports and diagnostics. It says that it checked recorded digests, not who produced the build. An OCI archive shows kind, platforms, size and digests. --json returns the full manifest. See build bundles.

oyzu run list starts with a count (Available tasks · 8 across 1 target), then one table with a Task / Source / Command header shared by every group. Tasks are grouped by target (for example cli and docs); your own ungrouped tasks are under Project. Each group heading shows its builder and task count. Listing prints no progress. Each row shows the full task name, its source and its command arguments. Tasks found by a builder (including package scripts) are labelled Inferred with their provider. Tasks from TOML show their file, relative to the project when possible. (override) marks a task that replaces an inferred or earlier one.

Cyan headings separate groups; inferred sources are muted and your own are purple. ui.color, NO_COLOR and terminal detection control color. ui.color=always or never wins; in auto mode NO_COLOR turns color off and CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 turns it on when NO_COLOR isn't set. Long rows become labelled records on narrow terminals. Unavailable tasks show why. Commands are shown for reading, not as a portable shell script. Dependencies and hooks may run more than the row shows. Command previews that look like they contain credentials are hidden, and terminal controls are escaped. Don't put credentials in task arguments.

Listing runs no tasks or tools and changes no files. JSON has the task map, and each task has an origin object: kind (inferred or user-defined), source (the configuration source, or null) and override (boolean).

Outside a project, oyzu run lists nearby projects by folder. It searches up to three levels down, skips hidden and generated folders, stops at each project and lists at most 32. It reads no child configuration and runs nothing. Change into a listed project or use oyzu -C <project> run. JSON returns status: "outside-project", directory, projects, searchDepth, limit and nextStep. With nothing found, it fails with PROJECT_NOT_FOUND. Asking for a task from the parent folder fails with TASK_PROJECT_REQUIRED. An unknown task fails with TASK_NOT_FOUND, the project folder, available task names and a spelling suggestion when there's a close match. When a task runs, its result row includes the exit code and duration, for example Failed (exit 7 after 0.20s). Oyzu exits with the task's exit code. JSON records have exit_code and duration_ms (run time only, not discovery or tool setup).
documents.s: Outside a project and unknown tasks

documents.t: Local tasks keep stdin. In text mode, tasks that record a bundle copy stdout and stderr both to your terminal and to dist/logs, even with --quiet. Their output is a pipe, not a terminal. Tasks with interactive = true get your terminal directly; their output can't be saved, so their bundle log files are empty. Tasks that don't record a bundle also get your terminal directly. With --json, task output is captured and stdout holds only the final result. See task output.

Flag Threshold (none) info -v, --verbose debug -vv trace -q, --quiet warn --log-level error|warn|info|debug|trace As given Flags work on either side of the subcommand. Arguments after -- belong to the child. More than two -v, more than one -q, or combining these flags is an argument error. Any of these flags overrides OYZU_LOG entirely. Without a flag, OYZU_LOG can set a level or comma-separated area=level entries, optionally starting with a default level (info if omitted): $env:OYZU_LOG = 'warn,oyzu::executor=trace' oyzu run foo oyzu run foo --json -v Remove-Item Env:OYZU_LOG Areas: oyzu::commands, oyzu::config, oyzu::discovery, oyzu::tools, oyzu::acquisition, oyzu::executor, oyzu::builders, oyzu::reports. Unknown or repeated areas, empty entries and invalid levels are errors. Help and version ignore OYZU_LOG, even invalid values. These aren't oyzu.toml settings. RUST_LOG has no effect on Oyzu.

--quiet hides routine progress and the interactive dashboard. Results, warnings, errors and child output stay. Verbosity never changes native flags, environment, plans, cache inputs, report checks or release eligibility. Logging is local and works offline. Environment variables, headers and full argument lists are never logged. Credential-bearing parts of messages are redacted (see Redaction). Child output and shell payloads you ask for aren't rewritten and may contain secrets. Trace isn't an HTTP dump.

Human diagnostics name the severity and the affected work. Operational failures also name the executable and version, the folder, the host platform and an ID when available. JSON diagnostic events have type, code and message, plus severity, target, invocationId, operationId and parentOperationId. Completed operations add duration_ms. Saved build logs carry the same IDs and every warning and error, whatever the console showed. Filtered console output can have gaps in its sequence numbers. Sequence numbers order events within one command; they don't show cause and effect between processes. New fields and event kinds may be added, so tolerate unknown ones. Reused actions can say which cache tier served them (local or remote).

A failed command prints ✗ <what failed and how to recover> with the diagnostic code underneath (for example COMMAND_FAILED). A message that already starts with its own code (✗ CONFIG_SYNTAX: …, ✗ REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED: …) doesn't repeat it underneath. --json prints {"error", "exitCode"}, and -q prints the plain error line. Internal phases are shown as words (Setup, Preflight, Source, Plan), and platform-specific targets as target · os/arch. Running a task prints a heading, the shared lifecycle rows and the result, followed by the tool's own output, unchanged.

Messages redact only the credential-bearing part. Ordinary URLs and text stay readable. Pattern Result A URL with a user name or password [sensitive diagnostic detail withheld] URL query and fragment ?[redacted] key=value or key: value with a credential-like name The name stays; the value is replaced. Authorization: or Bearer The rest of the line is redacted. Configuration display hides any value that looks like a credential. Child output isn't rewritten.

This is the style guide for every public command's human output: startup, progress, child output, results and failures. New and changed commands must follow it. A generic data dump or raw diagnostic envelope isn't a finished interface. Not every existing command has been reviewed against it yet. Lead with the outcome and the relevant selection (such as the active profile). Use short, descriptive section headings and aligned columns for comparable records. Keep empty collections compact ([] for configuration values) and leave out empty diagnostic sections. Never leave out failures or unresolved requirements. Keep identifiers exact: env.CARGO_HOME, env._.path, checks.coverageMinimum and cargo-llvm-cov are copyable identifiers, not prose. Never title-case them, split them, or change their underscores and punctuation. Humanize only labels the presenter owns. Group configuration settings by namespace, keeping full keys. Show booleans as true/false in configuration tables. Put long identities and low-priority metadata after the useful settings. Wrap long cells without dropping characters, and use labelled records on narrow terminals. Show Windows extended paths in normal form for people, but keep machine payloads unchanged. Use cyan headings, green success, yellow attention and red failures. Always include the meaning in text; color is never the only signal. Keep no-color output readable, escape terminal controls, and follow each command's redaction rules. Presentation must never reveal a value that was redacted upstream. Check the compiled command in human, no-color and JSON modes. Cover long identifiers and narrow layouts. JSON schemas and executable or native payloads don't depend on presentation. Human output leads with the outcome, then groups details into named sections. Comparable records use aligned tables; nested or long records use labelled fields without dropping values. The shared renderer uses the terminal width when it's known (100 columns otherwise) and switches to labelled records when a table would overflow. Color is extra: cyan headings, green success, yellow attention; errors keep explicit severity labels.

Shared result views use color on terminals and drop it for redirected output or TERM=dumb. A nonzero CLICOLOR_FORCE forces color, and NO_COLOR overrides forcing. No project configuration is opened just to style a result. JSON never contains ANSI sequences. Shell code, native streams and which paths keep their payload formats. Untrusted control characters in result values are escaped before styling.

pin shows one compact setup table per target. For Rust it lists each compiler component and test or coverage helper separately, with a purpose column. Formatting, linting, testing and coverage tools are required when those checks are enabled by the build or policy. The labels don't make checks optional. Being installable isn't the same as being installed. pin doesn't check for or install tools. Sources, profiles, compatibility constraints, configured requests and discovery limits are in --json rather than extra human tables. Unknown requirements stay visible. Results say whether resolution completed. Incomplete resolution lists what to do below the table. A platform coverage section lists the execution platforms the resolved metadata covers. That isn't a statement that tools are installed or run there. JSON keeps the full per-platform compiler_metadata. Environment inspection and shell profile results use the same layout.

Command behavior Required human presentation Quick lookup (which, version) Keep its short documented payload. No progress or decoration. Inspection or listing (env, config, tools current/list/versions/info, tools resolve, tools evidence, task list, pin preview) Descriptive title, useful selection context, grouped tables or labelled records, actionable unresolved items. Work (install, update, build, acquisition) Operation heading, named live steps, scoped child output, final outcome or receipt. Task or child execution (run, exec) Shared Oyzu preparation and progress; keep the documented native stream or pass-through behavior. Failure The failed operation and item, a readable cause, and recovery when known; keep the exit status and diagnostic code. A build summary shows each failed action's cause as an ERROR line even when the task never started (for example a rejected artifact handoff). Native text keeps its line breaks and has terminal controls escaped. Shell code and private protocols The exact payload, never decorated. Consistency means a shared hierarchy, vocabulary and state meanings, not identical headings on payload commands. Choose the pattern in the presenter before any work starts. Application commands return outcomes and lifecycle facts; they don't choose colors, terminal modes or human versus JSON formatting.

Before slow work, show the operation and what is being checked or done. Don't hold all feedback until the end. Instant lookups need no progress. Name the item or step (rust, Dependencies, Source evidence), not an internal scope like command or a repeated generic build. Context belongs in subtitles or explanatory text, not in something that looks like a work item. Use one state vocabulary: › running, ✓ done or ready, ✗ failed, ! attention, and the words Skipped, Blocked or Unresolved. Starting a check isn't finishing it: mark ready only after the owning operation confirms its checks. Close started steps on failure as well as success; never leave a step looking like it's still running in a finished receipt. Show elapsed or still-working feedback for long operations. Show a percentage only when there's a real total. Don't invent progress, and don't imply stalled work is healthy just because a heartbeat is printing. Keep the default linear. Small redraws may update active rows and short child output on capable terminals. Persistent panes, alternate screens and interactive input must never be required. Group concurrent work by target, task or tool. Indent and dim each child's recent output under its owner (about eight lines, within the shared terminal budget). Collapse it on success and keep the relevant part on failure. Never mix unattributed lines from parallel processes. Native pass-through commands keep their documented stream behavior. Finish with a short outcome and the useful results, artifacts or recovery steps. Don't repeat the whole progress history. Partial success, failed checks and missing requirements must stay visible. Routine progress must never default to envelopes like [Info] [oyzu::commands] [00:00.045] [command]. Subsystem names, timestamps and diagnostic metadata belong in requested diagnostic detail and structured logs. Warnings and errors still state their severity and keep useful codes; don't hide them to make output look clean. Example lifecycle (illustrative): Installing tools › rust Checking pinned installation… ✓ rust Ready · 1.95.0 · reused › cargo-nextest Installing… Downloading package… ✓ cargo-nextest Ready · installed Installation complete 2 tools verified · 1 installed · 1 reused A live terminal may replace the running rows; redirected output keeps a readable start and finish sequence. Both must show the same outcome.

Use the shared renderer's palette and color controls. Never add command-specific ANSI codes or a second styling policy. Dim native previews, not essential status or recovery steps. Without terminal capabilities, print append-only text with no cursor movement. Turning off color must not remove information. Forced color may style redirected output without turning on redraws. Never truncate copyable identifiers or paths at narrow widths. Keep progress and diagnostics on stderr and final results on stdout, apart from the JSON, shell payload and native stream exceptions above. --quiet removes routine progress, not results or failures. Verbosity adds diagnostics without changing what runs. Follow the owning redaction rules: don't redact ordinary configuration, paths or versions, and never reveal protected values just because verbose output is on.

For every new or changed public command: Pick its output pattern and reuse the shared presentation layer and invocation logging view. Look for an existing renderer first; extend the shared one rather than adding a local spinner, logger, palette or table formatter. Run the real compiled command. Check startup feedback, one successful outcome and a relevant failure, including that started steps are closed. A renderer unit test alone doesn't prove the command uses that renderer. Check normal human output, redirected or no-color output, JSON stdout/stderr separation and quiet mode. Check narrow and long layouts, and concurrent output where relevant. Use a real terminal for redraw changes. Say which terminals or platforms you couldn't check. Confirm payload exceptions, exit codes, redaction and the fast help/version path still work. Presentation must not change tool flags, plans, cache identity, recorded results or policy. Update the owning reference page and record what you checked. Fix inconsistencies in the command you changed; note unrelated gaps rather than claiming the whole CLI complies.

oyzu --help, oyzu help build, nested --help, --version and unknown-command errors come from the built-in command list. They work with an empty PATH, broken project files and a -C folder that doesn't exist. They don't load project configuration, refresh policy, open tool stores, start workers or contact services. No installation or account is needed. A native tool shim's --help still runs that tool's help. oyzu run list, oyzu discover and oyzu which are real operations, not help; they read the project and its configuration.

oyzu.toml settings, including tool pins, inherit from the Git worktree root. build.yaml doesn't inherit: the nearest build.yaml up the tree decides the builds (a build.yaml belonging to another tool never does). So a project nested in a repository sees the repository's tool pins. Pass --root . to make the current folder the root for both and stop inheritance. See configuration.

Human output can change between releases; don't parse it. Pass --json for pin, discovery, bundle and tool inspection, and configuration output. Each command has its own result shape; there's no universal result schema.
Build logging for live build progress and the heartbeat. Build bundles for inspect and history. CLI help for the help overview.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/configuration.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. This page explains how Oyzu combines configuration: where the files live, which value wins, how contexts, profiles and toolsets change values, and how policy limits them. For every oyzu.toml section and key with examples, see the oyzu.toml reference. The build.yaml rules are further down. Note: Configuration commands, their JSON output and several policy features are experimental and may change.

Configuration commands need no platform account, Docker, native toolchain or network. Save this as oyzu.toml in an empty directory named config-demo: [build] jobs = 2 [profile] default = "dev" [profiles.dev.build] jobs = 3 [ui] color = "never" From its parent directory: oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --no-profile config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config set build.jobs 4 --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config unset build.jobs --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs The get commands print 3, 2, 4 and 2. Validation succeeds (valid: true with --json). Removing the profile assignment exposes the base value; it does not restore the old 3. set and unset print the file they changed and the key.

Host Machine directory User configuration User state directory Windows ProgramData known folder + Oyzu RoamingAppData known folder + Oyzu/config.toml LocalAppData known folder + Oyzu/state macOS /Library/Application Support/Oyzu ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/state Linux /etc/oyzu $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/oyzu/config.toml, else ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml $XDG_STATE_HOME/oyzu, else ~/.local/state/oyzu The machine directory holds config.toml plus the protected files admin-settings.json (administrative policy) and management.json (enrollment). See administrative policy. Project files are oyzu.toml (commit it) and oyzu.local.toml (personal overrides; keep it out of version control). A relative XDG_* path produces a warning and the home fallback is used. OYZU_USER_CONFIG selects an absolute path for the user configuration file, which is useful for disposable environments. Relative paths are rejected. The file keeps user-level precedence, its sibling oyzu.lock holds user-default tool pins, and the variable cannot redirect machine policy, enrollment or state. On Windows, an absolute HOME that differs from the native profile moves persistent user data, including the tool store, to <HOME>/AppData/Local/Oyzu. This isolates tool caches in disposable homes. A relative HOME fails with CONFIG_SCOPE. Configuration and policy state locations and the action and image caches do not move, and existing data is not moved or deleted. Managed policy entries live under the user state directory. Integrity pointers are kept in the operating system credential store. A configuration file may be at most 1 MiB. There is no include mechanism and no executable configuration language. Oyzu does not enroll a machine automatically.

oyzu --root path/to/project config show --json oyzu --root path/to/project config explain build.jobs --json oyzu --root path/to/project config profiles oyzu --root path/to/project config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root path/to/project --profile integration run test oyzu --root path/to/project --no-profile run test

--root fixes the build root and the configuration root. -C / --directory sets the invocation directory; --root alone also sets it. Without --root, the nearest ancestor build.yaml that is an Oyzu inventory (see which build.yaml files are Oyzu's) within the current Git worktree selects the build. Configuration still inherits from the Git worktree root. Outside Git, the outermost ancestor with Oyzu configuration or a build declaration bounds inheritance, falling back to the invocation directory. A folder counts as a Git root when it has HEAD plus the objects and refs directories, or a .git file whose gitdir: pointer leads to them. Linked worktrees use their commondir pointer. An empty .git directory or a malformed pointer does not define a workspace. Oyzu reads this metadata without running Git. Entering an independent nested example and running oyzu build --plan selects that example. Its oyzu.lock and outputs belong to it, parent inventories are not merged, and automatic discovery skips nested build roots. An explicit parent target path still works. Composing roots and sharing a lock between roots are not supported. A selected build root may declare profile.default. Ordinary target subdirectories may not. A task cwd is relative to the TOML file that declares it. Two targets cannot own the same native build unit.

Lowest first: built-in defaults organization policy defaults (when the machine is enrolled) administrative defaults on the machine machine configuration user configuration each oyzu.toml from the project root down to the build's folder each included oyzu.local.toml in the same order invocation inputs (flags and OYZU_* variables) Each source applies its base values, then the selected profile. Each sibling target gets its own snapshot. Administrative constraints and project constraints are applied last. Arrays replace; they do not merge. A task replaces the whole task record. [overrides].remove removes explicit environment and task entries. Removed environment entries are also unset in development task environments. A task env can replace a global variable of the same spelling. Names that differ only in case (TOKEN and token) are rejected on every host. Tool aliases share the same precedence: a project node = "22" overrides a global "oyzu:node" = "latest". Inspection keeps the spellings with the winning source. Two aliases of one tool in the same overlay are ambiguous. Constraints bind a tool whatever its spelling.

Oyzu picks the profile in this order: --profile or --no-profile, the profile a task inherited, OYZU_PROFILE, the root profile.default, the inferred ci profile (empty unless you define it), then no profile. Profile names grant no authority. In CI, user computation settings and local files are left out and are not parsed. --local-overrides asks for local files, subject to administrative restrictions.

show, get, explain, profiles and validate never run project tasks. If resolution is blocked, show and explain report an unresolved status with no effective values, and exit successfully. validate is the failing command. Project and local files may not set platform.url, platform.account, cache.remote, cache.ciRemote, trust.enabled or trust.parents. Even show and explain fail with a CONFIG_SCOPE error that names the key, the file and where to set it instead. Environment values, credential-like names, recognizable sensitive values and task bodies are redacted. Use oyzu env to inspect the environment. Unknown optional settings produce a warning and have no effect. This covers unknown sections, fields under [toolsets.<name>], controls under [env._], and unknown fields inside tool requests, secret references, task report declarations, publication destinations, registry routes and engine or plugin package sources. A close spelling gets a hint. Known fields still validate. Unknown enum values and destination kinds are errors. If a project needs a feature older CLIs lack, declare it in [compatibility].requires so they refuse instead of ignoring it. Duplicate keys, known invalid values, unsupported required capabilities and unsupported schema majors fail. --strict also fails on warnings. --all-profiles also validates profiles that are not selected. Resolving an enrolled configuration can contact the policy endpoint and update its cache, so inspection is not always network-free.

The tables list every setting by area. Unless a row says otherwise, a setting can appear in machine, user, project or local configuration and in profiles, and administrative constraints can still limit it. "Scope" details for each key are in the oyzu.toml reference. An absent default means the setting has no value until you set one.

Key Values Default Meaning build.jobs Integer 1-65535 Logical CPUs (1 if unknown) How many independent preparation and build actions run at once. The smallest ceiling over the build root and the selected targets applies, and worker memory can lower it. oyzu build --jobs N (-j N), then OYZU_BUILD_JOBS, override every file. It does not change cache keys. See worker ceiling. build.isolation auto · docker · crun auto Sandbox for the isolated steps of Node targets on Linux. auto uses Docker when an engine answers and the daemonless sandbox otherwise. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun. Does not change cache keys. build.optimized true · false unset Selects the optimized or development profile. Unset means it follows where the output goes. build.executors Table of platform (os/arch[/abi]) to host · cross-toolchain · container unset The only executor that builds that platform. If it is unavailable the platform is not built here, and an explicit request for it fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. Nothing falls back. See platforms and executors. build.bundleDirectory dist · .oyzu/bundle dist Where collected outputs and evidence go. Root-only: component, context, profile and local values are refused. Choose .oyzu/bundle to keep a native dist folder. See bundle destination. build.host-workspaces-dir Absolute path native cache directory Where private source copies are parked between native host builds. User or machine scope only. Never part of a cache key. See source parking. version.strategy auto · native · tags · conventional auto How artifact versions are inferred. See version inference. ui.color auto · always · never auto Color in human task labels and statuses. auto colors only terminals. JSON is never colored. profile.default Profile name unset Profile used when none is chosen. Not allowed inside a profile or in a nested folder.

Key Values Default Meaning checks.tests, checks.coverage, checks.lint, checks.format off · advisory · enforce · required enforce How strict each check is. See check levels. checks.run required · all required locally, all in pr, ci and release Whether a build runs every check that is not off, or only required ones. --full runs every check. checks.coverageMinimum Integer 0-100 0 Minimum coverage percentage. A positive value makes the coverage report mandatory when coverage runs. With coverage off it is a configuration error. analysis.rules Table of rule id to off · advisory · enforce every rule advisory Experimental static-analysis levels. Unknown ids and levels are errors that list the valid ones. The nearest scope that sets it replaces lower scopes whole. See node static analysis. analysis.suppress List of { rule, path?, reason } none Experimental. reason is required; path is a project-relative glob. Suppressed findings do not fail and stay in --json. Unmatched suppressions are reported as stale. scan.jobs Integer 1-65535 2 How many independent scan checks run at once. scan.gitleaks.enabled, scan.gitleaks.failOnFindings Boolean false Select Gitleaks secret scanning and fail on findings. See scan. verification.<tool> List of tool lines ("22", "3.12") none Lines of a tool that need passing verification before oyzu publish accepts the build. See required tool lines. Does not change cache keys.

Key Values Default Meaning cache.local Boolean true Use the local action cache. false runs every action, like oyzu build --no-cache for one invocation. cache.remote oci://host[:port]/repository/prefix unset Experimental remote cache. User or machine scope only. Plain HTTP only for loopback hosts. No credentials, query or fragment in the URL. The sign-in token is never a setting: it comes from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or a CI job's ID tokens (OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL). Environment: OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE. cache.ciRemote Same as cache.remote unset The CI repository: a CI build reads and writes only it, other builds read it first and never write it. User or machine scope only. Environment: OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE. cache.read, cache.write Boolean true, false Whether the remote cache is read after a local miss, and whether local results are pushed to it. No effect without a remote or with the local cache off. cache.immutableTags Boolean false Declares that every configured cache repository refuses to replace a tag. Never set it for a registry that replaces tags. cache.dir Absolute path per-user cache (Linux $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/actions, macOS ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/actions, Windows %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\actions) Replaces the action-cache store. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file), not allowed in profiles, and ignored in CI. cache.nativeMaxMiB Integer 1-1048576 8192 Retained budget for native Rust compiler caches. See retention. cache.dockerMaxMiB Integer 1-1048576 20480 Budget for Docker images Oyzu pulled. Least recently used images are evicted after isolated builds. See Docker storage budget. Cache settings control transport and sizing. They do not grant cache credentials and do not change what an action produces.

Key Values Default Meaning tools.<name> Version string or { version = "..." } unset A tool request. See native pin files for how native version files combine with it. Not allowed in profiles or contexts. tools.ignore List of tool names none Silences best-effort detection of those tools for targets in that folder and below. Never removes a primary toolchain, and an explicit [tools] pin still provides the tool. Ignored detections show in -v and --json. tools.lockPlatforms List of execution platforms inferred See tool lock platform coverage. toolIndex.url HTTPS URL, or false https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/releases/latest/download/ Base URL of the signed public tool index. false uses no index, so registry packages resolve from the pinned registry. HTTP only for loopback. toolIndex.trustedRoot Absolute path Sigstore production root (built in, or newer from oyzu tools trust refresh) A trusted_root.json for a private Sigstore deployment. User or machine scope only. toolIndex.identity https: URI the index release workflow Certificate identity the index must be signed by, for a customer-signed index. User or machine scope only. toolCatalog.url HTTPS URL unset Delivery edge of the organization tool catalog. Tools then install only approved versions, using the token in OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN. toolCatalog.keys One to eight ed25519:<base64> keys unset Keys the signed organization catalog must verify under. Required with toolCatalog.url; pin two while the edge rotates keys. User or machine scope only. toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge 0, <n>h, <n>d (at most 366d) 7d How long the last good catalog may be used when the edge cannot be reached (network error or HTTP 5xx). 0 never uses it. User or machine scope only. toolCatalog.adminUrl HTTPS URL unset Admin API for oyzu tools request and --cancel. User, machine or administrative scope only. Environment: OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL. env.<NAME> Literal string or { secret = "reference" } unset Environment overlay. Names use ASCII letters, digits and underscores, start with a letter or underscore, and may not start with OYZU_. Values are not expressions. See environment values. env._.path Folders or { prepend, append } unset Development PATH additions. See shell activation. tasks.<name> Task table unset A task, replaced whole by a nearer source. See environment and tasks. The settings.* keys (auto-install behavior of developer commands) are listed in the oyzu.toml reference.

Key Values Default Meaning platform.url HTTPS URL unset Platform for sign-in, remote runs and secrets. HTTP only for loopback. No credentials, query or fragment. User or machine scope only. Environment: OYZU_PLATFORM_URL. platform.account Account id (lowercase letters, digits, hyphens) unset Account used for sign-in, remote runs and secrets. User or machine scope only. Environment: OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT. platform.authentication.provider session · environment · workload · private-key · execution unset Which credential provider platform commands use. Only session and environment are implemented. Environment: OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER. The access token is never a setting. It comes from oyzu auth login or OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN.

These select executable code, so they are accepted only from user, machine or administrative sources, never from project files, oyzu.local.toml or profiles. Key Values Default Meaning plugins.development Table of builder id (such as go/app) to absolute executable path unset Uses a local plugin executable for that builder id during this invocation. See local development plugin bindings. plugins.packages Table of builder id to { archive, sha256 } or { oci, identity?, trustedRoot? } unset A verified, installed plugin package that oyzu.lock pins. See plugin packages. plugins.preview Boolean false Makes preview plugin releases from the catalog eligible. See plugin catalog. engines.packages Table of engine identity to archive and digest unset Admits exact development engine archives. engines.development Boolean false Allows oyzu build --engine-development locally. Not allowed in CI, PR or release contexts. See engine staging for how engines are selected and which errors they raise.

Key Values Default Meaning docker.apparmorProfile Profile name oyzu-buildkit when the Linux host restricts unprivileged user namespaces, otherwise unconfined AppArmor profile for BuildKit. The older OYZU_BUILDKIT_APPARMOR_PROFILE variable is still read, with a diagnostic, and faces the same policy constraints. docker.frontends List of image references pinned by digest [] # syntax= frontends a Dockerfile may request. A request matches an entry with the same repository and digest, or the same tag when the request has no digest. Anything else fails with FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED. See Docker frontends. docker.load Up to 8 distinct destinations: docker or k3d:<cluster> unset Where oyzu run load puts a docker/image build's image. Put a team default in oyzu.toml and a personal cluster in oyzu.local.toml; [] in a nearer file turns an inherited list off. Without the build's with.repository the load task is unavailable. See loading the image locally. npm.sources HTTPS URL prefixes ending in / [] Extra places an isolated npm build may download locked packages from, besides https://registry.npmjs.org/. For example https://codeload.github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tar.gz/ admits a package pinned to a public GitHub commit tarball. The lockfile must record the tarball URL and its sha512, which is verified. git+https and github: specs are refused. npm.sessionEndpoint, nuget.sessionEndpoint, python.sessionEndpoint, cargo.sessionEndpoint, gradle.sessionEndpoint, maven.sessionEndpoint, oci.sessionEndpoint Numeric loopback HTTP URL unset Experimental dependency-session prototypes that need a separately running agent. See NuGet, Python, Cargo, Gradle, Maven and OCI sessions.

These are honored only from administrative configuration. Ordinary files and profiles cannot set them. Key Values Default Meaning config.localOverridesInCi Boolean false Whether --local-overrides may apply in CI. config.allowedProfiles List of names, including @none unset Restricts which profiles can be selected. tools.allowed List of tool ids unset Restricts which tools are eligible. tools.catalogs Ordered list ["public"] Catalog preference. An unavailable protected binding blocks execution. registries.routes List of { protocol, scope, connectorId } [] Routes package protocols (npm, pypi, maven, cargo, go, oci, tools, zig) through connectors. Standalone Node and Go installs support explicit host tool bindings. Other connector execution is not available yet. fetches.sources HTTPS URL prefixes ending in / unset (any HTTPS URL) Allowlist for declared fetches. When set, each fetch URL and every redirect must fall under a prefix or the build fails with SOURCE_DENIED or REDIRECT_DENIED. An empty list admits nothing. maven.snapshotRepositories HTTPS repository URLs ending in / [] Snapshot repositories captured Maven builds may use for snapshot version paths only. Everything else keeps the normal route. A build whose version is not a development snapshot fails rather than use one. See Maven snapshot repositories. engines.requirePin Boolean false Only a protected locked: true, value: true constraint requires an exact engine pin and a complete build lock. A policy default alone does not. See policy-required pins. scan.policy Scan policy table unset Organization scan policy.

A literal [env] value is the only value a task placeholder can read ({env.NAME}). Ambient variables and secret references never are. Literals can enter build inputs and evidence, so do not use one as a secret store. Secret references need an authorized consumer and are not substituted into build values yet. A task has either run (a shell command) or argv (an argument array), plus optional shell, cwd, env, depends_on, inputs, outputs, cache, interactive, reports, when and unless. argv elements and the task's own env values can use {namespace.name} placeholders. See task and hook conditions. cache = true with outputs makes an authored task cacheable by oyzu build. See authored tasks. Arguments after -- are appended to an argv task. A run task rejects them. oyzu run inherits stdin. Tasks that record a bundle copy stdout and stderr live and keep them in dist/logs. interactive = true keeps the real terminal and captures no logs, and for PowerShell it also drops -NonInteractive. JSON mode captures output and keeps stdin. See task streams and limits. A task needs a discoverable native project to run. [tasks.hello] argv = ["node", "-e", "console.log('hello')"] [overrides] remove = ["env.DEMO_MODE", "tasks.inherited"] oyzu --root path/to/project run hello runs the first task. [overrides].remove takes dotted keys.

Oyzu reads CI hints from the environment once, when the configuration session opens (before build workers set their own CI=true). Detection is offline and does not depend on terminals, hostnames, networks or the operating system. Detected context is a hint only. It never proves who is running the build and never grants publication, credentials or cache authority. A marker counts when it is set to a nonempty value other than false, 0, no or off (case-insensitive). Provider Marker pr signal release signal GitHub Actions GITHUB_ACTIONS GITHUB_BASE_REF set GITHUB_REF_TYPE=tag GitLab GITLAB_CI CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID CI_COMMIT_TAG Azure Pipelines TF_BUILD BUILD_REASON=PullRequest BUILD_SOURCEBRANCH starts with refs/tags/ CircleCI CIRCLECI CIRCLE_PULL_REQUEST CIRCLE_TAG Buildkite BUILDKITE BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST is not false BUILDKITE_TAG Travis CI TRAVIS TRAVIS_PULL_REQUEST is not false TRAVIS_TAG Bitbucket Pipelines BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER BITBUCKET_PR_ID BITBUCKET_TAG Drone DRONE DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=pull_request DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=tag AppVeyor APPVEYOR none APPVEYOR_REPO_TAG=true Jenkins JENKINS_URL CHANGE_ID none These providers are detected as CI without a pull request or release signal: Gitea Actions (GITEA_ACTIONS), TeamCity (TEAMCITY_VERSION), Bamboo (bamboo_planKey), Bitrise (BITRISE_IO), Google Cloud Build (BUILDER_OUTPUT), AWS CodeBuild (CODEBUILD_BUILD_ARN), Harness (HARNESS_BUILD_ID), Codefresh (CF_BUILD_ID), GoCD (GO_PIPELINE_LABEL), Prow (PROW_JOB_ID), Cirrus (CIRRUS_CI), Semaphore (SEMAPHORE), Netlify (NETLIFY), Vercel (VERCEL) and Xcode Cloud (CI_XCODE_PROJECT). TaskCluster needs both TASK_ID and RUN_ID (RUN_ID=0 counts). CI=woodpecker, CI_NAME=sourcehut and CI_NAME=codeship identify those providers. Any enabled CI value selects CI behavior even for an unknown provider. CI=false disables only that generic hint, not a vendor marker. A system with no recognized marker must set CI=true. A variable such as BUILD_ID alone is not enough. Several matching providers are kept in sorted order. With no signal the context is local. oyzu config explain shows executionContext with ci, the sorted providers and the matched variable names in signals.
