Reports are collected only if the command writes them to OYZU_TEST_REPORT / OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT (or a declared reports path). Missing reports are recorded as status: missing. Each test also gets a test-evidence record (oyzu.dev/test-evidence in the manifest, the Test evidence block in the output, evidence in oyzu run --json) with the status of the command, test results and coverage, and a verdict: Case Verdict Builder default or native runner, reports collected accepted Opaque command passed, reports missing, not required incomplete ("command passed; test results missing; coverage missing"); the run still succeeds Test command failed (any mode) rejected; the command fails and partial reports are kept A required report is missing (checks.tests = "required", checks.coverage = "required", checks.coverageMinimum, or a reports entry on the task) rejected with a report-missing error Builder default, but a report is missing The command fails Only reports written during this run count; older files are rejected. Oyzu never edits package.json or your configuration. You can also declare where a supported command writes a report: [tasks."project:test"] argv = ["node", "--test"] reports = [{ kind = "test", format = "junit", path = "reports/junit.xml" }] The path is relative to the task's folder. Missing parent folders are created. Declaring one report doesn't remove the other required kinds. No file may already match a declared path or glob before the run. Move or delete old files first. For a glob, your command must produce the matching files.

dist/manifest.json links the JUnit and coverage reports (LCOV for Node, Cobertura for Python and Rust, Go coverage profiles for Go), their summaries, the plan and the logs. It lists no new artifacts. The command fails when tests fail, a required report is missing or malformed, or coverage is below the configured minimum. Failed test reports are kept when available. A failing pre-hook blocks its test. A failing test skips its post-hook. A failing post-hook keeps the test's reports. Reports are collected after the post-hook, so a hook can transform them. A test that can't start is recorded as failed. Actions that never ran are marked blocked. Output is shown live and also saved in the bundle's numbered log files, including when tests fail. A task with interactive = true uses your terminal directly, so its output isn't saved. See task output. Only one oyzu run test can write a bundle at a time; a second one fails with a workspace-lock error.

Host tasks often build into dist/ before testing. A direct test keeps those files next to its reports and records their paths, sizes and digests under oyzu.dev/host-outputs. They aren't listed as artifacts of the test run. oyzu inspect checks this list. Earlier Oyzu reports and logs move to history. The previous dist folder moves to .oyzu/history/<run-id>. Native output must be ordinary files and folders. Links, reparse points and files that collide with new reports fail. manifest.json, plan.json, envelope.json and logs are reserved names in dist. Move an application file with one of these names before running. If the command fails early, the earlier bundle may still be in place. Check the command's result and run ID rather than assuming dist belongs to the last attempt. A later full build can keep a preserved file at an artifact's destination only when it matches the new artifact exactly (kind, digest, size and executable flag). Different content at the same path fails. See bundle retention and recovery.

A direct test run is local development evidence. The plan, envelope and manifest record oyzu.dev/invocation with: Field Value Meaning kind test A test-only run. execution host Ran on your machine. isolation none No sandbox; tests have your network and file access. source observed-before-run Source was hashed before the run; later changes aren't captured. toolIdentity unverified Ambient tools weren't verified. Actions declare network: host and aren't cached. Environment values are redacted in the plan. The tests' own output isn't scanned for secrets. In CI the producer is recorded as ci-unverified. A test run doesn't satisfy full-build checks and grants no publishing or signing rights. oyzu inspect checks integrity, not authenticity.

No test configuration is needed. Detection picks the runner, and the exact scripts jest, jest --ci, vitest, vitest run and mocha keep npm's pretest/posttest while Oyzu adds JUnit and LCOV. Your framework configuration still decides which tests run, reporters and coverage scope. Framework Tested version Also needs Jest 29.7.0 — Vitest 5.0.3 @vitest/coverage-v8 of the same version Mocha 11.8.0 c8 10.x in the project, or fallback tools in OYZU_NODE_REPORTING_HOME. See Mocha reporting. Install project dependencies before oyzu run test. Missing reporters aren't installed for you. Other major versions aren't tested. On Windows, npm is called through its JavaScript entry point, not a .cmd file. Scripted pnpm and Yarn combinations on the host aren't tested yet.

With no Node pin, oyzu build picks the latest LTS release that satisfies every engines.node range. If no LTS release does, it picks the latest matching stable release, and the plan explains why. For example, with 24.x as LTS and 26.x as Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 selects 26.x. Pins in configuration (latest, 26, exact versions, lts/<name>) work as usual and must satisfy engines. The build writes oyzu.lock and installs Node before any action runs. It doesn't run tests at this point. .nvmrc and .node-version aren't read. oyzu build --connector-bindings <file> supplies host bindings for tool sources routed by an administrator. See Node selection.

Direct tests are supported on Windows, Linux and macOS for Node frameworks and Rust (Rust on Windows needs MSVC; the windows-gnu toolchain lacks the profiler runtime). Helm direct tests are tested on Windows only. Docker targets have no test-only bundle. With the development node/app plugin binding, only single-package node --test and opaque report commands are supported. The built-in Jest, Vitest, Mocha and workspace integrations don't apply. Host tests aren't hermetic.
Build tasks for task order, hooks and output. Build bundles for bundle layout and history. Configuration for check levels and coverage minimums.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/directory-artifacts.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A directory artifact is a build output that is a whole folder, such as a static website in dist/, rather than a single file. Oyzu records every file and folder in it, lets you check the bundle later with oyzu inspect, and can copy it into another build with materialize. Note: Directory artifacts are experimental. Today they come from the Node application builder: conventional Vite builds and explicit node/app custom builds that write to dist/. Oyzu doesn't guess directory outputs for other build scripts.

In the build manifest, a directory artifact has the usual artifact fields (identity, target, producing action, version and bundle path) plus: Field Meaning kind directory. entries Every file and folder inside, sorted by relative path, including hidden files and empty folders. The root itself is left out. entries[].path, kind, size, executable Present on every entry. Folders have size 0 and executable: false. entries[].digest SHA-256 of the file's bytes. Files only. size Total bytes of all files. digest SHA-256 identity of the whole tree, computed from the sorted entries. It is not the checksum of an archive. Timestamps, absolute paths and user or group IDs don't affect the digest. Everything in the folder is collected, so names like dist, target or .hidden inside it are part of the artifact.

oyzu inspect <bundle> reads the folder without changing it and compares it with the manifest. Inspection fails when bytes changed, entries were added or removed, an empty folder is missing, entry metadata doesn't match, or a path is invalid. Inspection runs no tools or project scripts and uses no network. A passing check means the files match what the build recorded. It doesn't prove who produced them.

When a consumer build lists a directory output under materialize, the folder's contents land directly under the destination. An artifact containing index.html copied to site becomes site/index.html. The producing build must have succeeded. Oyzu checks the recorded content before copying and checks the copy afterward. Each consumer gets its own copy, so editing it never changes the producer's bundle. The copy fails if the destination already exists, two mappings overlap, or it collides with a source file. Producer and consumer must target the same OS and architecture. A consumer's platform requirement selects the matching producer variant; see matrix selection and Docker target selection. A directory output is never treated as platform-independent automatically.

Symlinks, special files, names that aren't portable and paths that differ only by case are rejected. To ship a tree with symlinks, produce a regular archive file instead. A tree can hold at most 100,000 entries and 10 GiB of file content. If a file changes while Oyzu is collecting or copying it, the operation fails. Unix executable bits are recorded and copied. On Windows every file is recorded with executable: false, so moving Unix executables through a directory artifact to Windows doesn't keep them executable. Static data folders aren't affected. Supported on Linux and Windows.
A failed collection can leave partial output on disk. It isn't a valid artifact and isn't reused. Fix the reported error, then rerun the producing build or restore an intact bundle.
Node applications Build bundles Host workspaces

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/discovery-selection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Discovery works out each Node or Python target's tools, such as its package manager or formatter, from your project files. When the files settle the question, you need no Oyzu configuration. When they don't, discovery stops and tells you which line to add to build.yaml. This page also covers how build.yaml and discovery decide which builds exist, and how Rust toolchain files are read. Discovery only reads files. It never runs a tool, script or configuration file, and it never picks a winner silently. oyzu build --plan shows every decision with its reason.

If discovery reports a conflict, add the selector the error names under with and run again: builds: pytest: uses: python/package with: formatter: ruff conflicting Python formatter candidates black, ruff: black via pyproject.toml tool.black; ruff via pyproject.toml tool.ruff; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {formatter: black}` or `with: {formatter: ruff}` Then check the result with oyzu build --plan; see decisions in the build preview.

A role is one tool choice a target needs, such as its package manager, test framework, linter or formatter. Each candidate comes with evidence of a certain strength, and the strongest wins: Strength Examples declared A test script that runs exactly one recognized test runner. native A lockfile, package.json packageManager, a framework configuration file, a pyproject.toml tool table. conventional A declared dependency, a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml, a uv.lock that locks no packages. default The default when nothing else applies: npm, ESLint, Prettier, pip or Ruff. Two different candidates tied at the strongest level are a conflict. A candidate Oyzu has no support for, such as packageManager: nub@0.8.3, is unsupported. Both stop discovery; file order never decides.

A lockfile beats a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml. pnpm can write this file just to store settings; only its packages list declares a workspace. Without packages, the file is conventional evidence, so package-lock.json (npm) wins. With no lockfile it still picks pnpm over the npm default. A file with packages, or one that isn't a YAML mapping, is native evidence and conflicts with another manager's lockfile. The runner a compound test script names. If the test script isn't exactly a recognized command (jest, vitest run, mocha, …), but its &&, ||, ; and | parts name exactly one of jest, vitest, mocha or node --test, that runner wins. Parts such as pnpm lint, npm run unit or yarn unit are followed into the referenced script. Leading NAME=value assignments, cross-env, npx and <manager> exec are skipped. A script with quotes, $, backticks, parentheses, redirection or flags such as --filter isn't read; other evidence decides. The script still runs as written. Oyzu adds test reporting only to an exact recognized command. A uv.lock that locks no packages. uv records the project itself in uv.lock, so a lock with no [[package]] entries is conventional evidence and yields to poetry.lock or [tool.poetry]. A uv.lock that locks packages is native evidence.
documents.s: Native rules that settle a role without configuration

documents.t: With a build.yaml, its builds are the full list. Discovery only fills in an omitted uses and reports folders the file leaves out (see builds build.yaml leaves out). Without a build.yaml, discovery uses a project at the root, or searches below the root for projects. The search stops going deeper once it finds a project; that project's builder handles everything inside it. Nested Git repositories and folders with their own build.yaml also stop the search. A build.yaml that belongs to another tool (its root has none of builds, members and exclude, such as Dart build_runner's file) doesn't stop the search. oyzu discover lists it under Skipped with its root keys (which build.yaml files are Oyzu's). If such a file is at the root, discovery works as if there were no build.yaml. The search skips generated and dependency folders, goes at most 32 levels deep and finds at most 1,024 targets.

Discovery stays inside the configuration boundary of the command. An empty or broken .git marker in a parent folder doesn't make that folder the workspace. For sibling projects with no shared Oyzu configuration, oyzu -C first run list lists only first's tasks. In a real Git workspace, discovery includes all its projects, and an unqualified task that several targets have is ambiguous. Use the qualified task name from the error, or --root first to choose a narrower root. Linked worktrees and .git pointer files follow the same rules.

When discovery stops, declare the target and add the selector the error names under with (see the quick start). If the files match more than one builder, choose uses first. For example, a root with both package.json and Dockerfile needs builds: {app: {uses: node/app}} before the Node test runner can be decided. Builder with key Values node/app, node/package package-manager npm, pnpm, yarn test-framework node-test, jest, vitest, mocha, custom linter eslint, biome formatter prettier, biome python/app, python/package, python/library package-manager pip, uv, poetry linter ruff, flake8 formatter ruff, black The keys match the role names shown by --plan. Your selection always wins. Discovery still records what it saw. Any other value, a non-string value or any other with key fails. A selection applies only to the target's own folder. It doesn't change packages inside a Node workspace. Tool versions don't go here; set them in oyzu.toml. Another example error: conflicting Node package manager candidates nub, pnpm (nub unsupported): nub via package.json /packageManager; pnpm via pnpm-lock.yaml lockfile; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {package-manager: pnpm}` The suggestions list the supported candidates that were seen, or every supported value if none was. Choosing a tool your project doesn't actually use can still fail later, when that tool runs.

oyzu build --plan shows a Discovered table per target with each role, the chosen tool and the reason. With --json, each target has a discovery object mapping the role to selected and reason: package-manager npm native package-lock.json lockfile; outranks pnpm (conventional pnpm-workspace.yaml settings without packages) formatter ruff build.yaml with.formatter; discovery also observed black A reason names the winner's evidence and every candidate it beat (other than defaults). A real build keeps all observations and any selector in the plan's oyzu.dev/discovery extension.

The Rust builder reads rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain in every form rustup accepts. Like rustup, it uses the nearest one, searching upward from the build folder and stopping at the project root. Form Meaning Legacy rust-toolchain holding only a name, such as stable, 1.95.0 or nightly-2020-07-10 The toolchain name. [toolchain] table, in either file channel (stable, beta, nightly, <major.minor>, <major.minor.patch>, optionally dated or with a host triple), components, targets and profile. A table without channel Oyzu uses its own default ([tools] rust in oyzu.toml, else Oyzu's default Rust) and keeps the declared components, targets and profile. path, a local toolchain folder Not supported. oyzu pin, oyzu build and build --plan fail with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID; set toolchain.channel to a release instead. A [tools] rust value doesn't override it.

A channel acts as a native pin only when [tools] rust would accept it: stable or an exact stable release such as 1.99.1. Any other channel (nightly, beta, 1.99, a dated or host-qualified name) makes builds, build --plan and oyzu pin fail with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID and a fix. oyzu discover still lists it.

An empty [toolchain] table, channel together with path, or an empty channel or one containing whitespace fails. Having both files fails with both rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain exist, even though rustup itself would prefer rust-toolchain.
With a build.yaml, only its builds exist; discovery never adds one. It does two things instead: it fills in an omitted uses, and it reports folders the file doesn't mention.

A build may leave out uses. When exactly one builder recognizes the build's folder, discovery uses it. oyzu discover shows the build as build.yaml; builder detected from project files (builder_selection: inferred in --json). Builds that name uses show as explicit. builds: web: {path: web} # discovery supplies uses: node/app cli: uses: rust/app # written out: reviewers see exactly what was chosen platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64] exclude: [tools/scratch, tooling/**] If no builder or several builders recognize the folder, discovery, planning and builds fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, naming the candidates and the line to write: build both: both is recognized by docker/image and node/app, so discovery cannot choose; write the one you want in build.yaml, for example both: {uses: docker/image, path: both}

A folder that a builder recognizes but no entry covers is listed, never built. Command What it does oyzu discover Lists each such folder, the builders that recognize it, and the line to add (web: {path: web} when one builder matches). A folder several builders match gets an example: line with a placeholder, such as both: {uses: <docker/image or node/app>, path: both}. oyzu build --plan Names up to five under Not in build.yaml, then a count of the rest. A real build doesn't look for them or fail because of them. oyzu discover --check Writes nothing. Exits 1 with error[INVENTORY_UNDECLARED] and a table of folders while any folder is neither declared nor excluded; otherwise exits 0 with Build inventory is current. Without a build.yaml, every discovered build counts as undeclared. Add it to CI to catch new folders that would silently not build. oyzu discover --write Declares every undeclared folder that exactly one builder recognizes. --check and --write can't be combined. --write details: Each folder is added as one line with uses written out (web: {uses: node/app, path: web}), at the end of the builds: block. Comments, order and your own entries stay as they were. It creates build.yaml if there is none. It refuses a file whose builds: isn't a block mapping at the start of a line, a symlinked file, a file changed meanwhile, or another tool's build.yaml. A folder several builders match isn't written. It's listed under Needs a choice and the command exits 1 (outcome incomplete). If nothing else was written, the first line says A choice is needed: …; nothing was written. When it writes, it adds # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu-releases/releases/latest/download/build.yaml.schema.json as the first line unless a schema comment is already there, so editors can validate the file (editor schemas). With --json, oyzu discover adds an inventory object with tracked, undeclared and excluded lists (or inventory.error, which never fails discovery). Plan JSON has undeclared: {total, folders, tracked}.

--write and --check print a build-inventory record with --json: Field Meaning mode The command mode. outcome current, undeclared, written or incomplete. path, tracked The build.yaml path and how files were counted. undeclared / added / needsChoice, excluded Folder lists. Each folder has path, builders, name, entry and, when excluded, glob. workspaceMembers Folders covered as workspace members, each with path, builders and the owning build. warnings Workspace manifests that couldn't be read. skippedBuildFiles Other tools' build.yaml files, each with its path and root keys. Plain oyzu discover --json lists them as skipped_build_files.

A folder listed as a member by the workspace manifest in a declared build's folder belongs to that build. It's never reported as undeclared, and --write never declares it. Builder Manifest in the build's folder Members rust/* Cargo.toml [workspace] members paths and globs (*, ?, […]), minus each exclude path and its subtree. A member listed by literal path stays a member even below an excluded path, as in Cargo. go/* go.work Each use folder (one module each, not its subfolders). node/* package.json workspaces (npm, Yarn; an array or {packages: [...]}) and pnpm-workspace.yaml packages The folder globs, minus those starting with !. A crate under crates/ that members doesn't list isn't a member (Cargo wouldn't build it), so it's still reported. Only the build's own builder counts: a docker/image build at the root doesn't own a Cargo workspace there. A build without uses asks every builder that recognizes its folder. A member covers only its own folder; the search continues below it. A manifest that can't be read owns nothing and never fails the check, plan or build. Its members stay reported, with a warning such as warning: build web: cannot read the workspace manifest package.json: …. Fix the file and run the check again. Human output counts members: Build inventory is current · 2 builds declared, 10 workspace members.

The walk starts at the build root and skips dependency and output folders, nested Git repositories and folders with their own build.yaml. It stops below a folder a builder recognizes. A declared folder owns everything below it, whether or not a builder recognizes it. The root never owns the whole tree while a build.yaml exists. A build declared at the root (path omitted or .) covers the root folder only; its workspace members are covered, and any other project below is listed until declared or excluded. Without a build.yaml, a recognized root is the only build, so --write declares just that. The walk continues below an excluded folder.

Without a build.yaml, --write keeps the existing zero-config names (project at the root, project-<path> below it, such as project-web), so dist/ paths and cache identity don't change. With a build.yaml, a new folder is named after the folder, then its path joined with -, then a numbered variant if needed.

exclude: lists folder globs relative to the build root. It silences the listing and the check; it never changes which builds exist. Use / on every platform. Matching is case-sensitive, as in Git. * stays within one folder, tooling/** covers everything below tooling, and . is the build root. Absolute paths, .., backslashes and drive letters are refused. The key is exclude, not ignore, so it isn't confused with tools.ignore.

Inside a Git work tree only tracked files count, so a file a CI job creates can't fail the check. A folder is considered when Git tracks a file directly in it (read with git ls-files, no network, no index writes). Outside Git, or without git, every file counts and the output says so (tracked: all-files).

Selections are read once from build.yaml. When npm workspace tests and checks run on the host, each package (including the root) is detected again without them, so a root that needed a selection fails there. Node output profiles and the Python test framework have no selector. Undeclared-folder detection works per folder: an untracked manifest next to tracked files still counts. The catalog detection budget applies to the whole walk. Going over it fails --check and --write (with a fix) and is reported, not fatal, in the plan. Workspace members come from the manifests listed above only. Cargo path dependencies that are automatically members, Maven modules, Gradle include, .NET solutions and uv workspaces aren't read, so those folders are reported until you declare or exclude them. npm doesn't document ! in workspaces; Oyzu reads a leading ! as pnpm does. Discovery is tested on Windows. The walk uses no platform-specific paths.
Configuration for build.yaml, native pin files and editor schemas. Local builds and build tasks for what builds do. CLI output for the oyzu discover output.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-frontend.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. docker/image builds run every Dockerfile through oyzu-buildkit-frontend, a BuildKit frontend that ships in the Docker plugin package. It runs the standard Dockerfile frontend of BuildKit v0.34.1 (the version its Go module pins) unchanged and adds two things: an approved list for Dockerfiles that request their own frontend with # syntax=, and a way to inject files into RUN steps. You normally only meet it when a Dockerfile starts with # syntax=. Oyzu loads the frontend from an OCI layout in the plugin package (share/buildkit-frontend), never from a registry. Preparation copies the layout into the prepared dependencies, which the BuildKit worker mounts at /oyzu-docker. A different plugin package changes the frontend and therefore the build plan.

A Dockerfile whose first line is # syntax=<reference> builds only if that reference is on the docker.frontends list (see configuration). Every entry must be pinned by digest: # oyzu.toml, user or managed configuration [docker] frontends = ["docker/dockerfile:1.17@sha256:<index digest>"] A request matches an entry when it has the same repository (docker/dockerfile and docker.io/docker/dockerfile are the same) and either the same digest, or the same tag if the request names no digest. An untagged request means latest. Oyzu copies the approved frontend image from your local Docker engine, for the build's platform, and loads it by digest. It never resolves the tag again. Anything else fails during preparation, before a worker starts: FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED: Dockerfile requests frontend docker/dockerfile:1, which is not on the approved list; approved: docker/dockerfile:1.17@sha256:... An entry without a digest fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Oyzu never ignores the # syntax= line or substitutes its own frontend. Oyzu still parses the Dockerfile with the plugin's pinned BuildKit parser during preparation. Syntax that parser does not understand fails even if the frontend you requested would accept it.

When a build plan carries injection files, the frontend gives every RUN step: a read-only mount of those files at /oyzu-inject, and APT_CONFIG and SSL_CERT_FILE set to the named files inside it (a RUN's own value for either variable is replaced). The mount and variables exist only while that step runs. No layer, image configuration entry or history line carries them, and the base image keeps its digest. Your Dockerfile is not edited. A RUN that mounts something at /oyzu-inject fails because the path is reserved. Nothing in Oyzu supplies injection files yet, so builds currently run without injection and RUN steps are unchanged.

Injection reaches only RUN steps. A requested frontend's own planning steps (for example, reading a file from a stage) run before Oyzu rewrites its graph and do not see the mount. The frontend follows the Dockerfile frontend of the BuildKit release its Go module pins. Updating it means releasing the Docker plugin again. Generated image recipes (such as Python containers) use BuildKit's built-in dockerfile.v0, not this frontend. A Docker plugin package built without its Linux helpers has no frontend and fails preparation.
Docker image inputs and offline builds Configuration for docker.frontends

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-images.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The docker/image builder turns a Dockerfile into a verified OCI image archive. Simple Dockerfiles that only add files to a base image build without any container engine. Everything else builds in an isolated, offline BuildKit worker. This page covers what the builder accepts, how base images and dependencies reach the build, and what a build records. Note: Image builds are experimental. The builder supports scratch, earlier stages in the same Dockerfile and base images that are already in your local Docker image store (or, for daemonless builds, public registry images pinned by digest).
documents.s: Docker image inputs and offline builds

documents.t: FROM alpine:3.22 COPY greeting.txt /greeting.txt RUN test -f /etc/alpine-release oyzu run list oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist No extra project configuration is needed. oyzu build --plan prepares the inputs, so the base image must already be provisioned and the base execution image must be available. The output is dist/<target>/<platform>/<target>-<version>.oci.tar, with its digest in dist/manifest.json. oyzu run build is a native development command. It does not give you the isolated, verified build that oyzu build does. The Docker plugin never takes the native host path. A workspace that selects an image target, including an image that packages a host-platform binary, takes the captured path along with its producers. That path needs a supported engine. Without one the build stops with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH (see plugin development).

The Docker builder ships as an external plugin package (oyzu-plugin-docker). It reads your Dockerfile and tells Oyzu what to run: assemble an image, run BuildKit, validate the result and copy outputs. Oyzu itself still fetches base images and OS packages, selects source files, runs the isolated steps, enforces policy and records artifacts. A plugin cannot grant itself credentials, mounts, frontends or publishing rights. The small compiled Go helpers that read Dockerfiles and image metadata, serve OS package snapshots and carry the BuildKit frontend ship inside the plugin package. Oyzu mounts them at /oyzu-plugin, so your machine needs no Go installation.

For BuildKit builds you need a Linux Docker engine. Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS works if it runs a Linux engine. Windows containers are not supported. Preparation and the quality checks run on the base execution image. The plugin package carries the metadata helpers, Oyzu's BuildKit frontend and the lint and format tools. RUN steps run in the rootless BuildKit worker oyzu-execution/buildkit:0.34.0, the upstream moby/buildkit 0.34.0 rootless image. Oyzu pulls it by its pinned digest when it is missing (see Published execution images). Base images for BuildKit builds must already be in your local Docker image store. Oyzu does not pull them or read registry credentials on this path. Provision them with your usual process. Daemonless builds need none of this. After a BuildKit action succeeds, Oyzu waits up to 30 seconds for Docker to confirm that the worker container is gone. If Docker does not, the build fails and its output is not accepted. Check the Docker daemon and build again. If a build stops with cannot verify the BuildKit worker's AppArmor boundary, Docker did not report its security options in the expected form (docker info --format '{{json .SecurityOptions}}' should return a list of strings). Wait until the Docker engine is fully running and try again.

An image can target a different platform than the worker when building it runs no target code. For example, a Dockerfile with only FROM scratch and COPY can build an arm64 image on an amd64 worker: builds: image: uses: docker/image platforms: [linux/arm64] Setting Values Default Meaning platforms linux/x86_64, linux/arm64 (linux/amd64 and linux/aarch64 are accepted; no ABI) The worker's platform The image's target platform. Variant suffixes and other platforms fail. List several platforms (platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64]) to build one image for each. Each has its own versioned archive and reports. A complete set also produces an OCI index. See matrix builds. Oyzu installs no image or emulator for you. A base image must match the platform of the stage that uses it: the target platform, or the worker's platform for a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM stage. A base with the wrong architecture fails before export, even if the tag matches. A target built from another target's output (see target workspaces) must have the same OS and architecture as its consumer. Setting the image's platform sets the producers' platforms too. Every image is checked against its target platform when it is tested, collected and inspected, so a valid image for the wrong architecture is never kept as a success. RUN and the target platform. Oyzu cannot run foreign-platform code. A Dockerfile with RUN in a target-platform stage needs the worker and target platforms to match. If they differ, preparation fails before any action runs, even if your machine has an emulator. RUN in a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM stage is fine.

If the final stage of a Dockerfile only adds files to one base and edits image settings, Oyzu builds the image itself without Docker, BuildKit or any container engine. Earlier stages may contain RUN if the final stage does not depend on them. They are skipped and not part of the image. Oyzu fetches the final base from its registry, adds each COPY as a layer and edits the image configuration. This is the approach ko, Jib and crane append use. Nothing selects it: the Dockerfile's content decides, per target. FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12:nonroot@sha256:7f0c72cd138b442ae0deeb69c08b1acf5525439ba251a49ad93c320a061567e5 COPY bin/server /server USER 65532:65532 EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

Instruction Supported form FROM The final base is scratch or a reference pinned by @sha256: digest (a tag may also be present), with optional AS name. No --platform. Earlier stages must also use scratch or digest-pinned bases. COPY Files or directories from the build context (no wildcards), shell or JSON form, --chown=user[:group] (names or ids) and --chmod=<octal>. Relative destinations resolve against WORKDIR. WORKDIR, USER, STOPSIGNAL One literal value. ENV, LABEL key=value pairs with shell quoting, or legacy ENV KEY value. EXPOSE Ports with optional /tcp, /udp or /sctp; no ranges. CMD, ENTRYPOINT JSON (exec) form, or shell form, which becomes /bin/sh -c. In an unused earlier stage the same instructions are read, but its RUN instructions are skipped. For example, FROM scratch AS unused, RUN exit 99, FROM scratch, COPY greeting.txt /greeting.txt builds only the last COPY. These use the BuildKit worker instead: a RUN in the final stage, stage references such as FROM unused or COPY --from=unused, ADD, ARG, HEALTHCHECK, VOLUME, SHELL and ONBUILD, unsupported COPY flags, heredocs and variable expansion, a # syntax= or non-default # escape= line, a base pinned only by tag, and a .dockerignore or Dockerfile.dockerignore file.

Oyzu first looks for the exact digest-pinned reference in your local Docker image store. A matching OCI index or manifest is exported and checked: the index must contain the requested platform exactly once, and the manifest, config and every layer must verify. A local image that fails the identity, platform or export checks is an error. Oyzu does not go and pull a different image. Classic Docker stores that expose only a config ID cannot be used for local capture. If Docker is missing or not running, you pass --no-docker, or the image is not in the local store, Oyzu pulls from the registry instead. Registry pulls use the OCI Distribution API by digest, so a moved tag can never change the content. For an index, Oyzu uses the entry for the target platform (linux/amd64 or linux/arm64). Verified content is kept in your image cache: %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\images on Windows, ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/images on macOS, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/images or ~/.cache/oyzu/images on Linux. The project's cache.dir does not move it. Later builds trust content already in the cache. Offline registry builds need it cached. Local images can be used offline. Under managed configuration, builds never contact a public registry. Only anonymous pulls are supported: Oyzu answers the registry's token challenge without credentials. That covers public images on Docker Hub, gcr.io, ghcr.io and similar. A private base fails preparation with an explanation and does not fall back to BuildKit. HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE apply as for other Oyzu downloads. A loopback registry (localhost:5000/...) is contacted over plain HTTP. A base with ONBUILD triggers, zstd or foreign layers, or a different platform from the target fails.

Base layers are copied byte for byte. Docker schema 2 bases are written with the equivalent OCI media types. Each COPY becomes one gzip layer, and so does a WORKDIR that creates a directory. Entries are sorted, stamped with 1980-01-01 UTC and carry numeric ownership only. Files are 0644, or 0755 when they are executable on a Unix host or start with an ELF header or #!. Directories are 0755. --chmod overrides both. New files and directories that COPY creates belong to --chown, or root. Names are looked up in the base image's /etc/passwd and /etc/group, and an unknown name fails the build. Without a group, the user id is also the group id, as in Docker. Directories already in the base keep their owner. The configuration comes from the base, with Env, Labels, User, WorkingDir, ExposedPorts, Cmd, Entrypoint and StopSignal edited as Docker does. An ENTRYPOINT drops an inherited CMD unless the Dockerfile sets one. An image without PATH gets Docker's default. COPY can read the files under each source in the target folder, plus artifacts you materialize into it. Nothing else in the workspace is visible. The output has the same layout, name annotations, checks and reports as a BuildKit build. Rebuilding the same inputs gives the same image digest on any machine. It is not byte-identical to what BuildKit would build from the same Dockerfile.

dist/dependencies/<target>.json names the adapter docker/oci-assembly and records: imageSource: registry or provisioned-local. The base's requested reference, manifest digest, config digest and content-tree digest (under images). The files selected from the context and the Dockerfile digest. Oyzu checks the Dockerfile and base against those identities before it writes anything. The build action records oci-assembly as its execution mode and that it used no container engine and ran no project code.

If Docker cannot provide the execution image (for example on a host or pod with no engine), a daemonless target still builds. Oyzu's own executable acts as the worker. oyzu build --isolated --no-docker accepts such a target when its selected work is just the build and packaging. The plan shows needsDaemon: false and isolation: in-process. Tasks that need the execution image still need Docker. --full adds Dockerfile lint (hadolint) and format checks (dockerfmt), so the build stops with NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON (exit 3) before preparation. Dockerfiles that are not daemonless have the same refusal. A digest-pinned base with ONBUILD triggers fails. Oyzu does not run the triggers or fall back to BuildKit.

Image selection can use ordinary Dockerfile ARG defaults, with no Oyzu configuration: ARG REGISTRY=docker.io/library ARG VERSION=3.22 ARG BASE=${REGISTRY}/alpine:${VERSION} FROM ${BASE} RUN test -f /etc/alpine-release Only ARG lines before the first FROM take part in choosing the base and platform. Defaults expand in order using BuildKit's own quoting, escaping and expansion rules. A later declaration with a value replaces an earlier one. A declaration without a value keeps the existing default. You can use expressions such as ${BASE:-alpine:3.22}. An empty base or empty explicit platform fails preparation. ARG inside a stage is not a global default, and host environment variables are never read. If an argument resolves to scratch or an earlier stage, it adds no external image. A stage's platform must be the target platform or the worker's (FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM). Anything else fails. A base for a worker-platform stage is captured for the worker's platform and bound as the BuildKit context <name>::<platform>, so one reference can serve both a build stage and the target stage.

Arguments Value TARGETPLATFORM, TARGETOS, TARGETOSVERSION, TARGETARCH, TARGETVARIANT The target platform. TARGETSTAGE The final stage name, or default if it has none. BUILDPLATFORM, BUILDOS, BUILDOSVERSION, BUILDARCH, BUILDVARIANT The Docker toolchain worker's platform. It is checked against the worker during planning. The target platform is never assumed to describe the worker. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH Set by Oyzu. A global ARG SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH makes it available to image selection and overrides the Dockerfile's default. Without that declaration it is not part of global selection. A declaration inside a stage can expose it to RUN commands separately. A global declaration can replace the target defaults. For example, ARG BASE=registry.example/runtime:${TARGETARCH} selects an architecture-specific image without reading the host architecture. These values do not let you run foreign-platform code. RUN still needs matching target and worker platforms. The common cross-compile pattern works: FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang AS build, then COPY --from=build into a target-platform stage with no RUN. It builds an arm64 image on an amd64 worker. RUN in the target-platform stage still fails before any action runs. Hadolint's rules about explicit FROM --platform flags still apply. You cannot override build arguments on the command line, and variables in stage-level mounts are not expanded.

with.repository names the image's registry repository (no scheme, tag or digest), such as registry.example.com/team/app. Building never publishes to it or contacts it. A helm/chart image binding reads it to name the image it uses. with option Values Meaning repository A repository name without scheme, tag or digest The image's repository. dependencies A provider name Selects the offline dependency provider. docker/image accepts only these two with options. oyzu config validate and every command that reads the build inventory reject others. Where a built image is loaded locally is set by docker.load, not by with.

The docker.load setting lists where oyzu run load puts an image you already built, so a local cluster can run it without a custom docker load step. # build.yaml builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/app # names the loaded image # oyzu.local.toml (Git-ignored), or oyzu.toml for a team default [docker] load = ["docker", "k3d:dev"] oyzu build oyzu run load # or: oyzu run image:load when several targets exist oyzu config explain docker.load --target image # where the list came from Which cluster you use is personal, so the list lives in configuration and not in build.yaml. Put a team default in oyzu.toml and your own cluster in oyzu.local.toml or user configuration. Like other per-target settings, it applies to the docker/image builds in its folder and below. The nearest file wins, and [context.<name>] and profile tables can vary it. The image is named by the build's with.repository. oyzu.local.toml is ignored in CI unless you pass --local-overrides (inspection and selection). Changing it does not rebuild anything. Destination What happens Needs docker docker load of the archive, docker tag as <repository>:<version>, then docker image inspect <repository>@<digest> must succeed. Docker Desktop Kubernetes shares this engine. docker on PATH, using Docker's containerd image store (which keeps OCI manifest digests). Another store fails the inspect with an explanation. k3d:<cluster> k3d image import of the archive, then on every server and agent node ctr -n k8s.io images tag names the image <repository>@<digest> and <repository>:<version>. docker and k3d on PATH (install k3d with oyzu install k3d) and a running cluster. The task never builds, pushes or contacts a registry. It reads the latest dist/manifest.json (the build must have succeeded and the archive must still match its recorded digest), picks the single OCI archive for this target, and makes the image available as <repository>@<manifest digest>. A bound chart uses that reference, so a deploy pulls nothing. Rules and failures: A list holds zero to eight distinct destinations. load = [] in a nearer file turns off a default from a farther one. If docker.load reaches a build without with.repository, the load task is listed as unavailable with that reason. Other commands are not affected. An unknown or repeated destination is rejected when the value is read. oyzu config validate reports it and every command that reads that configuration fails. The old with.load key is rejected with a message that points here. A platform matrix with several image variants is refused. Loading one chosen variant is not supported. Pushing to a registry is not part of loading. Use oyzu publish.

When a build needs one of Oyzu's execution images and your Docker engine doesn't have it, Oyzu pulls it by the digest pinned in src/executor/published_images.json and tags it with the name the build expects. The registry verifies the content, so a moved tag can't swap in a different image. No login or credentials are involved. Pinned today: the base execution image oyzu-execution/base:1, from ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/base (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64), and the BuildKit worker oyzu-execution/buildkit:0.34.0, from docker.io/moby/buildkit (0.34.0 rootless). Dockerfile base images and --image references you bring are never pulled. An image already on your machine is used as is, never replaced. Set OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL=1 to forbid pulling, for example on an air-gapped host. A missing image then fails with a message that says how to provide it. Limits: The pinned digests are not yet recorded in oyzu.lock. A pulled image is trusted by its pin and not re-checked on later runs. Pulls cannot go through a tool broker or private mirror.

Isolated builds add Docker resources, so Oyzu limits the ones it creates. It never touches anything it did not create. A resource is Oyzu's only if it carries the label dev.oyzu.owner=oyzu or is recorded in the per-user ledger docker-storage.json (in the cache folder of Oyzu's user data directory). Containers and volumes are labelled when created. Docker cannot label an image after a pull, so images are recorded instead: an execution image Oyzu pulled by its pin (images in ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/ that an earlier run pulled are adopted on the first pass) and container tools Oyzu installed. A locally built base image, Dockerfile base images and anything you pulled yourself are never listed, measured or removed. Setting Values Default Meaning cache.dockerMaxMiB 1 to 1048576 MiB 20 GiB The budget for recorded images. Set it in the ordinary configuration cascade. It is not part of any action key. After an isolated build that used a Docker image, Oyzu cleans up under a lock shared by builds: Images. Recorded images that lost their tag to a newer pinned image, and those unused for 60 days, are removed. Then the least recently used are removed until the recorded images fit in cache.dockerMaxMiB. Images used by the build that just finished are never removed, and Docker refuses to remove an image a container uses. Containers. Labelled containers that exited over an hour ago are removed along with their anonymous volumes. This includes the BuildKit worker's private store, so BuildKit's cache cannot outlive its worker. Volumes. Unused labelled volumes are removed. Persistent oyzu-tools-* volumes follow their own retention (see build logging). Cleanup is best effort. A failure leaves the work to the next isolated build and never changes a build's result. Host builds add no Docker resources and run no cleanup. The 60-day and one-hour ages are fixed. oyzu cache status shows the recorded image count, size and budget on its Docker line (and under docker in --json). It leaves the line out if Oyzu has recorded no image or cannot query Docker. oyzu cache clear empties the action cache only.

A native parser reads your Dockerfile to find the images it needs, without running any Dockerfile command. Global ARG defaults are expanded with BuildKit's own expansion library. Dynamic mount references, remote ADD, secret and SSH mounts and host networking are rejected. A # syntax= line builds only if it is on the digest-pinned docker.frontends list (see Oyzu's BuildKit frontend). To bring in a pinned download instead of remote ADD or RUN curl, declare a fetch and copy from the named context oyzu-fetch-<name>. Oyzu inspects each provisioned image and exports it by its immutable config identity, so a tag change in between cannot substitute another image. It never starts that image and never gives project code the host Docker socket. An offline Go adapter reads the exported archive, verifies its integrity and platform, and writes an OCI content store that keeps the original config, layers and media types. Images containing ONBUILD fail, because their hidden inputs are not part of discovery. Oyzu freezes the stores and records the reference, config digest, manifest digest and store digest for each image. Before the worker starts, it copies each store to private storage and checks it against the plan. BuildKit receives the stores as OCI named contexts. The worker and RUN steps stay offline. The stores are read-only inputs to the worker and are not mounted into RUN containers. No shared build cache is imported. The identities are recorded under extensions.oyzu.dev/docker.images in dist/dependencies/<target>.json, and they feed the dependency and build plan digests. metadata.selection records the target platform and the export epoch. Planning rejects values that disagree with the selected target. The manifest digest of a captured image can differ from the registry's original manifest, because docker save does not keep every registry representation. Oyzu verifies the config identity and the captured content, and does not invent registry provenance. A successful build keeps the versioned <target>-<snapshot-version>.oci.tar archive and its OCI digest in dist/manifest.json, plus integrity and platform JUnit results and lint and format results. These checks do not measure application code coverage. Producers you materialize into the image keep their own test and coverage reports. Version inference supplies a tag-derived base version and a source-derived snapshot suffix. The image reference uses the same version. A changed base image changes the plan and content digests even if the version string is the same.

Before the worker starts, Oyzu sets the file and directory access and modification times of its private copies of the source, Dockerfile, materialized artifacts and dependency contexts to the export epoch (1980-01-01 UTC). This makes identical inputs behave identically. Your originals and the prepared stores are unchanged. On Unix, file modes are also normalized, keeping executable bits and dropping umask differences. If a timestamp cannot be set, the worker does not start. This does not freeze application clocks, randomness or other file metadata. Installers keep their normal metadata, and the Dockerfile needs no change. Images built by an older Oyzu need to be rebuilt.

Within one oyzu build, each distinct base is exported with docker image save and converted once. Other targets that need the same base (same reference, Docker image ID, target platform and converter image) wait for it and get a verified copy. This keeps several targets on one large base from holding several copies in Docker's memory. Captures are kept in the system temporary directory and deleted when the build finishes. A failed capture is not reused, and separate oyzu build processes do not share captures. Oyzu gives the BuildKit worker each captured base as a private copy made with docker cp before the worker starts, not as a bind mount. The source context, definition and output folders are still bind-mounted. The copy is checked against its planned digest, owned by root inside the worker, and removed with it. A Dockerfile that changes while it is being copied is rejected rather than run. Python application packaging with container: true uses this path (see Python containers).
