documents.t: A dependency context is a read-only package store that Oyzu prepares before the offline build. A Dockerfile reads it through an external context named dependencies. The sections below each give a complete example. Provider Native inputs The base image must already contain python/pip requirements.txt Python 3.11 or later and pip python/uv pyproject.toml and uv.lock Python, pip and uv python/poetry pyproject.toml and poetry.lock Python, pip, Poetry and its export plugin node/npm package.json and a v2 or v3 package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json Node and npm node/yarn package.json and a Yarn Classic yarn.lock Node, Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 node/pnpm package.json and a single-project v9 pnpm-lock.yaml Node, pnpm 10.11.0 and yaml 2.8.1 go/modules go.mod or go.work Go and a POSIX shell (plus a C compiler for cgo) rust/cargo Cargo.toml and a checked-in Cargo.lock Rust/Cargo 1.94.0, a POSIX shell and the project's native compiler and linker All providers: Oyzu installs none of the tools. A missing tool in the base fails preparation. Preparation downloads from the public registry for that ecosystem, then the build runs offline. Private registries, direct URL or VCS dependencies, managed connector authorization and a persistent download cache are not supported. Oyzu puts no registry token in the image, build arguments or Dockerfile. Stale lock files, failed integrity checks and unsupported inputs fail preparation, before any action runs. Fix the inputs or the base and build again. The dependency record (dist/dependencies/<target>.json) keeps package identities and digests, source and lock identities, the observed tool versions and the base image identity. Package integrity is not a release approval. One matching provider is picked automatically. If several match, set with.dependencies (see Selecting a provider).

For a Docker target, an external context named dependencies asks for a prepared package store. With one Python ecosystem and a requirements.txt, you do not need to select a provider. Choose the Docker builder explicitly if the project also looks like an application: builds: image: uses: docker/image FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ pip install --no-index --no-cache-dir --no-compile --find-links=/dependencies -r requirements.txt COPY app.py . CMD ["python", "app.py"] Add application files with ordinary COPY. --no-compile avoids bytecode timestamps in the example. Use python -B for import checks during the build. A requirement such as six==1.17.0 is resolved by pip inside the exact base image, with its Python, pip, ABI and platform. Preparation downloads binary wheels through Oyzu's public-PyPI proxy. It adds no build, test or quality tools to the store and runs no project code or source builds. The Docker build then installs from the store with no network. Oyzu does not rewrite your RUN commands.

If other ecosystems' manifests make automatic selection ambiguous, name the provider with with.dependencies: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: dependencies: python/pip The value must be one provider name. oyzu config validate rejects anything else. The old top-level dependencies: build field is rejected with a message pointing at with.dependencies. Several matching managers need an explicit with.dependencies, even within Python. Unknown providers and missing native manifests fail. with.dependencies without an external dependencies reference also fails. A Dockerfile stage that is actually named dependencies stays a normal stage. Other external names are treated as image references.

uv uses its locked, offline export with --no-default-groups. Poetry uses its export plugin for the main group, with project plugins off. Stores exclude development groups and optional extras. A stale lock or hash mismatch fails. Local, path and VCS dependencies and extra indexes are not supported. uv and Poetry projects use their own lock, not a nearby requirements file. All three Python providers add a generated requirements.txt next to the wheels, pinning the whole selected closure with SHA-256 hashes. A uv or Poetry project can install from it without copying its lock into the image: RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ pip install --no-index --no-deps --require-hashes --no-cache-dir --no-compile --find-links=/dependencies -r /dependencies/requirements.txt uv's uv pip install can use the same file. uv sync and poetry install are not supported inside the build.

The base image must already be local and provide Python 3.11 or later with pip. The worker and target platforms must match for package preparation, even if the Dockerfile only copies files. With earlier named stages, the consumer is the stage's original base. Several different consuming bases, a scratch consumer or mismatched platforms fail instead of sharing an unchecked set of packages. Preparation uses the base's captured config, not a tag that may have moved. If later commands change the interpreter or libraries in the stage, compatibility is up to you. The dependency record keeps wheel identities and digests, source and lock identities, the interpreter and manager versions and a digest of the store. Only the wheels and the generated requirements enter BuildKit's context. Direct URL requirements, alternate-index directives and source distributions are rejected. Remote syntax frontends and secret mounts are not supported.

node/npm exports verified registry tarballs using the Node builder's locked acquisition. A Docker target with package.json and a v2 or v3 package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json picks this provider automatically (shrinkwrap wins, as in npm). With several ecosystems, set with.dependencies: node/npm. FROM registry.example.com/build/node:22-npm11 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ for archive in /dependencies/*.tgz; do npm cache add "$archive" --offline --cache /tmp/npm-cache --ignore-scripts; done \ && npm ci --offline --cache /tmp/npm-cache --ignore-scripts --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund \ && rm -rf /tmp/npm-cache COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] The example base is one you provision that contains Node and npm. Copy all workspace manifests and sources for a workspace install. Copy npm-shrinkwrap.json instead when you use shrinkwrap. The glob needs at least one captured package. A project with no dependencies can run npm offline with no store. A declared packageManager must match the base image's npm version, and npm checks engines. A package npm records as bundled inside its parent (inBundle, with no resolved URL or integrity of its own) is not fetched separately. It ships in the parent's tarball, whose integrity is verified. Any other inBundle entry is refused, naming the package. Packages outside the public registry, such as a package pinned to a public GitHub commit tarball (an HTTPS tarball URL in package.json and the lockfile, not a git spec), are fetched only from locations the project declares in npm.sources. Their locked integrity is still checked. The store contains only <sha256>.tgz files. Oyzu fetches every locked registry tarball, verifies the SHA-512 lock integrity and runs npm offline with lifecycle scripts off, which rejects stale locks and incompatible installs. Workspace links stay in the source. Development and optional packages are fetched too (the example omits development packages with --omit=dev). npm's cache, logs, configuration and Oyzu's own state are not exported. The example seeds a throwaway cache and deletes it in the same RUN, so no cache layer is left. Oyzu does not run project lifecycle scripts while preparing. Packages that need a compile step need a compiler in the base and an explicit offline command in your Dockerfile. Failures and limits: Missing or stale locks, unsupported lock versions, failed integrity checks, incompatible engines or a mismatched package manager fail preparation. The registry is https://registry.npmjs.org/. Private registries, VCS or direct non-registry sources and managed connector authorization are not supported. There is no persistent download cache or internet fallback during the build.

node/yarn exports a Yarn offline mirror after Oyzu validates the locked dependency graph. With package.json and yarn.lock and no competing ecosystem, it is selected automatically. With several native locks, set with.dependencies: node/yarn. A modern Yarn lock is not treated as Classic. FROM registry.example.com/build/node:22-yarn1 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json yarn.lock ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ printf 'yarn-offline-mirror "/dependencies"\ndisable-self-update-check true\n' >/tmp/oyzu.yarnrc \ && yarn install --offline --non-interactive --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --use-yarnrc /tmp/oyzu.yarnrc --cache-folder /tmp/yarn-cache \ && yarn cache clean --offline --non-interactive --cache-folder /tmp/yarn-cache \ && rm -rf /tmp/yarn-cache /tmp/oyzu.yarnrc COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] The image must already have Node and Yarn Classic 1.22.22. Oyzu installs neither. The @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 parser that reads yarn.lock ships in the Node plugin package, so the image doesn't need it. An OYZU_YARN_LOCKFILE path set in the image takes precedence. Only the verified mirror archives enter dependencies. The temporary configuration in the example lives inside the RUN and is removed there. Lifecycle scripts stay off. Preparation uses the base's Node and Yarn, checks engines and package-manager constraints and rejects a graph that changed. Yarn applies registry-only resolutions. Oyzu records every locked input with purpose build. It does not prune to runtime-only packages. Supported: a single project, Classic v1 locks, SHA-512 or legacy SHA-1 lock integrity, scoped and transitive registry packages, registry version-range resolutions, and the root .yarnrc and .npmrc settings listed in Yarn project settings. Copy those files into the consumer stage too if Yarn should apply them there. Not supported: workspaces, other .yarnrc and .npmrc settings, .yarnrc.yml, path and VCS dependencies, modern Yarn, private registries and managed connectors. Missing tools, stale locks, changed integrity or a changed base fail before any artifact is built. The build cannot fetch missing packages, and there is no persistent download cache.

node/pnpm prepares a pnpm store in the exact base image, using the Node builder's registry downloads and frozen-lock checks. package.json and a single-project v9 pnpm-lock.yaml select it if unambiguous. Otherwise set with.dependencies: node/pnpm. FROM registry.example.com/build/node:22-pnpm10.11 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ cp -r /dependencies /tmp/pnpm-store \ && pnpm --config.manage-package-manager-versions=false install --offline --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --ignore-pnpmfile --config.verify-store-integrity=true --config.side-effects-cache=false --store-dir /tmp/pnpm-store \ && rm -rf /tmp/pnpm-store COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] The image must already have Node and pnpm 10.11.0. The yaml 2.9.1 parser that reads pnpm-lock.yaml ships in the Node plugin package. An OYZU_PNPM_YAML path set in the image takes precedence. Other pnpm versions fail at export, because the store format is tied to this version. The context is read-only. Copy it so pnpm has a private writable store, and delete the copy in the same RUN. Installed packages keep working after the store is gone. Oyzu exports only pnpm's v10/files and v10/index records, sets each index file's checkedAt to zero and writes index keys in a fixed order. Package bytes and integrity values are unchanged, and pnpm rechecks the copied content. Links, special files, unknown store paths and side-effect caches are rejected, with limits of 100,000 files, 10 GiB and 16 MiB per index. An empty lock exports an empty store. User configuration and Oyzu's own state are not included. For a patched project, copy pnpm-workspace.yaml and patches/ before installing, or use the package.json patch declaration. pnpm applies and verifies the patches, and the record keeps the original package integrity and patch digests. Lifecycle scripts and side-effect caching are off. Every locked registry input is captured and recorded with purpose build. Not supported: workspaces, .npmrc, .pnpmfile.cjs, unsupported overrides, direct, path and VCS dependencies, other pnpm versions and private or managed registries. Stale locks, changed integrity, missing tools or unrecognized store data fail preparation. The build has no registry access, so an incomplete store fails and is never topped up from the internet.

go/modules gives the build Go's checksum-verified module download cache through dependencies. A Docker target with go.mod or go.work picks it automatically. With mixed ecosystems, set with.dependencies: go/modules. For a pure-Go command with a complete go.sum: FROM golang:1.24-bookworm AS build WORKDIR /src COPY . . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ GOMODCACHE=/tmp/gomodcache GOPROXY=file:///dependencies/cache/download GOSUMDB=off GOTOOLCHAIN=local CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o /app . FROM scratch COPY --from=build /app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] Go resolves workspace members, local replacements and test imports from your source and checksum files. Oyzu fetches the required modules through the public Go proxy, and Go verifies go.sum. Preparation does not change your manifests or checksum files. The base must already have Go and a POSIX shell, plus a C compiler for cgo. The example uses the standard golang:1.24-bookworm image. Preparation compiles a small metadata helper with that Go using only the standard library. It does not need oyzu-go-modulezip, version projection or module packaging, which belong to ordinary go/app and go/library builds. Toolchain download, VCS access and user Go configuration are off during preparation. The store is Go's download cache (module zips with their .mod and .info files), mounted read-only. The build uses it as a file proxy and extracts what it needs into its own writable GOMODCACHE, and Go verifies each zip against go.sum. Extracted trees are not stored, because many small files on a Docker Desktop bind mount were slow. No broker, credentials or acquisition metadata are in the store. Compiler output stays in the build stage, and the final scratch stage holds only the binary. Use a real runtime image instead of scratch for cgo or other runtime libraries. The record keeps the Go version and platform, lock and source digests and the module archives used. Its module-artifact list is empty because preparing dependencies does not publish your own module. The image's JUnit report checks the image, not your source. Build a separate Go target if you need source tests and coverage. Failures: missing checksums, stale manifests, workspace or replacement paths that escape the project, or an incompatible base fail preparation. Update and commit your Go files, or fix the base, and build again. Private modules, direct VCS sources, checksum database integration and a persistent cache are not supported.

rust/cargo gives the build a Cargo local registry. A Docker target with Cargo.toml and a checked-in Cargo.lock picks it automatically when no other ecosystem is present. Otherwise set with.dependencies: rust/cargo. The lock file is required even for a local-only workspace. FROM rust:1.94.0-slim-bookworm AS build WORKDIR /src COPY . . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ CARGO_HOME=/tmp/cargo-home CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/cargo-target CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 cargo \ --config 'source.crates-io.replace-with="oyzu-captured"' \ --config 'source.oyzu-captured.local-registry="/dependencies"' \ build --release --locked --offline \ && cp /tmp/cargo-target/release/oyzu-registry-example /app RUN test "$(/app)" = "Answer: 42" FROM debian:bookworm-slim COPY --from=build /app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] The base must already have Rust/Cargo 1.94.0, a POSIX shell and the compiler and linker your project needs. The example uses rust:1.94.0-slim-bookworm. Preparation does not need Python, nextest or llvm-cov. Oyzu checks the whole lock before downloading, using only crates.io registry sources whose index and archive SHA-256 checksums match. Cargo then validates the workspace and lock offline inside the exact base image. Preparation runs no build scripts, does not rewrite your lock and does not produce your crates' artifacts. Only *.crate archives and their index/ entries enter the read-only context. It uses Cargo's local-registry source replacement. Cargo unpacks into a fresh private home. The example's final stage copies the binary onto a Debian runtime that has the dynamic libraries it needs. A workspace with no dependencies needs no source replacement. Local workspace packages remain source inputs. The record keeps Cargo's metadata, the compiler and manager versions, the base identity, source and lock digests and the verified packages. It has no nextest or coverage evidence. The image's JUnit report checks the image, not your Rust tests. Build a separate Rust target if you need tests and coverage. Failures: a missing or stale lock, mismatched checksums, Git or alternate-registry sources, local paths that escape the project or missing tools fail before any artifact is built. Managed or private registries, a persistent download cache and other Rust versions are not supported.

For a dependencies context, Oyzu checks that the base image still has the captured OCI config digest, then runs it by its immutable Docker image ID. With Docker's containerd image store, a single-platform image's ID is its manifest digest. Oyzu then exports the image, checks the manifest bytes against the ID and reads the config digest from it. Classic storage reports the config digest as the ID. If the base reference changed, the build fails before the dependencies run. Oyzu never silently switches to a newer base. The dependency record keeps runtime_config separate from runtime.digest (the execution ID).

The Python and Cargo providers run Oyzu's compiled Linux worker inside the base image, so the image's own interpreter or compiler resolves the packages. Go and Node providers run only native tools and use no worker. Your base image does not contain the worker, and Oyzu never changes it. Oyzu mounts the invocation's engine read-only into the preparation containers, as in every other container action (see What runs in a container action). The selected engine member is recorded with the dependency record, so a different engine changes the plan. Requirements: An engine must be available for the base image's platform. Without an engine package, a Linux CLI of the same architecture mounts its own executable. Otherwise preparation stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE. An engine package's static Linux member runs on glibc and musl bases alike. When a Linux CLI mounts its own executable instead, the base needs that executable's glibc (2.39 or newer for release builds).
documents.s: Compiled worker in the base image

documents.t: Oyzu can use a base whose OCI index carries attestations. It selects and exports the runnable manifest for the requested platform, verifies its digest and config, and keeps the index identity for execution. This needs Docker image inspect and export to support --platform (Docker 29.8 is known to work). It does not verify signatures or trust the attestations. If selection or export is unsupported, the build fails and no image is substituted.

A missing image fails preparation with a provisioning message. There is no automatic internet fallback for BuildKit builds. A platform mismatch, malformed export, config mismatch, hidden ONBUILD, a modified frozen store or a native worker failure blocks artifacts. Fix the input or base image and build again. Lint and format failures still block the build (see Dockerfile linting and formatting). Limits: At most 64 distinct image references per build, 100,000 entries per image export and 10 GiB for an export or captured tree. Unsafe archive paths, duplicate member names and links are rejected without extracting layers on your machine. Unsupported archive forms fail. Equivalent references such as alpine:3.22 and docker.io/library/alpine:3.22 share one BuildKit context when their identities agree. Both requested references stay in the record. Conflicting identities fail planning, and reference order never picks between different images. Registry credentials, managed registry access, secret mounts, other package managers and a Dockerfile-free application image profile are not supported. An image in your local Docker daemon is not a statement that it is trusted or approved for release. Upgrading: Captures and plans made by older tools must be regenerated. They fail rather than assume defaults for missing platform or frontend facts. No project file changes are needed.

Check a build's result with oyzu inspect dist. For an image it confirms that the archive's digests and platform match what the build recorded. The build itself checks every image against its target platform, so an image for the wrong architecture is never kept as a success, and a valid archive hash is not enough. An image archive also carries a JUnit report with its integrity and platform assertions. These do not run the image or replace your application tests. Related: Dockerfile linting and formatting, Oyzu's BuildKit frontend, OCI indices, publishing an image, Helm charts.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Dockerfile projects get lint, a read-only format check and an explicit format task with no Oyzu configuration. Linting uses Hadolint 2.15.1 and formatting uses dockerfmt 0.5.4. Neither builds or runs your application.

oyzu run list oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build Task What it runs Changes files lint hadolint --no-color Dockerfile No format-check dockerfmt with --check No format dockerfmt with --write Yes. Only runs when you ask for it, and is not a build stage. Hadolint's rules, severities, configuration and inline suppressions decide whether lint passes. It reads a target-local .hadolint.yaml or .hadolint.yml. dockerfmt reads a target-local .editorconfig. With no .editorconfig, Oyzu adds --newline so formatted files keep a final newline. With one, dockerfmt's own defaults and your settings apply, including the end-of-file rule. Oyzu does not parse these files itself. Invalid native configuration is a native failure. The tasks are listed even before the tools are installed. If a tool is missing when you run the task, it fails with installation guidance. Oyzu does not download or skip it. Task overrides and pre/post hooks work as for other tasks. A task you replace owns its own behavior.

In an isolated oyzu build, lint and format-check are required gates before the image archive is collected. If either fails, the diagnostics are kept and no image artifact is produced. Your source and checkout are unchanged. Fix the findings, run oyzu run format if you want the formatter to rewrite the file, and build again. Lint results are not counted as application tests or coverage. The image's JUnit report comes from the OCI checks, and coverage is recorded as not applicable. .dockerignore controls what goes into the image, not what the checkers see. Oyzu keeps .hadolint.yaml, .hadolint.yml and .editorconfig available to the checkers even if .dockerignore excludes them from COPY. Configuration from folders above the target is not imported in a build. Keep required checker configuration inside the target folder so isolated and local runs agree. Local development runs also see configuration from your machine. Isolated builds do not mount any. dockerfmt defaults to four-space continuation indentation. If your repository has an .editorconfig in a parent folder, copy a Dockerfile example elsewhere before comparing native defaults.

oyzu run lint and oyzu run format on your machine need hadolint and dockerfmt on PATH. Isolated builds use the copies that ship in the Docker plugin package: Hadolint 2.15.1 as the unchanged upstream release, checked against its pinned SHA-256, and dockerfmt built from its Go module and checksum lock. The package keeps their upstream licenses and notices. Preparation copies the tools a build's enabled stages need into the prepared dependencies, checks they run and keeps their reported versions in the Docker dependency record. The actions run on the base execution image. A custom image given with --image docker=<image> needs neither tool, since the plugin supplies both. The host tasks run on Windows, Linux and macOS. Isolated image builds run on Linux amd64.

Hadolint is a static linter. It is not a vulnerability scanner and does not prove policy compliance. Inline suppressions change its result. dockerfmt has documented syntax limits, including escape directives and some shell grouping forms. See Hadolint and dockerfmt for their configuration.
Docker image inputs and offline builds

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/dotnet.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds a directory that has a solution (.sln, .slnx) or an SDK-style project (.csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj) without any Oyzu configuration. The dotnet/sdk builder runs restore, build, test and pack in a network-denied container and delivers a versioned NuGet package directory. Note: The .NET builder is experimental. It runs only in a Linux amd64 container (Docker required), so there is no host-native .NET build and no Windows or macOS build.

The dotnet/sdk builder is supplied by the oyzu-plugin-dotnet plugin. The plugin finds your projects, plans the build and runs the restore, test and pack steps. Oyzu itself still provides the SDK and source, the NuGet mirror, version resolution, credentials, and the checks on artifacts and reports. The plugin gets the NuGet mirror address from Oyzu and never sees your credentials.

oyzu run list oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Plain oyzu build selects the fast build and package path. oyzu build --isolated --full also runs the native tests. --isolated alone doesn't select tests. This builder has no host build path, so it always uses the container, with or without --isolated. The container needs Docker and the locked SDK described under Provisioning.

Builds run on the base execution image, which has no .NET SDK. The SDK comes from oyzu.lock and is restored read-only into every action (see Capturing a selected SDK). Without a [tools] dotnet setting, oyzu pin locks the default SDK, 10.0.401. The base image carries the shared libraries the official SDK loads (OpenSSL, ICU, Kerberos and zlib) and a C toolchain. Only Linux x64 GNU SDKs are supported, so .NET builds run on linux/amd64. Pass --image dotnet=<ref> to run on your own image, for example one with OS packages a project links against. It must meet the bring-your-own requirements, and the locked SDK is still the one restored. No image carries an Oyzu worker. Restore, test and pack run the engine and the .NET plugin that Oyzu mounts into the container, so updating the CLI never needs an image rebuild.

A directory is claimed when it directly contains a solution, or a project whose root element names an MSBuild SDK (Sdk="...", an <Sdk> element or an SDK import). Legacy non-SDK projects are not claimed. Discovery adds install, build and test tasks that run dotnet restore, dotnet build and dotnet test. A literal SemVer Version or VersionPrefix in the entry project or the root Directory.Build.props becomes the native version. Computed values stay native. Every native command receives one entry file: a single solution, otherwise a single SDK-style project. If there is more than one candidate, the build fails and lists them. Choose one: builds: app: uses: dotnet/sdk with: project: src/App.slnx Option Values Default Meaning with.project A solution or project file, relative to the target The single solution, otherwise the single SDK-style project The entry file every native command receives. Other with keys are rejected.

Setting Where Values Default Meaning [tools] dotnet oyzu.toml An exact stable SDK version, such as 10.0.402 10.0.401, locked by oyzu pin Downloads and uses that SDK (see below). lockPlatforms oyzu.toml [tools] ["linux/amd64/gnu"] The platform of the SDK archive to lock. sdk.version global.json in the target root An exact SDK version The build's native pin (native pin files). A configured SDK must also satisfy it. sdk.rollForward global.json Native roll-forward policies patch with a version, latestMajor without one Native SDK selection. sdk.allowPrerelease global.json true or false true Native SDK selection. test.runner global.json Microsoft.Testing.Platform Runs tests with Microsoft.Testing.Platform. Without it, tests use VSTest. msbuild-sdks global.json Literal versions NuGet-supplied MSBuild SDKs to restore (see MSBuild project SDKs).

By default the build uses the default SDK (10.0.401). To use another one, name an exact stable Linux x64 GNU SDK. Oyzu downloads it from Microsoft's builds.dotnet.microsoft.com release metadata and archives. This is experimental. [tools] dotnet = "10.0.402" lockPlatforms = ["linux/amd64/gnu"] Run oyzu pin, then oyzu build --isolated --full --frozen. Oyzu checks Microsoft's SHA-512 for the archive and records its SHA-256 in oyzu.lock. The archive is restored read-only and unchanged. Installation keeps all archive notices. DOTNET_ROOT, PATH and the exact version are fixed for restore, build, test and pack. The dotnet --version seen inside the container must equal your selection and satisfy global.json. Another SDK is never picked silently instead. Warm frozen or offline runs need the existing lock, the SDK archive and the NuGet inputs. They don't consult release metadata. Limits: The execution image provides the OS, linker and library prerequisites. An image of your own must provide them too. Oyzu doesn't provide an OS, a separate runtime, Windows, macOS or ARM SDKs, or a GNU fallback for musl. Prereleases and older SDK download layouts aren't supported. If the build is refused, the cause is one of these: Problem What to do Checksum mismatch, unsupported platform or archive layout Don't edit the lock digest to accept unexpected bytes. Restore the missing inputs online and rerun. global.json conflicts with the selected SDK Make the two agree, run oyzu pin, and retry the frozen build. You need a different SDK Change [tools] dotnet and run oyzu pin. Changing only the image doesn't override a locked SDK archive.

global.json in the target root selects the SDK the way the .NET host does: sdk.version, sdk.rollForward and sdk.allowPrerelease. patch can keep an exact installed SDK even when a newer patch is available. latestPatch takes the latest available patch. Oyzu runs dotnet --version in the target directory to see what the host would pick, instead of predicting it. Without global.json, the .NET host chooses the SDK supplied to the build, which is the locked SDK. A value that isn't an exact SDK version (10.0) is refused, with a hint naming an exact version such as 10.0.100. Only the target root's global.json is read. The .NET host's upward search for a global.json in parent folders isn't followed. global.json must be strict JSON. Comments are rejected. Custom SDK search roots (sdk.paths) aren't supported. oyzu build --plan lists the oyzu:dotnet tool requirement, with the global.json sdk.version as its constraint when there is one. The discovery record shows the request under sdk. Before restoring, preparation lists the SDKs installed in the container and checks which one the host would select in the target directory. Each check has a 30-second timeout. If no installed SDK is allowed, the build fails before restore. The message names the request, the SDKs provided and oyzu pin. The selected version must be installed and allowed by the request. The dependency record and the .NET SDK evidence record that version. Offline restore checks the selection again and requires the same answer. A failed or timed-out check, or an invalid answer, fails preparation.

Build actions run with the network denied: A prepare action restores offline from the prepared packages into /workspace/.oyzu-dotnet/packages (also NUGET_PACKAGES). It keeps --locked-mode when preparation used it. build runs dotnet build <entry> --configuration Release --no-restore --disable-build-servers -p:Version=<version>. When tests are selected (for example by --full), test runs dotnet test --no-build --no-restore and writes TRX results: VSTest uses --logger trx. Microsoft.Testing.Platform uses --report-trx and --solution or --project. Set test.runner: Microsoft.Testing.Platform in global.json to use it. All TRX files are converted into one JUnit report that keeps class names, failures and skipped tests. A passing run with no TRX results fails instead of reporting an empty suite. A custom test task must still produce the required JUnit report, or the action fails and no package is exported. dotnet pack --no-build --no-restore writes one directory artifact, nuget-packages-<version>. It fails if no project is packable. Environment: The version comes from version inference over the native version and your Git history. It is passed to restore, build and pack as -p:Version. CI is removed from the action environment, because ContinuousIntegrationBuild source mapping needs a .git directory that the captured source leaves out. Telemetry, first-run output, workload notices, MSBuild node reuse and online certificate revocation checks are off. Actions reserve 4096 MiB and time out after 30 minutes.

Preparation runs dotnet restore <entry> once, with the network denied, through a local mirror that forwards only the NuGet V3 flat container and vulnerability data of https://api.nuget.org/ to Oyzu's download broker. Restore reads only a generated NuGet.Config. Oyzu clears project RestoreSources, additional sources and fallback folders, so repository and user feeds, package source mappings and credentials are not used. If any packages.lock.json exists in the target, restore runs with --locked-mode. NuGet applies each lock to its own project, and projects without a lock restore normally. The lock files are recorded. Restored packages go into a NuGet global packages folder in the prepared tree. Each package's .nupkg digest and size is recorded. The recorded package source is the public index, so the prepared tree doesn't depend on the mirror's port.

Preparation restores with NuGetAudit=true and keeps warnings NU1900 to NU1905 as warnings, even under TreatWarningsAsErrors or WarningsAsErrors. The findings come from NuGet's own logs. Oyzu: shows a NuGet audit step with a summary, for example known vulnerabilities: 1 high; logs each finding as a NUGET_AUDIT warning; records them in the dependency record under oyzu.dev/nuget-audit, with complete: false when NuGet couldn't read vulnerability data. Audit findings never fail preparation. Build actions restore with NuGetAudit=false, so audit warnings can't turn into later compile errors.

Some MSBuild SDKs come from NuGet, such as Aspire.AppHost.Sdk or Microsoft.Build.NoTargets. A project names them with Sdk="Id/Version", an <Sdk Name Version> element, or msbuild-sdks in the root global.json. MSBuild restores them itself while it evaluates a project and ignores the generated NuGet configuration, so with the network denied the evaluation failed and restore skipped the project (NU1503). To avoid that, preparation scans the root global.json and every project, props and targets file for literal versions. It restores each SDK package through the broker into the prepared packages before restoring the entry, and the offline build restores them from there. The ids and versions are recorded under msbuildSdks in oyzu.dev/dotnet, and each package appears in the dependency record. SDKs bundled with .NET (Microsoft.NET.Sdk*) are never restored. A version written as a property, range or wildcard isn't restored and fails in MSBuild.

Every build checks its own results: A test failure keeps the JUnit report and blocks the package. A test run that exits successfully without a report fails. A changed dependency that doesn't match an existing lock fails restore. A SDK request nothing satisfies fails before restore. Run oyzu inspect dist to check the bundle, including the SDK, lock and package records and the test results.

These choices may change: the builder id dotnet/sdk; the default SDK; audit is reported but never enforced; CI is removed; the action memory and timeout limits; packing every packable project into one directory artifact; failing on an ambiguous entry, an unsatisfiable SDK request or missing TRX results. Not supported: private feeds, credentials, package source mapping and nuget.sessionEndpoint in captured builds; workloads, and MSBuild project SDKs whose versions MSBuild computes or a range names; global.json and Directory.Build.* files above the target directory; coverage, lint and format integrations; per-package file artifacts, dotnet publish outputs and NativeAOT publishing as a build stage; Windows and macOS builds; repositories with several projects and no root solution, unless with.project selects one. Resource limits: The download broker allows 1 GiB and 4096 requests per session, and 256 MiB per response. The prepared tree is limited to 100,000 entries and 10 GiB. NuGet's HTTP cache and extraction scratch use /scratch/nuget, which can grow with the action's 4 GiB memory reservation instead of being limited by the 512 MiB /tmp mount. Large packages such as Microsoft.Playwright fit. For managed NuGet sessions with oyzu exec, see NuGet sessions.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/ecosystem-support.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this page to see what Oyzu builds today, which reports it produces, and where each build runs. Oyzu is experimental. Support is for the project shapes and platforms listed here. A language or tool not listed on this page isn't supported yet, and neither is an unlisted combination.

Native builds run on your machine with the tools Oyzu installs for you. They have your account's access to files and the network. See native local builds. Isolated builds (oyzu build --isolated) run in a Linux container. They need Docker, collect dependencies first, and then build offline. The container is Linux (amd64). The host can be Linux or Windows (x86-64). Plain oyzu build is native when every selected target has a native build, and isolated otherwise. See which builds are native.

Platform Support Linux x86-64 Supported for native and isolated builds Windows x86-64 Supported for native builds. Isolated builds run Linux containers through Docker macOS Intel (x86-64) Zig native builds only macOS Apple silicon (ARM64) Not supported yet Linux ARM64 Not supported yet Windows ARM64 Not supported yet Rust can also build for other platforms from a supported host. See Rust cross-compiling.

Ecosystem What it builds Reports Native Isolated Rust (Cargo) Executables, plus crate archives in isolated builds. Packages and workspaces JUnit, Cobertura coverage, doctests Yes, on Linux and Windows. Cross-compiles other platforms with --platform Yes Go Application executables JUnit, Go coverage, go vet, format check One module with one main package, no go.work Yes. Libraries, workspaces and several binaries run here Node.js Application directories and npm packages JUnit, LCOV, lint, format check Yes, on Linux and Windows Yes Python with pip Wheels and source distributions JUnit, Cobertura coverage Wheels from pyproject.toml Yes Python with uv or Poetry Wheels and source distributions JUnit, Cobertura coverage No Yes Python applications Application artifacts from requirements files or distributions JUnit, Cobertura coverage No Yes. Native-extension builds aren't supported Java with Maven JARs and POMs from a reactor JUnit, JaCoCo Yes, with the Maven wrapper Yes Java with Gradle JARs from multi-project builds JUnit, JaCoCo Yes, with the Gradle wrapper Yes. Android isn't supported Java with Ant JARs JUnit, JaCoCo instruction coverage No Yes .NET SDK NuGet packages JUnit No Yes, on Linux x64 only. No lint, format or coverage Helm Charts, including subcharts Validation JUnit No Yes. helm-unittest isn't supported, and Oyzu doesn't deploy to a cluster Docker OCI images OCI validation JUnit Runs in a BuildKit container, so it needs Docker Yes Zig The installation tree of a build.zig project None. Zig test reports aren't supported Yes, on Intel macOS Yes, on Linux x86-64 (GNU) Each build produces the reports its checks select. A successful --full build doesn't create reports for checks that are off or not available for that ecosystem.

The right Node setup depends on the package manager and the project shape. This table shows what works for each combination. Project shape npm pnpm Yarn Classic 1.22.22 Yarn Berry 4.17.1 Single-root application (a dist/ directory, Node test runner reports) Native and isolated Native and isolated (pnpm 10.11.0 only in isolated builds) Native and isolated Native and isolated. node-modules linker only Single-root package (.tgz) Native and isolated Isolated, for projects with no dependencies Not supported yet Not supported yet Workspace packages (several .tgz files) Native and isolated Isolated Native Native Workspace application Isolated, with a private root Not supported yet Not supported yet Not supported yet Native Node builds are supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64), except where noted. Isolated builds use a Linux (amd64) container. A native npm single-root package is built when you declare it explicitly with uses: node/app. Native workspace packages: npm on Windows (plus TypeScript workspaces on Linux), Yarn Classic on Linux, Yarn Berry on Windows. Yarn Plug'n'Play, Yarn workspaces in isolated builds and per-member application artifacts aren't supported. See npm workspaces, pnpm and Yarn for workspace details. oyzu run test can run workspace tests for npm, pnpm 10 and Yarn Classic on Windows. Dependencies must already be installed. See workspace tests.

The Node test runner is supported in the shapes above. These also work for npm applications: Tool Support Vitest 5.0.3 with V8 coverage Native builds on Linux and Windows. Isolated builds and workspaces aren't supported yet Jest 29.7.0 Native builds on Linux and Windows. Isolated builds and workspaces aren't supported yet Mocha 12.0.3 with c8 Native builds on Linux and Windows. See Mocha Vite 8.3.3 application Native builds on Windows, and isolated builds. SSR, library mode and watch mode aren't supported Reports and linting for Node projects are described in Node quality checks, direct tests and Node applications.

CMake and C/C++ builds, SwiftPM, Xcode and Android aren't supported. You can run their tools with oyzu exec or a task, but Oyzu doesn't discover those projects, collect their artifacts or check their reports. Windows ARM64 and macOS Apple silicon hosts aren't supported. On Windows, Oyzu doesn't run Windows containers or use Windows SDKs for isolated builds.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/engine-staging.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The engine is the oyzu executable that runs a build. A project can pin an exact engine in oyzu.lock. When the oyzu you run is a different build, it hands the build to the pinned engine, which you supply as a local engine package. Note: Engine packages are local archives that you build and verify yourself, or that the install scripts compose from a release's own executables. There is no separate release channel, public catalog or automatic upgrade for engines. Engine staging works on Linux x86-64 and Windows x64 (MSVC). macOS is not supported yet. Isolated builds (--isolated) run the engine's Linux member inside the container. A Linux oyzu mounts itself. On Windows and macOS, oyzu needs an installed package that pairs it with the Linux oyzu built from the same source; see Installing this oyzu with its Linux member. The install scripts do this for releases.

Install a package you built and verified: oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> Run the executable the command prints. It reports identity, release, executable, registration and admission; add --json for machine-readable output. To make a project use a different engine, pin it in oyzu.lock and admit the archive in your user configuration: # oyzu.lock [engine] identity = "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab" # user configuration [engines.packages] "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab" = { archive = "/path/to/engine.tar.gz", sha256 = "sha256:<64 lowercase hex>" }

An engine identity is the first version token that oyzu --version prints. It leaves out the build profile, target and timestamp, so different dirty builds can share an identity. The archive digest identifies the exact content. Without a pin, the running oyzu is the engine. Every build records the engine identity it used and whether it was pinned. With a pin that differs from the running oyzu: oyzu looks for an admitted archive for that identity in engines.packages. It installs the engine beside your oyzu and hands the build to it before configuration is read, tools are resolved or plugins load. Your oyzu and the project lock do not change. oyzu build --plan and oyzu plugins update do the same, so the update check runs under the pinned engine's capabilities. A compatible engine change doesn't update plugin or tool selections, and a plugin update keeps the engine pin. If no admitted archive supplies the pin, the build stops with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH before doing any work. The project's oyzu.lock must be readable, even for build --plan. Captured builds (--isolated or an explicit --image) with a pin always need the admitted archive, even when the running oyzu already has the pinned identity. The archive supplies the Linux worker that runs inside the container. If the archive has no member for the platform, the build fails instead of using the worker built into the image. A build with no pin that you start from an installed engine (see below) uses that engine's package the same way.

engines.packages maps exact build identities to archives: Field Meaning key The exact engine identity archive Absolute path to the archive sha256 Archive digest, sha256: plus 64 lowercase hex digits The map holds at most 64 entries. There is no default source, tag lookup, newest cache lookup or network fallback. Set it in user or system configuration, never in a project file, local override or profile, so a project can't authorize its own engine. User configuration doesn't apply in CI. Edit it with oyzu config set --global (with --json-value) and oyzu config unset. The build's --store option selects the tool store. Engines live in engines/<archive-sha256>/ inside it.

oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> --json Option Meaning --identity The exact build identity declared by the package's engine.json --archive Local archive, with its platform members and notices --sha256 The archive digest you trust, with the sha256: prefix The command checks the archive digest, every executable listed in the manifest, and that the package has a member for this machine's exact OS, architecture and ABI. It needs no network. It doesn't change PATH, install system-wide or touch project locks. Payloads go in your per-user data directory under tools/engines/<archive-sha256>/. A separate registration file, tools/engine-installations/<archive-sha256>.json, binds the package to its installed executable. Only oyzu engine install creates it. Admitting an archive through engines.packages doesn't. An unpinned build uses an installed package only when the running executable is that registered, installed member with the matching identity and platform. For isolated builds on Windows and macOS, a copy of that member counts too when its bytes are identical (same executable digest, identity and platform), such as the oyzu the install scripts and oyzu run bootstrap put on your PATH. Any other copy, and every copy on Linux, doesn't inherit the registration. Warm use doesn't need the original archive, and installed files aren't re-hashed on each command. --store changes the tool store but not where registrations live. A registered engine can supply its own Linux worker for captured builds without any engines.packages setting. engines.requirePin and [engine] pins are still checked first, and engines.development doesn't affect registered packages.

oyzu engine install --linux ./oyzu-linux-x86_64 oyzu engine install --linux ./oyzu-linux-x86_64 --linux ./oyzu-linux-arm64 --json This packs the oyzu you run together with the Linux oyzu executables you name into one engine package, then installs and registers it exactly like an archive (see above). Afterwards, isolated builds on this machine run the Linux member from the package, whether you start the installed executable or the oyzu on your PATH with the same bytes. Rule Detail Members 1 to 4 --linux files; can't be combined with --archive Platform Read from the file: a 64-bit ELF for x86-64 or arm64. With a dynamic loader it is gnu (musl for musl's loader); statically linked it is musl Same source Each file must carry this oyzu's build identity (the first token of oyzu --version), or the command stops with ENGINE_IDENTITY_MISMATCH before installing anything Result The same fields as an archive install, plus platforms, every member of the package The identity check catches a Linux oyzu from another release or commit. Two builds of the same dirty checkout share an identity, so build both members from the same state. The Linux worker checks its exact identity and platform again before each isolated build. Run the command again after you replace oyzu: the new executable has different bytes, so the old package no longer applies.
