documents.t: An administrator can require every build in some contexts to have an exact engine pin and a complete lock, using the protected setting engines.requirePin. It is administrative-only, defaults to false, and can't be set in machine, user, project, local, invocation or profile settings. A nonbinding policy default doesn't require anything. For example, in a protected policy: { "engines.requirePin": { "locked": true, "value": true, "when": { "context": ["ci", "pr", "release"] } } } Put this in the administrative policy file, not in oyzu.toml. The build root and the stricter of the detected and requested contexts decide whether it applies. A weaker --context, a profile or an ordinary override can't waive it. Without an applicable requirement, local, CI and release builds can be unpinned. A build that requires a pin: Stops with ENGINE_PIN_REQUIRED if oyzu.lock has no [engine].identity, before discovery, plugin roles or preparation. Can't use --engine-development to skip the pin. Replays existing plugin selections and refuses unpinned local development plugin bindings. Checks that each selected tool has a portable lock entry before preparing tools. Never adopts or writes a missing plugin or tool selection. Prepare the whole lock before running the governed build. Removing --frozen doesn't remove the requirement. For a missing plugin selection, restore an approved complete lock, or run oyzu build in an approved context where policy allows adoption. Otherwise ask your policy administrator for a context where you can prepare the lock. oyzu plugins update replaces existing selections but doesn't adopt a missing first one, and oyzu pin and oyzu install don't repair a missing plugin selection. The requirement carries over when the build is handed to another engine. An older engine that doesn't understand it refuses the handoff.

To test a CLI you built from source while keeping the shared pin, first allow the override in user configuration (or ask your administrator to): oyzu config set --global engines.development true Then run that executable with --engine-development on each build: ./dist/cli/artifacts/oyzu -C ~/projects/app build app --engine-development Rule Detail Setting engines.development, boolean, default false. Not allowed in project or local files or profiles. Administrative constraints apply. Per build The setting only permits the flag; you pass the flag for every build. Where it works Local development only. Detected CI and requested CI, PR or release contexts refuse it, even with --context local. Combinations Not allowed with remote, isolated, image, all-platform or slice builds. Undo oyzu config unset --global engines.development The flag keeps the executable you started. It doesn't look for another executable, install the pinned engine, change the pin, or change PATH. Build inventory and local preview JSON record developmentOverride: true, pinned: false, the actual identity and executableDigest, and the requestedPin. The Context section of the human output names the override, its digest and the bypassed pin. Two builds with the same version label can have different content, so this record identifies bytes and is not a publisher attestation. Captured builds with external builders need an admitted engine archive and refuse this override.

For a captured build, --image go=<reference> picks the execution image for that ecosystem, separately from the engine, plugin and tool pins. Oyzu resolves the image to its immutable digest and platform once per build. Changing a tag later affects new builds, not one already running. To use the exact images of an earlier build again, keep that build's bundle outside the source tree and run: oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen \ --execution-images-from /retained/build-a This reuses the images only. It doesn't re-run the old plan. Oyzu checks the bundle's integrity (not who produced it), then checks that the source, the target, variant and builder selection, the lock bytes and the engine selection match. It then prepares and plans as usual under your current policy and checks. The new plan records which earlier build it took its images from. Rule Detail Required --isolated and --frozen Not allowed with --image, remote execution, previews, affected selection, slices, handoff, --engine-development, contract verification Supported Captured builds with an admitted engine archive, for built-in and external builders Not supported Derived application containers, in-process image assembly, and bundles recorded without the comparison facts (you can still inspect them) --offline Ordinary offline rules apply. It never permits missing tools or dependencies. Errors: Code Cause and recovery EXECUTION_IMAGES_SOURCE_CHANGED, EXECUTION_IMAGES_SELECTION_CHANGED The source or pins differ from the earlier build. Restore them, or run an ordinary new build. EXECUTION_IMAGE_UNAVAILABLE The recorded image isn't available, or your executor refuses it. The error names the target, digest and platform. Provide that exact image and retry. Oyzu never substitutes the current tag. On Windows, the frontend oyzu stays attached during Ctrl+C until the staged engine finishes cleanup and returns its exit status. The engine reports the interruption and keeps the failed build bundle. oyzu install --store <directory> and oyzu exec --store <directory> -- <command> use the same store when they read requirements from an already installed, locked external builder. Neither adopts a missing plugin; prepare it with a build first. On Windows, install oyzu.exe and oyzu-shim.exe together.

Captured builds run the engine, plugin and locked tools inside a Linux image. There are two ways they can get there: mounted: Oyzu mounts them read-only into the container. This is the default. image-installed: the exact files are already installed in the image, so Oyzu uses them in place without mounting or restoring anything. Image labels and PATH never choose versions. The engine archive, the plugin lock and the locked tool distribution do. When you install a package, the store keeps a record of its verified contents next to it. If that record is missing (older installs, or an interrupted install), builds use mounted placement. Reinstalling a removed package renews the record. Before a build, Oyzu compares the selected files with the image's filesystem once and caches the result for that image in your user cache. Only regular files and directories can be image-installed. A tree that contains links stays mounted. Anything that doesn't match stays mounted. Docker volumes, scratch paths and explicit overlays can't hide admitted files. An overlay that conflicts with one stops the build with ENGINE_CONTROL_CONFLICT. Evidence in the build records the selected engine member (identity, archive digest, platform and executable digest) separately from the engine baked into the image. Oyzu never runs the baked executable to observe it. The baked observation is for information only and never changes which engine is selected. An image from the classic Docker store can lack an OCI Descriptor. Then placement can't be observed, the baked engine shows as unavailable, and builds use mounted placement. A descriptor that is present but invalid is an error, not a fallback.

After a build has installed the exact engine, plugin and tools and filled the ecosystem's dependency cache, you can repeat it without the network. For Go: oyzu -C <project> install --frozen --offline --store <store> oyzu -C <project> exec --offline --store <store> -- go mod download oyzu -C <project> build app --frozen --offline --no-docker --no-cache --store <store> Keep the same GOMODCACHE, GOCACHE and GOPATH you used for preparation. To make Go itself refuse the network, also set GOENV=off, GOWORK=off, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, GOPROXY=off, GOSUMDB=off and GOVCS=*:off. --offline and these variables control the clients Oyzu and Go use. They don't block the network at the operating-system level, so an arbitrary project command could still reach it. Missing engine or plugin installations are restored from their admitted local archives, and a cached tool archive can restore a missing tool. If neither an installation nor an archive exists, the command stops. A missing Go module reports module lookup disabled by GOPROXY=off. Restore the content with an online build first. Don't edit the lock to match whatever is cached. Replaying means running the same command again with the same executable, arguments, directory, source, lock and package selections. There is no command that replays history. Current admission still applies: removing the engine's admission makes the build fail with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH, even if the bytes are cached. Matching evidence doesn't guarantee byte-identical output. If you cancel a build, the staged engine records it as interrupted, prints BUILD_INTERRUPTED, keeps no artifact from the run and exits with status 130. Other builds that share the installed engine are not affected.

An engine package is a gzip tar or ZIP archive with engine.json at its root and one executable per platform at the path the manifest gives. One admitted archive covers every platform member of the engine build. { "contract": "oyzu.engine.v1alpha1", "identity": "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab", "runtimes": [{ "platform": { "os": "windows", "arch": "x86_64", "abi": "msvc" }, "entrypoint": "bin/windows/oyzu.exe", "executableDigest": "sha256:<64 lowercase hex>" }] } Rule Detail Members 1 to 16 platform members with unique platforms and entrypoints Executables Each must be a regular file whose digest matches the manifest Platform match OS, architecture and ABI must match the running engine exactly. Oyzu doesn't infer ABI compatibility. Identity The running engine's compiled identity must match the manifest, so a manifest can't relabel a different build The digest you supply covers the whole archive, including the manifest. Oyzu verifies the archive before extracting it, extracts it without following links, checks the manifest and executables, then publishes the installation atomically. Installed files are trusted afterward. Admitting an archive by digest is not a publisher signature check and says nothing about official provenance.

Code Cause and recovery ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH No admitted archive supplies the pinned engine. Run the pinned engine, or admit its archive in user or system configuration. ENGINE_PIN_REQUIRED Policy requires an engine pin and oyzu.lock has none. Pin the engine and prepare the full lock. ENGINE_DEVELOPMENT_DENIED --engine-development isn't permitted here: the setting is off, the context isn't local, or policy requires the pin. Drop the flag or get permission. ENGINE_DEVELOPMENT_UNAVAILABLE The development executable couldn't be read. Make it readable and retry. CONFIG_SCOPE A project, local or profile source tried to admit an engine. Move the setting to user configuration or the administrator. ENGINE_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE The archive can't be read. Restore it. ENGINE_PACKAGE_DIGEST The archive doesn't match the digest. Get the expected archive; don't just change the digest. ENGINE_PACKAGE_INVALID The manifest or executables don't match the package rules above. Rebuild the package. ENGINE_INCOMPATIBLE The package's contract or platform isn't supported by this engine. Supply a matching build. ENGINE_IDENTITY_MISMATCH, ENGINE_HANDOFF_MISMATCH The manifest or the running build doesn't match the requested identity or entrypoint. Fix the package. No second handoff happens. ENGINE_HANDOFF_CHANGED The pin or the admitted release changed during the handoff. Retry with consistent settings. ENGINE_HANDOFF_INVALID The receiving engine can't take this handoff, for example an older engine that only supports builds, not updates. Run that engine directly or pick one that supports the operation. ENGINE_INSTALLATION_INVALID The registration and the installed executable disagree. Reinstall the package. Don't copy registrations between installations. ENGINE_START_FAILED The verified executable wouldn't start. Check host prerequisites and the package layout. ENGINE_CONTROL_CONFLICT An overlay or volume conflicts with an admitted engine file in a container. Remove the overlay. ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE An isolated build on Windows or macOS found no package with a Linux member for this oyzu. Run oyzu engine install --linux with the Linux oyzu built from the same source, or reinstall the release with the install script. A failure at this stage happens before the build does anything. Oyzu doesn't adopt plugins or tools or change selections. Complete engine installations stay in the store for reuse.

Engine packages are local archives. No separate release channel, catalog or automatic upgrade exists. oyzu run bootstrap doesn't build the Linux member on Windows or macOS yet; pass one with --linux. A nested build uses its own lock, not the parent's. Native (non-container) builds have no filesystem or network isolation from this feature. Updating plugins through an engine handoff works only when both the frontend and the receiving engine support it. macOS isn't supported yet.
Configuration Plugin packages Plugin updates

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/execution-image.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build --isolated runs every container action on one small Linux image, the base execution image oyzu-execution/base:1. It holds operating system pieces and a C toolchain and nothing else. Oyzu mounts everything a build needs into it: the invocation's own engine, the builder's plugin package and the tools oyzu.lock selects. Native builds (plain oyzu build on a host that has a native build for the project) don't use it. This page lists what the image contains, how Oyzu gets it, and what an image of your own must provide when you pass --image.
oyzu build --isolated # every builder runs on the base image, pulled on first use oyzu build --isolated --image npm=node:22-trixie-slim # one manager on your own image

Each action is assembled the same way, whichever builder it belongs to: Image. An explicit --image <manager>=<ref> for that manager, otherwise the base image for the action's architecture. Engine. The invocation's engine is mounted read-only. With an installed engine package (oyzu engine install, which the Windows and macOS install scripts run for you, or an [engine].identity pin in oyzu.lock), Oyzu mounts its Linux member for the image's architecture (the static musl one when the package has several). Without one, a Linux CLI of the same architecture mounts its own executable. On Windows and macOS hosts an engine package is required; without it the build stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE before any work. No image carries an Oyzu worker, so a new CLI release never needs a new image. Tools. Every language toolchain and stage tool comes from oyzu.lock and is restored read-only into the action: Rust and its components, cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov, Go, Node with npm, pnpm or Yarn, CPython, the .NET SDK, the JDK with Maven, Gradle or Ant, Helm and yamlfmt, and Zig. A builder whose tool isn't locked for the platform stops with the oyzu pin command that fixes it; the image has no copy to fall back to. Plugin. The selected builder plugin package is mounted read-only at /oyzu-plugin, with any helpers it ships: the Docker plugin's metadata, image and snapshot helpers, BuildKit frontend, hadolint and dockerfmt, and the Node plugin's pnpm and Yarn lockfile parsers. Pinned integration files. A few upstream files that aren't tools in the lock are fetched once, checked against a SHA-256 pinned in Oyzu, stored with your declared fetches and restored read-only: the default Node lint, format and coverage packages (Node quality), Checkstyle, google-java-format, JaCoCo, JUnit and Ant for Java builds (Java quality), the helm-unittest plugin when a chart has unit test suites (Helm), and the cross linkers of a Rust cross build (Rust). The plan and the build evidence record the image digest, the engine member, the plugin release and each tool's locked identity. Docker image builds that run RUN steps use a second image, the rootless BuildKit worker oyzu-execution/buildkit:0.34.0. It is the upstream moby/buildkit 0.34.0 rootless image pinned by digest, with nothing of Oyzu's added. See Docker image inputs.
documents.s: What runs in a container action

documents.t: The image is Ubuntu 24.04 (ubuntu:24.04, pinned by digest) with these packages, built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64: Package Why it is there gcc, g++, libc6-dev, make, cmake, ninja-build, pkg-config C and C++ compilers and build tools for Rust build scripts, cgo, native npm and Python extensions and Zig's C interop. Rust links with cc. musl-tools musl-gcc, for C code in a static musl build. git Native tools that read Git metadata, such as Go VCS stamping and Cargo Git dependencies. ca-certificates, tzdata TLS roots and time zones for tools and tests. libssl3t64, libgssapi-krb5-2, libicu74, zlib1g, libatomic1 Shared libraries the locked .NET SDK and Node releases load. bzip2, xz-utils, zstd, zip, unzip, patch, file Archive and patch tools native builds call, and .tar.xz restoration of locked tools. Oyzu builds and publishes both images and their index itself from tooling/images/build.yaml, installing the packages from an OS package lock that lists every version, including the dependencies apt pulled in; tooling/images/base/debs.lock.yaml is the committed copy, and each publishing run uploads the lock it actually built from. See Dogfooding in workflows. There is no language runtime, package manager, Oyzu engine or Oyzu plugin in it. PATH is the standard Ubuntu one; each action prepends the restored tools.

Ubuntu 24.04 ships glibc 2.39. Anything a build links against glibc in the container needs glibc 2.39 or newer wherever it later runs. A Rust or Go binary built for linux/* with the GNU target won't start on an older distribution such as Debian bookworm (glibc 2.36) or Ubuntu 22.04 (glibc 2.35). If your binaries must run on older Linux systems, build them statically: target musl in Rust (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, aarch64-unknown-linux-musl; Oyzu's isolated cross builds already link those with rust-lld), or build Go with CGO_ENABLED=0. A Docker image's own base decides its libc at run time; this note is about binaries built in the execution image and copied elsewhere.

When the image isn't in the local Docker engine, Oyzu pulls it from ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/base by the digest pinned in the CLI, so a moved tag can't substitute another image. The package is public and needs no login. An image already present locally is used as it is. To use an image built from source instead, build it under the same name before the first isolated build: docker build -t oyzu-execution/base:1 tooling/images/base from a checkout of the Oyzu repository. A local image of that name is used as it is, without a digest check. Set OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL=1 to forbid every pull, for example on an air-gapped host that preloads the image. The BuildKit worker is pulled the same way from docker.io/moby/buildkit by its pinned digest. Oyzu records pulled images and keeps them within the Docker storage budget. An organization registry allow-list and mirror for Oyzu-published images is designed in the platform repository and not implemented in the CLI yet.

--image <manager>=<ref> runs that manager's isolated actions on an image you choose, for example one with OS packages your native build links against: oyzu build --isolated --image cargo=registry.example.com/build/rust-base:2026-10 The manager is the one the target's builder uses, for example cargo, go, npm, pnpm, yarn, pip, uv or poetry. The reference must already be in the local Docker engine; Oyzu never pulls a bring-your-own image. The image's immutable identity is recorded in the plan and evidence. The image must provide: Linux on the action's architecture. A linux/arm64 action needs an arm64 image. A C runtime the engine can start on. An engine package's static Linux member runs on any libc. When a Linux CLI mounts its own executable instead, that executable's glibc requirement applies; release builds need glibc 2.39 or newer. A C runtime the locked tools can start on. The official Node, .NET, JDK and Rust releases need glibc, and Rust and cgo need a working cc. Alpine and other musl images only suit tools that are static. tar that extracts .tar.gz and .tar.xz archives with --strip-components, and sleep: Oyzu restores locked tools with the image's own tar and keeps tool volumes in use with sleep. Whatever OS packages the project's native build needs. Oyzu still mounts the engine, the plugin and the locked tools; an image's own copy of a tool is never used in place of the locked one.

Isolated uv and Poetry builds need an image with uv or Poetry installed, passed with --image uv=<ref> or --image poetry=<ref>; those two managers aren't restored from the lock yet. Rust builds for macOS link against Zig's libSystem stubs, with no Apple SDK in the image. Crates that link other Apple frameworks need an image that provides an SDK (SDKROOT). Only linux/amd64 runs have been exercised end to end; linux/arm64 images build but arm64 actions haven't been run on arm64 hardware. Remote pools don't use this image yet.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/go.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds Go modules and go.work workspaces without any Oyzu configuration. It finds go.mod and go.work, runs the native go tooling, and collects binaries, module archives, test reports and coverage into a build bundle. Use this page to see what the Go builder runs, how it picks the Go version and what it produces. Note: The Go builder is experimental. Captured builds run in a Linux amd64 container (Docker required) and work from Linux and Windows hosts. macOS is not supported yet. The builder is supplied by the oyzu-plugin-go plugin; see plugin catalog.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist oyzu run <task> runs a development task on your machine with your provisioned go and gofmt. oyzu build plans and builds the module in a Docker container (see Toolchain image). oyzu inspect dist checks the resulting bundle.

A go.work workspace owns the modules it declares. Listing tasks (oyzu run list) does not run Go. A project with no main package produces module artifacts instead of failing as an unsupported library. uses: go/library selects module packaging even when the project has commands. go/app and go/library are the two Go builds. Oyzu reads the module and package facts from Go, picks the tools and versions, and runs the build, test and archive steps.

Development tasks use your provisioned go and gofmt. The implicit tasks install dependencies, compile, test, vet, format and check formatting. oyzu run format changes your source. Builds use format-check, which fails when gofmt -l prints anything. In a go.work workspace, the member modules supply the package patterns for the build, test and vet commands. oyzu run test writes the test bundle described under Direct test evidence. Other development tasks don't produce a bundle.

Captured builds need Docker and the base execution image, which has no Go of its own. Go comes from oyzu.lock (see Pinned Go in isolated builds), and Oyzu mounts its engine and the Go plugin into each action. Preparation compiles the module archive adapter with the locked Go, against the golang.org/x/mod copy that the Go distribution vendors for its own go command. No image carries the adapter, and building it downloads nothing. Your own image (--image go=<image>) needs no adapter either. It must meet the bring-your-own requirements, and a locked Go takes the place of the image's own. Docker projects can also ask for an offline Go module context. It exports only the captured module cache, so the consuming image doesn't need the module archive adapter.

Oyzu runs Go with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so Go never switches or downloads a toolchain itself. Oyzu picks the Go from your project files instead. Other ecosystems' exact pins are in native pin files. The Go minimum is the newer of the go and toolchain lines in the build folder's go.work if there is one, otherwise in its go.mod. Go orders versions as 1.24 < 1.24rc1 < 1.24.0 < 1.24.5. A toolchain line is always honored. A suffixed name is read as Go reads it (go1.24.3-bigcorp and go1.24.3+auto mean 1.24.3). toolchain default and toolchain local are ignored. Any other value that isn't a Go release name is refused with a remedy. A go line from Go 1.21 on is a toolchain minimum. Before Go 1.21 it was a language level, so a line like go 1.16 only constrains the choice: with no toolchain line and no [tools] go, Oyzu uses the newest stable Go, and a configured value below the line fails resolution. In a workspace, the go.work lines decide. A go.mod beside the go.work keeps its go line as a constraint, and its toolchain line is ignored, as Go ignores it. Modules in subfolders are not read, because Go itself refuses a workspace whose go line is older than a module's. Project Go selected toolchain go1.24.5 (or go 1.24.5), no [tools] go Exactly 1.24.5 go 1.24 with no patch, or toolchain go1.25rc1 The newest stable release of that line (1.24.x, 1.25.x). Oyzu only installs stable releases, so a line that has only a release candidate fails resolution. [tools] go at or above the minimum, in any folder That value (1.25, 1.24 for a 1.24.5 minimum, latest). The minimum still binds its resolution. [tools] go below the minimum, in a folder above the module (the project root, or user configuration) The minimum. The farther value loses, and the Tools row shows overrides 1.23.4 from oyzu.toml. [tools] go below the minimum, in the module's folder or below it Refused before any work with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT, naming both files. A command-line, environment or policy value below the minimum (a toolset value is exempt) Refused with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT, naming its source and the native file. A policy value can't be changed in the project, so ask the policy owner or lower the minimum. For example, take toolchain go1.24.5 in app/go.mod, a root [tools] go = "1.25" and [tools] go = "1.24.0" in app/oyzu.toml. oyzu build stops after loading the configuration with exit status 3: ✗ TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT: hello: [tools] go = "1.24.0" in app/oyzu.toml is below the go minimum 1.24.5 that app/go.mod declares (toolchain line); set [tools] go to 1.24.5 or later in app/oyzu.toml, or remove it so the native file decides Next: Make the configured tool version reach the native minimum, or change the native file, then retry. With only a root [tools] go = "1.23.4", the build uses the minimum and says so in the Tools block: ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 0 installed now 1.9s go 1.24.5 already installed detected from go.mod · overrides 1.23.4 from oyzu.toml How requests are compared: Only plain releases and lines (1.23.4, 1.23) are compared with the minimum where they are written. Any other form, such as a range, is resolved against the minimum and fails when nothing satisfies it. Tool policy (a tools.go lock or allowed set) applies to the selected version, whichever file requested it, the minimum included. When policy refuses the minimum itself, TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT names the policy source. In a workspace that builds in the isolated executor, the same refusal stops the build during preparation with exit status 3, and the code appears in the bundle's diagnostics. oyzu config explain tools.go shows the configured value. The override appears only in the Tools block. Locking: The selection is locked in oyzu.lock like any request, with the minimum recorded as the constraint go-minimum:>=1.24.5. Changing [tools] go needs oyzu pin before the next build, as for any explicit request. So does a changed minimum. go get and go mod tidy rewrite the go and toolchain lines, and the next build stops and names the cause: ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:go 1.24.5; app/go.mod declares go 1.24.5 (toolchain line) but oyzu.lock pins 1.27.2; run oyzu pin Run oyzu pin and commit oyzu.lock. An oyzu.lock written before Oyzu read the Go minimum holds the request * and needs the same step once.

A project that pins Go (for example [tools] go = "1.23", locked with oyzu install go@1.23) builds with that exact Go inside the container. During preparation Oyzu: Reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for the pinned version in oyzu.lock. Downloads it through the tool broker, unless a copy in your user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256. Checks the bytes against the locked digest. Restores them read-only at /scratch/gotool. Puts that go first on PATH (and sets GOROOT) for preparation and every build action. The plan records the archive digest, so a different pin or archive changes the action identity. Without an explicit pin, the Go that preflight locked from the Go minimum is used the same way. The base image has no Go, so a captured build there needs Go in oyzu.lock. Run oyzu pin. Only your own image can supply its own Go when the lock has none. A lock with a changed digest is rejected, and a corrupted cached archive is replaced by a verified download. Offline builds need the archive already cached, or they fail with TOOL_OFFLINE.

oyzu run test runs the implicit go test ./... command with -json, a fresh -coverprofile and -count=1. Go owns test discovery and compilation. Oyzu converts Go's JSON events to JUnit and keeps the native coverage profile under dist/. The manifest records digests and summaries. Coverage is statement coverage, not branch or line coverage. A package with no tests gets an honest zero-test summary, and Go may succeed in that case. Missing or malformed reports, and configured coverage thresholds, can still fail the run.

For a go.work root, Oyzu uses the workspace's member packages and combines their test events and coverage. Members outside the task root fail. Forward selectors with oyzu run test -- -run TestGreeting. Forwarded arguments go only to the task you asked for. Go's cached test results are not reused, though Go may still reuse its compilation cache.

Hooks get OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT. The JUnit report is normalized before post_test runs and validated after it, so changes a hook makes are kept. An invalid event stream stays a failure even if a hook later writes valid XML. A failed test skips the success-only post hook and keeps the evidence it has. Exact argv = ["go", "test", "./..."] and run = "go test ./..." overrides get the same treatment. Other custom commands run unchanged and must write their own JUnit and Go coverage reports. An explicit coverage declaration redirects the native profile. An explicit JUnit declaration switches to file-based reporting, so your task or hook must produce that XML. The default Go command emits JSON, not JUnit. Declared paths must be fresh. See direct tests. This workflow needs a provisioned Go compiler and your dependencies. It needs no Docker and no account. It runs on your machine with your environment and network. For an offline run, use dependencies you already have and set GOPROXY=off, GOSUMDB=off and GOTOOLCHAIN=local. It is not an isolated build and produces no application artifacts. Direct tests covers provenance, output handling and recovery.

Go itself reports manifests, workspace members, main packages, dependencies and cgo use. Captured inputs must contain local modules and replacement paths. Paths that escape the project, or are missing, fail. Public modules are downloaded through Oyzu's scoped Go proxy and verified against go.sum. A redirect from the proxy to its storage bucket is followed (acquisition transport). Private modules and direct VCS downloads are not supported. Oyzu records the compiler and ABI for cgo, and an environment override can't turn off required cgo support.

Preparation captures the dependency cache and the module artifact candidates. Library candidates come from captured source, before any build output exists. Go works in a module cache on a container tmpfs (/scratch/gomodcache). The prepared store keeps only the download cache: module zips with their .mod, .info and .ziphash files. Each build action serves that store to Go as a file:// module proxy and extracts what it needs into its own tmpfs cache. go.sum verifies every zip.

Compile, test, vet and the read-only formatting check run with networking denied and the prepared module cache. Artifacts are collected only after the required checks pass. Applications build one primary binary or named multiple binaries, with -trimpath and without ambient VCS stamping. Libraries compile package patterns and produce no executable. Go's test JSON becomes JUnit, and Go coverage keeps its statement denominator. Both go under dist/, with paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. A failed test, vet, formatting check, missing report or compile error stops artifact collection. Your source is never changed. Read the task logs and reports, fix the problem and rebuild. Each scratch tmpfs has a 2 GiB minimum size and grows with the action's memory reservation. Go build actions reserve at least 4 GiB, so /scratch/gotmp holds large compiler and linker intermediates. The 512 MiB /tmp mount is separate.

For an application with pure-Go code, Oyzu plans one build action per main package and one test action per package. Only the actions whose inputs changed run again. Each test action gets the whole captured workspace and its own empty output and scratch directories. It can't see another action's reports or changes. Package tests run go test -json -count=1 and produce a separate JUnit report and statement coverage report per package. Binaries are written privately and exported with the module's current version in the file name after the required checks pass. A conflicting task environment fails validation before any result is reused. These targets run as one combined action instead: libraries, cgo, nested targets, native workers, targets with generated inputs, and configurations with any authored tasks or hooks. That keeps their command and hook order, including generated inputs and post-test report changes. This path runs the engine that Oyzu mounts into the execution image. Without one, the build stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE. Direct oyzu exec -- gofmt uses the formatter bundled with the selected Go (Go installation).

Each library or workspace module produces three files: Artifact Contents module-<index>-<version>.zip The Go module archive, with the <module>@<version>/ prefix module-<index>-<version>.mod The exact go.mod included in that archive module-<index>-<version>.info Go proxy version metadata, with no invented release timestamp The index follows the sorted order of module directories. Manifest artifact names are module-<index>-zip, module-<index>-mod and module-<index>-info. dist/dependencies/<target>.json lists module paths and directories, file names, versions and the h1: zip and go.mod checksums, so other tools can map the files to registry identities. Oyzu does not publish the modules.

Versions come from version inference: a base from Git tags when there is one, plus the build's -dev.g... suffix from the source. With no applicable tags the base is 0.0.0. Go packaging maps that to the module path's major where needed, for example v2.0.0-dev.g... for a /v2 module. A version from a tag must satisfy Go's module path rules. v3.0.0 for an unchanged /v2 module fails instead of silently changing the version. These are snapshot prereleases, not Go pseudo-versions, and they don't authorize a release. An exact RC tag keeps its qualifier, for example v2.6.0-rc.2.dev.g.... Binary file names and manifest coordinates use their module's inferred version. Oyzu doesn't inject version variables into your program. A Conventional Commit that declares a breaking change in the tool minimum doesn't change the Go module path. Under the default auto strategy that still infers a major bump, and packaging refuses the mismatch. A project whose released tags define its development line can choose the tag strategy instead. Path-major checks, tool selection and the required build and report checks still apply.

Each module in a workspace gets its own version, based on the tags and changes that affect it. Directory-scoped tags such as math/v2.4.2 and api/v1.4.2 give each module its own baseline. A root tag applies only to a module at the Git root. It doesn't coordinate the other modules. Files outside module directories count as shared inputs for every module. Custom tag namespaces and special major-directory layouts aren't supported yet. Oyzu freezes the versions in version-plan.json, uses them when it creates each zip, mod and info file, and rewrites local requirements to match. Recreate older captures after updating Oyzu.

The archive tool uses Go's own module zip library for allowed files, nested-module and vendor exclusions, case collisions and size limits, and Go's dirhash for checksums. It doesn't apply its own zip rules. Workspace dependencies point at the matching snapshot versions. Local imports, including test imports, supply the links between members even without a require entry. A local replace to a workspace module is removed from the packaged go.mod. Your source go.mod is unchanged. The files follow the Go module proxy protocol, so you can serve them from a local file proxy.

When the build container can't fetch a module, its local proxy answers HTTP 502 with a fixed category, for example module acquisition failed: BROKER_RESPONSE_BODY (broker HTTP 200). The HTTP status shown is the broker's reply, not a successful download. Messages never include file paths, JSON errors, credentials or redirect URLs. Category Meaning and fix BROKER_REQUEST_ID The worker couldn't generate a request ID. Check the worker's runtime. BROKER_REQUEST_WRITE, BROKER_REQUEST_PUBLISH The worker couldn't write or publish its request. Check the spool mount and its permissions. BROKER_RESPONSE_READ, BROKER_RESPONSE_METADATA The worker couldn't read the broker's reply. Check the spool mount. BROKER_RESPONSE_BODY, BROKER_RESPONSE_LIMIT The reply body was unreadable or larger than the 256 MiB limit. Check broker delivery or the module's size. BROKER_TIMEOUT The broker didn't answer within 55 seconds. Check the broker on the host. Upstream HTTP errors and the broker's own source and authorization messages pass through unchanged.

Linux amd64 is the supported captured platform. Arm builds and general cross compilation are not supported yet. Not supported: private module sources and direct VCS downloads, replace directives that point outside the selected workspace, registry replacements that need different publishing rules, and module publishing. An unsupported replace fails preparation instead of producing a module that depends on a local path. Source archives claim no compiled ABI and no build provenance. Full cgo and sysroot portability is not available. A platform matrix can pick the matching Go toolchain for each platform (platform selection). Preparation checks the actual Go OS and architecture, and tests run in each selected runtime. Pinned Go in the worker supports only linux/amd64 workers and the go/-prefixed tar.gz Go archive layout. Embedded files (//go:embed) are captured with the source that Go reports for them.
Local builds and build tasks for the shared build model. Build bundles for the dist/ layout these builds produce. Direct tests, version inference and Go installation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/gradle.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu detects build.gradle or build.gradle.kts without any build YAML, then builds, tests and packages the project with Gradle. A multi-project or composite build is one Oyzu target. Gradle still owns project membership, included builds, task dependencies and output paths, and Oyzu uses that model to plan artifacts and collect reports. The multi-project example has an application, a library and an included support build. Note: The Gradle builder is experimental. Captured builds run on Linux (Docker required). The builder is supplied by the oyzu-plugin-gradle plugin (profile java/gradle); see plugin catalog.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Captured builds also need Docker and the base execution image. The JDK and, for a project without a Gradle wrapper, Gradle itself are restored from oyzu.lock: oyzu -C examples/builds/java-gradle-multi-project/project build --isolated --full Note: Isolated Gradle builds on the base execution image are not supported yet. Isolated builds run in a Linux container.

oyzu run list doesn't run Gradle. It lists Gradle's build and test tasks and the shared Java lint and format tasks. Gradle's build already includes tests, so captured builds don't run a separate test stage. Qualified task names and TOML replacements work as in the common task engine. The default Java test tasks need no test or report configuration.

Command Runs Notes oyzu build Gradle on your machine Gradle's build lifecycle can run tests even in this fast mode. oyzu build --full Gradle on your machine Also runs Oyzu's quality checks. oyzu build --isolated --full In the container The captured path, with all checks. A custom Gradle JUnit directory doesn't change where JaCoCo coverage is read. Both are required evidence for a host build, and missing coverage blocks artifact export.

Need Detail Gradle 8.14.3. Set GRADLE_HOME or put Gradle on PATH. A Gradle wrapper in the project is used if present, and its distribution must already be installed. JDK 17, with JAVA_HOME set. Dependencies Your project and test dependencies, including JaCoCo 0.8.13. Gradle's user home and your project's repositories stay in charge. Direct tests need these tools installed. oyzu build on your machine prepares tools through the shared tool management and records the versions in oyzu.lock. A tool on PATH alone doesn't pin the build. Oyzu runs Gradle's model and test commands with --offline and turns off automatic Java toolchain downloads. Missing cached dependencies fail with an error. Offline resolution doesn't sandbox arbitrary build logic, and doesn't stop a wrapper from trying to install itself.

A JDK your project selects, through [tools] java or native requirements, is locked by build preflight. It is restored read-only at /scratch/jdktool from the verified Temurin archive in oyzu.lock, the same way as for Maven. Daemon JVM criteria​ An explicit toolchainVersion in gradle/gradle-daemon-jvm.properties selects the daemon JDK's feature release. For example, toolchainVersion=25 normally selects a stable Java 25. An explicit [tools] java must satisfy the same constraint. The declared vendor still applies when Gradle launches. Oyzu supplies Temurin. It refuses vendors other than ADOPTIUM or Eclipse Adoptium, and daemon requirements for a native-image-capable JDK, before downloading anything. The message gives the source path and field. Literal property names and whole-number feature releases are supported. Malformed or escaped criteria need to be corrected, or a matching JDK must already be installed. Without daemon criteria, Oyzu uses the highest literal Java level in the root and first-level build scripts (JavaLanguageVersion.of(21), sourceCompatibility) as the minimum compiler level, or Java 21 if none is declared. With explicit daemon criteria, your compilation and toolchain declarations are left for Gradle to enforce. They don't replace the daemon JDK. The container restores one JDK. A build that needs a second JDK for some task can still fail, because automatic downloads are off. JDK installation and Gradle versions​ The selected JDK is always offered to Gradle through -Dorg.gradle.java.installations.paths, including before daemon JVM selection. Automatic toolchain downloads stay off. The image's Gradle 8.14.3 runs on the selected JDK when that is release 24 or older. For a newer JDK, the launcher keeps the image's bootstrap JDK and offers the selected one to Gradle. A newer Gradle can then use it for the daemon criterion, but Gradle 8.14.3 may not support the newer JDK. A project's own wrapper version isn't installed in the container yet. A selected JDK older than 17 is refused with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION.

oyzu run test writes its reports to a bundle under dist/. After the usual task checks, Oyzu asks Gradle for the model of the root build and its included builds. The query runs only Oyzu's metadata tasks. It doesn't run your tests or compile your code on purpose. Gradle configuration, plugins and build logic still run normally. This is ordinary execution on your machine, not a security boundary.

Enabled test tasks that have test source files, with their JUnit destinations and JaCoCo destinations. Projects with no test sources don't create test obligations. A build with no tests fails instead of producing a passing empty suite. The implicit command runs the discovered tests across the composite, respecting task dependencies. Custom commands run unchanged and must produce the required reports. Forwarded extra arguments aren't supported by the default reporting.

Before each run, Oyzu removes previous XML from the selected test directories and the selected coverage XML. JaCoCo coverage is generated even after failed assertions. Each test task's suites are combined without dropping test cases, and fresh private JUnit and JaCoCo files are collected. dist/manifest.json links each report to its summary, plan and logs. Output stays in your project's build directories. Sources and versions are unchanged. Direct tests create no application artifact records and don't package, lint or format.

Pre and post hooks apply. A failed test skips its success-only post hook. Failed assertions, missing or malformed reports and unmet coverage thresholds fail the command and keep the evidence available. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle. See direct tests for output handling, history, report overrides and provenance. Direct execution isn't isolated, and a passing local test grants no publishing or signing authority.

Preparation reads Gradle's models and downloads Maven-layout dependencies through Oyzu's scoped public repository adapter. The build then runs offline against the captured repository. Private and custom repositories aren't supported. Gradle plugins come from the plugin portal. Version inference resolves native versions, scoped tags and commit changes, and Oyzu applies the versions in a private copy of the source. Gradle's archive tasks supply the file names and archive versions. JAR, WAR, EAR, ZIP, TAR and gzip archives are supported, and the bundle records their planned versions and digests. JAR manifest attributes are not rewritten to add implementation-version metadata. Tests and checks: Java tests supply JUnit and JaCoCo reports. Projects without sources are skipped. The shared Java quality checks run before artifacts are published to dist. Missing archives, unresolved dependencies and failed required stages or reports fail the build.

Oyzu reads the original versions first and freezes a version-plan.json for the project directories in the composite. Preparation checks the original versions and applies each decision, and the offline build uses the same result. A unique Gradle project name supplies the scoped tag name. Repeated names use directory paths. An unspecified version can take its version from a tag without adding a version to your build. Local project dependencies keep full build-tree identities, including substituted projects in included builds. Missing or unresolved graph facts fail preparation. Metadata-only queries on your machine don't resolve this graph. Changes in one project affect the projects that depend on it. Unrelated project directories keep independent bases.

Captured downloads come from two public sources: Maven Central and the Gradle plugin portal (https://plugins.gradle.org/m2/). The portal's artifact host, https://plugins-artifacts.gradle.org/, is also allowed so portal redirects for plugin JARs work. Redirects to Maven Central use the Central source. Plugins applied in settings.gradle or a project plugins {} block, and gradlePluginPortal() in pluginManagement, buildscript or project repositories, resolve through Oyzu during preparation: // settings.gradle plugins { id 'com.gradle.develocity' version '4.2' } How it works: An init script adds an Oyzu Central entry and an Oyzu portal entry to pluginManagement (replacing Gradle's implicit portal default) and routes each recognized repository to its own local path. Any other repository URL fails preparation with Gradle repository requires an approved source adapter. Files from both sources go into one Maven-layout repository that the offline build reads. repository-sources.json in the prepared tree records which source served each file, and the dependency snapshot lists each package under maven-central, gradle-plugin-portal or gradle-plugin-artifacts. A redirect to any other host fails with a source denial. Limits: Settings plugins resolve while Gradle evaluates the settings script, before Oyzu can reroute repositories that the script declares. Oyzu's own entries come first, so a plugin they serve is found. Plugin behavior that downloads at run time, such as Gradle toolchain provisioning, isn't covered.

Java projects are the supported case. Non-Java languages, custom coverage plugins, generated test sources and unusual plugin or composite setups may not work. Disabled tests and source-free tasks are skipped. Test tasks whose sources can't be attributed fail with an error. Private repositories and release authorization aren't supported. Daemon JVM selection for a Gradle build that needs a JDK newer than the image supports is limited by Gradle 8.14.3 itself (see JDK installation and Gradle versions).
Java quality tasks, direct tests, version inference. Maven builds and Java installation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/gradle-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this when a Gradle build should download from a private Maven-layout repository without storing a password in gradle.properties or init scripts. Each time you run gradle through oyzu, oyzu asks a local credential agent which repository to use, points every repository in the build at it and gives Gradle the password in memory. Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Gradle 8.14.3, JDK 17 and Bash. Isolated oyzu build runs don't use this.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [gradle] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning gradle.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain Gradle Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there.

With Gradle and a JDK installed: oyzu exec -- /opt/gradle-8.14.3/bin/gradle build # or, with Gradle on PATH: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" gradle build Use the real gradle executable; gradlew isn't supported. --help, --version, --status and --stop run without asking the agent.

Sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "gradle", "arguments": [...]}. Reads the agent's answer: { "repository": "https://packages.example.com/maven/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } repository is an HTTP(S) URL with no credentials, query or fragment. credentialEndpoint must be on 127.0.0.1. Starts Gradle with a bundled init script and --no-configuration-cache. The script fetches the password with a GET to credentialEndpoint (the response body is the password, up to 64 KiB) on every run. The init script points plugin, settings, buildscript and project repositories at the one repository, with those credentials, and adds it where a build declares none. Existing Maven-layout repositories (including mavenLocal()) are redirected to it. Other repository types fail the build. Gradle downloads directly from the repository; oyzu doesn't proxy the traffic. Your build files, lock files and other options aren't changed. Gradle's dependency cache and daemon keep working as usual. The temporary files are removed when Gradle finishes or fails. The agent is asked every time, even with a warm cache.

The password never goes into project files, command arguments or environment variables. It's in Gradle's memory, so build code and plugins can read it. The init script doesn't keep the password between runs, even when the daemon is reused. Read-only access has to be enforced by the repository account the agent uses. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command before Gradle starts. oyzu never falls back to running Gradle without a session.
Gradle's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID Bad endpoint, or the response has a bad repository or no user name Fix the endpoint or the agent GRADLE_SESSION_INVALID The agent's response couldn't be read, or an argument isn't valid UTF-8 Fix the agent's response GRADLE_SESSION_CONFLICT You passed --init-script/-I, asked for the configuration cache, or ran a task with publish in its name Remove the option. Publish with oyzu publish

One repository per run. Several repositories with different credentials aren't supported. Repository mode conflicts between settings and projects aren't resolved for you. Plugins that make their own HTTP calls aren't covered, and a build that changes repositories later isn't prevented from doing so. The configuration cache is turned off. Temporary files may be left behind if oyzu is killed. Linux and Bash only. Windows and macOS aren't supported yet.
Gradle builds Private Maven repositories Java installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/helm.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The helm/chart builder packages an application or library chart, renders it, lints it, checks its YAML formatting and runs your helm-unittest suites. It finds a chart at Chart.yaml or chart/Chart.yaml, so a basic chart needs no Oyzu configuration. If both locations exist, set the target paths in build.yaml, because ambiguous discovery fails. The chart example has a local library dependency and optional assertion suites. Note: The Helm builder is experimental. It is supported on Linux (x86-64) and Windows. Builds never contact a cluster.
documents.s: Helm charts and native chart tests

documents.t: oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist oyzu run list shows the tasks without launching Helm or reading assertion files. The tasks are: Task Runs Effect install helm dependency build May download dependencies and update locks build helm package Writes a chart archive lint helm lint None test Validation and helm-unittest Writes a test-only dist/ bundle format-check yamlfmt, read-only None format yamlfmt Rewrites your YAML files The group is named project. Explicit targets use their own names.

Direct tasks need Helm and the helm-unittest plugin in Helm's plugin folder, and yamlfmt on PATH for formatting. Isolated builds use Helm 3.22.0, helm-unittest 1.2.0 and yamlfmt 0.21.0. Declared dependencies must already be prepared (for example with oyzu run install), because testing doesn't download them. Builds do not install the plugin or run its installation hooks. The github:helm-unittest/helm-unittest@1.2.0 tool identifies the pinned plugin distribution. Isolated builds need Docker and the base execution image, which has no Helm of its own. Everything a chart build runs comes from the lock or a pinned release: helm must be in oyzu.lock for the worker's platform (see Pinned helm). Without it, preparation stops with a message that says how to lock it. yamlfmt, used by the format stages, is a locked stage tool. helm-unittest 1.2.0 is fetched when the test stage runs and the chart has unit test suites. Preparation picks the release for the worker's architecture (linux/amd64 or linux/arm64), checks it against the publisher's SHA-256 pinned in Oyzu and restores it read-only as the plugin folder /scratch/helm-plugins. The build fixes HELM_PLUGINS to that folder so a task can't redirect it to project code. Oyzu never downloads Helm plugins other than that pinned release. The image identity is recorded in the build's evidence. A Linux amd64 isolated --full build of a chart with a unit test suite ran its tests, lint and format checks and packaged the chart.

The Helm builder comes from the compiled oyzu-plugin-helm package. The package finds your chart and declares the Helm commands, the image bindings and the report translation. Oyzu itself captures dependencies, admits the locked Helm, picks the package and image, decides the version and checks reports and artifacts. Test suites are recorded by the digest of their YAML or archive and their location inside it. Discovery never runs the assertions.

Isolated chart builds need Helm in the lock. Pin the exact version: # oyzu.toml [tools] helm = "4.3.0" oyzu install helm@4.3.0 Helm takes an exact version only, and oyzu pin doesn't resolve it. Oyzu reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for that version in oyzu.lock. It downloads the archive through the tool broker unless a cached copy under the user data folder still matches the locked SHA-256, and verifies the bytes against that digest. It restores the archive read-only at /scratch/helmtool and puts that folder first on PATH for preparation and every build step. The pinned version and archive are part of the dependency record, so a different pin or archive changes the step's identity. A tampered lock is refused. Offline builds need the archive already cached, or they fail with TOOL_OFFLINE. A pinned Helm must be able to run the helm-unittest plugin.

A chart can use the identity of an image built in the same oyzu build, so a deploy needs no --set image.digest=...: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/greeting # the image's eventual repository chart: uses: helm/chart path: chart bindings: - from: image artifact: image type: image-reference repository: /image/repository digest: /image/digest Field Meaning from, artifact The producer build and its output, as in materialize type image-reference is the only type reference Destination that receives repository@sha256:... repository and digest A pair of destinations, used instead of reference Use reference or the repository and digest pair, not both and not neither. Binding the same values field twice fails during configuration. Destinations are JSON Pointers into the chart's values.yaml, and each must already hold a string there. An empty digest: "" is the usual shape. Nothing is created or templated. The image must set with.repository: a repository name without scheme, tag or digest. Building doesn't publish. The bound reference names the intended repository and the real manifest digest of the local archive, so the chart isn't deployable until the image is pushed there. If you change the repository, rebuild the chart. How it runs: A binding makes the chart depend on the image and copies the image's OCI archive into the chart target (.oyzu-bindings/<n>.oci.tar, recorded in dist/inputs/<chart>.json). After the chart is copied to its private workspace and before it is packaged, linted or rendered, the bind step reads the archive's manifest digest and rewrites the destinations in that copy's values.yaml. The packaged default values and rendered.yaml carry the produced reference. Your checked-in chart is never edited. The rewrite re-serializes values.yaml in the private copy, so comments in the packaged defaults are lost. A new image digest reruns the chart's steps, and an unchanged one reuses them. A failed or blocked image blocks every chart step. Image bindings work on Windows with Docker Desktop. A multi-platform image (more than one manifest) is refused. Linux and macOS hosts, bindings through a platform matrix, publishing and deployed clusters are not supported yet.

Discovery adds a read-only format-check build stage and a format task that edits your files. Both use yamlfmt. Selected files: .yaml and .yml files directly in each chart root (the folder with Chart.yaml), plus YAML below tests/ and crds/. Unpacked subcharts and sibling charts inside the target root are included. Left out: Go templates in templates/, __snapshot__ baselines, packaged chart archives, Chart.lock, generated output and hidden folders. Dependency archives are never edited or repacked. Template formatting isn't supported, so a passing check says nothing about template style. Oyzu runs yamlfmt with its own private configuration: LF line endings, a final newline, and yamlfmt's basic formatter defaults. Configuration in parent folders or your home folder is ignored. A formatter file in the target (.yamlfmt, .yamlfmt.yaml, .yamlfmt.yml, yamlfmt.yaml, yamlfmt.yml) fails the implicit task with a message telling you to override the tasks. Use normal TOML task overrides for custom formatting. format-check lists the files that differ and exits non-zero without changing anything. Invalid YAML also fails, with yamlfmt's message. Run oyzu run format, review the changes and try again. format writes files as it goes, so if a later file fails, earlier edits stay. Neither task downloads dependencies or contacts a cluster. Links and non-regular files are rejected. Limits are 100,000 traversed entries, 4 MiB per file and 64 MiB in total, and each yamlfmt run has a 30-second timeout. Direct tasks run as host processes with no sandbox. Isolated builds use the executor's isolation. The chart is packaged and rendered in the build even when you don't select the test stage, so plain oyzu build still writes rendered.yaml.

Declare unpacked subcharts in the parent's native Chart.yaml dependencies. For a subchart inside the chart, give its name and version and leave repository empty. That selects the existing charts/<name> folder. If you skip this, strict lint fails, even when the subchart's assertions pass. Oyzu doesn't add the dependency for you or turn the lint gate off. Keep checksum files out of charts/, or list them in .helmignore (for example charts/*.tgz.sha256), because Helm reads non-chart files there as dependencies.

Without assertion suites, the implicit test checks that an application chart renders and passes its values schema. A library chart is checked with strict lint with subcharts, because it can't be rendered as an installable chart. In isolated builds, rendering uses helm template --dry-run=client with an empty kubeconfig and no cluster access. This checks the chart. It doesn't show that a deployed application works.

Oyzu finds helm-unittest suites in each chart, including unpacked subcharts and local charts/*.tgz subcharts, even when the parent has none: flat tests/*_test.yaml recursive unittests/**/*.yaml (any .yaml name) .yml files, custom globs and recursive tests/ folders are not selected. Each subchart needs a regular Chart.yaml, and chart folders starting with a dot or underscore are ignored. Helm-unittest parses the YAML and runs the assertions, so malformed YAML is a native failure. For example, chart/tests/deployment_test.yaml: suite: deployment contract templates: - templates/deployment.yaml tests: - it: uses one replica asserts: - equal: path: spec.replicas value: 1 Oyzu passes both file patterns to helm-unittest explicitly, because helm-unittest 1.2.0 drops its defaults when you give it a pattern. Selected suites must produce at least one test case. You don't add a test section to build.yaml, and you don't set a glob. oyzu run test shows the logical task helm unittest --strict <chart>. It unpacks packaged subcharts in a private copy before calling the plugin. Isolated builds run both the render and schema validation and the unit tests, and ask the plugin for JUnit output. Suites are source files, so they go into the published chart archive unless you list tests/ in .helmignore. Oyzu doesn't change your packaging rules. Static discovery inspects archives without extracting them into your checkout. It stops at these limits: Limit Value Suites 128 Inspected entries 4,096 per scope Subchart levels 16 Archive nesting 16 Metadata file 4 MiB Expanded archive bytes 64 MiB per scope An archive needs one chart root with a Chart.yaml. Links, duplicate or case-alias paths, non-portable paths and mixed roots fail. Arbitrary tar layouts aren't accepted, only Helm-generated archives.

Preparation unpacks contained subcharts in its private workspace and captures the chart's local file:// dependencies. It rejects cycles and paths that escape, and runs dependency preparation offline. Existing locks are honored and stale locks fail. Lock timestamps and archive metadata are normalized. If a packed and an unpacked copy of a subchart both exist, the build fails instead of overwriting. Your source archives are never modified. The chart version comes from version inference over its native version and Git history, with a suffix from the source snapshot. appVersion and dependency versions keep their own meanings. A build packages the chart, runs the tests, strict lint and the read-only YAML format check, and collects the outputs if all pass. Application charts produce a versioned .tgz and rendered.yaml. Library charts produce the .tgz only. Building, generated files and the version change happen in private workspaces, so your checkout stays unchanged. The format check covers your source YAML, not the regenerated dependency chart. Reports are collected in dist/, and dist/manifest.json records their paths, digests and summaries: junit.xml is one render and schema check, or the library validation unittest.xml is required when suites are selected, and has the native test cases, failures and skips. A render success never covers a failed assertion Coverage is recorded as inapplicable: chart assertions have no source coverage. No coverage percentage is made up The manifest also lists framework discovery, step outcomes and artifacts. Testing fails for missing or invalid required reports, a plugin that won't launch, a native failure, a timeout, or a unittest run with zero test cases. Old report files are removed before each run, so an earlier success can't cover a failed launch. Validation and unit tests each time out after 120 seconds. Task replacements and hooks work as usual. A replacement keeps the required reports, and one that exits 0 without them fails collection. A valid bundle isn't a release approval. If a build fails, read the retained logs and reports, fix the suite, tool, values or lock, and rebuild. A format difference needs oyzu run format or a task override.

Helm-unittest can create missing matchSnapshot baselines even without --update-snapshot. Oyzu compares the files under __snapshot__ folders before and after the run. Creating, changing or deleting a baseline fails the task and blocks artifacts. The native JUnit can still show a passing assertion, so read both the step status and the reports. Create or update baselines on purpose with native helm-unittest outside the build, review them and commit them with the suite. Then a matching baseline passes and a changed value fails normally. Direct oyzu run test applies the same rule and also rejects creation or changes. Direct tests run on a private copy of the chart that leaves out .git, .oyzu and dist, so the live bundle isn't visible to Helm. The copy holds the chart tree only, so relative references to files outside it don't work. It rejects links and is limited to 100,000 entries and 64 MiB. Baseline scanning has the same entry limit with 16 MiB per file and 64 MiB in total. Exceeding a limit fails the task. This checks baseline changes and is not a file write monitor. Direct tasks are not a sandbox. Isolated builds use the executor's isolation.

To check a chart before you commit, run oyzu build --full, or oyzu run test, oyzu run lint and oyzu run format-check for the quick version, and read the reports with oyzu inspect dist. Not supported yet: Custom suite globs, templated test charts, and suites in sibling file:// dependencies that aren't prepared are not discovered. Remote and OCI chart dependencies aren't downloaded. Go-template formatting and custom yamlfmt configuration aren't supported. Publishing and signing aren't part of the Helm builder. Image bindings: see Image bindings.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/install-script.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. install.sh and install.ps1 install the oyzu executable from a GitHub release with one command. They pick the release asset for your platform, check its SHA-256 digest and put oyzu in a folder of your own. They need no administrator rights. They then run oyzu shell install, so your shells activate oyzu and both oyzu and its tool shims are on your PATH. Note: Every release is a preview. Releases are binaries and notices published on the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository, and both scripts default to it, so you need no account or token. No release has been published there yet. Until one is, a run stops with no published release. The scripts don't check release provenance (the *.sigstore.json files) yet.

On Linux or macOS: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | sh On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex A GitHub token is optional. It lifts the anonymous API limit, or lets you install from a private repository named in OYZU_RELEASE_REPO. With the GitHub CLI signed in: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) sh $env:GH_TOKEN = (gh auth token); irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex A successful run names the release, prints one summary line (tag, asset, SHA-256 digest, location), the installed oyzu --version and the result of oyzu shell install. Release values are placeholders here: Installing oyzu <tag> for linux/x86_64 from oyzuai/oyzu-releases Installed oyzu <tag> (oyzu-linux-x86_64, sha256:<digest>) to /home/you/.oyzu/bin/oyzu oyzu <version> (<build>; x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu; build <id>) Shells and PATH set up activation bash /home/you/.bashrc login-path bash /home/you/.profile Next Step: Open a new terminal (and restart IDEs) so they pick up the new PATH. To use Preview plugins, run oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true once. It is a user-level setting that applies to all your projects, and Stable defaults stay unchanged.

Piping a download into a shell runs whatever the server sent. Each script is under 250 lines, so you can read it first: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh -o install.sh less install.sh sh install.sh irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 -OutFile install.ps1 Get-Content install.ps1 powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install.ps1 Both are served from the documentation site over HTTPS.
documents.s: Read it before you run it

documents.t: install.sh install.ps1 Environment variable Default Meaning --version TAG -Version TAG OYZU_VERSION newest release with your platform's asset Install this release tag, for example v0.0.4 --dir DIR -InstallDir DIR OYZU_INSTALL_DIR ~/.oyzu/bin; Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\bin Folder that receives oyzu and oyzu-shim --no-modify-path -NoModifyPath OYZU_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 off Install the files only: skip shell activation and PATH changes (see Shell and PATH setup) --modify-path -ModifyPath Accepted and ignored. Shell and PATH setup is now the default --help -Help Print usage and exit An option wins over its environment variable. These variables have no option: Variable Default Meaning GH_TOKEN, then GITHUB_TOKEN none GitHub token for the API, for the rate limit or a private OYZU_RELEASE_REPO OYZU_RELEASE_REPO oyzuai/oyzu-releases Repository whose releases are read, for forks OYZU_API_BASE https://api.github.com GitHub API base, for GitHub Enterprise or a test server OYZU_DOWNLOAD_BASE https://github.com Base of anonymous release downloads To pass options through a pipe: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | sh -s -- --version v0.0.4 --dir "$HOME/bin" & ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1))) -Version v0.0.4

Without a version, the script reads the newest 30 releases and takes the newest one that is not a draft and has an executable for your platform. Previews count, and every release is one. Host Asset Linux x86_64 / aarch64 (glibc) oyzu-linux-x86_64 / oyzu-linux-arm64 Linux with musl (Alpine) oyzu-linux-x86_64-musl / oyzu-linux-arm64-musl macOS Intel / Apple silicon oyzu-darwin-x86_64 / oyzu-darwin-arm64; a shell under Rosetta still gets arm64 Windows x86_64 / ARM64 oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe / oyzu-windows-arm64.exe, by the native architecture even in an emulated shell If the release also has oyzu-shim-<platform>, it is installed beside oyzu as oyzu-shim. Releases so far publish no musl assets, so a musl host gets the no asset error. On macOS and Windows the script also downloads the same release's Linux oyzu for your architecture (oyzu-linux-x86_64 or oyzu-linux-arm64), checked the same way. Isolated builds (oyzu build --isolated) run that Linux oyzu inside the container. A Linux host doesn't need it: its own oyzu runs there.

Downloads the asset into a temporary folder and compares its SHA-256 with the digest GitHub reports for that asset. A mismatch or a missing digest stops the install. Runs the new oyzu --version from the temporary folder. An executable that can't run on this host leaves an existing install alone. Creates the install folder and replaces oyzu (and oyzu-shim) there, with the executable bit set. Running it again upgrades or reinstalls. On macOS and Windows, runs oyzu engine install --linux with the downloaded Linux oyzu. This installs the pair as the engine package of the new oyzu, so --isolated works. It prints Installed the Linux engine for isolated builds. If the release has no Linux oyzu for your architecture, or the step fails, oyzu stays installed and the script says so; only isolated builds are affected. Prints one line with the tag, asset, digest and location, then the version. Runs the installed oyzu shell install, unless you skipped it. The scripts never use sudo and never install toolchains.

The last step runs oyzu shell install with the new executable. It needs no network and edits only the files below. Running it again changes nothing. What Where Shell activation: bash, zsh, PowerShell 7 (each one found) ~/.bashrc, $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc or ~/.zshrc, and the PowerShell 7 current-user profile oyzu and the tool shims on the persistent PATH, Windows your user Path in the registry (HKCU\Environment), with %VARIABLE% entries unexpanded, announced to running programs oyzu and the tool shims on the persistent PATH, Linux and macOS a marked block in your login profile (~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile, whichever exists first; ~/.zprofile for zsh) The shims let IDEs, GUI programs, services and scripts that never start a shell run node, go or cargo at the version the project locks, without oyzu exec --. Programs that are already open keep the PATH they started with, so restart them or open a new terminal. If setup fails, the install still stands. The script says so on standard error and prints the command to run again. fish and Windows PowerShell 5.1 are not configured, so add the folders yourself. With --no-modify-path (-NoModifyPath, OYZU_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1) the script changes no profile or PATH. If the folder isn't on PATH, it prints how to set things up later: Shell Line any ~/.oyzu/bin/oyzu shell install (Windows: & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe" shell install) PowerShell, this session $env:Path = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin;$env:Path" See oyzu shell for what each file receives and how to undo it.

Run the same command again to move to the newest release, or pass a version to switch to that one. To uninstall, run oyzu shell remove to undo the shell and PATH setup, then delete the two files (and the folder if it is empty): rm -f ~/.oyzu/bin/oyzu ~/.oyzu/bin/oyzu-shim Remove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe", "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\oyzu-shim.exe" Tools that oyzu installed for projects live in its own store, not in this folder, so deleting these files doesn't remove them.

Integrity: the digest comes from the GitHub releases API over HTTPS, and the download must match it. This shows the bytes are the ones GitHub holds for that release asset. It doesn't show who built them, because the scripts don't check release provenance yet. Transport: install.sh restricts curl to HTTPS, including redirects, unless OYZU_API_BASE or OYZU_DOWNLOAD_BASE names a plain http: test server. Tokens: a token is sent only in a request header to the GitHub API. install.sh gives it to curl on standard input, never on the command line, so it needs curl when you use a token (wget is used only without one). curl and PowerShell drop the header when GitHub redirects a download to its storage host. The scripts never print a token. Scope: files go to the install folder and a temporary folder that is removed afterwards. oyzu shell install then edits the profiles listed under Shell and PATH setup. --no-modify-path skips it.

Script Runs on Needs install.sh Linux, macOS; also Git Bash on Windows POSIX sh, awk, curl or wget, and sha256sum, shasum or openssl install.ps1 Windows x86_64 and ARM64 Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7 install.sh uses no bash features, jq or Python. Running install.ps1 under PowerShell on macOS or Linux stops and points you to install.sh. The scripts are tested on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS, musl and ARM64 aren't tested yet.

Status Meaning 0 Installed 1 Failed: network, HTTP error, no release or asset for this platform, the executable doesn't run, or the folder can't be written 2 Usage error (unknown option or missing value) 3 Integrity refusal: the digest differs, the release reports none, or no SHA-256 tool is available install.ps1 sets the process exit status when run with powershell -File install.ps1. Under irm ... | iex it doesn't exit, because that would close your window. It prints the error and sets $LASTEXITCODE.

Errors start with oyzu install: and leave an existing install unchanged.
