Message Cause Recovery GitHub answered 404 Not Found for the release list of <repo> ... private OYZU_RELEASE_REPO names a private repository and no token was given, or it doesn't exist Pass GH_TOKEN with access, for example GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) GitHub answered 404 Not Found ... with your token The token can't read the repository, or the tag or asset doesn't exist Check the tag and the token's repository access GitHub rejected the token ... (HTTP 401) Invalid or expired token Create a new token or run gh auth login GitHub refused ... (HTTP 403) Anonymous API rate limit (60 requests an hour) or missing permission Wait, or pass GH_TOKEN no published release of oyzuai/oyzu-releases has <asset> No release has an executable for this platform (musl, other CPUs), or no release is published yet Build from source release <tag> ... has no <asset> That release lacks this platform Choose another --version <asset> ... has digest ..., but the release reports ... The download doesn't match the published digest Retry. If it repeats, don't use the file, and report it release <tag> reports no SHA-256 digest The release API returned no digest for the asset Choose another release could not connect to download ... Offline, DNS or proxy failure Check the network. curl, wget and PowerShell honor the usual proxy settings the downloaded <asset> does not run on this host Wrong ABI or a damaged download Build from source, or report the platform cannot write <path> No permission, or oyzu.exe is running on Windows Choose --dir, or close oyzu and retry
Getting started, including building from source. Shell setup for activating project tools.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/installer-recipes.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Some npm packages download extra files while they install or run: Puppeteer downloads a browser, node-gyp downloads Node.js headers. A captured build (oyzu build --isolated) runs without network, so those downloads would fail. For packages Oyzu recognizes, it downloads the matching file during preparation, checks it against a pinned SHA-256 and points the tool at it through the tool's own settings. Your project declares nothing. Note: Recipes cover Puppeteer and node-gyp on Linux x86-64 workers only, and there is no setting to turn one off yet. A native host build (without --isolated) has network access and downloads as the package intends.

After the package manager's captured install preparation, Oyzu reads the locked packages and the Node version. For each recognized package it looks up the pinned asset. If your version or platform has no pinned asset, Oyzu says so in the build log and guesses nothing (see When a package is recognized but not pinned). Oyzu downloads each asset the same way as a declared fetch, checks it against the pinned digest, stores it by digest under <user data>/cache/fetches/ and unpacks it under recipes/<recipe>/ in the prepared dependency tree. The build sees that tree read-only at /dependencies. Every command (install, tasks and package) gets the recipe's settings, so the install script skips its download and the tool finds the asset when it runs. If an administrator restricts downloads with fetches.sources, the asset's host must be allowed there, as for any declared fetch.

Recognized Every locked version of the registry package puppeteer, in npm, pnpm or Yarn locks Assets Chrome for Testing chrome and chrome-headless-shell for linux64, at the build Puppeteer pins for that release URL https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/<build>/linux64/<browser>-linux64.zip Layout recipes/puppeteer/<browser>/linux-<build>/<browser>-linux64/ (Puppeteer's cache layout) Settings PUPPETEER_CACHE_DIR=/dependencies/recipes/puppeteer, PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true Pinned releases Puppeteer 24.0.0 to 25.13.0, and 25.16.0 Puppeteer's install script sees PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD and doesn't try the network. puppeteer.launch() and puppeteer.executablePath() read PUPPETEER_CACHE_DIR and find the browser for their own pinned build, so your project needs no change. Both browsers are delivered because Puppeteer downloads both by default. Firefox is skipped by default and has no recipe. Limits: Only linux/amd64 workers have pinned assets. Chrome for Testing has no Linux arm64 build before Chrome 153. On other platforms the log says the browser isn't pinned. If you select another browser build (PUPPETEER_CHROME_VERSION, chrome.version in .puppeteerrc) or another cache directory, your setting overrides the recipe for that value and the install fails offline. The base execution image doesn't include the system libraries Chrome needs to start (libnss3 and others). The recipe delivers the browser. To launch it, use an image that has those libraries (--image npm=<image>).

Recognized A locked registry package whose archive has a top-level binding.gyp, or a binding.gyp in the project root Asset node-v<version>-headers.tar.gz for the Node version in use URL https://nodejs.org/dist/v<version>/node-v<version>-headers.tar.gz Layout recipes/node-gyp/<version>/node-v<version>/include/node/ Settings npm_config_nodedir=/dependencies/recipes/node-gyp/<version>/node-v<version> Pinned releases Node.js 18.0.0 to 26.11.1 node-gyp reads npm_config_nodedir and uses those headers instead of downloading them. The scripts that npm, pnpm and Yarn run inherit the variable. The headers alone don't compile an addon. You also need Python, make and a C++ compiler in the image. The base execution image has make and g++ but no Python, so a build that compiles an addon needs an image of its own: provide one with --image npm=<image>. Addons that download a prebuilt binary first (prebuild-install, node-pre-gyp) still fail offline unless they fall back to compiling.

Preparation continues and the build log shows one line for the recipe: Recipe puppeteer puppeteer@25.14.0 has no pinned Chrome for Testing build in this Oyzu release; its install script will try to download one Preparation doesn't fail here, because your project may already avoid the download with the tool's own settings. If it doesn't, the install fails as described next.
documents.s: When a package is recognized but not pinned

documents.t: When a captured npm install fails because a script couldn't reach the network, the error names the package, the URL and the fix, as far as npm's output shows them: DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING: the install script of cypress@13.6.0 tried to download https://download.cypress.io/desktop.json, and captured execution has no network. Oyzu has no recipe for this asset. Declare it as a pinned fetch in build.yaml (name, url, sha256) and point the package at OYZU_FETCH_<NAME> through its own setting; see the declared fetches reference. The original npm output follows the message. If Oyzu can't find a URL it names the host instead, and if there was no network error it reports npm's failure unchanged. This diagnosis covers npm installs. pnpm and Yarn report their native error. For the root package, npm reports the build version that version inference applied, which can differ from the version in your manifest. To supply the asset yourself, add a declared fetch and set the tool's own variable to its path. For Puppeteer on an unpinned release, fetch the Chrome for Testing zip with unpack: zip and set PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true and PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/dependencies/fetches/<name>/chrome-linux64/chrome.

Spotless steps backed by Eclipse formatters (<eclipse>, <greclipse>, <eclipseWtp> and <eclipseCdt> in the Maven plugin, and their Gradle equivalents) download Eclipse P2 bundles from download.eclipse.org at run time, into Spotless's own cache. There is no recipe for this, and a declared fetch can't be pointed at that cache. In a captured Maven build, spotless-maven-plugin:check fails during preparation with java.net.UnknownHostException: download.eclipse.org. To work around it, run that Spotless check outside the captured build, or keep the Eclipse step out of the captured lifecycle, for example with a Maven profile that sets spotless.check.skip=true.

Every recipe asset has a SHA-256 in a table inside Oyzu. A download whose bytes don't match fails with INTEGRITY_MISMATCH and nothing is stored. Oyzu never takes a digest from the network at build time. Chrome for Testing publishes no checksums. Oyzu's digests were computed from the downloaded zip after its bytes matched the checksum Google Cloud Storage reports for the file. Node.js header digests come from each release's SHASUMS256.txt. The signature of that file was not checked. The dependency snapshot records each asset with verification: digest-only: the bytes match the pinned digest, but no publisher signature was checked.

Each asset becomes a package in the target's dependency snapshot: Field Value id recipe:<target>/<recipe>/<asset>/<version>, for example recipe:web/puppeteer/chrome/136.0.7103.94 name, version The asset name (chrome, chrome-headless-shell, node-headers) and its upstream version sourceId fetch:<host> for a standalone build, or fetches.sources/<index> under an allowlist digest, size The verified bytes purpose, verification build, digest-only The extension oyzu.dev/recipes lists each applied recipe with the packages it serves, its settings and each asset's path and tree digest. Both are part of the snapshot digest, so the build plan is bound to the delivered assets.

Recipes apply automatically to every captured Node build that locks a recognized package. The digest tables cover a fixed range of releases. A newer release needs an Oyzu update. Recipe settings override the same variable from the builder plan. If a variable is delivered twice (for example by a recipe and a declared fetch), the build fails.

Recipe assets use the declared fetch errors. The message names the recipe, the asset and the package, for example web: puppeteer recipe asset chrome 136.0.7103.94 for puppeteer@24.9.0. Code Cause Recovery SOURCE_DENIED An administrative fetches.sources doesn't allow the asset's host Ask an administrator to allow it, such as https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/ INTEGRITY_MISMATCH The downloaded bytes differ from the pinned digest Report it. Don't change the digest without checking the upstream release. DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING An offline build needs an asset that isn't stored, or an install script without a recipe tried the network Run one online build, or declare the asset as above
Declared fetches Version inference

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/java-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Maven, Gradle and Ant projects get lint, format-check and format tasks without any configuration. They use Checkstyle 10.21.4 for linting and google-java-format 1.28.0 for formatting. Replace any of them with your own task if your project already has its own tooling. Note: These defaults are experimental. Oyzu does not install Checkstyle or google-java-format yet. For tasks on your machine you provision them once (see Provisioning and execution). Isolated builds fetch them for you. oyzu run list oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build In a workspace with several targets, qualify the task name, for example api:lint. oyzu run list needs no Java tools. It shows the linter and formatter that will be used. Running a task needs the tools installed. lint and format-check are build stages. format changes your files, so it is never added to a build. A failed quality check blocks the artifacts. Test and coverage reports that were produced stay in dist/manifest.json. Lint and format output is in the action logs, not in JUnit or coverage reports.

For tasks on your machine, install a JDK 17 or newer (Oyzu prepares the JDK itself, see Java installation) and the quality tools. The Oyzu repository has a provisioning script: python tooling/provision-java-quality.py --destination /absolute/path/java-quality Then set OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME to that absolute directory and put the JDK's java on PATH: # PowerShell $env:OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME = 'E:\tools\java-quality' # POSIX shell export OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME=/absolute/path/java-quality The script downloads checksum-pinned upstream JARs, keeps their licenses and notices, records their source URLs and copies the default lint configuration. It needs Python. The quality tasks themselves don't. Without the tools, a native oyzu build --full stops in preparation, before any action runs, and produces no artifacts. oyzu run lint refuses the same way. The message names Checkstyle, google-java-format, OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME and the provisioning command, and offers two alternatives: replace the task in oyzu.toml, or build without --full. Oyzu checks the tool home when the lint, format-check or format task is frozen, using the task's own OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME or the environment's.

Isolated builds need no provisioning. When lint or format-check is enabled, preparation fetches the pinned Checkstyle 10.21.4 and google-java-format 1.28.0 JARs, checks each against its SHA-256 and packs them with Oyzu's checks.xml into one archive. That archive is restored read-only on the base execution image at /scratch/java-integration/quality, which becomes OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME. Like your declared fetches, it is stored, so an offline rebuild reuses it. The JARs keep their upstream licenses and notices. Builds never read user-home caches. The quality checks run in the same network-disabled container as the build. Tasks run on your machine use the adapter copied in during provisioning, so run the script again after you update Oyzu. Containers use the adapter embedded in the CLI. Oyzu protects the tool-home setting from being replaced by a task environment. Tasks on your machine are ordinary development runs and aren't isolated. Failures that name a prerequisite (missing or relative tool home, missing tools, invalid Java, a tool failure, extra forwarded arguments) are fixed by correcting the prerequisite or the source and rerunning. The checks never change your source. If you used an earlier google-java-format 1.24.0, it fails on JDK 25 with NoSuchMethodError for Log$DeferredDiagnosticHandler.getDiagnostics. Version 1.28.0 fixes that. Reprovision the tools you installed for host tasks, because updating the CLI alone doesn't replace them. Isolated builds already fetch 1.28.0.

The lint defaults check for unused imports, redundant imports, empty statements and equals/hashCode consistency. Checkstyle does the parsing and rule checks. google-java-format formats and normalizes imports: format-check runs its dry-run mode, and format rewrites files. See the formatter CLI and Checkstyle CLI. Each task selects the .java files below its target, including custom source roots, reactor modules and included builds. It skips folders named .git, .oyzu, .oyzu-build, .oyzu-maven, .gradle, .idea, target, build, dist, out, node_modules and .venv, at any depth. It doesn't guess other output folders or tell generated files apart outside those names. If your authored source lives in a skipped folder, or you need a narrower scope or a different style, replace the task. Files are processed in sorted order. Up to 200,000 entries are visited and each Java file can be up to 16 MiB. Symbolic links aren't followed. Meeting a link outside the skipped names fails the task instead of reading outside the target. Files are passed to the tools in batches within a 16,000-character argument limit. If any batch fails, the task fails. With no .java files, the task reports that it doesn't apply. Build checks work on a private copy, so your checkout isn't modified. oyzu run format changes files in place and isn't transactional. A later malformed file can leave earlier files already formatted.

A native lint, format-check or format target in an Ant project wins over the default. TOML task replacements and hooks work as for any task. For example, a Gradle project that already has quality tasks can use them: [tasks.lint] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "checkstyleMain", "checkstyleTest"] [tasks.format-check] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessCheck"] [tasks.format] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessApply"] The tasks and plugins must exist in your project. These examples don't install them. Use ./gradlew or gradlew.bat if you use the wrapper. A replacement used in builds must work in the offline container. The default launcher rejects extra arguments, such as --replace on format-check. Put native flags in a replacement task.

Oyzu doesn't infer Maven quality-plugin bindings, Gradle quality tasks, custom Checkstyle XML or suppression files, Kotlin or Groovy tools, or per-module formatter differences. Checks you configured in your build still run through the native lifecycle and can coexist with the defaults. Replace the defaults if your rules differ.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/local-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Plain oyzu build runs your project's own tools (Cargo, Go, npm, pip, Maven, Gradle) directly on your machine and collects the results into a build bundle. These builders need no Docker. This page covers which builds run natively, how to choose platforms and executors, how to preview a build, and how to split a build into separate jobs. Note: A native build runs with your user account's access to files and the network. It is not a sandbox. Use oyzu build --isolated when you need the container executor.

oyzu build --plan # preview; installs and runs nothing oyzu build # host build with fast checks oyzu build --full # also run tests, lint and format checks oyzu build --platform linux/arm64 # build for one other platform oyzu build --isolated # use the container executor oyzu inspect dist # verify the bundle

Plain oyzu build runs natively when every selected target has a native host build (see the table below). Otherwise it uses the container executor. --isolated (or --image) always uses the container executor. --affected picks its targets first, then follows the same rule. --all-platforms builds every declared platform through the container executor and needs Docker. A failed build never retries with another executor. Running in CI doesn't change the choice. Native output is a runnable binary or package for this machine. Use --isolated when you need the packaging that the container executor produces. The bundle manifest still records each artifact's version: the builder's own version where it has one, otherwise the target's resolved version. When a consumer declares a platform other than the host, the build uses the container executor. For example, a docker/image with platforms: [linux/x86_64] that copies in a Go binary, built on Windows, gets a Linux Go binary built in the container. The container runs on the base execution image, and every tool comes from oyzu.lock there (see Go, Node and Helm). A tool that isn't locked for the platform is refused with the oyzu pin command that adds it.

These builders build on the host. Oyzu installs any missing tool into the shared tool store, then runs the ecosystem's own commands. Project Native build Version chosen when you don't pin one Rust (Cargo) Yes Latest stable Rust that satisfies Cargo rust-version. A rust-toolchain.toml channel or an explicit pin wins. See Rust installation. Node node/app with npm and a dist/ output Yes Latest LTS release that satisfies every engines.node range, else the latest matching stable release. See Node selection. Go go/app: one module, no go.work, exactly one package main Yes The Go minimum from the go.mod go and toolchain lines. See Go version selection. Python with pip and pyproject.toml Yes (wheel) Latest stable CPython that satisfies requires-python. See Python installation. Java Maven reactor (a committed mvnw is used) Yes (jars; tests run in verify) JDK from the declared language level; Maven 3.9 unless the wrapper supplies one. See Java installation. Java Gradle build (a committed gradlew is used) Yes (jars; tests run in build) JDK from the declared language level; Gradle 8 or 9. Go libraries, Go workspaces, several Go binaries; Ant and other Java; uv, Poetry or requirements-only Python; other Node projects No: container executor — When a builder without a native build is selected and Docker is unavailable, the build fails with a message that says so.

oyzu pin is optional for Rust, Go and Node. With no oyzu.lock, the first build resolves the tools, writes oyzu.lock and installs from it. Commit the lock to make later builds repeatable, or delete it to resolve again. Tools a builder detects on its own follow the same rule. For example, a Rust project whose Cargo.lock lists prost-build needs protoc. Its version is your folder pin, else the detection's hint, else the latest stable release in the catalog. The build locks and installs it with the other tools. oyzu pin records the same choice. A detected tool that has no catalog entry or checksum, or that can't be installed, is shown as an attention row and the build continues. Set tools.ignore to silence it. Only a tool you pinned in oyzu.toml fails the build when it can't be verified or installed.

[tools] go = "1.24" wins when it is at least the Go minimum. A module-folder value below the minimum is refused. The build runs go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so only the locked Go compiles and none is downloaded mid-build. --offline adds GOPROXY=off. Compiler errors show their file and line, the exit status is kept, and no earlier binary is republished. The artifact is the executable <target>-<version>. --full adds go test -json with coverage, go vet and gofmt -l. Dependencies use Go's module cache from your Go environment. It isn't separate per project.

One oyzu build can build several native targets, such as a Python wheel and a Node dist/ directory, into one bundle. Oyzu selects the targets you named plus everything they depend on, prepares their tools, and runs one shared task graph. Independent targets run at the same time, up to build.jobs. A depends_on in build.yaml makes the consumer wait for the producer's stages. A failed target blocks the targets that depend on it. Unrelated targets can still finish. Stages within one target run in order, because they share the target's files. Each target builds in its own private workspace. An ordering edge alone copies no files; use materialize to pass artifacts. Required reports must be produced and artifacts collected before a target counts as built. See build tasks. Two targets that would produce executables with the same file name are refused before anything runs. Ecosystem notes: npm runs npm ci and needs a lockfile. Installation is the target's prepare step. It runs before pre_build hooks, is skipped on a full cache hit, and runs again with --no-cache. A failed install blocks the build and publishes nothing. npm lifecycle scripts run as usual. pip uses its own PEP 517 wheel build, including downloading the build backend. CPython is installed as a managed tool and pip is the one bundled with it. The output is a wheel, not a runnable application. Offline, npm runs in offline mode and pip uses --no-index. The build fails if what they need isn't already cached.

Run oyzu build or oyzu build --plan in a nested folder that has its own build.yaml; you don't need --root. A source subfolder uses the nearest build.yaml above it. Repository configuration still applies, but the nested build has its own lock file and outputs. A parent build doesn't include nested builds. See configuration for how configuration is inherited.

oyzu pin --dry-run previews tool requirements and lock changes without installing anything or changing files. oyzu pin writes the lock; conflicts or incomplete inputs fail and leave the lock unchanged. See the lock file. With no oyzu.lock, the first build resolves the tools, writes the lock (it never edits your TOML files) and installs them. You don't need a compiler already installed. An existing lock is never changed by a build. A missing or incompatible entry fails with a request to run oyzu pin. oyzu build --offline never resolves versions or writes a lock. It needs the metadata, archives or installations already cached. Pinning reads files only. It works offline and currently runs from the workspace root. For Rust, discovery reads: rust-toolchain.toml or rust-toolchain, in every form rustup accepts (see Rust toolchain files). Having both files is an error. Cargo rust-version minimums. Declared components, targets and profile. The tools each selected stage needs (rustfmt, Clippy, nextest, cargo-llvm-cov). With no toolchain file, Rust is listed without a version and the build locks the latest stable release. A file with no channel keeps its components and uses your configured or default Rust. A local path toolchain fails unless oyzu.toml selects a release. Node is resolved the same way. For pip wheels, CPython comes from requires-python or .python-version and is installed from Python Build Standalone. uv, Poetry and older Python tools are not installed for you.

Oyzu names the system linker and SDK a Rust toolchain needs, but doesn't install them: Toolchain channel Needs *-windows-gnullvm LLVM-MinGW (UCRT) with Clang linking *-windows-msvc Microsoft Build Tools and the Windows SDK *-windows-gnu A toolchain with the profiler runtime if you need coverage Unqualified, such as 1.95.0 GNU/LLVM or MSVC, listed as alternatives Discovery doesn't run rustup, search PATH or check whether these are installed. The build checks them when it runs (see executor readiness). Requirements of dependency build scripts and toolchain files in parent folders aren't detected.

Two ideas stay separate. The target platform is what an artifact is built for. The executor is where its build steps run: this host, for its own platform; a native cross toolchain on this host; the container executor (--isolated, --all-platforms); a remote pool (--remote). The executor is part of the build's identity. The plan and manifest record it on each target (oyzu.dev/platforms), and cache keys include it. A cross-compiled or container result never stands in for a host build of the same platform, or the reverse.

Write every platform as os/arch[/abi]: linux/x86_64, linux/arm64, darwin/arm64, windows/x86_64, windows/x86_64/msvc. Input also accepts amd64 for x86_64 and aarch64 for arm64, in build.yaml platforms, --platform and --allow-incomplete. Output, records and dist/ folders always use the canonical form. The ABI is optional: gnu or musl on Linux, msvc, gnu or gnullvm on Windows. Without one, the builder picks its default (see Rust). The resolved ABI is recorded in the target's platform. For Rust it is musl for a Linux cross build, msvc on Windows and gnu on a Linux host. Published names (dist/ folders, asset names) include the ABI only when it isn't the OS default (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows). See release asset names. Container engines and registries keep their own spelling (linux/amd64). Note: musl is the default for Linux cross builds. If your code depends on glibc (dlopen, NSS name lookup), declare linux/<arch>/gnu.

Command Platforms built oyzu build The host platform. A target that declares no platforms builds for the host. A target that declares platforms, but not the host, builds the one declared platform this machine can build. With several it asks for --platform; with none it is skipped, with the reason. oyzu build --platform

(repeatable) Exactly those. A target that doesn't declare

is skipped for it. A declared platform that can't be built here fails before anything runs (PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE), as does a run where no target builds anything. --platform linux/arm64/gnu narrows a declared linux/arm64. Native executors build one platform per target per run, so use one --platform per CI job, or add --isolated. oyzu build --all-platforms Every declared platform, through the container executor. One the container executor can't build here fails before anything runs. --platform and --all-platforms can't be combined with each other or with --remote. An invalid platform name is a usage error (exit status 2). A platform-independent target, such as a static site in dist//any/, is built once. When a build sends a platform off the host, or a target declares platforms this run doesn't build, the Plan names each row's platform and shows what builds it. other lists platforms this machine could build with --platform; not here lists the rest, with the reason: ── Plan ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── format lint test build package hello · linux/arm64 skip skip skip run skip other windows/x86_64 · host with --platform linux/x86_64 · cross toolchain (rust-lld) with --platform not here windows/arm64 · missing MSVC arm64 build tools (Visual Studio VC/Tools/MSVC//lib/arm64); --isolated builds it with the container executor darwin/arm64 · needs a macOS runner (Apple SDK and linker); --isolated builds it with the container executor built by hello · linux/arm64 · cross toolchain (rust-lld) Only Rust has a native cross toolchain. Go, Node, Python, Java, .NET and Helm build only for the host natively. For other platforms Plan names the runner they need (needs a Linux runner) and whether --isolated could build them.

By default, a platform builds on the host when it matches, otherwise with a native cross toolchain if the builder has one (or the container executor under --isolated). You can fix the executor per platform in oyzu.toml, per folder and per context: [build.executors] "linux/arm64" = "cross-toolchain" # always cross-compiled, never built on an arm64 host "darwin/arm64" = "host" # only on a macOS arm64 runner [context.release.build.executors] "linux/x86_64" = "container" # releases build it in the container executor Values: host, cross-toolchain, container. A declared executor is the only one used for that platform. Nothing falls back to another. When it isn't available here (no cross linker, the wrong host, container without --isolated, or host/cross-toolchain with --isolated), the platform isn't built and Plan says why. Asking for it explicitly fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE before anything runs. In the release context the host platform counts as asked for, so a release build fails instead of skipping it. Plan, the preview (declaredExecutor) and the CI matrix (executor) show the declaration.

oyzu build --plan --json includes a top-level matrix you can feed to a CI matrix strategy. It has one include entry per declared platform of every selected target, with: platform; runner: os (linux, windows, macos) and arch, the machine that builds it natively; executor: the declared executor, else host; targets: the targets that declare it. The matrix doesn't depend on what the planning machine can build: a target that declares only darwin/arm64 still gets its entry when planned on Linux. unconstrained lists targets that declare no platforms. With --affected <ref>, the matrix holds only affected targets. Each target in the preview also has a platforms record: declared, declaredExecutors, one row per platform (selected, executor, declaredExecutor, reason, refused, runner), and the platform and executor this run would use. jobs: plan: runs-on: ubuntu-latest outputs: matrix: ${{ steps.plan.outputs.matrix }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - id: plan run: echo "matrix=$(oyzu build --plan --json --affected origin/main | jq -c .matrix)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" build: needs: plan strategy: matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix) }} runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner.os == 'macos' && 'macos-15' || matrix.runner.os == 'windows' && 'windows-2025' || 'ubuntu-24.04' }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: oyzu build ${{ join(matrix.targets, ' ') }} --platform ${{ matrix.platform }} Your workflow maps runner to real runner labels, including any arm64 runner. oyzu publish checks that every declared platform was built; see incomplete platform sets. Toolset verification runs are listed separately under .verify. Run them in the platform jobs, or pass --skip-verification to the platform jobs and run each .verify command in its own job. See fanning runs out in CI.
documents.s: A CI matrix from the plan

documents.t: oyzu build --plan shows what a build would do without doing it. It chooses native or container execution exactly as a build would. --isolated, --all-platforms, named targets, profiles and --full mean the same as in a build. You don't need Cargo or Docker installed to run it. The preview: reads configuration and project files, and shows each target's discovery decisions, stages (run or skipped), task order and tool requirements; doesn't install tools, download packages, run build tools or scripts, create a lock, or write a bundle; with --affected, reads local Git history and hashes local files, with no network access or writes. Some details are only known once a real build prepares: whether tools are installed, exact commands, artifact names and report paths. The preview marks these as unresolved. A stage marked run means configuration asks for it, not that its prerequisites will pass. A successful preview doesn't mean the build will succeed.

The Plan table shows targets by stage, with run, skip or - cells and one footnote per skip reason. A single target built for several platforms shows one row per platform. Above twelve rows, targets with identical stages share a counted row; -v lists every target. See result output. When every target needs the same tool, the requirements table shows "all N targets". --json still lists every target. Color follows your terminal (CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 forces it, NO_COLOR turns it off). --json returns a build-preview record with resolved: false, the selection, targets (each with a discovery map of role to selected and reason), tasks, requirements, unresolved details, effect flags and timings. The preview is not the executable plan. A real build writes that to dist/plan.json.

timings reports where the preview spent its time, in milliseconds: totalMs and phases, in this order: Phase What it measures discovery Configuration and target discovery. selection Selection, variants, task graph and requirements. source Listing the working tree from file metadata. Absent when analysis is off or fails. analysis Static analysis, with targets (one entry per target), finishMs and rulesMs. Absent when analysis is off or fails. planning Stage and task listing. Timings describe one run and aren't part of the analysis record.

oyzu build --remote --plan previews what oyzu build --remote would run on a platform pool. It doesn't contact the platform and needs no token. It uses the pool's settings: isolated execution, full checks and the normal platform selection. --remote doesn't imply --all-platforms. Named targets and --affected <base> work as in the remote run. --affected compares with the merge base of <base> and HEAD. The record's execution is remote. The preview reads your working tree, so it includes uncommitted changes, which a remote run never sends. --isolated, --all-platforms, --image, --check and --download can't be combined with --remote. Every preview target carries these placement facts: Field Meaning platform The artifact platform: from the target's variant, otherwise decided by the executor (unresolved until executor selection). platformSource variant, executor or host (a native host target). executionPlatform The platform the executor must run on, or null when any will do. A Rust cross-compile in the container runs on linux/x86_64 whatever it targets. A Docker image needs its own platform when its final stage uses RUN. needsDaemon, daemonReason Whether the work needs a Docker engine, and why. false for native host targets, for Node and supported external Go targets that can use the daemonless sandbox, and for RUN-free image assembly. Selected quality checks or hooks can make an image target need Docker. isolation What the executor must provide: host, crun (Linux with unprivileged user namespaces, or Docker), in-process (Oyzu's own image assembly) or docker. id, logicalTarget, variant The concrete target ID, its logical name, and its variant axes. Use the returned id; don't construct one. dependsOnTargets The concrete targets this one depends on. sliceable Whether another slice could reuse this target's results. false means build it in the consumer's slice. sliceReason, sliceDetail Why it isn't sliceable, or null: ALWAYS_RUN_HOOK, UNCACHED_TASK, UNSCOPED_INPUTS, UNBOUNDED_OUTPUTS, SECRET_ENVIRONMENT, CACHE_DISABLED, SOURCE_PROJECTION. platforms How each platform is built here; see a CI matrix from the plan. A target isn't sliceable when it has a hook (hooks always run), an authored task without cache = true and declared outputs, inputs outside its folder, stages with unbounded outputs, a secret environment, local caching turned off, or an image builder (its source isn't cached). A build can still fail to reuse a sliceable target, for example when the producer failed. The top-level placement object says which facts can change. Each target's platform, executionPlatform and needsDaemon are final, as are tool requirements whose status is discovered. The target list, task graph, stages and unsupported requirements can grow when a real build discovers more targets. OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 doesn't change the preview.

oyzu build --no-docker, or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1, is for executors with no Docker engine, such as a Kubernetes pool. Oyzu then runs no Docker command at all. Any value other than empty or 0 turns it on. Before preparing anything, the build works out the same placement as --plan. If any selected target has needsDaemon: true, it stops with exit status 3 and runs nothing: oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --json {"error":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON: cli need a Docker engine, which this executor does not provide (--no-docker); nothing was run","reason":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON","targets":["cli"],"exitCode":3} Exit status 3 means "wrong kind of executor", so a runner can tell it from a failed build (1) or a refused command (2) and requeue the job on a pool with Docker. What can still build without Docker: native host targets; Node targets and supported external go/app targets, in the daemonless sandbox; a RUN-free Dockerfile with FROM scratch or a digest-pinned base, with --isolated --no-docker (see Docker image assembly). --full adds Dockerfile lint and format checks, which need Docker, so the build refuses rather than skipping them. --no-docker can't be combined with --remote.

On Linux, the isolated steps of a Node target (npm, pnpm or Yarn) can run under crun, a rootless container runtime, instead of docker run. Each step gets the same sandbox as under Docker: no network, a read-only image root, no capabilities, no-new-privileges, a seccomp filter, Docker's masked /proc paths, the same mounts and tmpfs sizes, inside a user namespace that maps the workspace owner to itself. Each image's root filesystem is unpacked once per digest and shared by every build on the host. A root process gives unpacked files their archived owners. In a user namespace that does not map IDs 0–65535 (for example a planner sandboxed with unshare --user --map-current-user), a file whose archived owner is unmapped keeps the unpacking process's owner, as it would for a non-root process, and each step runs with only the workspace owner mapped, as for a non-root user. Such a root keeps its own copy of each image root rather than sharing the full-range one. Both backends produce the same cache keys and outputs, so a result cached by one serves the other. Unchanged npm builds can reuse earlier dependency downloads; see captured npm acquisition. Note: External Go plugin builds can also use crun on Linux x86-64. This is experimental. It needs a single application module, a packaged plugin, a locked Go and a compatible Linux image. Commit the full oyzu.lock and build with --frozen; add --offline once everything is cached. Built-in Go builds don't use crun.

build.isolation Behavior auto (default) Docker when an engine answers, otherwise crun. docker Always Docker. crun crun for eligible targets, even when Docker is present. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun for eligible targets whatever the setting says. oyzu install downloads a pinned crun release (1.24), checks its SHA-256 and keeps it in your user data folder. Set OYZU_CRUN to use a crun the executor already has. Images come from their digest-pinned published source, or from a running local Docker engine. A tag-only local image with no engine running fails before anything runs. crun runs without its own cgroup, so the executor pool's limits apply instead of per-step memory and CPU limits. Each action in the manifest records its sandbox in sandbox: backend (docker or crun), the crun runtime version, and resourceLimits (cgroup or pool).

Before running anything, a build that uses crun checks that crun works and that the host lets an unprivileged process create user, mount, network and PID namespaces. If not, it stops with NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES (exit status 3) and names the cause, such as kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1, a seccomp profile that blocks unshare, or cgroups in hybrid mode. Oyzu never runs the step without the sandbox. {"code":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES","error":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES: the daemonless sandbox (crun) cannot run on this host: cgroups are mounted in hybrid mode, which crun does not support; nothing was run","exitCode":3,"nextStep":"Run on a Linux executor that allows unprivileged user namespaces and has crun, or on one with a Docker daemon.","reason":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES"}

You can split a build into jobs that follow the target graph, each reusing what earlier jobs built. Each job builds a slice: the targets you name. Every other target it needs must come from a cache; it is never built. oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://registry.example.com/acme/web/ci web Input Meaning Target arguments One or more logical target names or concrete targets[].id values from the preview. A logical name selects variants as a normal isolated build does. A concrete ID builds exactly that variant, even for a non-host platform. --slice Build only the named targets (at least one). Every other target they need is looked up in the local cache and remote caches. A missing result fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED. Slices use the container executor. With --plan it prints the isolated preview of the slice. --slice-plan <target-id> Repeat once for every concrete ID in the original preview, including targets built in other slices. Pass the same set to every slice and retry. It lets a miss report whether the producer was in the original plan (inPlan). --handoff <oci-url> An OCI repository (oci://host/path, the same form as cache.remote). It is read first for upstream results, then cache.ciRemote and cache.remote, and every result this slice builds is written to it. It uses the same credential as a remote cache (OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or the job's ID token). An unusable URL is refused (exit 2) before anything runs. Plugin-built targets are handed off like any other: their results go to the --handoff repository, and their keys bind the plugin identity (action cache). cache.ciRemote and cache.remote are not read or written for them, so pass --handoff (or share one local cache) for a later slice to find them. Slices always run on the captured path. A plugin target that only builds on the native host lane is refused there with PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED; build it in a whole build instead. --slice can't be combined with --remote, --affected, --check, --no-cache or --verify-contract. It needs an active action cache when any upstream target isn't named. With cache.local = false, naming every target lets the slice run without reuse. With --no-docker, the same Docker check as an ordinary build applies. A slice builds the optimized profile, because its results leave the machine. Every upstream target's dependencies are still prepared, because its cache keys include them. Slices don't change cache keys. Per-target slices of a commit produce the same keys and artifact digests as one whole build. A producer that built something different shows up as a miss, never as a wrong reuse. A handoff hit is verified like any remote cache hit.
documents.s: Building a slice of a split run

documents.t: Reason Exit Raised when UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED 4 A result of a target the slice doesn't build wasn't found in any cache. Everything that needs it is blocked. HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED 5 A result of a named target couldn't be written to the handoff repository. The build fails even when every action succeeded, because later jobs would miss. Exit status 1 is a failed build, 2 a refused command and 3 a missing executor capability (NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON, NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES). When both 4 and 5 apply, UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED wins. A failed slice prints one JSON line last on stderr, in human and --json mode, so an executor that keeps only the tail of the log can act on it: {"action":"app:package","error":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED: app:package of upstream target app (key sha256:…) is not in the local cache or oci://registry.example.com/acme/web/ci; a slice reuses upstream targets and never builds them","exitCode":4,"inPlan":true,"key":"sha256:…","reason":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED","repositories":[{"location":"oci://registry.example.com/acme/web/ci","status":"active"}],"target":"app","why":null}

The build record (dist/manifest.json, printed by --json) carries an oyzu.dev/slice extension: Field Meaning targets The concrete targets this slice built. upstream The other targets it reused. handoff The --handoff location, or null. written Each result written to the handoff repository: target, action, key and outcome (pushed; converged when an identical entry was already there; conflicts when a different entry held the key and was kept). misses Each upstream result not found: target, action, key, repositories (each remote asked, active or unavailable), inPlan, and why when it was never looked up (for example a task without declared outputs, which is never cached). notWritten Each result that didn't reach the handoff repository: target, action, key, repository and status. failure null, or the first miss (exit 4), else the first unwritten result (exit 5). inPlan: false means the missing producer wasn't in the original preview, for example a dependency added since. inPlan: true means an expected producer didn't leave a reusable result. Both exit 4, and neither lets the slice build the producer. The action cache summary gains a handoff section beside ciRemote and remote.

Name a sliceable: false upstream together with its consumer, for example oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://localhost:5000/demo/ci generate web. If several consumers need it, keep them in one slice. An unnamed unreusable upstream fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED and its why.

Before compiling, a native Rust build runs a small Cargo compile-and-link check. It uses your Cargo linker settings and Rust flags, and asks for coverage instrumentation when tests are selected. Its temporary files are removed afterward. A failure reports EXECUTOR_PREREQUISITE_UNAVAILABLE with the cause. Install or fix the toolchain, linker or SDK and rerun. Oyzu doesn't install OS components. oyzu run runs the same check before a Rust task that compiles or links (cargo build, test, install, check, clippy, doc, run, rustc). Tasks like cargo fetch skip it. Without a linker, the task fails in under a second with guidance. For windows-gnullvm, the guidance is to put LLVM-MinGW's bin folder on PATH. Ready means the check passed. It doesn't check every library that dependency build scripts need. oyzu pin and discovery don't run this check; they report availability as not checked.

A plain local build runs compilation and checks set to required. --full, the pr, ci and release contexts, or the CI profile also run tests (with JUnit, coverage and doctests), Clippy and a read-only format check, except checks set to off. See check levels. Required checks, hooks and task prerequisites always run. Binaries are collected only after the selected stages succeed. oyzu run test, oyzu run lint and oyzu run format-check run those tasks on their own. Replacing the native build task isn't supported yet and is refused with a message. Quality stages need their tools: rustfmt, Clippy, and for tests nextest, cargo-llvm-cov and the compiler's LLVM tools and profiler runtime. With a pinned Rust, the build installs nextest and cargo-llvm-cov automatically when tests are selected. See Rust test reports. On Windows, test coverage needs MSVC or windows-gnullvm (LLVM-MinGW UCRT). The windows-gnu toolchain lacks profiler_builtins, so coverage fails there. The native path builds the development profile unless the build is optimized: --optimized, build.optimized = true, or a build whose artifacts leave the machine (a slice, a shared remote cache write, a packaging target, the release context). Optimized Rust builds run cargo build --release. Tests keep Cargo's test profile. See optimized builds.

Native Rust builds give artifacts the same inferred version as container builds. Local fast development builds keep the version from Cargo.toml when compiling, so editing one crate doesn't force every workspace member to recompile. CARGO_PKG_VERSION is the declared version; the version record shows it as compiledVersion beside the artifact's inferred version. Don't assume they're equal; read the build record. Everything else (full or CI builds, explicit version strategies, optimized, handed-off, remotely cached, packaged and release builds) compiles with the inferred version, so CARGO_PKG_VERSION matches the artifact version. Cache keys include the compiled version, so a local result never satisfies a version-stamped build. Oyzu writes versions into a private copy of the manifests; your Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock stay unchanged. See version inference.

Before running builder commands, a native build installs any missing tool from your pins into the shared user store. It uses the same download, checksum and policy checks as oyzu install. A build never changes pinned versions. Run oyzu pin for missing or stale entries. --offline forbids downloads and needs the installers' cached inputs. An installation error stops the build before compiling. A denied or damaged tool is never replaced with an unverified one from PATH. System linkers and SDKs are not installed. See helper installation.

The Rust builder first tries Cargo metadata offline. If something is missing and the build is online, it runs cargo fetch --locked with live output, then continues offline. Cargo handles downloads, checksums and its own cache using your Cargo configuration, credentials and network settings. Oyzu doesn't rewrite Cargo.lock. Compilation always runs offline. --offline never fetches. It reports missing inputs and suggests an online build or a manifest fix. Failures keep a category and recovery hint even when details that might contain credentials are withheld.

A native build can include docker/image targets, which run in a BuildKit worker (see image workers). Oyzu watches both the docker exec client and the worker: Code Meaning BUILDKIT_BUILDCTL_FAILED The client exited with a nonzero status. BUILDKIT_WORKER_UNAVAILABLE The worker stopped, was killed for running out of memory, or stopped answering. The container and daemon are checked every five seconds. A stopped or OOM-killed container fails at once; probe failures need three in a row. Diagnostics keep the buildctl exit code, the container exit and the memory limit. Exit 137 alone is reported as a possible OOM or external kill. Restore the worker or give it more memory, then retry. Failed actions publish no artifacts.

Native Rust builds keep Cargo's compiler state under .oyzu/native/rust/<host>/ in your project, so repeated builds stay incremental. Oyzu keeps Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock modification times unchanged when their contents didn't change, so Cargo doesn't rebuild for nothing. This also applies with --no-cache, which turns off Oyzu's action cache but keeps compiler caches.

After each build, Oyzu trims those compiler caches to a size budget: [cache] nativeMaxMiB = 8192 Setting Values Default Meaning cache.nativeMaxMiB 1–1048576 8192 (8 GiB) Total size kept across the host's Rust compiler caches. Works the same online and offline. Separate from remote cache settings. Progress shows the measured size and anything removed. With --json, these messages go to stderr.

When the caches are over budget: Oyzu runs cargo clean --workspace --offline on them, keeping compiled registry dependencies if that is enough. If still over budget, it removes whole cache folders with cargo clean, in this order: an old separate doctest target, the coverage target, the build target. Under budget, nothing is removed. Oyzu adds the standard CACHEDIR.TAG file to each cache folder, because Cargo won't clean a folder without one. A budget smaller than your working set saves disk space but can cause a full recompile on every build.

It limits what is kept after a build, not peak disk use. A crash or full disk can leave oversized caches until the next build. If cleanup fails at the end of a build, you get NATIVE_CACHE_RETENTION_FAILED but the build result stands. The next build retries before it starts, and a failure there stops it. Symlinked or redirected cache folders (including Windows reparse points) are refused. Use a normal folder. Only the Rust caches under .oyzu/native count. Installed tools, downloads, .oyzu/bin, dist, Cargo's own target folder and oyzu run tasks aren't touched.

Successful binaries go to dist/<target>/<platform>/ (for example dist/cli/windows/x86_64/; see the bundle layout) with their usual names, and are also linked at .oyzu/bin/<name>[.exe]. Outputs labels each binary development or optimized. Each is checked to be an executable for the host before it is collected. The bundle keeps the manifest, plan, reports and action logs. They record that the build ran on the host, the source it saw and the tools it used. Rust state lives in .oyzu/native/rust/<host>/: target for compilation and tests for test and coverage builds. Cargo decides what to rebuild. The previous bundle's artifacts move to history on every build, successful or not. Other files in dist are left alone. See bundle finalization and recovery. A file in dist that no bundle owns causes a collision error instead of being overwritten. A failed build exits nonzero and leaves .oyzu/bin at the last successful build. On Windows, the previous executable is renamed before the new one takes its place, so a running program isn't overwritten. An old copy that can't be deleted yet may stay as a hidden file. The source Oyzu records is hashed from your working tree with the usual source exclusions. Native builds read your checkout directly; they don't freeze a copy.

Output starts with Building <folder> (or Planning for --plan), the platform, local or isolated execution, and fast or full mode. Then it follows Preflight → Build → summary. Preflight covers configuration, discovery, tool preparation, dependency metadata and planning. Each tool row shows the tool, the requested version and its status: downloaded and installed, then verified, or reused and verified. External SDKs and linkers show as not checked until native tools run. Formatting, lint and test tools are hidden in fast builds unless those stages run. Press p for more environment and source detail, and d for detailed logs on small terminals. Running tools and subprocesses show their last eight output lines on capable terminals. Success collapses them; failure keeps them. Terminal behavior: auto and plain output modes print a linear log that keeps your scrollback. --output interactive opens a dashboard instead. ui.color=auto colors terminal output unless NO_COLOR is set; always also colors redirected output; never turns color off. A terminal counts as capable when TERM isn't dumb and, on Windows, when the console accepts virtual terminal sequences. --json emits a structured heading event on stderr; -q hides it. See build logging.

oyzu build --store <path> uses the same store as oyzu install --store <path>. The default is the shared user store. A relative path resolves against the current folder (or --root). The store is used for native installs and container tool preparation. It never changes pins, checks or image policy. A missing or broken tool in that store doesn't fall back to another store. Use the same --store on install, build and tool inspection commands, especially with --offline.

Native execution has your user account's access. Cargo's offline mode doesn't stop a build script from using the network. A local build, even with --isolated, can't grant production publication rights. --require-release refuses the build unless it is an authenticated release-candidate or release tag build; ordinary local tags and --context release don't count. See release staging. Native builds are tested on Windows and Linux (x86-64). macOS isn't supported yet.

These notes are for building the oyzu CLI itself from a source checkout. Build with cargo build --locked --release --bins, then copy target/release/oyzu[.exe] and target/release/oyzu-shim[.exe] together into a folder on your PATH outside the checkout. Check the build succeeded before copying, and keep a backup of the previous version. On Windows, updating your user PATH doesn't change terminals that are already open. Update the current PowerShell session: $fallbackBin = 'C:\path\to\oyzu-bootstrap\bin' $env:Path = "$fallbackBin;$env:Path" oyzu --version The repository adds ./.oyzu/bin to PATH through [env] _.path. After shell activation (in PowerShell 7.5+: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression), oyzu build puts the freshly built CLI first on your PATH inside the project. The Windows task flow uses a pinned MSVC toolchain, which needs Visual Studio Build Tools (the C++ workload) installed first. Then run oyzu pin, oyzu install and oyzu run install. If an older oyzu.lock fails with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS, delete it and run oyzu pin and oyzu install again. Keep machine-specific linker and CMake paths in an ignored oyzu.local.toml under [env].

oyzu run bootstrap rebuilds the CLI from the checkout and installs it, so the oyzu you type never lags the source. Run it from the checkout, on Windows or Linux: oyzu run bootstrap # development build oyzu run bootstrap -- --optimized # optimized build oyzu run bootstrap -- --dest ~/bin # install into this folder instead oyzu run bootstrap -- --linux <file> # also install the Linux engine for --isolated It first builds the rust/app and node/app plugins from the checkout into .oyzu/bin, since oyzu build cli needs them. If neither your user nor your machine configuration binds both plugins, it creates (or reuses) the checkout's own bootstrap file, .oyzu/bootstrap/config.toml, and uses it for this run only, as tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh does (see Repository source bootstrap). It then prints how to make other terminals see the bindings: set OYZU_USER_CONFIG to that file, or bind both plugins with oyzu config set --global plugins.development.<reference> <path>. It never changes your own configuration. If you have a user configuration file that binds neither plugin, it stops and prints those two commands. It runs oyzu build cli, then installs oyzu and oyzu-shim together into the checkout's .oyzu/bin and into the folder holding the first oyzu on your PATH outside the checkout (a link is followed to the real folder). With no such oyzu, it installs into the install script's folder (~/.oyzu/bin, or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\bin on Windows) and runs oyzu shell install so the folder stays first on PATH. Open a new terminal afterwards. Each replaced file is renamed to NAME.previous first, which works while the old oyzu is running; one backup is kept. If the replacement fails, the old file is put back. It then runs oyzu install --frozen in the checkout and prints the installed path and oyzu --version. Locked plugin selections change only with oyzu plugins update. Isolated builds run a Linux oyzu built from the same source. On Linux the new oyzu is its own. On Windows and macOS, pass the Linux oyzu built from the same checkout with --linux <file> (repeat it for each architecture): the bootstrap runs oyzu engine install --linux with it. Without it, the bootstrap says that --isolated has no Linux engine and still installs oyzu. It doesn't build the Linux oyzu itself yet: cross-compiling it on Windows or macOS fails, because a dependency compiles C and the host has no Linux C compiler. Needs Node.js on PATH. If your installed oyzu is too old to read this repository's configuration (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE), run tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh (Git Bash on Windows) and then .oyzu/bin/oyzu run bootstrap.
documents.s: Refreshing the oyzu on your PATH

documents.t: Rust projects get an install task automatically. To update your installed CLI from the checkout: oyzu run install -- --bins --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" This runs cargo install, not the full build checks. It builds the release profile; add --debug after -- for a development build. CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT also sets the destination. On Windows with an explicit root, Oyzu installs into a staging folder first, so your current CLI keeps working while Cargo compiles. Only after Cargo succeeds are the files replaced, keeping one .NAME.previous backup each. Cancelling or a failed install leaves the installed CLI unchanged. A killed process may leave a .oyzu-install-* staging folder; don't remove one that belongs to a running install. Files are replaced one at a time, not atomically. If replacement fails, check the named file and its backup, close programs still using the old copy, and retry. If your installed CLI is too old to run this, use Cargo directly with the provisioned toolchain: cargo install --path . --bins --locked --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" oyzu run fetch downloads Cargo dependencies, oyzu run install installs project executables, and oyzu install installs development tools.
documents.s: Updating this repository's bootstrap with Cargo

documents.t: Build tasks for stages, checks and tasks, and affected builds. Build bundles for the dist/ layout, and action cache for reuse. Rust, Go and Node applications for builder details. Target workspaces for passing artifacts between targets.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/maven.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu detects a pom.xml without any build YAML and treats a Maven reactor as one target. Maven still owns inheritance, active profiles, module order, dependency resolution and the lifecycle. Oyzu captures the inputs, assigns snapshot versions, runs the build in isolation and collects reports. The reactor example includes unit and integration test variations. Note: The Maven builder is experimental and runs captured builds on Linux (Docker required). It is supplied by the oyzu-plugin-maven plugin (profile java/maven); see plugin catalog. It doesn't publish, sign or promote anything.

oyzu -C examples/builds/java-maven-reactor/project run list oyzu -C examples/builds/java-maven-reactor/project build Captured builds need Docker and the base execution image. Oyzu pulls the image when it's missing. The JDK and, for a project without a Maven wrapper, Maven itself are restored from oyzu.lock. Development tasks use your provisioned Maven or the project's Maven wrapper. oyzu run list doesn't run Maven. Task Runs Notes install (implicit) Dependency preparation build (implicit) mvn -B verify Checks bound to verify run under Maven. test (implicit) mvn -B test The test task isn't repeated during a build. The shared Java quality defaults add lint and read-only formatting checks. You can replace them with your own tasks.

The base image has no JDK or Maven. Both come from the lock. A project without a locked JDK stops with the oyzu pin command that fixes it. The Maven extension and the Oyzu worker come with the Maven plugin and the CLI, so no image supplies them. A custom --image maven=<image> only has to meet the bring-your-own contract. Isolated Maven builds on the base execution image are not supported yet.

The execution image has no JDK. Your project selects one, through [tools] java or the root POM's declared level (see how versions are chosen), and build preflight locks it. The container uses it. Preparation: Reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) Temurin archive recorded in oyzu.lock. Downloads it through the tool broker, unless a copy in your user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256. Verifies it. Restores it read-only at /scratch/jdktool. Then JAVA_HOME and the front of PATH point at it for preparation and every build action, so Maven and the compiler run on it. The plan records the archive, so a different JDK changes the action identity. A selected JDK older than 17 is refused with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION. Maven and Oyzu's Java integration in the container need JDK 17. JDK 17 and newer can compile for older levels with --release. An oyzu.lock without a JDK entry stops the build with the oyzu pin command that fixes it.

Preparation captures the POMs and evaluates the reactor inside the container. Version inference combines native versions with scoped Git tags and relevant commit changes, and the Maven versions plugin applies each module's version, and local reactor references, in private copies of the POMs. Your checkout is unchanged. Supported packaging: pom, jar and war. Other types fail. Outputs keep their native final names, and the bundle records the planned snapshot versions.

Oyzu reads the Maven model first, decides each module's version, and freezes the result in version-plan.json. The final coordinates must match those decisions. If the facts change or the projection fails, the build stops. Maven evaluates version expressions. Oyzu never interprets POM expressions itself. A scoped tag uses the module's artifact ID when it is unique. A root tag doesn't coordinate a whole reactor. The reactor graph supplies each module's local upstream modules, including reactor parents. A library change therefore affects its consumers without advancing unrelated modules. Shared root inputs affect every module. A snapshot version never authorizes publishing. For a module with no version element of its own, preparation first writes the version Maven resolved into the private POM, so the versions plugin can set it independently of the parent. This may normalize the private POM's formatting. The POM in your checkout is never rewritten.

Maven downloads through a local mirror backed by Oyzu's scoped Maven Central broker. Upstream requests happen during acquisition. The captured repository is then copied into a private workspace for the offline build. Custom or private repositories and corporate credentials are not supported. The only other public source is an administrator-approved snapshot repository. There is no Maven lockfile. The prepared repository records what was actually captured, which doesn't guarantee that a later download resolves identically. Maven resolves parent dependency management, BOMs and conflicts first. Dependencies on other reactor modules are not fetched, so preparation needs no prebuilt JARs and doesn't compile or test. project-dependencies.xml in the prepared tree lists the external coordinates that were fetched. Plugin and go-offline downloads may add more versions to the repository, so it is not a minimal repository or a complete dependency report. Missing required bytes fail preparation, before any plan is frozen. Transient download failures are retried within limits (acquisition transport). A failed download blocks the build.

One offline lifecycle runs verify and JaCoCo reporting. Your project's JaCoCo version and prepare-agent execution take precedence, including inherited configuration, phase, skip settings and property names. Oyzu adds an initialize preparation only when the project declares none. Inherited pluginManagement version, configuration and executions are respected. JaCoCo 0.8.13 is used when nothing manages a version. Preparation fetches every effective JaCoCo plugin version, because go-offline alone can leave one module's plugin dependencies incomplete in a reactor with mixed versions. If you disabled preparation, it stays disabled and no agent is added. After a failed lifecycle, Oyzu still tries to produce the coverage report without rerunning tests, and keeps the failure.

Required reports, logs and artifacts, with their digests, are listed in dist/manifest.json. A failed check, or an invalid or missing required report, blocks artifact collection. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's integrity. It doesn't say whether a build may be released.

After acquisition, Oyzu asks Maven for the effective verify plan and records the report directories of the bound Surefire test and Failsafe integration-test goals. Defaults, inherited and execution-specific configuration, and paths with spaces all follow Maven.

If a Surefire or Failsafe argLine is a literal string, Oyzu prefixes it with @{argLine} in the private model. The JaCoCo agent can then add its flags while your JVM flags and execution-specific overrides stay in place. Your POM is unchanged. Where Oyzu adds this, a missing default property keeps its native user or system value or is set empty. Existing values are never replaced. Property expressions, custom JaCoCo property names and non-forking tests keep Maven's behavior, and Oyzu can't promise coverage for them. Missing coverage still fails the required report check.

Before the run, Oyzu removes old TEST-*.xml files from the declared directories in the private workspace. After the lifecycle it copies the XML unchanged into .oyzu-maven/reports/<reactor-index>/, using hashes of the source path to avoid name collisions. Every XML file is validated and its results recorded. Duplicate directories are collected once. A Surefire or Failsafe directory can be empty. A module with only integration tests doesn't need unit-test XML. A module with test sources needs at least one JUnit file across both directories, plus a JaCoCo report. If tests are skipped or reporting is off and no XML exists, the check fails. Malformed XML fails too. If a custom reporter suppresses some output, Oyzu can't tell which engine's files are missing. It never invents a passing report. Limits: Report paths must stay inside the captured workspace, outside the reserved .oyzu-maven folder, and not be redirected. Different modules need different report directories. Shared paths fail planning rather than credit the same tests to several modules. One XML file can be up to 16 MiB, and one module's reports up to 64 MiB. If a test fails, its XML and any coverage are kept and no artifacts are produced. Fix the test, the report configuration or the missing evidence, and rebuild. Reports from both engines are combined. Use the report records in the manifest, not assumed Surefire paths. JaCoCo reports are read from target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml under the module's build directory. Custom coverage destinations, aggregate reactor coverage and test source roots added only during the lifecycle aren't supported yet.

oyzu run test writes a test-only bundle to dist/. Each module with test sources gets named JUnit and JaCoCo reports, and oyzu inspect dist checks them. The implicit mvn -B test command (or the wrapper equivalent) is reported automatically, with no configuration. Qualified task names and hooks work as in the shared task engine. Custom task replacements keep their commands and must produce the required reports. Extra forwarded arguments and other lifecycle selections aren't supported for this automatic reporting.

Maven 3.9.11, a JDK 17 with java, javac and jar, and your project's plugins and test dependencies, including JaCoCo 0.8.13. MAVEN_HOME pointing at Maven and JAVA_HOME at the JDK, or the JDK executables on PATH. A wrapper must already have its distribution installed. Oyzu doesn't install wrapper distributions. Your Maven settings and environment apply. Oyzu runs Maven offline. A missing plugin or dependency fails instead of going online.

After task checks, a temporary Oyzu extension reads the effective reactor and the test plan in a dedicated Maven process, which exits before validate bindings or the default lifecycle run. Maven can load extensions while it builds its model, so this is ordinary execution on your machine. It is not a sandbox. oyzu run list stays static and doesn't run Maven. Captured builds look at the wider verify plan, which includes Failsafe integration tests. The run then clears old XML in the declared test directories and old JaCoCo execution and XML files, and runs prepare-agent, test and report. After a test failure it still tries to generate reports without rerunning tests. Native XML suites are wrapped into one JUnit document per module, and JaCoCo XML is copied to fresh private paths. Reports are validated and the bundle is finished after post hooks run. Empty suites and missing outputs never get invented passing reports. Limits: Direct tests don't run verify, package snapshots, run quality checks or run integration-only Failsafe suites. Use oyzu build for that. Missing tests or reports, failed tests and unmet coverage constraints fail the command and keep the current evidence. See direct tests for output handling and provenance. Custom JaCoCo destinations and aggregate reactor coverage aren't supported.

Captured preparation also fetches the dependencies declared on build plugins in Maven's effective model, in addition to dependency:go-offline. Oyzu gets the coordinates from the model and downloads them through the broker. It doesn't run the plugin to discover them. System-scoped plugin dependencies aren't supported. A dependency that a plugin chooses only while it runs is not found and can fail the offline build. Oyzu doesn't retry online. Spotless's Eclipse-based formatter steps are one such case: they download Eclipse P2 bundles from download.eclipse.org and fail with java.net.UnknownHostException. They aren't supported (Spotless Eclipse P2 artifacts). For private repositories, use the optional Maven session endpoint. Without it, downloads come from Maven Central. Ordinary JAR plugin dependencies are supported. A plugin's overridden or excluded dependency graph may fetch more than needed, and plugin dependencies produced by the reactor itself aren't supported.

Some plugins download an artifact named in their own configuration while they run. Oyzu fetches these ahead of time for a short list of known plugin parameters, read from Maven's effective model after property expansion: Plugin Parameter Requested type org.codehaus.mojo:animal-sniffer-maven-plugin signature signature com.github.siom79.japicmp:japicmp-maven-plugin oldVersion/dependency Configured type, default jar Both plugin-level and execution-level configuration are read. Animal Sniffer accepts the structured form and the groupId:artifactId:version[:classifier] shorthand: <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>animal-sniffer-maven-plugin</artifactId> <executions> <execution> <goals><goal>check</goal></goals> <configuration> <signature> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo.signature</groupId> <artifactId>java15</artifactId> <version>1.0</version> </signature> </configuration> </execution> </executions> </plugin> For japicmp, give an explicit old-version dependency inside the plugin's or execution's <configuration>: <oldVersion> <dependency> <groupId>org.jsoup</groupId> <artifactId>jsoup</artifactId> <version>1.23.2</version> <type>jar</type> </dependency> </oldVersion> An optional classifier and the artifact type are kept. A missing type means jar. Maven's artifact handler supplies a missing classifier (test-jar maps to jar:tests). An explicit classifier wins. The old artifact is fetched before the offline run so japicmp can compare it with the new one. A successful build alone doesn't prove the comparison happened: check japicmp's output for a warning that the old version was unavailable. File-based versions, newVersion, version ranges and versions japicmp computes aren't supported. The fetched signature file or old JAR is listed in the dependency snapshot's package inventory. A coordinate with a missing field, or an expression Maven didn't resolve, fails preparation and names the plugin. Fix the POM or its properties and rebuild. Other plugins, and parameters set only on the command line or computed by plugin code, aren't found and can fail the offline build.

Some projects inherit a parent that exists only as a snapshot. For example, jackson-core has a -SNAPSHOT jackson-base parent published to the Sonatype Central Portal snapshot repository and declared in the project's own <repositories>. Captured builds send every repository through one mirror to Maven Central, which serves no snapshots, so by default such a build fails preparation. Setting Values Default Meaning maven.snapshotRepositories A set of HTTPS repository base URLs ending in / Empty (off) The snapshot repositories Oyzu may use. Only corporate policy or the protected local admin-settings.json can set it. Project, local, user, machine and invocation configuration can't enable or widen it. For example, inside the settings object of admin-settings.json: "maven.snapshotRepositories": { "locked": true, "value": ["https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/"] } When the set isn't empty: Each URL becomes its own download source, maven-snapshots-<n>, numbered in sorted URL order. A URL with credentials, a query or a fragment, a plain HTTP URL, or one without a trailing / fails preparation. Admitted repositories can't carry credentials. The mirror and the repository identity stay the same, so the offline build reads snapshots from the captured repository exactly as it reads releases. Only snapshot version paths (group/.../artifact/<version>-SNAPSHOT/...) go to the approved repositories, which are tried in order until one returns the file. Every other path keeps the Central (or session-approved) route. The approved repositories, not the URLs your project declares, serve every snapshot. Maven only asks for snapshots when a declared repository enables them, so your project still declares its snapshot repository, as jackson-core does. The mirror replaces its URL. Each captured .pom, .jar, .module or .signature file under a snapshot version directory is listed in the dependency snapshot's package inventory with the maven-snapshots-<n> source that served it. The approved repositories are listed under extensions."oyzu.dev/maven".snapshotRepositories. Acquisition fails if one snapshot directory was served by two repositories. Release builds never use snapshot inputs. If any snapshot input was captured and any module's version decision isn't a development snapshot, or is production eligible, preparation fails with MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_RELEASE, even with the setting on. Today every captured build is a development snapshot build. A build without snapshot inputs is unaffected by the setting. Code or message Cause Fix Maven's "could not find artifact" error naming the snapshot The setting is off, and a snapshot parent or dependency can't be fetched Ask an administrator to admit its repository, or depend on a released version MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_REPOSITORY A captured snapshot package wasn't served by an approved repository.
