This applies whether or not the setting is on, so a snapshot served by a session-approved repository is refused too. The error names the file. Follow the approved-repository rules above MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_RELEASE A snapshot input was captured and a version decision isn't a development snapshot, or is production eligible The setting doesn't override this. Release builds never use snapshot inputs. CONFIG_SCOPE A project file sets maven.snapshotRepositories Remove it from the project file. Only corporate policy or the protected local admin-settings.json can set it.

Some POMs use os-maven-plugin properties to pick platform-specific artifacts, such as Netty's parent with <tcnative.classifier>${os.detected.classifier}</tcnative.classifier>. A project that only imports Netty's dependencies doesn't run the extension, so the expression is never resolved. Where the extension does run, it detects the machine Maven runs on. Captured preparation and execution therefore pass fixed Maven user properties taken from the job's target platform, not from the host or the execution image: Property linux/amd64 linux/arm64 darwin/arm64 windows/amd64 os.detected.name linux linux osx windows os.detected.arch x86_64 aarch_64 aarch_64 x86_64 os.detected.bitness 64 64 64 64 os.detected.classifier linux-x86_64 linux-aarch_64 osx-aarch_64 windows-x86_64 Names follow the plugin's own normalization (kr.motd.maven.os.Detector). Other platforms the plugin names, such as linux/ppc64le (ppcle_64) and linux/s390x (s390_64), map the same way. A target the plugin can't name fails preparation. os.detected.release* and kernel os.detected.version* aren't set, because a target platform has neither. A POM that needs them keeps Maven's behavior. Maven user properties win over the extension's detected values in interpolation, profile activation and plugin parameters, so ${os.detected.classifier} resolves the same way in every run, including in dependency POMs. A project that declares the extension still runs its own detection. Only these four properties are fixed. The properties are frozen in the prepared tree (properties.json) and listed in the dependency snapshot under extensions."oyzu.dev/maven".userProperties. Artifacts a plugin downloads from such a property while it runs, outside declared dependencies, aren't fetched ahead of time. Direct tests (oyzu run test) keep native detection.

Not supported yet: test providers other than JUnit through Surefire and Failsafe, custom or aggregate coverage, test sources generated during the lifecycle, private repositories and release builds. Captured builds run on Linux. A host Maven path exists for development tasks and direct tests only.
Java quality tasks, direct tests, version inference. Maven sessions for private repositories, and Java installation for JDK selection.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/maven-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this when Maven should download from private repositories without passwords in settings.xml. A local credential agent tells oyzu which repositories are allowed and supplies the credentials. oyzu uses the same agent for two things: running mvn yourself through oyzu exec or an activated shell, where Maven gets the password in memory; oyzu build for Maven projects, where oyzu downloads the dependencies itself and Maven never sees the password (see Captured build acquisition). Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Maven 3.9.11, JDK 17 and Bash.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [maven] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning maven.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain Maven and Maven Central Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there.

You need Maven 3.9.11 and a JDK with java, javac and jar on PATH: oyzu exec -- /opt/maven/bin/mvn verify # or, with Maven on PATH: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" mvn verify Use the mvn from a Maven installation; mvnw and other wrappers aren't supported. --help and --version run without asking the agent. You don't need any authentication files or extensions in the project.

oyzu sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "mvn", "arguments": [...]}. The agent answers with one or more mirror mappings: { "sources": [ { "id": "approved-libraries", "mirrorOf": "company-libraries", "access": { "repository": "https://packages.example.com/maven/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } } ] } Field Rules sources 1 to 64 entries, in Maven mirror order (exact matches before wildcards) id Unique. Letters, digits, -, _ or .. Can't be oyzu-source-denied mirrorOf A Maven mirror selector. Unique across entries access.repository HTTP(S) URL with no credentials, query or fragment access.username Not empty access.credentialEndpoint On 127.0.0.1. A GET returns the password as UTF-8 text Use "mirrorOf": "*" for one repository that serves everything, or separate entries for central, company-libraries, company-plugins and so on. Maven matches repository IDs, not group names.

Asks the agent before doing anything, even when Maven's cache is warm. Compiles a small bundled Maven extension against your Maven's libraries. Lets Maven read your normal settings.xml files (including -s and -gs). The extension then: keeps your blocking mirrors; adds the agent's mirrors, plus a catch-all that blocks every other repository, including ones declared in POMs; fetches each password into memory and authenticates only to that mirror's exact URL. Removes the temporary extension and files when Maven finishes or fails. An existing non-blocking mirror in your settings must match an agent mapping's URL, selector and layout (its ID may differ), or the run fails and names the settings file. <server> credentials in your settings are never used as a fallback. Profiles, properties, proxies and JVM settings work as usual. Maven downloads directly from the repositories; oyzu doesn't proxy the traffic.

With maven.sessionEndpoint set, oyzu build asks the agent for a session before it prepares a Maven project. The request has "tool": "mvn" and "arguments": ["oyzu-build-acquire"], a marker for the agent rather than a real Maven command. The agent answers with a single repository: { "repository": "https://packages.example.com/maven/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } The repository URL must end in /. oyzu fetches the password into memory and downloads the dependencies itself with Basic authentication. The build containers have no network access and never see the password; the build then runs offline from what was downloaded. Without the setting, dependencies come from Maven Central. If the agent denies or fails, the build stops. It never falls back to Maven Central. Snapshot versions are allowed only from administrator-listed snapshot repositories. If a plugin needs a dependency at build time that wasn't declared, the offline build fails. Declare it through the plugin's Maven configuration and build again. oyzu doesn't rerun the build online.

Passwords never go into settings files, command arguments or environment variables. When you run mvn yourself, the password is in Maven's memory, so plugins can read it. With oyzu build, Maven never receives it. The temporary files contain the credential endpoint, not the password, but treat them as sensitive. Read-only access has to be enforced by the repository account the agent uses. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command before Maven starts, with no fallback.
Maven's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID Bad endpoint, or a mapping has a bad repository or no user name Fix the endpoint or the agent MAVEN_SESSION_INVALID The agent's response couldn't be read, or has no mappings or more than 64 Fix the agent's response MAVEN_SESSION_PREPARE The JDK tools couldn't compile the extension Install a working JDK and Maven MAVEN_SESSION_UNSUPPORTED mvn isn't inside a Maven installation (no lib directory), or the project has .mvn/extensions.xml Use Maven's own bin/mvn; remove .mvn/extensions.xml MAVEN_SESSION_CONFLICT A mirror in your settings doesn't match the agent; duplicate IDs or selectors; or maven.ext.class.path or deploy in the arguments, MAVEN_ARGS, MAVEN_OPTS, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS or .mvn/maven.config/jvm.config Fix the setting or the mapping. Publish with oyzu publish

Plugins that make their own network calls aren't covered. Proxy authentication and custom TLS settings aren't supported yet. Credential rotation during a run, and cleanup after oyzu is killed, aren't handled. Linux and Bash only, with Maven 3.9.11. Windows, macOS and other Maven versions aren't supported yet.
Maven builds Private Gradle repositories Java installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/mocha.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The Node builder runs your Mocha tests with your own Mocha setup and collects a JUnit test report and an LCOV coverage report from them. Use it when your package already tests with Mocha and you want those reports in the build output. Note: This integration is experimental.

For a package that tests with npm and Mocha, add Mocha and c8 as dev dependencies and keep a plain mocha test script: { "scripts": {"test": "mocha"}, "devDependencies": {"mocha": "12.0.3", "c8": "10.1.3"} } Install dependencies with npm, then run the tests: oyzu run test oyzu build app --full --offline The test run writes junit.xml and lcov.info into the build's reports/ folder (see Reports). No Oyzu test or report section is needed in your configuration.

The builder detects Mocha from, strongest first: A test script that runs mocha, including a compound script that names only Mocha. A native .mocharc file or a mocha section in package.json. A mocha dependency. Oyzu reads configuration files without running them. If two frameworks have equally strong evidence, selection fails and names the with: {test-framework: <name>} selector in build.yaml. See discovery selectors. With no test script, a detected Mocha project gets an implicit test task that runs node node_modules/mocha/bin/mocha.js. oyzu run list shows it and oyzu run test runs it. Direct tests in single packages and npm workspaces also collect JUnit and LCOV into a test-only dist/ bundle. See direct tests and workspace test bundles.

Setup Mocha c8 Single npm package, direct tests and oyzu build 12.0.3 10.1.3 in your project Isolated builds and npm workspaces 11 (tried with 11.8.0) 10.x in your project, or Oyzu's default c8 The single-package setup is supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). For the platforms of isolated builds, see local builds. Other Mocha versions, pnpm and Yarn projects, and macOS are not supported yet.

This setup requires exactly mocha 12.0.3 and c8 10.1.3 in dependencies or devDependencies. It adapts an implicit Mocha test or a script that is exactly mocha, and keeps npm's script lifecycle and your configured Mocha reporter and options. Tests run serially. Watch mode and parallel mode are not supported. You cannot override the CLI reporter, and Oyzu rejects authored c8 configuration (.c8rc.json and similar). c8 reports the sources your tests load, not every file in the repository. Oyzu never downloads a reporting tool. The c8 in your project is always used. oyzu build app --full --offline uses your existing npm lock and cache and fails if a required input is not cached. Without --offline it prepares dependencies as usual.

Keep your existing project and native configuration: { "scripts": {"test": "mocha"}, "devDependencies": {"mocha": "11.8.0"} } Mocha must be a declared dependency that is captured with the build. c8 10.x in your project is used when present. A declared but missing c8 fails. Without any c8 dependency, Oyzu's default c8 is used. The test command runs under c8. Native thresholds, include and exclude rules and source-map handling in your c8 configuration apply. Only LCOV is exported, so additional coverage formats are not. No build action downloads reporting tools.

The engine collects the reports under dist/<target>/<platform>/reports/ and records their paths, digests and summaries in the manifest. Report File Test results (JUnit, from Mocha's XUnit reporter) junit.xml Coverage (LCOV, from c8) lcov.info The adapter combines your configured Mocha reporter with Mocha's XUnit reporter, so your reporter options keep working. A failed assertion keeps the reports that exist and blocks packaging. A failed coverage threshold fails the build even when every test passed. Passing coverage never turns a failed test into a success. A configuration or startup failure never reuses an earlier run's reports. A command that exits zero without writing a required report fails the required-report gate. Read the action log to see why a report is missing, fix the cause and rerun. A successful build also produces the normal Node package artifact. Build, test, lint and read-only formatting stay separate stages. The default lint rules know Mocha globals in conventional test folders and in test and spec files. Your own lint configuration takes precedence. See Node lint and formatting.

Workspaces use the same adapter. Each member resolves Mocha, its configuration and c8 from its own folder, including hoisted installs. A publishable root without a test script gets its own test suite. It excludes workspace members and Oyzu's own state with Mocha's --ignore option, and keeps your existing exclusions. An explicit script keeps its native file selection, including --file entries, which Mocha does not filter through --ignore. An explicit root test script produces one combined report pair. Otherwise each package gets its own JUnit and LCOV files, and a failure in one package keeps its siblings' results and blocks packaging. See npm workspaces.

Isolated builds recognize a bare mocha, its direct Node entry point and equivalent exact task overrides. Other shell commands, and scripts with extra flags, run as written. They must write their own required reports, and Oyzu does not guess a rewrite. Configure recognized runs through your Mocha configuration. Watch mode is turned off. Parallel Mocha reporting is not supported and fails when Oyzu detects it. Browser runners and custom reporters are not supported. Mocha configuration is project code. Development tasks run it on your machine, and isolated builds run it in an offline sandbox. The reporting adapter gets no credentials and no network access. A passing report shows the tests ran. It does not make a build eligible for release.
Node lint and formatting Direct tests npm workspaces Discovery selectors c8 options and Mocha's XUnit reporter

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-applications.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The node/app builder builds a Node application and produces a directory artifact, normally the contents of its dist/ folder. Use it to ship a front-end site or another static application as a directory that other targets, such as a container image, can consume. Note: Node application builds are experimental. They support a single package root (npm, pnpm, or Yarn, see Yarn builds), Vite 8 projects, and a private npm workspace root. See Limits.

If your package's native build script writes dist/, declare the build in build.yaml: builds: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend oyzu run list oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Oyzu runs the native build script with your package manager, then stages the contents of frontend/dist/ as the primary directory artifact application-<snapshot-version>. A consumer that uses materialize: [{from: frontend, to: site}] receives site/index.html directly, without a nested dist directory. A package with a vite dependency and "scripts": {"build": "vite build"} needs no build.yaml. Package discovery selects node/app for it (see Vite projects). Builds use the Node builder plugin. See plugin packages for how plugins are installed and pinned in oyzu.lock.

Selecting node/app is how you tell Oyzu that your build script follows the dist convention. Oyzu does not read your script to find out. The output must be a freshly produced directory inside the package: A missing output directory, a file where the directory should be, linked entries and special files fail the build. Contents left by an earlier build never count. Build, test, lint and read-only format checks still run. The default quality checks skip the generated dist. Browser globals are not assumed from the application selection alone. The artifact keeps the platform it was built on. Reusing one artifact across platforms is not supported. How Oyzu picks a builder: Discovery reports builder_selection: explicit and the dist-application output profile. A recognized framework such as Vite has its own output rules and validation. uses: node/package always builds a package archive instead (see npm workspaces and plugin packages). If discovery infers a Node target whose script is unknown, it builds a package archive. Add uses: node/app only when the script writes dist/. A custom output directory other than dist is supported only for Vite (see below).
documents.s: How the output directory is chosen

documents.t: A docker/image target can take the application directory as input: builds: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: frontend to: site The image's Dockerfile can use COPY site/ /site/. It receives site/index.html and the generated assets with no extra dist layer. The image build uses the recorded artifact and the matching platform. The image build context is made from the selected source files plus the materialized directories: Directory inputs keep all their files, including empty directories and names like dist that source capture normally skips. Linked inputs, name collisions and paths outside the image target are rejected. The combined inputs may hold at most 100,000 entries and 10 GiB of file data. Oyzu checks that the copied content did not change during the copy. Source ignore rules do not filter materialized artifacts.
documents.s: Use the directory in an image

documents.t: Discovery recognizes a vite build script and selects node/app without a build.yaml.

To write somewhere other than dist/, use vite build --outDir public-site as the native script. The script must be exactly vite build, optionally followed by one literal --outDir <path>. The path must stay inside the project and use only ASCII letters, digits, /, _, - and .. Parent (..) segments, absolute paths, shell expansion, quoting and compound commands are not interpreted. Any other Vite flag fails planning with a diagnostic.

Oyzu uses Vite's own loader for vite.config.js, .ts, .mjs, .mts, .cjs and .cts. Your configuration can pick a mode, add plugins and emit extra assets. Discovery and dependency installation never run the configuration. During the build, Oyzu replaces the private copy's build script with a small wrapper. Your checkout is not changed. Your package manager still runs the prebuild, build and postbuild scripts. The wrapper calls Vite 8's build API and records the resolved configuration and the files written. A literal --outDir takes precedence over the configuration's output directory. Files that postbuild adds to the output directory are included. If your build script is replaced by something that writes no Vite output, the earlier site is not published.

Select node/app with an installed Node plugin. No extra build option or helper file is needed. These commands build a Vite application: oyzu --json build app --full --no-cache oyzu --json build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image npm=<node-image> The second command runs the build in an isolated Linux amd64 worker with network access disabled during execution (see Isolated builds). The build checks that the resolved output path is inside the source, not linked, and was not left over from an earlier run. It then lets Vite write. After your npm command succeeds, Oyzu copies the output tree, including postbuild additions, into the planned artifact. A failed build leaves no usable artifact. Fix the command or configuration and rebuild. Before a build finishes, the implicit lint and format checks may evaluate your Vite configuration separately to find generated-output paths to skip. This does not run the build.

Artifact Name Notes Primary application-<snapshot-version> The output directory. Consumers that don't name an artifact get this one. build-metadata vite-output-<snapshot-version>.json Media type application/vnd.oyzu.vite-output.v1+json. Records the Vite version, snapshot version, project root, output directory and mode. Both artifacts are covered by the bundle's integrity checks.

One client environment and directory output only. Library and SSR builds, multiple environments, watch mode and write: false fail with a message. The project root and output must stay inside the project, with no linked parent directories. Rollup output options must agree with the resolved directory. Vite versions other than 8 are not supported. Your Vite plugins are project code. They run under the build sandbox but are not trusted release evidence. A failed build produces no output record. Missing, malformed or version-mismatched metadata fails the build. Fix the cause and rebuild.

With --isolated, Oyzu captures your dependencies first and then builds in a Linux worker with no network access. Use the usual build options. To use your own image instead of the base execution image, add --image npm=<node-image>: oyzu build app --full --no-cache --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --image npm=<node-image> Docker and the base execution image are required. Tool versions belong in oyzu.toml, not in build.yaml. Isolated builds run on Linux amd64 workers, including from a Windows coordinator. A platform matrix can select matching images (see toolchain platforms).

Select node/app at the root of a private npm workspace that has a current package-lock.json. npm decides workspace membership and linking. For example, a root that depends on a shared member and builds it first: {"scripts":{"build":"npm run build --workspace @oyzu-example/shared && node build.mjs","test":"node --test"}} The member builds its module before the root imports it, and the root writes a self-contained dist/. oyzu build app --full --no-cache --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --image npm=<node-image> How it behaves: Your root build script runs once. Oyzu does not expand it into separate member builds. Recognized Node tests at the root produce one aggregate JUnit and one LCOV report. Member tests may run inside that invocation, but members get no reports or versions of their own. Before the build, Oyzu checks workspace membership, the lock and the installed links. Dependencies are replayed offline during execution. Lifecycle scripts run in the private workspace. If a member build fails, the rest of the root script and the artifact export are skipped. Read the native error and fix the member. This produces one directory artifact. It does not create a package archive per member (see npm workspaces). Supported: private npm root with one shared member, isolated on a Linux amd64 worker. Native (non-isolated) workspace applications, member applications, and pnpm or Yarn workspace applications are not supported.

The Node plugin builds a single-root pnpm application whose build script writes dist/. Declare an exact stable version in packageManager (for example pnpm@10.11.0), or configure pnpm under [tools] if there is no declaration. Keep a current pnpm-lock.yaml. Run oyzu build app --full. Oyzu runs pnpm install --frozen-lockfile before the build and checks. Node tests get JUnit and LCOV reporters. Your lint and format checks stay as package scripts. An offline build reuses pnpm's prepared store and fails if bytes are missing. Workspaces, conflicting package managers, and packageManager values that are ranges or prereleases are refused. Isolated pnpm builds are supported with pnpm 10.11.0 on Linux amd64 (see plugin packages). For pnpm settings and lock rules, see pnpm builds.
Single-root Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and Yarn Berry 4.17.1 applications are supported with node/app. See Yarn builds for requirements and commands.

Tasks: oyzu run list shows your native build and test scripts, inferred lint and read-only format checks, and explicit formatting. Listing runs nothing. oyzu build installs dependencies, runs the build, test, lint and format-check steps, then packages. For Vite projects, the fallback ESLint setup includes browser globals as well as Node globals. The output directory is excluded from implicit quality checks. Your own scripts and configuration are never overridden. After a build, implicit quality tasks use its recorded output directory. Before that, they resolve your Vite configuration in production mode. That can run your configuration code on the host for development tasks, or inside the sandbox for isolated tasks. See Node quality for the lint and format defaults. Reports and output: Native Node tests produce JUnit and LCOV. The artifact is at dist/<target>/<platform>/application-<snapshot-version> in the build bundle. Read its path from the manifest instead of building the path yourself (see bundle layout). Only the selected output directory is staged. Source files, dependencies and tests are not copied into it. Failed tests or quality checks stop the artifact from being published. Their reports stay in the bundle. Integrity: The manifest records kind: directory, the version, the producing action, a full file inventory and a content digest. oyzu inspect dist checks them (see directory artifacts). materialize copies verified content into a fresh consumer context and keeps the producer's evidence references. A failed operation can leave partial output. It is not recorded as an artifact.

If your project pins Node ([tools] node = "22.12", locked with oyzu install node@22.12), isolated builds run on that exact Node instead of the image's copy. Oyzu: Reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for that version in oyzu.lock. Downloads it, unless a cached copy under the user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256. Verifies the bytes against the locked digest. Restores them read-only at /scratch/nodetool. How it is used: The directory is placed on PATH just before the image's system directories. The image's package manager (npm, pnpm or Yarn) keeps running and only the runtime changes. Preparation and every build action see the same environment. A different pin or archive changes the action identity. Without a pin, the Node that build preflight locks is used the same way (see Default Node selection). If an engine range has no matching LTS release, a newer stable runtime can be selected even though the image carries Node 22. Projects whose oyzu.lock has no Node entry, managed builds and non-Linux workers use the image's Node. To test other Node versions, use verification toolsets, which run natively and never in the isolated worker. Limits: Oyzu's test reporting passes Node 22 flags such as --test-coverage-exclude. With a pin older than Node 22, the build works but the native test stage fails with bad option. Pin Node 22 or later if you run tests. Only linux/amd64 workers are supported, and offline builds need the archive already cached. Pinning was tried with the npm image only. How the pnpm and Yarn images handle the changed PATH has not been tried. A locked npm or pnpm release (from [tools] or an exact packageManager) replaces the image's manager the same way. See npm and pnpm installation.

Without a configuration pin, the default request is lts, whether or not engines.node is set. Oyzu picks the greatest stable release marked LTS in Node's index.json that satisfies every engine constraint. If no LTS release satisfies them, it picks the greatest stable release that does. Example: if 24.x is LTS and 26.x is Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 selects 26.x. node = "latest", node = "26", exact pins and lts/<name> keep their usual meaning and must satisfy engines. The nearest .nvmrc or .node-version above the build folder (up to the project root) with an explicit version (22, v22.14.0) is used as the request instead. If neither file exists, an exact devEngines.runtime version is used. An alias such as lts/* is refused with a hint, and a [tools] node value must agree with the file (see native pin files). Explaining and locking: oyzu build --plan shows the LTS default and fallback rule as the requirement source. Pin previews and locks keep the lts request. A matching lock keeps its exact version, including a fallback, without checking today's LTS data. Engine constraints are still checked offline. A lock from the old default (*) does not match the lts default. Resolve it online once before building offline. Under an organization catalog, the signed index has no LTS markers. Use an approved exact version or a named line such as lts/krypton. The moving alias fails with TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE and does not contact a publisher outside the catalog.
The base execution image installs libatomic1, which newer Node binaries need. An image you pass with --image npm=<ref> (or pnpm=, yarn=) must provide it too.

Node and a supported npm or pnpm release, installed through tool management. Native builds need compatible tools and your project's dependencies already installed. Installing Node doesn't install your test or quality dependencies (see Node quality). Isolated builds need Docker and the base execution image, with the locked Node and the pinned quality defaults. Dependencies are captured through your package manager before isolated execution, then replayed offline. No new download route or credential channel is added. For native builds on the host, see local builds.

Platforms: native builds are supported on Windows and Linux. Native Vite configuration output is supported on Windows only. Isolated builds run on Linux amd64 workers, including from a Windows coordinator. macOS, Windows ARM64 and Linux ARM64 are not supported yet. Vite SSR and library modes, compound Vite commands, native workspace application output and cross-platform reuse of one directory artifact are not supported. Project build scripts are project code. They run under the build sandbox. Executable file modes in directory artifacts are not preserved when a Windows coordinator transfers them (see directory artifacts). The consumers tested read the output with a limited DOM, not a real browser. Browser behavior is not checked.
npm workspace builds, pnpm builds and Yarn builds Directory artifacts and build bundles Node quality

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Node packages get lint, format-check and format tasks without any Oyzu configuration. lint and format-check only read your files and run as gates in oyzu build. format rewrites files and only runs when you ask for it. Note: This integration is experimental. It works for single packages using npm, pnpm or Yarn, and for npm workspaces. Other workspace forms are not supported yet.

From the package or npm workspace root: oyzu run list oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format Your own scripts and oyzu.toml task replacements win. If package.json defines lint, format-check or format:check, Oyzu runs that script instead of the built-in check. A script named format:check is treated as the read-only formatting task.

Oyzu picks one linter and one formatter from your project's files: Role Default Chosen instead when Linter ESLint A biome.json or biome.jsonc selects Biome Formatter Prettier A biome.json or biome.jsonc selects Biome Your native ESLint or Prettier configuration counts as stronger evidence than the default. Oyzu reads configuration files without running JavaScript or launching tools. If your files point to two different tools for the same role, discovery fails instead of picking one. Resolve the conflict by removing one configuration, or choose in build.yaml: with: linter: eslint formatter: prettier Task overrides do not bypass this check. See discovery selectors.

Task What it does Changes files lint Runs ESLint or biome lint on your source files No format-check Runs prettier --check or biome format No format Rewrites files with Prettier or biome format --write Yes oyzu build runs lint and format-check before it collects artifacts. A failure stops the build and no artifacts are collected. format is never part of a build. format is not transactional. If a later file or package fails, earlier edits stay. The built-in lint and format-check reject extra arguments, so an argument cannot turn a check into a write. To pass custom flags, write a package.json script or an argv task. Oyzu does not guess whether a custom script is read-only from its name. ESLint never applies automatic fixes. With no ESLint configuration, Oyzu uses recommended JavaScript and TypeScript rules. Prettier uses your options, EditorConfig and ignore files. Biome gets explicit file arguments and uses your Biome configuration and ignores. It does not read from stdin. Long file lists are split into batches, and a failure in any batch fails the task. Native diagnostics are shown as they are, with the tool's own exit status. Files a tool ignores can produce no check.

The built-in tasks check JavaScript and TypeScript files (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, and their CommonJS and ESM variants). They do not format JSON, CSS or other files, even though Prettier and Biome can. To format those, write your own script. Source discovery skips dependency folders, .git, .oyzu, .oyzu-build, dist, build and coverage output. It never follows symlinks and stops at 100,000 files. In an npm workspace, the root checks skip member folders, and each member's checks skip nested members. See npm workspaces. For a Vite application, the build output folder is skipped and browser globals are enabled in the default ESLint rules. If the output folder is not known yet, the task reads your Vite configuration in production mode to find it, which can run your configuration code. Discovery and oyzu run list never do this. An invalid or uncontained output path fails the check. In a Mocha project, the default ESLint rules know Mocha globals in test and tests folders and in test and spec files. The default rules also know Jest globals in test files, and Node globals everywhere. A custom test location needs its own ESLint configuration.

Tool Version Oyzu provides Notes ESLint 10.13.0, with recommended JavaScript and TypeScript rules Uses your configuration when you have one. Legacy eslintrc needs a compatible ESLint 8 or 9 installed in your project, or a move to flat configuration. Prettier 3.9.10 Your configuration, EditorConfig and ignore files Biome 2.5.15 Biome 2 only. Other major versions are rejected. TypeScript 6.0.3 backs the default TypeScript parsing (typescript-eslint 8.72.0 supports TypeScript >=4.8.4 <6.1.0). TypeScript 7 is not supported by that parser. Your project can still compile with TypeScript 7. The listed versions are the ones Oyzu provides and uses by default. Other versions in the same major range can work but are not guaranteed.

Tools installed in your project win, including hoisted ones. If your package declares a tool that is missing from its installed dependencies, the task fails. Oyzu does not substitute a different version. Otherwise Oyzu uses the default. Isolated builds restore the defaults without any Node quality image. When a lint, format-check or test stage is enabled, preparation fetches every registry tarball the worker's platform needs, checks it against the lock's integrity and a SHA-256 pinned beside it, and restores one read-only archive at OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME (/scratch/node-quality). Lifecycle scripts never run, and no build action downloads checkers. For development tasks, set OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME to a directory that has a package.json and installed node_modules with the tools you want. Oyzu does not download checkers for development tasks either. Biome's platform binary package must be installed. A missing binary fails the task with no fallback install. Supported on Linux and Windows. macOS is not supported yet.

Oyzu recognizes a single-root Jest command, either a jest script or the inferred test task, and asks Jest for JSON and LCOV output. Your Jest reporters, transforms and test selection stay as you configured them. The native JSON result is converted to JUnit. It is written next to the JUnit destination with .jest.json added to the name. Coverage goes to lcov.info beside the LCOV destination. Failed tests or loading errors, and missing required reports, fail the task. Oyzu refuses to overwrite an existing report file. Move or delete it, then retry. A script that is not a plain jest command keeps its own body and must write its own declared and required reports. If your test script is jest --ci and you want a different report location, declare the reports. An authored task needs run or argv; reports alone does not inherit a command. [tasks.test] argv = ["npm", "run", "test"] reports = [ {kind = "test", format = "junit", path = "reports/custom/junit.xml"}, {kind = "coverage", format = "lcov", path = "reports/custom/lcov.info"}, ] Jest 29.7.0 with npm is supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). Other versions and package managers are not supported yet.

Oyzu runs Vitest through your own Vitest configuration (or your Vite configuration as a fallback) and adds JUnit and LCOV output while keeping your reporters. Scripts that are exactly vitest or vitest run keep their package manager lifecycle. For a project without such a script, Oyzu runs the installed Vitest CLI. Custom scripts are left alone and must meet their own report obligations. Oyzu requires Vitest 5 and a matching installed @vitest/coverage-v8 or @vitest/coverage-istanbul, whichever your configuration selects (V8 by default). A missing or mismatched provider fails before the tests run. Install your project's dependencies with its package manager and retry. Native coverage is always on for the required report, even when your configuration leaves coverage.enabled off. Vitest may read source files that no test imports, so the test action keeps the whole target's source. Your include and exclude rules, reporters and thresholds still apply, and Oyzu does not waive their result. Automatic Vitest commands skip .oyzu/** and .oyzu-build/**, so retained copies of your source do not add test suites. The Vitest reporting adapter runs one worker at a time. This does not change test selection, your timeouts, coverage, reports or gates, but a large suite can take longer within the 600-second action limit. Vitest 5 (tried with 5.0.3) and the V8 provider with npm are supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). Istanbul, browser mode, other versions and package managers are not supported yet.

Situation What to do A tool is declared in package.json but not installed Install your project's dependencies with your package manager, then retry. A default tool is missing for a development task Provide it in a directory named by OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME. Two tools are indicated for the same role Remove one configuration, or set with: {linter: <name>} or with: {formatter: <name>} in build.yaml. Extra arguments rejected on lint or format-check Use a package.json script or an argv task for custom flags. An existing Jest report file is in the way Move or delete it and retry. Invalid configuration or failed rules Fix them as the tool reports. The native diagnostics are authoritative.

Native configurations and plugins can run their own code. Development tasks run on your machine with your task environment. Isolated builds run in the prepared offline environment. These tasks do not fetch anything or deliver credentials. Global inherited configuration, some plugin forms and configuration inherited across package managers are not supported. Original-metadata formatting of files that a build rewrites is not supported. Built-in formatting does not cover JSON, CSS or other non-code files.
Mocha Node applications npm workspaces Discovery selectors Biome CLI

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-static-analysis.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu can read a Node package's source and scripts, without running anything, and predict what each build stage will read and write. Use it to see why a build depends on a file, to catch problems that only show up across files (an undeclared dependency, a secret in a browser variable), and to let the isolated build give each stage only the files it needs. Note: This feature is experimental. Names, output and rules can change.

Preview the analysis for a target: oyzu build --plan api Each Node target ends with a Static analysis section. This target never declares ../shared, but its build script copies a file from it, and the analysis reports that read with the script line that does it: api:build · confidence: over-approximate · scope: predicted 10 exact, 1 over-approximate, 0 unknown Reads Path or name Confidence Source Why package.json exact api/package.json manifest ../shared/src/greeting exact api/build.mjs:3 file-read · copyFileSync · outside the target directory .mjs build.mjs exact api/package.json:7 script-entry ! ../shared/src/greeting.mjs is outside api/. Declare it as a source input or a dependency, ... Output shortened. For each stage the section lists the files it is predicted to read, the paths it writes, the environment variable names it reads, the workspace targets it depends on, the tools it needs, and anything the analysis could not bound. Every line shows a confidence and a source (file:line). The analysis only reads and parses files. It never runs project code, scripts, package managers or the network.

oyzu build --plan api # analysis for every stage of the target oyzu build --plan api --stage build # one stage oyzu build --plan api --why ../shared/src/greeting.mjs oyzu build --plan api --unknown # only unknown and over-approximate facts oyzu build --plan api --facts # raw facts, one table row per fact oyzu build --plan api --no-analysis # skip analysis; whole-target scope oyzu build --plan api --json # everything, including the full analysis record oyzu build --check # apply the rule levels; runs nothing Flag Meaning --stage <name> Show one stage, for example build or test. Needs --plan. --why <path> Say, for each stage, whether the path is an input and why. The path is relative to the target or to the repository root. Needs --plan. --unknown Show only facts that are unknown or over-approximate. Needs --plan. --facts Also list every raw fact, grouped by kind. Needs --plan. --no-analysis Skip the analysis. Every stage uses the whole target. Needs --plan. --check Apply rule levels and exit non-zero on a blocking finding. The answer to --why is one of: Answer Meaning input A fact names the path. not-an-input No fact names it and nothing could cover it. covered-by-bound No fact names it, but the limit of an unknown fact covers it. covered-only-by-fallback No fact names it, but an unknown fact with no limit widens the stage to the whole target. --plan analyzes your working tree. A normal oyzu build analyzes the snapshot of the source it captured, before any action runs. Both give the same facts for the same files. When planning, Oyzu lists the tree from file names and sizes and opens only the files the analysis reads, so a large checkout costs a directory walk, not a read of every file.

Confidence Meaning exact Proven from literal text, for example copyFileSync("../shared/src/greeting.mjs", ...). over-approximate A superset that contains the truth: a glob, several resolution candidates, a dynamic import with a known directory. unknown Not pinned down: a computed require, a computed file path, a command the analysis does not model. An unknown only ever widens the result. If it has a limit (a relative import that is missing, a test pattern that is not expanded, a command with no tool profile), it widens its stage only by that limit. If it has none, the stage falls back to the whole target. See bounded unknowns.

Source What the analysis takes from it package.json, lockfiles, .npmrc Ancestor manifests, lockfiles, engines and packageManager tools, main, module, types, bin and exports entry points, files as outputs, and workspace:, file: and workspace-name dependencies Workspaces workspaces globs and pnpm-workspace.yaml members. A bare import of a member resolves to its exports or main. Scripts build, test and lint, with their pre and post hooks, using the script graph tsconfig The extends chain, include, exclude and files, paths aliases, references, and outDir and tsBuildInfoFile outputs Imports import, export ... from, require, literal import() and import x = require(), for relative, alias and workspace specifiers. Every resolution candidate is kept (all extensions, the TypeScript .js to .ts mapping, index files). File access fs read, write, copy, stat and readdir calls with constant paths, including path.join(__dirname, ...), import.meta.dirname, new URL(..., import.meta.url) and process.cwd(). Computed paths are unknown. Environment variables process.env.X, process.env["X"], import.meta.env.X and destructuring. Computed names and whole-object use are unknown. Dynamic access require(expr) and import(expr). A template with a literal directory prefix is limited to that directory (over-approximate). Anything else is unknown, and so is every child_process call. Paths in facts are snapshot-relative with forward slashes, so results are the same on every checkout path and host. Only the build, test and lint stages are modeled.

Human output leads with the outcome, uses aligned tables and reads fine without color. With --json, oyzu build --plan adds an analysis object to its document: Field Contents analyzedFrom working-tree or captured-snapshot snapshotDigest For the working tree, a digest of paths, kinds and sizes. It does not change when a file's bytes change at the same size. per-target stage views confidence, fallback (predicted or target-directory) and counts diagnostics The rule findings record The complete analysis record, with every fact A normal oyzu build reports unknown facts and analysis failures only in the debug log (--log-level debug), with the file, line, construct and what it widens.

Rules read the facts and report problems that are only visible across files and targets. They are advisory by default. A finding never fails oyzu build --plan. It fails oyzu build --check or oyzu build only when you set its rule to enforce. Warning (phantom-dependency): app:build imports `left-pad` at packages/app/build.mjs:2, but packages/app/package.json does not declare it; it resolves today only because package.json declares it and the package manager hoists it. Fix: add `left-pad` to the dependencies of packages/app/package.json. With --json, each finding has rule, severity, message and facts, the ids of the facts behind it. Messages name variables, never values. Severity is warning for a violation and note when the rule could not decide. A finding that rests on an over-approximate fact says so. Rule Reports phantom-dependency A bare package import that the importing file's own package.json does not declare (any dependency section, its own name, or the matching @types package). When the import works only through hoisting, the message names the ancestor manifest that declares it. escaping-reference An import, import glob, CSS reference or literal file read that leaves the target's directory, when the target has no workspace dependency on the package that holds the path. undeclared-env A literal process.env.X or import.meta.env.X read for a name that no task environment of that stage sets and no environment file the stage reads defines. NODE_ENV, MODE, BASE_URL, DEV, PROD, SSR and CI are never reported. A computed name is a note. public-env-secret-name A variable inlined into browser output (VITE_, NEXT_PUBLIC_, PUBLIC_, NUXT_PUBLIC_) whose name has a SECRET, TOKEN, PASSWORD or PRIVATE segment. A bare KEY is not reported, so publishable keys are left alone. exports-target-missing A main, module, types, bin or exports path that is neither in the source nor under anything the build is known to write. If the build's outputs are unknown, the finding is a note. Patterns containing * are not expanded. output-outside-declared A build script or source write to a path outside every output location the build is known to use (a compiler outDir, a framework output or generated directory, warm state). A target with no known output location is not judged. config-unreadable A configuration file (framework config, tsconfig, manifest, environment file, test-runner config such as next/jest) the analysis could not read statically. Always a note. The stage falls back to the whole target. script-wrapper-opaque A script step the closed shell grammar cannot resolve, for example a redirection. Always a note. lockfile-manifest-drift The nearest lockfile no longer matches the target's package.json: a declared range differs from or is missing in the lockfile, or the locked version does not satisfy the range. The fix names the package manager's command (npm install --package-lock-only, pnpm install --lockfile-only, yarn install). redundant-declaration A build.yaml inputs entry inside the target's own directory, which is always captured. An input outside the directory is never reported. lockfile-manifest-drift reads package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json (version 2 or 3), pnpm-lock.yaml (version 5 to 9) and both Yarn lockfile formats. If a directory has several lockfiles, it uses the one packageManager names. It skips what it cannot judge: non-semver specs (tags, git, URLs, file:, link:, workspace:, catalog:, npm: aliases), prerelease locked versions, and packages under overrides, resolutions or pnpm overrides. It does not check transitive entries. phantom-dependency compares manifests only. It cannot see installed node_modules, so it cannot confirm whether an import resolves through hoisting today. A file is judged against its nearest package.json. escaping-reference ignores authored inputs, so a path you already list there is still reported.

Set a level for each rule in the oyzu.toml cascade (see configuration): [analysis.rules] phantom-dependency = "enforce" # off | advisory (default) | enforce [[analysis.suppress]] rule = "escaping-reference" path = "legacy/**" # optional glob over the finding's file reason = "vendored fork, tracked in the migration plan" # required Level Meaning off The rule's findings are dropped from --check and from build logs. advisory Reported, never fails anything. This is the default for every rule. enforce A blocking finding fails oyzu build --check and oyzu build. A finding blocks only if its rule is enforce, it is a warning (never a note), and every fact it cites is exact. An enforced finding that rests on an over-approximate or unknown fact is reported as not blocking, with its confidence, and never fails a build. --check counts those so you can see how much enforcement is held back. A suppression needs a rule and a non-empty reason. path is a project-relative glob over the file the finding cites first (* stays within a directory, ** crosses directories). Without path, the suppression covers every file. A suppressed finding does not fail and is listed under Suppressed. With --json its reason is in suppressedBy. A suppression that matches no finding is reported as a stale note and never fails a build. Suppression changes reporting only, never a stage input or cache key.

oyzu build --check is static analysis only: it prepares, installs, downloads and executes nothing. It selects targets the way build --plan does (including --affected), and you cannot combine it with --plan or the analysis view flags. Exit status Meaning 0 No blocking finding. 1 At least one blocking finding, or the analysis could not complete (the error is shown, never a pass). 2 Usage error. ✗ Check failed: 1 blocking finding in enforced rules phantom-dependency · enforce Blocking packages/app/build.mjs:2 app:build imports `left-pad` at packages/app/build.mjs:2, but ... Fix: add `left-pad` to the dependencies of packages/app/package.json. With --json, the build --plan --json document gains a check object: Field Contents outcome passed or failed counts blocking, advisory, nonBlocking, suppressed, staleSuppressions findings rule, level, severity, status, target, path, line, message, fix, confidence, and suppressedBy when suppressed staleSuppressions Suppressions that matched nothing A normal oyzu build applies the same levels to the snapshot it captured (or, for native host builds, to the working tree) before any action runs. A blocking finding stops the build with the same file, line and fix, and the failed bundle records it. Advisory findings stay in the debug log. A native host build that enforces no rule skips the analysis. Limits: An unknown rule id, a level other than the three, an empty reason, an unknown suppression field or an invalid glob is a configuration error that names the valid ids. analysis.rules and analysis.suppress are whole-value settings. The nearest scope that sets one replaces the lower ones instead of merging per rule. A managed policy can pin a value. build --plan lists every finding and ignores levels and suppressions. Per-rule severity overrides and expiring suppressions are not available.

Each stage script (build, test, lint, with pre<name> and post<name>) is read with a closed shell grammar and resolved into a graph whose leaves are tool invocations. Scripts are read, never run. Every script it visits is reported as an exact fact at its line in package.json, with its command, the tools and unknown constructs it ends in, the scripts it calls, and the chain that led to it (build > build:compile > compile). Construct Handling &&, ||, ;, newline, | Every segment is analyzed, which is a superset of what runs. Comments, quotes and \ escapes are honored. $VAR, ${VAR} A read of that variable, except inside single quotes or after \$. NAME=value cmd, cross-env, env, npx, pnpx, time, command Stripped, and the real program is classified. Unknown flags of these wrappers are unknown. dotenv [-e file] -- cmd The env files are exact reads (default .env). -c cascades are unknown. cd dir Later commands in the same script use that directory. npm run, npm test, pnpm run, pnpm <script>, yarn <script>, node --run Delegation to the script of the same package, with hooks. --prefix, -C, --dir and --cwd select another package. --if-present tolerates a missing script. A missing script is unknown. -- and trailing arguments Appended to the last command of the delegated script. npm run s -w <name>, --workspaces, pnpm -r, pnpm --filter, yarn workspace, yarn workspaces foreach Fan out to the workspace members that define the script. A selector that matches nothing is unknown. A dependency or git-range selector selects every member, which is a superset. npm-run-all, run-s, run-p Script names and name:* patterns. A pattern that matches nothing is unknown. node, tsc Entry files, preloads (--require, --import, --env-file), --test, directories and extensionless names resolved like Node. For tsc: -p, -b, project lists, files on the command line, and --outDir, --declarationDir, --tsBuildInfoFile and --outFile as writes. node -e, node -p and watch modes are unknown. rimraf, del, rm, mkdir, touch, cp, copyfiles, mv, cat, echo, sleep, ... Known utilities. Deletes, creates and copies are writes (over-approximate), reads are reads, and echo-like commands have no effect. A glob or computed target of a write is unknown. Tools with a framework profile Run through the profile when the command runs in the analyzed target's directory. In another workspace member it is unknown. ./script.sh, bash file The file is an exact read. Its body is not analyzed, so it is also unknown. >, >>, < The command is still analyzed. Each target other than /dev/null is unknown. Subshells, $(...), backticks, &, eval, unterminated quotes, other programs unknown. Delegation deeper than 8 levels, or more than 256 script instances in a stage, stops with an unknown fact that names the chain. A cycle is an unknown fact that names the cycle. An unknown leaf widens only its own stage. The generated build command for npm, pnpm and Yarn workspaces runs the member builds, checks their public entries and packs them as one operation. Native packing also reads each package's files selection, ignore rules and lifecycle inputs, so the analysis treats this command as an unbounded read of the target source and keeps the whole target for confinement and cache inputs. An authored root build script keeps its own analyzed bounds. Not supported in scripts: if, for, while, case, functions, aliases, here-documents, glob expansion of shell arguments (an argument glob is unknown except for cp-like reads), concurrently, turbo, nx, lerna, bun and Yarn plug-and-play specifics. Arguments passed to a hook script and .npmrc settings that change scripts (script-shell, ignore-scripts) are not modeled. This is the build stage of a project that uses run-s build:*: Entry points, scripts and frameworks Path or name Confidence Source Why prebuild exact package.json:7 npm run clean build exact package.json:8 run-s build:* build:assets exact package.json:9 build > build:assets · cross-env NODE_ENV=production node scripts/assets.mjs --minify build:compile exact package.json:10 build > build:compile · npm run compile -- --pretty false compile exact package.json:11 build > build:compile > compile · node scripts/stamp.mjs && tsc -p tsconfig.build.json postbuild exact package.json:12 node scripts/report.mjs clean exact package.json:13 prebuild > clean · rimraf dist The entries these scripts reach (scripts/assets.mjs, scripts/stamp.mjs, scripts/report.mjs) are listed as well. In the same project, --stage lint lists redirection to or from "lint.log" is not analyzed as an unknown fact.

tsc -p, tsc -b, project lists and a bare tsc (which searches upward for tsconfig.json; tsc -b looks only in its own directory) predict the compiler's own file list from: The extends chain. This includes extends of a workspace-member package, read through the member's package.json. Any other package is unknown. files, include and exclude. The default exclude applies only when none is set. allowJs, and the priority between a.ts, a.d.ts and a.js. references, with each referenced project's own set. Build-info files for composite and incremental, as warm state. The imports reached from those files, plus the package.json of every directory above each program file and of every workspace member an import resolves to. Not predicted: extends of an installed package, types and typeRoots, lib files and anything under node_modules. Command-line compiler options other than -p, -b, the output flags and files are not applied to the file set. Oyzu does not run tsc --listFilesOnly to check its prediction.

A profile tells the analysis what a build tool reads and writes. It is used when a stage's script runs the tool's command. A value in your configuration beats the convention: an explicit Next.js distDir or Vite build.outDir replaces .next or dist. A value the analysis cannot read makes only the facts derived from it unknown. Script configs (.js, .mjs, .cjs, .ts, .mts, .cts) are evaluated by a small built-in interpreter, never by running your code. It understands object and array literals, string concatenation, path helpers, __dirname, import.meta.dirname and import.meta.url, new URL(...), spread, top-level const, defineConfig(...) wrappers, and relative imports of other config files and JSON. Anything else (another call, a loop, a function parameter, a binding changed after its declaration) is unknown for that value only. process.env.X is recorded as an environment read with an unknown value. Very large or deeply nested configs also become unknown and the message names the limit. Tool Recognized command Notes Vite vite build [--mode m] [--config f] Reads the config and what it imports, index.html (or build.rollupOptions.input or build.lib.entry) and the module graph from there, public/, tsconfig, PostCSS and Tailwind CSS v3. Writes build.outDir (default dist). resolve.alias, import.meta.glob, CSS @import and url(), and new URL(..., import.meta.url) are followed. A plugin other than the React plugins makes the stage unknown. Vitest vitest [run] Reads the config (vitest.config.*, else vite.config.*), files matching test.include minus test.exclude, setupFiles, globalSetup and their imports. test.workspace, projects, includeSource, typecheck, coverage and a workspace file are unknown. Next.js next build Reads the config, app/ route files and metadata files, pages/, src/ variants, root middleware, proxy and instrumentation, public/, and the file set of tsconfig (the type check). Writes distDir (default .next), out/ for output: "export", and the cache. webpack, turbopack, experimental.turbo, swcPlugins, images.loaderFile and cacheHandler make the stage unknown. See route handlers. SvelteKit vite build with sveltekit() in the Vite config (also under Vitest) Reads svelte.config.*, route files under kit.files.routes, static/, hooks, app.html, .env* from kit.env.dir, $lib and kit.alias, and the module graph through each component's <script> and <style>. Writes .svelte-kit (or kit.outDir) plus the adapter's output. Modeled adapters: adapter-static, adapter-node, adapter-vercel, adapter-netlify, adapter-cloudflare and adapter-auto. Any other adapter, a non-constant adapter option, a preprocessor other than vitePreprocess(), a component whose markup uses import( or import.meta, or a <style lang> other than CSS makes the stage unknown. Astro astro build [--mode m] [--config f] [--root d] Reads astro.config.*, src/pages, public/, middleware, actions, content collections loaded by glob() or file(), .env*, tsconfig, and the module graph through .astro frontmatter, scripts, styles and Markdown or MDX. Writes outDir (default dist) and .astro. Any adapter, an integration other than @astrojs/sitemap and mdx() without options, Vite options that can add files, Markdown plugins, a custom image service, experimental or legacy flags, and --outDir make the stage unknown. Nuxt nuxt build, nuxt generate (also nuxi) Reads nuxt.config.*, the source directory and its scanned directories, server/, shared/, public/, .env, css and plugins entries, the standard aliases, and the module graph through each .vue component. Writes .nuxt and .output (and dist for the static preset). modules, extends and layers, local layers/ and modules/ directories, nitro.config.*, .nuxtrc, a Nitro preset other than node-server, node, node-listener, node-cluster or static, and a CSS preprocessor make the stage unknown. React Router (framework mode) react-router build [--mode m] Reads the Vite config with reactRouter(), react-router.config.*, the app directory, every route module named by the route configuration, public/, .env*, tsconfig and aliases. Writes the build directory (default build) and .react-router. buildEnd, presets, serverBundles, a route list the evaluator cannot read, and a Vite plugin other than reactRouter() and vite-tsconfig-paths make the stage unknown. Remix v2 remix vite:build [--mode m] Reads the Vite config with vitePlugin(), the app directory, every route module, public/, .env* and tsconfig. Writes the build directory (default build). routes, presets, buildEnd, serverBundles, SPA mode and another Vite plugin make the stage unknown. The classic remix build is not modeled. Angular CLI ng build [project] [-c name] with the application builder (@angular/build or @angular-devkit/build-angular) or the webpack browser builder Reads angular.json, the build target's options merged with the selected configurations, the tsConfig program, browser or main, polyfills, index, styles, scripts, assets, fileReplacements and each component's template and style files. Writes outputPath (default dist/<project>) and .angular/cache. Other builders, ssr, prerender, serviceWorker, localize, Sass or Less styles, and a PostCSS or Tailwind CSS configuration make the stage unknown. ng test and ng serve are unknown. Nest nest build [--path p] [--config f] [--builder tsc|swc] Reads nest-cli.json, the selected tsconfig and its file set, compilerOptions.assets, and for swc the .swcrc and every source file under sourceRoot. Writes the tsconfig outDir (default dist) and each asset's own output. The webpack and rspack builders, compiler plugins (under swc only with a type check), watch modes and an @nestjs/cli major other than 11 or 12 make the stage unknown. nest start is not modeled. Jest jest Reads the config (jest.config.* or package.json jest), every file under roots, files matching testMatch, setup files, and Babel config for the default transform. preset, projects, moduleNameMapper, testRegex, custom transforms and configs built at runtime (such as next/jest) are unknown. ESLint eslint [paths] Reads the flat config found from the target directory upward, its imports, and the files and directories on the command line. Package presets and plugins, type-aware parsing and legacy eslintrc files are unknown. PostCSS and Tailwind CSS v3 (inside Vite and Next.js) n/a Reads the PostCSS config, tailwind.config.* and what it imports, every file the content globs match, and Browserslist files. Tailwind CSS v4 scans the whole project and is unknown. A test file under src/ is a build input in a Tailwind CSS project (the content scan reads it) and in a Next.js project whose tsconfig includes it (the type check reads it). Excluding tests in tsconfig or the Tailwind content globs makes them non-inputs. Jest lists every file under its roots, so its stage scope is the roots. Next.js next.config.* functions such as rewrites(), redirects(), headers() and generateBuildId are not executed. If one reads a file, that read is not predicted. Sass and Less @import, repeated extglobs, and inline <script type="module"> in HTML are not modeled.

From Next 15, app-router GET route handlers are dynamic unless the file opts into static generation. Environment reads inside a handler that runs only at request time are not build inputs. The analysis decides this per build and per route file, and records its decision as next-get-handler-default with the Next version it used and where that version came from. Input Effect Next version The version your nearest lockfile installs, else the lowest major your declared range allows. Tags such as latest and non-registry specs resolve nothing. Version below 15, or unknown Next 14 default: GET and HEAD reads are build inputs unless the file exports dynamic = "force-dynamic". next.config.* not readable, output: "export", or cacheComponents or dynamicIO set Next 14 default. Next 15 or later otherwise GET and HEAD reads are request-time unless the file opts in. Opt-in An exported dynamic other than "auto" or "force-dynamic", a revalidate other than 0, generateStaticParams, or export *. Metadata routes Routes such as robots, manifest, sitemap, icon and opengraph-image stay static. Reads inside POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and OPTIONS exports are always request-time. A handler defined in another module and re-exported is not recognized, so its reads stay exact. Partial prerendering is not modeled.

For the mode of the command (production for vite build and next build, test for Vitest, or the value of --mode), the candidate environment files are inputs whether they exist or not, because creating one changes the build. Tool Files read, lowest precedence first Vite, Vitest .env, .env.local, .env.<mode>, .env.<mode>.local in envDir (default: the project root) Next.js .env, .env.<mode>, .env.local, .env.<mode>.local (.env.local is skipped in mode test) Nuxt .env at the root, then Vite's .env, .env.local, .env.production, .env.production.local in srcDir Each file fact lists the variable names it defines. Values never enter facts. Names with a prefix the framework inlines into browser output (VITE_* or your envPrefix, NEXT_PUBLIC_*) are reported as public. A mode that is not a constant name, for example --mode $MODE, is unknown.

Facts belong to the stage that needs them. The test stage lists the runner's test files and setup files, and the build stage does not. A test-only edit therefore leaves every build fact unchanged: oyzu build --plan --why tests/extra.test.ts --stage build # not-an-input oyzu build --plan --why tests/extra.test.ts --stage test # input When the runner's configuration cannot be read statically (a computed test.include, a config built by next/jest), only the test stage falls back to the whole target. The build stage does not depend on test discovery and stays bounded. Vitest's test action always keeps the whole target view. Oyzu's reporting adapter turns on native coverage, which can read source files that no test imports. Your Vitest coverage settings and thresholds still apply.

On the isolated (captured) executor path, the analysis narrows the cache key and the source each action can see, for analyzed packages whose command it models: build, test and the builder-owned stages below. See confined actions. --affected and the native host path do not use it. Rule findings fail a build only when you enforce them.

Five stages of a Node package run commands the builder chooses instead of a project script. --plan lists their reads under these stages (for example oyzu build --plan --stage package). Stage Command version The version stamp prepare The npm install package npm pack lint, format-check The default ESLint and Prettier checks, for a package without such scripts Absent files are reads. A tool that looks for a file reads its absence. The version stamp probes npm-shrinkwrap.json, .npmrc and .npmignore. ESLint probes every eslint.config.* and .eslintrc* in and above the target. Prettier probes every configuration name and .editorconfig. Creating one changes the stage's cache key. Whole-package reads. npm pack without files (or with a glob in it) reads the whole package directory. The quality checks read every JavaScript and TypeScript file below the target. Implicit native install. If a package has a binding.gyp, gypfile is not false, and there is no install or preinstall script, npm defaults to node-gyp rebuild. The analysis treats this as an unbounded unknown, so preparation keeps the whole target. A postinstall script does not stop the native default. Not modeled. Workspace roots and members, pnpm and Yarn installs and packs, application package commands, Biome, legacy ESLint configuration, Prettier script configurations and plugins, install lifecycle scripts, dependency install scripts, and local, Git or URL dependencies. Each is unknown for its stage only, so that stage keeps the whole-target key and the others stay confined.

Supported on Linux and Windows. macOS is not supported yet. Profiles cover the tools in the table above. Other build tools, and commands or builders they do not model, are unknown. package.json exports conditions, packages in node_modules, .d.ts lookups in @types and tool installations are not analyzed. A bare import of an installed package yields no read fact, only evidence for phantom-dependency. Limits protect the analysis from hostile input: 1 MiB per file, 256 MiB and 20,000 files per snapshot, 400 open brackets (or an estimated 1,000 levels of nesting) per parse, and a 5,000-file import graph. A file that hits a limit makes its stage unknown and the message names the construct. The depth check over-estimates, so a very deep but legitimate file can lose precision. Non-UTF-8 files are treated as opaque. Symlinks are never followed. A specifier that differs from a file name only by case or Unicode normalization resolves to that file. Other lookups that miss only that way make the target unknown (case-variant-path). A leading byte order mark in a file is ignored, and CRLF files report the same lines and columns as LF files. The analysis is not a replacement for the tools themselves. A prediction is a superset, so a build may read fewer files than listed.

The Oyzu repository has a development script, tooling/measure-node-analysis.py, that compares predictions with what real builds read and checks that hiding every file a stage was not predicted to read changes nothing. It is not part of the oyzu CLI.
Action cache for how unknown reads and confined actions affect reuse Configuration for analysis.rules and analysis.suppress Node applications and npm workspaces

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-workspace-tests.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu run test runs the tests of an npm, pnpm 10 or Yarn Classic workspace and collects each package's JUnit and LCOV reports into a test-only dist/ bundle. Your package manager decides workspace membership. Oyzu picks each package's test runner and collects the reports. No build YAML or reporting section is needed. Note: Workspace test bundles are experimental. They hold results from your machine, not the versioned artifacts of an isolated build. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist

Install the project's dependencies and provide Node and your package manager first. Oyzu does not install tools or dependencies during this operation. Manager Version tested npm 11.11.0 pnpm 10.11.0 Yarn Classic 1.22.22 Node 22 and 24 were used. pnpm and Yarn must expose their JavaScript entry point on PATH through a normal package install or native executable link. This works with package-local .bin directories and ordinary global installs on Windows and Unix. Corepack and standalone bundled pnpm executables are not used. A missing prerequisite or an unsupported manager major version fails with a message.

oyzu run list reads native markers and scripts without running a package manager. workspaces in package.json marks an npm or Yarn workspace. pnpm-workspace.yaml marks a pnpm workspace, even before a lock exists. Lockfiles and packageManager declarations take part in the normal manager conflict rules. Actual membership is read only when you run tests. npm uses its installed dependency graph, pnpm uses its recursive JSON list (pnpm list), and Yarn Classic uses its workspace info output (yarn workspaces). Oyzu has no workspace glob parser of its own. pnpm runs with automatic manager-version management turned off. Yarn runs in offline mode and ignores yarn-path. Your other project settings still apply.

Without a root test script, oyzu run list shows the manager's recursive test command. When you run tests, Oyzu reads membership, fixes each package's scope and report files, then runs each member's script or inferred Node, Jest, Vitest or Mocha suite. An explicit root test script owns one aggregate report pair and runs once. A publishable root without a script also gets its own implicit suite, where the manager allows that layout. Yarn Classic needs a private workspace root. Package scripts keep their manager's argument and lifecycle behavior. Arguments reach each selected test command, and a root script receives them once. Inferred suites skip nested members. Explicit scripts keep their own selection. Test frameworks and reporters must already be installed (see native reporting prerequisites). Each package's current JUnit and LCOV files go into the bundle with the plan, logs and manifest summaries. Package names give stable report identities. A failing assertion fails the command but lets later suites run, and available reports are kept. A missing tool, malformed metadata or unresolved framework can stop the run before any suite starts. Missing or invalid required reports are errors, including under task overrides. Oyzu never invents a pass for a command that writes no reports. Hooks: Oyzu pre and post hooks use the common task engine. A failed test blocks its success-only post hook. Exact implicit commands get report instrumentation. Replacements in TOML keep their bodies and must write the required reports. Member commands receive OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT. Replacing a whole workspace task means providing each package's reports or explicit report collection paths.

It doesn't rewrite package versions or locks, build archives, or run unrelated quality gates. Test scripts can write host files and use the host environment and network. Offline manager flags only restrict the manager's own downloads. Installed dependencies are used as they are. Nothing records where they came from. pnpm and Yarn direct host member builds and quality defaults are incomplete. Modern Yarn releases are not supported. A pnpm pnpm-workspace.yaml with a packages list selects workspace planning. Patch-only settings keep the single-project path. See direct tests for how existing output is preserved and how to inspect a failed bundle.
npm workspace builds, pnpm builds and Yarn builds for isolated builds and packaging Direct tests and Mocha

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/npm-workspaces.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds and tests an npm workspace using npm's own workspace membership and installed dependency graph. It handles private aggregation roots and publishable root packages, producing an independent package archive and test reports for each package. Run it from a conventional npm workspace root with no Oyzu configuration. Note: npm workspace support is experimental. Affected-only selection, member task groups and duplicate target selection are not available. See Limits. Builds use the Node builder plugin, which must be installed and selected (see plugin packages). There are three ways to build a workspace: Mode Where it runs Output Section Development tasks Your machine, with oyzu run Test-only bundle Direct test bundles Native workspace packages Your machine, with oyzu build One archive per package External native workspace packages Captured workspace packages Isolated Linux worker (Docker) One archive per package External captured workspace packages

From a workspace root that has package.json, its native lock and installed dependencies: oyzu run list oyzu run build oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format For an isolated build, which needs Docker and the base execution image: oyzu build oyzu inspect dist
