CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-development.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A builder plugin is a separate program that tells oyzu how to build one kind of project: which tasks it has, which tools it needs, which command builds it and where the output lands. This page shows how to run a plugin from a local path while you develop it, how plugins work, what a plugin has to provide, and how to package it. It also covers the Node plugin's behavior, since it's the largest first-party plugin. Note: The plugin interface (plugins-v1alpha1) is experimental. It's edited in place and can change without a new version. The Rust crates in the oyzu repository that help write plugins are internal and not a supported SDK. You can write a plugin in any language that speaks the JSON contract below.

Bind your executable to a builder reference in your user configuration (~/.config/oyzu/config.toml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml on macOS, %APPDATA%\Oyzu\config.toml on Windows, or the file OYZU_USER_CONFIG names): [plugins.development] "go/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/target/debug/oyzu-plugin-go" "node/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/target/debug/oyzu-plugin-node" Then build as usual: oyzu build oyzu build --full oyzu run test Oyzu runs your executable for that reference instead of a catalog package. The build shows the plugin-owned output directory in its commands (for example go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o .oyzu/native/plugin/…), the Context facts in dist/logs/events.jsonl include Plugins go/app → local development <path> (sha256:…), and the plan, envelope and manifest carry extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"] (see plugin packages). Remove the entry to stop using the local executable. The next build then has to find the package some other way: the catalog, a plugins.packages binding or the lock. There's no built-in fallback.

Key Type Default Where plugins.development Table of builder reference to absolute executable path none User, machine or administrative configuration Keys are short builder references without a major version (go/app, not go@1/app or an OCI reference). Values are absolute paths. At most 64 entries. The setting selects code to run, so a project oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml or a profile is refused with CONFIG_SCOPE: plugins.development is not permitted in this scope. In CI, user configuration is ignored as usual; a machine-level binding still applies. Pass --ci-machine-binding to the repository bootstrap to create one on an ephemeral runner (see CI machine binding). The table is replaced as a whole by a later source. Bindings are read once per command, before targets are discovered. A missing or unreadable executable fails with PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID; a malformed or versioned key fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A local binding has no download, signature check, manifest check or oyzu.lock entry. The executable is recorded by file name and SHA-256 digest only.

A plugin doesn't have to match a built-in family. To develop a new profile such as independent/app, bind its id and name it in build.yaml. The names and path are illustrative: [plugins.development] "independent/app" = "/home/me/src/plugin/target/debug/independent-plugin" builds: app: uses: independent/app Run oyzu build app to build with it. An independent profile must be named in uses; the binding adds no detection, no with options, no dependency preparation and no isolated execution. Tool versions still come from your configuration or native files, and oyzu installs the tools the plugin's requirements answer names under the usual policy. A local binding can't ask oyzu to run task-command observations (see below), even for an installed tool. When tools.allowed is set, oyzu run admits a task of a plugin-built target only if every tool the plugin's requirements declare for that task is on the list. A task whose binding declares no tool for it is refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED before anything launches. Registry routes and approved catalogs stay fail-closed for local bindings, as for any other builder.

For every operation, oyzu starts your executable once, with no arguments, a minimal environment and a fresh scratch directory as its working directory. It writes one JSON request to standard input and reads one JSON result from standard output. The process gets no credentials. Stream Content Standard input One request, then end of input Standard output One result and nothing else Standard error Diagnostic lines as JSON. Other lines are kept only for troubleshooting Documents use snake_case, schema_version: "v1alpha1" and a constant type. Unknown members, duplicate keys, null members and numbers written with a fraction or exponent are invalid. A request carries an operation_id, role (builder), operation, required_features, deadline_ms, the target (name, uses, whether the reference was inferred or explicit, absolute source root for reading, and the base version) and the operation's input. Your result echoes operation_id and operation and has an outcome: completed (with output), failed (with error{code, message}), unsupported (with reason) or, for task-command, observe. Oyzu accepts a result only if it's valid, the process exited with status 0 and the ids match. A valid result followed by a nonzero exit is a failure. Limits: 16 MiB for a request or result, 1 MiB of kept diagnostics, at most 64 observations. Oyzu never truncates and accepts. Each operation has a deadline (60 seconds by default). At the deadline, or when the build is cancelled, oyzu terminates the whole process tree (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 seconds on Unix; the job object on Windows). Termination is a failure whatever the process wrote. Plugins keep no state between calls. Oyzu supplies every fact each time. Target-relative paths use /, never .. or spaces, and at most one leading dot per segment.

An operation you don't implement answers unsupported. Operation Called to Your answer describe Confirm identity and roles Protocol generations, plugin identity, roles with their profiles, operations and features tasks Discover conventional tasks The package manager, optional native package name and version (with the file they came from), and tasks (name, argv, build stage, whether it changes source, optional environment defaults) requirements Find the tools a target needs Tools (for example oyzu:go), stages, components, version constraints with their source files, and why. Read-only native-admission Decide whether the plugin can build this target on the host {admitted, reason}. Read-only native-build Plan a host build The build operations and the artifacts. Oyzu supplies the version, a fresh output_dir, offline and the execution platform native-test Plan the direct test run An optional test command and the reports it must write, into a fresh report_dir task-command Adjust a task's command An optional replacement command, or observe to ask oyzu to run tool commands and call again once captured-plan Plan an isolated build Build and test intent, from read-only source. No observations or downloads What oyzu keeps for itself: the build version (the plugin must echo it), where output is written, scheduling, tool installation, running processes, collecting artifacts and the report gates. The plugin supplies intent: tasks, requirements, commands, artifact paths and report formats. Report formats are junit, cobertura, lcov, go-cover and jacoco; sources are file, go-test-events, jest-json and jest-lcov. A plugin that needs nonempty with options must declare the build-options feature. A task-command observation names a core tool identity and its command line. Oyzu checks that the tool is one the builder may use and that argv[0] is that tool's command, runs it once on the task's PATH (stdout up to 1 MiB, stderr up to 64 KiB), then calls task-command again in a new process with the results. One round only. A local development binding may not use observations. Artifacts must have unique names and sources (compared without regard to case). A default artifact lives inside output_dir. An artifact marked executable is promoted to .oyzu/bin after a successful build.

Some builds decide their own output location: npm run build writes dist, and the plugin can't steer it into output_dir. For those, the plugin marks the artifact "origin": "target" with a target-relative source, and the build operation runs the task's own command (oyzu sends it as input.task.argv): {"name": "primary", "producer": "build", "kind": "directory", "filename": "application-1.4.0", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "source": "dist", "executable": false, "origin": "target"} Before any build action runs, oyzu checks the source and refuses it otherwise: Rule Refused with It names something below the target: not ., no segment that starts or ends with a dot (.git, .oyzu), is node_modules (any case) or is a Windows device name (con, nul, COM1.txt) PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: … invalid result Sources are unique, ignoring case PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: … invalid result It doesn't equal, contain or lie inside output_dir PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: … overlaps the output directory It doesn't equal, contain or lie inside a file or directory of the target's source selection PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_REFUSED: … overlaps the frozen source selection at <path> No existing segment is a symbolic link or reparse point, and none above the last is a file PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_REFUSED: artifact … names … Oyzu then moves anything already at the path into a fresh directory beside the output (never deleting in place) and discards that directory after collection. The plan records moved paths under extensions["oyzu.dev/retired-outputs"]. A build whose script writes nothing fails with native artifact collection failed rather than republishing an old output. Collection then applies the usual rules: no links, no reserved names. On the native host lane the target directory is a private copy rebuilt from the selected source before each build, so nothing is ever moved there and previous is always false. In an isolated build, the output is moved aside in the private execution workspace, never in your project. To recover from a refusal, name a project output that isn't source, version control state or a dependency tree, and remove any link in its path.

tasks can report native_package with an optional name and version and the file (origin{path,digest,location}) they came from. Oyzu checks that the file is inside the supplied source and that its digest matches. A missing declaration stays unknown, even when the target's version is 0.0.0. The Node plugin reports package.json; the Go plugin doesn't. See version inference.

Targets built by a plugin are reused from the local action cache like other targets. The cache key includes the plugin's executable digest and runtime, so rebuilding the plugin reruns its targets. Bind the executable itself, not a wrapper script, because a script's digest doesn't cover the program it starts (see external builder targets). An unchanged one-module rebuild launches the plugin five times (tasks, requirements, native-admission, native-build, and one task-command per command; two when the command asks for an observation). Launches scale with the number of plugin targets.

A package is the archive described in plugin packages: plugin.json plus one executable per platform. The manifest (schema) requires: Field Meaning identity publisher, name and version. A builder reference is <name>/<profile>. The publisher oyzu is reserved for official releases (see below) protocol_generations Must include v1alpha1 profiles, roles The builder profiles you serve and, per role, the contract and features (for example go-test-events, captured-plan, build-options) runtimes One entry per platform: os (linux, darwin, windows), arch (amd64, arm64), optional abi (gnu, musl, msvc), entrypoint and its SHA-256 digest requirements Baseline tools needed whatever the project contains, with stages and a reason effects What the plugin needs: source-read, output-write, native-process, native-network. These limit what oyzu brokers; they don't remove a native executable's own operating system access provenance Source revision and maintainer Example manifests for each first-party plugin are in the repository. tooling/package-plugin.py in the oyzu repository packages one built executable for the host platform and prints the archive digest: python3 tooling/package-plugin.py --executable target/debug/oyzu-plugin-go --out go.tar.gz # prints sha256:<archive digest> To distribute your plugin through an OCI registry, publish a release root laid out as in the OCI package contract, with a Sigstore signature attached. Users then have two ways to trust it: Bind it by tag. A tag outside ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/ needs a plugins.packages entry with the exact signer identity to require. Binding by digest trusts the digest instead. See OCI sources. List it in an organization catalog. Your organization's tool index can list your package. For a publisher other than oyzu, the signed catalog's digest is the trust. A package named oyzu/* always needs the official signature, on any registry. You can't publish under that publisher yourself.

Before you ship a plugin, run it against the sample requests in the repository. oyzu-plugin-conformance <plugin-executable> docs/contracts/plugins-v1alpha1/examples (from the oyzu repository) sends every request.*.json through oyzu's real plugin launcher, so limits, deadlines and acceptance are the same as in a build. It checks that each result is valid and echoes its request, that the outcomes match the operations describe declares, and that the plugin is stateless (every request runs again in a new process in reverse order and must answer the same). It checks the protocol only. It runs no native tools, so it can't tell you whether your commands build anything. Then try the plugin in a real project through a local binding.

Error Cause Recovery CONFIG_SCOPE: plugins.development is not permitted in this scope The setting is in a project file or profile Move it to user or machine configuration PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID: … cannot read plugin executable The path is missing or not a regular file Build the plugin or fix the path CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: plugins.development A key isn't a short unversioned reference, or a path isn't absolute Use an id such as independent/app and an absolute path PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: observation … which this builder does not admit The plugin asked for an observation with a tool it may not use. Local bindings may use none Return command intent without an observation PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: <id> plugin <path> (<operation>) The plugin failed, answered unsupported, broke the protocol, exited nonzero, wrote no result or ran past its deadline. The cause and the plugin's diagnostics follow Fix the plugin PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED or ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE An isolated build lacks a package feature, platform member, supported profile or engine files. If the plugin also declined the target for the host build, the message ends with ; target <id> was not admitted to the native host lane: <reason> Fix what the reason names, or supply the isolated build prerequisites plugin … sets command env, which the native host lane does not carry yet A build operation or test command carried env Set the environment in the native-build output env. Per-command env isn't supported PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_REFUSED: artifact … names … A project-written artifact overlaps the source, passes through a link, lies below a file, or oyzu couldn't move the previous output aside Name a project output that isn't source and has no link in its path A failed operation fails the build or task. No partial plugin result is used.

A plain oyzu build tries the host build first. If the plugin declines a target, the build continues on the isolated path, as oyzu build --isolated would, with the engine that path mounts. Without an [engine] pin in oyzu.lock or an installed engine, a Linux oyzu mounts its own executable (see execution image); on Windows and macOS the build stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE and how to install the Linux engine (oyzu engine install --linux). A pinned engine is installed only by an explicit isolated build, so a plain build with a pin stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE naming the pin and oyzu build --isolated. If the isolated path can't take the target either (a raw executable binding has no isolated package, for example), the build fails during preparation, before any build action or tool installation, with the code above and the plugin's reason. The message lists every target the plugin kept off the host build, not only the first. A plugin that fails native-admission is named the same way. Human and --json output carry the same message. oyzu build --plan doesn't fail; its "Unresolved until preparation" list (unresolved in JSON) adds a Target <id> was not admitted to the native host lane: <reason> line for each one. With --isolated or --all-platforms, oyzu selects the engine first without launching plugins, so you see the engine's own refusal until an engine is available: ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH for a pin no admitted engine archive supplies, or ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE on a host that can't mount itself. After that, a target that can't be planned fails with its PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED message and the same clauses. This asks each selected plugin for native-admission once if it isn't cached, and a hanging plugin can cost its full 60-second deadline per target.

A binding runs the named executable with your user's permissions whenever oyzu discovers a workspace. Bind only executables you built or trust. The recorded digest says which bytes ran; it isn't a signature and grants nothing. The plugin gets no credentials and no inherited environment.

The Go plugin builds only go/app with one module and one package main on the host. go/library and workspaces keep task execution through the plugin, but oyzu build refuses them. Per-command env in native-build operations and the native-test command is refused. Observation commands are matched by tool short name (go for oyzu:go) on the task's PATH. Oyzu doesn't verify that the resolved file belongs to the locked tool. Ctrl-C (or SIGTERM and SIGHUP on Unix) stops a running plugin and its child processes. oyzu build reports a cancelled build. If oyzu run or oyzu build --plan ends from a signal, the private copy of the bound executable (an oyzu-plugin-* temporary directory) isn't removed. Diagnostics from successful operations aren't shown.

The Python plugin (python/package) builds pip and pyproject.toml projects into wheels with pytest and Ruff checks, using the same binding. It adds no installer, PATH change or PYTHONPATH bridge: dependencies, pytest, coverage and quality tools must already be in the project's environment, and a target-local .venv is used when present. A mismatched environment is refused. Direct oyzu run tasks don't use this binding. Tested on Linux amd64 (GNU). No Python plugin is published yet. See Python preparation and, for the isolated path, captured pip Python packages.

The Node plugin serves node/app for npm, pnpm and Yarn (Classic and Berry). It's experimental and isn't published yet, so you supply the package or a local binding. The host build takes a node/app target that is declared with uses: node/app, isn't a workspace root, and has a non-empty scripts.build that writes dist. Anything else is refused with the plugin's reason, and because a plugin-served id has no fallback, that target can't build until it's changed or the binding is removed. Workspace projects and package output are covered on npm workspaces, pnpm, Yarn and plugin packages. It builds on Windows and Linux x86-64. Windows ARM64, macOS and Linux ARM64 aren't tested.

Action Command When <target>:install npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, Yarn Classic yarn install --frozen-lockfile or Berry yarn install --immutable. Offline handling follows the manager The project has dependencies, devDependencies or optionalDependencies <target>:build The selected build task, normally <manager> run build Always <target>:test Your test script, or the detected default Tests are selected <target>:lint Your lint script, or the native ESLint or Biome adapter Lint is selected <target>:format-check or <target>:format:check Your check script, or the native Prettier or Biome adapter Format is selected. A script that changes files is never selected The shared check levels decide which checks run, and --full runs every check that isn't off. Your own scripts win over the defaults. format:check, build:prod and similar names are kept; unsupported names fail discovery with an explicit error. An authored install task in oyzu.toml replaces npm ci, and disabling the install stage drops it. Authored tasks run with your ambient environment, not oyzu's pinned tools, so an authored npm ci can fail where the plugin's own install works (on Linux without a global npm: cannot execute npm: No such file or directory). The artifact is the dist directory your build script writes (project-written outputs), named application-<version> from the version oyzu resolved (0.0.0-dev.g<source hash> for an unversioned checkout), not the version in package.json.

Dependencies need the manager's lock file, or planning fails before any action with a diagnostic like node.lock-file: host npm dependency preparation requires package-lock.json; create it with npm before building. npm: package-lock.json (an npm-shrinkwrap.json alone isn't enough). pnpm: pnpm-lock.yaml. A stale lock fails the install (--frozen-lockfile) and isn't rewritten. Update it with pnpm, then retry. Yarn: yarn.lock.

If packageManager is present it must be an exact stable release such as pnpm@10.11.0. Oyzu checks it against explicit tool configuration, and a conflicting release fails before any action. Ranges, tags and prereleases are refused. Without packageManager, select pnpm in [tools]. A pnpm-workspace.yaml that contains only settings is allowed. A packages key, or anything oyzu can't classify as settings, makes the project a workspace and it's refused. Competing manager evidence is also refused. pnpm owns install scripts and their policy. Oyzu adds no script approval. Offline builds add --offline and need the dependencies already in pnpm's own store. Missing bytes fail without going online. This is the host's ordinary pnpm configuration and store, not a hermetic replay, and --no-cache doesn't clear it.

Accepted exact releases: yarn@1.22.22 (Classic) and yarn@4.17.1 (Berry). Berry needs nodeLinker: node-modules in .yarnrc.yml (a quoted value is fine). Plug'n'Play is refused. See managed Yarn. Direct tests need dependencies installed in the source project. A full build installs into a private workspace. For Berry, run oyzu exec -- yarn install --immutable, then oyzu run test. Not supported: isolated Yarn builds, extra rc settings, workspaces on this path, project plugins, yarnPath, custom registries and non-registry sources.

An npm project whose build script is recognized vite build, with an optional literal --outDir, Vite as a dependency and a native Vite 8 configuration, builds as an application. Oyzu keeps the npm lifecycle around one Vite build and stages the output after the native postbuild step. Tested with Vite 8.3.3. Other Vite flags, pnpm or Yarn with Vite, SSR, library and multi-environment builds, and watch or no-write modes aren't supported. See Node applications.

For non-workspace npm, pnpm and Yarn targets, oyzu run test adds JUnit and LCOV reporting to a default node --test, to flag-only test scripts it recognizes, and to exact vitest and vitest run commands. See Vitest and Jest for those frameworks (Vitest was tested with npm and Vitest 5.0.3; Jest with npm and Jest 29.7.0). The matching coverage provider must already be installed, because oyzu doesn't download it. pnpm and Yarn pass reporter flags directly after <manager> run test, with no npm-style -- separator. Other test commands run unchanged. They can write to OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT or to report paths you declare. A missing optional report makes the evidence incomplete. A missing required report, a malformed report or a failing test fails the command. Workspace tests and other managers fail with node.test-lane. Lint and format checks use your project's installed ESLint, Prettier or Biome. A directory you point OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME at can supply packages the project doesn't declare. A declared but uninstalled package fails instead of falling back. Native configuration and ignore files are authoritative. oyzu run format changes source; format-check doesn't. To run a named task such as format:check, use oyzu run app:format:check or [tasks."app:format:check"]. Environment defaults from native files go through the normal configuration and policy checks; reserved OYZU_* names stay unavailable.

This section is for people working on the oyzu repository itself. Releases use the shared package store instead. tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh builds the CLI, native shim, Rust plugin and Node plugin (this repository declares both a cli and a docs build, so both builders must resolve before oyzu build cli). It compiles with the pinned Rust, locked and offline, and honors CARGO_TARGET_DIR and CARGO_BUILD_TARGET. It needs no Python, Node or jq just to read configuration; only the read-back in the CI machine binding below uses Python. On a machine with no user configuration file and no existing plugin choices, the script writes the two development bindings to .oyzu/bootstrap/config.toml and prints the OYZU_USER_CONFIG export (or records it through CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, or through GITHUB_ENV for later GitHub Actions steps). It doesn't touch your own user configuration, project or local files, or shell profiles. If any step fails, it removes the file it created. Running it again with the same unchanged file prints Reusing this checkout's unchanged bootstrap USER file and the same export. If you already have a user configuration file or other plugin choices, the script refuses instead of merging. Bind the two plugins yourself, then run it again; with both present it passes them through. From the checkout root: oyzu=.oyzu/bin/oyzu # .oyzu/bin/oyzu.exe on Windows bin="$(pwd -W 2>/dev/null || pwd)/.oyzu/bin" "$oyzu" config set --global plugins.development.rust/app "$bin/oyzu-plugin-rust" # add .exe on Windows "$oyzu" config set --global plugins.development.node/app "$bin/oyzu-plugin-node" # add .exe on Windows tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh Or edit the user file by hand: [plugins.development] "rust/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/.oyzu/bin/oyzu-plugin-rust" "node/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/.oyzu/bin/oyzu-plugin-node" In CI the user file is ignored, so the script refuses fresh user setup there; a CI job uses the machine binding below instead.

Pass --ci-machine-binding (used by the repository's own setup action and release workflows) to bind the two plugins in machine configuration on a GitHub Actions runner (GITHUB_ACTIONS=true; anywhere else the switch does nothing). Before the configuration check above, the script: Checks that the runner is ephemeral: a GitHub-hosted runner (RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT=github-hosted), or a runner image that declares itself ephemeral with a root-owned, read-only /etc/oyzu-runner-ephemeral and provides a machine directory owned by the runner user, as the repository's self-hosted runner image does with /etc/oyzu. Owning the machine directory alone isn't enough. Otherwise it fails and writes nothing. Refuses an existing machine config.toml or an existing plugin copy. It never merges into or replaces machine configuration. Builds both plugins from source (and the CLI too, unless a published release's oyzu is in use) and copies oyzu-plugin-rust and oyzu-plugin-node into the machine directory's plugins/ folder: /etc/oyzu/plugins on Linux, /Library/Application Support/Oyzu/plugins on macOS (both with sudo on a GitHub-hosted runner) and %ProgramData%\Oyzu\plugins on Windows. The checkout's own executables are never bound. Creates the machine config.toml with only [plugins.development] entries for rust/app and node/app naming those copies. Reads the configuration back with oyzu --json config explain plugins.development (parsed with Python, which GitHub-hosted runners and the runner image provide) and requires exactly those two values, from machine scope only. The configuration check must then report the choices complete (unchanged), or the script fails. Machine configuration isn't personal configuration, so CI keeps it. The binding lasts as long as the runner, and a GitHub-hosted runner or runner container is discarded after its job. This applies only to these executable bindings on ephemeral runners. A refused run keeps the executables it built in .oyzu/bin. If it used an oyzu already on your PATH, it built nothing, so check that both plugin files exist. Remove those entries to stop using the checkout's plugins; the script never edits or removes them.
Plugin packages, the store and lock selections Plugin catalog and builder selection Go builder preview Configuration

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu plugins shows which plugins the catalogs offer, which are installed, and which one each target in your project uses and why. Inspection never installs or runs anything and never changes a file. Note: Plugins are experimental. oyzu plugins search go oyzu plugins versions go/app oyzu plugins explain For catalogs, detection and the build's Selection section, see plugin catalog. For the store and oyzu.lock records, see plugin packages. To change a locked selection, use oyzu plugins update. To clean up revoked copies, use oyzu plugins prune.

Command Shows oyzu plugins search [QUERY] [--type build] The uses references the catalogs offer, with package, capability, description, newest stable version, the version oyzu build would pick, and status. oyzu plugins versions REFERENCE Every known release of a reference, labelled, with why each can or can't be selected here. oyzu plugins info REFERENCE[@VERSION] One release: package, publisher, contracts, profiles, platforms, payload digests, download routes and what is verified. oyzu plugins list Releases installed in the plugin store, with the references that name them. A release a catalog has withdrawn or revoked is marked (withdrawn) or (revoked) (JSON catalogStatus). oyzu plugins current This project's locked selections: installed or not, still eligible or not, the update candidate, and one line per plugin-backed target. oyzu plugins explain [TARGET] Why each target uses its plugin, and how to change it.

Option Meaning --json One JSON object on standard output. Before or after the subcommand. --store DIR The plugin store to read, as for oyzu build --store. --refresh Update the cached catalog first. Never downloads a plugin. --offline Never use the network. Can't be combined with --refresh. --type build Filter search by capability. build is the only value. The commands work in any folder. Outside a project, search, versions, info and list work as usual, and current and explain find no targets.

search, versions and info read the same catalog a build uses (see the catalog snapshot): the verified official catalog, or your organization's catalog, which replaces it. A version shown as selectable is one a build can select. Mode Behavior default Uses the cached catalog. Nothing is fetched. --refresh Updates the catalog cache first. The official catalog is fetched only when plugins.preview is on, as for builds. --offline Never fetches. Anything not cached is shown as unavailable, with the reason. An expired catalog is shown as history only: eligibility is reported as snapshot expired, and current shows it as unknown. Its withdrawals still apply. A catalog that failed verification isn't shown; you're told why no catalog is usable. Search covers the official and organization catalogs only; it doesn't crawl OCI registries. A plugin you name directly (in uses: or plugins.packages) can work without being listed. Under an organization catalog the official one isn't consulted, so a company replacement shows as its own package (for example acme/go for go/app).

oyzu plugins prune removes plugin releases from your local store after a catalog has revoked them. You name each release by its exact digest. Without --apply, it only previews. oyzu plugins list --refresh --store /path/to/store oyzu plugins prune sha256:<64-lowercase-hex-digits> --store /path/to/store oyzu plugins prune sha256:<64-lowercase-hex-digits> --apply --store /path/to/store Each argument must be sha256: and exactly 64 lowercase hex digits. Copy it from the list output. Only a current revocation of that exact release allows removal. A withdrawal, a release missing from the catalog, an expired catalog or unavailable metadata doesn't. Prune uses the cached catalog only. Run plugins list --refresh first if you need a newer one. --apply checks eligibility again; an earlier preview doesn't count. There's no whole-store scan, no force option, and builds, updates and inspection never prune on their own. A release in use by a running Oyzu command is kept. So is one with uncertain identity, malformed metadata or unreadable files. Project lock files aren't changed. If a project still locks a pruned release, Oyzu can install an eligible release again the normal way. See store maintenance. With --json, the result is kind: "plugin-prune" with apply, store, the catalog used, and releases (each with release, state and reason): State Meaning eligible Preview: revoked, identity matches and not in use. retained Not removed. The reason says why. removed The release and its metadata were removed (including leftovers from an interrupted earlier removal). absent Nothing of the release remains. incomplete Removal started but an operating-system error or an outside change stopped it. Some files may be gone. Fix the reported error; you may need to clean up the remaining files by hand. Preview exits 0 when it returns a result. --apply exits 1 if any release is retained or incomplete, otherwise 0. Invalid digests fail before anything is opened. Each release is handled independently.

Label Meaning latest-stable Newest release that isn't a prerelease or withdrawn. It may be incompatible or outside your adopted major version. latest-compatible Newest stable release that fits this engine and host: contract, builder profile, support status and platform. update-candidate Newest selectable release inside the major version your project has locked. adoption-candidate What oyzu build would adopt now, for a reference your project doesn't lock yet. locked The release oyzu.lock holds. A compatible major version 3 can be latest-stable and latest-compatible for a project locked to major 1; it shows outside the adopted major 1 and is never the update candidate. A prerelease shows preview only unless plugins.preview is on, and is never a default. Reasons (in JSON reasons): withdrawn, revoked, preview only, stable releases come from the official catalog, unsupported, no supported protocol generation, no such builder profile, no payload for this platform, outside the adopted major N, snapshot expired. Compatibility is checked for the running engine and this host only. A requested [engine] pin is shown separately (JSON requestedPin, human "Engine pin"), but its capabilities aren't guessed. Remote worker platforms aren't checked, and the output says so.

explain shows the same record oyzu build prints in its Selection section, for every plugin-backed target, followed by what it was checked against. With --json: { "kind": "plugin-explain", "target", "evaluation", "coverage", "lock", "selection" }. coverage.choice (also selection.catalogChoice) says which catalog was used: Value Meaning published The official catalog. organization Your organization's catalog. no-index toolIndex.url = false, so there is no catalog. official-unavailable The official catalog was never fetched, failed verification or expired. coverage.unavailable gives the reason. Two states appear only in inspection, because a build would act on them: state Meaning not-adopted A release is selected but oyzu.lock has no entry yet. The next oyzu build records it. not-installed oyzu.lock selects a release that isn't in the store, and a source for it is known. The next online, non-frozen oyzu build installs it without changing the lock. JSON route (and the explain human view) names the source. Where a build would fail, explain and current fail with the same error: Error Cause PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE The locked release isn't in the store and no binding or catalog entry supplies it. PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH A binding names a different release from the lock. PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE A catalog release isn't in the store and has no download route. PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE The catalog failed verification. PLUGIN_DETECTION_CONFLICT Two detections match the same folder. The error shows the smallest build.yaml selector that settles it. oyzu build --plan never downloads. With an empty store it stops with PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE; the message mentions --offline even if you didn't pass it. For a selection you disagree with, the output lists the same fixes as a build: declare the target in build.yaml (or set uses:), bind a different package, undo an adoption, or pin a tool in oyzu.toml. A plugin's tool requirements come from running the plugin, which inspection never does. So tools is absent from the JSON, the human view says deferred, and a generic oyzu pin <tool>@<version> suggestion appears instead. oyzu build lists the real tools. current returns { "kind": "plugin-current", "evaluation", "coverage", "lock", "locked", "selection" }. lock has path, exists, selections and enginePin. Each locked entry has the reference, package, major, version, release, installed, eligible (null when no usable catalog lists it), reasons, latestStable, latestCompatible and updateCandidate. A newer release in the store doesn't change what oyzu.lock selects. list shows both; current shows the locked one.

list reads <store>/plugins/* and shows package, version, release digest, profiles, platforms, the references that name each release, and whether this project locks it. It can't tell which other projects use a release; the store doesn't track that.

Human output leads with the outcome and uses aligned tables that wrap without losing text on narrow terminals. Meaning never depends on color. --json prints one object per command, and errors use the usual error shape. Human and JSON output always agree.

Code Cause PLUGIN_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN No catalog lists that reference. The error names what is listed. PLUGIN_VERSION_UNKNOWN No release matches the version you asked for. PLUGIN_TARGET_UNKNOWN No plugin-backed target has that name or path. Build resolution errors (PLUGIN_DETECTION_CONFLICT, PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED and others) are reported unchanged.

Inspection doesn't run the platform and package checks a build runs when it installs a plugin. A release already in the store that this host can't run shows as not-adopted, where a build would fail with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED. A bound source that isn't installed isn't opened or checked. Only the host platform is evaluated, not remote workers. --type has one value, build. Organization policy beyond the catalog's own withdrawals isn't shown. The official catalog is refreshed only with plugins.preview on. Inspection is supported on Linux. prune is supported on Linux and Windows. macOS isn't supported yet.
Plugin catalog Plugin packages Updating plugins

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-packages.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A plugin package is the archive that holds a builder plugin: its manifest and one executable per platform. Oyzu verifies a package, installs it into a plugin store, pins the exact release in oyzu.lock and launches it for your builds. This page covers where packages come from, how they're verified, how they're locked and how builds record them. Note: Plugins are experimental. Builders are not built into the CLI, so every target needs a package. A package comes from the plugin catalog, from a plugins.packages binding, or from a direct oci:// reference. Only the Go preview is published. For the other first-party builders, build the package yourself and bind it, or use a development binding.
documents.s: Plugin packages, the plugin store and lock selections

documents.t: A package is a .tar.gz or .zip archive containing: plugin.json at the root, the plugin manifest (schema); the platform executables that the manifest's runtimes name by entrypoint. Installation refuses a package that: hashes to a different digest than the one configured (checked before extraction); exceeds the archive bounds (512 MiB archive; at most 4096 entries, 1 GiB extracted, 512 MiB per file, depth 16, expansion ratio 100), or contains path traversal, absolute paths, hard links, symbolic links that leave the payload, or non-portable names. Relative symbolic links inside the payload are allowed, but an entrypoint must be a regular file; has no valid plugin.json, or one with unknown fields. Fields that name another plugin (dependencies, preferences, successors) are unknown fields, so a plugin can't depend on another plugin; names an entrypoint that's missing, isn't a regular file, or whose SHA-256 differs from the manifest's runtimes[].digest; isn't the package the bound reference names (go/app needs package name go with builder profile app), or supports no protocol generation v1alpha1. Nothing in a package runs during installation. There are no install hooks. To build a package for development, see plugin development.

A binding tells oyzu which package serves a builder reference. Set it in user, machine or administrative configuration, never in a project file or profile (CONFIG_SCOPE): [plugins.packages] "go/app" = { archive = "/home/me/plugins/go-0.1.0.tar.gz", sha256 = "sha256:…" } # or "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0" } Keys are short references without a major selector (go/app), or exact direct OCI target references. At most 64 entries. archive is an absolute path. sha256 is sha256: plus 64 lowercase hex digits and must match the archive. A reference can be bound by plugins.packages or by plugins.development, not both (PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID). A binding applies only to the references your project's targets use. A Go binding never affects a Python or Rust project, and writes no lock entry for it. If the archive digest equals the release digest of the release the catalog selects, the binding is that release's local archive route, and the package must also be the catalog's package and version. Any other digest is a local package binding. Neither can bypass a catalog's withdrawal: a binding for a withdrawn or revoked release is refused with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN or PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED before it's recorded or launched. Oyzu records how each OCI or HTTPS release was accepted (including whether it's a preview) alongside the installed release. A damaged record is an error; an older installation without one is treated as an ordinary release.

A uses entry in build.yaml can name an OCI release and builder profile directly: builds: app: uses: oci://registry.example/team/opaque@sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa#app The repository path says nothing about which package it is. Oyzu reads the package's own plugin.json, checks the requested profile, protocol and engine features, and records the original URI, the real package and version, and the release root in oyzu.lock. A digest must equal the bound and locked release. A tag is resolved once, when the selection is adopted. Later builds use the locked root and never resolve the tag again. A tag outside the official namespace needs a plugins.packages binding keyed by the complete URI, with the signer to require (see OCI sources). If you later remove that binding, an already installed release still replays without a registry request, but a missing one can't be downloaded until you restore the binding. A configured archive can supply a direct digest only when the archive's digest equals that release. A URI doesn't bypass a refused catalog, a withdrawal or the preview rules. A package named oyzu/* on any registry needs the official signature (below). HTTPS is a catalog route, not a uses syntax.

A binding can name a release in an OCI 1.1 registry, such as GHCR, a distribution registry or Harbor, whose token endpoint (if any) is on the registry's own origin. The release is laid out as the Oyzu OCI package contract defines: an immutable release root binding the plugin manifest and one manifest per platform payload, with a detached Sigstore signature attached to the root. [plugins.packages] # Official release by tag: signed by oyzuai/oyzu's plugin-release.yml. "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0" } # Another registry by tag: say whose signature to require. "go/app" = { oci = "registry.example.com/team/go:1.2.0", identity = "https://github.com/acme/plugins/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" } # By digest: the digest is the trust (no signature is checked unless identity is set # or the reference is in the official namespace). "go/app" = { oci = "registry.example.com/team/go@sha256:…" } Field Value Meaning oci registry/repository:tag or registry/repository@sha256:<hex>, no scheme The release root. A tag and a digest together are refused identity https:// certificate identity (SAN URI) The signer the root signature must come from: a GitHub Actions workflow identity on a GitHub-hosted runner, as with toolIndex.identity. Required for a tag outside ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/. Refused for an official reference trustedRoot Absolute path A Sigstore trusted_root.json that replaces the production root (for a private Sigstore deployment). Needs a signer. Refused for an official reference

A reference under ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/ (also written ghcr.io:443/…) is official. It must be signed by exactly https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/.github/workflows/plugin-release.yml@refs/heads/main, issued by GitHub Actions OIDC on a GitHub-hosted runner and verified against Sigstore's production trusted root. A copy of the workflow on another branch signs as @refs/heads/<branch> and is refused. An official binding with identity or trustedRoot is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Configuration can't replace the official signer or let a private CA vouch for it. Any other tag without identity is also CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, when configuration loads. A release found through a catalog (no binding) follows the package's publisher instead: publisher oyzu needs the same official signer on every route, a company mirror included, and any other publisher is trusted by the digest the signed catalog lists. See Who may sign a release. A package named oyzu/* needs the official signature and production root on any network OCI route, even on an arbitrary registry or digest.

On a glibc Linux host, when a release has no payload without an ABI or for gnu, oyzu uses the musl payload for that architecture. Musl payloads must be statically linked. A dynamically linked musl entrypoint is refused on a glibc host with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, naming the loader it needs. A package this machine can't run is refused before it's installed. The official Linux payloads are static musl.
documents.s: Choosing a payload for your machine

documents.t: Downloading runs only where an archive would be read: a real oyzu build adopting a selection, or installing a locked release that's missing from the store. It needs no Docker, ORAS, crane or login. Oyzu speaks the OCI Distribution API itself, anonymously, following a registry's Bearer challenge to its token endpoint without credentials, as public GHCR packages allow. A loopback registry (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1) uses plain HTTP; every other registry uses HTTPS through your configured proxy and certificate trust. It fetches, in order: The release root, by the locked digest, the binding's digest, or (only at first selection) the tag. The digest is the SHA-256 of the bytes received, never a registry header. The signature, when one is required: referrers of the root, through the referrers API or the sha256-<hex> referrers tag. Each Sigstore bundle is verified against the root digest, the signer and the trusted root until one verifies. The metadata manifest and plugin manifest, checked against the bound reference. The manifest and payload for this platform only. Other platforms are never downloaded. Every object must hash to its descriptor before use, and the extracted entrypoint must match its manifest digest. Only then is the release published into the store. Moving a tag afterwards changes nothing, because later builds, --frozen replays and reinstalls into an empty store use the locked digest. An archive digest and a root digest never match, so switching a binding from an archive to OCI is an explicit re-adoption (PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH). Not supported: registries whose token endpoint is on another host (Docker Hub's auth.docker.io); credentials for private registries. A private package fails with PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE; payloads over 512 MiB (a payload is held in memory); organization route settings (list a mirror as a catalog route instead), a command that fills a mirror, and offline export or import.

A verified catalog release can list a route such as {"type":"https","url":"https://mirror.example/plugins/go.tar.gz"}. The URL serves a tar or gzip tar of a standard OCI image layout: oci-layout, index.json and blobs/sha256/<hex> at the archive root. The index names the catalog's exact release root and any detached signature manifests. See the layout contract. Unlike a local plugins.packages archive, the lock and the installed directory use the canonical OCI root digest, not the hash of the transport archive. Changing a release from an OCI route to an HTTPS mirror of the same root keeps the lock valid. Oyzu checks the layout, blob digests, descriptor sizes, metadata, the selected runtime and the extracted entrypoint before installing. Publisher oyzu still needs its fixed GitHub-hosted release signer and the production Sigstore root. The mirror carries the original signature unchanged. Other publishers use the root digest the signed catalog lists. A catalog can't name another signer. The transport uses your configured proxy and SSL_CERT_FILE. HTTPS is required even for loopback. URLs can't carry credentials, a query or a fragment, and redirects must stay within the same origin and directory. Downloads are anonymous and limited to 256 MiB. The whole archive is downloaded, even if it includes other platforms; only your platform's payload is installed. Extraction uses the archive limits above and refuses links and unexpected paths. An installed release needs no archive request. --offline makes no request. --frozen can refresh catalog metadata but never downloads this route. Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE (a PEM file containing the inspection CA). This adds TLS trust only. It never changes the official signer, the production Sigstore root, the route or the locked release. Loopback destinations bypass proxies. Go builds through an inspecting proxy have been tested on Linux and Windows; see acquisition transport. A failed route is PLUGIN_ROUTE_FAILED. Invalid contents keep PLUGIN_PACKAGE_DIGEST or PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID, and missing signatures keep their signature errors. Builds never choose a newer release to recover from unavailable content. Restore the route or the exact content.

Packages live in the tool store (--store, default the shared user store) under plugins/<hex>/, where <hex> is the release digest (the archive digest, or the OCI release root digest). Releases sit side by side, and a build uses the payload for your platform. Concurrent first builds extract once. A release is published with an atomic rename, so nobody sees a partial extraction. A shared lease on the release is held for the whole command to protect a running executable (this matters on Windows). An installed release is trusted. Later builds don't hash it again, and only a missing release needs the archive.

oyzu plugins prune removes a revoked release from your store. It previews by default and needs --apply to remove anything. It acts only on exact digests you name, and only when the current verified cached catalog revokes that release. It doesn't refresh the catalog. A withdrawal, or an expired or unverified revocation, never allows deletion. It takes the store's lock for the release, then an exclusive use lease, so a release in use by another oyzu command is kept. On Windows it also checks that no process has the executable open. Uncertain, malformed, linked or inaccessible content is kept. If the operating system interrupts removal, the result says incomplete, not retained. It touches only plugins/<hex> and the release's package-contents/plugin-<hex>.json. Other releases, catalogs, installed tools, the permanent locks/plugin-<hex> files and every project lock stay as they are. It doesn't check whether other projects' locks name the release. A normal build can download it again if a later selection allows it. To recover a project that still selects a revoked release, adopt an eligible one with oyzu plugins update. Pruning never changes a selection.

The first time oyzu resolves a plugin for a project, it appends the selection to oyzu.lock in the project root. Existing records, comments and ordering aren't touched. [[plugin]] reference = "go/app" profile = "app" package = "oyzu/go" major = 0 version = "0.1.0" release = "sha256:…" [[plugin.payloads]] os = "linux" arch = "amd64" digest = "sha256:…" Field Meaning reference, profile The builder reference and its profile package The publisher/name of the package major The major version of the manifest, set at first resolution version The exact release version release The archive digest, or the OCI release root digest payloads The executable digest per platform from the plugin manifest. For an OCI release, every platform the root lists The lock never records local paths, download times or the platform of the machine that wrote it. oyzu pin and other tool commands keep [[plugin]] entries. A lock that holds only a plugin selection doesn't count as pinned tools: your first oyzu build still pins the tools the builders need. Only a real oyzu build (not --plan or --check) can install a bound package and record a selection. Only oyzu plugins update can install a release to replace a selection that's already locked. Every other command that discovers the project replays the lock and the store and writes nothing. Situation What happens Bound, not locked, oyzu build Installs the package, records the selection, builds Bound, not locked, any other command PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED. Nothing is installed or written. Run oyzu build Locked, release installed Reuses it. The archive isn't read Locked, release missing, binding present oyzu build installs it from the binding (an archive, or an OCI reference fetched by the locked digest), only if the binding names the locked release. Other commands report PLUGIN_NOT_INSTALLED Locked, release missing, no binding An online, non-frozen oyzu build downloads that exact release from its entry in the current verified catalog, without changing the lock. An unlisted release or an absent or expired catalog gives PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE. A refused catalog gives PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE. A listed release with no usable route gives PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE. A plugins.development binding for the reference still replaces the locked package Locked, release missing, no binding, --frozen or --offline PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE. Nothing is downloaded and the lock isn't rewritten. Prepare the release online first Binding names a different release than the lock PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH. Builds never change a selection. Use oyzu plugins update <reference> Installed release differs from the lock PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE oyzu build --frozen, selection missing PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING. Nothing is resolved, installed or written. Restore a complete lock, or adopt with a normal oyzu build where your policy allows it. Removing --frozen never waives policy oyzu build --frozen, selection present Replays it. Missing content can still be installed from a bound local archive, but never from an OCI binding or a catalog route Two builds of one project at once The second is refused ("another oyzu build is using this workspace") Lock this oyzu can't parse, with [[plugin]] visible in it Discovery refuses with the lock error rather than guess tasks for a project whose package it can't know Lock with sections or fields this oyzu doesn't know Refused before anything changes ("use the oyzu release that wrote it") Builds of different projects that share a store converge: a build that loses a race on the lock reuses the pins the other build published, or retries for up to 30 seconds, instead of failing with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. Offline native builds also need their ordinary tool metadata in the same user context. oyzu tools check --catalog --json seeds the signed tool index into the default user metadata store; add --store DIR to target another store. An explicit plugin store doesn't replace the default metadata that native Go reads for its locked-version withdrawal check. Prepare both while online. A catalog revocation refuses installed releases, even when replaying against an expired catalog. Selection refusal doesn't delete bytes; use oyzu plugins prune. @vN major selectors in bindings aren't supported.

Every build records the engine that ran it: the version token of oyzu --version (for example 0.1.0-local.36bdcec27267, without the profile, target and timestamp). It appears as Engine in the build Context and in the retained inventory. You can pin it by hand: [engine] identity = "0.1.0-local.36bdcec27267" A protected administrative policy can require this pin and a complete lock (policy-required pins). CI alone doesn't make the pin mandatory. If the pinned engine isn't the one running, oyzu uses engine staging before discovering the project, when an allowed user or system source provides the archive. Otherwise it fails with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH. A development override keeps the running executable and records its actual content and the bypassed pin. A package lists the engine features it needs (such as go-test-events or captured-plan). If the running oyzu lacks one, the build fails with PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT before any plugin operation, naming the missing feature and the running engine. Use an oyzu that supports it, or a compatible plugin release. The catalog skips releases whose required features oyzu doesn't support.

A package's entrypoint runs in place from the store, where its digest was verified at installation. A plugins.development executable is copied to a private per-command file and hashed as it's copied, so the recorded digest is that of the file as launched. Replacing the source afterwards changes nothing in the running command. The copy is removed when the command ends. If oyzu is killed by a signal, the copy stays in the temporary directory as oyzu-plugin-*; delete it by hand. For a wrapper script, the digest covers only the script, not the program it starts, so its targets are never reused from the action cache. Bind the plugin executable itself. Action cache keys include the plugin's identity (reference, release, version, executable digest and runtime), recorded on each target as extensions["oyzu.dev/builder-plugin"]; see external builder targets. Every plan, execution envelope and manifest of a build or oyzu run carries extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"] when a plugin is used, so plugin-built output is distinguishable from other output: {"reference":"go/app","source":"package","package":"oyzu/go","version":"0.1.0", "release":"sha256:…","executableDigest":"sha256:…","selection":"adopted"} {"reference":"go/app","source":"local-development", "executableName":"plugin","executableDigest":"sha256:…"} A development record keeps only the executable's file name, never your absolute path. Nothing refuses to publish plugin-built output; the record makes it visible. oyzu inspect requires the records in the plan, manifest and envelope to be identical (see build bundles). oyzu run --store DIR, oyzu scan --store DIR and oyzu lock --store DIR move the plugin store with the tool store, as oyzu build --store DIR does. The set of bindings is fixed by the first discovery in a command. If a later discovery in the same command asks for different bindings (another executable, changed bytes or another reference), it fails with PLUGIN_BINDING_CONFLICT.
documents.s: Which bytes run, and how output records them

documents.t: --isolated builds run in a sandbox with no network, in Docker or the Linux daemonless sandbox. The plugin plans the build without running it (the captured-plan feature), and oyzu does everything that needs the network or a toolchain: it installs the locked tools and dependencies, then runs the plan offline. Note: Isolated builds with plugins are experimental and are limited to Linux amd64 targets. An isolated build with a plugin needs all of these: A package whose manifest declares captured-plan and has runtime members for both your host and the Linux execution platform. One member can serve both when the platforms match. For an isolated build, exactly one member must match the image's OS and architecture; none or several refuse selection. An accepted engine archive and a usable immutable Linux image. The locked tools for that platform. A raw development executable binding can't run an isolated build. Any missing piece fails explicitly with PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED or ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE, and oyzu never falls back to another builder. The plugin supplies build, artifact and test report intent; it can't fetch dependencies in this role. JUnit and coverage reports stay required checks.

Supported: one conventional Go application module with one main package, with a Linux artifact and execution platform declared in build.yaml. oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full Add --no-docker to require the daemonless sandbox. On Linux amd64, a normal build adopts the package selection. Commit the complete oyzu.lock, then use --frozen to replay it, and add --offline when every exact input is retained. A missing input fails without using the network. --full produces the executable with native JUnit and Go coverage. Go libraries, workspaces, missing capabilities and unsupported execution settings fail explicitly.

Supported: python/package targets built with pip and PEP 517. The package must declare captured-plan. No Python plugin is published yet, so you supply the package and bind it yourself. oyzu -C <fixture> --json build demo --isolated --full --frozen --no-cache --jobs 1 Oyzu freezes the selected CPython archive and the prepared dependencies, then lowers the plugin's intent to a wheel or sdist build. Put tool versions in native pin files or oyzu.toml, not in build.yaml. Installed-artifact tests and quality reports are required checks. Python builds with uv, Poetry or legacy distributions don't use this path. A refusal never falls back to another builder. See Python preparation.

Supported: npm node/app applications. The package must declare captured-plan. The Node plugin is not published yet, so you supply the package. oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen --image npm=<node-image> Oyzu prepares the locked Node and npm archives and dependencies and runs an offline install before the plugin's build and check steps. JUnit and LCOV reports are required. A dist directory written by your project is moved aside in the private workspace before the build and exported with the usual containment checks. Select tools in oyzu.toml (they resolve into oyzu.lock). The image must be one your engine can run; a bare image without the right runtime fails explicitly. Yarn, workspaces and frameworks need their own pages (Yarn, npm workspaces, pnpm). pnpm applications use the same flow with --image pnpm=<node-image>. Export of the native pnpm store currently needs exactly pnpm 10.11.0, selected in packageManager or the tool configuration, with pnpm-lock.yaml and oyzu.lock up to date. The default base execution image is enough: the YAML parser the pnpm adapter needs (yaml 2.9.1, ISC license, shipped with its license) comes in the Node plugin package. An image you pass with --image pnpm=<ref> must meet the bring-your-own requirements.

Supported: a single-root npm project that produces a .tgz through npm pack. Oyzu uses this path when build.yaml has uses: node/package, or when there's no build.yaml and the project's output facts select a package: builds: package: {uses: node/package} oyzu build package --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen --image npm=<node-image> oyzu inspect dist You need a package.json with a package name, a current npm lock, selected Node and npm tools, the required checks and a matching package that declares captured-plan. With no build.yaml, the command is oyzu -C <project> --json build --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image npm=<node-image>. Dependencies are installed offline. Oyzu applies the build's resolved version to a private copy of package.json and the lock, runs your build script and checks, then runs npm pack --json --ignore-scripts. Your checkout and its locks are not changed. A package with no build script skips the build step. Read the artifact's path, version and digest from its recorded manifest. Don't guess the file name npm produced. Failed tests or missing required reports block packing and export. Tested with Node 22.23.3 and npm 11.11.0 on a Linux amd64 worker. Failure Recovery Missing native lock, incompatible package or engine, or a workspace target Supply current inputs, or use a flow that supports your project Lock mismatch or install failure Regenerate the lock with npm, then update the frozen inputs. Nothing is projected or packed Build, required report or pack failure Fix the failure and rerun. No archive is exported Packed archive name or version doesn't match, or the path is unsafe Inspect the retained packing log and the package's name and version

An inferred single-root pnpm project produces a .tgz the same way, through pnpm pack --json --out. You need a real pnpm-lock.yaml, exactly pnpm 10.11.0 (tested with Node 22.23.3), the required checks, and a matching package that declares captured-plan. Vite projects and pnpm workspaces aren't covered here (see pnpm). oyzu -C <project> --json build --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image pnpm=<node-image> An explicit uses: node/package selects the same profile. A package with no scripts exports straight from the checked-in source with setup, checks and packing, and no build step.

Supported: an explicit single-root npm package built on your machine (no sandbox) with the Node plugin. Declare only the package intent and keep your npm lock: builds: package: {uses: node/package} oyzu --json build package --full --no-cache The first build records any missing selection in oyzu.lock. Lint, format and similar quality checks need the project's own packages or an OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME you provisioned. Oyzu doesn't install fallback tools. A build with a missing quality tool stops before export. Oyzu applies the version to a private copy, runs your checks and hooks, then runs npm pack --json --ignore-scripts into a fresh scratch directory. Read the artifact's path, digest and version from the manifest. Failed checks or missing reports prevent export. Tested on Windows x86-64 with Node 22.23.3 and npm 11.11.0. Inferred and Vite packages, pnpm and Yarn packages, and other platforms aren't supported on this path. For workspace packages, see npm workspaces and Yarn.

Code Cause Recovery PLUGIN_PACKAGE_DIGEST Archive bytes differ from the configured digest, or an OCI object differs from its descriptor Fix the digest or archive. For OCI, the registry or mirror is serving wrong bytes PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID The manifest, entrypoint or archive broke a rule Rebuild the package PLUGIN_PACKAGE_MISMATCH The package doesn't provide the bound reference Bind the right package PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE The archive is missing and the release isn't installed, an OCI object is missing, or the registry refused anonymous access or is unreachable. The missing digest is named Restore the archive, complete the mirror or make the package public PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_MISSING No Sigstore signature is attached to the OCI release root. For an oyzu/* package on a catalog mirror, the message says the mirror must serve the official signature Publish the required signature. A package from another publisher can be bound by digest. For a mirror of an official package, copy the release's signature referrers (the sha256-<hex> tag or referrers entries, with the signature manifest and bundle) into the mirror unchanged PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_INVALID No attached signature verifies for the root digest, signer and trusted root Check identity and trustedRoot. For a mirror of an official package, serve the official release and its original signature. A company's own build can't stand in for oyzu/*; list it as the company's own package PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED No runtime for this OS, architecture and ABI. The message names your machine and what the package provides Use a package that has one PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING, PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH, PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE, PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED, PLUGIN_NOT_INSTALLED See the lock table above PLUGIN_BINDING_CONFLICT A second discovery in one command asked for different bindings Bindings are fixed for the command PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT The package needs an engine feature this oyzu lacks Use an oyzu that supports it, or another release ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH The running engine isn't the pinned one Run the pinned oyzu
Plugin catalog and builder selection Inspecting plugins Updating plugins Go builder preview Writing and testing a plugin

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-preview.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu/go is the first published Oyzu builder plugin: it builds Go projects. It's a preview release, published as an OCI package on GHCR and listed in the official plugin catalog. This page says how to select it, what it supports, how long releases are supported, and what happens when a release is withdrawn. Note: The Go builder is a preview. Its plugin interface (v1alpha1) can still change, and a later preview may behave differently.

Add this to your user configuration (see Selecting the preview): [plugins] preview = true Then build any Go module: oyzu build Oyzu downloads oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 from ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go, checks its signature, records the exact release in oyzu.lock and builds with it. You need no account, login or Docker. The build's Selection section shows the source as official default. To undo it, remove oyzu.lock, then run oyzu config unset --global 'plugins.packages."go/app"' and oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false. The build prints this line for you.

Immutable releases. A published version never changes. A fix, a changed payload or a new platform is a new version. Verified bytes. Oyzu accepts a release only when it's signed by the plugin-release.yml workflow on refs/heads/main from a GitHub-hosted runner, and it checks every object by digest (signature rules). No surprises. A lock never silently changes the implementation. A newer release, a newer preview or a new catalog serial changes nothing until you run oyzu plugins update. Visible and reversible selection. The build shows which builder each target got and prints the line that undoes it. A preview does not promise that the plugin interface is stable, that a later preview behaves like this one, that every platform in the package is tested, or that it's supported after a newer release replaces it. Previews are left out of ordinary stable resolution and updates.

Selection is deliberate and per user. A project file can't select a preview (CONFIG_SCOPE), because the release is code that runs on your machine. Set it in user, machine or administrative configuration: [plugins] preview = true The build then downloads the release from the route in the verified catalog (ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:25f830bd…f9bf). Optionally, a plugins.packages binding supplies the bytes instead and takes precedence: [plugins.packages] "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0-preview.1" } A tag binding has these consequences: The tag can move. GHCR tags are mutable. Oyzu resolves the tag once, at first selection, so a fresh checkout without a committed oyzu.lock can resolve different releases at different times. The lock is what pins the release: it records the root digest, and later builds, --frozen replays and fresh stores fetch that digest. Commit oyzu.lock, or bind by digest (ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:<root>). It's a local package binding. The catalog's supported, deprecated and unsupported statuses don't apply to a release a tag supplies. A withdrawal or revocation still refuses it. oyzu plugins update still never selects a preview you didn't name. A digest binding equal to the release the catalog would select counts as the official default. With plugins.preview off, a build never refreshes the official catalog and can't select the preview, so a Go build fails with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE unless you bind a package. oyzu plugins update never moves a selection to a preview unless you name it (go/app@0.1.0-preview.2, which needs the opt-in). A routine update stays inside the adopted major version and skips previews.

Oyzu ignores the whole user configuration when it sees a CI marker (CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS and similar variables). A project file can't select a preview, so the settings above have no effect in a CI job. Instead, write them to the machine configuration before the build. On a GitHub-hosted Linux runner: - name: Select the Go preview run: | sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/oyzu sudo tee /etc/oyzu/config.toml > /dev/null <<'TOML' [plugins] preview = true TOML - run: oyzu build Keep the file owned by root and not writable by group or others. Oyzu doesn't check the owner or mode of the machine config.toml, so this is advice, not enforcement. The recipe replaces any machine configuration already on the runner, so use it on throwaway runners. The machine file is /Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml on macOS and %ProgramData%\Oyzu\config.toml on Windows; those paths use the same rule but haven't been tested.

These statements are for oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1. They change only with a new release or a new catalog entry, never with a new oyzu release. What Supported Not supported or untested Plugin interface Protocol generation v1alpha1. Builder role with the go-test-events feature. Profiles go/app and go/library Any other generation or required feature fails before work starts Oyzu version The first oyzu release that carries this preview (tested with 0.1.0) and later ones that still speak v1alpha1. The catalog can name an incompatibility Older releases have no plugin support Platforms in the package Linux amd64 and arm64 (static musl, used on glibc and musl hosts), macOS arm64 and amd64, Windows amd64 (MSVC) A host with none of these fails with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, naming what the package provides.
