Support. Only the newest preview is supported. When a newer preview or a stable release replaces it, the catalog marks it deprecated for at least 30 days, with a message naming the successor, then unsupported. Fixes ship as a new preview. There are no backports. Withdrawal. A defective release is withdrawn at once, without waiting for the deprecation period. Retention. Release roots, platform payloads and signatures stay on GHCR for at least 12 months after the release is replaced. A withdrawn or revoked release's bytes and evidence are kept as long as its withdrawal is listed. Catalog entries. The catalog lists supported releases within their retention. Withdrawals are kept for good. A release removed from the catalog is unlisted, not withdrawn: new builds no longer offer it, but a lock that names it still replays while its bytes are in your store or on GHCR. Transparency log. Each signature is a public Sigstore (Rekor) entry. It can't be deleted, and withdrawing a release doesn't remove it. Freshness. The catalog is re-signed daily and is never valid for more than 31 days. With the opt-in, oyzu refreshes it at most once an hour. Oyzu treats these cases differently. A deprecated or unsupported release still replays. Missing bytes fail with PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE. A withdrawn or revoked release is refused with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN or PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED.

When the catalog selects the release (the usual path): Status New selection (an unlocked build) Adoption (oyzu plugins update) Replay of an existing lock supported Offered A candidate Replays. An online, non-frozen build with an empty plugin store downloads the exact locked digest again without rewriting the lock deprecated (even past its end date) Offered, with no build warning. oyzu plugins info shows the status and message, and --json also the end date A candidate Replays unsupported Not offered. The build fails with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE unless you bind a digest, which still installs it Not a candidate ("up to date"). An explicit binding of the release still adopts it Replays preview, without plugins.preview Not offered Never chosen by a routine update (PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED) Replays preview, with plugins.preview Offered Only when named exactly (go/app@<version>) Replays unlisted (removed after retention) Not offered Not a candidate Replays from the store. A fresh store needs a binding of the locked digest, or fails with PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE withdrawn Not offered. A plugins.packages binding of it is refused (PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN) before it's recorded or run Refused by name or binding Refused on every command, including --plan and --frozen, naming the lock entry. The lock isn't rewritten revoked As withdrawn, with PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED As withdrawn As withdrawn With a plugins.packages binding (which takes precedence over the catalog's route), the catalog is consulted only for withdrawals: Binding New selection oyzu plugins update Lock replay Tag (oci = "…/go:<version>") Support status doesn't apply. Oyzu resolves the tag once and the lock pins the digest Never adopts a preview (PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED) Replays by the locked digest Digest (oci = "…@sha256:…", or archive with sha256) An unsupported release installs Adopts an unsupported release through the binding. Refuses a preview as above Replays Locked, no binding n/a n/a Replays A withdrawn or revoked release is refused for every kind of binding, before it's installed. Support is advice and withdrawal is authority: unsupported and deprecated never stop a lock, while withdrawn and revoked always do. Known limits: A passed end date doesn't change a status by itself. The catalog is re-published as unsupported. A build shows no deprecation warning. A revocation can't reach a machine that never verified a catalog, or stop an installed copy that isn't replayed through a lock.

A catalog change reaches you as the next serial of the tool index. With the opt-in, oyzu picks it up at its next refresh, at most an hour later, and applies its withdrawals on every command. Situation What you see What to do A release is defective and withdrawn Builds and --plan fail with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, naming the catalog serial and the lock entry Run oyzu plugins update go/app (it needs a binding or the store to supply the replacement). oyzu plugins versions go/app shows why a release is excluded A release is revoked (its content or signing is compromised) PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED ("it will not run") on every command. Installed copies outside a lock aren't removed Recover as above. Remove the copy with oyzu plugins prune The catalog is wrong and rolled back Oyzu ignores a lower serial, the same serial with other bytes, or a higher serial generated earlier, and keeps the last verified copy and its withdrawals Nothing to do The catalog is tampered with or its signature fails Oyzu refuses it and keeps the last verified copy. Unlocked references fail with PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE. A lock replays only against a verified copy. With no network or an expired copy, withdrawals still apply and a PLUGIN_CATALOG_EXPIRED warning appears Bind a package explicitly to continue without the catalog GHCR is unreachable or the package is private PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE naming the missing object or "refused anonymous access". A release already in your store keeps working with no network Retry when the registry is reachable A signed release can't be deleted: the signature log entry is permanent and the bytes stay for the retention period. It can only be withdrawn.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-updates.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu plugins update changes the plugin selections already recorded in oyzu.lock. Use it for a routine update within the major version you adopted, to move to a new major version on purpose, or to select one exact version or release (which is also how you undo an update). A ready-made GitHub workflow can run it on a schedule and open a pull request. Note: Plugins are experimental. oyzu plugins update # every locked selection, each within its adopted major oyzu plugins update go/app # only go/app oyzu plugins update go/app@v2 # move go/app to major 2 oyzu plugins update go/app@1.0.0 # exactly version 1.0.0 of go/app's package oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:… # exactly this release (the printed undo) oyzu plugins update --dry-run # check and show the change without writing oyzu.lock For how a selection is first adopted, see plugin catalog. For the [[plugin]] lock record, see plugin packages. For read-only views, see inspecting plugins.

Option Meaning --dry-run Check everything and show the change, but don't write oyzu.lock. --offline Use the cached catalog only. --store DIR The plugin store, as for oyzu build --store. --json One JSON object on standard output. No account is needed. Publishing or caching a newer plugin release never changes your lock; builds keep using the locked release. Only this command (or deleting the entry) changes it.

You write Picks go/app, or nothing (every locked reference) The newest eligible release in the adopted major. Never an older one while the locked release can still be used. go/app@v2 or go/app@2 The newest eligible release of major 2. go/app@1.4.2 Exactly version 1.4.2 of the package the catalog binds, newer or older. go/app@sha256:… Exactly this release, which also fixes the package. The printed undo uses this form. "Eligible" means the same as for a build: listed by the catalog, not withdrawn or revoked, supported, on the current plugin contract, with the right builder profile and a payload for this host. A plugins.packages binding for the reference supplies the package instead, as it does for a build, and must still match the selector. Previews. Routine and @v<major> updates never pick a preview release (PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED). A release is a preview if its version is a prerelease or the catalog lists it as one. An exact @<version> or @sha256:… can pick a preview, but only with plugins.preview on. Package changes. A routine update never switches to a different package. If an organization catalog or a binding now points the reference at another package, you get PLUGIN_PACKAGE_CHANGE; adopt it with an explicit selector such as @v1.

If oyzu.toml pins an exact engine, that engine is set up first (see engine staging). Required features it doesn't support fail before anything changes. Then: Refresh the catalog. Unless you pass --offline, the verified catalog is refreshed first. If there's no current verified catalog (refused, expired or missing), the whole update fails with PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE. This is stricter than a build: a build continues with an older cached copy after a refused refresh; an update doesn't. Pick each candidate using the selector. Check it. Each new release is installed into the plugin store (from the store, a plugins.packages binding, or the OCI route in its catalog entry) and checked like a first adoption: digest, package and version, builder profile, protocol and a payload this host can run. It must also pass the build's lock rules: not withdrawn, not revoked, not rebound by an organization catalog. Write once. Only when every requested reference passes is oyzu.lock rewritten, replacing just those [[plugin]] entries (comments above them are kept). Other selections, tool records and the engine pin are untouched. If another process changed those entries in the meantime, nothing is written (PLUGIN_LOCK_CHANGED). Any failure leaves the lock exactly as it was. An update never runs a plugin and never edits configuration or other project files. Releases it installed stay in the store, even after a failed or --dry-run update.

Updated 1 plugin selection in oyzu.lock Changes Reference Before After Change Why go/app acme/go 1.0.0 acme/go 1.0.1 patch the plugins.packages binding supplies this release go/library acme/go 1.0.0 — unchanged newest eligible release in major 1 Releases go/app sha256:a9713fde…7583 → sha256:d660c518…06ca · installed now from /home/me/acme-go-1.0.1.tar.gz Undo oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:a9713fde547a6353975dd14aad1c837a4c70b475961ec37563ae320fb32d7583 Restores the earlier releases while they remain eligible; reverting the oyzu.lock change does the same. Lock ./oyzu.lock (updated) Evaluated against Engine 0.1.0 (running engine) … Review and commit oyzu.lock to share the update. Nothing was launched and no configuration changed. Change Meaning patch, minor A newer release in the same major. major A new major, chosen explicitly. rollback An older release, chosen with @<version> or because the locked one can't be used anymore. package A different package now serves the reference, chosen explicitly. unchanged Nothing newer is eligible. With --dry-run, the heading says Would update … and the undo is labelled Undo (once adopted). Notes point out things like a binding that holds the locked release while a newer one is eligible. --json prints the same information: {"kind":"plugin-update","dryRun":false,"wrote":true,"lock":"/work/app/oyzu.lock", "changes":[{"reference":"go/app","selector":null, "from":{"package":"acme/go","major":1,"version":"1.0.0","release":"sha256:…"}, "to":{"package":"acme/go","major":1,"version":"1.0.1","release":"sha256:…"}, "level":"patch","reason":"…","installedNow":true,"route":"/home/me/acme-go-1.0.1.tar.gz"}], "undo":"oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:…","notes":[], "evaluation":{"engine":"…","engineSource":"running engine","platforms":["linux/amd64"],"…":"…"}, "coverage":{"choice":"organization","snapshots":[{"label":"acme catalog serial 2","…":"…"}],"…":"…"}} evaluation and coverage match the inspection commands.

The undo line selects each changed reference's earlier release by digest, so it fixes the package as well as the version. It goes through the same checks, so it works only while that release is still available and allowed: A release the catalog has since withdrawn or revoked is refused with PLUGIN_UPDATE_UNAVAILABLE. If a catalog now binds the reference to another package, the earlier package is refused. The message names both packages and your options: ask the catalog's owner to bind the package you want, or update the bound one with an explicit selector. Under an organization catalog, builds refuse a lock of the other package too (PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED), including a reverted oyzu.lock. If a plugins.packages binding supplied the new release, the binding has to name the earlier release again (or be unset) before the undo works. The update's notes say so, and an undo against the binding fails with PLUGIN_UPDATE_CONFLICT and the oyzu config unset line to run. Reverting the oyzu.lock change in version control has the same effect; the next build checks it under the same rules.

Every failure says oyzu.lock was not changed. Code Cause and fix PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE No current verified catalog. Restore access and run again. PLUGIN_UPDATE_NOT_LOCKED The reference isn't in oyzu.lock. Run oyzu build to adopt it first. PLUGIN_SELECTOR_INVALID The selector isn't v<major>, an exact version or a sha256: digest, or a reference appears twice. PLUGIN_UPDATE_UNAVAILABLE No eligible release fits the selector. The reasons are listed (for example outside the adopted major 1, no payload for this platform). If the locked release is still fine, a routine update reports unchanged instead. PLUGIN_MAJOR_CHANGE A binding supplies a release outside the adopted major. Run the printed @v<major> update. PLUGIN_UPDATE_CONFLICT A plugins.packages binding supplies a different release from the one you asked for. PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED The release would be a preview. Use an exact selector with plugins.preview on. PLUGIN_PACKAGE_CHANGE A routine update would switch packages. Run the printed explicit selector. PLUGIN_UPDATE_REFUSED The new selection fails the build's lock rules (PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED or PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED). PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE The release isn't in the store, no binding supplies it and the catalog lists no OCI route (or --offline prevents using it). The message shows the plugins.packages line to add. PLUGIN_ROUTE_FAILED The catalog route couldn't be reached, doesn't hold the release, or has an unusable address. Nothing was installed. PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, PLUGIN_PACKAGE_MISMATCH, PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID, digest errors The downloaded package failed its checks. No other release is picked instead. PLUGIN_LOCK_CHANGED oyzu.lock changed while the update ran. Run it again. When a build fails with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED, PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED or PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH, its suggested fix is oyzu plugins update <reference>.

workflows/oyzu-plugin-update.yml is a standard GitHub workflow. Copy it to .github/workflows/ in a repository whose oyzu.lock selects plugins. It runs weekly and on demand, in three jobs, so that nothing an unreviewed plugin does can change what gets proposed: update runs oyzu plugins update --json, which never runs a plugin. If oyzu.lock didn't change, it stops. Otherwise it uploads the new oyzu.lock, the JSON report, the change levels and the pull request text as one artifact. verify puts that oyzu.lock into a fresh checkout and runs BUILD_COMMAND (default oyzu build --frozen), which runs the new plugin. It has no repository write credential and uploads nothing. It's a pass/fail gate only. propose runs only if both passed. It downloads the update job's artifact, refuses it unless it contains exactly body.md, levels, oyzu.lock and report.json, commits only oyzu.lock to the oyzu/plugin-update branch, force-pushes it, and opens (or refreshes) a pull request listing each change, its level, the reason, notes and the undo line. It never merges directly. Setup: Item Meaning OYZU_UPDATE_TOKEN secret A GitHub App or fine-grained token with contents and pull-requests write access, used by the propose job only. The default GITHUB_TOKEN won't do: pull requests it opens don't trigger your required checks. Install oyzu steps Replace with your pinned, checksummed oyzu installation. AUTO_MERGE_PATCH: 'true' Optional. When every change is a patch, turn on GitHub auto-merge, which still waits for branch protection and required checks. jq Needed by the update job. GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners include it. When the workflow refreshes an open pull request with anything other than patch changes, it turns auto-merge off and confirms it's off before pushing, so an earlier auto-merge request never applies to the new proposal. If that check fails, the job stops without pushing.

Only this host's platform is checked for payloads. Other platforms you build for (a declared matrix, remote workers) aren't checked. Only a catalog's OCI route is used for downloads. A release whose catalog entry lists only an HTTPS archive route needs a plugins.packages binding. @vN works only on this command, not in uses:. The verify job runs an unreviewed plugin. It has no repository write token, but on a GitHub-hosted runner the plugin runs as the job's user (with passwordless sudo). It can read the job's ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN and use it to write Actions caches for the default branch, which other workflows may restore, or to upload artifacts. The propose job is protected because it checks the artifact it uses; other workflows that restore default-branch caches are not. Setting permissions: {} doesn't help, since that limits GITHUB_TOKEN, not the runtime token. Where you can, run verify on an ephemeral, isolated runner and key important caches so this workflow can't produce them. The workflow hasn't yet run on GitHub-hosted runners against a real plugin project. Supported on Linux. Windows and macOS aren't supported yet.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/pnpm.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds Node projects that use pnpm and a pnpm-lock.yaml. Single projects and conventional pnpm workspaces need no Oyzu build configuration. Use it to build, test and package a pnpm project with dependencies captured from the public registry and checked against the lockfile's SHA-512 integrity values. Note: pnpm support is experimental. Oyzu captures and verifies the archives, then lets native pnpm validate the frozen lock and install. It is not full pnpm compatibility (see Limits). Builds use the Node builder plugin (profiles node/app and node/package), which must be installed and selected. See plugin packages.

Pin Node and pnpm (see Prerequisites and use), then run from the project: oyzu --root path/to/project run list oyzu --root path/to/project build oyzu --root path/to/project inspect dist oyzu run list shows your package scripts and the inferred test and quality tasks. oyzu build produces a snapshot-versioned .tgz under dist/ with its test and coverage reports. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's recorded content integrity.

Isolated builds run on the base execution image with Docker. Node and pnpm both come from oyzu.lock, so pin both: Node in [tools], pnpm with an exact packageManager (or pnpm in [tools]). The tested profile is pnpm 10.11.0 on Node 22. Setting Value Meaning Docker and the base image oyzu-execution/base:1 Required for isolated builds. See Execution image. --image pnpm=<image> An image name Runs pnpm's isolated actions on an image of your own. The locked Node and pnpm are still the ones that run. Lockfile parser yaml 2.9.1 Ships in the Node plugin package and reads pnpm-lock.yaml for planning. No image needs it. packageManager An exact stable release, such as pnpm@10.11.0 When present, must agree with the pnpm that runs. An exact stable release is pinned as a tool and locked as oyzu:pnpm, so pnpm never downloads itself in the worker. Corepack digest suffix pnpm@10.11.0+sha512.<hex> Accepted and ignored in that comparison. Node requirements Native strict engine validation Incompatible Node requirements are rejected. How tasks run: oyzu run <task> uses the tools installed on your machine. oyzu run list shows native package scripts and inferred test and quality tasks. oyzu build runs native build and test work plus read-only lint and format checks in the isolated worker. Node's built-in test runner gets JUnit and LCOV reporting. Other frameworks use their own adapters. Formatting during a build never rewrites your checkout. See Node quality for quality selection and defaults. To test other Node versions, use verification toolsets in oyzu.toml. matrix.node in build.yaml is refused. Verification runs execute on the native host executor, and pnpm builds use the isolated executor. A pnpm build that has verification runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED. Private registry configuration is not supported.

A pnpm workspace has a private root, a native pnpm-workspace.yaml, a version 9 lock and locally linked packages (see the pnpm workspace example). Run oyzu build from the root with no Oyzu configuration file. oyzu run list shows build, test, lint and format-check. Development builds dispatch pnpm --recursive run build. Development tests use the workspace report collector.

Acquisition runs a frozen pnpm install with scripts disabled, then asks pnpm to list its members. Workspace commands use the first pnpm executable on PATH, including a standalone executable. They do not fall back to a lower-priority pnpm. Corepack pnpm shims are refused because they can download a package manager. JavaScript pnpm layouts run through the selected Node. Version projection reads the project lock with the yaml package the Node plugin ships (an OYZU_PNPM_YAML path takes precedence). Planning and execution: Local links come from the lock's importer records. They must point to captured members or to a named, publishable workspace root. A private root can't be a link target. Oyzu orders the root and members, fixes their snapshot versions and declares each package's JUnit and LCOV. In its private tree, Oyzu rewrites root and member versions, workspace dependency selectors and matching importer specifiers, then runs a fresh frozen install. pnpm pack turns workspace selectors into published snapshot dependencies. The publishable root is packed once, separately from member packages. Your source and lock are unchanged.

Select node/package to build a pnpm workspace into package archives in the isolated worker. Supported: pnpm 10.11.0 and Node 22.23.3, on a Windows x64 coordinator with a Linux amd64 worker. Three archives install in a fresh offline pnpm project with the source absent. Frozen reuse and failures in dependencies or package tests are caught. Not supported: private roots, other pnpm versions, native-host workspace packages, Linux coordinators, Linux ARM64, Windows ARM64 and macOS. It needs: A publishable root and publishable members. Native pnpm-workspace.yaml membership. A genuine version 9 lock. Recognized package-local build lifecycles and implicit Node tests. Aggregate or opaque root builds, explicit test scripts and replaced build or test tasks are not supported. How it works: Oyzu fixes versions and dependency decisions from native pnpm facts. In the private tree, it changes local workspace specifiers and importer specifiers but keeps link: resolutions and registry integrity data. pnpm builds each package and packs the archives. Each package must produce its JUnit and LCOV before anything is published. Your source and lock stay unchanged. Use the ordinary package binding and a matching coordinator and worker engine. Tool versions come from native pins or the configuration cascade. build.yaml only selects uses: node/package. The first build with a real, non-frozen run adopts the plugin and creates oyzu.lock. Later --frozen runs reuse it: oyzu -C <workspace> --json build workspace --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image pnpm=<image> Generate the lock with pnpm 10.11.0. For oyzu exec, select pnpm in the tool configuration, because packageManager alone doesn't select it.

A root script keeps ownership of its stage. Otherwise member build scripts run in dependency order, and member tests and quality use native scripts or inferred defaults. Required test or quality failures stop artifact collection. Available reports stay in the failed bundle. Overrides, prerequisites and hooks come from Oyzu's shared task scheduling. Format checks during a build are read-only. Registry inputs come from a local loopback server (see Acquisition and execution). pnpm's connection to it doesn't allow external downloads. An opaque root build keeps the native root script and runs it once. Oyzu does not guess which member scripts it covered. A root test script of the form tsc -p <relative-config> && vp test --run keeps its native pnpm script and TypeScript step, while Oyzu adds JUnit and LCOV reporters to the final vp test command. The Vitest and Vite configuration comes from your Vite+ package graph. The coverage provider must be a declared dependency matching the runner's version. Other custom root scripts must write their own reports. Oyzu adds no flags to them. A root format script that is only vp fmt --check with directory-prefixed operands can serve as the format check when you have no format-check, format:check, preformat or postformat script. An opaque or mutating format script does not become a check.

Before packing, Oyzu resolves each concrete public import and require entry from the package and requires the selected file to be a regular file. Declaration files selected by the types condition and a literal legacy declaration path must also exist. Existence is checked, not TypeScript validity. A missing declared JavaScript entry fails the build. Types-only and assets-only packages need no JavaScript entry. Null exclusions and conditional alternatives are left to Node. Wildcard-only entries without a concrete specifier can't be checked. One pnpm pack --json result records the archive's name, version, file name and files. An archive missing a selected public file is rejected before its artifact receipt is written. Browser or custom conditions, declaration validity and every wildcard path are not checked. Cyclic workspace graphs, affected selection, member task groups and full direct host build and quality composition are not supported. pnpm's own layout and peer rules stay in charge.

Checked-in patchedDependencies work in a single project's pnpm-workspace.yaml or in the pnpm object in package.json: patchedDependencies: is-number@6.0.0: patches/is-number@6.0.0.patch Create the patch with pnpm patch and pnpm patch-commit, and commit the patch, settings and updated lock together. No Oyzu setting is needed. A pnpm-workspace.yaml with patch settings doesn't make the project a workspace. A packages list turns on workspace discovery. Patch-only settings stay single-project. The workspace settings below are also accepted. Other configuration keys are not. Checks: Declared and locked patch paths must be regular files inside the project. Absolute paths, .. segments, backslashes, symlinks, missing files and patches over 4 MiB are refused. pnpm checks the lock and configuration agree and verifies patch hashes, then applies the patch in its private installation. Oyzu has no patch engine of its own. A changed patch with a stale lock fails before project lifecycle hooks run. Your source files and the registry archives stay unchanged. Recorded in the build output: The dependency inventory still identifies the original downloaded archives. The oyzu.dev/pnpm.sourcePatches extension records each patch's selector, captured relative path, SHA-256, size and the native lock hash. The source digest and dependency-snapshot digest include the patch inputs. Patched source is distinguished from the pristine upstream archive. This is not a full runtime SBOM.

Captured builds honor these pnpm-workspace.yaml settings as declared: catalog and catalogs, overrides, minimumReleaseAge, allowBuilds and trustPolicy. Each is either fixed by the committed lock or makes acquisition stricter, so none can widen what a build downloads or runs. No Oyzu configuration is needed. catalog: is-odd: 3.0.1 is-number: 6.0.0 overrides: is-number: 'catalog:' minimumReleaseAge: 1440 trustPolicy: no-downgrade allowBuilds: esbuild: false Oyzu never re-resolves dependencies for these settings. It checks them before any native invocation, then native pnpm applies its own --frozen-lockfile checks. See the settings example. Setting What Oyzu checks Effect with pnpm 10.11.0 catalog, catalogs Each catalog maps names to specifier strings. catalog is the default catalog, so also declaring catalogs.default fails. Every importer dependency whose specifier is catalog: or catalog:<name> needs a lock catalogs entry with the same specifier. pnpm compares the same entries and installs the locked versions. overrides The lock's overrides must equal the declared map after pnpm's normalization ($name takes the root package.json specifier, and catalog: takes the catalog entry for the target package). Overrides come from pnpm-workspace.yaml, or else from package.json pnpm.overrides merged over resolutions. Declaring them in both places fails. A mismatch fails with pnpm lock overrides differ from configuration for <selector>. pnpm makes the same comparison (LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH). The locked graph already reflects the overrides. minimumReleaseAge Must be a whole number of minutes. Not read: pnpm 10.11.0 predates it (added in 10.16). A frozen lock resolves nothing new, and Oyzu fetches no registry metadata to check ages. trustPolicy no-downgrade or off. Not read: pnpm 10.11.0 predates it (added in 10.21). Newer releases apply it during resolution, which a frozen install doesn't do. allowBuilds Each value is true or false. A placeholder such as set this to true or false fails. When any entry is true, pnpm must be 10.26.0 or newer, the first release that reads it. Otherwise it fails with pnpm allowBuilds approves <selector>, but provisioned pnpm <version> predates allowBuilds. Denials are honored: pnpm 10 runs no dependency build scripts unless approved, and acquisition disables lifecycle scripts entirely. An approval needs a newer pnpm, which then runs only the approved packages' scripts during execution.

In package.json, the pnpm object may hold only patchedDependencies and overrides, because pnpm 10 reads other settings only from pnpm-workspace.yaml. Any other key in either file fails with pnpm capture does not yet support configuration <key> in <file>. The message names the key, not its value. That includes minimumReleaseAgeExclude, trustPolicyExclude, trustPolicyIgnoreAfter, onlyBuiltDependencies, ignoredBuiltDependencies and blockExoticSubdeps. Remove such keys to build.

After pnpm validates the lock, the oyzu.dev/pnpm.workspacePolicies extension records the declared minimumReleaseAge, trustPolicy and allowBuilds values, which leave no trace in the lock. The dependency-snapshot digest includes them. A recorded policy states what the project declared. It does not prove pnpm enforced it. Catalogs and overrides are covered by the recorded lock and source digests. If a catalog or override check fails, regenerate and commit the lock with the pnpm version the project declares. Newer pnpm releases can enforce minimumReleaseAge and trustPolicy during a frozen install, using publisher metadata. The captured adapter supplies the full publisher metadata and the attestation responses pnpm requests (see Acquisition and execution). pnpm makes the decision. Oyzu doesn't invent acceptance or treat a broker failure as missing metadata. With pnpm 12.6.0, a satisfiable release age passes and an unsatisfiable one fails with ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION before any action or artifact. Projects that use these settings together with other unsupported keys or .npmrc files, or that pin a pnpm version that isn't provisioned (10.33, 11.9, 12.4), still fail.
This section explains what is downloaded, from where, and what is checked.

Oyzu reads lock format v9 with a root importer and, for workspaces, member importers. pnpm 12 can write the lock as two YAML documents: an environment document pinning pnpm itself under packageManagerDependencies, then the usual v9 project document. The project document is captured exactly like a single-document lock. The environment document is checked but not captured, because Oyzu provisions the package manager. It may hold only lockfileVersion, importers, packages and snapshots, one . importer, and only configDependencies and packageManagerDependencies in it. A non-empty configDependencies fails, because it would need its own captured inputs. Version projection rewrites only the project document and writes the environment document back unchanged. A lock with more than two documents fails. pnpm 10.11.0 can't read a two-document lock. An exact packageManager release is a locked tool requirement when the tool provider offers it, for both older and pnpm 12 packages. A full isolated build with pnpm 12.3.4 and a two-document lock works. Other pnpm 12 projects aren't supported yet.

Every registry package in the project document's packages section needs an exact SHA-512 integrity value. Native frozen pnpm install in the build image asks for the archives it needs. Oyzu captures only those requests, through the scoped npm-public route to https://registry.npmjs.org/. Optional archives for other platforms are fetched only if pnpm asks for them. Your lock is unchanged, and project lifecycle scripts are disabled during acquisition. Unsupported pnpm configuration and hook files are rejected before any native invocation, including the version query. Archive digests are verified before the bytes reach pnpm. An unknown route, or a failed broker or integrity check, fails preparation even if pnpm would tolerate a missing optional package. The snapshot holds content-addressed tarballs in lock order. It does not keep pnpm's mutable store. pnpm requests at most eight packages at once. Its loopback wait is 120 seconds during acquisition and 15 seconds when replaying captured bytes. Neither raises the broker's network deadline or byte allowance.

Oyzu creates a fresh private store and serves the captured archives to pnpm from a loopback port. The isolated worker has no external network. The server holds no registry credentials, forwards nothing, and fails unknown routes and methods. During execution it serves only the frozen subset. pnpm needs HTTP access to it, so pnpm's own --offline flag isn't used. For pnpm 12, Oyzu also captures full publisher metadata for the locked packages through the npm-public broker, and the attestation responses pnpm requests for locked name and version pairs. It records their bytes and digests in extensions["oyzu.dev/pnpm"].attestations and policyMetadata (source ID, URL, locked versions, SHA-256, size). A source-backed 404 records absence. A broker denial or timeout never becomes absence. This is source and content data, not proof of authenticity or a runtime SBOM. pnpm evaluates its own attestation and supply-chain policy. Oyzu doesn't set trustLockfile. Execution mounts no broker, rechecks captured response identity, and turns native lifecycle behavior on. The private store lives in scratch space and is discarded. Lock and manifest checks run with --frozen-lockfile. Oyzu verifies the lock bytes are unchanged and that the pnpm and Node versions match between preparation and execution. oyzu build --offline is rejected for this builder before preparation. Capture online, then execute with no network. pnpm 10's dependency-script approval rules apply. Oyzu doesn't approve scripts for you. Credentials never enter the inventory or loopback endpoint. Private registries are not supported.

A successful build produces a snapshot-versioned .tgz under dist/. The package's embedded version matches the artifact version. The manifest records artifacts and the collected test and coverage reports. Native logs and the dependency snapshot are in the bundle. Failed tests keep their reports and block packaging. oyzu inspect dist checks content integrity. It doesn't check release eligibility or who produced the bundle. Dependency records use adapter layout 1. They list each captured archive with its name, version, source ID, size and SHA-256, and record lockfile-sha512 verification in oyzu.dev/pnpm. Every package counts as a build input. Runtime and test classification and registry dependency edges aren't recorded, so this is not a runtime SBOM. Workspace captures also keep local package edges for planning and version projection. Failure Recovery Stale lock Regenerate and commit the lock with the intended pnpm version, then rebuild. Digest mismatch, denied acquisition, missing captured archives, metadata or attestation responses, or changed runtime versions Fails instead of refetching during execution. Fix the cause and rebuild from acquisition. Your sources are never changed by an isolated build.

The Node plugin can build a single-root pnpm project into one native .tgz. You need an installed Node plugin package, Docker, a genuine pnpm-lock.yaml, and Node 22.23.3 and pnpm 10.11.0 in your tool configuration. No build.yaml is needed for the package fallback. An explicit node/app keeps its directory output (see Node applications). Vite projects are not supported here. See plugin packages for usage. Inferred, explicit node/package and scriptless packages each produce a versioned archive, Node test JUnit and LCOV, and install in a source-free, network-free consumer. A package with no build script has no build action. A failing assertion blocks packing and export. Supported: an empty dependency graph, a Windows x64 coordinator and Linux amd64 execution. Native-host single-package builds are npm only. Other versions, macOS, Windows ARM64 and publication are not supported.

This is incremental pnpm support, not full compatibility. Supported: single-project public registry packages with integrity-only lock resolutions, native dependency patches, the workspace settings above, and captured workspace packaging. pnpm 11 and later: Oyzu passes pmOnFail=ignore so pnpm doesn't download itself, and still checks the selected locked version. Not supported yet: .npmrc, .pnpmfile.cjs, .pnpmfile.mjs, other configuration, packageExtensions, explicit tarball, Git or file resolutions, and private registries. hoistPattern and nodeLinker settings are refused. Workspace registry dependencies, peer and alias combinations, and framework variations beyond those above aren't covered. Yarn Classic has its own adapter.
Node quality, Yarn Classic, verification toolsets and the workspace report collector pnpm tool installation for the pinned packageManager tool

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/publish.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu publish sends files from a finished build to an OCI registry or an existing GitHub release. It needs no Oyzu account: you configure destinations in oyzu.toml, supply signed build provenance, and Oyzu uploads the files, signs a record of what it published and reads everything back to check it. If you use the Oyzu platform, oyzu publish can instead register the build there and follow a publication the platform runs (see Governed publication). Publishing is optional. oyzu build and every other command stay local and work without an account. Note: Publishing is experimental. Supported destinations are OCI registries (files and single-platform images) and GitHub releases. npm, PyPI and tag-based OCI publishing are not supported.

Configure a destination and the evidence you accept, then publish a finished build: # oyzu.toml [publish] default = "sandbox" [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "oci" artifacts = ["app/archive"] # optional when the build has exactly one artifact registry = "https://registry.example.com" repository = "team/artifacts" usernameEnv = "REGISTRY_USERNAME" passwordEnv = "REGISTRY_PASSWORD" [publish.sets] release = ["sandbox"] [publish.requirements.provenance] bundlePath = "evidence/build.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/release" [publish.requirements.signing] keyEnv = "PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 publication public key>" oyzu build oyzu publish --destination sandbox This is an example: use your own public keys, provenance bundle and credentials. Keep secret values out of the TOML. The file names environment variables that hold them. oyzu publish reads dist/manifest.json by default (or the configured build.bundleDirectory). Pass --manifest FILE to publish a different bundle.

Oyzu reads the build manifest, which must record a succeeded build, and selects the artifacts each destination asks for. It checks the selection and all evidence before it contacts any destination: the file's bytes and size, your signed provenance and the publication signature. It uploads the files and the evidence. It downloads what it uploaded and checks every digest and size. Upload acknowledgements alone never count as success. Publishing never builds, scans, repackages or runs project hooks, and it never creates missing provenance. It needs network access, and there is no offline mode.

Run oyzu publish --destination sandbox, or omit --destination to use publish.default. Repeat --destination to publish to several destinations, or name a set from publish.sets. All selected destinations are required. A later destination can fail without undoing earlier ones. Successful publications stay, and the receipt lists the unfinished destinations.

Publishing settings use the ordinary configuration cascade, but only in the project root's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml. A [publish] table in any other folder's file is a CONFIG_SCOPE error naming the file and line (root-only settings). Setting Values Default Meaning publish.default A destination name The destination used when --destination is omitted. publish.destinations.<name>.kind oci, github-release oci The destination kind. publish.destinations.<name>.artifacts Build output IDs The outputs this destination publishes (see Selecting artifacts). You can omit it only when the manifest has one artifact. publish.destinations.<name>.registry An HTTPS URL The OCI registry. Plain HTTP is allowed only on loopback (for example a local test registry). publish.destinations.<name>.repository A repository name The OCI repository. publish.destinations.<name>.usernameEnv, passwordEnv Environment variable names Registry credentials. Set both or neither. Registries that use the same-origin bearer token challenge work. publish.sets Named lists of destinations Sets you can select with --destination. publish.requirements.provenance bundlePath, publicKey, builderId, or a byArtifact map The build provenance you accept (see Provenance evidence). publish.requirements.signing keyEnv, publicKey Signing for the publication record. keyEnv names an environment variable holding a base64 32-byte Ed25519 seed. Its public key must match publicKey. Rules: publish.destinations, publish.sets and publish.requirements each resolve as a whole. A later source in the cascade replaces the entire table and does not merge entries. Profiles and mandatory configuration constraints apply. An evidence path is relative to the file that declares the requirements. Artifact paths are relative to the bundle that holds the manifest.

kind defaults to oci, so older configurations need no change. github-release uses the adapter described in Existing GitHub release. npm, pypi and unknown kinds fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE before Oyzu loads evidence, reads credentials or uses the network. Unknown destination fields are errors.

Each destination lists the build outputs it publishes in artifacts. An ID is target/name for the output called name, or just target for that target's primary output. It is not the file's name. artifacts = ["app/archive"] selects output archive of target app. artifacts = ["app"] selects the primary output of app. Each destination can name different files. Nothing fans out implicitly. Empty or duplicate entries fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Oyzu checks selectors long before you publish (names that cross files): oyzu config validate, oyzu build --plan and every build refuse a selector (or byArtifact key) whose build does not exist, or whose @os/arch is not one of the build's platforms. The error is CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN, with the file, line, column and the nearest build name. Each build's Prepare step refuses an output name the build does not produce, and lists the outputs it does. At publish time, an unknown or ambiguous ID, or a missing selection in a bundle with several artifacts, fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before any evidence loading, signing or upload. Platform selectors​ Add @os/arch to select one platform of an output, such as cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64. The platform is the one the builder recorded for the file, in the canonical spelling x86_64 or arm64. amd64 and aarch64 are accepted and normalized. An unqualified selector such as cli/bin-oyzu selects every platform of that output in the bundle. Each platform is a separate file with its own evidence. A qualified selector fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID, listing the platforms present, when the bundle lacks that platform or the output has no recorded platform. Two artifacts of one output and platform also fail. Listing an output both with and without a platform, or the same platform twice, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. oyzu build writes one platform per bundle. To publish several platforms together, pass several bundles (see Incomplete platform sets). A bound chart needs its image​ A helm/chart build whose bindings write an image's with.repository into its values is published only when the same oyzu publish also pushes that image to that repository. That means an OCI destination whose registry host and repository equal with.repository, and whose artifacts select the image. Otherwise publishing fails with PUBLISH_BINDING_UNPUSHED before any evidence, signing or upload. The message names the chart's destination and the destination to add. Mirrors elsewhere are still allowed. Publish the chart and image together, for example oyzu publish --destination charts --destination images. See Publishing an OCI image. Oyzu applies the same check to publish.default and each publish.sets entry when it reads the configuration (CONFIG_BINDING_UNPUSHED).

Oyzu publishes only files it can tie to signed build provenance that you supply. The file must be a regular file whose bytes and size match its recorded SHA-256 digest. Other outputs in the manifest are validated but their files are not read or published. The accepted provenance is: a Sigstore v0.3 bundle with one DSSE application/vnd.in-toto+json envelope, holding an in-toto Statement v1 with SLSA build provenance v1, signed with the Ed25519 key in publicKey, from the exact builder in builderId, and covering the exact digest of the file being published. This profile uses keys you manage. It makes no transparency-log, trusted-time or keyless-identity claim and does not assert a SLSA level. Standalone publishing rejects --no-upload, --provenance and --policy-evidence before reading configuration or using the network. It takes provenance only from publish.requirements.provenance. If different outputs have different provenance, replace the single form with a map keyed by output ID: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."app/archive"] bundlePath = "evidence/app.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/package" [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/cli.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" Keys use the same IDs as artifacts. Only the selected output's entry is used and unselected bundles are not read. A selected output with no entry fails with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING. Oyzu never substitutes another output's evidence. Combining byArtifact with the single form, an empty map or ID, or a malformed entry fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Provenance is one bundle per file, so an output published on several platforms needs one bundle per platform. Use a key per platform ("cli@linux/arm64"), or one unqualified key whose bundlePath contains {artifact.platform}: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/{artifact.platform}/cli.sigstore.json" # evidence/linux/x86_64/cli.sigstore.json publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" {artifact.platform} is the only placeholder. Any other { or } in bundlePath fails validation. An unqualified key without the placeholder that would cover several platforms, or a placeholder on an output with no recorded platform, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A missing bundle for one platform fails the whole publish with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING naming the key. Nothing is published. Evidence problems report one of these codes: PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_INVALID (malformed bundle, bad signature, wrong statement type), PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_SUBJECT_MISMATCH (provenance does not cover this file's digest), PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_BUILDER_DENIED (builder is not the accepted builderId) and PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_UNSUPPORTED (the bundle carries transparency-log or timestamp material this profile does not accept).

Before uploading, Oyzu signs a publication intent with your publication key. The intent is a small signed record of exactly what this publish will do: the file's identity and media type, where it will go, the digest of your provenance, the digest of the whole plan and the operation publish. The intent cannot claim an earlier build origin or a finished upload. It does not contain the invocation ID, so publishing the same plan again reuses the same OCI coordinate. Oyzu verifies every signature before it uploads anything. A signing key that does not match publish.requirements.signing.publicKey fails with PUBLISH_SIGNING_INVALID. The OCI artifact holds the unchanged file, plus your provenance bundle and the publication-intent bundle as layers that anyone can download. The coordinate is registry/repository@sha256:<manifest-digest>. Tags are not supported. A mutable tag could be replaced by another writer between the check and the upload. Matching content already in the registry is reported as already-present. A different manifest, layer or digest at that coordinate is a PUBLISH_CONFLICT. Success requires Oyzu to fetch the manifest, config and every layer back from the registry and match their digests and sizes.

A docker/image build produces an OCI image archive (dist/<target>/<platform>/<target>-<version>.oci.tar). Select it by its output ID <build>/image, and Oyzu pushes it as an image rather than as a file: [publish.destinations.images] kind = "oci" registry = "https://registry.example.com" repository = "team/app" artifacts = ["image/image"] oyzu build oyzu publish --destination images docker pull registry.example.com/team/app@sha256:<image digest> Oyzu pushes the image's manifest, config and layers unchanged, by digest. The coordinate is the image digest the build recorded as ociDigest, which is also what a bound chart writes into its values. Before it touches evidence, signing or the network, Oyzu verifies the archive (every blob digest and layer diff ID) and checks that its image matches the recorded digest. If not, it fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED. An archive that holds a multi-platform image index, or an image selected by a github-release destination, fails with PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED. The image cannot carry evidence without changing its digest. Oyzu pushes the provenance and publication-intent bundles as a separate artifact in the same repository whose subject is the image (an OCI referrer with artifactType application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json). Its reference is the entry's evidenceReference, and registries that support the OCI referrers API list it under the image. As for files, success means Oyzu fetched the image and the evidence back and matched every digest and size. In the receipt, reference and manifestDigest name the image, and verification.artifactDigest is the archive's SHA-256. An image already present without this publication's evidence gets the evidence pushed and counts as published. If the registry refuses a write, the entry fails with PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED. If it cannot be reached, the entry fails with PUBLISH_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE. Both name the registry. Run the same publish again: content already pushed is matched by digest. When one OCI destination selects images of the same output for two or more platforms, oyzu publish also pushes an OCI image index of them, by digest. Each platform usually builds on its own host, so pass each build's manifest: oyzu build # on an amd64 host, its dist/ copied to amd64/ oyzu build # on an arm64 host, its dist/ copied to arm64/ oyzu publish --destination images --manifest amd64/manifest.json --manifest arm64/manifest.json docker pull registry.example.com/team/app@sha256:<index digest> The index lists each image by digest, size and platform, sorted by platform, so the same images always give the same index digest. Images that share an OCI platform, such as glibc and musl builds for one architecture, form no index and are published alone, because the OCI platform has no ABI. The signed plan covers the index digest and its members. If a member changed since the plan, publishing fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED or PUBLISH_PLAN_CHANGED before anything is sent. Oyzu pushes the index only after every selected image succeeded, then reads it back. The receipt lists it under indexes, with output, artifactIds, manifestDigest, outcome and reference (or error). If an image failed, the index's outcome is unfinished. Governed publication doesn't compose an index yet. It pushes each image alone.

Human output shows the operation, each selected output, each destination's result, the exact reference and the digest Oyzu retrieved. With --json, the receipt has operationId, status, planDigest, artifacts and destinations. Each destination has a kind and entries. An entry lists the artifact ID, coordinate, reference, payload outcome and how its evidence was stored and verified. An artifact's id is output-id@os/arch when the file has a recorded platform (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64), and the output ID otherwise. Such artifacts also carry compatibility (kind target, native or independent, plus the canonical platform), which the signed intent covers. unselectedArtifacts lists, in sorted order, outputs you did not select. Human output lists them as unselected and not published. Each destination reports published, already-present, failed or unfinished, with the digests Oyzu verified. Outcome Exit code Published 0 A failed or unfinished destination in the receipt 2 A check failed before publishing (missing evidence, wrong subject, conflicting existing asset) 1 Invalid command syntax 2 After you fix a failure, run the same publish again. Successful destinations are matched by digest and not repeated.
Publishing needs network access. Each file and each response is held in memory, so very large files need that much memory. A destination's credentials come only from environment variables you name.

The GitHub adapter uses the same configuration, evidence checks and signing as OCI. It uploads files as assets of a release that already exists. It never creates tags or releases. Replace the destination in the Quick start example with: [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "github-release" apiUrl = "https://api.github.com" repository = "your-owner/your-test-repository" tokenEnv = "GITHUB_SANDBOX_TOKEN" artifacts = ["app/archive", "cli"] [publish.destinations.sandbox.evidence] mode = "destination" Setting Values Default Meaning kind github-release oci Selects the GitHub Releases adapter. apiUrl An API origin The GitHub API root. repository owner/name The repository that holds the release. tokenEnv An environment variable name Holds a token with Contents read and write access to that repository. artifacts Output IDs As for OCI. evidence.mode destination destination Where evidence is stored. destination (evidence next to the files, downloadable from the destination) is the only supported value for OCI and GitHub. receipt and managed are not accepted. Create the tag and release yourself first, and give Oyzu the token by environment variable. Oyzu never creates refs or releases, publishes a draft, changes release metadata or deletes assets. It records the repository, release ID, tag commit, upload route, draft and prerelease state, and filenames, and stops before writing if any of them changes. A draft release can receive and verify assets. Publish the draft separately afterwards. If GitHub's tag endpoint returns 404, Oyzu looks for the exact tag in the release list. No match, or more than one, fails. Authentication and other HTTP errors are not treated as a missing tag.

A GitHub destination stores no tag in configuration. oyzu publish picks the release in this order: --tag <tag>, if given. It applies to every GitHub destination in that publish. Use it for manually started releases or tags version inference does not read. Otherwise the exact version tag that version inference recorded for the packages the destination publishes. A single-package repository tagged v1.4.0 at the built commit publishes to release v1.4.0. The api package of a workspace tagged api/v1.4.2 publishes to api/v1.4.2, even if another package has the same version. Oyzu decides the tag before any evidence loading, signing or network access, and the signed intent records it. --tag need not point at the built commit. If it replaces a different recorded tag, Oyzu warns with PUBLISH_TAG_OVERRIDDEN and continues. A tag key in a github-release destination is an error everywhere configuration is read: CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: publish.destinations: PUBLISH_DESTINATION_TAG_REMOVED. Delete the key. Without --tag, Oyzu stops and sends nothing in these cases: Code Cause Fix PUBLISH_TAG_UNKNOWN A published package has no recorded version tag: the built commit has no version tag that applies to it. Tag the built commit (v1.4.0, or <package>/v1.4.0 for one workspace package), rebuild and publish again, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_CONFLICT The destination's packages have different tags, a package has several tags, or some have a tag and some do not. The message lists each tag and package. One release has one tag. Give each independently versioned package its own destination, delete a duplicate tag, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_AMBIGUOUS Several packages of a build share the artifact's version with different tags, and the build did not record which package made the artifact. Rebuild with this version of oyzu, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_COMMIT_MISMATCH The derived tag points at a different commit than the one built, in your checkout or on GitHub. Also when packages record the tag on different commits. Build the tagged commit and publish again, or pass --tag to publish to that release anyway. PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED --tag is given but no selected destination is a GitHub release, or the publication is governed. Drop --tag. The recorded tags are what the checkout looked like when you built. Oyzu does not authenticate them against source control. The tag is tied to the built commit, not to a clean tree: a build of the tagged commit with uncommitted changes still publishes to that tag.

Oyzu derives each asset's name when you publish, from the file's local name and the compatibility its builder recorded. This lets one release hold several platforms of one operating system. File bytes and local dist/ names do not change. Recorded compatibility Asset name Example target (built for one platform) <stem>-<os>-<arch><ext> oyzu for linux/x86_64 becomes oyzu-linux-x86_64. oyzu.exe for windows/x86_64 becomes oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe. app.tar.gz for linux/arm64 becomes app-linux-arm64.tar.gz. independent (no platform restriction) the filename site.tar.gz native (the package's own name encodes the platform, such as a wheel) the filename pkg-1.0-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl pending, unknown or missing refused with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID The builder must record what the file is for. Platforms use the canonical spelling (x86_64, arm64, never amd64). An ABI is added only when it differs from the OS default (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows, none elsewhere). A GNU Linux build is oyzu-linux-x86_64, a musl build is oyzu-linux-x86_64-musl, and a GNU Windows build is oyzu-windows-x86_64-gnu.exe. Evidence files follow the derived name. Qualified selectors (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64/musl) and {artifact.platform} paths use the same form, so a GNU and a musl build of one output can sit in one release. In the evidence path the platform renders as linux/x86_64 for the default ABI and linux/x86_64-musl otherwise. A selector that names the default ABI (@linux/x86_64/gnu) never matches. Oyzu refuses it and shows the form to write. Two artifacts that publish to the same platform are refused with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before any evidence loading or network access. Names carry no version, so releases/latest/download/oyzu-linux-x86_64 keeps working across releases. Assets uploaded earlier under unqualified names are left alone. They are never renamed or removed. Extension rule: the extension is the longest case-insensitive match from .tar.gz, .tar.xz, .tar.zst, .tgz, .zip, .exe, .msi, .dmg, .pkg, .deb, .rpm, .dll, .so, .dylib, keeping its original case. Without a match, the platform is appended. Name checks (all fail with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before any evidence loading, signing or network access): Names use ASCII letters, digits, dot, underscore and dash only, at most 220 bytes, with no leading dot. A name must not end in a reserved evidence suffix. The evidence assets are <asset>.provenance.sigstore.json and <asset>.publication.sigstore.json. Two names that differ only in ASCII case collide. Executor records: each artifact also records how it was built (host, cross-toolchain with its target, or container). That record is part of the plan, the signed intent and the receipt. An unknown executor kind or field is PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID. A cross toolchain whose target does not match the artifact's platform is PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_INVALID. A release publication refuses a platform-specific (target or native) artifact that has no executor record, with PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_UNKNOWN. Rebuild it with this version of oyzu. Publishing does not otherwise judge how the artifact was built.

Before any upload, Oyzu checks the whole plan for name collisions and for assets that already exist on the release. Identical existing content is reused. Different bytes at the same name fail with PUBLISH_CONFLICT. Oyzu never overwrites or deletes. A GitHub API failure (an unexpected HTTP status, invalid JSON, or a release or asset list that is too large) fails with PUBLISH_GITHUB_API and the status. It uploads and re-downloads your provenance and the signed publication intent before the file they describe. Success requires downloading each asset and matching bytes, sizes, digests and evidence claims. An upload acknowledgement is not enough. An interrupted upload can leave an asset on the release. The receipt lists which assets were completed, failed or unfinished. Run the same publish again. Matching assets stay and only missing work is done. If the subject, coordinate or evidence changed, make a new plan. A same-name asset with different evidence is a conflict. Oyzu will not replace it. Other people can still edit release metadata, so a read-back is a check at that moment and not a permanent guarantee.

For GitHub.com, Oyzu talks to the configured API origin, the release's upload route on uploads.github.com and asset downloads on release-assets.githubusercontent.com. API path prefixes are preserved. Requests stay on the same origin, and upload routes are tied to the repository and release ID. Redirected downloads are anonymous. The token is never sent to a redirect target. GitHub Enterprise endpoints are supported only when all routes are on the API origin under its prefix. Translating /api/v3 to /api/uploads is not supported. GitHub Actions artifacts and GHCR are not supported destinations.

A build records the platforms each target declares (platforms: in build.yaml). When you publish, Oyzu compares them with the platforms of the artifacts you selected, combining the variants of one target. A declared platform with no selected artifact is a gap. It may never have been built (for example a build on only one runner) or you may not have selected it. In the release context a gap refuses the whole publish with PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_INCOMPLETE, naming each missing target and platform, before any evidence loading, signing or network access. In any other context it is a warning. A target that declares no platforms is not checked. A bundle with no platform records (built by an older oyzu) is refused in release with PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_UNKNOWN and warned about elsewhere. If you never ship a platform, remove it from the declared platforms. An allowance below covers one publication, not a standing exception. To publish anyway, name each missing platform with a reason: oyzu publish --destination github \ --allow-incomplete darwin/x86_64=no-intel-mac-runner \ --allow-incomplete windows/arm64="arm64 runner not available yet" Each value is <platform>=<reason> (aliases are accepted; the reason is 1 to 200 printable characters). A malformed value, a repeated platform, or a platform that no published target is missing fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, so the record never claims a gap that does not exist. Every gap, with the reason you gave (or null for a warned gap), is part of the plan digest, is recorded in every signed publication intent as incompletePlatforms, and appears in the receipt. Governed publication does not check completeness and refuses the flag (PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED). Several bundles as one publication. If you build one platform per job, publish every platform at once by repeating --manifest, one per bundle: oyzu publish --destination github \ --manifest bundles/linux-x86_64/dist/manifest.json \ --manifest bundles/darwin-arm64/dist/manifest.json \ --allow-incomplete windows/arm64=runner-unavailable The artifacts from all bundles are selected, checked for completeness together and published in one plan. Each artifact keeps its own bundle's files and executor record. Giving the same bundle twice is PUBLISH_REQUEST_INVALID. Governed publication takes one manifest (PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED).

If the build's configuration requires verification for certain tool versions (verification.<tool>, usually set by policy), standalone publishing checks each line against the verification the given bundles recorded. This happens after selection and the completeness check, and before any evidence loading, signing or network access. Each required line must be one of: outside the build's native version range (so it does not apply), covered by the build's own passing tests on a version in that line, or covered by a passing verification run of the same build, from any --manifest bundle, that verified its source or the published artifact. Otherwise publishing fails with PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING. The message names each uncovered line, why it is not covered and the commands of the runs the build left to other jobs. Oyzu resolves the requirement at publish time, in the build's folder and the publication's context. To cover a line, run a separate verification job (oyzu build --verify-only) and pass its bundle beside the platform bundles. That bundle is evidence only, and nothing is published from it. The receipt lists under verification how each line was settled. See required tool lines. Governed publication does not check verification evidence.

Oyzu publishes its own releases with this same path. Each platform is built in its own job. One oyzu publish then runs in the release context with a --manifest per platform and a --tag, uploading binaries as assets of a release in the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository. Follow that repository's releases to download them. Releases are binary-only, and the source repository stays separate. To cut a release: Merge a commit whose Cargo.toml says X.Y.Z, tag it oyzu/vX.Y.Z and push the tag to oyzuai/oyzu. Create and publish the release with the same tag in oyzuai/oyzu-releases. Start the release workflow: gh workflow run release.yml -f tag=oyzu/vX.Y.Z. The workflow attaches assets to that release. It never creates the release or the tag. It writes to oyzuai/oyzu-releases with the OYZU_RELEASES_TOKEN secret, a token with Contents read/write on that repository only, because the workflow's own token can't write to another repository. If OYZU_RELEASES_TOKEN is missing, or the release repository differs from the committed destination, the run stops before publishing. A fork sets the repository variable OYZU_RELEASE_REPO and edits the destination's repository. The release build: Runs one job per platform. Each downloads the newest earlier release's oyzu for its platform, builds the release tag with it (oyzu build cli) and signs provenance with the witness. Audits the build for binary-only distribution, which refuses any shipped component that needs source delivery. The corresponding-source companion stays in the run's retained bundle and isn't uploaded. Runs Linux x86_64 and the publish job, which hold the signing seeds and the release token, on the main runner pool named by the repository variable OYZU_MAIN_RUNNER (a JSON runs-on value that includes the oyzu-main label). If it's unset or lacks that label, the run stops in its first job, before anything that holds a secret, rather than falling back to a hosted runner. The first job runs on that pool too. The other five platforms build natively on GitHub-hosted runners; a platform the incomplete input leaves out only records that it was skipped, so it runs on the main pool and needs no hosted runner. Never reads a shared action cache, so every shipped output is built by the release job itself. The publish job first publishes each platform's oyzu-notices-<os>-<arch>.txt and reads it back, then publishes the binaries to the committed [publish.destinations.github] with --tag. It then attaches the configuration schemas build.yaml.schema.json and oyzu.toml.schema.json, printed by oyzu config schema, which editors reach at https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu-releases/releases/latest/download/<asset> (see editor schemas). Re-run a release with the same gh workflow run command. oyzu's own CI jobs​ Oyzu's own CI jobs start from the newest published release of oyzu and run Cargo through oyzu exec, so the project builds itself with the tool it ships. Setup action. The setup step runs tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --release --require-release --ci-machine-binding, reading releases from the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases (OYZU_RELEASE_REPO names another repository, for forks). It uses the downloaded executable only when its SHA-256 digest matches the one GitHub reports for the asset, as the install script does, then puts .oyzu/bin on PATH and writes one summary line naming the release tag, asset and digest of the oyzu used. CI ignores user configuration, so --ci-machine-binding builds only this checkout's Rust and Node plugins and binds them in a new machine configuration on the job's ephemeral runner (see CI machine binding). Node and Python. Repository checks and the CLI job's harness scripts get Node and Python from the checks toolset in oyzu.toml, pinned in oyzu.lock (oyzu --toolset checks install --frozen), so they don't use actions/setup-node or actions/setup-python. The checkers' Python packages go into a virtual environment outside the tool store. The task and build scenario jobs still use the setup-* actions, because those host tools are what the scenarios run the candidate against. No source build. The setup step never builds the oyzu CLI from source. If no release has an executable for the runner's platform, or the release's oyzu can't read this checkout's configuration, the step fails with that reason; publish a release to fix it. Run the bootstrap without --require-release locally to build from source. The base execution image is published by a separate workflow using the released oyzu. With --root tooling/images, that folder is its own project root, so its configuration never mixes with the CLI's. Without --root, the repository root's configuration applies and refuses the folder's [publish] table with CONFIG_SCOPE. Each platform builds on a runner of its own architecture (linux/arm64 on GitHub's arm64 runner), which runs: oyzu --root tooling/images lock --update base # re-lock the apt packages on this runner oyzu --root tooling/images build base # RUN installs them offline from the lock node tooling/release-witness.mjs sign --manifest tooling/images/dist/manifest.json \ --out tooling/images/.oyzu/release-evidence --artifact base/image@linux/x86_64 A publish job then downloads both builds and publishes them together: oyzu --root tooling/images --json publish --destination base \ --manifest base-amd64/dist/manifest.json --manifest base-arm64/dist/manifest.json Both images and their image index are pushed by digest to ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/base with the same release keys as the CLI, as in Publishing an OCI image. The registry credential is the job's GITHUB_TOKEN. The lock is observed again on each run, because replaying debs.lock.yaml needs the signed apt metadata in the machine's own store (see OS package lock limits). The job summary shows how the lock changed against the committed one, and the run uploads the lock it built from. When it changed, the provenance records the source as dirty. The job needs a released oyzu that has the Docker plugin, pins the published base image, locks Ubuntu packages with epoch versions and composes image indexes, plus a committed tooling/images/oyzu.lock that selects that release's Docker plugin. Until then, the job fails at its first oyzu step. Each runner locks its own architecture and keeps the committed lock's entries for the other. After a Dockerfile change, run oyzu lock on an amd64 and an arm64 host and commit the result. oyzu publish pushes by digest only, so a last step points the tag 1 at the index with docker buildx imagetools create --prefer-index=false, which copies it unchanged, checks the tag's digest and prints the index digest. The job needs a Docker engine, so it runs on GitHub-hosted runners, and each run needs the maintainer's approval.

Release assets for the oyzu CLI are named per host. The install script and the repository bootstrap pick the one for your host and check the SHA-256 digest GitHub reports for it before installing: Host Asset Linux x86_64 / aarch64 oyzu-linux-x86_64 / oyzu-linux-arm64 macOS x86_64 / arm64 oyzu-darwin-x86_64 / oyzu-darwin-arm64 (a shell under Rosetta gets arm64) Windows x86_64 / ARM64 oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe / oyzu-windows-arm64.exe On Windows, oyzu-shim-windows-<arch>.exe is installed beside oyzu.exe as oyzu-shim.exe. See the install script for how installation works.

With the Oyzu platform, oyzu publish registers the build, uploads its file, and asks the platform to run a publication. The platform decides which destinations and evidence requirements apply. Your command line cannot widen that authority. Choose it by giving a server, account and project: oyzu build oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json --provenance FILE is required. It is a signed provenance bundle you already have, sent unchanged. --destination cannot be combined with this mode. It publishes one staged file artifact. --no-upload does not work with it. Optionally pass --policy-evidence FILE, an existing signed policy report that the platform's policy may require. Oyzu sends the file unchanged as policyEvidence.bundle. It does not verify the report, evaluate policy or treat it as an approval. The platform decides whether to accept it. What the command does: Reads the manifest, uploads the artifact and registers the build with its components. Starts a publication operation: POST /publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/operations with the registration build, the artifact's identity and reference, and the provenance. Follows that operation (GET /operations/{operationId}) until it finishes and prints its decisions and receipts. Registering or staging a build is never reported as completed distribution. If following the operation times out, the CLI reports status: "unfinished" and a recovery message. The operation continues on the platform, so inspect it before you submit another request. Server URL path prefixes are preserved, with or without a trailing slash. Note: Governed publication needs an Oyzu platform that serves this API. It is separate from standalone publishing, which works on its own.

For governed publication: A finished oyzu build whose manifest records status: succeeded. A failed, cancelled or interrupted build is refused before anything is sent (PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED). The platform URL, account and project, as flags or environment variables. A credential the project accepts: the pipeline's OIDC token for a trusted CI connector, or a publish token from the project's CI connector. See Credentials. Commit, repository and ref come from the CI system's environment or from flags.

Flag Environment Default Meaning --server URL OYZU_URL required The platform's URL. Must be https, except http://localhost, http://127.0.0.1 or http://[::1] for local development, so a token never crosses a network unencrypted (PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER). --account ID OYZU_ACCOUNT required The account to publish to. --project ID OYZU_PROJECT required The project to publish to. --manifest FILE Standalone: the root's build.bundleDirectory. Governed: dist/manifest.json The build manifest, relative to -C. Repeat it to publish several bundles as one standalone publication. For governed publication, pass --manifest .oyzu/bundle/manifest.json if your bundle is elsewhere. --provenance FILE required for governed publication The signed provenance bundle, sent unchanged. --policy-evidence FILE none Optional signed policy report for the platform's policy. Governed only. --version VERSION none The build's version, if the pipeline names one. --commit SHA from CI The built commit. --repository OWNER/NAME from CI The repository the build came from. --audience AUDIENCE OYZU_AUDIENCE oyzu The audience to request for OIDC tokens the CLI gets from a CI system. --token-env NAME none Read the OIDC token from this environment variable instead of discovering one. --no-upload OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 upload Register the build without uploading artifacts. Governed publication needs the upload and refuses this. A flag wins over its environment variable. Account and project IDs use lowercase letters, digits and inner hyphens, 1 to 63 characters, starting and ending with a letter or digit. With --json, the CLI prints the final operation record, including registrationBuild. Transport errors use the usual {"error": ..., "exitCode": 2} shape.
