jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 permissions: contents: read id-token: write # lets oyzu publish request an OIDC token steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: oyzu build - run: oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json

oyzu publish uses the first credential it finds, in this order: --token-env NAME, else OYZU_ID_TOKEN: an OIDC token the pipeline already has. A --token-env variable that is unset or empty is an error and does not fall through. GitHub Actions: when ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN are set (the job has permissions: id-token: write), the CLI requests a token for the audience and uses it. Bitbucket Pipelines: BITBUCKET_STEP_OIDC_TOKEN (a step with oidc: true). CircleCI: CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2, then CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN. Buildkite: when BUILDKITE is set and buildkite-agent is on PATH, buildkite-agent oidc request-token --audience oyzu. OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN: a scoped, revocable publish token (oyzp_...) issued on the project's CI connector, for CI tools without OIDC. How each CI system provides its token: CI system How GitHub Actions Set permissions: id-token: write on the job. Oyzu finds the token automatically. GitLab CI/CD Add id_tokens: to the job, for example OYZU_ID_TOKEN: {aud: oyzu}. Oyzu reads OYZU_ID_TOKEN (or name another variable with --token-env). Bitbucket Pipelines Set oidc: true on the step. Bitbucket fixes the audience, and the project's trust must accept it. CircleCI Oyzu finds CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2 or CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN, whose audience is the CircleCI organization. For an oyzu audience, run circleci run oidc get --claims '{"aud":"oyzu"}' and put the result in OYZU_ID_TOKEN. Buildkite Oyzu uses buildkite-agent oidc request-token. The pipeline's OIDC policy must allow it. Jenkins with the OIDC provider plugin Bind the plugin's credential to a variable and pass --token-env (or bind it as OYZU_ID_TOKEN). Jenkins without OIDC, TeamCity Use OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN from a credentials store or secure parameter. The platform decides which tokens a project accepts, based on the trusts on the project's CI connector. Oyzu sends the token only in the Authorization header of the publish request. It never prints, logs or writes it to disk. Progress output names only the source, for example "a GitHub Actions OIDC token". If a source is present but fails (GitHub refuses the token request, the Buildkite agent fails), the command stops with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE and does not fall back to another credential. If none is found, it fails with PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL. In GitHub Actions the message names the missing id-token permission.

The platform accepts a CI OIDC token once per privileged operation (build registration, upload grant, and publication create or retry). Reusing a token for the same operation is refused with HTTP 401. GitHub Actions and Buildkite can issue tokens on request, so Oyzu gets a new token for every attempt, including each retry after a connection failure or a 502, 503 or 504. Reads, such as polling an operation, use no token. Oyzu requests one token up front so a missing permission or failing agent stops the command before anything is sent. A failure to issue a later token stops the command with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE. A fixed token (--token-env, OYZU_ID_TOKEN, Bitbucket, CircleCI, OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN) is sent as is on every attempt. If a retry is refused with a 401 (or the platform says replayed), the command fails with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_REPLAYED. The earlier attempt may already have taken effect, so check the platform before you publish again with a new token. The Buildkite helper has a fixed 30-second deadline, including output capture. If it stalls, Oyzu tries to stop it and fails with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE and external command deadline exceeded. Oyzu does not fall back to the publish token or wait on a process holding the output open. There is no timeout setting or automatic retry. Token output stays in memory and is not included in the timeout message. Check the Buildkite agent and its OIDC policy, then run oyzu publish again, or pass an already issued token with --token-env. Stopping the helper does not guarantee that remote work or child processes stopped.

Before registering the build, Oyzu uploads each artifact that is not an OCI image or index to the platform's registry as an OCI artifact. Pass --no-upload or set OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 to skip this. Images and indexes keep their oci_digest and are not uploaded this way. Only a regular file with its recorded size and SHA-256 digest is uploaded. A missing or changed file stops the publish with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED before Oyzu asks for any credential. A directory artifact is skipped with a warning and published without an oci_ref. Oyzu asks the platform for temporary registry access (POST .../builds/uploads, 1 to 1000 artifacts) and signs in to the registry with the standard token flow. The registry and its token endpoint must be on https and on the same origin (plain http only on loopback), so the grant token never goes elsewhere. It then pushes each file's bytes, skipping blobs the registry already has, and an OCI manifest addressed by digest (never a tag). The manifest carries the file's media type and name, and the output name in the annotation dev.oyzu.output. If the platform answers 404 (no artifact storage), Oyzu warns and publishes without upload. 401, 403 and 422 fail the publish with the platform's problem, and 502, 503 and 504 are retried like the publish request. Registry requests that fail with a server error or in transport are retried up to three times. Any other registry refusal fails with PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED and nothing is published. Each uploaded artifact then carries "oci_ref": "<registry host[:port]>/<repository>@sha256:<manifest digest>".

POST {server}/publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/builds with Authorization: Bearer <credential> and a JSON body: { "version": "1.4.2", "commit": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567", "repository": "acme/web", "ref": "refs/heads/main", "run_url": "https://github.com/acme/web/actions/runs/42", "outputs": [ {"path": "dist/manifest.json", "kind": "manifest", "media_type": "application/vnd.oyzu.build-manifest.v1alpha1+json", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 2101}, {"path": "dist/api/linux/x86_64/server", "kind": "artifact", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123, "target": "api", "name": "binary", "version": "0.1.0-dev.g111111111111", "oci_ref": "registry.example/acme/web/artifacts@sha256:…"} ] } outputs lists the manifest file and one artifact per artifact in the manifest, with its path, media type, digest, size, target, name and version. OCI images and indexes also carry oci_digest. Fields Oyzu cannot determine are left out. Paths are relative to the checkout root (the manifest's directory relative to -C, then the artifact's bundle path). Oyzu checks the platform's limits before sending (PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID): at most 1000 outputs, paths up to 1024 bytes, media types 255, targets 256, names 64 and versions 255. Every artifact needs a target, name, version, SHA-256 digest and safe relative path. Commit, repository, ref and run link come from the first CI system that announces itself: CI system commit repository ref run_url GitHub Actions GITHUB_SHA GITHUB_REPOSITORY GITHUB_REF $GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID GitLab CI_COMMIT_SHA CI_PROJECT_PATH refs/tags/$CI_COMMIT_TAG or refs/heads/$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH CI_PIPELINE_URL CircleCI CIRCLE_SHA1 CIRCLE_PROJECT_USERNAME/CIRCLE_PROJECT_REPONAME CIRCLE_TAG / CIRCLE_BRANCH CIRCLE_BUILD_URL Buildkite BUILDKITE_COMMIT (not HEAD) from BUILDKITE_REPO BUILDKITE_TAG / BUILDKITE_BRANCH BUILDKITE_BUILD_URL Bitbucket BITBUCKET_COMMIT BITBUCKET_REPO_FULL_NAME BITBUCKET_TAG / BITBUCKET_BRANCH https://bitbucket.org/<repo>/pipelines/results/$BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER Jenkins GIT_COMMIT from GIT_URL GIT_BRANCH without origin/ BUILD_URL TeamCity BUILD_VCS_NUMBER none (use --repository) none none

The platform answers 200 with the build, its eligibility (candidate or snapshot), one entry per component and the outputs that belong to no component: Build registered · 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 (candidate) ✓ published api 1.4.2 (candidate) = already published web 2.0.0 ! skipped worker 0.3.0: the build did not publish [worker/config] Outputs in no component (never shipped) web/build-metadata This only records components. Nothing is distributed until the publication operation finishes, and its receipt controls success. A malformed response (missing build, eligibility or component fields) fails with PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID. The server may already have published the build, so check its state and the platform and client versions. Retrying the same build is safe.

Governed publishing failures exit 2 and print one diagnostic. Nothing the platform refused is retried. Code Meaning PUBLISH_NOT_CONFIGURED A server, account or project is missing or malformed (or, standalone, destinations or requirements are not configured). PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER The server uses plain http and is not localhost. PUBLISH_MANIFEST_MISSING / PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID No manifest at the path, or it breaks a rule above. Nothing is sent and no token is requested. PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest records a build that did not succeed. PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED An artifact is missing, not a regular file, or no longer has its recorded size or digest. Nothing is sent. Build again. PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED The registry refused or failed a sign-in, blob or manifest request after retries. Nothing is published. PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's upload grant or answer is malformed, or names a registry that is not https. PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL / PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE No credential was found, or a CI system did not issue one. PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_REPLAYED (401) The platform refused a fixed CI token on a retry, or said it was reused. The earlier attempt may have taken effect. Check the platform, then publish again with a new token. GitHub Actions and Buildkite send a new token per attempt. PUBLISH_UNAUTHENTICATED (401) The platform did not accept the credential: expired, wrong audience or revoked. 403 (PUBLISH_<code>) The token is valid, but no trust on the project's CI connector accepts this pipeline (repository, branch or workflow). other PUBLISH_<code> The platform's RFC 9457 problem: its detail, each errors[] entry as field: message, and the request ID. PUBLISH_UNREACHABLE The platform could not be reached after retries. Connection failures and 502, 503 and 504 answers are retried up to five attempts with backoff, honoring Retry-After (at most 30 seconds). Each retry carries its own token where the credential source can issue one. Standalone publishing codes are explained where they arise: Code See CONFIG_SCOPE, CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN Settings, Selecting artifacts PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_INVALID, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_SUBJECT_MISMATCH, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_BUILDER_DENIED, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_UNSUPPORTED Selecting artifacts, Provenance evidence PUBLISH_SIGNING_INVALID What is published PUBLISH_BINDING_UNPUSHED, CONFIG_BINDING_UNPUSHED A bound chart needs its image PUBLISH_TAG_UNKNOWN, PUBLISH_TAG_CONFLICT, PUBLISH_TAG_AMBIGUOUS, PUBLISH_TAG_COMMIT_MISMATCH, PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED Which release: the release tag PUBLISH_CONFLICT, PUBLISH_GITHUB_API Uploads and conflicts PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_INCOMPLETE, PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_UNKNOWN, PUBLISH_REQUEST_INVALID Incomplete platform sets PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING Required verification evidence PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_INVALID, PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_UNKNOWN Asset names

Publishing needs network access, and each file is read into memory. Standalone destinations are OCI registries and existing GitHub releases. Native npm and PyPI publishing, mutable OCI tags and multi-platform image indexes are not supported. Governed publication handles one staged file artifact and needs an Oyzu platform. A registry whose token endpoint is on another origin is refused. Commit, repository and ref are what the CI system reports. The platform decides what it trusts from the token's claims.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-applications.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A python/app target with static PEP 621 metadata and one console script produces a runnable, versioned .pyz application next to the usual wheel and source distribution. Use it to ship a Python service or tool as a single archive built from tested inputs. The application holds the built wheel's files and the runtime dependencies. It doesn't copy other files from your checkout. Note: Python applications are experimental. Isolated builds run in Linux containers, so they need Docker and the base execution image. See Compiled builder and provisioned images.

Declare the target in build.yaml: builds: api: uses: python/app Your pyproject.toml says what to build: [project] name = "example-api" version = "0.1.0" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] example-api = "api:main" [build-system] requires = ["setuptools==80.9.0"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [tool.setuptools] packages = ["api"] Build, inspect and run it: oyzu run list oyzu build oyzu inspect dist python <application-path-from-manifest> api.main is an ordinary console function. Oyzu doesn't add a server, port, health check or supervisor. Read the application artifact's path from dist/manifest.json.

Artifact Name Notes application <target>-<version>.pyz The runnable archive. The version is the package's PEP 440 build version, such as 0.1.0.dev0+g0123456789ab wheel Native wheel A separate artifact sdist Native source distribution A separate artifact Select artifacts by name, not by position: an application build produces more than two files. Version inference combines your metadata with exact tags, the nearest release tag and Conventional Commits. A v1.4.2 baseline plus a feature commit can give 1.5.0.dev0+g... for all three artifacts without editing your checkout. A local build or tag doesn't authorize a release. Applications with only a requirements.txt use SemVer versions such as 0.0.0-dev.g<source>, and no distribution metadata is invented.

With several console scripts, or none, planning fails with a message. There is no setting yet to choose one. Auto-detected python/package projects may have several console scripts. A requirements-only application runs app.py or __main__.py.

Oyzu prepares the dependencies (Python dependency preparation). It runs your native build backend once. It assembles the application. It tests the sources extracted from that archive. It runs the lint and read-only format checks. Reports go to dist/ with their paths, digests and summaries in the manifest. See Python testing for overrides, empty suites and coverage thresholds. Direct tasks (oyzu run) run your native commands. They don't assemble archives or collect build reports.

Assembly: checks the wheel's name and console entry point against the plan installs the runtime wheels only (offline, without resolving dependencies) with pip. Build and test tools stay out removes installer-specific provenance and launchers tied to one interpreter generates a launcher from the package's entry point metadata records the source, version, project files, runtime packages, entry point and original wheel digest in oyzu-application.json inside the archive The archive has sorted paths and normalized ZIP metadata. Oyzu refuses unsafe paths, case collisions, symlinks and oversized payloads. Packaging confirms the archive is the one that was tested and that the wheel and sdist didn't change. If tests, quality checks or reports fail, or an artifact changed, the artifacts aren't collected. Read the logs and reports in dist/. These checks guard the build and are not a security boundary against malicious tests.

Native pip builds run on your machine and make a wheel only. Oyzu can install CPython for them from requires-python or .python-version (Python installation). See native local builds. The .pyz application comes from isolated builds, which also handle requirements-only, uv, Poetry and legacy projects. They use Linux containers through Docker with Python 3.12 and pip, uv or Poetry. CPython comes from oyzu.lock, so installing CPython on your machine doesn't replace it. Isolated builds download dependencies during preparation. After that, assembly and tests run with the network off. If an input is missing, fix it during preparation. There is no network fallback in the build. The archive needs pure Python wheels and ZIP-compatible code and data. Native extensions, .pth startup files and libraries that need real files fail with an error. Test the app to check how it loads resources. Python is not bundled. Running the .pyz needs a compatible interpreter. Legacy setup.py applications, dynamic console metadata, editable installs, entry point overrides and native application layouts are not supported. To put the archive in an OCI image, see Python application containers.

Isolated builds run on the base execution image. Oyzu mounts its engine and the Python plugin into each action, so no image carries an Oyzu worker and none needs rebuilding when the CLI changes. CPython comes from oyzu.lock and is restored into each action. The base image has no Python. uv and Poetry aren't restored from the lock yet. For those builds, pass an image that provides the manager: --image uv=<ref> or --image poetry=<ref>. An image you pass must meet the bring-your-own requirements. A locked CPython still takes the place of the image's own. The oyzu CLI itself doesn't need Python. Builds run Oyzu's own steps in compiled code. Small embedded Python helpers run inside the selected Python only to call the packaging, Poetry export, setuptools, pytest, coverage and quality-tool APIs. Ruff runs as a native program. The container that runs your finished application uses a plain python:3.12-slim-bookworm and doesn't need the Oyzu engine.
Python application containers Python testing Python dependency preparation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-containers.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Set with.container: true on a python/app build to package the tested application archive into an OCI image. You need no Dockerfile and no second application build. Note: Experimental. Supported for isolated builds on Linux. There is no startup smoke test of the application, and the image is built for CPython 3.12 only. builds: api: uses: python/app with: container: true Build with oyzu build --isolated. A native build refuses a container request with native build does not support these declared relationships; select --isolated explicitly. oyzu build runs the application's build, test, lint and format steps as usual, and then adds the image steps under a derived target named api-container in the plan and manifest. You can't run those derived steps directly with oyzu run or override them with hooks. If one of your own targets already has the derived name, the build fails instead of overwriting it. with.container belongs to python/app. oyzu config validate and every command that reads your builds check it. It is refused on any other builder, including python/library, and so is the older top-level container: field (the message names with.container).

The Python toolchain and dependencies described in Python applications python:3.12-slim-bookworm in your local Docker image store The base execution image. The image helpers ship in the Docker plugin package (Docker images) The right AppArmor profile, where your host needs one Oyzu doesn't pull any other missing image, install Docker or change host security settings.

The python-pure-zip-3.12-v1 profile needs a pure-Python, ZIP-compatible application and CPython 3.12. Oyzu checks the local base image's implementation and Python version without using the network and uses exactly that image content. If the image changes during the build, the build fails. Provision base images by a process you trust. Oyzu does not authenticate to registries, and a matching image is not an approval of its contents. Setting Default Archive path /app/application.pyz User and group 65532:65532 Working directory /app Entrypoint ["python", "/app/application.pyz"] CMD Cleared Oyzu doesn't add ports, health checks, a server lifecycle, deployment settings or secrets. Nothing is installed during image assembly. The archive already contains its runtime dependencies.

Use an object to change the defaults. Every field is optional, and {} behaves like true. builds: api: uses: python/app with: container: base: registry.example/python-runtime:3.12 user: "1000:1001" workdir: /srv/api entrypoint: [python, /app/application.pyz] Field Values Notes base An image reference, up to 512 bytes Must already be in your local store with CPython 3.12. It gets the same check as the default base. No pull and no public fallback user Numeric UID:GID, each up to 4294967295 Names and negative IDs fail. This identity also owns the copied archive workdir Absolute path, up to 1,024 bytes, using letters, digits and /._-, with no .. Doesn't move the archive from /app/application.pyz entrypoint 1 to 64 non-empty arguments, up to 4,096 bytes each, no control characters Used as given. No shell or variable expansion Unknown keys, wrong types and explicit null values fail validation. A custom entrypoint is recorded as launch metadata. It doesn't prove that the program exists or that your service starts. The runtime check still runs, and changing the entrypoint doesn't choose between several console scripts in the application. The overrides give no production approval. with.container: false means no container everywhere. The build counts as having no image.

The application, wheel and sdist artifacts are still produced. The derived target adds an image artifact, for example api-container/artifacts/api-0.1.0-dev.g<source>.oci.tar. The image version uses the SemVer spelling, not Python's PEP 440 version. The manifest records the file digest and the OCI digest. Image steps start after the application's tests, required reports and quality checks pass. A failure there blocks the image. Oyzu copies the exact tested archive into an empty private build context. Generated image files never enter your checkout. Assertions on the image's content and platform produce their own JUnit report. No application coverage is invented for the image. Failed image assertions block the image from reaching the bundle. Read the logs and reports, fix the error and rebuild. The configuration engine applies precedence and policy. Docker's eligibility is checked together with the application before preparation. docker.apparmorProfile comes from your resolved configuration and is fixed for the image step, and no environment variable overrides it. A profile name doesn't grant signing or publishing rights. In a managed setup, connector restrictions apply to application downloads, and there is no managed fallback.

The application's startup is not tested. Passing archive tests and image assertions doesn't show that it starts. Legacy and native Python application layouts, container matrices, other language runtimes and centrally configured runtime profiles are not supported. Discovery doesn't turn on containers for you. Related: Python applications, Docker images, configuration.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-preparation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Before an isolated Python build runs, Oyzu prepares your dependencies. A worker that can reach only PyPI downloads binary wheels, and every build, test and quality step then installs them offline. This page explains which inputs Oyzu reads and how it treats dependency-group includes, editable references to your own project, dynamic versions and packages that must be built from source. pip, uv and Poetry keep their own behavior; Oyzu reads only the declarations listed here. Note: Python builds are experimental. An isolated build needs Docker and the base execution image, plus any system libraries your dependencies need. See Python applications.

The python/package builder (also available as python/library) and python/app come from the oyzu/python plugin package. The plugin reads your project files, picks the package manager and quality tools you already use, and declares the commands, reports and artifacts. Oyzu itself downloads dependencies, runs the steps offline and checks the reports. If the plugin refuses a project, the build fails. There is no fallback to another builder. An isolated pip build needs a plugin package built for Linux, not a raw development executable. See plugin packages. A Linux environment image and its system libraries are also required; choosing a CPython version does not provide them.

An isolated build uses the CPython version recorded in oyzu.lock. It comes from [tools].python and from your project's own requirements (requires-python, .python-version). oyzu pin records the choice, and oyzu build --isolated --full --frozen reads it without rewriting the lock. Oyzu checks the CPython archive against its locked digest and mounts it read-only in the worker. If the lock has no entry for the platform, the build stops and tells you how to fix it. It never falls back to the image's Python. Offline builds need the archive already cached. That one interpreter is used for environment markers, dependency inventory, pip downloads, wheel compatibility, the project version, virtual environments, source builds and tests. Your own task commands see it first on PATH. How each manager uses it: Manager Interpreter pip The selected CPython uv The selected CPython, passed explicitly. uv's managed Python and downloads are turned off Poetry The exporter runs in the image's own interpreter, where Poetry is installed. Your PATH is unchanged The image still supplies pip, uv or Poetry and any compilers or system libraries you need. A Docker image that asks for runtime-only dependencies uses its own interpreter, markers and compatibility, not the producer project's CPython. If a Python pin from your configuration or policy conflicts with that interpreter, the build fails. Legacy setup.py projects with runtime dependencies are refused. A legacy package takes its version from the shared version decision, and planning fails if its metadata disagrees.

A native python/package pip build runs on your machine, not in a container. Supported on Linux x86-64 (glibc). Oyzu installs the managed CPython and, before copying your source, reads its runtime. You provide the dependencies: With no .venv in the target, Oyzu uses the managed CPython directly. With a .venv, it must be a standard virtual environment created from that exact managed interpreter, with system site packages off. A mismatch fails the build. A linked or shared environment root, or a source input inside .venv, fails the build. Ordinary interpreter symlinks inside a valid environment are fine. Each check has a 20-second limit. Install your project dependencies, pytest, pytest-cov, coverage and the quality tools you use into your own .venv by running the managed interpreter. Oyzu does not install them, copy the environment or repair it, and the source copy leaves .venv out. Missing packages fail as usual, and offline builds need them already present. The interpreter is used for the wheel build and for pytest and coverage reporting. Ruff runs from the environment's own entry point. Black and Flake8 run through the interpreter with -I -m. Task replacements and hooks keep their commands and still owe their reports. If the environment does not match, recreate it from the managed CPython. This applies to full native builds only. It does not apply to direct tasks, to VIRTUAL_ENV selection, to environments found in parent folders, or to uv and Poetry.

Input Used for project.dependencies in pyproject.toml Runtime build-system.requires (or the locked legacy tools, with fixed defaults for tools not locked) Build The dev dependency group, with its includes Test requirements.txt Runtime Default test and quality tools you have not declared or locked Build or test How the closure is resolved: A uv project uses uv export --locked, and a Poetry project uses its lock export. That hashed export decides the closure for the project and its groups. Extra backend requirements, requirements.txt and injected tool requirements are resolved by pip, with your lock as constraints. They keep their extras and transitive dependencies. A pip project resolves all its declarations. Oyzu records every wheel's digest in the dependency snapshot. An authored build-system.requires is always authoritative, even when it conflicts with a lock. When it is missing, the default setuptools and wheel backend uses versions your lock already selects. For a tool the lock does not select, Oyzu falls back to setuptools==80.9.0 or wheel==0.45.1. Oyzu never refreshes a lock or drops one of your requirements to hide a conflict.

A package can provide its own quality tool, for example building Black and formatting with Black. The offline build installs your wheel before the quality checks, so the checks use that installed copy. Oyzu skips the default download of a quality tool whose name matches the current package. Explicit requirements, locked constraints and the report gates are unchanged.
documents.s: The current package as a quality tool

documents.t: [dependency-groups] follows PEP 735. An entry is a requirement string or an { include-group = "name" } table, and includes expand in place. Group names are compared after PEP 503 normalization, so Runtime_Checks and runtime-checks are the same group. [dependency-groups] dev = [{ include-group = "tests" }, "pytest-cov==6.0.0"] tests = [{ include-group = "runtime-checks" }, "pytest==8.3.5"] runtime-checks = ["packaging==24.2"] This captures packaging, pytest and pytest-cov as test inputs. Preparation fails, naming the group, for an include of an undefined group, two groups with equivalent names, a cyclic include, or any other table entry. Only the dev group is used, as in uv. For uv projects, the native export applies the same includes.

Requirements files often install the project itself (-e .[cli]), and dependency groups often reference it with extras (name[tests]). Oyzu builds the project from your source, so it never downloads it. It replaces the reference with what installing the project would add: project.dependencies plus the project.optional-dependencies for the extras you chose, following extras that reference the project again. Extra names are compared after normalization. An undefined extra fails preparation. A reference whose environment marker does not apply to the build interpreter is skipped, as pip skips it. In requirements.txt, the accepted editable forms are -e ., -e ./, --editable . and --editable=., each optionally followed by [extras]. The project needs a static project.name. Any other directive (-r, -c, an editable path to another folder, option lines) fails with Unsupported requirements directive; no alternate source fallback.
documents.s: The project itself as a requirement

documents.t: A dependency can require the project you are building, with extras. For example, a Litestar plugin requires litestar[cli]>=2.0.1. Oyzu satisfies that from your own source, without downloading it. Oyzu checks the declared requirements, the requested extras and their closure with native marker and extra rules. It fails on unknown extras, missing dependencies, unapproved direct URLs and a package that would be both downloaded and built from source. Dynamic dependency metadata can't be checked without running your build backend, so it is refused. Your source version can differ from the final version of the build. Before creating the virtual environment, Oyzu compares each constraint with the version it assigned to the build. It fails if there is no planned version, the project identity differs, or a constraint doesn't accept the version. This does not apply to apps or runtime-only dependency contexts.
documents.s: Dependencies that require the current project

documents.t: A project can list version in project.dynamic. For the pdm.backend, Oyzu reads the version from a file without running the backend or importing your code: [project] name = "example" dynamic = ["version"] [build-system] requires = ["pdm-backend"] build-backend = "pdm.backend" [tool.pdm.version] source = "file" path = "example/__init__.py" Oyzu reads that UTF-8 file with PDM's default rule: the first line that matches __version__ = "1.2.3" or VERSION = '1.2.3' wins, with an optional trailing comment. The value is validated as a PEP 440 version. Version inference then picks the build's version from it. The wheel and sdist metadata carry the build version, and the manifest keeps the original as nativeVersion. The path must be relative, inside your captured source, free of links, and name a regular file of at most 4 MiB. Bad paths, invalid UTF-8, a missing default literal and an invalid version fail preparation. Fix the declaration or the file and rebuild. Other dynamic forms use tag-based inference and are not executed: setuptools [tool.setuptools.dynamic] version = { attr = ... } Hatch file and VCS providers PDM call, SCM and custom-pattern providers PDM projects with backend-path, a tool.pdm.build.custom-hook, or a pdm_build.py Without applicable tags, the base is 0.0.0, which gives a version such as 0.0.0.dev0+g0123456789ab. The native strategy fails with version-needs-native when no native version exists. In its private build tree, Oyzu removes version from project.dynamic, removes tool.setuptools.dynamic.version if present and writes the build version as the static project.version. The wheel, sdist and their metadata then agree. Your checkout is unchanged. A pyproject.toml with neither a static nor a dynamic version fails with Python project version must be static or listed in project.dynamic.

Some locked packages have no wheel to download: a uv.lock package whose source is a Git repository pinned to a commit a uv workspace member or path dependency, which uv export lists as -e ./PATH or ./PATH a registry package that uv.lock locks with a source distribution (sdist) and no wheel Oyzu builds these from source, only inside the isolated worker that has no network, never during preparation. This works for uv projects only. Splitting. Oyzu separates these lines from the uv export and downloads only the registry wheels, with their hashes. A declaration that names such a package, including one that repeats the source as a direct URL such as advanced-alchemy @ git+https://github.com/..., is satisfied by the source build. A direct URL for a package that uv.lock doesn't build from source is still refused. Sdists. An sdist is downloaded from the files.pythonhosted.org route, checked against the SHA-256 in uv.lock and unpacked without running any of its code. A missing hash or a URL outside that route fails. Only regular files are written, names must be portable with one top-level folder, and archives are limited to 256 MiB. Git sources. Oyzu fetches the commit recorded in uv.lock with Git over a read-only route. Only public HTTPS GitHub repositories work. The checkout is stored without Git metadata, and no hooks, filters, submodules or credentials are used. Build requirements. Oyzu reads each source's build-system.requires (or the locked legacy tools for a setup.py package) and downloads them as build wheels, using the lock as constraints. No backend code runs. Build. In the worker, after the captured wheels are installed, each source is copied into the private build state and built with pip wheel --no-index --no-deps --no-build-isolation. A missing build requirement fails before the backend runs. The wheel must carry the locked name and version. Then all wheels are installed from a digest manifest with --require-hashes. For example, this declaration makes uv lock sampleproject at the commit: [project] dependencies = ["sampleproject"] [tool.uv.sources] sampleproject = { git = "https://github.com/pypa/sampleproject", rev = "621e4974ca25ce531773def586ba3ed8e736b3fc" } The dependency snapshot records each Git source with the digest of its captured tree and lists every source package in the oyzu.dev/python-sources extension, with its kind, path, commit, purpose and build requirements. An sdist source also records its URL and SHA-256. Workspace members belong to your project source and have no separate record. Because Git metadata is not captured, Oyzu sets SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION to the locked version during the source build, so setuptools-scm and hatch-vcs read it. A source that requires maturin or setuptools-rust needs Rust and Cargo crates, which Python preparation doesn't capture. Preparation fails naming the requirement, as it does for pydantic's pydantic-core member. A python/app whose runtime closure includes a package built from source fails at packaging, because application archives contain captured wheels only. Runtime dependency contexts for Docker refuse such packages.

The worker keeps everything it creates for a Python target outside your project, in /out/.oyzu-python of the target's private output root: Path Contents venv/ The build environment with captured wheels and source builds installed dist/ The wheel and sdist before packaging copies them sources/, source-builds/, source-wheels/ Copies and wheels of packages built from source application/, application-project/, application.pyz, test-application/ Application staging, the archive and its extracted test copy The output root lasts across the target's actions and is never inside /workspace. Because of that, build backends can't pack the build environment into your sdist, and Ruff, Black and Flake8 check only your project files. This state is private and not an input or output contract. Packaging copies artifacts to the bundle folder /out/<target>/<platform>/ (available to the adapter as OYZU_OUTPUT), and reports go to its reports/ folder. See the bundle layout. Hooks that used to look in a .oyzu-build/ folder inside the project no longer find it.

Preparation failures stop the build before any action runs and keep the worker's message. Fix the input and start a new build. Message Cause and fix Dependency group NAME is not defined / includes itself Fix the include in [dependency-groups] Project extra NAME is not defined Declare the extra in project.optional-dependencies or fix the reference An editable project reference needs a static pyproject.toml project name Declare project.name statically Source package NAME needs build requirement maturin... The source builds Rust code, which isn't supported Source package NAME build requirement REQ is not in the captured dependency set A build requirement of a source package wasn't captured. The build stops before running its backend Isolated source build of NAME failed The backend failed offline with only captured inputs. pip's output is in the action log Locked path requirement PATH: only workspace members and path dependencies inside the captured project can be built The export names an absolute path, a parent folder or a file: URL Git sources currently require a public HTTPS GitHub repository / Git source must lock a full commit identity Pin a public GitHub repository by full commit Git source NAME uses submodules, which preparation does not fetch The locked commit has a .gitmodules file Git sources need the git client in the Python preparation image The base execution image includes git. An image you pass with --image must too Packages built from source are supported only for uv projects with uv.lock / ...not supported in runtime dependency contexts Source builds work for uv projects only, and not for a Docker runtime context uv.lock sdist-only package NAME: has no locked SHA-256... / ...outside the approved registry file route The sdist entry can't be trusted. Re-lock from PyPI The sdist of NAME does not match the SHA-256 recorded in uv.lock The download differs from the lock. Nothing is built Python applications cannot package runtime dependency NAME built from source yet A python/app runtime dependency is built from source Direct URL requirements need an approved source adapter A declaration or requirements file pins a direct URL or Git source outside uv.lock Current project dependency REQ is incompatible with planned version VERSION A dependency on your project doesn't accept the build's version Current project extra is not defined: NAME / Current project dependency closure requires static metadata The closure can't be worked out from static metadata Poetry lock is missing or stale; update it with poetry lock Run poetry lock and commit the result

Installed-artifact tests measure the installed package, not your checkout. A coverage setting such as omit = ["*/site-packages/*"] under [tool.coverage.report] can exclude every measured file. Then the tests may pass but coverage reports No data to report, the required Cobertura report is missing and packaging is blocked. Narrow or remove that exclusion in your coverage configuration so the installed package is measured, then rerun. See Python testing.

Source builds work only for uv. Poetry Git and path sources, and Git or path lines in a pip requirements file, are refused. Git sources need a public HTTPS GitHub repository and a full commit. Sdist-only packages need files.pythonhosted.org sdists in uv.lock. Submodules and Git LFS content are not fetched. Sources that build Rust (maturin, setuptools-rust) or need other non-Python toolchains beyond what the image provides are not supported. A source package that is itself a build requirement of another source is refused, environment markers on member lines are refused, and virtual members are skipped as uv skips them. Source-built wheels are not checked for reproducibility. Only the source tree and the captured build requirements are digest-recorded. A Poetry lock whose content hash no longer matches the project is rejected, as poetry install rejects it. Oyzu doesn't refresh it. Only the PDM default file form supplies a native dynamic version. Other computed versions use tags, and dynamic dependencies are not computed. Only the dev dependency group is used, and you can't select others.
Python testing Python applications Version inference Python installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this when pip or uv should install from a private package index without a password in pip.conf, uv.toml, .netrc or environment variables. Each time you run pip or uv through oyzu, oyzu asks a local credential agent which index to use and gives the tool the password through its keyring support. You don't need the Python keyring package or any per-project authentication file. Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Python 3.12, pip 25.0 and uv 0.12, using Bash. Isolated oyzu build runs don't use this yet.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [python] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning python.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain pip and uv Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there.

With Python and pip, or uv, on PATH: oyzu exec -- python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt oyzu exec -- uv lock oyzu exec -- uv sync --locked eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt An activated Bash shell routes python, python3, pip, pip3 and uv through oyzu when they're installed. oyzu exec also recognizes versioned names such as python3.12 and pip3.12. Running Python itself is unchanged; only python -m pip goes through the agent. Tool Supported commands pip install, download, wheel uv lock, sync, pip install, pip sync --help and --version run without asking the agent. Other commands, including uv run and uv publish, fail with PYTHON_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED. Publish with oyzu publish.

Sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "pip" or "uv", "arguments": [...]}. This happens on every run, including warm or offline installs. Reads the agent's answer: { "index": "https://packages.example.com/simple/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } index is HTTP(S) with no credentials, query or fragment. username can't be empty. credentialEndpoint must be on 127.0.0.1. Adds the user name to the index URL and puts oyzu itself on PATH as keyring. Replaces the tool's index configuration for that run: pip gets PIP_CONFIG_FILE set to the null device, PIP_INDEX_URL, PIP_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess and no interactive prompts; uv gets UV_NO_CONFIG=1, UV_DEFAULT_INDEX and UV_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess; extra-index and find-links variables and UV_CONFIG_FILE are removed. When the tool runs keyring get <service> <username>, oyzu POSTs {"ecosystem": "python", "service": "...", "username": "..."} to credentialEndpoint, which must answer {"password": "..."}. The agent should check the request against the index it approved. Because pip and uv configuration files are switched off for the run, other options in them are ignored too. Requirements files, pyproject.toml, uv.toml and lock files aren't changed. Package caches and installed packages work as usual.

The password never goes into generated configuration, command arguments or environment variables. It passes through the keyring helper into the tool's memory, so the process can read it. Read-only access has to be enforced by the index account the agent uses. Helper failures show a generic message. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command before pip or uv starts, with no fallback to cached or direct access.
The tool's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID The endpoint or credential endpoint isn't 127.0.0.1 HTTP, or the response is too large Fix the endpoint or the agent PYTHON_SESSION_INVALID The response couldn't be read, or the index or user name isn't valid Fix the agent's response PYTHON_ROUTING_CONFLICT You passed an index, extra-index, find-links, keyring-provider, config-file, --isolated, --project or --directory option Remove the option PYTHON_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED The command isn't in the supported list Use a supported command

One index per run, for ordinary named packages (including hash-pinned requirements and uv locks). Direct URL, VCS and path dependencies, source directives in requirements files, uv source and workspace overrides, and credentials in .netrc or other auth stores aren't covered. Poetry and scripts that run pip or uv internally aren't covered. Turning off pip and uv configuration isn't a network sandbox. Temporary files may be left behind if oyzu is killed. Linux and Bash only. Windows and macOS aren't supported yet.
pip documentation on configuration uv configuration files Python installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-testing.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Python projects built with pip, uv or Poetry get an implicit test task that runs pytest. The task exists, and runs as part of the default build, even if your project has no tests/ or test/ folder. Pytest decides at run time which tests exist. Oyzu never imports conftest.py, runs Python or collects tests while it discovers your project. Note: Python support is experimental. Direct oyzu run test is supported on Windows and Linux. Isolated builds run in Linux containers.
oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Pass extra arguments to pytest after --: oyzu run test -- -k smoke.

Oyzu looks for pytest settings in pytest.ini, .pytest.ini, [tool.pytest.ini_options] in pyproject.toml, [pytest] in tox.ini or [tool:pytest] in setup.cfg. With none of these, pytest is still the default. Several configuration files are not treated as competing frameworks. Detection only records your intent. Pytest owns testpaths, file name patterns, markers and collection errors. This configuration needs no Oyzu setting: [pytest] testpaths = checks python_files = spec_*.py The implicit command depends on the project's manager: Manager Command pip python -m pytest uv uv run --locked pytest Poetry poetry run pytest Install Python, the manager and your dependencies first. Direct runs use the manager's own environment and behavior, including any synchronization it does, and are not isolated. TOML task replacements and pre/post hooks work as for any task.

oyzu run test runs the pytest command and writes JUnit and Cobertura reports into a test-only bundle in dist/. Pytest still collects the tests, and your manager picks the environment. See direct test reports for hooks, overrides, retention and inspection. Requirements: Python 3.11 or newer in the selected environment. pytest and pytest-cov in that environment. Oyzu does not install them. It works with pytest 8.3.5 and 9.1.1 with pytest-cov 6.0.0. Other versions can fail with an error instead of producing partial reports.

A direct run measures your checkout, not an installed package. It keeps your coverage configuration (COVERAGE_RCFILE or the usual coverage files), including source settings, branches, exclusions and thresholds. Without source settings, it measures the task's working directory, including modules that no test imports. Collected tests, files matching pytest's name patterns, conventional test file names, conftest.py files and .oyzu and .venv folders are left out of application coverage. Helper modules that tests import are not guessed to be tests. Use coverage exclusions for them. Omissions apply below the measured source root. A project that Oyzu copied into .oyzu/host-workspaces is still measured. Each run uses its own temporary coverage configuration and data file. An existing .coverage file or COVERAGE_FILE can't add old results and isn't overwritten. pytest-cov source and output options on the command line don't override the report locations Oyzu sets. Selectors such as -k work normally. Pytest caches and Python bytecode can still be written.

Oyzu adds reporting to the exact python -m pytest, pytest, and the implicit manager commands. python -m pytest uses the python on PATH, even in a uv or Poetry project. Bare pytest also uses python from PATH. Any other command (a custom shell program, for example) runs as written and must write the required reports to the declared paths or the report environment variables. Assertion and collection errors, coverage thresholds and missing reports fail the run, and the reports that exist are kept. An empty suite keeps pytest's exit code 5 and a zero-test JUnit file. A zero-denominator coverage report is not rewritten to 100 percent.

oyzu build runs tests in a Linux container after dependency preparation. Preparation adds pytest 8.3.5 and pytest-cov 6.0.0 unless your project or lock already selects them. Your versions win, and an incompatible integration fails instead of downloading a replacement. Dependencies come from PyPI. Packages are tested as installed: pytest runs against the built wheel in importlib mode, and coverage measures the installed wheel's Python files. Your coverage settings, including thresholds, are kept. Applications are tested from the sources extracted from the generated application archive. See Python applications. Pytest creates JUnit and Cobertura reports. Oyzu stores them in dist/ and records their paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. You don't configure test or output paths. Artifacts are collected only when tests and quality checks pass. An assertion failure, collection error or failed coverage threshold blocks the artifacts. An empty suite keeps pytest's exit code 5 and any zero-test JUnit file, and does not count as a pass. A suite with skipped tests keeps pytest's skip counts and exit code. A custom replacement that exits 0 can't satisfy a missing required report. If a project had no test folder before, the build now runs pytest and fails when it collects no tests. Add tests or fix your pytest configuration.

Package tests can import ordinary test helpers, including namespace folders such as docs_src and test packages with relative imports. Pytest keeps your working directory, collection paths and test resources. Tests see your checkout's helper modules, but not the checkout's copy of the package being tested. Anything the installed wheel provides (modules, packages, namespace roots, native extension names, as listed in its RECORD) comes only from the install. A missing submodule never falls back to your source. Configured pythonpath entries inside your project (relative or absolute) work. Entries outside the project, file or ZIP entries, and entries that enter an installed package fail with an error. Selected tests or conftest.py files inside a package that the wheel installs fail too. Move those tests into a separate test folder. Oyzu keeps importlib mode even if you pass another mode to pytest. These rules apply to package tests only, not to direct runs or application tests. Helpers are shared with shallow links (copies where Windows can't make symlinks). They don't grant network access, install packages or change your source.

Problem What to do No tests collected Check pytest's file name patterns and configuration, and run the same manager command to see what it collects Reporters missing Add pytest and pytest-cov to your declared dependencies or environment and prepare again Report or coverage failure Read the native logs and report records in dist/ Coverage says No data to report See Coverage reports no data Test configuration and plugins run during testing. In isolated builds they run offline. In direct runs they have your normal permissions.

Pytest is the only supported framework. It runs unittest.TestCase suites, but there is no dedicated unittest runner, other frameworks, distributed pytest or other pytest and pytest-cov versions. Coverage of native extensions is not measured. If no measurable Python source exists, that is a failure.

Oyzu runs the test steps itself. It chooses the command, creates private coverage files and starts the selected interpreter. Small pytest and pytest-cov hooks are built into the oyzu executable. They only read your pytest configuration, source metadata and framework events. Oyzu never searches your project for its own scripts. Python is required because you selected a Python build, not by the CLI. Pytest exit codes and report requirements are unchanged. For a full native pip build, Oyzu binds one explicit interpreter, either the managed CPython or your validated target .venv. It uses that interpreter with -I and fresh JUnit and Cobertura paths, and ambient PYTHONPATH or an activated environment doesn't select one. See native preparation. For package helpers, the pytest hook normalizes the resolved pythonpath list before pytest uses it, and guards conftest.py imports so that a protected package in your checkout is refused before either runs. Test selection stays with pytest. A pytest change that breaks this hook fails the run with an error. Related: direct test reports, Python applications, pytest configuration and pytest exit codes.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/release-check.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu release check asks the Oyzu platform, before you publish anything, what a release of your finished build would do in each of the project's environments. Run it after oyzu build. Note: This command is experimental. The Oyzu platform doesn't serve the would-ship check yet, so the command can't get an answer from a live platform today. oyzu build oyzu release check --project web oyzu release check --project web --environment production oyzu release check --project web --json For each environment the answer is one of: Verdict Meaning would ship Nothing waits on a person or a gate. would wait It would go out once the named approvals, gates or blockers clear. refused A policy or fact would refuse it. The reason is named. The platform works out the plan a release would get right now from the project's saved facts and policies. Nothing is published, saved or started.
documents.s: Checking whether a build would ship

documents.t: A finished oyzu build whose manifest says status: succeeded (dist/manifest.json by default). platform.url and platform.account in your configuration. A platform credential: an oyzu auth login session or a token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. See which credential a command uses. The check runs as you, so you need read access to the project. The project name, from --project or OYZU_PROJECT.

Flag Default Meaning --project OYZU_PROJECT The project to check in. --environment every environment Answer for this environment only. Repeat for more. --manifest dist/manifest.json The build manifest to check. --version each artifact's own Use this version for every component. --commit the checkout's HEAD The built commit.

The manifest's artifacts, named the way oyzu publish names them: each artifact's target, or target/name for an artifact that isn't the target's primary one. OCI images and indexes are identified by their OCI digest. The commit, the GitHub repository the checkout pushes to (if any), and the environments you asked about. The build is always checked as a candidate build.

Each environment gets one line, with its reasons and the policy behind each one underneath: Would this build ship? · web (checked as a candidate build) ✓ qa would ship … production would wait Approval from release-managers (1) (promotion policy prod-approval) ✗ eu would refuse it api has not been verified in staging (verification policy eu-staged-check) Once published (start policies) agents: joins the open batch of jobs (2 versions so far) and rides the release cut at 2026-10-11T15:02:00Z; 2 releases already wait in the queue ahead of it The Once published section appears when a start policy covers the build. It says whether publishing would join an open batch, open a new one or cut a release at once, and how many releases already wait ahead of it. With --json, the command prints the platform's ship-check record with account added.
The command exits 1 when any environment would refuse the build. Waiting on a person or a gate isn't a failure.

Code Cause Fix RELEASE_CHECK_NOT_CONFIGURED No project, or no platform.url / platform.account. Pass --project and set the platform settings. RELEASE_CHECK_UNAUTHENTICATED No credential, or the platform refused it. Run oyzu auth login in a terminal, or set OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Unattended runs never use a stored session on their own. RELEASE_CHECK_NO_COMMIT Not a Git checkout with a commit. Run from a checkout or pass --commit. RELEASE_CHECK_NOTHING_TO_SHIP The manifest lists no artifacts. Build something first. RELEASE_CHECK_RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND The project doesn't exist, or you can't read it. Check the name and your access. RELEASE_CHECK_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's answer is missing required fields or has an unknown verdict. Check that your CLI and the platform are compatible. An invalid answer never counts as "would ship". PUBLISH_MANIFEST_MISSING, PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID, PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest is read exactly as oyzu publish reads it. See publishing.
Authentication Publishing

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/release-provenance.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu inspect can check a downloaded artifact against its detached Sigstore provenance and a build profile you choose independently. Use it to confirm that a file was built by the exact GitHub repository, commit and workflow you expect. Verification runs offline and never runs the artifact or any project code. Note: This is experimental. Only one evidence format is supported: public GitHub Actions provenance (in-toto Statement v1, SLSA provenance v1, GitHub workflow/v1) in a Sigstore bundle v0.3. A passing check doesn't assess the producer's build controls or establish a SLSA level. oyzu inspect application.tar.gz --provenance application.sigstore.json \ --release-profile expected-build.json For a file inside an Oyzu build bundle, name its recorded path: oyzu inspect dist --artifact app/linux/x86_64/application \ --provenance application.sigstore.json --release-profile expected-build.json --json

Option Default Meaning --provenance <FILE> none The detached Sigstore bundle. Turns on provenance verification and requires --release-profile. --release-profile <FILE> none JSON file with the exact producer, source and build parameters you accept. Never read from the artifact. --artifact <PATH> none The recorded file path inside a bundle directory. Required for a bundle; not used for a plain file. --trusted-root <FILE> the built-in public Sigstore root A Sigstore trusted-root JSON file you supply. Never taken from the artifact or its evidence. Each input file can be at most 1 MiB. Keep profiles and trusted roots somewhere you control, separate from downloaded content. Oyzu never fetches or refreshes trust material over the network.

A release profile lists exact values. It isn't a policy language. Unknown fields and duplicate JSON keys are errors. Every field is required except stagingBuilderWorkflow. Field Meaning signer The signing workflow's certificate identity: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/.github/workflows/FILE.yml@COMMIT, pinned to a full 40-character lowercase commit. signerRevision That same commit. stagingBuilderWorkflow Optional. A separate workflow URL, pinned to a full commit, that ran the build job. Used only by oyzu build --release-profile (see below). When absent, the signer is assumed to have built. null, empty or branch references are errors. builderId https://github.com/actions/runner/github-hosted sourceRepository The application repository, as https://github.com/OWNER/REPO. sourceCommit, sourceRef The application commit and its full Git ref. repositoryId, repositoryOwnerId GitHub's numeric IDs, as decimal strings. workflowPath, workflowRevision The calling workflow under .github/workflows/ and its commit in the application repository. eventName The GitHub event, such as push. externalParameters The exact JSON object of build parameters you accept. Its workflow.repository, workflow.ref and workflow.path must agree with the source and workflow fields. The signer workflow's commit and the application's commit are different things. A valid signature from an unexpected repository, fork, workflow commit, builder or set of parameters fails. If your build job can mint its own OIDC token, the signer has to be a different workflow file. Separate jobs in one workflow don't give you that separation. Use stagingBuilderWorkflow for the build workflow and signer for the attesting one: { "stagingBuilderWorkflow": "https://github.com/example/builders/.github/workflows/build.yml@1111111111111111111111111111111111111111", "signer": "https://github.com/example/builders/.github/workflows/attest.yml@2222222222222222222222222222222222222222", "signerRevision": "2222222222222222222222222222222222222222" } These fields go alongside the other required fields.

For a bundle, ordinary bundle inspection and the required native report checks run first. A valid attestation can't rescue a failed build or a missing required report. The actual file is hashed. The certificate, issuer, signature and transparency-log or timestamp evidence are verified. The signed subject must match the file's digest. The signed source, repository IDs, calling and called workflows and build parameters must match the profile. Standard GitHub provenance doesn't name an intermediate build workflow. If stagingBuilderWorkflow differs from signer, the result reports that workflow as not-covered-by-standard-provenance, and human output says it wasn't authenticated. A plain file has no report inventory, so a passing check on one says nothing about tests or other reports.

With --json, the inspection result gains a releaseVerification object: Field Meaning passed All standard provenance checks passed. expectationsScope standard-provenance. signature, subject, expectations Each check's own result. Replaced bytes with genuine evidence show a verified signature and an unmatched subject. profileDigest, evidenceDigest, trustRootDigest Identify the exact inputs used. stagingBuilderWorkflow Present when a separate staging workflow was named; see above. builderAssurance Always unassessed. productionEligible Always false. Verification never changes manifests, versions, source, trust stores or publishing permissions. oyzu inspect without these options behaves as before.

A failed verification exits nonzero. Invalid input and ordinary bundle failures use the usual error output. Failure Fix Missing or invalid profile, unsafe --artifact path, unreadable file Correct the input. Nothing is rewritten. Replaced bytes or invalid signature Get the expected artifact and its genuine evidence. Don't edit the profile to accept the mismatch. Wrong source, signer, workflow, IDs, build type or parameters Check the profile against the producer you approved. A valid signature alone isn't enough. Missing or wrong trusted root Supply a complete trusted root. There is no network fallback. Failed build or missing required report Fix the producing build.

oyzu build --release-profile expected-build.json uses the same profile while building, for authenticated release staging. A reusable-workflow job must present signed job_workflow_ref and job_workflow_sha values that match stagingBuilderWorkflow (or signer when that field is absent). The calling source, tag, workflow and run checks still apply, and a job that doesn't match the profile is refused rather than built without it. --require-release still refuses a build when release evidence is missing. Profiles can't be forwarded to --remote builds.
documents.s: Staging a release build with a profile

documents.t: Only public GitHub Actions provenance is supported. GitHub Enterprise Server, private GitHub trust services, other CI providers and self-hosted runners are not supported. SLSA provenance doesn't authenticate each tool or test result recorded in the bundle. This doesn't sign anything, attest local builds or grant permission to publish.
Build bundles Version inference Publishing

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/remote-runs.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Add --remote to oyzu build or oyzu run <task> to run the same command on a platform pool instead of your machine. The pool checks out the exact commit you pushed, runs the build or task there with full checks in isolation, and streams the output back. Oyzu follows the run to the end and exits with the remote exit code. Note: Remote runs are experimental and have been run on Linux pools only. Everything else Oyzu does is local and works without an account. git push oyzu build --remote

A Git checkout whose HEAD is pushed to a github.com repository that is linked to a project in your platform account. git must be on PATH. platform.url and platform.account in user, machine or administrator configuration. Project and local files can't set them, so a checkout can't send your credential somewhere else. oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments In CI you can set OYZU_PLATFORM_URL and OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT instead. A platform credential: an oyzu auth login session (used at a terminal, or when platform.authentication.provider is session) or a token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. See which credential a command uses. Unattended runs with neither fail with REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED.

Command Runs remotely oyzu build --remote Every target. oyzu build cli web --remote Targets cli and web, plus what they depend on. oyzu build --affected origin/main --remote Targets affected since the merge base of origin/main and HEAD. oyzu run policy-check --remote Task policy-check (target:task also works). ... --remote --download out The same, then downloads every output into out/. To see what a pool would run without starting anything, use oyzu build --remote --plan; see planning a remote run. Oyzu sends the repository from the current branch's remote (or origin), the full HEAD commit and the branch. For --affected it sends the merge-base commit, not a local ref name. Uncommitted changes aren't part of the run; you get a warning.

The terminal view looks like a local build. Each streamed log line is attributed to the target or task that wrote it, and the pool's own lines (checkout, start, finish) appear under runner. At the end you get a summary: ✓ Remote build succeeded Run 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 Commit 3f2a9c1d4b5e (main) Project oyzu/platform Oyzu 0.9.0 Outputs manifest dist/manifest.json 4.0 KiB sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaa report dist/cli/linux/x86_64/reports/junit.xml 2.0 KiB sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbb Use --download <DIR> to fetch outputs; nothing was written locally. With --json, standard error carries the same events a local build emits, and standard output carries one remote-run record: Field Meaning invocationId This invocation. submission What was sent: repository, commit and selection. run The final run resource. result State, exit code, reason and outputs. resultAvailable says whether the full result was fetched. downloads Each downloaded path, digest and local file. observation The last seen run state, time and log position, and any known log gaps. cancelled This invocation asked for cancellation. It doesn't mean the run stopped. cancellation requested, acknowledged and confirmed, as separate facts. If Oyzu loses track of a run after creating it, the outcome is unknown, with the last state it saw. That doesn't mean the run failed, and Oyzu never starts local work instead. Check the run in the platform (using the web link, if one was shown) before starting another.

Remote outcome Exit code Succeeded 0 Oyzu exited non-zero on the pool That exit code Failed before Oyzu ran, skipped, cancelled, timed out, or unknown 1 Refused before or while creating the run (configuration, Git or platform problem) 2 Interrupted with Ctrl-C 130

The first Ctrl-C asks the platform to cancel and keeps following the log while the pool stops the work. cancellation.confirmed is set once the run reports cancelled. A second Ctrl-C exits at once with 130. There's no confirmation prompt, so it behaves the same in CI. Cancelling a run that just finished is harmless; you see its real outcome. Closing the terminal (SIGHUP) doesn't cancel. It stops only the local follower; the run continues on the pool.

Outputs are listed by digest and never written into dist/. With --download <DIR>, Oyzu fetches each one through a short-lived download link (no platform credential is sent to it), checks its SHA-256 digest and writes it at its recorded path under DIR. A path that would land outside DIR is refused. Outputs are the manifest, artifacts and required reports. They aren't a complete local build bundle, so oyzu inspect can't check them as one. If the platform can't verify the work a pool sent back, the run fails with CONTRIBUTION_UNVERIFIED and no outputs, even if the native build succeeded. Check the run's diagnostics before retrying.

A refused remote run never falls back to a local build. Platform errors keep the platform's code with a REMOTE_ prefix, plus the platform request id. Code Cause Fix REMOTE_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account is missing or set in the wrong scope. Set them at user scope. REMOTE_NOT_A_CHECKOUT Not a Git checkout. Run from a checkout. REMOTE_REPOSITORY_UNSUPPORTED The remote isn't on github.com. Only github.com is supported. REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED HEAD isn't on any branch of the remote. Push first. REMOTE_AFFECTED_BASE_INVALID The --affected ref can't be resolved. Fetch the ref or pick another. REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED No credential, or it was refused. Run oyzu auth login, or set a current token. REMOTE_REPOSITORY_NOT_LINKED The repository isn't linked to a project. Link it in the platform. REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_FOUND The platform can't see the commit. Push first. REMOTE_VALIDATION_FAILED The platform rejected the request. Correct the named field. REMOTE_RESPONSE_INVALID The run result is missing output details. Check CLI and platform compatibility. The run isn't restarted. CONTRIBUTION_UNVERIFIED See Outputs. Check the run's diagnostics. Requests that fail on the network or get a 503 are retried up to five times with backoff, honoring Retry-After. Retried creation uses the same idempotency key, so it never starts a second run. Logs are followed with 30-second long polls over plain HTTPS, which works through proxies (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE) with outbound access alone.

The credential is sent only to platform.url. platform.url must use HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host. Never put a token in command arguments, copy a browser session, or give a coding agent your personal token. Run ids and digests from the platform are checked before they're used in a URL or file name. Streamed log text is escaped before it reaches your terminal.
Only GitHub repositories on github.com. Task arguments (-- args) aren't supported remotely. There's no --detach, no way to list runs and no way to reattach to a run. Tested on Linux pools only.

A platform executor can hand private files, such as a signing key, to the native actions of a remote run. You don't configure this in your project, and ordinary local builds don't use it. The runtime-input contract describes the details. Files are mounted read-only at /oyzu-runtime, and an environment variable points to each file only while the action runs. The project can't name host files. The files never affect source, plans or cache keys. Affected targets skip the action cache so tests always see the current files. Where the executor provides an egress gateway, an HTTP client that can use a Unix socket can reach it through OYZU_HTTP_PROXY_SOCKET. Direct TCP networking stays off. Supported for Unix process actions on Linux x86-64 in Docker. Anything that doesn't match (unsupported host, missing or unsafe files, conflicting variables) is refused. Fix it and submit a new job. Removing the files afterward is cleanup, not secure erasure.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/runtime-matrices.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. To test a build on other runtime versions, add verification toolsets in oyzu.toml. To ship a build for several platforms, list platforms: in build.yaml. The two never mix: a toolset only changes how a build is checked, while a platform changes what ships. Runtime versions are never written in build.yaml; the old matrix.<runtime> axis is refused (see migration).

The build that ships is built and tested once, with the [tools] versions. Each toolset adds a verification run: the build's runtime-dependent stages, repeated with the toolset's tools. A run never produces an artifact, so a release always has one artifact per output, however many toolsets run. # build.yaml: nothing about runtime versions builds: app: uses: node/app # oyzu.toml [tools] node = "22.14.0" # builds, tests and ships the app [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" # also tested on Node 24, in pr, ci and release oyzu pin # locks Node 22.14.0 and the node24 toolset's 24.14.1 oyzu build # local: the app alone oyzu build --verify-with node24 # local: the app and its Node 24 run oyzu build --context ci # ci: the app and its Node 24 run

Question Rule In which contexts? Every context except local, unless the toolset lists contexts = [...] (local, pr, ci, release). contexts = [] turns it (or an inherited definition) off. --verify-with NAME (repeatable) adds a toolset's runs in any context. For which builds? Builds in the toolset's folder chain whose builder uses one of its tools in its build or test stages. A node toolset adds nothing to a Go build. The nearest definition of a name applies as a whole, as for --toolset. On which platform? One run per toolset, on the build's first declared platform (the host if it declares none). A toolset that lists platforms = [...] gets one run per listed platform. Runs aren't multiplied by the build's platforms. In which job? A job runs the runs assigned to the platform it builds: a plain local build runs the host's; a --platform job runs that platform's. Runs for other platforms are listed under Verification elsewhere and in the plan, never dropped. What runs? The build's build and test stages and its hooks, with the toolset's tools. Never lint, format, packaging or publication. Every check that isn't off in some context runs, as with --full. Test and coverage reports are collected; outputs aren't. What is verified? Each run records verifies: source (it rebuilt and tested the source). Every current builder does this. A builder that tested the built artifact instead would record verifies: artifact. Errors before anything runs: Code Cause CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN A named toolset isn't defined in any selected build's folder. Lists the defined ones. TOOLSET_NOT_APPLICABLE No selected build uses the toolset's tools. VERIFICATION_RUN_NOT_HERE --verify-with or --verify-only named a toolset none of whose runs is on the platform this job builds. Names each run, its platform and command. TOOLSET_INVALID Policy refuses the toolset's tools. Only a build that would run it here fails; plans, --skip-verification jobs and jobs whose run is elsewhere list it and continue.

A run is its own target, <build>-verify-<toolset> (with the platform appended when the toolset lists several), and its own Plan row: -- Plan ------------------------------------------------------------------------ format lint test build app off off run run app-verify-node24 off off run run The Tools block lists each version once (node 22.14.0 and node 24.14.1). The run's target has no artifacts, and the manifest marks it with oyzu.dev/verification: {"build": "app", "toolset": "node24", "platform": "windows/x86_64", "verifies": "source", "reason": "context", "tools": {"node": "24.14.1"}} reason is context when the toolset runs in this context, and requested for --verify-with/--verify-only. tools are the toolset's requests as written; oyzu.lock resolves them.
