A failing test in a run fails the build, and the shipped build's evidence is kept. Verification evidence. Every native build's manifest records what its builds and runs verified, under oyzu.dev/verification-evidence. oyzu publish checks it: {"verifyOnly": false, "builds": [{"build": "app", "tests": "passed", "source": {"commit": "5f3b…", "tree": "9c1e…", "digest": "sha256:fc29…"}, "tools": [{"tool": "go", "id": "oyzu:go", "request": "1.24.13", "version": "1.24.13", "ranges": [{"dialect": "go-minimum", "expression": ">=1.24.0", "file": "go.mod", "field": "go"}]}], "notApplicable": [{"tool": "go", "line": "1.23", "native": "go.mod go >=1.24.0", "requiredBy": "project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])"}]}], "runs": [{"id": "app-verify-go125", "build": "app", "toolset": "go125", "platform": "windows/x86_64", "verifies": "source", "status": "here", "command": "oyzu build app --verify-only go125", "subject": {"source": {"commit": "5f3b…", "tree": "9c1e…", "digest": "sha256:fc29…"}}, "stages": ["build", "test"], "result": "passed", "tools": [{"tool": "go", "id": "oyzu:go", "request": "1.25", "version": "1.25.14"}]}]} A build entry is each shipped build in this job: source is the source revision it built; tools are the tools its build and test stages use, with resolved versions and the native ranges that constrain them (package.json engines, go.mod go); tests is passed, failed or not-run (fast local builds skip tests); notApplicable lists required lines outside those ranges. A run entry is every run of the selected builds, with status here (ran in this job), other-platform or skipped (--skip-verification), and the command that runs it. A run that ran here adds its subject (the source revision), the tools it used, the stages that ran, and result: passed only when every action passed and its tests ran. verifyOnly is true for a --verify-only job; its bundle is evidence only. Source revisions​ verifies: source evidence is tied to a source revision: digest: always present. A SHA-256 over the selected files' paths and contents, with CRLF read as LF and executable bits ignored, taken before any action runs. commit and tree: present when the build's folder is in a Git work tree and none of its selected files differ from HEAD or are untracked. The HEAD commit and the Git tree of the build's folder. Two revisions are the same source when their digests match and, if both have a tree, their trees match. Because the digest is always compared, an edit hidden from Git's index (--assume-unchanged, --skip-worktree, a filter) still counts as different source. The commit is for reference only: another commit with the same tree and content is the same source. A Windows checkout with core.autocrlf and a Linux checkout of the same commit are the same source.

oyzu build --plan --json keeps .matrix for platform builds and lists runs under .verify. Each entry has id, build, toolset, platform, runner (OS and architecture), verifies, requested, source (the file defining the toolset), tools, status (here, other-platform, skipped) and the command for a dedicated job. The command includes --platform when the build declares platforms. "verify": [{"id": "app-verify-node24", "build": "app", "toolset": "node24", "platform": "linux/x86_64", "runner": {"os": "linux", "arch": "x86_64"}, "verifies": "source", "requested": false, "source": "oyzu.toml", "tools": {"node": "24.14.1"}, "status": "here", "command": "oyzu build app --verify-only node24"}] By default, one job builds and then runs every verification run for its platform. To give runs their own jobs, read .verify in a planning job (GitHub Actions: fromJSON) and: run each entry's command in a job on its runner. oyzu build app --verify-only node24 runs only that toolset's runs (the builds it depends on are still built); build the platform jobs with --skip-verification, which runs no verification and warns VERIFICATION_RUN_SKIPPED for each run, with its command. --verify-with and --verify-only can't be combined with --skip-verification, --isolated, --all-platforms, --image or --remote. Pass every job's bundle to oyzu publish (--manifest once per bundle). Platform jobs supply the artifacts and their builds' evidence; verification jobs supply the runs' evidence. Publication never takes an artifact from a --verify-only bundle, so the same output isn't offered twice.

Policy requires tool lines, not toolset names. The setting verification.<tool> lists the lines of a tool ("22", "3.12", "1.24": one to three numbers) that must have passing verification evidence before a build is published. Name the tool without a namespace (verification.node, not verification.oyzu:node). It's an ordinary per-folder setting: central policy and a root oyzu.toml [constraints] table can require lines with required, limited by when/unless, and a project can list its own. # root oyzu.toml [constraints."verification.go"] required = ["1.23", "1.24", "1.25", "1.26"] when = { context = ["pr", "ci", "release"] } # optional For each required line of a tool the build uses, in the build's folder and context: Not applicable. A line entirely outside the build's native range (package.json engines.node, the go.mod go minimum) is never run. The manifest records it under notApplicable with the native file and range (go.mod go >=1.24.0), and publication accepts it. Other native ranges (requires-python, rust-version) aren't evaluated: such a line runs, and tool resolution reports the conflict. To enforce a support floor, constrain tools.<name> instead. Covered. The build's own [tools] version in that line covers it in every context. A toolset with a version in the line covers it only in the contexts its runs run in: contexts = [] never does, contexts = ["release"] only in release (or when named with --verify-with/--verify-only). Otherwise, a run is added, as if the root oyzu.toml defined a toolset policy-<tool>-<line> (policy-go-1_26, dots become _). Its target is <build>-verify-policy-<tool>-<line>, listed in .verify with requiredBy and its command (oyzu build app --verify-only policy-go-1_26). It runs where toolset runs do: every context except local (unless the constraint's when names local), in contexts no toolset covers, on the build's first declared platform. --verify-with policy-go-1_26 adds it in any context. oyzu pin locks a policy run's tools in a set labelled toolset = "policy-go-1_26" when the requirement applies in pin's context and some context has no covering toolset. For a release-only requirement, run OYZU_CONTEXT=release oyzu pin. A build whose lock lacks the line fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE; run oyzu pin. oyzu build --plan shows the requirement as a CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE (or policy override) note. oyzu config explain verification.go shows where each line comes from.

oyzu publish resolves verification.<tool> again at publish time, in each published build's folder and the publication's context, so a requirement added after the build still applies. Each required line must be settled by the bundles given with --manifest, in one of three ways: Not applicable: outside the recorded native range. The build's own tests: its bundle records tests passed with a version in the line. Fast local builds skip tests; build with --full, or in a ci or release context. A run: a run of the same build in any given bundle that ran here, passed, used a version in the line, and verified the published build. For verifies: source, its subject must be the build's source revision; for verifies: artifact, its artifact digests must include the published artifact. Otherwise publication fails before loading evidence, signing or any network access. The error lists every unsettled line, why, and the commands for runs left to other jobs: ✗ PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING: no passing verification evidence for app go 1.25 (required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])): no run with go 1.25 was given. … Run what is missing (the runs this build left to other jobs: oyzu build app --verify-only go125) and pass every bundle with --manifest. Nothing was sent A bundle from the container executor has no verification evidence, so publication refuses its build when any verification.<tool> line applies in the build's folder. The publish receipt lists how each line was settled under verification, and the output shows it under Required verification: Required verification app go 1.23 not applicable: outside go.mod go >=1.24.0 · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints]) app go 1.24 the build's own tests (1.24.13) · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints]) app go 1.25 run app-verify-go125 (1.25.14) · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])

oyzu pin locks every toolset's tools beside the [tools] tools, each toolset in its own set labelled toolset = "NAME", whatever the context and whether or not a build uses them. oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks one toolset. oyzu update re-resolves [tools] and then every toolset. A build whose lock lacks a run's tools installs and locks them like any other tool. See toolset lock rules. A toolset that can't be locked (defined in a nested folder, TOOLSET_NESTED_LOCK, or refused by policy) is listed under Toolsets not locked (toolsetsNotLocked in JSON) with the reason. The rest is still locked and the command succeeds. A run that needs that toolset fails when it runs. Native ranges still apply: a toolset Node outside package.json engines fails when resolved, naming the constraint.

Runs execute only on the native host executor. A build that uses the container executor (--isolated, --image, --all-platforms, slices, remote pool builds, or builders without a native path such as pnpm and Yarn Node builds) and has runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED, and so does its --plan. Build natively, or add --skip-verification. oyzu build --remote can't pass --skip-verification to the pool. A pool job runs as ci (or release), never local, so a toolset with default contexts makes a remote build fail. For remote builds, list contexts the pool doesn't use, such as contexts = ["local", "pr"]. oyzu build --remote --plan evaluates toolsets in your local context; pass --context ci to see what a pool job would refuse. No builder records verifies: artifact yet. Only native builds record verification evidence. The check that the work tree matches HEAD covers the build's folder only. An uncommitted change to an inputs file outside it doesn't stop the revision naming the commit. "Not applicable" is decided only for engines.node and the go.mod go minimum. Every builder repeats the same stages (build and test) in a run. When this job builds a platform with a cross toolchain, whether tests run follows the builder's cross-build rules.

build.yaml no longer accepts matrix. A runtime axis is refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE and the equivalent toolsets, built from the file's own values: CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: app: matrix.node is no longer accepted: build.yaml says what ships, and tool versions belong in oyzu.toml. The build ships once, built with [tools]; each other version is a verification-only toolset that tests the build in pr, ci and release (add one locally with oyzu build --verify-with NAME). Remove matrix from build.yaml and add to oyzu.toml: [tools] node = "22.14.0" [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" See docs/reference/runtime-matrices.md The old axis built and kept one artifact per runtime. A toolset builds one artifact and verifies the other versions, so a release no longer holds two artifacts for one output. Shipping a separate artifact per runtime ABI isn't supported. matrix.platform is also refused; use platforms:.

builds: api: uses: go/app path: api image: uses: docker/image platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64] materialize: - from: api to: bin/server This expands into two image variants, each using an api variant built for the same platform. Platform requirements pass through materialize transitively, including named artifacts and directories. Ordering-only depends_on and other targets' task prerequisites don't pass them on. A producer's own platforms list limits what consumers can ask for. A conflict names the consumer's required platforms and the producer's allowed ones. platforms is the only way to declare artifact platforms. The old platform: <os/arch> and matrix.platform forms fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Aliases are accepted and stored in canonical form. Each builder checks the platforms against what it can actually run. Language builders need a toolchain that runs on the target platform, so the example fails before running if the only Go worker is x86-64. Cross-compiling a binary wouldn't prove its arm64 tests pass. See toolchain platforms. Docker can assemble x86-64 and arm64 scratch images on one x86-64 worker when no target code runs; see Docker platform admission. A complete set of image platforms also produces an OCI index. A partial selection keeps the individual images without an index.

A producer with no platforms keeps a standalone instance for commands like oyzu build api. Selecting image builds only the matching producer variants. A full workspace build skips the extra standalone instance when consumers already need platform variants, unless an ordering or task dependency requires it. If a standalone instance can't choose among a dependency's declared platform variants, selecting it fails with an ambiguity error before preparation. Resolve it with a platform declaration on the producer or consumer; Oyzu never guesses from the host.

A target that declares exactly one platform keeps its name. Several platforms give each instance a platform-qualified ID, and inferred producer variants always get one. IDs are deterministic and portable, derived from the name and platform, with a digest suffix when needed. Don't assume the logical name is the artifact's target ID; use the selection record and materialization receipts. Case-insensitive ID collisions are refused. A workspace can have at most 256 target instances and 16,384 copied tasks. Standalone instances count. Each instance gets its own copy of the build's tasks and hooks, including root hooks and stage replacements that reach it. Expansion never rewrites build.yaml.
Configuration for toolsets and constraints. Native local builds for the platform CI matrix. Publish for publication. Toolchain platforms for picking platform-specific images.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/rust.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds Cargo packages and workspaces with no Oyzu configuration. It finds Cargo.toml, runs Cargo, and collects binaries, crate archives, test reports and coverage into a build bundle. Use this page for what the Rust builder runs, the options it accepts, and how host builds differ from isolated (container) builds. Note: The Rust builder is experimental. Private Cargo registries, private Git sources and Git LFS aren't supported in isolated builds. See Limits.

oyzu build --plan # preview the stages and tool requirements oyzu build # build for this machine oyzu build --full # also run tests, doctests, Clippy and rustfmt oyzu inspect dist # check the bundle Plain oyzu build builds natively for the host. --platform <os/arch> cross-compiles one other platform. --all-platforms builds the declared matrix in the container executor. See build selection and checks. oyzu build --isolated runs the build in a Linux container. See Ordinary tasks and isolated build prerequisites. oyzu run <task> runs a development task such as build, test, lint or format-check with the Cargo you have installed. oyzu run list shows them. Cargo owns workspace membership, package metadata and dependency resolution. A checked-in Cargo.lock is required, and Oyzu runs Cargo with --locked.

The Rust builder is the oyzu-plugin-rust plugin. It reads your Cargo metadata, plans the build, and turns Cargo's output into binaries, crate archives and reports. Oyzu itself installs tools, downloads dependencies, projects versions, caches work and checks every artifact and report before it reaches dist/. Oyzu selects the plugin for rust/app and rust/library targets from its plugin sources (see plugin packages). There is no built-in fallback: if no Rust plugin is available, the build stops and says so. To use a locally built plugin, see local plugin bindings. Building Rust needs no Python or other unrelated runtime.

A host build runs Cargo on your machine and keeps Cargo's state under .oyzu/native/, so repeat builds stay incremental. oyzu build followed by oyzu build --full can reuse the same executable and run the extra checks concurrently. Each action uses a private source workspace and its own writable Cargo state. Clippy and tests use separate target directories, and coverage builds are kept apart from ordinary ones. Hooks and replaced tasks run without that reuse. See native action caching. Tests, coverage, doctests and the other checks need their tools: rustfmt, Clippy, cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov, and the compiler's LLVM tools and profiler runtime. See native execution for what Oyzu installs for you and what it checks first. Native Rust builds are supported on Linux (GNU) and Windows (x86-64, MSVC). macOS isn't supported yet.

A named build uses the shared fields in build inventory migration plus builder-owned with options. builds: cli: uses: rust/app platforms: [linux/x86_64] with: features: [integration] artifacts: binaries Option Values Default Meaning with.features List of unique Cargo feature names none (Cargo's default features stay on) Applied to metadata, builds, lint, tests, doctests and package verification. with.artifacts all, binaries all all delivers the binaries and the crate archives of publishable workspace packages in isolated builds. binaries delivers only enabled Cargo binaries and never packages crates. Unknown with keys fail. Options are never raw command strings. binaries fails if the build has no enabled binary. Feature-gated binaries need their Cargo features turned on. binaries still compiles, runs the selected checks and validates the executables. Cargo can't package a publishable crate that depends on an unpublished path dependency. If you only need executables, select binaries. The old rust: object is no longer accepted. Cargo features go in with.features and cross-compilation targets go in platforms. Legacy language objects, tool versions, runtime matrices, unknown shared fields, and empty, repeated or suffixed platform entries are refused.

oyzu build builds for the host. oyzu build --all-platforms builds every declared platform in the container executor. Without platforms, a build targets the platform of the executor that runs it. The container executor needs the Linux Rust image described below and downloads crates.io inputs before it runs offline. Outputs and reports end up in the verified dist/ bundle. To pin the compiler, see Locked Rust compiler.

Name the platforms a Rust build ships in platforms, not Cargo target triples. builds: cli: uses: rust/app with: features: [mise-integration] platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64/musl, windows/x86_64, darwin/arm64] Cargo triple platforms entry x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu linux/x86_64 on a Linux x86-64 host, otherwise linux/x86_64/gnu aarch64-unknown-linux-musl linux/arm64 (musl is the cross default) or linux/arm64/musl x86_64-pc-windows-msvc windows/x86_64 on Windows, or windows/x86_64/msvc x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, -gnullvm windows/x86_64/gnu, windows/x86_64/gnullvm aarch64-apple-darwin darwin/arm64 oyzu build --platform <os/arch[/abi]> builds one of them on this host: the host platform as a host build, another one with the cross toolchain. oyzu build --plan --json lists every declared platform with the runner and executor it needs, so a CI matrix can build each on its own runner. A project that needs a particular executor declares it with build.executors. with.features applies to every platform. Outputs go to dist/<target>/<platform>/. Only x86_64 and arm64 on Linux, Windows and macOS have platform names. Other triples, such as riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu, can't be built yet. A build isn't a raw cargo build --target: Oyzu also applies tool requirements and artifact collection. A native executor builds one platform per target per run.
documents.s: Platforms instead of Cargo target triples

documents.t: oyzu build --platform <os/arch[/abi]> builds for another platform with your pinned toolchain: cargo build --target <triple> with the target's linker. Planning only looks at the host and the files it can see. It installs and runs nothing. Platforms and executors shows how the Plan reports each platform. Target platform Triple Linker Available when linux/<arch> (default, published as -musl), linux/<arch>/musl <arch>-unknown-linux-musl rust-lld (ships with Rust) always, for pure-Rust crates linux/<arch>/gnu <arch>-unknown-linux-gnu <arch>-linux-gnu-gcc it is on PATH windows/<arch> on Windows, windows/<arch>/msvc <arch>-pc-windows-msvc MSVC Visual Studio's VC/Tools/MSVC/<version>/lib/<x64 or arm64> is installed windows/<arch> elsewhere, windows/<arch>/gnullvm <arch>-pc-windows-gnullvm <arch>-w64-mingw32-clang (LLVM MinGW) it is on PATH windows/<arch>/gnu <arch>-pc-windows-gnu <arch>-w64-mingw32-gcc it is on PATH darwin/<arch> <arch>-apple-darwin Apple clang the host is macOS; elsewhere the Plan says needs a macOS runner The defaults are musl for Linux, MSVC on a Windows host and LLVM MinGW elsewhere. An ABI in the platform name (linux/arm64/gnu) overrides them. The host's own machine and default ABI (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows) build as a host build. A musl build of the host's machine is a cross build. The target's standard library must be in the pinned toolchain. A cross build adds rust-std@<triple> to its tool requirements, and fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE if the toolchain has none. Output goes to dist/<target>/<platform>/ with the target's executable suffix. Oyzu checks the binary format and architecture against the target platform without running it. Limits: A crate whose build script compiles C (such as ring, through the cc crate) needs a C cross compiler, which the rust-lld route doesn't provide, so the build script fails. Use the container executor instead (--isolated, or "linux/arm64" = "container" under build.executors), which restores pinned cross linkers and C compilers for each target (details), or build on a runner of that platform. Tests, coverage and doctests don't run for a cross-built platform. cargo-zigbuild isn't used. A project can require a cross build with build.executors. A release then cross-compiles that platform as declared or fails.

oyzu run list shows the Rust tasks without running Cargo: oyzu run list oyzu run build oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check Tasks use the Cargo, rustfmt and Clippy you already have. The implicit tasks are fetch (cargo fetch --locked), install (cargo install --path . --locked), build, test, lint, format, format-check and archive. oyzu run format changes your source. Builds only run the read-only format-check. oyzu build never runs fetch or install unless your tasks or hooks connect them. Test tasks write JUnit, Cobertura and doctest reports under dist/<target>/<platform>/reports/, not relative to the Cargo workspace. Required reports must be collected and are limited to 16 MiB.
documents.s: Ordinary tasks and isolated build prerequisites

documents.t: Isolated builds need Docker and the base execution image, which has a C toolchain and no Rust. Host builds don't use it. Rust, rustfmt, Clippy and the LLVM tools come from oyzu.lock (see Locked Rust compiler). cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov are locked stage tools for the test stage. If a tool the enabled stages need isn't in the lock, the build stops with a message that names oyzu pin. Oyzu mounts its engine and the Rust plugin into each action, so you never rebuild an image when the CLI changes. Python isn't needed. Cross builds add the pinned linkers described under cross-platform execution: Target Linker C code in build scripts Linux musl (linux/x86_64, linux/arm64) The compiler's own rust-lld zig cc, through cargo-zigbuild macOS (darwin/x86_64, darwin/arm64) cargo-zigbuild, against Zig's libSystem stubs zig cc, through cargo-zigbuild Windows gnullvm (windows/x86_64, windows/arm64) LLVM MinGW clang LLVM MinGW clang Zig 0.15.2, cargo-zigbuild 0.21.2 and LLVM MinGW 20260616 are each fetched once, checked against a SHA-256 pinned in Oyzu, stored with your declared fetches and restored read-only under /scratch/rust-cross-*. They're fetched only for a build that targets those platforms, and they run on linux/amd64 workers. The image has no Apple SDK. Crates that link Apple frameworks other than libSystem need your own image (--image cargo=<ref>) that provides one through SDKROOT. A custom --image cargo=<image> must meet the bring-your-own requirements, including a working cc. Oyzu still uses the locked tools. Docker dependency contexts use the narrower rust/cargo provider. Isolated Rust builds run on Linux with Docker.

oyzu run install -- --root /path/to/bootstrap --force oyzu run fetch -- --offline oyzu run install runs cargo install --path . --locked in the target's directory. With several Rust targets, qualify it (oyzu run cli:install). Arguments after -- go to Cargo. Installation uses Cargo's release profile. Use --bin to choose a binary and --force to replace an existing one. --root and CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT choose the install root. Otherwise Cargo's default applies, and its bin directory must be on PATH. Cargo reports its own errors for packages without installable binaries and for virtual workspace roots. A lock selects dependencies but doesn't make Cargo offline. Forward --offline when your caches are enough. Use oyzu run fetch for cargo fetch --locked. oyzu install provisions tools, not this task.
Isolated builds first collect everything Cargo needs, then build offline.

Oyzu reads the complete registry inventory from Cargo.lock before it makes any request. Only crates.io is supported: index entries from https://index.crates.io/ and archives from https://static.crates.io/crates/. Another registry or an unsupported Git host fails. Oyzu never falls back to Cargo's own network access. Every locked registry package needs a SHA-256 checksum. Oyzu requires the index metadata and archive bytes to match, then stores the archive and only the locked version's index entry in Cargo's local-registry format. If a cached index entry lacks the locked version, an online run fetches it once and checks it again. An offline run fails and tells you to run online. Duplicate matching entries and checksum disagreements are errors. Cargo extracts the archives, verifies checksums, resolves and compiles. No project code runs during acquisition. If the lock contains only local workspace packages, no registry replacement is written. Acquisition needs crates.io to be reachable on each fresh preparation. Once preparation succeeds, the build runs with the network denied.

Public GitHub sources need a full commit in Cargo.lock. Cargo fetches them through a repository-scoped broker inside a container with no network. The broker allows only Git smart-HTTP discovery and upload-pack requests, within size, redirect and request limits. Oyzu keeps the fetched object database and recreates the checkouts privately for the offline build. Repositories with Unix symlinks work on Windows hosts. Private Git, other hosts, submodule routing and Git LFS aren't supported.

Isolated builds archive only publishable workspace packages as .crate files. A package with publish = false (or an empty publish list) never gets a .crate. A private application delivers its executables instead. A private library is workspace internals. Private packages still build, lint and test. Publishable packages keep Cargo's own packaging and verification. One that depends on a private library fails with Cargo's own message.

For a workspace with local path dependencies and registry inputs, Oyzu packages members in dependency order. Each runs cargo package --locked --offline --allow-dirty --registry crates-io --package <name> with verification on. Each archive's name, version and SHA-256 are checked before dependent members can use it. Ordinary and build dependency cycles, and paths outside the workspace, fail planning. The captured registry stays unchanged. A temporary registry copy is removed when the action ends. An index over 4 MiB, an archive over 128 MiB, or an identity or checksum conflict fails packaging. Fix the manifest and rebuild. Native manifest publish restrictions still apply, and only the crates.io profile is supported. Development-dependency cycles between local members are supported when their ordinary and build edges are acyclic. Oyzu packages the cycle group together without verification, admits the results to a private registry, then packages and verifies every member separately and requires each final archive to match its provisional one byte for byte. Archives from a cycle group don't include Cargo.lock, so cargo install --locked doesn't work on them. If the original lock holds a different registry version of one of these members, Oyzu lets Cargo align its private lock with the verified workspace archives, offline, and restores the original lock afterward. Before packaging, Oyzu checks the original lock offline and writes workspace versions and local requirements into private manifests with a regenerated private lock. Your source files stay unchanged. Registry packages keep their locked versions and aren't delivered as artifacts.

Ordinary versions are snapshots with a source-derived suffix, such as 1.2.3-dev.g<source-prefix>. Workspace packages resolve independently unless they join a fixed version group. Snapshots are never marked eligible for release. A package's version follows its path-dependency closure. A relevant dependency commit changes the consumer's version, and an unrelated member's commit doesn't. Changes to root workspace inputs affect every member. Private manifests and packaged local requirements use each member's selected version. See version inference for strategies and tags. In a supported GitHub Actions tag job, release staging can select exact release coordinates. It's experimental and covers Linux x86-64 Cargo projects without repository hooks. --require-release refuses when the event or source evidence is insufficient. Cargo fixed version groups​ Workspace members can share one version using a subset of cargo-release's metadata. Oyzu reads the project-local settings and doesn't run cargo-release or its hooks. Fixed groups are supported on Linux x86-64. shared-version = true joins the workspace's shared group. A nonempty string such as "suite" names a group (case-sensitive; boolean true and the string "true" differ). shared-version = false opts a package out of an inherited group. Without effective membership, packages stay independent, even when their versions match or use version.workspace = true. Private and unselected members still count toward membership. This workspace groups App and Core and keeps Helper independent. Each package uses version.workspace = true. The root has: [workspace] members = ["app", "core", "helper"] resolver = "2" [workspace.package] version = "1.4.2" [workspace.metadata.release] shared-version = "suite" tag-prefix = "suite/" tag-name = "{{prefix}}v{{version}}" helper/Cargo.toml overrides both inherited fields: [package.metadata.release] shared-version = false tag-prefix = "helper/" With tags suite/v1.4.2 and helper/v1.4.2, an App-only feat: add API commit moves both App and Core to base 1.5.0. Helper stays at 1.4.2. All of them are still source snapshots. Each field merges separately, lowest to highest precedence: Workspace-root release.toml. Root Cargo.toml under [workspace.metadata.release]. Member-directory release.toml. Member Cargo.toml under [package.metadata.release]. A missing field inherits. An explicit false or empty prefix is a value. Home-directory configuration and cargo-release command-line overrides aren't read. Release, publish, signing and push settings don't control groups. For tag-based versions, every group member needs the same literal, slash-terminated tag-prefix (such as suite/). tag-name can be {{prefix}}v{{version}} (the default) or {{prefix}}{{version}}. An empty prefix means root tags and requires exactly one release subject at the Git root. Wildcards, crate-name templates and other tag formats are refused, as are partial prefixes, conflicting tags and unreadable controls. Fix the named declarations and rerun. --plan doesn't run Cargo or fetch history to fill in missing facts. Every member must declare the same normalized version, including qualifiers. Full builds write the common version and local requirements into private manifests and the private lock. Fast local builds can keep native versions and record compiledVersion. A registry backreference that needs a different member version is refused rather than splitting the group. The bundle records group membership, tag prefixes, where each setting came from and the resolved versions in oyzu.dev/version-subjects, beside each package's oyzu.dev/versioning entry. See Cargo groups in version inference for the strategy and conflict rules.

An isolated build runs release compilation of the workspace, native tests with reporting, Clippy, a rustfmt check, verified crate packaging and final collection. Commands use locked, offline inputs and the executor denies the network. Build scripts and proc macros run in that environment and must work with the collected inputs. The compiler's host target, the .oyzu-build/target output root, the private Cargo home and the offline setting are fixed by the plan. A task environment can't change them. Custom Cargo source replacement isn't supported and can fail offline resolution. Other Cargo settings in the project still apply. Compilation, tests, lint, formatting and archive verification are required. If one fails, no final artifacts are collected. The logs and any reports show which stage failed. Fix it and rerun. A bundle from an earlier successful build stays in .oyzu/history and isn't reused as this build's output.

Tests run through cargo llvm-cov nextest. JUnit and Cobertura reports land under dist/ and are indexed with paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. Test failures and coverage failures are reported separately. A missing or invalid required report fails collection. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's integrity. The Cobertura report omits per-function records and keeps line and branch details, which keeps it under the 16 MiB report limit. Oyzu's coverage gate uses covered and valid source-line counts. Cargo doctests run as part of the same test gate, since nextest doesn't run them. Oyzu runs cargo test --doc --locked --offline --package <name> for each workspace package that has a doctest-enabled target (doctest = false is honored). Binary-only targets and registry dependencies don't run doctests. doctest.xml has one case per package invocation, not per documentation example. A package with doctests enabled but no examples still passes. A non-zero Cargo exit is a failure and a launch error is an error. Output streams live, and the report keeps the start of each diagnostic. All selected packages run even if one fails. A failed doctest blocks artifact collection even when nextest passes. Coverage covers nextest runs only. It doesn't include doctests or individual doctest cases. Custom nextest configuration isn't supported.

oyzu run test produces nextest JUnit, LLVM Cobertura coverage and doctest reports, and you can follow it with oyzu inspect dist. It's supported on Windows (MSVC) and Linux. See direct tests for the bundle layout.

Rust with the llvm-tools-preview component and the compiler's profiler runtime, cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1. On Windows, use an MSVC or windows-gnullvm compiler with its linker and SDK. The windows-gnu compiler isn't supported for coverage because it lacks profiler_builtins (see native build prerequisites). Dependencies must already be installed so Cargo can resolve them offline with --locked. This task doesn't install tools. If the LLVM tools are missing, it fails before llvm-cov tries to download them. LLVM_COV and LLVM_PROFDATA can point at installed copies.

Cargo's metadata --no-deps --locked --offline supplies the workspace members and doctest-enabled packages. oyzu run list never runs Cargo. The default cargo test --locked --workspace task is instrumented automatically. A task you replace keeps its own command and still has to produce the JUnit, coverage and doctest reports. No Oyzu configuration is needed for the default. A temporary nextest profile inherits your default profile and writes fresh JUnit output. Your .config/nextest.toml isn't edited. Compilation and coverage use private temporary target directories, so project build state isn't reused. Extra command arguments go to nextest. Alternate nextest profiles, arbitrary cargo test arguments and filtered doctest selection aren't supported here. The task runs nextest, generates coverage even if tests failed, and runs doctests. Any failing phase fails the task. Build scripts and proc macros run normally. Cargo's offline flags aren't a network sandbox on the host. See direct tests.

With the default with.artifacts: all, an isolated build produces <package>-<selected-version>.crate for each publishable workspace package, plus <binary>-<selected-version>-<compiler-host> for each enabled binary. with.artifacts: binaries selects only executables and fails if there are none. The selected version is normally a projected snapshot. See Registry backreferences for the exception. Manifest names use the crate- and bin- prefixes. A publishable library-only package gets a crate archive and no invented executable. Duplicate binary names fail planning.

Cargo's resolved features decide whether a binary with required-features exists. A binary whose features aren't on is left out. Turn the features on through Cargo's defaults or with.features to include it.

Oyzu reads Cargo's JSON compiler messages and matches each expected binary by its manifest path and target name. It takes the executable path from Cargo's own compiler-artifact events rather than guessing filenames, and never publishes test binaries. Cached results count as well as fresh compilation. A missing, unexpected or conflicting output, a failed Cargo process, or an executable outside the target root fails the build. Oyzu clears its staging directory before each Cargo run, so an old executable can't stand in for a disabled feature or a failed compile. A task you replace must still produce the planned artifacts. This builder doesn't publish, sign or promote anything. Crate archives don't include Oyzu's private .oyzu-build files.

Cargo package verification re-resolves through a private registry. A projected prerelease version of a member can then conflict with a registry dependency of the same name. When the resolved graph has a registry dependency named after a workspace member, Oyzu keeps that member's declared version, and local path requirements use it. Only affected members keep declared versions. Others get snapshot versions. An inactive dependency declaration doesn't count. These artifacts are still snapshots. oyzu.dev/versioning records reason: cargo-registry-backreference, the source digest, intent: snapshot and productionEligible: false, even if the version looks like a release. Use the bundle's source identity and artifact digest to tell apart snapshots with the same version.

A [tools] rust = "1.95.0" declaration in oyzu.toml, installed into oyzu.lock, selects the compiler for isolated builds. The container worker uses the linux/<architecture>/gnu installation from the project's .oyzu/tools store. That's the compiler's own platform. Artifact platforms in build.yaml don't change it. Only a Rust-only tool selection works this way. Before any package is downloaded or Cargo runs, Oyzu verifies the lock, the installer, the installation receipts and the payload. It copies the installation into the private dependency snapshot while holding a lease, and verifies the copy. The build uses that copy's Cargo, rustc and rustdoc. The live tool store is not mounted into containers. The dependency record keeps the identities of the request, the installation, the lock and the copy. If anything is missing or stale, the build fails: a missing or stale lock, a missing worker distribution, an absent installation, an unsupported layout or a changed payload. Install the matching compiler first. Oyzu doesn't resolve versions, edit the lock or use the network to restore the compiler. oyzu install provisions only its own host, so installing a Linux compiler from a Windows host isn't supported yet. The base image has no Rust, so an isolated build without a locked compiler stops with a message that names oyzu pin. The image provides only OS prerequisites and a C toolchain. Formatting, lint and test tools come from the lock too.

Build manifests list oyzu.dev/tool-requirements for each Rust target. Oyzu reads literal package.rust-version values and Rust toolchain channel constraints, with their source files and locations, in every form rustup accepts (details). It lists compiler components, standard libraries for the platforms you build, and the formatting, lint and test tools that the selected stages need. Fast builds leave out the quality tools they don't run. Components named in your toolchain file stay required. A rust-version inherited from the workspace needs workspace metadata. Without it, the build fails with a clear message instead of ignoring the value. For a locked compiler, isolated builds choose their recipe from the same build-stage requirements as oyzu pin. A build with tests selected therefore needs the locked llvm-tools-preview component, even if the lock also holds a smaller recipe for fast builds. An incomplete lock stops the build. An environment override doesn't replace it. The helper tools cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov are restored from the lock as stage tools.

Declaring artifact platforms in build.yaml runs isolated builds on the execution image with the pinned cross linkers listed under the isolated-build image. Supported platforms are linux/x86_64, linux/arm64, darwin/x86_64, darwin/arm64, windows/x86_64 and windows/arm64. Linux builds musl and Windows builds gnullvm. Other ABIs are refused. Baselines: musl for Linux, Apple Darwin with a macOS 13 deployment target, and LLVM MinGW for Windows. They don't guarantee compatibility with older operating systems. The locked compiler and target standard libraries are restored separately from the linkers.

Declare the compiler in oyzu.toml and install it into oyzu.lock. On Windows, oyzu install also fetches the Linux compiler when the project declares a Rust build. Equivalent locked selections in one build share one verified compiler extraction per archive digest and worker image. It's mounted read-only. Cargo homes, outputs and workspaces stay private. The extraction is released when the build ends. The persistent oyzu-tools-* volumes are reused by identity, and superseded ones are pruned (see build logging). The build runs without network access. Compiler sharing is automatic and adds no build.yaml options. It doesn't deduplicate crate downloads or preparation, and it isn't a persistent compiler cache.

Each cross-platform Rust action reserves 8 GiB of memory and may run up to two hours. Oyzu limits concurrent targets by Docker's available memory and keeps 25% as headroom. A Docker engine needs about 11 GiB to run one such action. Preparing the locked compiler reserves 4 GiB. Tests and coverage run on the Linux worker. Cross-compiled executables are checked for the right binary format and architecture, but not run on the target OS. Cargo extraction and Git checkouts use a private Linux scratch filesystem of at least 2 GiB that grows with larger memory reservations. Only the Git object databases are copied back, which keeps registry extraction and symlinks off Windows host mounts. Build inputs and workspaces live under the project's .oyzu directory on the same volume as the project, not in the system temp folder. They're private, and excluded from source snapshots and bundles. cargo fmt runs with the same locked compiler and never receives feature arguments.

Isolated builds support single packages and local workspaces, including libraries, binaries, proc macros and build scripts. Only crates.io registry dependencies and public GitHub Git dependencies work. Private or alternate registries, private Git and Git LFS don't. Isolated Rust builds run on Linux with Docker. Cross-compiling needs the platform's linker or the container executor (see above). Custom nextest configuration, doctest coverage and individual doctest cases aren't supported. Release and registry publication aren't done by the Rust builder.

Local builds, build tasks and build bundles for the shared build model and output. Version inference, direct tests and Docker images for adjacent behavior. Rust installation for provisioning the compiler. Private Cargo registries for private sparse registries on the host.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/scan.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu scan runs security and quality scanners against a build you already made: Gitleaks, Trivy, Grype and SonarQube. It checks the same source files and artifacts that oyzu build recorded in dist/, and tells you whether the result passes the thresholds you set. No platform account is needed. Note: oyzu scan is experimental and has been tested on Windows only (native Gitleaks, and container scanners through Docker Desktop with Linux containers). oyzu build oyzu scan oyzu scan --json scan never rebuilds, runs tests or publishes. Each call starts a new scan.

There are two ways to choose scanners: Method Scanners Where Project settings Gitleaks, run natively [scan.gitleaks] in oyzu.toml Administrator policy SonarQube, Trivy, Gitleaks, Grype, run in Docker scan.policy in administrator configuration only If no scanner is selected, you get SCAN_SELECTION_REQUIRED with the setting to add.

[scan.gitleaks] enabled = true failOnFindings = true Setting Values Default Meaning scan.gitleaks.enabled boolean false Run Gitleaks natively on the recorded source. scan.gitleaks.failOnFindings boolean false Fail the scan if Gitleaks finds anything. When false, findings are recorded but don't fail the scan; Gitleaks errors still fail it. These settings follow the normal configuration cascade and its constraints. They can't replace or loosen an administrator's container selection; failOnFindings can only make it stricter. Oyzu installs Gitleaks like any other tool: from your [tools] request if there is one, otherwise a compatible pin or the default version. It doesn't edit your configuration or oyzu.lock, and it never falls back to a Gitleaks on PATH or a container.

Option Meaning --store <DIR> Use this native tool store instead of the shared user store. A relative path is resolved from the project root. --offline Use only tools, images and inputs already on this machine. See offline scans. --json Print only the result on standard output; progress events go to standard error. Works before or after scan.

Only administrator configuration can set scan.policy. In the protected admin-settings.json file: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "scan.policy": { "locked": true, "value": { "sonar": { "image": "sonarsource/sonar-scanner-cli@sha256:a3f4215076706c95a17a68c19322ee916e40a3acd081a8c1a1e839e0194afa57", "endpoint": "https://sonarqube.example.com", "projectKey": "example", "sources": ["app/src/main/java", "library/src/main/java"], "requireClasses": true }, "trivy": { "image": "aquasec/trivy@sha256:af6acf9a6b85dfe389a1941505c0ce9efef52a4719635e1a962f022a3d855daa", "maximumFindings": 0 }, "requireQualityGate": true } } }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Each scanner (sonar, trivy, gitleaks, grype) is optional, but at least one is required. Images must be pinned by digest. Oyzu pulls missing images through Docker before scanning and reuses ones you already have. Private tool catalogs and custom registry routes aren't supported for scanner images. Key Meaning <scanner>.image The scanner image, by digest. <scanner>.maximumFindings The most findings allowed before the scan fails. Omit for no limit. (Trivy, Gitleaks, Grype.) requireQualityGate Require a passing SonarQube quality gate. Needs sonar. Default false. sonar.endpoint, sonar.projectKey The SonarQube server and project. sonar.sources Source folders to analyze, relative to the project. sonar.requireClasses Give SonarQube compiled classes taken from the build's JAR artifacts. trivy.rules Extra Trivy secret rules; see Trivy. gitleaks.config Gitleaks TOML rules; see Gitleaks. Container scanners need Docker on the machine running oyzu scan. Scanners never get the Docker socket. For SonarQube, set up the SonarQube server and project yourself, and put SONAR_TOKEN in the environment (never in the policy file). The token needs permission to submit analysis and read tasks, quality gates and project issues. endpoint may use HTTP for a local server. Tool versions belong under [tools] or in the policy image, not in other scanner settings.

scan rebuilds the exact list of source files the build recorded, and their digest must match the build's. It doesn't rediscover inputs or reread ignore files, and a Git commit alone isn't enough. If source changed since the build, the scan fails with SCAN_SOURCE_MISMATCH before any scanner runs. Restore the files or build again. A bundle without a recorded source selection fails with SCAN_SOURCE_SELECTION_MISSING; a malformed one with SCAN_SOURCE_SELECTION_INVALID. Build again with the current CLI. For Cargo, adding an ignored release.toml or a file that could become a workspace member can make the scan refuse even if the recorded digest still matches. Declare the file as a build input or fix the workspace members, then build again. Differences between machines' filesystems can prevent a match. They aren't smoothed over. Artifacts are copied and digest-checked for the scan. The original dist/ is checked before and after and never changed. Source isn't fetched from Git and remote bundles aren't downloaded.

Each scan is saved under .oyzu/scans/<run-id>/: File Contents manifest.json The final result, with digests of the other files. plan.json The policy, tool versions and inputs used. events.jsonl Progress events. <scanner>/report.json The scanner's own JSON report (Trivy, Gitleaks, Grype). <scanner>/native.log The scanner's own output. sonarqube/provider.json The SonarQube server's response. grype/database.log Grype database download output. Each check records whether its tool was installed or reused, and the exact image or native tool version. If a scan fails partway, a failure manifest names the phase. A configuration error caught before the scan starts writes nothing. Scanning never pins tools or writes oyzu.lock. Reports can include secrets or source text, so protect .oyzu/scans. Human output shows only counts, never matched text.

The terminal view follows the build layout: a Preflight phase (install or reuse each scanner), a Scan phase with each scanner's progress, then a table of scanner, analysis type, subject, result and duration. Details below list findings, quality gates, the pass or fail decision, report links and the result path. NO_COLOR turns color off and --quiet hides progress, not the result.

Exit Meaning 0 Every check ran and the result passes. 1 A scanner failed, a threshold or quality gate failed, or SCAN_SOURCE_MISMATCH. 2 Invalid flags or input. 3 Configuration or policy errors (CONFIG_*, POLICY_*). If one scanner fails, the others still run and keep their reports, but the overall pass/fail decision is skipped. Findings by themselves never count as a scanner failure; they're compared with the threshold afterwards. A nonzero scanner exit or a malformed report is a failure.

A successful scanner exit only means the analysis was submitted. Oyzu then waits up to three minutes for the server to finish and reads that analysis's quality gate. The dashboard and issue links in the result show the project's current state, not a snapshot of this analysis; the result says so and keeps the analysis and task IDs. Issue snapshots are cut off at 500 issues and don't affect the result. A passing quality gate doesn't mean zero findings or permission to publish.

Trivy runs secret detection on the recorded source only. It has no vulnerability database, network, credentials or Docker socket. Repository trivy.yaml, ignore files and secret rules are ignored. Administrators can add trivy.rules: an array of custom secret rules with id, title, regex and severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH or CRITICAL). Built-in rules stay on. An invalid regex fails the check.

Add gitleaks to scan.policy, alone or with other scanners: { "gitleaks": { "image": "zricethezav/gitleaks@sha256:691af3c7c5a48b16f187ce3446d5f194838f91238f27270ed36eef6359a574d9", "maximumFindings": 0 } } This selects Gitleaks 8.30.0. It scans the recorded source files (gitleaks dir), not Git history. gitleaks.config can supply Gitleaks TOML rules. Without it, Gitleaks' default rules apply. Project .gitleaks.toml, .gitleaksignore and gitleaks:allow comments are ignored. A config error fails the check. Source is mounted read-only. There's no network, credentials or Docker socket. Gitleaks redacts matches in its report, but treat reports as sensitive anyway. See the Gitleaks documentation for rule syntax.

Add grype to scan.policy to check the build's JAR artifacts (application/java-archive) for known vulnerabilities: { "grype": { "image": "anchore/grype@sha256:af65fbc0c664691067788fe95ff88760b435543e45595eb2ca6f102fc476fbe1", "maximumFindings": 0 } } This selects Grype 0.110.0. Each scan downloads a fresh vulnerability database into the scan folder, then analyzes the JARs with networking off. This uses disk space and bandwidth on every run. Project Grype configuration is ignored. Grype's own database age and hash checks stay on. Findings count vulnerability matches, not unique CVEs. Only packages Grype finds in the recorded JARs are checked. Container images, SBOMs, lock files and other artifacts aren't. A clean result isn't a full dependency audit. See Grype database behavior and the Grype CLI reference.

Concurrency. scan.jobs (1 to 65535, default 2) sets how many scanners run at once. Set 1 for one at a time, or 4 to run all four together. A failed scanner doesn't stop the others. Results keep plan order. Offline scans. oyzu scan --offline works when tools, images and inputs are already on the machine. A missing image fails with TOOL_OFFLINE, native Gitleaks without a recorded installation or pin fails before resolving a version, SonarQube fails with SCAN_OFFLINE and Grype with SCAN_DB_OFFLINE. Checks are never skipped to make an offline scan pass. Scanners are never run during oyzu build, and scan never runs Maven or other build tools. Native installation is available for Gitleaks only. Trivy, Grype and SonarQube run in Docker. Grype's database isn't cached between scans. Results prove the files weren't changed; they aren't signed provenance. Docker administrators on the machine can see scanner environment variables, including SONAR_TOKEN. Missing JAR artifacts for Grype fail with SCAN_INPUT_MISSING. For nested projects, inputs from sibling folders outside the project are checked against the build but may not be passed to scanners.
Build bundles Configuration

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/secrets.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu secrets manages the secrets your Oyzu platform account keeps for the account, one of its organizations or one of its projects. A secret is either a token a build job receives (build exposure) or a webhook secret the platform uses to check incoming deliveries (internal exposure). Values are write-only. You can set or replace a value, but no command or API ever shows a stored value back to anyone, including account owners. Note: This command is experimental and hasn't been tested against a live platform yet. Everything else Oyzu does is local and works without an account. oyzu secrets create release-webhook --exposure internal --description "Release tool deliveries" oyzu secrets set release-webhook --generate oyzu secrets list

platform.url and platform.account in your configuration, usually at user scope: oyzu config set --global platform.account payments. A platform credential: an oyzu auth login session (used at a terminal, or when platform.authentication.provider is session) or a token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. See which credential a command uses. Unattended runs need an explicit provider or token and never use your stored session. Don't copy a browser session into a token. Permission for the operation on the platform. Having a credential isn't enough on its own. You don't need a Git checkout.

Command What it does oyzu secrets list Lists the account's secrets: name, type, exposure, value version and description. oyzu secrets create <name> --exposure build|internal Creates a secret with no value. Add --type file for exact bytes such as a key file (default text) and --description. oyzu secrets set <name> < value.txt Sets or replaces the value from standard input. oyzu secrets set <name> --file key.pem Sets or replaces the value with a file's exact bytes. oyzu secrets set <name> --generate Generates a value, sets it and prints it once. oyzu secrets set <name> ... --overlap 24h Keeps the replaced value valid for this long, up to 168h. Units: h, m, s. oyzu secrets rm <name> --previous Ends an overlap now, for example if the old value leaked. oyzu secrets rm <name> Deletes the secret and all its values. Add --org <org> or --project <project> to any command to work in that scope; without them, commands act on the account. Use the organization's or project's identifier. set and rm accept a secret's name or id. set never creates a secret; if it doesn't exist you get SECRETS_NOT_FOUND with the create command to run. Exposure, type and scope are fixed when you create a secret. To change one, create a new secret.

oyzu secrets set release-webhook --generate --overlap 24h # update the sender with the new value oyzu secrets rm release-webhook --previous Both values are accepted during the overlap, so no deliveries are dropped.

Values come from standard input, --file or --generate, never from a command-line argument, so they don't end up in shell history or process listings. Standard input must be piped or redirected. If it's a terminal, set fails with SECRETS_VALUE_REQUIRED rather than echo what you type. Bytes are sent exactly as read. echo token | oyzu secrets set x stores a trailing newline; use printf '%s' "$TOKEN" or a file without one. A value can't be empty and can be at most 64 KiB. A text value must be UTF-8. --generate takes 32 bytes from the operating system's secure random source and uses them as 64 lowercase hex characters, which webhook senders accept. The value is printed once, after the platform has stored it. If the platform refuses, the value is thrown away and never shown.

A listing is a table. The Value column shows the version (and, during an overlap, when the old one stops working) or not set: Secrets · project web of payments Name Type Exposure Value Description npm-token text build version 2 (version 1 valid until 2026-10-11T09:05:00Z) hook text internal not set Release tool Values are write-only: no command shows a stored value. Replace one with `oyzu secrets set <name>`. A generated value is shown once: ✓ Set the value of release-webhook (version 1) Generated value 3f9c…(64 hexadecimal characters) Copy it into the sender's webhook settings now. It cannot be shown again; if it is lost, set a new one. With --json, standard output holds one record with kind, account and scope: kind Extra fields secrets secrets (metadata only) secret-created, secret-overlap-ended secret secret-value-set secret, and generated_value for --generate only secret-deleted name, id The JSON from --generate contains the value, so treat it as sensitive.

Exit status is 0 on success and 2 on any failure. Platform errors keep the platform's code with a SECRETS_ prefix, plus the platform request id. Code Cause Fix SECRETS_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account is missing. Set them. SECRETS_UNAUTHENTICATED No credential, or it was refused. Run oyzu auth login, or set a current OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. SECRETS_PERMISSION_DENIED You can't do this in that scope. Ask for access. SECRETS_NOT_FOUND No secret with that name in that scope. Check the scope, or create it first. SECRETS_RESOURCE_CONFLICT Name already taken, no previous value to end, or a sign-only secret. Pick another name, or leave platform-managed secrets alone. SECRETS_VALIDATION_FAILED The platform rejected a field (named in the error). Correct that field. SECRETS_VALUE_REQUIRED, SECRETS_VALUE_EMPTY, SECRETS_VALUE_TOO_LARGE, SECRETS_VALUE_UNREADABLE No usable value. Pipe the value, use --file or --generate. SECRETS_OVERLAP_INVALID Bad --overlap duration. Use a value like 24h, at most 168h. SECRETS_UNREACHABLE The platform couldn't be reached. Retry later. SECRETS_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's reply was malformed. Run oyzu secrets list to see what happened before retrying. Check CLI and platform compatibility. list retries a 503 or network failure with backoff. create, set and rm are sent once, because retrying a value could create an extra version and, with an overlap, retire the value you meant to keep. If one fails in transit, run oyzu secrets list to check before trying again.

No command reads a value back. Values never come from arguments, are never logged and are never written to disk by the CLI. The credential is sent only to platform.url, using your proxy and trust settings. Redirects aren't followed. A reply that contains a secret value is rejected, not printed. sign-only secrets (the platform's own integration keys) are listed but can't be created or changed here.
There is no hidden prompt for typing a value. Pipe it or use --file.
Platform sign-in Remote runs

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/shell-activation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Shell activation puts a project's tools and [env] settings into your terminal as you cd into it, and puts your environment back when you leave. Use it for everyday work in an interactive shell. For a single command, use oyzu exec; to see what would be applied, use oyzu env. Supported shells: Bash and Zsh on Linux and macOS, and PowerShell 7.5 or newer on Windows.

Bash or Zsh: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # or: oyzu activate zsh cd ./project-a cd ../project-b oyzu deactivate PowerShell: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression Set-Location ./project-a Set-Location ../project-b oyzu deactivate Entering a project applies its environment and tools. Moving to another project or leaving restores what you had before. The first time, a project's [env] values may be skipped until you trust the folder. To set up every supported shell and keep oyzu and the shims on the persistent PATH, run oyzu shell install (the install scripts do); for one shell, run oyzu shell install SHELL --rc-file PATH. See installing activation in a shell profile.

A project that only sets environment variables needs no tools, lock file, install or account. [env] APP_MODE = "development" _.path = ["./bin", "./node_modules/.bin"] _.path adds directories to the front of PATH, in order. To add some to the end as well: [env] _.path = { prepend = ["./bin"], append = ["./scripts"] } Shell activation, oyzu exec and shims apply these values once the folder is trusted. oyzu run and oyzu build always apply them.

env._ is reserved for settings like _.path. It's never exported as a variable. Values are literal. There's no variable expansion, scripts, .env loading or command substitution. Setting env.PATH directly is an error. Use _.path. Relative paths are relative to the file that declares them (including local and profile files), not to your current folder. Use "." for the declaring folder. Directories don't have to exist. Empty entries, NUL, control characters and an embedded PATH separator are errors.

Normal configuration precedence applies. The winning _.path replaces any inherited one entirely. [] clears project additions. The final PATH order is: tool shims, project prepends, your existing PATH, then project appends. Directories already on your PATH stay where they are.

Inside Git, the project root is the repository root unless you pass --root. Outside Git, it's the outermost folder with Oyzu configuration. Nested files affect only their own subtree. Installed tools live in the shared user store, not in the project. oyzu activate --store <dir> uses a different store. A relative path is resolved from where you run the command. Use the same store for install and activate.

oyzu run <task> --store <path> runs a task with tools from that store. The path is resolved from where you run the command, and applies to the whole task, including hooks and prerequisites. Missing tools aren't installed and there's no fallback to another store. oyzu run list --store <path> only lists tasks; it doesn't open or create the store. Put task arguments after --. A --store after -- goes to the task.

You can activate outside any project. Changing folder applies the new environment before your next command. Edits to configuration are picked up at the next prompt. Run _oyzu_hook to refresh by hand. Hooks never install tools, run tasks or use the network. Tools in [tools] must already be installed and locked. Each terminal keeps its own state. A nested shell can activate and change projects without affecting its parent. oyzu deactivate restores the environment the shell started with. Ordinary oyzu commands in an activated shell run the first oyzu on PATH (so a project-local build of oyzu takes over). Activation hooks keep using the oyzu that activated the shell. Bash has no native folder-change hook, so Bash activation defines cd, pushd and popd functions that call the builtin with the same arguments. A failed change returns the builtin's status and runs no hooks. After a successful change, a defined chpwd function runs first, then each defined function named in the chpwd_functions array, in order, stopping at the first failing hook; the change still succeeds. Oyzu adds its own _oyzu_hook_chpwd entry, keeps entries other tools registered and works under set -u; oyzu deactivate removes only Oyzu's entry. Activation replaces a cd, pushd or popd function of your own. Zsh uses its native chpwd hook. PowerShell 7 uses its native location-changed event. Windows PowerShell 5.1 has no such event, so there the new environment is applied at the next prompt: cd .\project; node -v typed on one line still runs with the previous folder's variables. Removing the profile block affects new shells only. Run oyzu deactivate in the current one.

Switching projects first undoes the previous project's changes. A variable is restored only if it still has the value Oyzu set. If you edited or unset it, your change is kept. A new project's value can override your edit temporarily; your edit comes back when you leave. An empty variable and an unset one are treated as different. PATH restoration keeps directories you added and removes the ones Oyzu added, even if they were reordered. If a duplicate makes that ambiguous, the entry is kept and you get a message. To unset a variable inside a project: [overrides] remove = ["env.APP_MODE"] It's restored when you leave, unless you changed it.

If configuration is invalid or a required tool isn't available, the previous project's changes are undone and OYZU_TOOL_STATUS is set to unavailable. Nothing from the failing project is half-applied. Fix the configuration or install the tools; the next prompt tries again. A working environment sets ready. Managed environment values and secret references aren't supported and fail with an error. Hooks never sign in or refresh credentials.

Environment variables can make shells, loaders and interpreters run code, so Oyzu won't apply a checkout's [env] and _.path in your shell until you say you trust it. Review the settings, then: Command Effect oyzu trust [path] Trust the project root (the current project if no path). oyzu trust --revoke [path] Remove the trust record. oyzu trust --list List trusted folders. All forms support --json. Trust is tied to the folder's real path (symlinks resolved) and survives edits to oyzu.toml. It never writes into the checkout or contacts a service. Records live under trusted-projects in the user state directory.

Tools still work. Only project and local [env], _.path and their removals are skipped. Your user-level environment values still apply. Prompt hooks, shims, exec and oyzu env --shell follow the same rule. A short hint about oyzu trust is printed once per command, or once per activated shell. oyzu run, oyzu build and build planning always apply project environment settings, trusted or not, so they match CI. oyzu config also shows them.

Setting Where Default Effect [trust] enabled = false User or administrator configuration true Turns the check off. [trust] parents = ["/absolute/projects"] User or administrator configuration none Trusts every project under these folders (for example E:\\projects on Windows). OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=false Environment, one command Turns the check off. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=true Environment, one command Turns the check on, overriding files. CI (including CI=true) Automatic Trusted. Platform executors count as CI. Project and local files can't change these settings. Local coding agents get no exemption. --revoke removes only the explicit record. A parent rule, a disabled check or CI can still trust the folder.

oyzu env shows configuration sources, the resulting variables and the selected executables in separate tables. It doesn't change your shell. Sources show which file and profile won for each value, including oyzu.local.toml and _.path. PATH entries are listed in search order. Tool-provided variables and your existing PATH are included. In an untrusted folder, project entries are marked skipped until trusted. The PATH shown is the configured one, not what activation has applied. oyzu env --json lists the values and selected commands, with sources in the configuration array. projectEnvironmentSkipped says whether project values are being held back, and affected rows carry the same skipped until trusted status.

Ordinary values are shown in human and JSON output. Values with credential-like names (token, secret, password, API key, auth, private key) are redacted, as are values that look like credentials. This is a best-effort guess. Don't put secrets in innocently named variables.

oyzu exec -- program runs a command with the trust-filtered environment, including unsets, without changing your shell. A bare command name must be a declared tool; use an absolute path for anything else. oyzu env --shell SHELL prints one-time changes with no hooks. Use activate if you want them undone when you leave. _.path isn't passed to tasks as a variable and isn't a build input.

Directories Oyzu adds to PATH use normal drive or UNC paths, without \\?\ prefixes. Your existing entries keep their original spelling. Windows PowerShell 5.1 activates and switches environments when you change folder, applying the change at the next prompt rather than mid-line. Keeping empty variables needs PowerShell 7.5 or newer.

Supported shells are Bash, Zsh and PowerShell 7.5+. PowerShell before 7.5 can't keep empty environment values (Microsoft documentation). Other shells, managed values and secret references aren't supported.
Configuration for the cascade and the user state directory. Tool shell environment for oyzu env details, shims and profile installation. Tool commands for installing a project's tools.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/target-workspaces.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A native oyzu build gives each target its own private copy of its source before it prepares dependencies. The target's hooks and stages share that copy, but other targets can't see the files it generates. To pass files from one target to another, use materialize. This page covers which source goes into a target's workspace, how artifacts are passed between targets, and how Python wheels and Docker images fit in. Note: Private workspaces keep targets apart; they aren't a sandbox. Native processes still have your user's access to files and the network. oyzu run tasks run in your checkout as usual.
documents.s: Host target workspaces and artifact inputs

documents.t: Each target's folder is copied with your current edits and untracked files, minus the usual exclusions (.git, .oyzu, dist, target, node_modules, virtual environments). Files outside the target's folder must be listed in inputs, unless they already belong to the same native project: builds: api: uses: node/app path: api inputs: [../../shared/schemas] inputs is a list of file or folder paths relative to the build.yaml that declares them, not to the target's path. Paths must stay inside the Git repository, or inside the build root when there is no repository. Absolute paths and paths that escape fail. On the container path, an input must stay under the folder holding build.yaml and match at least one captured file. It becomes part of the target's cache scope (declared inputs). Copies keep the repository-relative layout. Each target gets its own copy. Symlink and reparse-point restrictions still apply. Only selected targets and their dependencies need their inputs. For example, oyzu build cli doesn't need the docs target's inputs, but oyzu build docs and a full build do. A missing input of a selected target fails before anything runs. Use artifact relationships, not inputs, for another build's generated output. Oyzu doesn't infer what a script reads.

Private workspaces live in .oyzu/host-workspaces and persist between builds: Each build updates them in place. Files whose size, modification time and read-only flag match aren't rewritten; others are copied again, and files no longer selected are removed. Every source file is still hashed on every build. At the end of a build, files the build generated inside the workspace are removed. An interrupted build leaves state that the next build cleans up. Copies keep modification times, and paths stay the same between builds, so native tools can stay incremental. Rust compiler caches stay in the original project's .oyzu/native/rust, under the cache budget. Cleaning workspaces never removes bundles, installed tools or compiler caches.

builds: server: uses: rust/app path: server consumer: uses: node/app path: consumer materialize: - from: server to: inputs/server - from: server into: inputs/original Field Meaning from The producer target. Required. artifact The producer's logical output name. Optional when the producer has one primary artifact. to Exact destination for a file, or the folder to fill with a directory artifact's contents. into Folder to place a file in, keeping its file name. If the file name is only known after the build (a native wheel), the real name is used; see file name discovery. Directory artifacts use to. usage runtime (default), build or data; see artifact compatibility. runtime A local image that must accept a native Python wheel; see native wheels. Only with usage: runtime. Set exactly one of to and into. Destinations are relative to the consumer target. Archives aren't extracted, source files aren't overwritten, and destinations can't overlap. materialize already orders the targets; don't add depends_on as well. Platform compatibility and artifact identity are checked. Artifacts are passed after all of the producer's actions and required reports succeed, and before the consumer's first action. Each consumer gets its own copy, checked against the collected digest, and the manifest records each handoff. Inputs that the consumer needs during dependency preparation (for example, files npm ci reads) aren't supported. The producer's pre_build, build and post_build actions share its workspace, so changes a post-hook makes to the output are included. A failure in any of them means no artifact is passed, even if output files were written. A failed producer blocks its consumers; independent artifacts can still appear in the failed bundle. A host-built Python output is a wheel folder named primary, so use to. A python/package built in a worker image (--image pip=<image>) exports files named wheel and sdist; choose one with artifact: wheel and into.

materialize.usage says how the consumer uses the artifact: usage Compatibility checked against runtime (default) The consumer artifact's platform. build The platform the consumer's build runs on, for a tool that runs during the build. The producer must be unambiguous. data Nothing: the bytes are included without any runtime claim. The output must still be unique, the producer successful and the bytes verified. Artifacts carry oyzu.dev/artifact-compatibility: Value Meaning target Built for a specific platform. pending Must be inspected by the builder before use. independent Runs anywhere, such as a pure Python wheel. native Bound to one platform, and checked against the consumer's runtime. unknown Compatibility can't be established. pending and unknown artifacts can't be used at runtime. The handoff record notes the consumer's platform and usage under oyzu.dev/artifact-consumer. These checks don't certify arbitrary binaries or ABIs. When a consumer has several platforms, each gets the producer variant built for its platform. A producer with no platforms that outputs a python/package wheel can serve several consumer platforms: pure wheels are shared, native wheels go through the runtime check. A plain native build always uses host outputs; for a native binary feeding an image for another platform, use --all-platforms.

A native build can also include docker/image targets. Images build in a rootless BuildKit worker, while the other targets still run on the host. Docker is needed only when an image target is selected. No build container gets the host Docker socket, and no nested Docker daemon is started. Note: Image workers in native builds are experimental and tested on Windows. Image targets need the base execution image and, for RUN steps, the pinned rootless BuildKit worker; the Docker plugin package supplies the helpers. Oyzu pulls both by pinned digest on first use. Base images must already be in the Docker daemon. Preparation records their identities, and worker actions run offline. Your docker.apparmorProfile setting still applies. An image tag doesn't satisfy a tool pin. A Linux producer and image: builds: package: uses: python/package path: package image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: package to: payload oyzu build image --plan shows the producer, the artifact edge and each target's executor without contacting Docker. oyzu build image runs it.
