The Dockerfile can use COPY payload/ /wheels/ without knowing the wheel's versioned name. Installing the wheel into the image is up to the Dockerfile. The image's build context follows its source selection and .dockerignore, plus the materialized artifacts. Files your hooks generate don't join the context unless they were already part of it. Named image platforms must include the worker's platform. Use --all-platforms for several platforms. Fast builds assemble and verify the image. --full adds image assertions, lint and formatting. Image content and platform are always verified before publication. --isolated builds the whole graph in containers instead. Host Python wheel folders are inspected after collection. A wheel tagged pure Python and none-any can go to any platform. A host-built wheel whose tags all name one Linux x86_64 or aarch64 platform (linux_*, manylinux*, musllinux_*) is native and goes through the runtime check below. Other native tags, such as Windows or macOS, fail the handoff, even on the same OS.

Before a native wheel enters the consumer's workspace, Oyzu runs pip install --dry-run --no-index --no-deps for it in the consumer's runtime image, with networking off. pip decides whether the Python version, ABI and wheel tag fit. The runtime image is: the input's runtime: <image>, a local image (never pulled) that must match the consumer's platform; else the consumer's pip dependency base image (a requirements.txt used with a pinned base; see Docker images). materialize: - from: package to: inputs runtime: registry.example/python:3.12-slim # only needed without a pip base A consumer with neither, such as a plain COPY into scratch, can't receive a native wheel. Use usage: data to include it without the check. For generic linux_x86_64 and linux_aarch64 wheels, Oyzu also checks: libc. Oyzu inspects the wheel's .so files and the consumer's Python. A clear glibc/musl mismatch is refused before the image builds, naming the wheel, file, linkage and image. If it can't tell, it reports NATIVE_WHEEL_LIBC_UNVERIFIED and lets pip decide. Extension suffix. For a *.cpython-<version>-<platform>.so file, Oyzu compares the suffix with the consumer Python's supported suffixes. A mismatch, or a consumer that can't report them, gives the warning NATIVE_WHEEL_EXTENSION_SUFFIX_UNVERIFIED. The build continues. If you see it, check that the module imports in the final image; if not, build the wheel with that image's Python. Plain .so and .abi3.so files aren't compared. manylinux* and musllinux_* wheels skip these extra checks; pip decides. A rejection fails the consumer with the wheel name, the image and the libc mismatch or pip's message. It appears as an ERROR line, in diagnostics with --json, and in full in the action log. Wheels built for a version (cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64) are accepted only by the matching Python; abi3 wheels are accepted by any compatible Python. Host-built native wheels need a Linux host. Windows and macOS hosts build win_*/macosx_* wheels, which a Linux consumer refuses.
documents.s: Native wheels and the consumer runtime

documents.t: To get a Linux native wheel from any host with Docker, build it in a container with oyzu build --image pip=<image>. Use an image with a C compiler (not -slim) that meets the bring-your-own requirements; Oyzu mounts its engine, so the image needs no Oyzu worker. The wheel's tag comes from the Python that runs the build, the locked CPython when there is one, for example cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64. Oyzu finds the file (below), reads its tags from the wheel's WHEEL metadata and records it as native for the image's platform, so the consumer check applies.
documents.s: Wheels built in a worker image

documents.t: A planned output normally has an exact file name. The one exception is when a builder can only know the name after building: Python's python/package wheel output: if no file exists at the planned path, Oyzu looks for the single file {name}-{version}-*.whl next to it. No match fails with missing bundle path; several matches fail and name them. A file at the planned name, such as a pure py3-none-any wheel, is always used as is. Symlinks are ignored, and the usual containment, regular-file, digest and size checks apply. The bundle records the real file. The plan and --plan keep the planned name, so the two can differ for a native wheel. materialize with into writes the real name. to needs an exact name, so use into for a discovered file. An existing file is never overwritten. sdist, applications and other builders don't use discovery. This also applies to an older setup.py wheel whose planned tag is missing: a different tag is collected and classified from its metadata.

oyzu build --plan shows declared inputs and artifact relationships without installing, copying or building. During a build, Ctrl+C on Windows or SIGINT/SIGTERM on Unix cancels it. Oyzu stops starting actions, stops running processes and workers, keeps available logs and a failed bundle, blocks pending dependents, and exits with code 130. Post-hooks aren't guaranteed to run. After a forced kill (SIGKILL), check for leftover processes and build files yourself. To recover from an invalid input path, artifact selector, collision or failed command, fix it and rebuild. You never need to copy files into a consumer by hand. Each rebuild starts from a fresh private copy of the source.

Private workspaces are separation, not sandboxing, and don't make a build eligible for production publication. Native workspaces and image workers are tested on Windows. Linux and macOS hosts aren't supported yet. The usage: build path is tested on Linux x86-64. Native wheel handling covers Linux x86_64 and aarch64 tags. A Linux arm64 consumer, deeper libc version checks and Windows or macOS tags aren't supported. Choosing a build tool from a producer with several platform variants isn't supported.
Native local builds for the native build path. Directory artifacts and build bundles for artifact layout. Docker images for image builds.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-aqua.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Registry packages are command-line tools described by the aqua registry, the same catalog mise's aqua backend reads. Oyzu installs them with an oyzu: tool ID and verifies each download against the publisher's SHA-256. Use them for tools Oyzu doesn't provide itself, such as terraform, gh or ripgrep. Note: Experimental. Error codes, field names and the pinned registry snapshot may change. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. When a tool index is configured (the default), packages it lists install from the index. The rest of this page describes what Oyzu does when it resolves a recipe from the registry itself.
documents.s: Registry packages (oyzu: ids, from the aqua registry)

documents.t: oyzu install terraform@1.9.8 # a curated name oyzu install gh@2.49.2 # a catalog short name, stored as oyzu:gh oyzu install oyzu:burntsushi/ripgrep@14.1.1 oyzu install aqua:go-task/task@3.54.0 # mise spelling, rewritten to oyzu:task oyzu exec -- gh --version # runs the installed binary oyzu tools info oyzu:gh # provider, source, commands, platforms, verification oyzu tools versions oyzu:gh # releases, newest first, with excluded ones explained oyzu uninstall oyzu:gh Configuration stores the tool's canonical ID: [tools] "oyzu:task" = "3.54.0" "oyzu:gh" = "2.49.2" terraform = "1.9.8" # curated names can be written bare All tool commands work (scopes, --dry-run, --frozen, --offline, update, tools current, tools list). No account and no mise executable are needed.

mise's table form of a [tools] entry is accepted for every tool, with one option, version. It means the same as the plain string: [tools] "oyzu:gh" = { version = "2.49.2" } [tools."oyzu:jq"] version = "1.7.1" oyzu install gh@2.50.0 changes only version inside the table, keeping its form and comments. A table under an aqua: or core: key is replaced by a plain entry under the new key. Other options (os, exe, bin, asset_pattern, install_env, postinstall, ...) are ignored with a warning. They never run hooks or change the installation. oyzu config validate --strict turns the warnings into errors. A table without a valid version string is refused (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE). Arrays of versions aren't supported.

Every spelling of a package resolves to one canonical ID, and configuration and the lock store that ID, so how you typed it never changes the lock. IDs never carry an aqua: prefix. Package Canonical ID Also accepted In the curated set (for example hashicorp/terraform) oyzu:<name> (oyzu:terraform) terraform, oyzu:hashicorp/terraform, aqua:hashicorp/terraform Any other registry package oyzu:<owner>/<repo>[/<name>], lowercased (oyzu:burntsushi/ripgrep) aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep; a catalog short name (ripgrep) with oyzu install A GitHub repository's release assets github:<owner>/<repo> Oyzu's own providers (Node, Go, Rust, ...) oyzu:<name> (oyzu:go) go, and the older core:go Curated names are built into Oyzu, so they resolve without the network. Each is the package's primary name in mise's catalog, except cli/cli, which is oyzu:gh (mise's github-cli also works). Names that would clash with an Oyzu provider (kubectl, helm, k3d) or a Cargo helper aren't curated; those packages keep their owner/repo ID. aqua: is accepted as input wherever an ID is (commands, [tools] keys, policy) and rewritten. Oyzu never writes it. Installing a tool declared under an aqua: or core: key moves the declaration to the new key. The lock records the origin. Each lock entry lists the registry package in components (package:<owner>/<repo>), next to registry: and tag:. Older locks with aqua: or core: IDs are stale. oyzu install reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE naming the rename, and oyzu install --frozen fails. Run oyzu update to re-lock the same versions under their oyzu: IDs (same archives and digests). [tools] keys written as aqua: keep working and aren't rewritten.

As in mise, oyzu install gh@2.49.2 looks up a short name that Oyzu neither provides nor curates in mise's name catalog, expands it to the first backend Oyzu supports (aqua:cli/cli) and stores the canonical ID (oyzu:gh). oyzu:gh is looked up the same way. $ oyzu install gh@2.49.2 $ cat oyzu.toml [tools] "oyzu:gh" = "2.49.2" The catalog is the registry/*.toml data from the mise crate release 2026.10.5. Oyzu downloads it from static.crates.io, checks it against a pinned SHA-256 and caches it as <store>/catalogs/mise-registry-<digest>.crate. Once cached, it works offline. No mise code is run. A name Oyzu provides itself (node, go, ...) always resolves to Oyzu's provider. Short names work with oyzu install only. Other commands and [tools] keys need a curated name or the canonical ID. Situation Result Unknown name TOOL_NAME_UNKNOWN, suggesting the oyzu:<owner>/<repo> spelling. Only available through backends Oyzu lacks (cargo:, npm:, asdf:, ...) TOOL_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED, listing them. Catalog can't be fetched, or its digest differs TOOL_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE or TOOL_REGISTRY_DIGEST_MISMATCH.

Request Meaning Needs the GitHub release list 3.54.0 or v3.54.0 Exactly this release. No latest Newest stable release the recipe covers. Yes 2.49 Highest stable 2.49.x the recipe covers. Yes An exact version tries the tag spellings <version_prefix>v<version> and <version_prefix><version>, and uses the first whose checksum file exists. Pinned installs make no GitHub API request, so they can't hit its rate limit. latest and prefixes read GitHub's releases API (the newest 300 releases). Set GITHUB_TOKEN to raise the anonymous limit; it's sent to api.github.com only. Drafts are never offered. Pre-releases are only used when named exactly. The lock keeps your request and the exact release. A latest lock stays valid without re-reading the release list.

Registry. One pinned snapshot, aqua-registry v4.573.0, downloaded from raw.githubusercontent.com, checked against its SHA-256 and cached in the tool store as catalogs/aqua-registry-<digest>.yaml. Each Oyzu build uses a fixed snapshot. Resolution. Declaring or updating a tool evaluates its recipe for each default platform (linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native, windows/amd64/msvc) with the recipe evaluator, reads the publisher's checksum file and writes one lock entry per platform. A platform with no build is recorded as unavailable. Recipe types. github_release (a GitHub release asset) and http (a direct download URL, such as https://releases.hashicorp.com/...). Other types (go_install, cargo, github_content, ...) are refused with SOURCE_KIND. Formats. The recipe's format decides how the download is unpacked: format Installed as tar.gz, tgz gzip tar tar.xz, txz xz tar tar.zst zstd tar tar plain tar zip ZIP raw (or an asset with no archive extension) The file is the executable. It's stored under the first command's name (<name>.exe on Windows) and every declared command runs it. Other formats (tar.bz2, tbz, single-file gz, bz2, xz or zst, 7z, dmg, pkg) fail with TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED. Archives are unpacked with limits on entries, size, depth and expansion ratio. The lock is the pin. Each lock entry holds the archive URL, its SHA-256, and in components what install needs: kind:, bin:<command>=<path in the archive>, tag: and registry:. A locked tool installs without the registry, and oyzu install --frozen into an empty store needs only the locked URLs. Download. Only the host archive is downloaded, and its SHA-256 must match the lock. GitHub's release hosts are always allowed. A recipe that downloads from elsewhere is allowed that host only over HTTPS on port 443, with a public DNS name (no IP address, single-label or .local-style name) and no credentials in the URL. Tool routes for registry packages aren't supported (TOOL_ROUTE_UNSUPPORTED). Commands. The executables a recipe declares (files) become the tool's commands. Without files, the command is the last part of the package name (kubectl for kubernetes/kubernetes/kubectl). On Windows, .exe is added as the registry specifies. With several commands, each is available through oyzu exec -- <command>, and each command's folder is added to PATH for child processes. When several names share one file (superfly/flyctl declares flyctl and fly), each works through oyzu exec, but a child process searching PATH only finds the file's own name.
documents.s: What is installed, and from where

documents.t: Install checks the publisher's SHA-256: the lock records the checksum from the recipe's checksum file for each platform, and the download must match it. A checksum file whose body is a single digest with no file name (like dl.k8s.io's kubectl.sha256) is read as that asset's digest. Recipes can also declare GitHub artifact attestations, cosign, SLSA provenance or minisign. Oyzu doesn't check those yet, and they don't stop an install. For example, oyzu install oyzu:gh@2.102.0 installs on its checksum even though the recipe declares an attestation. tools info says so. A successful install means the archive matches the checksum the publisher listed when you resolved it. It doesn't prove the publisher or the checksum file is authentic. Code Cause TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING The recipe declares no checksum, and the package isn't on the GitHub-reported digest list. TOOL_CHECKSUM_UNSUPPORTED The checksum isn't SHA-256, or the checksum file uses the regexp format. TOOL_CHECKSUM_UNVERIFIABLE The checksum file doesn't list the archive, or lists conflicting values.

A recipe without a checksum normally can't be locked. For a short, reviewed list of packages, Oyzu instead locks the SHA-256 that GitHub reports for the release asset in the package's own repository. The list currently holds protocolbuffers/protobuf/protoc. It isn't open to every checksum-less recipe, because that would weaken checks for tools nobody reviewed. Any other checksum-less package reports TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING. For a tool a builder detected, that's a warning row and the build continues; for a tool you pinned, it's an error.

Code Cause and fix TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED Another backend (asdf:, vfox:, ...) isn't supported. The message lists what is. TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Not oyzu:<name>, oyzu:<owner>/<repo> (or <owner>/<repo>/<name>), github:<owner>/<repo> or the aqua: alias. TOOL_NAME_UNKNOWN oyzu:<name> isn't curated. Use oyzu:<owner>/<repo>, or oyzu install <name>. TOOL_NOT_IN_REGISTRY The package isn't in the pinned snapshot. Check the spelling. TOOL_VERSION_NOT_FOUND No such release, or nothing matches a prefix in the newest 300 releases. Run oyzu tools versions. TOOL_RATE_LIMITED GitHub refused the release list (anonymous limit or access policy). Set GITHUB_TOKEN, or request an exact version. TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED The format isn't in the format table. CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE A [tools] table has no valid version string. See option tables. TOOL_RECIPE_UNSUPPORTED The recipe uses something the evaluator doesn't support. See recipe resolution. TOOL_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE, TOOL_REGISTRY_DIGEST_MISMATCH The pinned snapshot couldn't be fetched, or doesn't match its digest.

oyzu tools versions oyzu:<name> lists releases, newest first, for this host. A release the recipe doesn't cover, with no build for this platform, or whose verification Oyzu can't perform appears under excluded with the reason, so the list shows what install would accept. oyzu tools info shows the provider, source, commands (once locked), platforms, eligibility under tools.allowed, declarations and the verification rule. Both support --json.

Supported on Linux x86-64 only. Formats: tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.zst, tar, zip and raw executables only. Only SHA-256 checksum files. Attestations, cosign, SLSA and minisign aren't checked. A command name that differs from its file's name (such as flyctl's fly) works through oyzu exec but isn't on the child PATH. Option tables honor only version. Other mise backends aren't supported (github: is separate; see the github: backend). A hand-written declaration with no lock entry needs oyzu install <id> or oyzu update; plain oyzu install reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE. The registry snapshot is fixed per Oyzu build. Your own registries and a floating registry aren't supported. Tool routes aren't supported for registry packages, and version listing needs GitHub's API. Recipe vars and musl builds aren't supported. tools.allowed matches the canonical oyzu: ID.
Tool index Resolving recipes into artifact sets The github: backend Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-catalog.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. An organization tool catalog lists the tools and versions your organization approves. Set toolCatalog when your organization runs a delivery edge (the server that publishes the catalog and serves approved downloads): Oyzu then installs registry packages and Oyzu's own providers (oyzu:java, oyzu:node, ...) only from that signed catalog. Note: Experimental. Setting names, error codes and the catalog format may change. Supported on Linux x86-64 and Windows x86-64; macOS is not supported yet.

Point Oyzu at the signed tool index and the delivery edge, and pin the edge's public signing key: # ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml [toolIndex] url = "https://index.example.test/" [toolCatalog] url = "https://dl.example.test/" keys = ["ed25519:7sb4o1W0lRKR712+E7DQ8uYEeTX2sUXSzJMTpKc0lzI="] Put the organization token in OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN. Then: oyzu tools versions <tool> lists the versions your organization approves. oyzu tools check --catalog checks the declared tools the way an install would. oyzu tools request <tool>@<version> asks for a version the catalog doesn't offer yet.

The catalog is the signed public tool index, narrowed to the approved versions, with each version's state and how its files are delivered. With a catalog configured: Only approved versions resolve. Any other version fails before anything is downloaded. A blocked or quarantined version fails with your organization's reason. Oyzu only uses a catalog signed by a key in toolCatalog.keys. The catalog can only narrow the index. An entry whose SHA-256 differs from the signed index is refused, so the edge can't substitute other files. Files the catalog marks proxy download from the edge with the organization token. Files marked direct (for licenses that forbid redistribution) download from the publisher, and Oyzu still checks the catalog's SHA-256. Oyzu doesn't fall back to local recipes, registry files, GitHub release lists or publisher APIs. If the edge is unreachable, Oyzu uses the last good catalog for a limited time (toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge) and warns you.

The signed tool index doesn't yet carry Node's LTS markers. Under a catalog, node@lts fails with TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE, and tools check --catalog reports it unavailable. Use an approved exact version or a named line such as lts/krypton. Without a catalog, an unpinned Node requests lts, even when engines.node is set. Oyzu picks the newest stable LTS release that satisfies every engine constraint, or, if none does, the newest stable release that does. The build plan explains which rule applied. Explicit latest, major, exact and named LTS requests keep their meaning and must satisfy the engines. A locked lts version installs offline without refreshing.

A signed tool index (toolIndex.url). The catalog approves versions from the index; it isn't an index by itself. An organization token from the edge's operator. The edge's catalog signing public key (ed25519:<base64>), from the edge's operator.

Setting or variable Values Default Meaning toolCatalog.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback) unset Base URL of the delivery edge. Unset means registry packages resolve from the index or locally. toolCatalog.keys One to eight ed25519:<base64> public keys unset Keys the catalog must be signed with. Required when toolCatalog.url is set. Pin two while the edge rotates its key. User or machine configuration only. toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge 0, <n>h or <n>d (up to 366d) 7d How long after the edge built it the last good catalog can be used while the edge is unreachable. 0 turns this off. User or machine configuration only. toolCatalog.adminUrl HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback) unset Delivery admin API, used by tools request. Also OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL. Can't be set in a project file, because your sign-in token is sent there. OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN environment variable unset Organization token, sent as Authorization: Bearer. It is never a setting, so it can't end up in a committed file. Settings marked "user or machine configuration only" fail with CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file. Oyzu fetches <url>v1/catalog once per command, with the ETag of its saved copy, so an unchanged catalog isn't downloaded again. Proxied files are fetched from <url>v1/upstream/<host><path>.

To make the catalog mandatory on a machine, set it as a locked setting in the machine's protected admin-settings.json (see configuration). User and project files can then neither remove nor change it: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "toolCatalog.url": { "locked": true, "value": "https://dl.example.test/" }, "toolCatalog.keys": { "locked": true, "value": ["ed25519:7sb4o1W0lRKR712+E7DQ8uYEeTX2sUXSzJMTpKc0lzI="] }, "toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge": { "locked": true, "value": "3d" }, "toolIndex.url": { "locked": true, "value": "https://index.example.test/" } }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Pair it with a network allowlist that permits the edge and the index host but not the publishers' hosts. Distribute both through device management.

For an aqua: package: The index picks the version from those the catalog approves on any platform, so every platform in the lock gets the same version. Each platform's entry must be approved for that platform, not refused, and carry the index's SHA-256. A version approved only for other platforms is treated like a release with no build for this one, and that platform is left out of the lock. The download follows the catalog's delivery for that URL: proxy through the edge, direct from the publisher. A URL the catalog doesn't list is refused. Reinstalls and the lock: Reinstalling from a cached archive still checks the current catalog first. A cached, verified archive isn't downloaded again. install --offline uses the saved catalog (under the rules in When the edge is unreachable) and never contacts the edge. Both the catalog and the archive must be available locally. The lock is the same as without a catalog: the publisher URL and SHA-256, never the edge's host or the token. github: packages are refused under a catalog, because the catalog doesn't list their files.

A version withdrawn from the signed index (see the index) stays in the catalog with state withdrawn, and the edge won't serve it. Oyzu refuses it with TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN, the reason and the newest version the catalog serves for your platform: TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN: oyzu:golang-migrate 4.20.0 was withdrawn from the tool index: upstream release assets were deleted (404). The newest version the acme tool catalog serves for linux/amd64/gnu is 4.19.1. If nothing else is available, the message suggests oyzu tools request. A prefix or latest skips withdrawn versions. A lock that names one is refused on the next install. tools versions lists it under excluded, and tools check --catalog reports it as withdrawn.

Oyzu's archive providers (Java, Node, Go, Python, Maven, Gradle, kubectl, k3d, Helm, Liquibase, Tailscale, npm and pnpm) follow the same three steps under a catalog, instead of reading the publisher's live metadata. The index lists them under their oyzu: ID (for example oyzu:java, from core:java). The catalog can use either name. The version and SHA-256 come from the index as narrowed by the catalog. The lock records oyzu:java, the publisher URL and the SHA-256, the same as without a catalog. Accepted requests: An exact release (21.0.8), a release-line prefix (21, 1.25) or latest. For Java, lts and * pick the newest approved LTS release (8, 11, 17, 21, 25, ...). Node's named lines (lts/jod, lts-iron). The moving lts alias is refused, as described above. A range (^20, ~1.24, >=3.12 <3.14) picks the newest approved release it matches. Native constraints (>=17) narrow every request. Tools the index doesn't carry: A provider missing from the index fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX. oyzu:rust installs from an approved Rust channel manifest in the index, and each download is verified. See indexed Rust. An unapproved version fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG. cargo: helpers (cargo:cargo-nextest, cargo:cargo-llvm-cov) are refused with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX.

With toolCatalog.url set, oyzu tools check --catalog fetches the catalog (or reads the saved copy with --offline) and judges each declared tool as an install would. The selected version must be approved for the host and for every platform listed in tools.lockPlatforms. Other default lock platforms are optional. Status Meaning Refused approved Installs version through the catalog. no not-in-catalog No approved release matches the request. Also every github: package. yes refused Your organization refuses version (with its reason), or the catalog names different files than the index. Also cargo: helpers and Rust missing from the index. yes withdrawn The version was withdrawn from the index. The reason names the newest available one. yes not-in-index The index doesn't carry the tool. yes unavailable No approved build for the host or a required platform. yes excluded, blocked, unknown Same as without a catalog. yes The command exits 1 if anything would be refused. JSON adds catalog (org, built, source and any saved-copy warning).

oyzu tools versions <tool> lists, newest first, the versions the catalog approves and serves for your platform. A version your organization refused appears under excluded with TOOL_REFUSED and the reason, in a "Refused by the catalog" table. A version whose catalog SHA-256 disagrees with the index shows TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH. A withdrawn one shows TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN. Versions never approved aren't shown. A tool the catalog doesn't list fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG. In JSON, source is organization catalog, and catalog shows org, built and whether the copy was fetched or cached.

oyzu tools request <tool>@<version> [--reason TEXT] asks your organization's administrators to approve a version. The version can be a prefix (kubectl@1.31). oyzu tools request yq@4.44.3 oyzu tools request kubectl@1.31 --reason "cluster upgrade" oyzu tools request --status 7 oyzu tools request --cancel 7 oyzu tools requests What you need: toolCatalog.adminUrl (or OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL). Without it the command fails with TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL_MISSING. A personal sign-in: oyzu auth login (with platform.url and platform.account) or OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Your personal token is sent to the admin URL, not the organization token. You need the catalog.request permission. OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN, to read the catalog. What it reports: The request's id, state and what to do next. The state is pending, or approved if one of your organization's auto-approve rules accepts it immediately. Asking again for the same tool and version returns the pending request. A version the catalog already serves reports served. A tool missing from the index, or a version with no verified download, fails with TOOL_REQUEST_INVALID. A request stays pending until an administrator approves or denies it, you cancel it, or it expires after 30 days (unless your organization sets another limit). An expired or cancelled request can be asked for again. --status ID shows a request's state (pending, approved, denied, cancelled or expired), when it was made and expires, who asked, who decided and why. --cancel ID cancels your own pending request. Only the person who asked can cancel it. oyzu tools requests lists the newest 50 requests made from this machine with the current organization token, with their state read now. Oyzu remembers only the IDs, tools and versions, in the default store under state/tool-catalog/. A request the edge no longer has shows as unknown. Neither command waits for a decision. Run it again later.

The edge serves the catalog as a DSSE envelope with payload type application/vnd.oyzu.tool-catalog+json. Each signature is Ed25519, and its keyid is the hex SHA-256 of the public key. Oyzu accepts the catalog when one signature verifies with a pinned key; anything else fails with TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED. Payload field Meaning org The organization the token belongs to. revision SHA-256 of the catalog's content; changes whenever the catalog does. index {serial, sha256} of the signed index the catalog was built from. policy_revision Revision of the organization's policy. built, expires When the edge signed it, and when a fetched copy stops being accepted (24 hours later by default). entries Approved entries: ID, aliases, version, platform, sha256, delivery, state, refusal and upstream URL. Oyzu checks, in order: The signature. For a fetched copy, that it hasn't expired (TOOL_CATALOG_STALE; also check your clock). If Oyzu's index has the same serial as the catalog's index, that both have the same SHA-256 (TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH). A catalog built from a neighboring index release is accepted, since the edge and Oyzu update on their own schedules. Every entry is still checked against Oyzu's own index.
To rotate keys, the edge's operator adds the new key next to the old one (the edge signs with both), you update toolCatalog.keys to the new key, and the operator removes the old key.

Oyzu keeps each verified catalog in the default tool store under catalogs/tool-catalog/<key>/catalog.json (~/.local/share/oyzu/tools/... on Linux), exactly as the edge sent it. The signature is checked every time the copy is read. An edited copy, or one signed by a key you no longer pin, is refused. The <key> comes from the catalog URL and a hash of the token, so switching edges or organizations never reads another catalog's copy. Only a newer catalog replaces the saved copy. When fetching fails with a network error or HTTP 5xx: The saved copy is used if the edge built it no more than toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge ago, and you see TOOL_CATALOG_CACHED with its age. Its expires time doesn't apply offline. Entries are still checked against the signed index. An older copy fails with TOOL_CATALOG_STALE. A refused token (401, 403), a missing catalog (404), a bad signature or a malformed document is never replaced by the saved copy. When less than a quarter of maxOfflineAge remains (under 42 hours at the default 7d), you also see TOOL_CATALOG_EXPIRING. Oyzu also records when the newest catalog it ever fetched was built. A saved copy older than that fails with TOOL_CATALOG_STALE, so restoring an old backup can't bring back a version your organization has since withdrawn. oyzu tools versions --offline uses the saved copy and the cached index without contacting the edge. oyzu install --offline replays the lock.

Oyzu accepts index records for Linux amd64 and arm64 (GNU), macOS arm64 and Windows amd64 (MSVC). macOS amd64 records in the index aren't installable. Tailscale has Linux archives only. Someone who can write to your own tool store can put back an older genuine catalog and use a withdrawn version offline, but only until maxOfflineAge after that copy was built. Someone between you and the edge with a valid token can replay a genuine catalog until its expires (24 hours by default). While offline, a withdrawal made after the last fetch isn't seen until the next fetch.

Code Cause Fix TOOL_CATALOG_UNAUTHENTICATED OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN is empty or the edge rejected it. Get a current token from your administrator. TOOL_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE The catalog couldn't be fetched and there is no usable saved copy, or the edge has no catalog for your organization (404). Check the network path to the edge. TOOL_CATALOG_STALE The saved copy is older than maxOfflineAge or than the newest one fetched, or the edge sent an expired catalog. Reconnect to the edge; check your clock. TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED toolCatalog.keys is missing, or the catalog isn't signed by a pinned key. Pin the edge's current public key; report a bad signature to the edge's operator. TOOL_CATALOG_CACHED (warning) The edge is unreachable; the saved copy was used. None while it's recent enough. TOOL_CATALOG_EXPIRING (warning) The saved copy has less than a quarter of maxOfflineAge left. Reconnect before it runs out. TOOL_CATALOG_INVALID The catalog is malformed. Report it to the edge's operator. TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH The catalog names different files than the signed index, or a different index with the same serial. Nothing was installed. Report it to the edge's operator. TOOL_CATALOG_NOT_CONFIGURED tools request or tools requests without toolCatalog.url. Requests only work with a catalog. TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL_MISSING tools request without toolCatalog.adminUrl. Set it to the delivery admin API URL. TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX The index doesn't carry the tool, a cargo: helper, Rust missing from the index, or no index configured. Ask an administrator. TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG Your organization hasn't approved this tool or version, or the download URL isn't listed. oyzu tools request <tool>@<version>. TOOL_REFUSED The version is blocked, quarantined or otherwise refused (with the reason), or the edge refused the download. Use another approved version. TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN The version was withdrawn from the index. Use the version the message names, for example with oyzu update <tool>. TOOL_REQUEST_INVALID Not <tool>@<version>, or the edge refused the request. Fix the spec or pick an indexed version. TOOL_REQUEST_UNAVAILABLE The admin API has no such organization or route (404), or the edge takes no requests. Check toolCatalog.adminUrl; ask an administrator directly. TOOL_REQUEST_UNAUTHENTICATED No personal sign-in, or it was refused (401). oyzu auth login. The organization token isn't accepted here. TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account isn't set. Set them. TOOL_REQUEST_UNKNOWN --status or --cancel with an ID your organization doesn't have. oyzu tools requests shows the IDs made here. TOOL_REQUEST_FORBIDDEN You lack catalog.request, or tried to cancel someone else's request (403). Ask an administrator, or the requester. TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_PENDING --cancel on a request that's already decided, cancelled or expired (409). Nothing to cancel; --status shows it.
Tool index Tool commands Configuration

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-commands.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use these commands to add, lock, install, update and inspect the tools a project or your user account needs. Each command changes the declaration ([tools] in configuration) and the lock (oyzu.lock) together, so the two never drift apart. Use them instead of editing oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock by hand. Note: These commands are experimental, and their syntax and error codes may change. They are fully tested on Linux x86-64; Windows x86-64 works with less test coverage, and macOS isn't supported yet. No account is needed. oyzu install go@1.26 # this project: declare, lock, install oyzu install -g node@22 # your user configuration, all projects oyzu install go # declared: make sure it is installed; undeclared: go@latest oyzu update go # newer version within the requirement; config untouched oyzu uninstall go # remove the project declaration and lock entry oyzu tools current # what is in effect here oyzu tools list # what is in the store, and what uses it oyzu tools versions go # what could be installed oyzu tools info go # provider, verification, eligibility Supported tools: Archive providers: node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm, yarn. Rust: rust and the Cargo helpers cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov. Experimental registry packages: aqua:<owner>/<repo> (see the aqua: backend) and github:<owner>/<repo> (see the github: backend).
documents.s: Tool commands: install, update, uninstall and inspection

documents.t: Each command acts on one scope. The default is the current project. Flag Configuration written Lock written none, inside a project project oyzu.toml (created if missing) project oyzu.lock -g, --global your user configuration file (OYZU_USER_CONFIG or the platform default) the oyzu.lock next to it --local oyzu.local.toml project oyzu.lock --toolset NAME (global option) [toolsets.NAME.tools] in oyzu.toml, or in oyzu.local.toml with --local that toolset's entries in oyzu.lock; [tools] entries are untouched (toolsets) The project is --root, or the workspace root when it holds oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml, build.yaml or a Git marker. Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT and writes nothing. -g ignores project files, even when you run it inside a project. --global and --local can't be combined, and --toolset can't be used with --global. Profiles never hold tools. --profile with install SPEC or uninstall fails with TOOL_PROFILE_DECLARATION. If the same tool is declared in another scope, the command prints a note.

oyzu install with no arguments installs everything declared in the effective configuration. It accepts --frozen (require a matching lock), --offline (use only locks, installations and cached archives) and --store DIR. oyzu install --global installs your global tools using your user configuration and its oyzu.lock, independent of the current project. oyzu install --global --frozen --offline restores a locked global selection from local data. A missing lock fails with TOOL_LOCK_MISSING.

A spec is [provider:]name[@version], split at the last @. Spec Meaning go@1.26 Newest version starting with 1.26. go@1.26.8 Exactly this version. go@latest Newest eligible version. go Keep the declared requirement and make sure it is installed; if undeclared, use latest. Several specs are applied together or not at all. Naming a tool twice fails with TOOL_SPEC_INVALID. Configuration stores what you typed ("1.26"). The lock stores the exact version. Core tools (node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, rust) are written under the name you typed. Other tools are written under their full ID (for example "cargo:cargo-nextest"). An existing declaration keeps its spelling. An ambiguous bare name fails and lists the exact spellings to retry with. Replacing a requirement prints Replaced "1.25" (1.25.9) -> "1.26" (1.26.8) and reuses an installation already in the store. Other declared tools in the same lock that aren't locked yet are locked and installed in the same run, keeping their current versions. What install does, in order: Parses the specs. Checks tools.allowed. Resolves lock entries for every platform your builds declare, plus the host. tools.lockPlatforms replaces the inferred platform list (the host is always kept). Downloads and installs only the host archive. Writes configuration and lock in one transaction. Any failure leaves both files unchanged. A concurrent edit fails with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT.

--dry-run resolves versions (reading publisher catalogs) and reports versions, files and platforms. It downloads no archive and writes nothing. Specs with --frozen, --offline or --update fail with TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT, as do --dry-run and --local without specs. Archive tools and Rust tools can't be mixed in one command (TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT). Run two commands.

✓ Installed go 1.26.8 Declared "1.26" in ./oyzu.toml (project) Locked in ./oyzu.lock for 3 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc) With --json the result has tools[] (tool, key, request, version, previous, status, platforms, otherScopes) plus configuration, lock, scope and store.

If the publisher has no artifact for a platform, that platform is left out of the lock and reported as unavailable (a warning in human output, unavailablePlatforms in JSON). The other platforms lock and the host installs normally. Selecting the unavailable platform later fails. For example, oyzu install node@14 locks Linux and Windows only, because Node 14 has no macOS arm64 build. This applies when a tool is first declared or its request changes, and only for Node, Go and Java. update re-resolves only platforms that are already locked. A tool with no artifact on any platform fails, as does any other resolution problem (for example a missing checksum file).

oyzu install oyzu:NAME@VERSION --artifact-set FILE [--artifact-set-digest sha256:D] installs a tool from a resolved artifact set instead of a built-in provider. This is experimental, works in the project scope only, and doesn't yet make the tool runnable. See artifact sets.

oyzu update [TOOL...] moves locked versions forward within each existing requirement, locks the result for all platforms and installs the host selection. It never edits configuration. With no arguments it updates every tool in the scope. It takes names, not versions. In a project without --toolset, it also updates every toolset: [tools] first, then each toolset. The Set column (toolset in JSON) shows which one each row belongs to. A named tool is updated wherever [tools] or a toolset declares it. --dry-run reports the versions that would be locked. Tools you removed from configuration by hand aren't pruned from the lock. install --update still works but is deprecated.

oyzu uninstall TOOL... removes the declaration and every lock entry for the tool in the selected scope, in one transaction. Comments elsewhere in the file are kept. Installed files stay in the store and show as unreferenced in oyzu tools list. A tool that the scope doesn't declare fails with TOOL_NOT_DECLARED, naming the scope that does. --dry-run writes nothing.

oyzu pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 adds the requests to the project's [tools] and locks their exact archives for the configured platforms, in one transaction. It installs nothing. Run oyzu install --frozen afterward to install. --dry-run previews the result. Specs can't be combined with --refresh or --offline. Bare oyzu pin locks what your builds need, and accepts --refresh and --offline. Bare oyzu pin covers every toolset. oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks only that toolset. Configuration precedence and policy still apply. A request that another scope overrides fails without changing files. oyzu --json pin ... returns the same facts with status: "pinned". Pinning reads publisher metadata or the tool index. For some checksum formats it downloads the archive to compute a SHA-256. The default platforms include linux/arm64/gnu. A platform the provider doesn't publish is left out and reported.

These commands are read-only. They install nothing, don't re-check installed files (tools are verified when installed, then trusted) and print the store path. All accept --store DIR. Command Shows oyzu tools current [-g] [--all] [--details] One row per tool in effect: requested and selected versions, scope and status. -g shows only global declarations; --all adds declarations a closer scope overrides. oyzu tools list [--details] Installations in the store, with size and what uses each: global, project or unreferenced. oyzu tools versions TOOL [--offline] Versions you can install, newest first. oyzu tools info TOOL Provider, accepted names, commands, platforms, verification, eligibility, declarations by scope and current state. oyzu tools check --catalog, oyzu tools migrate [--write] Check declarations against the tool index, or move mise.toml tools to Oyzu names. See tool index. Statuses in tools current: Status Meaning ok Installed and locked. not installed Locked but not in the store. Run oyzu install. blocked Excluded by tools.allowed; the rule is named. stale lock No lock, or no entry for this tool, platform or provider. Run oyzu pin. ambiguous Conflicting lock entries or names. Notes: tools list only knows about the global lock and the current project. An "unreferenced" installation may still be used by another project. tools versions reads the publisher's catalog, or the tool index when it lists the package (which also works offline). Otherwise it needs the network and fails with TOOL_OFFLINE under --offline. Pre-release and nightly versions aren't offered. A version blocked by tools.allowed says why. Rust and the Cargo helpers have no version catalog (TOOL_VERSIONS_UNSUPPORTED).

Supported on Linux x86-64 only. Archive and Rust tools need separate commands. Installing one tool also installs the other declared tools in its lock. These commands don't run in managed (enrolled) mode.

Code Cause and fix TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Unparseable spec, empty version or a tool named twice. TOOL_NO_PROJECT No project here. Run inside a project or use --global. TOOL_NOT_DECLARED uninstall or update of a tool this scope doesn't declare. TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT Flags that don't combine, archive and Rust tools mixed, or a declaration overridden in this invocation. CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED tools.allowed excludes the tool. The rule is named; nothing is written. TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT A configured version is below the minimum in Go's go.mod or go.work. Both sources are named. Exit status 3. See Go version selection. TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT A [tools] value in the pin file's folder or nearer the build, or set by policy, names a different version than a native pin file (rust-toolchain.toml, .nvmrc, .node-version, .python-version, packageManager). Exit status 3. See native pin files. TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID A native pin file holds a value [tools] doesn't accept (an alias such as lts/* or nightly, a range, several versions, or a Rust toolchain.path). The file and a fix are named. Exit status 3. TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_OVERRIDDEN Warning: oyzu.local.toml overrides a native pin. oyzu pin locks the pin, not the override. TOOL_LOCK_STALE The lock has no entry for a request, or a native pin or minimum changed (for example go get rewrote go.mod). Run oyzu pin. PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT Another process changed the files at the same time. Retry.

If a configuration and lock write was interrupted, the next oyzu install, oyzu update, oyzu uninstall or oyzu pin finishes or rolls it back before doing anything else. Read-only commands report PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED with the affected folder and the command to run. If the files were edited by something else in the meantime, recovery stops with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT and leaves its journal for you to inspect. A concurrent edit while a command reads configuration reports CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT. Retry the command.

If installation recipes are out of date, the error names the tool, version and lock. Run oyzu pin --refresh (keeps selected versions), then oyzu install. Tool preparation failures name the tool, version, store path and the command to recover. Windows paths in errors use the plain C:\... or \\server\share\... form.
Shell activation to use installed tools in your shell. Configuration for [tools], toolsets and native pin files. Tool index and tool catalog for where tools come from and organization policy.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-github.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. github:<owner>/<repo> installs a program from a GitHub repository's release assets. It uses the same [tools] syntax as mise's github: backend. No account and no mise executable are needed. Note: Experimental. Tested on Intel macOS with Pandoc 3.12.1 and Poedit GettextTools 1.0. Linux, Windows and Apple Silicon are not supported yet. $ oyzu install github:cli/cli@2.49.2 $ cat oyzu.toml [tools] "github:cli/cli" = "2.49.2" You need network access to api.github.com, github.com and GitHub's release-asset host. The lock covers every platform your builds declare, plus the current host. Use tools.lockPlatforms to lock other platforms (the host is always kept).

An exact MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH request reads the release tagged v<version> or <version>. latest and prefixes such as 2.49 pick the highest stable matching release. oyzu tools versions github:owner/repo lists them. For each platform, Oyzu picks the asset whose name best matches the OS, architecture and libc. A wrong architecture is never used as a fallback. Checksums, signatures, packages (.deb, .rpm, .msi) and source archives are never picked. The SHA-256 is the digest GitHub reports for the asset, or one from a checksum file published next to it. Oyzu downloads the asset once per platform, checks it against that digest and finds the command: the file named after the repository, or else the only executable. The lock records the asset URL, its SHA-256 and the command path. oyzu install --frozen doesn't need the GitHub API again. Only the publisher's SHA-256 is checked. Attestations, signatures and SLSA provenance are not verified.
documents.s: How a release is chosen and pinned

documents.t: github:poedit/gettext-tools version 1.0 installs the GNU msgfmt from Poedit's GettextTools.xcframework.zip on macOS (11.5 or newer). Oyzu runs Versions/A/Helpers/msgfmt from the unmodified framework, so its bundled libraries load without extra settings. The package version (1.0) is separate from the gettext version the binary prints. [tools] lockPlatforms = ["darwin/amd64/native"] "github:poedit/gettext-tools" = "1.0" Oyzu only uses this command path for that exact archive (SHA-256 04dcba5b92ad8d0ff475e29baee72180f096431af220a858f0d29a9ec8988dcd). Other packages use the normal command detection, which refuses archives with more than one candidate.

Code Cause and fix TOOL_RATE_LIMITED GitHub refused the request (anonymous rate limit or access policy). Set GITHUB_TOKEN; it is sent to api.github.com only. TOOL_VERSION_NOT_FOUND No release matches the request. TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING The release publishes no SHA-256 for the chosen asset. Nothing is installed. TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH The download doesn't match the published digest. TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED The chosen asset isn't tar.gz or zip (for example a bare binary or tar.xz). TOOL_RECIPE_UNSUPPORTED The archive has no single identifiable command. TOOL_SPEC_INVALID The ID isn't github:<owner>/<repo>.

Supported on Intel macOS only. Not supported: bare-binary assets, tar.xz and tar.zst, options such as asset_pattern, bin and version_prefix, private repositories and GitHub Enterprise hosts. tools versions lists releases without looking at their assets, so a listed version may have no build for your platform. Resolving downloads each platform's asset once, which can be large.
Tool commands The aqua: backend

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-go-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install the official Go distribution for your project and run go and gofmt from it, so you don't need Go installed on the machine. The exact release and archive digest are recorded in oyzu.lock.

Declare a version in oyzu.toml: [tools] go = "1.24.13" Then install and run it: oyzu install oyzu which go oyzu exec -- go version oyzu exec -- gofmt -l main.go oyzu exec -- go run ./main.go gofmt -l main.go prints the file name when the file needs formatting and nothing when it's already formatted. With --json, the command's output is in the stdout field. To reinstall later without changing anything or touching the network: oyzu install --frozen --offline

Source Role [tools] go in oyzu.toml The request, when set go.mod / go.work The Go minimum (the newer of the go and toolchain lines). It becomes the request when [tools] go is unset, and an incompatible [tools] go is rejected oyzu.lock The exact release, reused until you update it See Go version selection for how builds use this. To move to a newer release that matches your request, run oyzu update go (oyzu install --update go does the same). --frozen and --offline commands never pick a new version.

oyzu exec, shims and activated shells: put the installed Go bin directory first on PATH; set GOROOT to the installation; set GOTOOLCHAIN=local so Go uses the locked compiler instead of downloading another one. You can override this with an environment setting in oyzu.toml. Module downloads are still done by Go itself, using your normal Go proxy settings. When you activate a shell, oyzu creates go and gofmt shims. A shim runs the Go selected for the current directory and refuses commands that aren't part of that selection. oyzu env --json shows the selected tool.
documents.s: What oyzu sets when Go runs

documents.t: oyzu reads the release list from https://go.dev/dl/?mode=json&include=all and downloads archives from https://dl.google.com/go/. Before installing, it checks that the archive's size and SHA-256 match the release list and its .sha256 file. The lock records the digest. Go releases have no publisher signature to check.

An administrator can send downloads through a mirror with a tools route scoped to go, oyzu:go or * (see proxy acquisition). The mirror must serve an index.json with the official all-release catalog, plus the archives and their .sha256 files, at its base URL. When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.

Installations made by older oyzu versions keep working for go, but may not expose gofmt. Run oyzu update go once to refresh the installation for the same Go version, then use frozen commands as usual. oyzu pin --refresh updates lock metadata only, not the installed files.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 Supported macOS Intel Installs from an exact version or version line; automatic default pinning isn't available yet macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet Linux musl Not supported

oyzu selects the compiler only. Module downloads and proxies are Go's own behavior, and choosing a compiler doesn't make a build hermetic. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive already cached.

Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install helm, so a project that packages or deploys Helm charts doesn't need Helm installed on the machine.

[tools] helm = "3.16.2" # exact release # helm = "latest" # the publisher's current stable release oyzu install helm@3.16.2 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one oyzu exec -- helm version --short oyzu which helm The installed command is helm (helm.exe on Windows).

Request Result 3.16.2 or v3.16.2 That release latest The release named by the publisher's helm-latest-version marker Ranges, minor lines such as 3.16 and pre-releases are refused, because the Helm download site has no list of releases. For the same reason oyzu tools versions helm fails. latest currently points at a Helm 4 release. Pin an exact version if your project depends on Helm 3 behavior. The lock keeps the resolved version until you run oyzu update.

oyzu downloads the release archive for each platform from https://get.helm.sh/ (.tar.gz on Linux and macOS, .zip on Windows) and checks it against the SHA-256 in the publisher's .sha256sum file on the same site. The digest is recorded in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to helm, oyzu:helm or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-index.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The tool index is a public, signed list of every registry package's versions, with per-platform download URLs and the SHA-256 Oyzu verified for each file. oyzu install and oyzu tools versions read it instead of asking GitHub or each publisher, so only the download itself goes to the vendor. You don't need to configure anything to use it. Note: Experimental. Settings, error codes and exit statuses may change. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. By default Oyzu reads the index published as GitHub releases of oyzuai/tool-index, refreshed daily. The file format is tool-index.schema.json.
documents.s: The public tool index (toolIndex, tools check --catalog, tools migrate, tools trust)

documents.t: The index can carry Oyzu's own providers: Java, Node, Go, Python, Maven, Gradle, Helm, kubectl, k3d, Liquibase, Tailscale, npm, pnpm, Yarn and Rust. Archive records name the exact download URL the provider uses. Rust records approve a channel manifest and carry its component digests; see Rust installation. Without an organization catalog, a provider request uses the newest verified index record that matches. It reads the publisher's live metadata only when the index has nothing for it (no index, a provider the index doesn't carry, or no verified record). Once an indexed version is selected, a platform it has no record for is unavailable; Oyzu doesn't look it up at the publisher. Under a catalog, a tool missing from the index fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX, and an unapproved version with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG. Cargo helpers aren't available under a catalog. Index records are produced with oyzu --json tools evidence --provider <name> --version <exact-release>. See provider records for the publisher sources and checksum formats. The default matrix is Linux amd64 and arm64 (GNU), macOS arm64 and amd64, and Windows amd64 (MSVC). macOS amd64 records exist for Rust, Node, Go, Python, npm, pnpm, Yarn and Zig when the publisher provides them; other providers report it unsupported. Tailscale reports macOS and Windows as unsupported.

Setting Values Default Meaning toolIndex.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback), or false https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/releases/latest/download/ Where the index is. false reads no index, and registry packages are resolved locally from their recipes (refused under managed configuration). toolIndex.trustedRoot Absolute path Sigstore's production trusted root (built in, or newer from oyzu tools trust refresh) A Sigstore trusted_root.json to verify against instead, for a private Sigstore deployment. User or machine configuration only. toolIndex.identity https: URI https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main The signing identity the index must have, for an index you sign yourself. User or machine configuration only. Settings marked "user or machine configuration only" fail with CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file. # ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml [toolIndex] # A mirror instead of the public index (or `false` for no index): url = "https://index.example.test/" # Only for an index signed by another workflow or another Sigstore instance: # identity = "https://github.com/example/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" # trustedRoot = "/etc/oyzu/sigstore-trusted-root.json" The URL can point at a GitHub release directory, an Oyzu host or your own mirror. Trust comes from the signature and the pinned identity, not from the host. The default URL redirects to the newest release (releases/download/index-v<serial>/) and then to release-assets.githubusercontent.com. If your network blocks that host, use a mirror.

Each index release has three files: index.json, index.json.zst (the same content compressed, used only for transfer) and index.json.sigstore.json, a Sigstore bundle. The index is signed keylessly by the index repository's GitHub Actions release workflow, and the signature is recorded in the public Rekor transparency log. Oyzu verifies the bundle itself, offline, against the trusted root (no cosign and no extra network call). It checks that: the bundle has exactly one log entry and one signature; the log entry is signed by a Rekor key that was valid at signing time (Rekor v1 signed entry timestamps and Rekor v2 inclusion proofs with RFC 3161 timestamps are both accepted); the certificate chains to a Sigstore Fulcio CA valid at signing time; the certificate names toolIndex.identity, the GitHub Actions OIDC issuer and a GitHub-hosted runner (an index signed on a self-hosted runner is refused); the signed statement names the SHA-256 of the exact index.json bytes. Oyzu doesn't check certificate transparency timestamps, the Rekor v1 inclusion proof, or the timestamp authority's signing-certificate attribute. Only ECDSA (P-256 or P-384) timestamp authorities are supported. Then the document itself: Unknown fields are refused, tools must be sorted with lowercase oyzu: IDs, and every record's digests must recompute. expires must be in the future. serial can't go below the highest one accepted before, and the same serial can't have different content (rollback protection). Oyzu downloads index.json.zst (up to 256 MiB uncompressed), or index.json if the server returns 404 for the compressed file. The signature is checked on the uncompressed bytes.

The last verified index is kept under <store>/catalogs/tool-index/<key>/. The highest accepted serial is kept separately in <store>/state/tool-index/<key>.json, so deleting the cache doesn't reset rollback protection. Each store has its own history. A copy fetched less than an hour ago is used without a request (index.source is recent). After an hour, Oyzu checks for a new one. If a newer copy can't be fetched or fails verification, the cached copy is verified again and used while it hasn't expired. index.source is cached and index.warning says why. With --offline (tools versions, tools check --catalog, tools migrate), only the cached copy is read. install --offline replays the lock and doesn't read the index. With no valid copy, the command fails with TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE, naming the fetch failure and the cache state.

For a registry package (oyzu: IDs and their aqua: aliases, not github:), after checking the lock: The index. The package matches an index tool by ID (oyzu:terraform) or by its origin package (oyzu:hashicorp/terraform, aqua:hashicorp/terraform), ignoring case. The request (1.16.5, v1.16.5, 1.16 or latest) picks a version with a record for the platform. Prefixes and latest skip pre-releases. The lock gets the record's URL and verified SHA-256. Local recipe evaluation (standalone only), when the index doesn't list the package, has no matching release, or has no verified SHA-256 for it. Under managed configuration, step 2 never runs; a miss fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX. A tool the index lists as excluded fails with TOOL_EXCLUDED. A listed version with no build for the platform fails as an unavailable platform. A configured index that can't be verified is always an error, never a silent fallback. With an organization tool catalog, step 1 considers only approved versions, and step 2 never runs.

The index can withdraw a version, for example when its upstream files were deleted or the release was broken. The version keeps its records, so a lock still matches it by name, and gains a reason (1 to 512 characters): { "version": "4.20.0", "released": {...}, "sets": [...], "withdrawn": { "reason": "upstream release assets were deleted (404)" } } A prefix or latest skips withdrawn versions, for registry packages and for the providers that read the index (Java, Node, Go, Python). An exact request for a withdrawn version, a prefix whose every match is withdrawn, and an existing lock entry for one are all refused: TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN: oyzu:golang-migrate 4.20.0 was withdrawn from the tool index: upstream release assets were deleted (404). The newest available version is 4.19.1. The last sentence names the newest stable version with a build for your platform, if there is one. A lock is checked against whatever index the install can read (fetched, or cached with --offline). If no index is readable, a locked install proceeds. tools versions lists a withdrawn version under excluded with the reason, and tools check --catalog reports it as withdrawn. Under an organization catalog, the message names the newest version the catalog serves; see the catalog reference.

oyzu tools versions aqua:owner/repo lists an indexed package's versions, newest first, with tags, release time (publisher or first-seen) and versions excluded for this platform. With --offline it reads only the cached copy. It needs no GITHUB_TOKEN. In JSON, source is tool index, and index gives the URL, version (the serial), expires and whether the copy was fetched or cached.

Checks every tool declared here (the project, or your global configuration outside a project) against the index. It installs and writes nothing. With toolCatalog.url set, it checks against the organization catalog instead (see the catalog statuses). Availability is judged for this host plus any platforms listed in tools.lockPlatforms. Missing records for other default lock platforms don't count against a tool. oyzu tools check --catalog Status Meaning Refused indexed Installs from the index at version for the host and every tools.lockPlatforms entry. no local Not in the index (or no matching release); would be resolved locally from its recipe. no (standalone) refused Same as local, under managed configuration. yes direct A github: package, or one of Oyzu's own providers (uses the index when it has a record, the publisher otherwise). no unavailable Listed, but no build for the host or a required platform. yes withdrawn The version was withdrawn; reason gives the reason and the newest available version. yes excluded The index excludes the tool. yes blocked tools.allowed doesn't list it. yes unknown Not a tool Oyzu recognizes. yes Exit status: 0 when nothing is refused, 1 when something is, 2 when toolIndex.url is false (TOOL_INDEX_NOT_CONFIGURED). JSON has tools[], the refused count, outcome and index.

Moves tool declarations from mise.toml (or .mise.toml) into oyzu.toml under Oyzu names. By default it's a dry run that shows every change and the complete proposed oyzu.toml (after). --write replaces oyzu.toml atomically, keeping comments and formatting. mise.toml is never changed. oyzu tools migrate # show what would change oyzu tools migrate --write # apply it mise spelling Becomes node, go, ... and core:<name> The bare name. A short name for a supported backend (gh, terraform) Unchanged; bare names resolve against the index. aqua:owner/repo (also when already in oyzu.toml) The tool's index name (terraform), or oyzu:owner/repo (lowercased) if the index doesn't list it. github:owner/repo Unchanged. ubi:owner/repo github:owner/repo. asdf:, vfox: and short names only available through them Left out, with the reason. Other backends (npm:, pipx:, cargo:, go:, ...) Left out, with the reason. A version array keeps its first entry, and a table keeps its version. Anything dropped is noted. A tool oyzu.toml already declares is reported as a conflict, and the existing declaration is kept. Running it again after --write reports no change. Short names are resolved from mise's name list, downloaded once into the store. --offline reads only the cached index.

Oyzu ships with a copy of Sigstore's production trusted_root.json. When Sigstore rotates a key or adds a log, oyzu tools trust refresh fetches the newer root without waiting for an Oyzu release: oyzu tools trust refresh # from https://tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev/ oyzu tools trust refresh --from /media/sigstore # from a copy, on a machine without network oyzu tools trust status # which root verifies the index now --from takes an HTTPS URL of a TUF repository mirror or a directory. The directory can hold the repository files as Sigstore serves them (16.root.json, timestamp.json, 166.snapshot.json, 14.targets.json, targets/<sha256>.trusted_root.json) or be a checkout of github.com/sigstore/root-signing. The refresh runs the standard TUF client checks, starting from the TUF root built into Oyzu (or the last refresh): each newer root must be signed by the previous and its own root keys; the timestamp, snapshot and targets files must be properly signed, unexpired and not older than before; and trusted_root.json must match the length and SHA-256 the targets file lists. The result is saved in <store>/state/sigstore-root.json and verified again, offline, every time it's read. An edited file fails with TOOL_TRUST_INVALID; delete it to go back to the built-in root. A refreshed root is used only while it's newer than the built-in one. A later Oyzu release with a newer built-in root takes over. toolIndex.trustedRoot, when set, wins over both. Expiry is only checked when refreshing. Sigstore's timestamp expires within about a week, so an offline copy must be recent. refresh reports status (refreshed or unchanged), the TUF root and targets versions with their expiry, the trusted root's SHA-256, and inUse (refreshed or built-in). status reports inUse (built-in, refreshed or configured), the built-in root and the saved refresh. While the TUF root Oyzu starts from expires within 30 days (or has expired), commands that load the index warn with TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING. Index verification still works; run oyzu tools trust refresh to clear it. The built-in TUF root (version 16) expires on 2027-04-22.
documents.s: oyzu tools trust refresh and status

documents.t: Code Cause and fix TOOL_INDEX_UNTRUSTED The toolIndex.trustedRoot file can't be read or isn't a trusted root. Inside a TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE reason: the signature didn't verify. TOOL_INDEX_URL_INVALID The URL isn't HTTPS (or loopback HTTP). TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE No verified, unexpired copy could be obtained. TOOL_INDEX_INVALID The signed document is malformed (wrong format, no serial or expires, unsorted, digests don't match). TOOL_INDEX_NOT_CONFIGURED tools check --catalog with toolIndex.url = false. TOOL_INDEX_EXPIRING (warning) The index expires within three days, so publishing has stalled. After it expires, commands that need it fail with TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE. TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING (warning) The TUF root expires within 30 days. Run oyzu tools trust refresh. TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX Managed configuration, and the index lacks the package or release. TOOL_EXCLUDED The index lists the tool as excluded. TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN The requested or locked version was withdrawn. Install the version the message names, or run oyzu update <tool> for a lock. TOOL_MIGRATE_NOTHING tools migrate found nothing to migrate. TOOL_MIGRATE_INVALID A TOML file can't be parsed. TOOL_TRUST_REFRESH_FAILED tools trust refresh couldn't fetch or verify the TUF repository. The reason names the file and the check. TOOL_TRUST_SOURCE_INVALID --from is neither an HTTPS URL nor a directory. TOOL_TRUST_INVALID The saved refresh no longer verifies. Delete it or refresh again.

A release published in the last hour may not be seen until the hour is up. There is no flag to force a fetch. If a new release is published between Oyzu's two downloads, they won't verify together, and the cached copy is used (with a warning) until the next run. The built-in trusted root is never refreshed automatically. Update Oyzu or run oyzu tools trust refresh. tools evidence always uses the built-in root. There is no minimum-release-age rule. Supported on Linux x86-64 only.
