CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-java-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install a JDK, Maven and Gradle itself, so a fresh checkout of a Maven or Gradle project builds without any of them on the machine. See native host builds for which projects build this way. Note: Supported on Linux x86-64 only.

Pinning is optional. For a Maven project that builds natively, oyzu build picks a JDK and Maven, writes oyzu.lock, installs them into the shared tool store and builds: oyzu build # no Java or Maven on PATH, no pin needed oyzu pin --dry-run # preview: oyzu:java 17 and oyzu:maven 3.9, with where each came from oyzu exec -- mvn -version To choose versions yourself, set them in oyzu.toml. This takes precedence: [tools] java = "21" # latest 21.x; also "lts" or an exact "21.0.8" maven = "3.9" # latest 3.9.x; any Maven release range

Tool Default Override JDK The Java level in the root POM (maven.compiler.release, maven.compiler.target, maven.compiler.source or java.version; 1.8 means 8), raised to 17 if lower. Without one, lts: the newest long-term-support release [tools] java Maven 3.9, which supports Java 8 and newer [tools] maven Gradle Gradle 8, or Gradle 9 when the project declares a Java level above 24 [tools] gradle A property that isn't a literal number counts as undeclared. The declared level is a minimum, not the newest JDK: a project declaring 21 gets JDK 21. A project declaring 8, 9 or 11 gets JDK 17, the oldest JDK that Maven, Gradle and oyzu's Java support run on. JDK 17 still compiles for older levels correctly (--release 8 checks against the Java 8 API). Gradle projects follow the same rule. The lock records the exact versions. Isolated (Docker) builds use the same locked JDK instead of the image's (see Maven). An explicit [tools] java below 17 still installs for use on your machine, but an isolated build refuses it with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION.

Tool Source Check JDK Eclipse Temurin, found through the Adoptium API and downloaded from the adoptium GitHub organization SHA-256 published by the Adoptium API Maven The Apache distribution server (maven-3 and maven-4 listings) The publisher's SHA-512; the lock records the SHA-256 of the checked bytes Gradle The catalog at services.gradle.org/versions/all; the zip is served from Gradle's GitHub releases SHA-256 from the catalog Maven and Gradle use one archive for every platform. Downloads are fetched in 2 MiB pieces, each with its own 45-second timeout, so a slow server makes the first build slower but doesn't make it fail. Checksums come from the publisher; no signatures are checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to java, maven, oyzu:java, oyzu:maven or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.

JAVA_HOME points at the installed JDK (on macOS, its Contents/Home). Build tasks see JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_HOME and GRADLE_HOME from the installed tools. Values already set on your machine are ignored, so a machine-wide JDK can't change which Java a build uses. Shims are provided for java, javac, mvn and gradle.
documents.s: What oyzu sets when Java runs

documents.t: If the project commits mvnw or gradlew, oyzu runs the wrapper instead of mvn or gradle and installs only the JDK. The wrapper downloads its own Maven or Gradle: The Maven wrapper in bin form needs Java plus unzip or tar. The only-script form also needs curl or wget on PATH. That download is the wrapper's own, so oyzu's mirror routes, credentials and checksum checks don't apply. Set distributionSha256Sum in gradle-wrapper.properties or maven-wrapper.properties to have the wrapper verify it.

Maven runs verify, so tests run as part of the build. Each module with tests must produce Surefire XML in target/surefire-reports. Results show as Tests N passed · M failed. A failing test fails the build and no artifacts are published. JaCoCo 0.8.13 runs around verify, and each tested module's target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml is collected as coverage. A module that declares maven-failsafe-plugin and has an IT*, *IT or *ITCase test class must also produce target/failsafe-reports, collected as integration tests. Custom report directories aren't collected. An authored build command supplies its own reports. Gradle runs gradle --no-daemon --console=plain build. oyzu adds an init script that reads Gradle's own model to find each project's archive and test tasks. It publishes the jar and archive outputs, collects JUnit XML and build/reports/oyzu/<test task>/jacoco.xml (JaCoCo 0.8.13). Archive types oyzu doesn't recognize are refused with a reason. Archives with the same name are told apart by project path. Integration-test source sets are collected only when Gradle reports them as Test tasks. Coverage tools are downloaded by Maven or Gradle from Maven Central, so a failed or throttled download fails the build, and offline builds need them cached. --full lint and format checks need Checkstyle and google-java-format provisioned separately (see Java quality); the error says how.
documents.s: What a native Maven or Gradle build runs

documents.t: Native Maven builds need every jar's name to be readable from the POMs: literal or inherited versions, jar packaging, no finalName or classifier. Other projects use the isolated (Docker) build. Ant isn't built natively. oyzu doesn't install Ant. Without Docker, oyzu build stops before doing any work and says it needs the isolated Docker executor (see native host builds). With Docker and the base execution image, the isolated build works. Maven still downloads your project's dependencies from Maven Central, which can throttle shared IP addresses. Pinning records Java requirements for every Maven target, including ones that build in Docker. Windows (including mvn.cmd and the Windows JDK zip) and macOS aren't supported yet.
Maven Gradle Native host builds Liquibase installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-k3d-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install k3d, so a project that runs a local Kubernetes cluster in Docker doesn't need k3d installed on the machine. oyzu installs only the k3d binary; creating clusters still needs a running Docker engine.
[tools] k3d = "5.7.4" oyzu install k3d@5.7.4 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one oyzu exec -- k3d version The installed command is k3d.

Only exact versions are accepted: 5.7.4 or v5.7.4. Ranges, minor lines such as 5.7, latest and pre-releases are refused, because oyzu doesn't query GitHub for a list of releases. For the same reason oyzu tools versions k3d fails.

oyzu downloads the binary for each platform from the k3d GitHub release (https://github.com/k3d-io/k3d/releases/download/v<version>/k3d-<os>-<arch>, with .exe on Windows). It checks the binary against the SHA-256 listed in the release's checksums.txt and records that digest in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to k3d, oyzu:k3d or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64, macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS Intel, Linux musl Not supported
oyzu doesn't install or start Docker. --offline needs the tool installed or its binary already cached.
Tool commands kubectl installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-kubectl-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install kubectl, so a project that deploys to Kubernetes doesn't need kubectl installed on the machine.

[tools] kubectl = "1.31.2" # exact release # kubectl = "1.31" # newest stable 1.31 patch # kubectl = "latest" # current stable release oyzu install kubectl@1.31 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one oyzu exec -- kubectl version --client oyzu which kubectl The installed command is kubectl (kubectl.exe on Windows). oyzu sets no environment variables for it.

Kubernetes doesn't publish a list of every release, so oyzu can't resolve ranges. Use one of these forms: Request Resolved through 1.31.2 or v1.31.2 Used as is 1.31 https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable-1.31.txt latest or * https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt Ranges such as >=1.30, channels and pre-releases are refused, and oyzu tools versions kubectl fails. The lock keeps the exact version, so 1.31 stays on the patch it resolved to until you run oyzu update.

oyzu downloads the binary from https://dl.k8s.io/release/v<version>/bin/<os>/<arch>/kubectl (the site redirects to cdn.dl.k8s.io) and checks it against the .sha256 file published beside it. The digest is recorded in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to kubectl, oyzu:kubectl or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64, macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS Intel, Linux musl Not supported

Tool commands Helm installation k3d installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-liquibase-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install liquibase, so a project that applies database changelogs doesn't need Liquibase installed on the machine. Liquibase runs on Java, so pin a JDK beside it (see Java installation). The JDK oyzu installs sets JAVA_HOME, which the Liquibase launcher uses, so no machine-wide Java is involved.

[tools] java = "21" liquibase = "5.0.4" # exact release # liquibase = "latest" # newest stable release oyzu install java@21 oyzu install liquibase@5.0.4 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one oyzu exec -- liquibase --version oyzu exec -- liquibase --url=jdbc:h2:file:./db/app --username=sa --changelog-file=changelog.xml update The installed command is liquibase (run through liquibase.bat on Windows).

Request Result 5.0.4 or v5.0.4 That release latest The newest GitHub release that isn't a draft or pre-release Ranges, minor lines such as 5.0 and pre-releases are refused, and oyzu tools versions liquibase fails because oyzu doesn't list releases. The lock keeps the resolved version until you run oyzu update. Only releases 4.33.0 and later can be installed (see below).

Liquibase publishes no checksum file. oyzu reads the release from the GitHub API (api.github.com/repos/liquibase/liquibase/releases/) and uses the SHA-256 digest GitHub records for the archive: liquibase-<version>.zip on Windows and liquibase-<version>.tar.gz on Linux and macOS. It checks the download against that digest and records it in the lock. The digest is computed by GitHub when the file is uploaded; it isn't a signature from the Liquibase project. GitHub records these digests only for recent uploads. Releases from 4.33.0 have one; 4.32.0 and earlier don't. oyzu refuses a release without a digest rather than install it unchecked. Unauthenticated GitHub API requests are limited to 60 per hour per IP address, and an install reads the release once per platform. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to liquibase, oyzu:liquibase or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
Liquibase 5.x is source-available under FSL-1.1-ALv2, not an open-source license. Check that it fits your use before you adopt it.
Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 Supported macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS Intel, Linux musl Not supported

On Windows, run liquibase.bat from a normal Windows shell. It calls find /i and fails in a shell that puts a POSIX find ahead of find.exe on PATH. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive already cached.
Java installation Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-lock-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu.lock records the exact tool versions, download URLs and digests a project uses. This page describes what the lock contains, how oyzu pin decides which platforms to lock, and how to check a lock file with oyzu tools inspect-lock. Note: Experimental. The lock format may change.

All tool locks use format = 1. One file can hold two kinds of records, and neither implies the other: resolved_environment and resolution records: what oyzu pin resolved (versions, URLs and digests per platform). environment and tool records: verified installations. It can also hold optional [[requirements]] records, which list what Oyzu discovered your builds need. Their resolved and installed fields are always false. oyzu pin updates resolution records and keeps installation records; oyzu install keeps resolutions. Any other format value fails. A set locked for a toolset carries toolset = "NAME". Sets for [tools] carry none. The label only decides which sets a command changes; the same requests get the same identity in every toolset. Entries have no scope or profile field. The format is described by the lock JSON schema. If Oyzu rejects a lock written by an older development build, run oyzu pin --refresh, then oyzu install. Existing installed files are kept. oyzu pin --dry-run previews what would be locked, and oyzu pin writes it without installing. See requirement discovery.

oyzu tools inspect-lock [PATH] checks that a lock file is well formed. It doesn't resolve, download, install or run anything, and it doesn't check that the tools are installed. oyzu -C /path/to/project tools inspect-lock oyzu tools inspect-lock path/to/oyzu.lock PATH defaults to oyzu.lock in -C, then --root, then the current directory. An absolute path also works. Output is readable text by default; --json returns the structured result. Exit 0 on success, 2 on a validation or read error. The file must be a regular UTF-8 TOML file of at most 8 MiB. Symlinks to a regular file are followed; FIFOs are refused. It doesn't read project configuration or mise files, make network requests or change the lock. The whole file is checked, whatever profile or toolset is selected.

The command rejects: unknown or duplicate fields, an unsupported format and malformed digests; record keys that don't match their content, and verification subjects that differ from artifact digests; duplicate sets, missing dependencies, cycles, unreachable tools, conflicting IDs in one set and missing platform entries; source or artifact identifiers containing colons, path separators or control characters. Limits: 1,024 environments, 4,096 tools, 64 platform entries per tool, 16,384 dependency edges, depth 64 and 256 roots per environment.

The format, environment and tool counts, and the sorted list of platforms. A selection digest for each environment and platform. It covers every tool in the set, including dependencies, their file digests, verification and layout. Comments and ordering don't affect it; changing any dependency's file changes it. installation_keys, mapping each tool to the identity of its installation. Changing a dependency changes its key and the keys of tools that depend on it. Adding a platform leaves the existing keys unchanged. These keys name intended content; they don't mean the installation exists. The result says validation: "structure-and-identity-only". A pass means the file is consistent. It doesn't prove the publisher is authentic, that policy allows the tools, or that installed files are intact. A carefully crafted malicious lock can pass. Request digests are checked for shape, not recomputed against your configuration. If the check fails, fix the records or restore a known good lock (or regenerate it with oyzu pin). Don't edit digests to make it pass. The command never repairs files.

Node and Go projects can run oyzu pin --dry-run, oyzu pin, then oyzu install --frozen: Set node or go in [tools]. For Go, the minimum in go.mod or go.work (the newer of the go and toolchain lines) is a request by itself when [tools] go is unset; see Go version selection. Node also checks engines.node in package.json. Neither tool is run to find this out. If a configured version is missing, the preview is incomplete, explains why and exits 2. It never writes an empty lock. Pin records the selected version, the archive URL and its SHA-256. It doesn't download the archive. Node and Go entries keep your request (including prefixes and ranges) next to the exact version. Validation checks that the version satisfies the request, using the provider's rules (including Node aliases). --frozen doesn't re-read the publisher's catalog. Rust and Cargo helper requests must be exact versions.

By default, the lock covers the platforms declared by every build in the project, plus the host, whatever command you run. Platforms a provider doesn't support are listed in platformsNotLocked (human output: Inferred platforms not locked). The host and any platform you list explicitly must be covered. Oyzu never borrows another platform's artifact. Offline pin needs existing matching entries; it may leave other inferred platforms unlocked. oyzu install installs the host entry and keeps the rest of the lock. A repeat offline install reuses the verified copy in your store. To lock platforms explicitly, for example for another machine that runs your builds, set tools.lockPlatforms: [tools] rust = "1.95.0" lockPlatforms = ["windows/amd64/gnullvm", "linux/arm64/gnu"] The list must not be empty and must use exact supported platforms. The host is always included. tools.platforms is no longer accepted. Remove it, or rename it to lockPlatforms. See mapping and migration.

oyzu pin locks Rust for linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/amd64/native, darwin/arm64/native, windows/amd64/msvc, windows/arm64/msvc, windows/amd64/gnullvm and windows/arm64/gnullvm. Windows GNU/LLVM entries also lock the rust-mingw component. Windows amd64 installs use MSVC. Pin resolves every requested platform and its components before writing. Missing publisher data fails without writing a partial lock. Offline pin needs existing entries for every requested platform. Rust versions must be exact stable releases. The Cargo helpers are cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1, with URLs and SHA-256 digests from their GitHub releases. Windows helpers are MSVC binaries, even next to a GNU/LLVM compiler. macOS cargo-nextest is a universal binary. Locking a platform doesn't mean Oyzu can install or run tools on it. Windows GNU/LLVM component installation and ARM64 execution aren't supported yet.
Store inspection Tool commands Configuration

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-npm-pnpm-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install npm, pnpm and Yarn as their own tools (oyzu:npm, oyzu:pnpm and oyzu:yarn), separate from the npm bundled with Node. Choose a release in [tools] or with packageManager in package.json; the lock records it with the registry's integrity hash.

[tools] node = "22.12" npm = "11.6.2" # exact release, a range such as "11", or "latest" # pnpm = "10.20.0" oyzu install npm@11.6.2 # declares, locks, installs oyzu exec -- npm --version oyzu exec -- npx --version oyzu install pnpm@10.20.0 oyzu exec -- pnpm --version oyzu tools versions npm and oyzu tools versions pnpm list the registry's stable releases.

Selecting Node also gives you its bundled npm and npx, through oyzu exec, activated shells and shims, with no separate npm declaration. Both run on the selected Node. Declare npm only when you want a different npm release; its npm and npx then take precedence over the bundled copy. npm needs Node: when oyzu:npm is selected, select oyzu:node too. A lifecycle script that calls npm through PATH during oyzu exec still finds Node's bundled npm; in an isolated build it finds the locked one. After upgrading oyzu, run oyzu reshim to refresh existing shims. A shim doesn't pick a version itself: it uses the project or global selection each time it runs.

pnpm releases combine the older platform packages and the pnpm 12 packages. latest follows the pnpm package's latest tag. If that release isn't available for your platform, latest fails, but exact pins and ranges still work.

A Node build uses the nearest package.json with a packageManager field, searched from the build folder up to the project root (as Corepack does). If it names an exact stable npm or pnpm release, such as "packageManager": "pnpm@10.20.0", that release becomes a tool requirement: It's a native pin file. When the project has no oyzu.lock, the build locks it beside Node. A [tools] npm or [tools] pnpm value must agree. A disagreeing value in the same folder or nearer the build fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT; one further away loses to packageManager. A Corepack hash suffix (+sha512.<hex>) is accepted but not compared. The lock records the registry's integrity hash instead. A range, tag, bare major, pre-release or URL fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID. Write an exact stable release, or remove the field and set [tools]. If oyzu.lock already exists without that release, add it with oyzu install npm@<version> or oyzu install pnpm@<version>. When there's no packageManager, an exact devEngines.packageManager version with onFail: "error" is the request. For Yarn, see Managed Yarn. engines.node constrains Node's version instead; see Node selection.

Isolated builds use the locked release instead of the copy in the build image, for dependency installation and every action: pnpm is placed at /scratch/pnpmtool and comes first on PATH. npm is placed at /scratch/npmtool. Dependency installation writes npm and npx launchers to /dependencies/manager/bin, which comes first on PATH for every action. The build's dependency record lists the locked release under the oyzu.dev/locked-manager extension. A changed digest in oyzu.lock is refused. Isolated builds run on linux/amd64 workers only, and an offline build needs the archive already cached. On a Windows machine, pnpm workspace links stay inside the Linux build workspace. oyzu reads them without following them on the host, and doesn't restore cached action results that contain links.

Note: Managed Yarn is experimental. It supports Classic 1.22.22 and Berry 4.17.1 with Node 22.23.3 for single-package applications on Linux and Windows (x86-64). Isolated builds don't support Yarn yet. oyzu installs Classic Yarn from the yarn package and modern Yarn from @yarnpkg/cli-dist on the npm registry. latest follows the modern package's tag. Both yarn and yarnpkg run bin/yarn.js on the selected Node. Declare Node too: Yarn doesn't install its own runtime or use Corepack. [tools] node = "22.23.3" yarn = "4.17.1" oyzu pin oyzu install --frozen oyzu exec -- yarn --version oyzu exec -- yarnpkg --version Both commands print 4.17.1. Use yarn = "1.22.22" for Classic.

Yarn builds go through the Node plugin with a declared node/app target and a yarn.lock generated by Yarn. A full frozen build exports fresh dist output with JUnit and LCOV reports. A failed test or missing required report blocks the export. To run tests directly, install dependencies first (for Berry, oyzu exec -- yarn install --immutable). Requirements: packageManager names exactly yarn@1.22.22 or yarn@4.17.1. Berry needs a .yarnrc.yml with nodeLinker: node-modules (or the quoted "node-modules"). oyzu never converts a Plug'n'Play project. Berry needs Node >=18.12.0 as well as the project's engines.node. Workspaces, Yarn plugins, yarnPath, custom registries and Git, file or patch dependencies aren't supported. Dependency installation needs yarn.lock. Classic runs install --frozen-lockfile (plus --offline for offline builds). Berry runs install --immutable, with YARN_ENABLE_NETWORK=0 for offline builds. Offline builds need the tools and Yarn's cache already present. A failed install stops dependent actions and artifact collection.

Before running Yarn, oyzu checks the project, parent-folder and home rc files. For Berry, nodeLinker is the only setting allowed. For Classic, oyzu also checks .config/yarn/config, .config/yarn, .yarn/config, the XDG or Windows config location, /etc/yarn/config, /etc/yarnrc and npm's global npmrc under the selected Node's prefix. Directories at those paths are ignored, as Classic does. Any other setting, an unusual or oversized rc file, or an environment override of the registry or linker (including YARN_CONFIG, YARN_REGISTRY, an alternate npm user config or DESTDIR) fails with YARN_CONFIG_UNSUPPORTED before Yarn runs. Remove the setting, then retry.

Each tarball is checked against the registry's SHA-512 integrity and the original files and notices are kept. Classic includes a BSD-2-Clause LICENSE file. The Berry package has its bundled notices but no standalone LICENSE; its source license is BSD-2-Clause.

All three tools come from https://registry.npmjs.org/. oyzu reads the package's metadata and refuses a release whose tarball isn't at <registry>/<package>/-/<file>-<version>.tgz or that has no SHA-512 integrity. It downloads the tarball, checks it against that integrity and locks the SHA-256 of the checked bytes. Tool Releases up to 11 Releases from 12 Commands npm npm, one tarball for every platform Same package npm and npx, run on the selected Node pnpm on Linux x86-64 @pnpm/linux-x64 @pnpm/exe.linux-x64 pnpm pnpm on Linux ARM64 @pnpm/linux-arm64 @pnpm/exe.linux-arm64 pnpm pnpm on macOS Apple silicon @pnpm/macos-arm64 @pnpm/exe.darwin-arm64 pnpm pnpm on Windows x86-64 @pnpm/win-x64 @pnpm/exe.win32-x64 pnpm.exe npm's own bin/npm and bin/npx launchers (and their .cmd and .ps1 forms) run Node's bundled npm, so oyzu leaves them out and runs bin/npm-cli.js and bin/npx-cli.js directly. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to npm, oyzu:npm, pnpm, oyzu:pnpm or * (see proxy acquisition). Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.

pnpm is supported on Windows x86-64 for isolated builds. Other platforms for the dedicated npm and pnpm tools aren't supported yet, and neither is offline dependency installation. Nested npm calls from lifecycle scripts inside builds aren't supported yet. Linux ARM64 is recorded in the lock but not supported yet; musl isn't supported.
Node applications pnpm Yarn Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-proxy-acquisition.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. You can send Node downloads through a corporate proxy or mirror instead of the public Node site. An administrator routes Node to a named connector, and you pass a binding file that says where that connector lives and which credential to use. Note: Node only. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. Not available in managed mode.

An administrator adds a route to the protected admin-settings.json, inside its settings object: "registries.routes": { "locked": true, "value": [{"protocol": "tools", "scope": "oyzu:node", "connectorId": "corp-node"}] } You then pass a binding file to install: format = 1 [connectors.corp-node] base_url = "https://proxy.example/node/" authorization_env = "CORPORATE_NODE_AUTHORIZATION" oyzu install --connector-bindings /absolute/path/to/host-bindings.toml

Routes are administrative settings. They can't appear in project TOML. A node or oyzu:node scope wins over *. Setting both node and oyzu:node is ambiguous and fails. Only tools routes affect Node downloads. tools.allowed is checked before Node is selected or installed. Non-public tools.catalogs aren't supported and fail without falling back to the public source.

Key Meaning base_url Must end in / and serve the Node distribution layout: index.json, each version's SHASUMS256.txt and the archives. HTTPS is required, except plain HTTP to a loopback address. authorization_env Optional. The name of an environment variable holding the complete Authorization header value. redirects "server" or "client". Used only by artifact set routes; Node ignores it. A relative path to the binding file is resolved from the directory you run in (including -C). Oyzu doesn't look for this file in your project; you always pass it explicitly. Set the credential variable through your usual secret provisioning. Don't put credentials in project files, binding files or command arguments. Both version metadata and archives are fetched through the binding.

A missing binding, a missing credential variable or a denied request fails. Oyzu doesn't retry against the public source. Fix the binding or credential and run install again. A failed download doesn't write a new lock. The lock records the logical source (node-releases) and the archive digest, never the proxy address or credentials. oyzu install --frozen from cached archives needs no binding and no credentials. In offline mode, a missing cached archive fails without contacting the proxy.
Artifact sets for routing recipe-tool downloads Configuration Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-python-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install CPython itself for a Python build, so a fresh checkout builds without Python on the machine. See native host builds for which projects build this way.

Pinning is optional. For a Python project that builds natively, oyzu build picks a CPython release, writes oyzu.lock, installs it into the shared tool store and builds with it: oyzu build # no Python on PATH, no pin needed oyzu pin # optional: preview or refresh the selection oyzu exec -- python --version To choose a version yourself, set it in oyzu.toml: [tools] python = "3.12" # latest 3.12.x; ranges such as ">=3.11 <3.14" also work

Source Role .python-version (one release such as 3.12 or 3.12.4), the nearest one from the build folder up to the project root The request. It's a native pin file [tools] python in oyzu.toml The request when no .python-version applies. Otherwise it must agree with the file (3.12 agrees with 3.12.4). A disagreeing value further from the build than the file loses to it; one in the same folder or nearer fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT [project] requires-python in pyproject.toml A constraint every selection must meet None of these The newest stable release oyzu picks the newest stable CPython that meets the request and every constraint. Pre-releases, free-threaded and debug builds are never picked. A .python-version holding anything other than one CPython release (system, pypy3.10, 3.13t, several versions) fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID. Blank lines and # comments are ignored. requires-python follows PEP 440: <=3.12 means at most 3.12.0, and ~=3.10 means >=3.10, <4. !=, === and local or pre-release specifiers can't be used as a tool range and fail with the specifier named. Set [tools] python instead. When nothing matches, the error names the request, each constraint and the file it came from.

oyzu installs the install_only builds from Python Build Standalone. It reads the publisher's latest-release.json and that release's SHA256SUMS, then records the archive URL and digest in oyzu.lock. Downloads are checked against that digest; no signatures are checked. With a lock in place, oyzu doesn't need to read the release list again. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to python, oyzu:python or * (see proxy acquisition). The mirror must serve latest-release.json and the release files under the same relative paths. When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install. If the signed tool index marks a platform unsupported, installation fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE even when the publisher has an archive.

python runs the real interpreter (bin/python3.X). python3 and python3.X also work through oyzu exec and shims. When pip is included, pip, pip3 and pip3.X run python -m pip on the selected interpreter. You don't need to declare pip separately. The distribution's bundled terminfo database (share/terminfo) is left out, because it contains file names that differ only by letter case. Python's curses module uses the system's terminfo instead. After upgrading oyzu, run oyzu reshim to refresh an existing shims directory.

oyzu checks the archive digest and layout when it installs Python and trusts the installation after that. Builds, tasks, oyzu exec and shells don't re-check it, so Python can write __pycache__ files next to its standard library as usual. If an installation is damaged or edited, oyzu doesn't notice in advance; the interpreter fails when it runs. Delete that tool installation to reinstall it.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported, including native wheel builds macOS Intel Installing and running the interpreter (Python 3.11) Windows x86-64, macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Not supported yet Linux musl Not supported

The native build covers pip wheel builds from pyproject.toml. Isolated builds with pip, uv, Poetry and other managers use the same locked Python in Docker; see interpreter selection. pip downloads the project's build backend from the package index during the wheel build, so --offline builds fail unless it's already cached. With nothing declared, oyzu picks the newest stable CPython, which may be very recent. Declare requires-python or pin a version to avoid surprises.
Python preparation Native pin files Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-resolve.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Many tools are single-binary releases described only by community recipes (the public aqua registry). These two commands turn a recipe into a file that lists exactly what to download for each version and platform, and then check those downloads against what the publisher published. Use them to build or audit an artifact set or tool index records. Neither command installs anything. Note: Experimental. Command and field names, exit code 3 and limit values may change. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. oyzu tools resolve evaluates a recipe snapshot offline and writes one record per tool, version and platform (the discovery tier). It reads only the snapshot file you name and its flags, and writes to stdout. oyzu tools evidence takes that output, downloads each artifact and its checksum file from the publisher, records the SHA-256 and size, compares them with the published checksum and fills in the verified tier. With --provider, it first builds the records for one of Oyzu's own providers from the publisher's listing. Neither command reads or changes configuration, locks or the tool store, and neither needs an account. They ignore oyzu.toml, oyzu.lock, -C and --root.
documents.s: Recipe resolution and evidence (oyzu tools resolve, oyzu tools evidence)

documents.t: # 1. Download a registry snapshot yourself (resolve never fetches one) curl -sSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry/v4.573.0/registry.yaml # 2. Evaluate offline, pinned to the snapshot digest oyzu --json tools resolve --registry registry.yaml \ --registry-digest sha256:52a43b0b2817a56fe7566625809d7cca41a1178ccae2b152941221b516e70228 \ --snapshot-tag v4.573.0 \ --tool hashicorp/terraform --version v1.16.5 > terraform.discovery.json # 3. Download and check the real files (needs the network) oyzu --json tools evidence --set terraform.discovery.json > terraform.verified.json Without --json, both commands print a summary: the outcome, a table of records, unsupported platforms and errors with reasons, and next steps.

Flag Meaning --registry FILE The merged registry.yaml. A directory (the per-package tree form) is rejected with SNAPSHOT_INVALID. --registry-digest sha256:HEX Reject the snapshot unless its SHA-256 matches (SNAPSHOT_DIGEST_MISMATCH). --snapshot-tag, --snapshot-commit Labels recorded in the output. Not checked. --tool NAME (repeatable), --tools-file FILE Registry package names such as hashicorp/terraform. The file has one name per line; # starts a comment. --version V (repeatable) Exact upstream version as the recipe sees it, including any prefix (v1.16.5). Required. --platform OS/ARCH/ABI (repeatable) Default: linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native, windows/amd64/msvc, whatever the host. OS: linux, darwin, windows. Architecture: amd64, arm64. Other ABIs (for example musl) give an error record, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED. --limit NAME=VALUE (repeatable) Lower a limit: recipe_nodes, recipe_bytes, recipe_depth, recipe_overrides, string_bytes, expression_steps, url_bytes, record_urls, regex_bytes, snapshot_bytes, output_bytes. Limits can't be raised. Every tool and version is evaluated for every platform. The output is sorted by tool ID, version and platform, so flag order doesn't matter. Tool IDs are aqua:<package> (for example aqua:cli/cli), the same spelling mise uses.

Packages of type github_release and http. Oyzu has its own evaluator for the registry's data format, which supports: Version selection: version_constraint, the first matching version_overrides entry, version_prefix and version_filter. The record's version.branch is top-level, override[N], or null when no branch applied. Expressions: Version, SemVer, string and list literals, semver("..."), ==, !=, in, matches, startsWith, endsWith, contains, not/!, and/&&, or/||. semver() is false for a non-semver version. Pre-release versions only satisfy constraints that name a pre-release. Templates: {{.Version}}-style fields, pipes, parentheses, if/else/end, and the functions trimV trimPrefix trimSuffix replace title semver regexFind index splitList eq ne. supported_envs (with rosetta2 and windows_arm_emulation), replacements, platform overrides (first match), no_asset, error_message, complete_windows_ext, files, checksum, cosign, minisign, slsa_provenance, github_artifact_attestations. Anything else (a loop, an unknown function, recipe vars) is reported as RECIPE_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED for that record, never guessed.

One JSON document (format: 1, kind: "artifact-sets") matching artifact-set.schema.json. It holds the engine, the snapshot (its digest plus your labels), the limits used and the records. Each record has a status: Status Meaning Exit resolved URLs (artifact, checksum, signatures, ...), archive facts and declared evidence. 0 unsupported A normal result: PLATFORM_EXCLUDED, NO_ASSET, RECIPE_MESSAGE, SOURCE_KIND (build-from-source packages), VERSION_NOT_COVERED, PRIVATE_PACKAGE. 0 error Couldn't decide: LIMIT_EXCEEDED, RECIPE_INVALID, RECIPE_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED, RENDER_FAILED, URL_NOT_HTTPS, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED. 3 Each record carries digests.declared (the record without its verification results) and digests.full (everything except digests), computed over canonical JSON (RFC 8785). The output contains no time, host, user or path, so the same inputs always produce identical output. GitHub release downloads are stored as the recipe renders them (github.com/...). Redirect targets are never stored.

Exit Meaning 0 Complete; every record is resolved or unsupported. 1 Bad input, no records: SNAPSHOT_INVALID, SNAPSHOT_DIGEST_MISMATCH (and for evidence: SET_INVALID, SET_SCHEMA_INVALID, SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH). With --json, the standard error object (error, code, nextStep, exitCode) is on stdout. 2 Usage problem, no records: FLAGS_CONFLICT, REQUEST_EMPTY. 3 Complete, but at least one record is error (resolve) or a resolved record stayed at the discovery tier (evidence). 5 Not found, no records: TOOL_NOT_IN_SNAPSHOT. A process killed by the system (memory, time limit) writes nothing. Run one tool per process if you need to contain that.

Flag Meaning --set FILE or - A tools resolve document (or standard input). Every record's digests are checked first; a mismatch is SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH and nothing is downloaded. --allow-host HOST (repeatable) Allow a host beyond those in the set's own URLs. --verify METHOD (repeatable) Run only these methods; others are reported not-run. --provider NAME Build the records for one of Oyzu's providers from its publisher instead of reading a set, then verify them the same way. Can't be combined with --set. --version V (repeatable, with --provider) Exact provider release, such as 21.0.8. Required with --provider. --platform OS/ARCH/ABI (repeatable, with --provider) Default: linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native, darwin/amd64/native, windows/amd64/msvc. Platforms the provider doesn't install get an unsupported record.

For each resolved record, evidence downloads the artifact (hashed as it streams, never stored, up to 2 GiB) and the checksum file (up to 4 MiB, once per URL), and records verified.artifact (digest, size, publisher_digest, agree). Up to five redirects are followed. Each hop must be an allowed host, or github.com to release-assets.githubusercontent.com. The hosts seen are listed in verified.observed_redirect_hosts. HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE are honored (see acquisition transport). Each download is retried up to twice on network errors and HTTP 408, 429 and 5xx. Credentials are never sent to publisher hosts. GITHUB_TOKEN, if set, goes to api.github.com only. Each evidence entry gets an outcome in verified.results[].outcome: Outcome Meaning verified For checksum: the checksum file lists the artifact's name with a matching sha256 or sha512. For attestations and provenance: see below. failed The checksum file lacks the name, has conflicting or malformed values, couldn't be fetched, or doesn't match; or no attestation or provenance verifies. The detail says which. verifier-unavailable Oyzu has no verifier for the method (cosign, minisign, openpgp), or the algorithm (md5, sha1) or format (regexp) isn't supported. Never counted as verified. not-run Excluded by --verify. A record becomes tier: verified only when at least one entry verified and none failed. verified.lock then holds the strongest result: attestation when a GitHub attestation or SLSA provenance verified, otherwise digest-only. Otherwise the record stays discovery with verified.status: failed, and the command exits 3. What a result means: A checksum-verified record means these bytes match what the publisher's checksum file listed when fetched. It doesn't prove the checksum file is authentic, that a signature holds, or that you're allowed to use the tool. An attestation-verified record also means a GitHub Actions workflow in the release's repository attested these exact bytes, or, for SLSA provenance, that a slsa-github-generator release built them from that repository. It says nothing about whether the workflow's source is trustworthy.

For github-attestation evidence (aqua's github_artifact_attestations), Oyzu asks GitHub for the attestations of the artifact's digest (GET https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/attestations/sha256:<digest>?predicate_type=https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1). The repository comes from the artifact's GitHub release URL; other URLs fail. Set GITHUB_TOKEN to raise GitHub's anonymous limit of 60 requests an hour. Each Sigstore bundle is verified offline against Sigstore's public-good trusted root built into Oyzu. A bundle verifies when: its Rekor entry timestamp is signed by a trusted Rekor key, and its certificate chains to a Fulcio CA valid at that time; the certificate's issuer is GitHub Actions, its source repository is https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>, and, if the recipe names a signer_workflow, the certificate names that workflow (like gh attestation verify --repo --signer-workflow); the signature verifies and the signed statement names the artifact's SHA-256 with an SLSA v1 provenance predicate. The first bundle that verifies wins; identity shows its signing workflow and verifier is sigstore-public-good. Not checked: certificate transparency timestamps, inclusion proofs, RFC 3161 timestamps (so bundles from GitHub's private Sigstore instance, used for private repositories, don't verify), the runner environment and the provenance contents.

For slsa-provenance evidence (aqua's slsa_provenance, typically {{.Asset}}.intoto.jsonl), Oyzu downloads the provenance file published by slsa-github-generator (up to 4 MiB, same host rules as checksum files). As slsa-verifier does, it finds the matching log entries in Rekor's public API by the artifact's digest (rekor.sigstore.dev, at most 16 entries, no credentials sent). Everything Rekor returns is verified offline against the built-in trusted root: the file is an in-toto statement with an SLSA v0.2 or v1 provenance predicate naming the artifact's file name and SHA-256; a Rekor entry with a trusted signed timestamp records this envelope; the certificate chains to a Fulcio CA and was valid at that time; the issuer is GitHub Actions, the certificate names a slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator workflow at a v* release tag, and the source repository is the recipe's source_uri (or the release's repository); with source_tag, the source ref must be refs/tags/<source_tag>; the signature verifies. identity shows the builder workflow. Not checked: certificate transparency timestamps, inclusion proofs and the provenance contents (builder ID, build type, materials). Any generator workflow at a v* tag is accepted, and for delegated (BYOB) builds the delegated builder isn't checked.

For Java (Eclipse Temurin), Oyzu reads the publisher's GA release list for each feature release once (api.adoptium.net, the newest 20 releases) and writes one record per version and platform: tool.id is core:java (the index tool oyzu:java lists it as its origin). The version is the release (21.0.8). A resolved record names the archive and its .sha256.txt file on github.com/adoptium/temurin<feature>-binaries, the same archive the Java provider installs. release carries the publisher's release time when known. A platform the provider doesn't install is unsupported (PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED); a release with no build for the platform is unsupported (NO_PLATFORM_ARTIFACT); a release not in the list is an error (VERSION_NOT_FOUND); an unreadable list gives error records (SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE). oyzu --json tools evidence --provider java --version 21.0.8 --version 17.0.16 > java.verified.json Only Temurin JDK builds are recorded, and only the newest 20 GA releases of a feature; an older release is VERSION_NOT_FOUND.

These follow the same rules (tool.id is core:<name>, the same status codes, and each record names the archive the provider installs): Node reads nodejs.org/dist/index.json for the release and its date, then the release's SHASUMS256.txt. Go reads go.dev/dl/?mode=json&include=all. The release must be stable and list the platform's archive. The checksum is the archive's .sha256 file on dl.google.com. Python reads python-build-standalone's latest-release pointer, then that release's SHA256SUMS. Only versions that release ships as install_only builds for all four install platforms are recorded; any other is VERSION_NOT_FOUND. The archive URL includes the release tag, so a lock doesn't depend on the pointer.

--provider also accepts maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, zig, npm, pnpm, yarn and rust (optionally prefixed with oyzu: or core:). Versions must be exact stable three-part releases. Without --platform, all five index platforms are recorded. Intel macOS records are produced for Rust, Node, Go, npm, pnpm, Yarn and Zig when the publisher supports that release; other providers record it as unsupported. Provider Source and check Maven Apache archive listing, binary tarball and SHA-512 file. Gradle services.gradle.org release list's SHA-256 and binary ZIP. Zig ziglang.org stable index's tar.xz URL and SHA-256. Helm get.helm.sh archive and its SHA-256 file. kubectl dl.k8s.io binary and its SHA-256 file. k3d GitHub release binary and its checksums.txt entry. Liquibase The digest GitHub's release API reports for the asset (no publisher checksum file). Tailscale pkgs.tailscale.com stable Linux tarball and its SHA-256 file. npm, pnpm, Yarn npm registry tarball metadata and SHA-512, converted to SHA-256 after the archive is verified. Rust static.rust-lang.org channel manifest and its SHA-256 file, every available component URL and digest, plus a checksum-verified rustup bootstrap. Registry metadata is limited to 64 MiB; checksum files to 4 MiB. Liquibase 5.x records carry params.license = "FSL-1.1-ALv2", a source-available license. This records the license; it isn't a legal approval. For Rust, the artifact is dist/channel-rust-<version>.toml. Its checksum entry's params.rust_distribution lists each component and target with its URL and digest, plus the rustup bootstrap. evidence verifies the manifest checksum, checks the component list against the manifest and verifies the bootstrap. Component tarballs are checked when installed, not downloaded here. An unreachable publisher produces error or discovery records, never a verified result. oyzu --json tools evidence --provider kubectl --version 1.34.1 oyzu --json tools evidence --provider helm --version 3.22.0 oyzu --json tools evidence --provider rust --version 1.95.0

tools resolve makes no network calls, starts no processes and writes no files. It doesn't add an operating-system sandbox; run it in one (for example an empty network namespace) if you need that. Recipes are untrusted data. Recipe text in human output has control characters escaped. The evaluator contains no registry data or code from another project. Credentials are never sent to publisher hosts.

Only merged-file snapshots are supported, not the per-package tree form. Checked: checksums, GitHub artifact attestations and SLSA provenance. Not checked: cosign, minisign and OpenPGP. Rekor's search is best effort; an artifact whose entries it doesn't list fails. evidence runs downloads one at a time, has no stall timeout, and doesn't refuse private or loopback addresses after DNS resolution. Its allowed hosts come from the set's own URLs. On Windows, .exe is only added for raw assets, not for files entries. Edge cases of pre-release and build-metadata versions in semver() may differ from the registry's own engine. Duplicate YAML keys fail the whole snapshot. version.branch is null when no branch was selected (PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED, a limit hit on the whole entry, or VERSION_NOT_COVERED). Supported on Linux x86-64 only.
Installing from resolved artifact sets Tool index Registry packages

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-rust-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install the Rust toolchain for your project (rustc, Cargo, rustdoc, rustfmt, Clippy and the LLVM coverage tools) and the Cargo helpers the Rust builder uses, so you don't need rustup or Rust installed on the machine. The exact release is recorded in oyzu.lock.

Pinning is optional. With nothing declared, oyzu pin or your first oyzu build picks the newest stable Rust and records it in oyzu.lock. To choose a version, set it in oyzu.toml or in rust-toolchain.toml: [tools] rust = "1.95.0" oyzu install rust oyzu which cargo oyzu exec -- rustc --version oyzu exec -- cargo build oyzu install rust --frozen --offline oyzu install rust checks that rust is configured, then installs the project's whole tool selection into one lock. Bare oyzu install does the same for every configured tool.

Source Role rust-toolchain.toml or rust-toolchain, the nearest one from the build folder up to the project root The request. It's a native pin file; see Rust toolchain files [tools] rust (or [tools]."oyzu:rust") The request when no toolchain file applies. Otherwise it must agree with the file rust-version in Cargo.toml A minimum every selection must meet None of these stable: the newest stable release Accepted requests are an exact stable version (1.95.0) or stable. oyzu resolves stable to one exact release and keeps it in the lock; offline commands and oyzu pin --refresh don't move it. oyzu install rust and oyzu update rust need an exact version in configuration. Beta, nightly, partial versions such as 1.95, dated channels and ranges aren't supported. A fresh stable request needs the network. Offline, it works only when the lock already has the selection.

When it installs Rust, oyzu: Downloads the official channel manifest for the exact release and its published SHA-256, and checks that every needed component has a URL and digest. Downloads each component and a fixed rustup installer, checking each against its digest. Runs rustup against a private local copy of those files, with its own private Cargo and rustup homes, a minimal profile, the listed components and targets, and self-update turned off. Nothing outside those files is downloaded. Stores the finished toolchain as an archive in oyzu's tool store, with its license files. Reinstalling from the lock (--frozen) restores that archive and doesn't run rustup. If both the installation and the archive are gone, run an online update; oyzu won't silently build a different archive for an existing digest. The default profile also installs the standard libraries for the targets the Rust builder supports. Having a target's standard library doesn't mean you have a linker for it.

The toolchain's bin directory goes first on PATH. RUSTC and RUSTDOC point at the installed binaries. RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN points at the installed toolchain, so Cargo subcommands from your own Cargo home can't pick a different global Clippy or rustfmt. Cargo still downloads crates and Git dependencies itself, and your Cargo cache and configuration are separate from the installed toolchain.
documents.s: What oyzu sets when Rust runs

documents.t: oyzu doesn't install system linkers or SDKs: Platform You need Windows (MSVC) Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload and a Windows SDK. The IDE isn't needed macOS Apple Command Line Tools, which provide the SDK, linker and Git (oyzu uses Git to infer versions). Check with xcode-select -p, xcrun --show-sdk-path and git --version; install with xcode-select --install. Some builders may need full Xcode GNU or LLVM targets LLVM or MinGW installed yourself, if you select those toolchains CMake and other build tools your crates need are also up to you.

On Windows x86-64, for a Rust-only project: oyzu pin oyzu install oyzu run install oyzu run install runs the Rust builder's executable installation task; it doesn't install tools. The compiler platform is windows/amd64/msvc. If an installation was made by an older oyzu or for a different pin, run oyzu install --update rust. oyzu run uses tools from the default user-level tool store. It puts them on PATH (and sets RUSTC/RUSTDOC) for the whole task and its hooks. If a needed tool isn't installed, the task fails before any hook runs and tells you to run oyzu install. Listing tasks and help don't need tools. To use a custom store, use oyzu exec --store; oyzu run doesn't accept one.
documents.s: Pinned native Rust and task execution

documents.t: The Rust builder needs cargo-nextest 0.9.146 for tests and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 for coverage. You don't have to list them: after oyzu pin, oyzu install installs everything the enabled build stages need; oyzu build --full installs and runs the quality stages; plain oyzu build installs only what compiling needs, unless configuration turns on more checks; oyzu run test uses the pinned helpers but needs them installed first. You can also set them in [tools] as cargo:cargo-nextest and cargo:cargo-llvm-cov (short names work too). Other versions fail with a clear error. oyzu never runs cargo install or builds helpers from source. oyzu tools current, oyzu which, oyzu exec and activated shells use the selection of the nearest build target. Child targets don't change a parent shell's tools. If pins are missing, run oyzu pin; oyzu build never re-pins on its own. If installations are missing, run an online install; --offline reuses installed tools and cached archives only. Installations live in the shared user store and are reused across projects; the project lock stays portable.

When toolCatalog.url is set (see organization tool catalog), pin, install and build only use an approved release from the signed index: The downloaded channel manifest must match the index's SHA-256, and its full component list must match the indexed one. Every component selected by rust-toolchain.toml and the rustup installer must match an indexed URL and digest. There's no fallback to the public site. Locked selections are checked against the current catalog before install or reuse. Error Cause TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG The release isn't approved TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX The tool isn't indexed, or its record has no component list TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH The indexed and locked inputs differ A downloaded file with the wrong digest fails before rustup starts. cargo: helpers are refused under a catalog. Corporate mirror routes for Rust aren't supported. To see what an index entry would contain, run oyzu tools evidence --provider rust --version 1.95.0 (see tools evidence).

All tool selections live in one oyzu.lock (see lock inspection). oyzu pin updates what's selected; oyzu install records what's installed. Neither edits oyzu.toml or native files. Command What it does oyzu pin Resolves every tool the project needs, on every platform it builds for, and writes oyzu.lock. Doesn't install anything oyzu pin --dry-run Shows the result without writing. With --json, the proposed lock is in proposed_files. Exits 0 when complete, 2 when something couldn't be resolved oyzu pin --refresh Re-fetches installation details for the versions already selected, without upgrading. Needs the network oyzu pin --refresh --dry-run Previews the refresh A failed or incomplete pin doesn't replace the lock. If two sources disagree on a version, the error names both files and versions and confirms nothing changed. oyzu writes the lock and related files through a recovery journal (.oyzu-pin-journal.json). If a pin is interrupted, the next pin finishes it. Commands that read tools refuse to run while the journal is unfinished. If a file was changed by something else in the meantime, pin keeps the journal and fails with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT.

Isolated builds use the locked compiler too. With no oyzu.lock, the first build resolves and writes one before it starts. Linux ARM64 builds use the arm64 execution image, oyzu-execution/base:1-linux-arm64 until the image is published. oyzu checks its architecture but doesn't install emulators. oyzu install never sets up a Linux worker just because build.yaml declares Rust targets. The installer container gets 6 GiB of scratch space, 8 GiB of memory and two CPUs, with no network and a read-only root. Make sure Docker allows that much.

oyzu build --offline needs an existing lock and a cached compiler. It doesn't resolve versions or change the lock, and it fails without running an installer if the compiler is missing. Offline builds work only for projects whose Cargo.lock has no registry or Git dependencies (local workspace packages are fine). Otherwise the build fails before fetching, because cached crate replay isn't available yet.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 (MSVC) Supported macOS Intel Supported with an existing lock; automatic default pinning isn't available yet Windows ARM64 (MSVC) oyzu install installs Rust from a lock that covers windows/arm64/msvc; building on this platform isn't verified yet macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Not supported yet Helper installation (cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov) is supported on Windows x86-64; on other platforms it isn't supported yet.
Rust toolchain files Lock inspection Tool commands Organization tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-shell-environment.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. This page covers the ways to put a project's locked tools on PATH outside oyzu run and oyzu build: a one-time oyzu env --shell, an activated shell that switches tools as you change directory, a shell profile block, and a shims folder for IDEs and scheduled jobs. It also lists the settings that control when tools install themselves on first use. For the overall model (provenance, PATH views, nested shells), see shell activation. Note: Activation and env --shell are supported in Bash and Zsh on Linux and macOS, and in PowerShell 7 on Windows. Writing a shell profile with oyzu shell install is supported for Bash and Zsh on Linux; macOS and PowerShell profiles are not supported yet.

oyzu env shows the selected tools' executables and the effective environment variables. oyzu env --json returns the same as JSON. Credential-like fields and values that look sensitive are redacted. Tools that aren't installed are left out; env never installs anything. Invalid locks, damaged install records and policy denials still fail. The environment is the same one oyzu exec uses: the literal values from [env] in your configuration, plus the selected tools' folders added to the front of your PATH. To apply the environment to your current shell once, pick a shell: # Bash (use --shell zsh for Zsh) eval "$(oyzu env --shell bash)" node --version oyzu env --shell pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression node --version With --json, the code is returned in a script field next to the shell name. No network access and no installs. Values stay literal: quotes, dollar signs and shell metacharacters are escaped, never interpreted. Values must be valid UTF-8. If you installed into a shared store, pass the same --store here. This changes the current shell once. It doesn't add a prompt hook, switch on cd or restore old values. Use activation for that.

Activation, env --shell, prompt hooks, shims and oyzu exec only apply a project's [env] and PATH additions after you trust the project folder, because those values end up executed by your shell. An untrusted project still gets its selected tools, without those additions and without a prompt. oyzu env marks such entries skipped until trusted. oyzu run, oyzu build and build planning always apply those settings.

oyzu exec -- COMMAND runs a command with the project's environment. Put Oyzu flags before --. By default the command's output passes straight through; with --json, Oyzu captures it in stdout and stderr fields next to exitCode.

Activate a Bash or Zsh session from a project with installed tools: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # use zsh for Zsh node --version cd ../another-installed-project node --version # the other project's Node oyzu deactivate In PowerShell: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. --store /absolute/store uses a shared store. Without it, the default user store is used. --root, --profile and --toolset given to activate stay in effect for the session. On every prompt, Oyzu checks whether the directory, relevant environment variables or configuration and lock files changed. If nothing changed, it does nothing. If something changed, it applies the new project's locked tools and [env] values. The prompt hook never uses the network, installs tools or runs project tasks. cd alone never installs anything or writes a lock. Running a missing command may install it, depending on the invocation controls. In PowerShell, missing-command installs only trigger for a command you typed in the interactive session, not for lookups inside scripts. The prompt check looks at file metadata only. Installed tools aren't re-checked on each prompt: they were verified when installed and are trusted afterward. oyzu env can take longer than oyzu config show because it fully reads the selection.

Invalid configuration or a denied tool clears the previous project's changes, sets OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=unavailable and prints a message once. Missing installations don't stop a valid environment from applying. OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=ready means the environment was composed, not that every tool is installed. Check with oyzu tools current. A trusted project's PATH additions come before the selected tool folders.
documents.s: When the selection fails or is incomplete

documents.t: Oyzu saves what it changed in a private per-user shell-sessions folder so oyzu deactivate can undo it. The shell holds only a random token. On Unix the folder is private (0700) and linked directories are refused. On Windows it lives under your LocalAppData and reparse points are refused. oyzu deactivate restores a variable only if it still has the value Oyzu set, so your own edits survive. An unchanged PATH is restored exactly. Entries Oyzu added are removed even if you added or reordered others; ambiguous duplicates are kept with a message. oyzu --json deactivate only previews; the session stays active. If the record is missing or unreadable, you get a warning and the hooks are removed, but old values can't be recovered. Open a new terminal or activate again. Records older than 30 days are cleaned up on activation, but only when their shell is gone. Activation adds the Oyzu executable's folder to PATH if it isn't there. That entry stays after deactivation. The oyzu shell function that activation defines evaluates the output of oyzu deactivate for you. Running the binary by full path with deactivate only prints the code. Global flags such as oyzu -q deactivate work. --log-level and -q can't be combined; a rejected command leaves the session active.

oyzu shell install with no shell is the machine-level setup that the install scripts run. It does not install tools or use the network. It edits, once: the activation block of each supported shell found: bash (login shell, or ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile exists, including Git Bash on Windows), zsh (login shell, or $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc or ~/.zshrc exists) and PowerShell 7 (when pwsh is on PATH or in %ProgramFiles%\PowerShell\7); the persistent PATH, with the fixed shims folder (STORE/shims/bin, refreshed first as oyzu reshim does) ahead of the folder holding the running oyzu. On Windows that is the user Path value in HKCU\Environment: entries such as %USERPROFILE%\bin keep their raw spelling, the value kind is kept (REG_EXPAND_SZ for a new value), entries already present are not duplicated (compared after expanding variables, ignoring case and a trailing separator) and WM_SETTINGCHANGE is broadcast so programs started afterwards, such as IDEs, see it. On Linux and macOS it is a marked PATH block in the login profile: the first existing of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile (~/.profile when none exists), and $ZDOTDIR/.zprofile or ~/.zprofile when zsh is set up. oyzu shell remove with no shell reverses it: it removes intact blocks from those files and the two folders from the user Path, and leaves other content. Only entries spelled exactly as install wrote them (the running oyzu and its store folders) are removed, so entries added by an oyzu installed in another location, and your own %USERPROFILE%\bin-style spelling of a folder, stay. A block that was edited is refused as below. Reports list each file or the registry value under entries with changed. Windows PowerShell 5.1 and fish are not configured. Programs already running keep the PATH they started with. Checked by unit tests for planning, PATH list editing and (on Linux) install, repeat and remove over a temporary home, a unit test of the registry code on a scratch key, and the compiled CLI on Windows. macOS and fish are not checked.
documents.s: Set up all shells and PATH

documents.t: oyzu activate never edits files. To activate in every new shell, add a block to your startup file: oyzu shell install bash oyzu shell remove bash --rc-file ~/.bashrc oyzu shell install pwsh --rc-file $PROFILE oyzu shell remove pwsh --rc-file $PROFILE Default startup files: Shell Default bash ~/.bashrc zsh $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc, or ~/.zshrc pwsh PowerShell 7's current-user console profile: Documents/PowerShell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 on Windows, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/powershell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 on Unix (falling back to ~/.config/powershell/...) --rc-file PATH picks another file. A relative path resolves against the current directory (or -C). For another PowerShell host or version, pass --rc-file $PROFILE. The global --profile option selects an Oyzu configuration profile, not a shell file. Oyzu creates missing folders and files, appends one marked block and leaves the rest of the file and its permissions unchanged. The block calls the oyzu executable by its full path. If you move or upgrade it, run oyzu shell install again to update the block. Running it again with the same executable changes nothing. The block uses the default store and configuration. It doesn't include a project, profile, credentials or store path. For a custom store, add your own oyzu activate <shell> --store PATH line outside the block. Install the project's tools before opening a new shell. Editing the profile itself uses no network. --json reports changed, shell, profile_path, installed, shims, activation, check and nextStep. Install and remove refuse a block that is modified, incomplete, duplicated or written by a different oyzu. Fix or restore the block by hand first. A symlinked profile needs the real target path, and a non-UTF-8 profile must be converted first. oyzu shell remove deletes only the intact block and leaves the rest of the file byte for byte. A file Oyzu created stays as an empty file. Removing the block affects new shells; run oyzu deactivate to end the current session.
documents.s: Install activation in a shell profile

documents.t: oyzu install and oyzu activate create a launcher (shim) for every command of every installed tool, including companions such as npm, npx, kubectl and helm. Each shim works out the project, configuration and lock from the directory it runs in. On Unix, shims are symbolic links to oyzu. On Windows, oyzu-shim.exe must sit next to oyzu.exe. Install or copy both. Shims for activated shells live under STORE/shims/native/. Run oyzu install, oyzu activate or oyzu reshim to refresh them; oyzu install also refreshes shims in already activated shells, so newly installed commands appear there. A shim keeps the command's arguments, exit status and signals unchanged. A tool can call another shim (for example, a Node script starting another Node process); each call selects its tool again. Prompt hooks don't create shims. Oyzu doesn't delete old shim folders automatically, since running shells may still use them.

IDEs, CI jobs and scheduled tasks never run a prompt hook. For them, put the store's shims folder on PATH. It holds one launcher for each installed command, and each launcher picks the right tool for the project it runs in: oyzu reshim # refresh launchers and print the folder eval "$(oyzu activate bash --shims)" # put it first on PATH in this shell oyzu shell install bash --shims --rc-file ~/.bash_profile oyzu shell install zsh --shims --rc-file ~/.zprofile On Windows, add it to your user PATH: $shims = (oyzu reshim --json | ConvertFrom-Json).directory [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', "$shims;" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path', 'User'), 'User') The folder is STORE/shims/bin. The PATH line removes any existing copy of the folder and puts it first, so an unmanaged copy of a tool earlier on PATH can't win. A store path containing the PATH separator (:, or ; on Windows) fails with SHIMS_PATH_INVALID. On Windows, Bash and Zsh lines use Git Bash or MSYS/Cygwin path spelling (/c/Users/...). Generate Cygwin profiles from inside Cygwin. activate --shims only prints the PATH line. Run oyzu reshim once first, and again after moving or upgrading oyzu. shell install --shims runs that refresh for you. If a shim has no selected tool, it falls back to the next matching command on PATH, unless you turn that off (see invocation controls). oyzu reshim refreshes the shims folder and the activation shims owned by the running oyzu, using local install records only. It downloads nothing and edits no startup file. --json reports the folder as directory and the command names as commands. On Windows, run it after updating both executables.

These settings control when a tool installs itself the first time you use it. They go in the usual configuration files (including profiles), and administrators can constrain them. The values shown are the defaults: [settings] auto_install = true offline = false exec_auto_install = true not_found_auto_install = true not_found_auto_install_registry = false not_found_system_fallback = true auto_install_disable_tools = [] windows_executable_extensions = ["exe", "bat", "cmd", "com", "ps1", "vbs"] windows_shim_mode = "exe" [settings.task] run_auto_install = true Setting Meaning auto_install Master switch. false turns off the exec, missing-command and task installs below. offline Use only cached downloads; never fetch. Same as oyzu exec --offline. exec_auto_install oyzu exec installs configured tools that are missing. not_found_auto_install A shim, or a command your shell couldn't find, installs its configured tool. not_found_auto_install_registry A command the shell couldn't find, and that no configuration declares, is looked up in Oyzu's tool list, installed and added to your global configuration as latest. not_found_system_fallback A shim with no selected tool runs the next matching command on PATH. auto_install_disable_tools Tools (short or full IDs) that never install themselves. oyzu install still works for them. windows_executable_extensions Extensions treated as executable on Windows. windows_shim_mode How shims are created on Windows (below). task.run_auto_install oyzu run installs missing tools for the task. How they behave: A compatible lock entry always wins. Running a command never upgrades a locked version, and a missing locked tool isn't replaced by another installed version. In a project with no compatible lock entry, shells, exec, tasks, env and which can reuse a matching version you already installed. This writes no lock. A command may create a missing lock when it installs a configured tool. With not_found_auto_install_registry, a name that matches more than one tool is skipped. A project declaration still overrides the global entry. Progress goes to stderr, so the command's stdout is unchanged. To make unresolved shims fail instead of running a system command, set both not_found_system_fallback and not_found_auto_install to false. Fallback skips Oyzu shim folders and keeps PATH order. A failed install, invalid lock, denied tool or unavailable managed integration is an error. It never silently falls back to a system command. Prompt hooks, env, which and oyzu build --plan never install tools. which shows the selected tool; a shim on PATH doesn't mean the tool is installed. oyzu build ignores these settings. It requires the full locked selection, and never accepts a system command in place of a locked tool or a denied tool.

For each target, oyzu build prepares the tools its builder needs for the selected steps, plus the tools pinned in the oyzu.toml files from the project root down to that target's folder. A root pin reaches every target; a pin in docs-site/ reaches only targets in that folder. So oyzu build cli doesn't download a tool only docs uses. oyzu exec, shells and oyzu install still provide every pinned tool. Host prerequisites are checked, never installed.

Node provides node, npm and npx. A separately configured npm takes over npm and npx. On Windows, PATH lookup follows PATHEXT order. PowerShell and VBScript files run with their own interpreters. Bare bash and sh resolve to Git for Windows; WindowsApps aliases are skipped. Unix commands get interrupts forwarded and keep terminal control. --json reports the numeric exit status.

windows_shim_mode Behavior exe A native launcher (oyzu-shim.exe) per command. Default. hardlink Hard links to oyzu. Needs a filesystem that supports them, on the same volume. symlink Symbolic links to oyzu. Needs symlink permission (usually Developer Mode). file CMD and Git Bash forwarder scripts. CMD's own rules apply: PowerShell's default argument passing can change empty arguments and embedded quotes, and delayed expansion changes ^ and !. After changing the mode, run oyzu reshim (with the same --store). If the mode isn't available (missing permission or unsupported filesystem), Oyzu reports it instead of picking another mode. Other platforms always use symbolic links.
Shell activation Tool commands Configuration

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-store-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The tool store is the folder where Oyzu keeps downloaded archives and installed tools. Every project, shell and build on your machine shares it, so a tool version is downloaded and installed once. This page explains what's in the store, what Oyzu checks when it installs a tool, how concurrent installs and running tools are kept safe, and how to inspect an installed tool's files. Note: Experimental. The store layout may change.

Platform Default Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/oyzu/tools, or ~/.local/share/oyzu/tools macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/tools Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\tools Most tool commands accept --store DIR to use another store. A relative path is resolved from the current directory. Pass the same --store to install, inspect and activate. oyzu tools list --json shows the store in use. Archive providers, registry packages and Rust all use the same store.

Folder Contents installs/<key>/ One installed tool: payload/ (its files) and receipt.json (what was installed, from where, and its commands). blobs/sha256/<digest> Downloaded archives, named by their SHA-256. staging/ Installs and downloads in progress. quarantine/ Cached archives that failed their digest check, kept for you to inspect. locks/ Lock files that coordinate concurrent installs and running tools. Never delete these while Oyzu is running. leases/ Records of which installations are in use. catalogs/, state/ Cached tool index, catalogs and trust state. shims/ Command launchers (see using tools in your shell).

Oyzu checks a tool thoroughly when it installs it, and trusts it afterward: Every download must match the SHA-256 from the lock, index or publisher before it is used. A new installation's files are checked against its receipt before it is committed. Later commands, shells and builds check that the installation exists and that its receipt matches the lock. They don't re-hash the files. A tool that is damaged or edited after install simply fails when it runs.
