An organization catalog or the tool index can still refuse an unapproved or withdrawn version when you install or reuse it.

Archives are downloaded to a temporary file, checked and then moved into blobs/. Memory use doesn't grow with archive size. A download is limited to 8 GiB and must be exactly the expected size. A short, long or mismatched download stores nothing. A cached archive is checked again whenever it is used. If it no longer matches, it is moved to quarantine/ and downloaded again (online) or reported as missing with its path (offline). If a lock records a digest but no size, Oyzu uses the cached archive's size. Offline installs need the archive already in the cache. The error names the missing digest; retry online.

Installs unpack tar, tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.zst, ZIP and single-file (raw) downloads, within these limits: Limit Value Entries 200,000 Total size 8 GiB Single file 1 GiB Path depth 64 Expansion ratio 200:1 (some reviewed tools allow up to 1024:1) Paths that escape the folder, absolute paths, Windows device names, names that differ only by case, and conflicting entries are refused. Tar archives can contain files, directories and relative symbolic links. Hard links and sparse files aren't supported. ZIP archives can contain stored or deflated files, directories and Unix relative symbolic links. Encrypted, multi-volume and ZIP64 archives aren't supported. Symbolic links are created after all files are written, and must stay inside the tool's folder. This keeps macOS framework layouts intact. Symbolic links inside archives aren't supported on Windows. Ownership, set-ID bits and the archive's directory permissions aren't applied. Files are private to you, and Unix executable bits are kept.

Before an installation is committed, Oyzu prepares it in staging/ and checks it: The archive layout (how it's unpacked, which prefix is stripped, which files are commands) must match the layout recorded in the lock. Every command file must exist. On Unix, declared executables are set to mode 0700. Commands and environment values may only refer to files in the tool itself or its direct dependencies. The receipt is written last, with the digests of the final files. Nothing in the tool is run during this step, and oyzu.lock isn't changed. If a step fails, the staging folder is discarded and no installation is created.
documents.s: Checking an installation before it is committed

documents.t: Each installation is moved into installs/ in one atomic step, and never replaces an existing one. When a tool has dependencies, each one is committed separately. If a later one fails, earlier ones stay as valid, unreferenced installations. The lock is never edited. An existing valid installation is reused. A damaged one fails; Oyzu doesn't replace it or fall back to another download. Windows supports long store paths, including UNC paths.

Installs of the same tool or archive wait for each other, for up to 30 seconds. While a command, shell or build uses a tool, it holds a shared lock on the installation, so it can't be removed underneath it. Each such use writes a small record in leases/ with its process ID, start time and installation keys. It contains no paths, environment values or credentials. The record is removed when the command ends. A crash can leave a record or a .pending file behind. Oyzu cleans these up when it next starts an install, but only once their locks show nobody is using them. It never deletes an installation during cleanup. Records it can't verify are left for manual review.
documents.s: Concurrent installs and tools in use

documents.t: Installs work in their own folder under staging/. If an install is interrupted, the next install removes abandoned staging folders, but only when no other install is running. Older leftover staging files (.tmp* and top-level blob-*) and quarantined archives are kept for you to inspect and delete.

oyzu tools inspect-tree lists the files of an installed tool, with their digests, so you can compare or audit an installation. It's a diagnostic command; Oyzu never runs it automatically. oyzu tools list --details # find installation paths oyzu tools inspect-tree <store>/installs/<id>/payload Payload inspection Bytes: 3 Digest: sha256:79a94bbfa8c76fb62b27ce178116533fb1e8239516c2015be5e8e8123793b851 Entries: Digest Executable Path Size Target Type not specified 73 bin not specified not specified directory sha256:98ea6e4f216f2fb4b69fff9b3a44842c3 73 bin/x 3 not specified file 8686ca685f3f55dc48c5d3fb1107be4 Manifest digest: sha256:7a8aea237bd28004828e36b056b48fbdb164f8c7dd1cb244c288f9111ad1a718 Validation: payload-observation-only --json returns bytes, digest, entries[] (path, type, size, digest, executable, target), manifest_digest and validation. Each file's entry has its digest, size and Unix executable bits (always zero on Windows). Directories and relative symbolic link targets are listed. Timestamps, owners and ACLs aren't included. It never runs files, follows links inside the tree or changes anything. Exit 0 on success, 2 on error. A relative path is resolved from -C, --root or the current directory. The path must not contain .. or pass through a symbolic link. Hard links to files outside the tree, special files and files that change during the scan fail. Limits: 200,000 entries, 8 GiB in total, 1 GiB per file, path depth 64 and 64 link hops. validation: "payload-observation-only" means this is a snapshot of what was on disk when read. It doesn't prove the files are authentic or haven't been changed by another process at the same time.

Store cleanup (pruning unreferenced installations) isn't available yet. oyzu tools list shows unreferenced installations. Locks coordinate Oyzu processes. They don't protect the store from other programs running as your user.
Tool lock files and inspection Tool commands Using tools in your shell

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-tailscale-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install tailscale and tailscaled on Linux, so a project or CI job that joins a tailnet doesn't need Tailscale installed on the machine. oyzu installs the two binaries only. It doesn't start the daemon, log in or grant any network capability.

[tools] tailscale = "1.78.1" # exact release # tailscale = "latest" # newest version on the stable track oyzu install tailscale@1.78.1 # declares, locks, installs on Linux oyzu exec -- tailscale version oyzu exec -- tailscaled --version tailscaled usually needs root or a TUN device, or its userspace-networking mode. How you run it is up to you.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Linux ARM64 (glibc) Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS No download: Tailscale ships only a GUI app and a .pkg installer Windows No download: Tailscale ships only .exe and .msi installers Other Linux architectures, musl Not supported Platforms without a download are left out of the lock, and oyzu install prints a warning naming them. Running oyzu install tailscale on macOS or Windows fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE and changes nothing. A lock created on Linux still works for Linux CI.

Request Result 1.78.1 or v1.78.1 That release latest The TarballsVersion in https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/?mode=json Ranges, minor lines and pre-releases are refused, and oyzu tools versions tailscale fails because oyzu doesn't list releases. The lock records the resolved version.

oyzu downloads https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/tailscale_<version>_<arch>.tgz (arch is amd64 or arm64) and checks it against the .sha256 file on the same site. The digest is recorded in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. The installed commands are tailscale and tailscaled; the systemd unit files in the archive aren't installed as services. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to tailscale, oyzu:tailscale or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
oyzu doesn't run or configure tailscaled. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive already cached.
Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-zig-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install a stable Zig compiler from the official download index and run it for your project, with no existing Zig installation or account. The exact archive is recorded in oyzu.lock. Note: Zig installation is experimental and currently supported on Intel macOS only.

Create oyzu.toml in your project: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 oyzu install --frozen oyzu which zig oyzu exec -- zig version $ oyzu exec -- zig versionCopy 0.15.2 Commit oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock. Later, oyzu install --frozen --offline reinstalls without the network. oyzu install zig@0.15.2 declares and installs in one step. oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 works before the project has any discovered build; plain oyzu pin needs one. The names zig, oyzu:zig and core:zig all select the same tool. The installed command is zig. Setting Meaning [tools] zig An exact stable version, a release line, latest or a semver range tools.lockPlatforms Optional list of platforms to lock oyzu.lock The exact version, platform, archive URL and SHA-256 oyzu doesn't read a compiler version from build.zig.zon. A minimum version there is a constraint for the Zig builder, not a pin.

oyzu reads the official index and picks stable releases only (no master or nightly builds). It downloads the archive, checks it against the SHA-256 the index publishes, and installs the full distribution, including libraries and license files. Zig releases are checked by digest; no publisher signature is verified. Under an organization tool catalog, only an approved release can be selected, and a missing record fails instead of falling back to the public index. Frozen installs rebuild the download from the URL in the lock without reading the index again. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive cached. Zig's own package fetching is separate: pinning the compiler doesn't make package downloads offline.
Platform Status macOS Intel Supported Linux x86-64 (glibc) Not supported yet Other architectures, musl, Windows Not supported

Failure Cause and recovery TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE The platform isn't supported. Use a supported platform No stable version matches Choose a published stable version that fits your constraints. Master and nightly builds aren't supported Invalid or missing archive or checksum Nothing is installed. Check the official release before retrying Archive URL doesn't match the expected layout Restore the original lock or update the selection. Custom mirrors and archive names aren't supported TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX / TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG Ask your organization to approve that release and platform TOOL_LOCK_STALE Run the suggested oyzu update or oyzu pin command. Frozen commands never change the selection
Zig builds Tool commands Organization tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/toolchain-platforms.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Container builds run each language build on the base execution image, with the language's tools restored from oyzu.lock for the action's platform. When a target is built for another platform, such as linux/arm64, Oyzu picks the base image for that platform. No project configuration is needed. Language builders need an image whose OS and architecture match the target platform, because they run tests and other target code. The Docker image builder can assemble images for another platform on its usual worker when it doesn't run target code.

Oyzu looks up the base image oyzu-execution/base:1 and inspects its platform. If the platform matches, that image is used. Otherwise it looks for a sibling named oyzu-execution/base:1-<os>-<arch>, such as oyzu-execution/base:1-linux-arm64, and checks that the image really has that platform (a matching tag isn't enough). A missing image or sibling is pulled from the pinned index for that architecture. Running another architecture's image still needs emulation in Docker; Oyzu doesn't install emulators. For example, with Docker and arm64 emulation already set up: oyzu build image oyzu inspect dist When an image target declares two platforms and copies in a Go binary, Oyzu builds two Go producers, each running its build, tests and checks on the base image for its platform with the Go locked for that platform. Docker then assembles both images and Oyzu writes an OCI index for them.

--image manager=reference sets the image for every selected variant that uses that manager. Oyzu uses it as given and doesn't look for siblings. An override with the wrong platform fails before preparation, so one override generally can't serve both sides of a platform matrix. oyzu run tasks use host tools and never pick container images.

Plans and dependency records include the image identity and the platform it ran on, separately from the artifact's target platform. Go preparation also checks that Go's OS and architecture match the image.

A missing sibling, a sibling with the wrong platform, or an execution failure stops the build. Oyzu never silently builds on the wrong architecture. Provision the right image (and emulation, if needed), or fix the --image override, then rebuild.

The container executor accepts Linux images only. Every ecosystem uses the same lookup. arm64 actions haven't been run on arm64 hardware or under emulation since the move to the base image. Records don't say whether a build ran on native hardware or under emulation. Your Docker host provides any emulation; Oyzu never installs it. See Docker's multi-platform guide. Cross-compiling an arm64 binary doesn't replace running its tests in an arm64 image. Dockerfiles that RUN commands for another platform have separate rules; see Docker platform admission. Image selection only uses the local daemon. Remote worker pools aren't discovered.

When Oyzu locks tools that it installs from archives, it resolves them for these hosts: Linux x86-64 and arm64 (GNU), macOS arm64 and Windows x86-64 (MSVC). Locks include linux/arm64/gnu entries even when resolved on another host. A tool with no release for a host reports it as unavailable; for example, Tailscale has Linux archives only. macOS x86-64 and musl hosts aren't included. Installing tools on an arm64 host or on macOS isn't supported yet.
Native local builds for platforms and executors. Verification toolsets and platform matrices for how producers are matched to platforms. Docker images and OCI indices.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/version-inference.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build works out a version for every artifact from your native version declarations, your Git tags and your Conventional Commit messages. You don't configure anything: build as usual and each artifact gets a version that says which release it's heading for and exactly which source it came from. Supported builders: Cargo, Node (npm, pnpm, Yarn), Helm, Go, Docker, Python, Maven, Gradle and Ant.

A single-package repository declares version 1.4.2, has the tag v1.4.2, and one newer commit feat: add endpoint. oyzu build resolves the next version to 1.5.0, and artifacts get: 1.5.0-dev.g<12-character-source-hash> The suffix comes from the content of the build's source files, not the Git commit SHA. There's no counter or timestamp, so the same source always gives the same version. Artifact digests, not version strings, identify the exact bytes. Every ordinary build produces a snapshot version like this. Only release staging produces exact release versions.

Run oyzu build in a supported project. No Oyzu configuration is needed. Git must be on the host. Oyzu reads your repository before the build starts. If history is missing (for example in a shallow CI clone), Oyzu can fetch it read-only. A folder exported without Git uses the native version, or 0.0.0 when the builder has no native version, plus the source suffix. Oyzu never edits your checkout. Inferred versions are written only into the private copies of manifests used for the build.

Choose a strategy in oyzu.toml if the default doesn't suit you: [version] strategy = "tags" Strategy How the base version is chosen auto (default) Combine the native version, exact tags, the nearest stable tag and commit impacts. Fall back to the native version or 0.0.0 when history can't supply a baseline. native Use the native version. Ignore tags and commit bumps. Fails if there's no native version. tags Use an exact tag on the commit, otherwise the nearest stable tag. No bump is inferred and the native version doesn't have to match. conventional Like auto, but requires complete history and a baseline or exact tag, and rejects relevant commits that aren't Conventional Commits. Every strategy still produces snapshot versions, and none changes who may publish or sign. The setting follows the normal configuration cascade, including profiles and administrative constraints. Unknown values fail validation.

The first stable tag that applies to the package, walking first-parent history, is the baseline. Commits after it (including merged ones) bump the version once, by the largest impact: a breaking change bumps major, feat bumps minor, fix bumps patch. Other Conventional Commit types don't bump. A native version already ahead of the baseline is kept if it's at least the computed minimum. An RC tag matching a stable native version keeps its prerelease label in the snapshot.

An exact tag on the built commit still produces a snapshot version and doesn't allow publishing by itself. It does name the release: oyzu publish uses the exactTags a build records as its GitHub release tag, so the version and the release tag always agree. Builds for one destination must agree, and oyzu publish --tag overrides it. See which release. Only tags that apply to the package are recorded (see tag names). For example, an unscoped v1.4.0 on a member of a multi-package Cargo workspace records nothing, so publishing it needs --tag. Artifacts from the Rust builder and Node workspace packages carry extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"].package, naming the package their version came from.

Each target in dist/plan.json and dist/manifest.json has extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"] with the native version, resolved base and version, source digest, commit, baseline tag and commit, exact tags, contributing and unclassified commits, whether history was complete, the reason, the strategy used and the configured requestedStrategy. extensions["oyzu.dev/version-history"] records the Git facts each decision used: HEAD, the repository prefix, shallow status, tags (names, object IDs and commits), and the commits read (parents, messages, paths). Decisions point to it with historyDigest, and record baselineDistance and analyzedCommits. These are local observations. They aren't authenticated source-control facts and don't make a build releasable. History records include commit messages and paths, so treat bundles as repository information when you share them.

Code Cause Fix version-needs-native The strategy needs a native version and there isn't one. Declare the version natively, or pick another strategy. version-needs-tags, version-needs-history The strategy needs tags or complete history. Fetch complete history and tags, or pick another strategy. version-unclassified-commits conventional found relevant commits that aren't Conventional Commits. Reword the commits' intent, or pick a less strict strategy. unsupported-version-strategy tags or conventional on a native version scheme Oyzu can't map. (auto and native keep a native snapshot instead.) Use auto or native. version-conflict, ambiguous-version-tags An exact tag conflicts with the native version, one commit has two version tags, or the native version is too low. Fix the native declaration or the tags and rerun.

Oyzu reads Git history once per repository per build. How much it reads depends on the build: Build What is read CI, --full, a ci profile, or the tags / conventional strategy Commit messages and changed paths back to each package's nearest stable tag. Older history can't change the result. If an origin is configured and the build is online, Oyzu also fetches complete ancestry and a fresh tag list first. Local fast build with auto, or native Only the head commit, shallow state and tag list. No commit messages. So in a local fast build with auto, an exact tag can still set the version, but otherwise the version falls back to the native version (or 0.0.0) plus the source suffix, with reason native-fallback-local-history-skipped and historyComplete: false. A local artifact's version can therefore differ from CI's for the same commit. Use --full, the CI context or the tags/conventional strategy to get the version a release build would use.
documents.s: What history is read, and when

documents.t: When a build needs history it doesn't have, Oyzu can fetch it read-only from a public https://github.com/owner/repository origin. Credentials, SSH and file URLs, queries and fragments are refused. Plain HTTP is allowed only for loopback hosts. The administrative fetches.sources allowlist also applies. Fetching is refused whenever organization management or registries.routes is in effect. Authenticated or managed Git connections aren't supported; provide complete history locally instead. History is fetched into a private store under cache/git-history in the user data directory. Your checkout's refs, tags, index and commit are never touched. A checkout that moves during the build, or a local tag that disagrees with the remote one, stops the build. Fetched tags never grant release permission. --offline never fetches, but reuses earlier fetched history for the same origin and HEAD. Local fast auto builds, native and --plan never fetch. If history can't be fetched, auto keeps its snapshot fallback; tags and conventional stop before any build actions if their inputs are still missing. Diagnostic Cause Fix SOURCE_DENIED The origin URL or fetches.sources doesn't allow this source. Use a credential-free HTTPS GitHub origin, or ask your administrator to allow it. CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED Organization management or registry routing is in effect. Provide complete history and tags locally. HISTORY_INPUT_MISSING Offline, with no earlier fetch for this origin and HEAD. Run once online, or provide complete history. HISTORY_ACQUISITION_UNAVAILABLE The source couldn't be reached or exceeded its limits. Restore access or provide complete history. HISTORY_INTEGRITY_CONFLICT Fetched or stored history failed validation. The build stops. Investigate, remove the bad stored copy and retry. version-conflict Local and remote tags disagree, or the checkout moved. Reconcile the tags and retry from a stable checkout. The manifest records fetch outcomes and times in extensions["oyzu.dev/history-acquisition"]; they don't affect the version. Each online fetch currently downloads a full fresh copy, even if an earlier one had the same objects, and old copies aren't cleaned up. This can add network and disk use to full builds.

A standalone package at the repository root, or a single-package Cargo workspace, uses unscoped tags such as v1.4.2. Independent Cargo and Node members use package-name tags. Maven modules use the artifact ID (or groupId.artifactId when IDs collide). Gradle projects use the project name (or directory path when names collide). Multi-project builds need scoped tags such as library/v1.4.2. Go workspace modules use directory-scoped tags. Equal native versions never imply that packages are released together. For that, see Cargo fixed release subjects.

Within a workspace, a change to a package also bumps the packages that depend on it. For example, with app -> bridge -> shared and a separate independent package, a feat that changes only shared moves the first three from 1.4.2 to 1.5.0; independent stays at 1.4.2. Each package is compared with its own tag, and each consumer's metadata gets its dependencies' chosen versions. Dependencies come from the native model (Cargo and Node local dependency edges, Maven's reactor, Gradle's resolved project graph, Go imports). Development, build, optional and peer dependencies count. This is a cautious view of build inputs, not a claim about public API changes. A changed file belongs to the most specific member folder that contains it. Files outside every member (workspace manifests, lock files, root build inputs) count for all members. inputScope in each decision records the directories and workspaceDirectories used. Oyzu doesn't guess undeclared imports between members.

Separate targets can depend on each other through depends_on, tasks and artifact relationships, and through inputs paths in build.yaml (including paths outside the producer's folder). A change in a producer can then bump its consumer's version against the consumer's own tag, without bumping unrelated targets. Changed paths are matched against the build's recorded source selection, including your ignore overrides. Deleted paths count too. Git paths are relative to the repository root, even in a nested workspace. Decisions record inputScope.declaredPaths. Inputs in a different Git repository fail with version-inputs-outside-repository. This works for Node (isolated builds), and for native Go and Rust builds.

For isolated builds on Unix, Oyzu can narrow a target's source suffix to the files its shipping commands actually read, so an unrelated shared file doesn't change every target's version. It applies only when every selected command has a complete, confinable stage contract and stays cacheable. The scope includes files the shipping commands read, declared inputs, and the configuration, build and lock files. Files only checks read are left out when the checks' outputs can't reach a shipping command. An optional file that a command would read stays in scope while absent, so creating it changes the version. Windows, native host builds, cross-target prerequisites, hooks, custom replacements and materialized inputs keep the full source scope. So does any target whose command details are incomplete.

For isolated Node builds, a pre_build hook that declares outputs counts as a generator. The version hash covers the target's source without the hook's own script, plus the files the hook wrote to its declared outputs. Editing the script without changing what it writes keeps the version; changing what it writes changes it. The script stays in the hash if a build stage reads or writes it, or if it isn't an argument of the hook's command. plan.json records the version before the hook runs; the final version is in plans/<target>.post-hooks.json and the manifest. See hooks as always-run actions. --no-cache gives the same version. Other builders and hook phases use the plain source hash.

Inferred versions and local package references are written only into Cargo's private build copy. Full, CI, tags/conventional, optimized and distributed builds compile the inferred version into CARGO_PKG_VERSION. Local fast development builds keep the declared Cargo versions so incremental compilation can reuse work, and record the actual compiledVersion beside the artifact version. --full alone doesn't change this. See local builds. Executable names don't change.

The native package name and version from package.json drive the version, for isolated and native host builds alike. With native, a package without a version fails before the build; add the version to package.json. Native host builds never change package.json. Isolated builds write the version into private copies of the root and member manifests and their local references. Native Node facts and host policy​ Node plugins report the native package name and version with their source path and digest. A target's alias is separate from the package name. The decision sets the plan version, the artifact file name and version, and the default OYZU_VERSION. The native compiled version may differ from the artifact's snapshot; both are recorded.
The root chart version is written into the private build copy. appVersion and dependency chart versions keep their native meaning.

Go uses the version in artifact names and the manifest. It doesn't inject a version into compiled code. Docker uses it in the OCI archive name, image reference and manifest. Both record nativeVersion: null. An exact tag supplies the base; otherwise an ancestor tag is the baseline for commit impact, or 0.0.0. Go resolves each workspace module separately, using imports and test imports. Module zip, mod and info outputs keep native v prefixes and RC qualifiers. See Go native module artifacts.

Native PEP 440 versions are normalized by Python's packaging library. Stable versions with up to three components, and alpha, beta and RC versions, take part in tag inference. For example, base 1.5.0-rc.2 becomes 1.5.0rc2.dev0+g<source-hash>. Epochs, post-releases, existing dev versions and longer version tuples keep a native snapshot (reason native-ecosystem-source). Static PEP 621 projects (pip, uv, Poetry) get the version in their private pyproject.toml. Projects with a dynamic version take it from tags (or 0.0.0); see dynamic versions. Legacy setuptools projects get the version through their distribution metadata. The source archive includes a generated setup.py wrapper so rebuilding it keeps the version. Custom distribution code beyond standard setuptools and distutils entry points isn't supported. Requirements-only applications have no native version and use SemVer application versions. Recreate dependency captures made by older Oyzu versions.

A trailing -SNAPSHOT is removed when the rest is SemVer. Other forms keep their value and get a native snapshot. Gradle's unspecified lets tags set the base. Ant falls back to 0.0.0 when there's no version property. Maven and Gradle read native models in an isolated step, then apply the chosen versions in the private workspace. Maven writes module, parent and dependency versions; Gradle archive tasks use the chosen versions; Ant records it in the JAR manifest. Requires the Gradle 8.14.3 profile and a current Maven image. Reprovision an older Maven image if reactor dependencies are missing. Recreate older dependency captures. Releasing inherited Maven versions together isn't supported.

Cargo workspaces can declare packages that always share one version, using cargo-release's shared-version setting: shared-version = true joins the shared group. A string names a separate group. false opts out of an inherited group. See Rust fixed version groups for an example, field precedence, and the supported tag-prefix and tag-name forms. Membership comes from all packages in the workspace, including private and unselected ones. Other ecosystems don't support fixed groups. A change to any member bumps the whole group once, by the largest impact. A package that depends on a member sees that change too, while keeping its own tag. Every member must declare the same native version, including qualifiers. Strategy Group behavior auto, fast local Common native snapshot, with exact group tags. No commit history read. auto, full or CI Common exact tag or nearest stable baseline, and the combined commit impact. native Common native snapshot. Ignores tags and commits. tags Needs a declared tag prefix and enough tags. conventional Needs a tag prefix, complete history and Conventional Commits. If no member declares a tag prefix, auto and native record a native snapshot with reason native-group-missing-namespace, and strict strategies refuse. A prefix on only some members is refused. Non-native strategies reject conflicting per-package tags on HEAD or the baseline commit. Private Cargo manifests, local requirements and the lock get the chosen versions. Your checkout isn't changed. Fast local builds report compiledVersion as usual. extensions["oyzu.dev/version-subjects"] records the group, members, tag prefixes and resolution; each member's oyzu.dev/versioning entry points to it with releaseSubject. --plan never runs Cargo or fetches history to fill in missing facts. Fixed groups are supported on Linux x86_64.

Release staging builds exact release-candidate or stable versions, instead of snapshots, in a CI job triggered by a tag push. Use --require-release when the job must fail rather than fall back to a snapshot. Note: Release staging is experimental. It supports only a GitHub Actions job triggered by a tag push in the same repository, building Cargo for Linux x86_64, and it hasn't been run end to end on GitHub yet. Staged versions are never marked production-eligible. oyzu -C app build app --require-release --full The native version and the tag together choose the version. Native 1.5.0-rc.1 with a matching exact tag stages a release candidate; native 1.5.0 with its tag stages a stable release. Each needs a fresh build: renaming an RC archive doesn't make it stable. A native/tag conflict fails, and native doesn't let a tag override the native version. Option Behavior (none) If the job's facts match, the build can stage exact versions. Otherwise it keeps snapshot versions and records why. --require-release Missing, offline, unsupported or contradictory evidence refuses the build before any build, check or package action runs. --release-profile FILE Accept only the exact reusable workflow and source in this release profile. --context release, OYZU_CONTEXT Only set the context. They never authenticate a release. --optimized Only chooses the build profile. --plan Read-only preview. Shows what evidence is missing. --check --require-release Reports missing release evidence as a blocking finding. A staged build always runs every required check, including real test and coverage reports. A nested target can't turn those off.

Job permissions: contents: read, actions: read and id-token: write. Oyzu requests a fresh GitHub OIDC token and checks the signed repository, ref, commit, workflow, run attempt and job against GitHub's API (using the job's GITHUB_TOKEN). CI variables, a local tag, a JWT file or OYZU_ID_TOKEN can't stand in for this. The built files and their modes must match the tagged commit exactly, and the tag must stay the same until the build finishes. Refused: uncommitted changes, forks, the wrong job or attempt, a moved tag, repository hooks, Git symlinks or submodules in the selected source, and inputs outside the repository. Reusable workflows need --release-profile, and both signed workflow claims must match. The manifest records GitHub's answers and any unresolved reasons in extensions["oyzu.dev/release-staging"]. If a check fails, or the source or tag changes before the end, no final output is accepted. A job token proves the job's identity and event. It doesn't prove where Oyzu ran, who built the artifact, that checks were correct, or that the build was isolated.

If GitHub is unavailable or permissions are missing, a build without --require-release keeps snapshot versions. With --require-release it fails, naming the missing fact. Retry online in the matching job after fixing access. Saved manifests and earlier attempts can't be reused, and offline builds can't stage.

Release staging is limited as described above. No other CI providers, events, builders or platforms are supported. Fixed release groups are Cargo-only. Native version schemes Oyzu can't map to SemVer (some Python, Maven and Gradle forms) keep native snapshots and don't get tag or commit bumps. History can be fetched only from public GitHub HTTPS origins.
Rust, Go, Python preparation Publishing Release provenance verification

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/yarn.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds and tests Node projects that use Yarn. Yarn Classic (1.22.22) projects and workspaces are discovered from native manifests and the lock with no Oyzu build file. Single-root applications also work with Yarn Berry 4.17.1. Note: Yarn support is experimental. Each setup below lists the exact versions and platforms it supports. Anything not listed there is not supported yet. Builds use the Node builder plugin, which must be installed and selected (see plugin packages). Native Yarn always owns dependency layout, peer behavior and lifecycle scripts.

Setup Yarn Platforms Section Isolated Classic builds (package archives, workspaces) Classic 1.22.22, Node 22 Isolated Linux amd64 worker (not fully tested yet) Capture and installation, Workspace builds Isolated single-root application Classic 1.22.22, Node 22.23.3 Windows x64 coordinator with Linux amd64 worker External captured Classic application Isolated single-root application Berry 4.17.1, Node 22.23.3 Windows x64 coordinator with Linux amd64 worker Captured Berry application Native single-root application Classic 1.22.22 or Berry 4.17.1, Node 22.23.3 Windows x64 and Linux x64 Managed Yarn Native workspace packages Classic 1.22.22 Linux x86_64 (GNU) Native Classic workspace packages Native workspace packages Berry 4.17.1 Windows x64 Native Berry workspace package continuation Berry setups need an existing literal nodeLinker: node-modules in .yarnrc.yml. Yarn Plug'n'Play is not supported.

The tested profile is Yarn Classic 1.22.22 on Node 22. Isolated builds run on the base execution image with Docker. Node and Yarn both come from oyzu.lock, so pin Node in [tools] and Yarn with an exact packageManager (or yarn in [tools]). oyzu --root path/to/project run list oyzu --root path/to/project build oyzu --root path/to/project inspect dist Oyzu never installs a replacement package manager during a build. --image yarn=<image> runs Yarn's isolated actions on an image of your own. Its immutable identity is recorded, and the locked Node and Yarn still run. The @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 parser ships in the Node plugin package, and the default quality tools are restored from their pinned lock, so no image needs either. An exact packageManager declaration must agree with native Yarn's version. A Corepack suffix such as yarn@1.22.22+sha512.<hex> is accepted and ignored in that comparison. Incompatible Node engine requirements fail. Your native scripts appear as tasks. During isolated builds, the conventional build and test work and read-only lint and format checks run. oyzu run uses host tools, and explicit formatting can modify your source (build format checks cannot). Node test scripts produce JUnit and LCOV. See Node quality.

Oyzu reads Yarn Classic v1 lock syntax with Yarn's own parser, including grouped selectors. It needs a lock that parses, current direct dependency selectors, conventional HTTPS registry archive URLs and an integrity value for every entry. SHA-512 is the normal form. Older Classic locks also carry integrity sha1-... values for packages locked before the registry published SHA-512. Those are accepted only when the SHA-1 value matches the #<sha1> fragment of the resolved URL. They are verified against that SHA-1 and named in the dependency record. SHA-1 is weaker, so regenerate those entries with native Yarn if you need SHA-512 throughout. Several selectors for one archive share its captured identity. Conflicting identities and ambiguous offline-mirror file names fail. Every locked archive is captured, including optional and transitive ones. Git, file and other non-registry resolutions are refused. Preparation uses the scoped broker routes for https://registry.npmjs.org/ and https://registry.yarnpkg.com/, recorded as npm-public and yarn-public. Redirects stay subject to broker authorization. Your lock keeps its original URLs and hashes. The archive inventory strips URL fragments from transport addresses and verifies the lock's SHA-512 before installation. Credentials never enter the inventory or mirror. The snapshot holds content-addressed archives and an inventory, not Yarn's extracted cache. Each install creates a fresh private mirror and cache and a temporary Yarn configuration outside your source. Installation uses the mirror, includes development dependencies, and has no network in the worker. Before lifecycle scripts are allowed, Oyzu runs yarn install --offline --ignore-scripts --force in the private tree and compares the resulting lock with the captured one. Any change in dependency resolution fails. Cosmetic serialization changes are discarded, so your lock bytes stay as they were. During execution, yarn install --offline --frozen-lockfile --force runs the lifecycle without a broker. Acquisition never enables scripts. Native Yarn and Node versions must match the captured versions. The comparison matters because suppressing lock writes alone doesn't show that changed resolutions agree with the lock. Registry version overrides in package.json resolutions are supported, including a different transitive version alongside a direct one: { "dependencies": {"is-odd": "3.0.1", "is-number": "6.0.0"}, "resolutions": {"is-odd/is-number": "7.0.0"} } Generate and commit the matching lock with native Yarn first (see the yarn-resolutions example). Yarn's own warnings and selective-resolution limits apply. File, Git, URL and alias-protocol resolution values are rejected before any native invocation. See Yarn's selective resolutions. Oyzu uses Yarn's offline mirror and does not reimplement package resolution or Yarn's cache layout.

Yarn Classic reads a project .yarnrc and .npmrc itself. Oyzu accepts these files only when every setting is on a fixed list that can't redirect archive sources, the offline mirror, caches, credentials or the Yarn executable: File Accepted settings .yarnrc ignore-engines, save-prefix, save-exact, disable-self-update-check, version-tag-prefix, version-git-message, version-git-tag, version-sign-git-tag .npmrc package-lock, loglevel, progress, save-exact, save-prefix, fund, audit, update-notifier For example, webpack's .yarnrc has ignore-engines true and its .npmrc has package-lock=false. Both are accepted and Yarn applies them. Any other key fails acquisition with Yarn capture does not yet support <file> setting <key> before any native invocation. That includes registry, scoped @scope:registry, //host/:_authToken credentials, yarn-path, yarn-offline-mirror, cache-folder and ---prefixed command-line settings. The message names the key, not its value. .yarnrc is read with Yarn's lock parser. .npmrc is read as key=value lines, and an ini section header is rejected as an unknown key. Settings files inside workspace members are not supported. .yarnrc.yml is Yarn Berry configuration. In a Classic build it fails with a message saying Berry needs its own setup.

To test other Node versions, use verification toolsets in oyzu.toml. matrix.node in build.yaml is refused. Toolset verification runs on the native host executor, and isolated Yarn builds use the isolated executor, so a build with verification runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED. A successful build emits snapshot .tgz packages with normalized archive metadata. The embedded package version matches the artifact version. dist/manifest.json lists artifacts, tests and coverage, with dependency snapshots and native logs beside it. Failed tests keep their reports and block packaging. oyzu inspect dist checks content integrity, not release trust. Dependency records use adapter layout 2. They list names, versions, source IDs, SHA-256 digests and sizes. The oyzu.dev/yarn extension records lockfile-sha512 integrity and the all-locked-registry-tarballs inventory. If any archive was verified by a legacy SHA-1 value, integrity is lockfile-sha512-or-legacy-sha1 and legacySha1Packages lists those archives as name@version. Packages are classed as build inputs. Registry dependency edges and runtime or test classification aren't recorded, so this is not a runtime SBOM. Workspace captures also keep local package edges for build ordering and version projection. Failure Recovery Stale or conflicting lock Fix it with native Yarn and commit the result. Corrupt archive, missing captured input, disallowed source or runtime mismatch Fails instead of downloading a replacement during execution. Fix the cause and rebuild. Layout-1 dependency-free capture Capture again. It can't be replayed as layout 2. Unsupported source configuration Rejected before any native invocation, including version queries.

A Yarn Classic workspace has a private native root, a committed Classic lock and locally linked packages (see the Yarn Classic workspace example). Run the commands above from that root with no Oyzu configuration. oyzu run list includes build, test, lint and format-check. A plain oyzu run build runs yarn workspaces run build when there is no root script, so every member needs a build script. The isolated oyzu build also handles packages without build scripts. Acquisition asks Yarn for its workspace list after lock validation. Member locations and local dependency edges become captured facts. Oyzu does not read Yarn's workspace globs itself. Oyzu orders members by those edges, assigns snapshot versions and declares each package's reports. It rewrites versions and matching local references only in the private tree, before a fresh offline install. Your manifests and lock are unchanged. An explicit root script owns its stage once. Otherwise build scripts run in dependency order, and tests and read-only quality checks combine member scripts with inferred defaults. JUnit and LCOV are collected per package. yarn pack --ignore-scripts creates each archive. Oyzu normalizes archive metadata and publishes the packages to dist only after the required stages pass. Failed assertions or quality checks block artifact collection and keep the failure evidence. Hooks and overrides follow the shared task and report rules. For a coarse root build, Oyzu checks the concrete public JavaScript entries selected by Node's import and require conditions before packing. It also checks declaration files selected by the types condition and literal legacy declaration paths. Existence is checked, not TypeScript validity. Missing regular files fail. Null exclusions and conditional alternatives are left to Node. The check doesn't look inside Yarn's archive, and skips browser or custom conditions and wildcard paths. Limits: Classic needs a private workspace root. Cyclic local graphs, custom registry configuration, affected selection and member task groups are not supported. Direct host build and quality composition is less complete than the isolated build. Direct tests use the workspace report integration. Workspaces with external dependencies and broader framework setups aren't covered beyond a linked two-package project.

A single-root application with Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and Node 22.23.3 builds into an application directory plus Node-test JUnit and LCOV. It runs on a Linux amd64 worker, driven from a Windows x86_64 coordinator. Workspaces, other versions and other platforms are not supported. Select node/app and keep the package manager declaration: builds: app: {uses: node/app} {"packageManager":"yarn@1.22.22","dependencies":{"semver":"7.7.2"}} You need: A current Classic yarn.lock. Tool selections in oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock. An installed Node plugin package that supports multiple platforms (see plugin packages). Ordinary native build, test and quality scripts, an exact packageManager, public HTTPS registry dependencies with supported lock integrity, and no workspaces, project plugins, yarnPath or non-comment rc settings. oyzu -C path/to/app --json build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen --no-cache --image yarn=<image> oyzu -C path/to/app inspect dist The plugin and tool selections and your lock must already be in oyzu.lock for --frozen. On first adoption a normal build creates them. Don't delete an existing oyzu.lock to retry a failed build. You don't need installed project dependencies or a Yarn lock parser in the image. Oyzu orchestrates, and native Node and Yarn do installation and scripts. Acquisition captures authorized registry archives with their original integrity data and without lifecycle scripts, then validates the lock with scripts off. Execution installs from the private mirror with network disabled, then runs lifecycle, build, test and quality steps. --frozen freezes selections but doesn't make acquisition offline. On success, dist holds a versioned application directory and fresh required reports, with dependency and tool identity and action logs in the manifest. Failed assertions keep available reports and block export. A test that exits zero but writes no JUnit and LCOV still fails the build. Problem Recovery Stale lock Run native Yarn to generate the intended lock, and keep it with the manifest. Missing yarn.lock Restore it. Admission can report the generic PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED: no owned captured dependency provider. A selected tool was lost during the build Retry with the corrected coordinator. Don't purge caches by hand. Both lock problems fail before lifecycle scripts run.

An isolated Berry build needs exact packageManager: yarn@4.17.1, Node 22.23.3, a current lock and an existing literal nodeLinker: node-modules: nodeLinker: node-modules It handles a single root with public registry dependencies. Plug'n'Play, child workspaces, yarnPath and project plugins are not supported. It runs on a Linux amd64 worker, driven from a Windows x86_64 coordinator. Other combinations, macOS, Windows ARM64 and Linux ARM64 are not supported yet. Use the same node/app declaration and isolated command as above. Oyzu prefetches public-registry metadata and archives through the broker, with SHA-512 checks, and serves only those fixed local GET and HEAD routes. Yarn creates and validates its own ZIP cache with install --immutable --mode=skip-build. Execution copies that cache into private scratch and runs install --immutable --immutable-cache with network disabled, before your commands run. Your .yarnrc.yml, package.json and lock are not rewritten. Archive integrity and Yarn's ZIP checksums are separate checks. The worker also gets an executable alias archive for yarn and yarnpkg, bound to the selected Node and Yarn. Executable modes survive Windows coordination, and the files are read-only for every action, including your commands and their child processes. The image's own Yarn is never used. Problem Recovery Lock drift (YN0028) Regenerate the lock with the selected Yarn only when you intend to change dependencies. Missing lock Restore it. Plug'n'Play project Fails admission. Oyzu doesn't convert PnP projects. Stale or missing lock, a checksum failure, or a request outside the prefetched routes Fails preparation. Fix the lock or dependency and rebuild. Child workspaces, yarnPath, project plugins, custom sources or extra rc settings Refused.

Note: Experimental. Supported on Linux x86_64 (GNU) only. Windows, macOS and ARM64 are not supported for this setup. A native build (without Docker) of a Classic workspace into package archives, using Node 22.23.3, Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and node/package. Your project needs: A named, semver-versioned private coordinator (root) with two publishable members. A genuine Classic yarn.lock, and local references such as *. Flat cp source.cjs dist.cjs builds and implicit package-owned Node tests. Select tools through normal configuration and the lock, and declare the output: builds: package: uses: node/package oyzu --json build package --full --no-cache --jobs 1 How it works: Oyzu runs the selected yarn install --frozen-lockfile task, after a script-free preparation with --ignore-scripts. Yarn's workspaces info supplies member links, and installed links confirm local targets. The private root is a build, test and report owner even though Classic leaves it out of its membership map. Oyzu rewrites versions and local references to exact versions in the private tree only. Classic packs each publishable member with --filename. Your manifests and lock keep their bytes. First adoption may add plugin and tool selections to oyzu.lock. The output is two TGZ archives and six JUnit/LCOV reports. A failing root assertion blocks both member archives and all export. A replaced install task is refused before any action. Native build scripts and helpers keep their implicit pre/post lifecycle and the protected-path rules. Not supported: pack hooks, peer dependencies and their metadata, active rc overrides, private members, aggregate builds and isolated Yarn workspaces. Empty or comment-only rc files are accepted.

Note: Experimental. Supported on Windows x64 with Node 22.23.3 and Yarn 4.17.1 only. A native build of a Berry workspace into package archives. It needs an existing literal nodeLinker: node-modules, a named and versioned root, publishable app and shared members, literal workspace:* local dependencies, recognized package-local build bodies and implicit package-owned Node tests. Declare the output in build.yaml, keep the genuine yarn.lock, and select tools through configuration and the lock: builds: package: {uses: node/package} oyzu --json build package --full --no-cache { "status": "succeeded", "runId": "45292-1792727760814863500" } Output shortened. A root, app and shared project produces three .tgz archives and six owner reports. Oyzu runs the ordinary immutable install, does a script-free preparation, fixes native membership, links and versions, then builds and tests in the private tree. Yarn packs the archives. Private version projection leaves the lock untouched and lets Yarn translate workspace:* when packing.

A root with "private": true still builds, runs implicit tests and writes its JUnit/LCOV, using its Oyzu-resolved version. Only publishable members get archives. Two members mean two archives and six reports. A failing root assertion blocks member export. Keep the root named and semver-versioned. Private members are not supported.

Authored install replacements are refused. prepack and postpack bodies are accepted only when Oyzu can show they have package-local effects before preparation or your commands. Recognized copy bodies and local Yarn helpers keep the protected-path rules. Coarse JavaScript bodies and foreign writes are refused. The whole script and helper map must match its analyzed value just before packing. Yarn runs each accepted hook in one native pack. prepack can generate archive content. postpack runs after the archive is made and can't change it. A postpack failure blocks export of the target, including archives packed earlier. Yarn's own postinstall stays ordinary native behavior. Berry doesn't run arbitrary pre and post build hooks automatically the way npm does.

Active .yarnrc.yml files in member directories and parents must be absent, comments, or the same node-modules setting. Other or malformed active settings fail before preparation. Settings changed by installation fail the frozen-facts comparison before member execution. Managed environment admission also applies to the install task. An alternate rc file name doesn't bypass it. Explicit npm or pnpm helper delegation is refused. Yarn options before a helper's selected script that can change script or binary ownership, such as -T/--top-level and -B/--binaries-only, are refused. Arguments after the script or -- are forwarded. Not supported: Classic, Plug'n'Play, isolated Yarn workspaces, aggregate scripts and other platforms.

Supported versions and platforms are in Supported setups. Modern Yarn (Berry) is not supported for isolated workspace builds. Berry .yarnrc.yml settings beyond the literal nodeLinker: node-modules are not supported. Custom registry layouts, private registry credentials, member settings files and other .yarnrc or .npmrc settings are not supported. Lifecycle scripts that need external downloads fail in the isolated worker. Yarn Plug'n'Play and project plugins are not supported.
Node applications, npm workspace builds and pnpm builds Managed Yarn for tool selection and direct-test preparation Workspace test bundles and Node quality

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/zig.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The zig/project builder runs a native Zig project's build.zig and collects what it installs. Use it when your build.zig defines the programs, libraries and resources you want in the build bundle. Note: Experimental. Zig 0.15.2 is the supported compiler. Native builds are supported on Intel macOS, and isolated builds with dependencies on Linux (x86-64, GNU). Other compiler versions and platforms aren't supported yet. Zig test reports and coverage aren't available.

The Zig builder isn't in the plugin catalog yet. Build it from the Oyzu source checkout and bind it in your user configuration: oyzu exec -- cargo build --locked -p oyzu-plugin-zig --features plugin Create build.yaml beside your build.zig: builds: hello: uses: zig/project Pick the compiler in oyzu.toml: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" Bind the compiled plugin by absolute path in a user configuration file: [plugins.development] "zig/project" = "/absolute/oyzu/target/debug/oyzu-plugin-zig" Set OYZU_USER_CONFIG to that file's absolute path and run oyzu build from your project. The installation tree is collected as the install directory artifact in dist/manifest.json. On Intel macOS its bundle path is hello/darwin/x86_64/install. Check the manifest for the real path before running install/bin/hello. See local plugin bindings and build bundles.

Input Meaning build.yaml with uses: zig/project Required. Zig targets aren't detected automatically. [tools] zig and oyzu.lock The compiler request and the exact installation Oyzu selected. build.zig The native build program. Only Zig runs it, during the build. build.zig.zon Optional. Oyzu reads the package name, version and minimum Zig version from it. with.steps Native build steps to run. with.definitions Project options passed to zig build as -Dname=value. with.install-format directory (default) or tar.gz. .minimum_zig_version in build.zig.zon is a minimum, not a pin. Choose a compiler that satisfies it through [tools]. Task Command Notes build zig build Oyzu redirects the install prefix and both caches into its own output directory. test zig build test Runs the command only. Zig test reports aren't supported, so a build that requires test reports fails with a message saying so. format zig fmt . Changes your source. format-check zig fmt --check . Read-only. A build task you write yourself keeps its own command and working directory, and must produce the install artifact itself. Oyzu doesn't add arguments to it. Build options (with.steps, with.definitions, with.install-format) only work with the conventional build, so combining them with your own build task fails before anything runs.

Oyzu reads build.zig.zon without running Zig. It accepts strings, enum package names, fingerprints, comments, literal containers, package versions, minimum compiler versions and string paths. A root .description string is accepted as plain metadata. Duplicate fields, expressions, other unknown fields and unsupported escapes are errors, reported with file, line and column. A package .version is major.minor.patch, optionally followed by exactly -dev. Minimum compiler versions must be stable releases. The manifest is limited to 1 MiB, 32 nesting levels and 20,000 values.

Tools pinned in the target folder's oyzu.toml apply to every selected build in that folder. The Zig compiler stays first on PATH, and other tool directories follow it. For example, a build that runs Pandoc needs the GitHub provider named explicitly: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" "github:jgm/pandoc" = "3.12.1" Then pin, install and build: oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 oyzu pin 'github:jgm/pandoc@3.12.1' oyzu install --frozen oyzu build --isolated This works with Pandoc 3.12.1 on Linux x86-64 GNU. Plain pandoc has no entry in the tool index, so the GitHub provider is the way to ask for it. Oyzu accepts complete publisher tar.gz or tar.xz trees. Interpreter commands, command aliases, partial payloads and other archive types are refused. Oyzu never changes file modes on downloaded bytes to make an archive executable. Normal tool-index and download policy checks apply before a cached tool is reused. A missing tool or platform fails. The image or host never substitutes for a pin. Offline builds need the tools prepared by an earlier online build, including the exact cached archives. An installed executable alone isn't enough, and TOOL_OFFLINE asks you to prepare online first. Isolated builds run with the network denied. If the build step fails, nothing is exported. Pandoc runs during the build but isn't part of the collected installation tree.

with.steps selects native build steps and with.install-format: tar.gz collects the install tree as one archive. This works at an ordinary checkout root. Keep your build.zig and tracked files in place and move the bundle out of the way in oyzu.toml: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" builds: ghostty: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: steps: [lib-vt] install-format: tar.gz Evidence and collected files go in .oyzu/bundle, and the native dist directory comes in as a declared source input. oyzu inspect picks that bundle by default. Git and source containment checks still apply, and an unowned destination is refused. Oyzu doesn't translate your Zig build graph into YAML. build.zig owns the compile, documentation and install steps. The YAML says what to collect and which native entry point to run. Option Values Default Effect steps 1 to 16 distinct names. Each starts with an ASCII letter and has at most 64 letters, digits, _ or -. Zig's default install step Selects native build steps. Flags, paths, shell text and an empty list are refused. definitions Map of up to 16 option names to strings, booleans or signed 64-bit integers Empty Each entry becomes one -Dname=value argument. install-format directory, tar.gz directory tar.gz packs the install tree into install.tar.gz before collection. Definitions let you set project-defined Zig options: builds: ghostty: path: ghostty uses: zig/project inputs: [ghostty/dist] with: definitions: xcframework-target: native install-format: tar.gz The project decides what an option means. Here xcframework-target: native tells Ghostty to build only its host Mac application. Keep tool versions in oyzu.toml. Don't put ordered actions or commands in definitions. Rules for definitions: Names follow the same grammar and 64-byte limit as steps. String values can be up to 1,024 UTF-8 bytes with no control characters. Empty strings are fine. Booleans become true or false, and integers become decimal numbers. The rendered arguments total at most 4,096 bytes and are sorted by name. Spaces and punctuation stay inside one argument and are never run through a shell. Null, floats, nested objects and arrays are refused. Names that control the compiler, target and CPU, optimization, release or version, install prefix and caches, toolchain, system packages, fetching or job count are reserved (including case and underscore variants). Any other option goes to your project's own build.zig, and its failures show up normally. Oyzu owns the Zig binary and the prefix, cache and --system paths. Steps and definitions don't grant tool, source, network or credential access. Native build exit codes stay separate from JUnit and coverage, and required-report checks still apply.
documents.s: Native steps and linked installation archives

documents.t: After the native build succeeds, Oyzu writes install.tar.gz and collects it as a regular file. It keeps relative links inside the tree and executable bits, and refuses links that escape, dangle or loop, and unsupported file types. Limits are 100,000 entries, 10 GiB of file content, and 64 nested link expansions. Plain directory collection rejects links, so use tar.gz for trees that contain them. oyzu inspect checks the archive's bytes. It doesn't unpack it.

On Intel macOS, a Zig project with dependencies is prepared before the build, using the Oyzu-managed compiler. Oyzu downloads each original archive through its broker, checks the archive hash and Zig's package hash, and then builds with --system pointing at its prepared package tree and -j1. A build task you wrote yourself doesn't get this preparation. Required isolated execution is refused on this path. Native builds run with your account's access. oyzu build --offline fails with OFFLINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE. The prepared packages aren't kept between builds, so dependency builds need to be online. Preparation runs in a macOS sandbox with network and host-read access denied, a private HOME, and no registry credentials or inherited environment. If your project refers to installed resources through zig-out, the build keeps zig-out available in its private workspace as a view of the real install prefix. An existing path or a case collision is refused, and your checkout is not changed. XZ package metadata is checked with Apple's system liblzma from the selected SDK. If the SDK can't provide it, the build fails. There is no other decoder. An Xcode flow is also supported for a nested project, limited to Xcode 26.3 (build 17C529), Apple Swift 6.2.4 and a finite Sparkle 2.9.0 binary package recipe on Intel macOS. One canonical Package.resolved is recognized. Unknown pins, manifests, layouts and multiple resolutions are refused, and arbitrary SwiftPM projects aren't supported. Packages come from the broker through a separate swiftpm route, SwiftPM runs with its network denied, and its caches stay private. Only TZ=UTC, LC_ALL=C and the selected DEVELOPER_DIR are accepted as explicit environment for this flow. Other task environment values or PATH changes are refused before anything downloads. Xcode tools write to temporary files under your user's Darwin temp root. Oyzu allows only the specific paths Xcode's tools use, on top of a sandbox that still denies network and unrelated reads. Other builds by the same user can share those temporary files, and Oyzu doesn't delete them. Required stronger isolation is refused. Authored Swift or Xcode arguments for CLANG_MODULE_CACHE_PATH are refused, because Oyzu sets it.

This configuration builds the installed documentation and C library of Ghostty (tested with upstream v1.3.1) as one native build: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" "github:jgm/pandoc" = "3.12.1" [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" builds: ghostty-docs: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: definitions: emit-docs: true emit-exe: false install-format: tar.gz oyzu build ghostty-docs runs the project's default install step. There is no separate docs step. The tree has section 1 and 5 Markdown, standalone HTML, man pages, and the VT library with headers and pkg-config files. It leaves out the application resources that belong to the executable. The project's native build graph decides all of that. The output keeps the version fallback 1.3.1-dev+0000000 and the pkg-config build prefix. pkg-config paths aren't relocated. Two builds in one folder can't own the same native build unit, so a library build and a docs build need separate configurations. The build reserves 4,096 MiB for its native action, so Docker needs more than its 4 GiB default. A 6 GiB Docker budget on an 8 GiB machine worked, with jobs set to 1. Keep at least 2 GiB of disk free.

This builds Ghostty's VT library from an ordinary Git checkout and checks it with a small C program that uses only what the build collected. [tools] zig = "0.15.2" [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" builds: ghostty: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: steps: [lib-vt] install-format: tar.gz The checkout must be clean: tracked changes or unexpected untracked files are refused. Generated root files and .oyzu/ state are allowed. The project's own oyzu.toml, build.yaml and oyzu.lock are the only files a configuration adds. Run oyzu build first. Until the plugin is adopted, oyzu config validate fails with PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED and installs nothing, and a lock alone doesn't install its plugin into a fresh store. After lib-vt succeeds, the collected archive holds the public header and a versioned shared library. A C99 consumer compiled against only those two files accepts a safe string and rejects a newline and a bracketed-paste end sequence. Repeat builds with unchanged inputs reuse results. A changed C export triggers a rebuild, and --offline replays work after the source is restored. Executed builds use fresh private Zig caches. The required test-lib-vt step doesn't compile yet, so Zig tests of this library aren't supported. Native test reports, the Linux GUI and macOS aren't covered.

For the conventional build, Oyzu runs zig build --prefix <output>/install --cache-dir <output>/cache --global-cache-dir <output>/global-cache and exports only the install directory, keeping the executable bits of installed files. The directory isn't promoted into .oyzu/bin. The plugin reads static source metadata and plans the build. It doesn't launch the compiler, download anything or use observation tools. Oyzu selects the compiler, verifies archives, runs the build, applies policy and reports, and collects the bundle. The plugin can't waive required checks. Native host builds refuse declared dependencies (including path and lazy ones), except in the Intel macOS flow above. Use an isolated build, described below, for projects with dependencies on Linux. Zig test reports, coverage and app packaging aren't supported. A fast build proves only that it built and collected its artifacts. A tree with links fails directory collection. Use install-format: tar.gz. A build that installs nothing fails artifact collection. A failed Zig command never produces a successful artifact. Fix invalid metadata at the reported location. Choose a compiler that satisfies the minimum, and keep the real failures from your build.zig. Don't replace them with an ambient compiler or remove required checks.

Isolated builds prepare every URL, transitive, contained path and lazy dependency before build.zig runs. This needs a Linux amd64 GNU compiler and a multi-platform Zig plugin build. A single local plugin binding can't do captured planning. Oyzu's broker downloads the archives and records each archive's SHA-256 separately from Zig's package hash. Zig sees only local files. The build uses the prepared packages/p tree through --system with separate writable caches and serial -j1. Your own build task doesn't receive these arguments.

HTTPS archives: the URL can't contain user information, queries, fragments, percent encoding, control characters, backslashes or path traversal. Archive types are .tar, .tar.gz (.tgz), .tar.xz, .tar.zst and .zip, or their media types. Other types fail with ZIG_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED. GitHub commits: git+https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>#<40-hex-commit>. Oyzu downloads the commit tarball over HTTPS, with no Git executable and no branch or tag lookup, and the compiler must produce the exact hash you declared. Credentials, queries, abbreviated commits, .git suffixes, extra path segments and other hosts are refused. A matching native hash doesn't verify a Git object or signature. Registry routes: registries.routes with protocol zig maps a source host[:port]/prefix/ (HTTPS implied) to an administrator-configured connector. Once any Zig route exists, all package routing is closed. A missing source or connector, an overlap, an unapproved redirect or an unavailable mirror is refused with no public fallback. Project and user configuration can't grant route authority. The connector's credentials stay in Oyzu and Zig never sees them. Authenticated downloads aren't reused from the cache.

A dependency normally has a regular build.zig.zon. A dependency without one is accepted only after Zig's hash check and a bounded scan of the original archive proves no build.zig.zon appears anywhere in it. This works for gzip and XZ tars. The scan has limits of 64 MiB compressed, 256 MiB decoded and 10,000 members, runs in a separate worker for XZ (4,096 MiB and 120 seconds), and fails closed. Code Meaning and fix ZIG_SOURCE_INVALID The dependency declaration isn't a supported exact source. Fix it. SOURCE_DENIED The download or a redirect isn't on an approved route. ZIG_HASH_MISMATCH The downloaded bytes don't produce the declared hash. Oyzu doesn't substitute another source. ZIG_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED The archive type isn't supported. ZIG_MANIFEST_UNAVAILABLE Oyzu can't prove the dependency's manifest. Keep a regular build.zig.zon or use a supported original archive. ZIG_CACHE_INVALID Reused data no longer matches its recorded receipt. Prepare again online.

Linux dependency package trees keep regular filenames that end in a dot, such as ._., and direct symlinks from one regular file to a sibling regular file (the target is a single portable name). Chains, directory links, dangling links and absolute or traversing links aren't supported. Project sources, build artifacts, directories, trailing spaces and other filename rules are unchanged. Packaging for Docker image dependency contexts still applies portable names and can refuse these trees.

Reuse needs identical dependency contents, compiler and plugin identities, and source mapping, and checks current routes again. Offline builds replay prepared dependencies from an earlier online build. Tests and coverage are refused before preparation until a Zig report adapter exists. Private connector sessions and live organization endpoints aren't supported. Zig's native caches are fresh for each executed isolated build, so native incremental compile speed isn't available there.

Oyzu is an early release. The core local workflow works without an account; some areas are experimental or limited to certain platforms. This page is a summary; each linked reference page has the details. Area Status Help and machine-readable output Every command has offline --help and --json output Discovery, tasks and local builds Available for the supported ecosystems. Support for each builder varies by platform; see ecosystem support Tool management Available. Fully supported on Linux x86-64 Build bundles and history Available: every build writes a bundle you can inspect, and recent builds are kept Local action cache On by default. Experimental Remote OCI cache Experimental. Supported on Linux Isolated (container) builds Experimental. Supported on Linux hosts Publishing Experimental. OCI registries and existing GitHub releases Remote builds Experimental. Needs an Oyzu platform account See Known limitations for the details behind each experimental area.
CLI output Local builds Action cache Remote runs
Read this before you choose Oyzu for a project. Each section links to the page with the full details.

Every release so far is a preview. The release repository is not public yet. The install script works for people with access who pass a GitHub token. There is no Linux musl executable; build from source on those systems. The install script checks the release's SHA-256 digest but not its provenance files. There is no package-manager distribution.

Support for tool versions, operating systems, builders and dependency handling varies. See ecosystem support, local builds and tool commands. Tool management is fully tested on Linux x86-64. Windows x86-64 works with less test coverage, and macOS isn't supported yet. Isolated (container) builds are experimental and supported on Linux hosts.

The local action cache is on by default and experimental. The remote OCI cache is experimental and supported on Linux. Entries are not signed, and entries larger than 256 MiB are not pushed. Cache keys cover the inputs Oyzu can see. Something outside them, such as an environment variable a tool reads on its own, doesn't trigger a rebuild. See Cache build results.
Publishing is experimental. It supports OCI registries and existing GitHub releases only; npm and PyPI publishing are not available. See Publish artifacts.
Remote builds are experimental and need an Oyzu platform account. See Remote builds.
The site uses the Segoe UI font when it is installed on your system and a fallback font otherwise.
If something on this site doesn't match your installed CLI, include oyzu --version, your platform, the command you ran, its full output (with -v) and the relevant --help output when you report it.

Google loads only after you choose Allow analytics. No thanks leaves every page and local search available without sending analytics requests to Google. With JavaScript disabled, analytics does not load. Use Analytics settings at the bottom of any page to change your choice. This browser remembers it for 180 days on the docs site, separately from the marketing site. If storage is unavailable, your choice applies only to the current document. Rejecting after acceptance stops measurement, clears the docs analytics cookies and reloads the page. It does not delete data already collected by Google. What is collected After acceptance, Google receives page visits, GitHub and download click events, browser and device information, approximate geographic information, and cookie identifiers. Your IP address reaches Google through the network connection. Analytics cookies expire after 180 days; visits can renew them. A download click does not prove installation or use of Oyzu. We remove query strings and fragments from reported page addresses and report only the referring website’s origin. Valid campaign labels may be included; do not put personal information or secrets in campaign links. We do not send search terms, copied code, user IDs or link addresses in action events. Google Signals and advertising personalization are disabled. Our setup uses explicit events rather than automatic enhanced measurement. Google processes analytics data under its terms. Read Google’s Privacy Policy and how Google uses information from sites using its services.
